parts.problemMd:
Table 1.2 shows the 5th to 8th successive ionisation energies of three elements, **X**, **Y** and **Z**, which are in Period 3 of the Periodic Table.

**Table 1.2**

| element | 5th IE / kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> | 6th IE / kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> | 7th IE / kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> | 8th IE / kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **X** | 6274 | 21269 | 25398 | 29855 |
| **Y** | 7012 | 8496 | 27107 | 31671 |
| **Z** | 6542 | 9362 | 11018 | 33606 |

i) Deduce the group of the Periodic Table to which element **Y** belongs. Explain your answer.

Group ...............................

Explanation ..............................

[2]

ii) State and explain the general trend in first ionisation energies across Period 3.

[2]

iii) Explain why the first ionisation energy of element **Y** is less than that of element **X**.

[2]

iv) Complete the full electronic configuration of an atom of element **Z**.

1s<sup>2</sup> .................

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) Element **Y** belongs to:
> 
> - Group 16 / Group 6 **[1 mark]**
> - Large increase between the 6th and 7th ionisation energies **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The general trend in first ionisation energies across Period 3:
> 
> - First ionisation energy generally increases across Period 3 / increases from Na to Ar **[1 mark]**
> - Nuclear charge / number of protons increases; shielding remains approximately constant / electrons are added to the same shell **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The first ionisation energy of **Y** is less than that of **X** because:
> 
> - **Y** has a paired electron in a 3p orbital (3p<sup>4</sup> configuration) / one 3p orbital in **Y** is doubly occupied **[1 mark]**
> - Electron pair repulsion makes the paired electron easier to remove / reduces the ionisation energy of **Y** **[1 mark]**
> 
> iv) The full electronic configuration of an atom of element **Z** is:
> 
> - (1s<sup>2</sup>) 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup> 3s<sup>2</sup> 3p<sup>5</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part (i): to deduce the group number from successive ionisation energy data, look for the large jump. For Y, the jump is between the 6th and 7th values (8496 to 27107), meaning the 7th electron is in an inner shell. Y therefore has 6 outer electrons and belongs to Group 16.
> 
> For part (ii): note there are two slight downward steps in Period 3 (Na to Mg to Al, and P to S) but the overall trend is an increase. These exceptions involve subshell changes and spin-pair repulsion.
> 
> For part (iii): X is in Group 15 (3p<sup>3</sup>, half-filled with one electron in each 3p orbital). Y is in Group 16 (3p<sup>4</sup>, with one 3p orbital doubly occupied). The paired electrons in Y repel each other, making the first electron easier to remove than expected from nuclear charge alone.
> 
> For part (iv): the large jump for Z is between the 7th and 8th values (11018 to 33606), so Z has 7 outer electrons and belongs to Group 17 (chlorine). Its electronic configuration is 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup> 3s<sup>2</sup> 3p<sup>5</sup>.

parts.problemMd:
All elements have a value for a first ionisation energy.

i) Define the term first ionisation energy of an element.

[2]

ii) Construct an equation to represent the first ionisation energy of aluminium. Include state symbols.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The first ionisation energy of an element is:
> 
> - The enthalpy / energy needed to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms **[1 mark]**
> - To form one mole of gaseous 1+ ions / ions with +1 charge **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The equation for the first ionisation energy of aluminium is:
> 
> - Al (g) → Al<sup>+</sup> (g) + e<sup>-</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> Equations without state symbols do not gain the mark.

> **[exam-tip]**
> When writing an ionisation energy equation, always start with the neutral gaseous atom, not a positive ion. For the 1st ionisation energy, you remove the 1st mole of electrons from neutral Al (g) atoms to form Al<sup>+</sup> (g) ions. A common mistake is to write Al<sup>+</sup> on the left-hand side, which would represent the second ionisation energy.
> 
> The number of the ionisation energy tells you which mole of electrons is being removed: the 1st IE removes the 1st mole of electrons to form 1+ ions; the 2nd IE removes the 2nd mole of electrons to form 2+ ions, and so on.
> 
> State symbols are essential in ionisation energy equations. The definition specifically requires gaseous atoms and gaseous ions, so (g) on all species is part of the correct answer.

parts.problemMd:
Table 3.1 shows successive ionisation energies of an element **A**, found in Period 3 of the Periodic Table.

**Table 3.1**

| ionisation | 1st | 2nd | 3rd | 4th | 5th | 6th | 7th | 8th |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ionisation energy / kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> | 1012 | 1904 | 2914 | 4964 | 6274 | 21 268 | 25 431 | 29 872 |

Use data from Table 3.1 to deduce the identity of element **A**. Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The identity of element **A** and the evidence for it are:
> 
> - Phosphorus / P **[1 mark]**
> - There is a large jump in ionisation energy between the 5th and 6th ionisation energies / after the 5th ionisation energy **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> To deduce the identity of an element from successive ionisation energy data, look for the large jump, the point where the ionisation energy increases significantly compared to the previous steps.
> 
> Here, the values from the 1st to the 5th IE increase by roughly 1000 to 2000 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> each time. The jump from the 5th to the 6th is nearly 15 000 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>, far larger than any previous step. This means the 6th electron is much harder to remove because it is in an inner shell, closer to the nucleus.
> 
> A common mistake is to identify the element as being in Group 6 because the large jump occurs between the 5th and 6th IEs. But if the jump comes after the 5th IE, there are 5 outer electrons, placing the element in Group 15 / Group V. The electronic configuration of phosphorus is 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup> 3s<sup>2</sup> 3p<sup>3</sup>, confirming it has 5 electrons in its outer shell.

parts.problemMd:
Fig. 3.1 shows the trend in ionisation energy for Period 3 of the Periodic Table.

![Graph of first ionisation energy plotted against element for Period 3, from sodium to argon, showing a general increase with anomalies at aluminium and sulfur](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/1-atomic-structure/1-4-ionisation-energy/assets/010-graph-of-first-ionisation-energy-plotted-against.png)

**Fig. 3.1**

i) State and explain the general trend in first ionisation energies across Period 3.

[3]

ii) Explain the deviations from the trend shown in Fig. 3.1.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The general trend and reasons for it are:
> 
> - There is a general increase in first ionisation energy across Period 3 **[1 mark]**
> - Nuclear charge increases / a proton is added to the nucleus **AND** shielding stays the same / electrons are added to the same shell **[1 mark]**
> - Atomic radius decreases **OR** outermost / outer / highest energy / valence electrons are closer to the nucleus **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The deviations from the trend are:
> 
> - Aluminium deviates because its outermost / highest energy / valence electron is in a 3p orbital **[1 mark]**
> - The 3p orbital is further from the nucleus **OR** the 3p orbital has a slightly higher energy than the 3s orbital **[1 mark]**
> - Sulfur deviates because its outermost / outer / highest energy / valence electron is paired / shares an orbital with another electron **AND** there is repulsion between the electrons in the orbital **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For the general trend across Period 3, your answer needs three elements:
> 
> 1. State that IE generally increases
> 2. Explain it using nuclear charge and shielding
> 3. Bring in the consequence (smaller atomic radius or outer electrons closer to the nucleus). Make sure you give both the increased nuclear charge and the unchanged shielding together, as both are needed for that one mark.
> 
> Aluminium (Group 13) and sulfur (Group 16) are the two anomalies in this trend, and they arise for different reasons.
> 
> - For Al, the outer electron is in a 3p orbital, which is at higher energy than the 3s orbital of Mg, so it is easier to remove.
> - For S, one 3p orbital holds a paired electron; the repulsion between those two electrons makes it easier to remove one compared to the half-filled 3p orbitals in P.
> 
> The same reasoning applies in Period 2: boron has a lower 1st IE than beryllium, and oxygen has a lower 1st IE than nitrogen, for the same reasons.

parts.problemMd: Explain why the second ionisation energy of aluminium is greater than the first ionisation energy.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The second ionisation energy of aluminium is greater because:
> 
> Any **one** from:
> 
> - Electrons are removed from a positive ion rather than a neutral atom
> - The electron being removed is closer to the nucleus
> - The Al<sup>+</sup> ion is smaller than the Al atom
> - The electron is being removed from a 3s orbital rather than a 3p orbital
> 
> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Successive ionisation energies always increase because once an electron has been removed, the remaining electrons experience a stronger effective nuclear charge. There are the same number of protons but fewer electrons, so each remaining electron is held more tightly.
> 
> For aluminium specifically, there is a second factor: the 2nd electron is removed from a 3s orbital rather than a 3p orbital. The 3s orbital is at a lower energy and sits closer to the nucleus than the 3p orbital, so removing an electron from it requires more energy. This is why the 2nd IE of Al is noticeably higher than the 1st.

>

**Extract:**

The first six ionisation energies of an element **X** are given below in Table 5.1.

parts.problemMd:
The first ionisation energies of the elements in Group 14 are given below in Table 5.2.

**Table 5.2**

| element | C | Si | Ge | Sn | Pb |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1st ionisation energy / kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> | 1090 | 786 | 762 | 707 | 716 |

Explain the trend shown by these values in terms of the atomic structure of the elements.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The general decrease in first ionisation energy down Group 14 is due to:

> - Atomic radius increases (down the group) / outer electrons are increasingly further from the nucleus **[1 mark]**
> - Electrons are added to new / additional shells **[1 mark]**
> - More / increased shielding (from inner shell electrons) **[1 mark]**
> - Nuclear charge increases (down the group) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When explaining why ionisation energy decreases down a group, address both why the outer electrons are easier to remove (greater distance and shielding) and acknowledge that nuclear charge is also increasing. All four points are needed for full credit.

>

parts.problemMd:
Ionisation energies provide evidence for the electronic structure of atoms.

i) Define the term first ionisation energy.

[2]

ii) Construct an equation to represent the second ionisation energy of magnesium. Include state symbols.

[1]

iii) Explain the trend in first ionisation energies across Period 3 (sodium to argon). Refer to nuclear charge and shielding in your answer.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) First ionisation energy is:
> 
> - The energy required to remove one electron from each atom (in one mole of gaseous atoms) **[1 mark]**
> - From one mole of gaseous atoms **[1 mark]**
> 
> Marks cannot be awarded if energy is released
> 
> The ionic equation, including state symbols, X (g) → X (g) + e<sup>−</sup> scores **[2 marks]**
> 
> ii) The equation for the second ionisation energy of magnesium is:
> 
> - Mg<sup>+</sup> (g) → Mg<sup>2+</sup> (g) + e<sup>-</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The trend in first ionisation energies across Period 3 is:
> 
> - The nuclear charge / number of protons increases across the period **[1 mark]**
> - The shielding by inner shells remains approximately constant
> **OR**
> There is the same number of inner shells **[1 mark]**
> - This means that the attraction between nucleus and outer electron increases, so more energy is needed to remove the electron
> **OR**
> The effective nuclear charge increases, so more energy is needed to remove the electron **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For ionisation energy definitions, precision matters. A very common slip is writing that energy is “released” or forgetting the word “gaseous”. Ionisation is endothermic, so energy is required, and the definition is for gaseous atoms.
> 
> For the second ionisation energy equation, start from the 1+ ion, not the neutral atom. The first electron has already been removed, and state symbols (g) should be included.
> 
> For the trend across a period, avoid only stating what happens. Make the key comparison the marks are looking for: nuclear charge increases across the period, while shielding stays about the same because electrons are added to the same shell. This increases attraction to the outer electron, so more energy is needed to remove it.

parts.problemMd:
Silicon(IV) oxide, SiO<sub>2</sub>, and phosphorus(III) chloride, PCl<sub>3</sub>, have different structures and physical properties.

i) Describe the structure and bonding of silicon(IV) oxide.

[2]

ii) Predict the shape and bond angle of a molecule of phosphorus(III) chloride.

[2]

iii) Explain the difference in melting points between silicon(IV) oxide and phosphorus(III) chloride in terms of their structure and bonding.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The structure and bonding of silicon(IV) oxide is:
> 
> - Structure: giant molecular
> **OR**
> Giant covalent
> **OR**
> Macromolecular **[1 mark]**
> - Bonding: each Si is bonded to 4 O atoms and each O atom is bonded to 2 Si atoms **[1 mark]**
> 
> Describing the structure as simple molecular, ionic lattice or metallic does not score the first mark.
> 
> ii) The shape and bond angle of a molecule of phosphorus(III) chloride are:
> 
> - Shape: trigonal pyramidal **[1 mark]**
> - Bond angle: 107°
> **OR**
> 107.5° **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The difference in melting points between silicon(IV) oxide and phosphorus(III) chloride is because:
> 
> - SiO<sub>2</sub> has many strong covalent bonds that must be broken **[1 mark]**
> - PCl<sub>3</sub> has weak intermolecular forces (London / van der Waals') between molecules which must be overcome **[1 mark]**
> - More energy is needed to melt SiO<sub>2</sub> than PCl<sub>3</sub>, so SiO<sub>2</sub> has a much higher melting point **[1 mark]**
> 
> Breaking covalent bonds in PCl<sub>3</sub> means the second and third marks cannot be awarded.

> **[exam-tip]**
> For shapes and bond angles, start by counting bonding pairs and lone pairs on the central atom.
> 
> In PCl<sub>3</sub>, phosphorus forms three bonds and keeps one lone pair. Lone pairs repel bonding pairs more strongly than bonding pairs repel each other, which reduces the bond angle from 109.5° to about 107°.
> 
> A common bonding mistake is mixing up what breaks when a substance melts.
> 
> - In giant covalent structures (for example SiO<sub>2</sub>), you must break strong covalent bonds within the lattice.
> - In simple molecular substances (for example PCl<sub>3</sub>), the covalent bonds stay intact and you only overcome weak intermolecular forces.

> iv) Helium / He **[1 mark]**
> 
> v) Magnesium / Mg **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> i) Oxygen has the electronic configuration 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>4</sup>. Gaining 2 electrons forms O<sup>2-</sup> with configuration 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup>, which is the same as neon.
> 
> ii) Silicon has a giant covalent structure. Much more energy is needed to break the strong covalent bonds throughout the lattice compared to the metallic bonding in Na to Al, or the weak van der Waals forces between molecules in P to Ar.
> 
> iii) Sodium has the largest atomic radius of the first three periods. It has 3 electron shells (more than any element in Periods 1 or 2) and the lowest nuclear charge of the Period 3 elements, so its outer electrons are held least tightly.
> 
> iv) Helium has the highest first ionisation energy from H to Ar. It has only one shell of electrons very close to the nucleus, and two protons providing a strong nuclear attraction. Although neon has more protons, helium's outer electrons are in shell 1 (not shell 2), so they are held more strongly.
> 
> v) The large jump occurs between the 2nd and 3rd ionisation energies, indicating that the 3rd electron is in an inner shell. The element has 2 outer electrons and is therefore in Group 2. The Period 3 Group 2 element is magnesium.

parts.problemMd:
Fig. 1.2 shows the first ionisation energies for six consecutive elements labelled **A**–**F**.

![Graph showing first ionisation energy plotted against six consecutive elements labelled A to F, illustrating increases and decreases characteristic of a period](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/1-atomic-structure/1-4-ionisation-energy/assets/008-graph-showing-first-ionisation-energy-plotted-ag.png)

**Fig. 1.2**

Complete the graph to show the first ionisation energies of elements **G**–**K**.
parts.solutionMd:
The completed graph is:

![Graph showing first ionisation energies of elements A to K, with G and I starting new sub-periods and a drop from G to H due to spin-pair repulsion](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/1-atomic-structure/1-4-ionisation-energy/assets/009-graph-showing-first-ionisation-energies-of-eleme.png)

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for G plotted above F **AND** H plotted between F and G
> 
> 1 mark for I plotted above H and below A **AND** J plotted above I and below B
> 
> 1 mark for K plotted below C

> **[exam-tip]**
> Element B is the noble gas in the sequence, because there is a large drop after B to C. The outer electron of C is in a new, higher energy shell at the start of a new period, so C is a Group 1 element.
> 
> From C onwards, the pattern repeats across the next period. G starts at a similar level to C (both are Group 1), then the IE generally increases toward J (noble gas), with two characteristic dips: one from D to E (outer electron moves from s to p subshell, higher energy and further from nucleus) and one from G to H (spin-pair repulsion in a doubly occupied p orbital lowers the IE of H below G).
> 
> K starts the following period and will have a lower IE than C or G, because it has one more shell of electrons further from the nucleus.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Fig. 1.2 shows the first ionisation energies for six consecutive elements labelled **A**–**F**.

Explain why the value of the first ionisation energy for **D** is greater than for **C**.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The first ionisation energy of **D** is greater than that of **C** because:
> 
> - **D** has one more proton / higher nuclear charge **OR** the outer electron in **D** is closer to the nucleus **[1 mark]**
> - The electrons being removed from **D** and **C** are in the same (s) subshell **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> In this sequence, B is the noble gas (it has the highest IE before a large drop to C), so C is a Group 1 element starting a new period and D is the Group 2 element that follows. D has one more proton than C but the same number of inner shells, so its outer electron experiences a stronger nuclear attraction.
> 
> The key point to include is that both C and D have their outer electrons in the same s subshell, so shielding is the same for both. The only difference is nuclear charge, which makes D's outer electron harder to remove.

parts.problemMd:
Successive ionisation energies provide evidence for the arrangement of electrons in atoms. In Table 2.1, the successive ionisation energies of oxygen are given.

**Table 2.1**

| ionisation | 1st | 2nd | 3rd | 4th | 5th | 6th | 7th | 8th |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ionisation energy / kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> | 1314 | 3388 | 5301 | 7469 | 10 989 | 13 327 | 71 337 | 84 080 |

i) Construct an equation to represent the third ionisation energy of oxygen. Include state symbols.

[2]

ii) Explain how this data shows evidence of two energy shells in oxygen.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The equation for the third ionisation energy of oxygen is:

O<sup>2+</sup> (g) → O<sup>3+</sup> (g) + e<sup>-</sup>

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct formulae: O<sup>2+</sup> (g) → O<sup>3+</sup> (g) + e<sup>-</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for correct state symbols: (g) on all three species
> 
> ii) The data shows evidence of two energy shells because:
> 
> - There is a very large jump / increase in ionisation energy between the 6th and 7th ionisation energies **[1 mark]**
> - This indicates the 7th electron is removed from a different / inner shell / energy level, closer to the nucleus **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For the third ionisation energy equation, start from the 2+ ion as two electrons have already been removed. The equation shows one mole of electrons removed from one mole of gaseous O<sup>2+</sup> ions to form O<sup>3+</sup> ions. State symbols on all three species are required.
> 
> To interpret successive IE data for evidence of shells, look for the largest jump. Here the values increase gradually from the 1st to the 6th IE (all within the outer shell), then there is a dramatic rise from the 6th (13 327 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>) to the 7th (71 337 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>). This jump indicates the 7th electron is being removed from a shell much closer to the nucleus. Since there are 6 electrons in the outer shell and 2 in the inner shell, this is consistent with oxygen having two energy shells.

parts.problemMd:
Give the full electronic configuration of the following atoms and ions.

i) Te

[1]

ii) Zn<sup>2+</sup>

[1]

iii) Cu<sup>2+</sup>

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The full electronic configuration of Te is:
> 
> - 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup> 3s<sup>2</sup> 3p<sup>6</sup> 3d<sup>10</sup> 4s<sup>2</sup> 4p<sup>6</sup> 4d<sup>10</sup> 5s<sup>2</sup> 5p<sup>4</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The full electronic configuration of Zn<sup>2+</sup> is:
> 
> - 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup> 3s<sup>2</sup> 3p<sup>6</sup> 3d<sup>10</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The full electronic configuration of Cu<sup>2+</sup> is:
> 
> - 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup> 3s<sup>2</sup> 3p<sup>6</sup> 3d<sup>9</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Always write full electronic configurations in order of principal quantum number (n = 1, 2, 3, 4...), placing 3d before 4s and 4d before 5s in the written form, even though the s subshells fill first.
> 
> For ions, the s subshell empties before the d subshell. Zinc is [Ar] 3d<sup>10</sup> 4s<sup>2</sup> as a neutral atom; forming Zn<sup>2+</sup> removes both 4s electrons, leaving [Ar] 3d<sup>10</sup>.
> 
> Copper has an anomalous configuration: [Ar] 3d<sup>10</sup> 4s<sup>1</sup> rather than [Ar] 3d<sup>9</sup> 4s<sup>2</sup>, because a completely full 3d subshell provides extra stability. When forming Cu<sup>2+</sup>, the 4s<sup>1</sup> electron is removed first, then one 3d electron, giving [Ar] 3d<sup>9</sup>. The other anomalous first-row transition metal is chromium, which has a half-filled 3d subshell: [Ar] 3d<sup>5</sup> 4s<sup>1</sup>.

parts.problemMd:
i) Give the electronic configuration for the zirconium 2+ ion, Zr<sup>2+</sup>, starting with [Kr].

[1]

ii) Construct an equation to represent the third ionisation energy of zirconium, Zr. Include state symbols.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The electronic configuration of Zr<sup>2+</sup>, starting with [Kr], is:
> 
> - [Kr] 4d<sup>2</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The equation for the third ionisation energy of zirconium is:
> 
> - Zr<sup>2+</sup> (g) → Zr<sup>3+</sup> (g) + e<sup>-</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are required for this mark.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Zirconium (Z = 40) is in Period 5 and has the configuration [Kr] 4d<sup>2</sup> 5s<sup>2</sup> as a neutral atom. When forming Zr<sup>2+</sup>, the 5s electrons are removed first (the s subshell empties before the d subshell), leaving [Kr] 4d<sup>2</sup>.
> 
> For the third ionisation energy equation, start from the 2+ ion: Zr<sup>2+</sup> (g) → Zr<sup>3+</sup> (g) + e<sup>-</sup>. Each ionisation energy equation removes exactly one mole of electrons and must include state symbols on all three species.

choices.label: B
choices.textMd: $\frac{1}{12}$ of the mass of an atom of carbon-12

choices.label: C
choices.textMd: the mass of an atom of hydrogen-1

parts.problemMd: Which expression defines the unified atomic mass unit?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- The **unified atomic mass unit (u)** is defined as exactly $\frac{1}{12}$ of the mass of an atom of carbon-12.

- This is distinct from **relative atomic mass (*****A***<sub>**r**</sub>**)**, which is the weighted average mass of naturally occurring atoms of an element on a scale where an atom of carbon-12 has a mass of exactly 12 units.

**A** is incorrect as the mass of an electron is approximately $\frac{1}{1836}$ u, which is negligible compared to 1 u.

**C** is incorrect as an atom of hydrogen-1 has a mass of approximately 1.0078 u, not exactly 1 u. Hydrogen was the original standard before being replaced by carbon-12 in 1961.

**D** is incorrect as the mass of a proton is approximately 1.0073 u. The formal definition uses the entire carbon-12 atom, which accounts for protons, neutrons, electrons, and nuclear binding energy.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Do not confuse the unified atomic mass unit with relative atomic mass.
> 
> - The atomic mass unit is a fixed quantity, defined as exactly 1/12 the mass of one carbon-12 atom.
> - Relative atomic mass is a dimensionless ratio that uses this unit as its reference scale and takes into account the natural isotopic abundances of an element.

parts.problemMd: What is the relative formula mass of ammonium sulfate, (NH<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- The **relative formula mass** of ionic and giant covalent compounds is calculated from all the atoms in the empirical formula.

- *M*<sub>r</sub> = 2*A*<sub>r</sub>(N) + 8*A*<sub>r</sub>(H) + *A*<sub>r</sub>(S) + 4*A*<sub>r</sub>(O)

*M*<sub>r</sub> = 2(14.0) + 8(1.0) + 32.1 + 4(16.0)

*M*<sub>r</sub> = 28.0 + 8.0 + 32.1 + 64.0

*M*<sub>r</sub> = **132.1**

**A** is incorrect as this has used the IGCSE atomic mass for sulfur (32.0 instead of 32.1) **AND **forgot to multiply the ammonium ion by 2, giving NH<sub>4</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> = 114.0.

**B** is incorrect as this has used the correct A Level atomic mass for sulfur (32.1) but forgot to multiply the ammonium ion by 2, giving NH<sub>4</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> = 114.1.

**C** is incorrect as this has correctly multiplied the ammonium ion by 2 but used the IGCSE atomic mass for sulfur (32.0 instead of 32.1), giving 132.0.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The most common error on this question type is forgetting to multiply all the atoms inside a bracket by the number outside. For (NH<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, the subscript 2 outside the bracket applies to both N and H, giving 2N and 8H in total.
> 
> At A Level, always use the atomic masses from the CIE Data Booklet rather than the integer values you may have used at GCSE. For sulfur, the Data Booklet value is 32.1, not 32 and this is the key discriminator between options C and D.

parts.problemMd:
Iron has many different naturally occurring isotopes.

| **Isotope** | **% Abundance** | **Isotopic mass** |
|---|---|---|
| <sup>54</sup>Fe | 5.845 | 53.9396 |
| <sup>56</sup>Fe | 91.754 | 55.9349 |
| <sup>57</sup>Fe | 2.119 | 56.9354 |
| <sup>58</sup>Fe | 0.282 | 57.9333 |

What is the relative atomic mass of iron?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- To calculate the **relative atomic mass**, multiply each isotopic mass by its percentage abundance, sum the results, and divide by 100.

*A*<sub>r</sub> = `\frac{\Sigma (\% \text{ abundance} \times \text{isotopic mass})}{100}`

*A*<sub>r</sub>(Fe) = $\frac{(5.845\times53.9396)+(91.754\times55.9349)+(2.119\times56.9354)+(0.282\times57.9333)}{100}$

*A*<sub>r</sub>(Fe) = **55.845**

**A** is incorrect as 55.800 is the value given in the CIE Data Booklet for iron. This traps people who read the answer from the periodic table instead of performing the calculation on the data provided.

**C** is incorrect as 56.186 is the simple unweighted average of the four isotopic masses, ignoring the percentage abundances.

**D** is incorrect as 56.250 is the simple unweighted average of the four mass numbers (54, 56, 57, 58), ignoring both the isotopic masses and the percentage abundances.

parts.problemMd:
A sample of neon contains only the isotopes <sup>20</sup>Ne and <sup>21</sup>Ne.

The relative atomic mass of this sample is 20.2.

What is the percentage of <sup>21</sup>Ne atoms in this sample?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Since the sample contains **only** these two isotopes, their percentage abundances must sum to 100%.

- Let the percentage of <sup>21</sup>Ne = *x*, so the percentage of <sup>20</sup>Ne = (100 - *x*).

- Substituting into the relative atomic mass expression:

$\frac{21x+20(100-x)}{100} = 20 . 2$

$21 x + 2000 - 20 x = 2020$

*x* = **20%**

**A** and **D** are incorrect as these values do not satisfy the equation above.

**C** is incorrect as 80% is the percentage of <sup>20</sup>Ne when the algebra is set up correctly but *x* is assigned to the wrong isotope.

parts.problemMd:
A sample of metal **Z** was analysed by mass spectrometry. The relative abundance of each isotope in a mass spectrum of the sample is shown.

| ***m*** **/** ***z*** **value** | 70 | 72 | 74 |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Relative abundance (%)** | 24.4 | 32.4 | 43.2 |

What is the relative atomic mass of metal **Z** to 3 significant figures?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- To calculate the relative atomic mass:

*A*<sub>r</sub> = $\frac{(70\times24.4)+(72\times32.4)+(74\times43.2)}{100}$

*A*<sub>r</sub> = $\frac{1708+2332.8+3196.8}{100}$

*A*<sub>r</sub> = 72.376

*A*<sub>r</sub> = **72.4** (to 3 significant figures)

**A** is incorrect as 72.0 is the simple unweighted mean of the three *m*/*z* values: (70 + 72 + 74) / 3 = 72.0, ignoring the percentage abundances.

**B** is incorrect as 72.2 is the result when the abundances for *m*/*z* 72 and *m*/*z* 74 are swapped in the calculation.

**C** is incorrect as 72.38 is the correct calculated value (72.376) rounded to 4 significant figures rather than the 3 significant figures requested.

parts.problemMd:
Hydrated copper(II) sulfate has the formula CuSO<sub>4</sub>·*x*H<sub>2</sub>O and a relative formula mass of 231.6.

What is the value of *x*?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Calculate the relative formula mass of anhydrous CuSO<sub>4</sub>:

*M*<sub>r</sub>(CuSO<sub>4</sub>) = 63.5 + 32.1 + 4(16.0) = 159.6

- Find the mass contributed by the water of crystallisation:

231.6 - 159.6 = 72.0

- Divide by the relative formula mass of water (18.0) to find *x*:

*x* = $\frac{72.0}{18.0}$

*x* = 4

**A** is incorrect as CuSO<sub>4</sub>·2H<sub>2</sub>O has *M*<sub>r</sub> = 159.6 + 36.0 = 195.6

**B** is incorrect as CuSO<sub>4</sub>·3H<sub>2</sub>O has *M*<sub>r</sub> = 159.6 + 54.0 = 213.6

**D** is incorrect as CuSO<sub>4</sub>·5H<sub>2</sub>O has *M*<sub>r</sub> = 159.6 + 90.0 = 249.6

parts.problemMd:
An element, **X**, consists of only two isotopes, <sup>69</sup>**X** and <sup>71</sup>**X**, with percentage abundances of 60% and 40% respectively.

What is the relative atomic mass of element X?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- To calculate the relative atomic mass:

*A*<sub>r</sub>(**X**) = $\frac{(69\times60)+(71\times40)}{100}$

*A*<sub>r</sub>(**X**) = $\frac{4140+2840}{100}$

*A*<sub>r</sub>(**X**) = **69.8**

**A** is incorrect as 69.2 is not produced by any standard calculation error on these values.

**C** is incorrect as 70.0 is the simple unweighted mean of 69 and 71, ignoring the percentage abundances.

**D** is incorrect as 70.2 is the result when the abundances for <sup>69</sup>**X** and <sup>71</sup>**X** are swapped in the calculation.

parts.problemMd:
A sample of strontium was analysed by mass spectrometry. The relative abundances of some of the isotopes are shown.

| ***m*** **/** ***z*** **value** | 84 | 86 | 87 | 88 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **% abundance** | 0.56 |   |   | 82.58 |

The relative atomic mass of this sample of strontium is 87.71.

Which row gives the percentage abundances of <sup>86</sup>Sr and <sup>87</sup>Sr?

|   | <sup>**86**</sup>**Sr** | <sup>**87**</sup>**Sr** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | 6.96 | 9.90 |
| **B** | 8.43 | 8.43 |
| **C** | 9.90 | 6.96 |
| **D** | 11.58 | 5.84 |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Find the total percentage of the two unknown isotopes:

100 - (82.58 + 0.56) = 16.86%

- Let <sup>86</sup>Sr abundance = *y*, so <sup>87</sup>Sr abundance = (16.86 - *y*).

- Set up the relative atomic mass equation:

$\frac{(84\times0.56)+(86y)+(87(16.86-y))+(88\times82.58)}{100} = 87 . 71$

- Expand and simplify:

$47 . 04 + 86 y + 1466 . 82 - 87 y + 7267 . 04 = 8771$

$8780 . 90 - y = 8771$

*y* = **9.90%** (<sup>86</sup>Sr)

<sup>87</sup>Sr = 16.86 - 9.90 = **6.96%**

**A** is incorrect as these are the correct values but assigned to the wrong isotopes.

**B** is incorrect as 8.43% is obtained by dividing 16.86% equally between the two isotopes without performing the algebraic calculation.

**D** is incorrect as 11.58% and 5.84% are obtained when the <sup>84</sup>Sr abundance (0.56%) is ignored, incorrectly treating the unknown total as 17.42% rather than 16.86%.

parts.problemMd:
Aspirin is a common analgesic used for the relief of aches and pains.

![Skeletal formula of aspirin showing a benzene ring with an ester group (OCOCH3) and a carboxylic acid group (COOH)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/2-atoms-molecules-and-stoichiometry/2-1-relative-masses-of-atoms-and-molecules/assets/001-skeletal-formula-of-aspirin-showing-a-benzene-ri.jpg)

Which row correctly describes aspirin?

|   | **Empirical formula** | **Molecular formula** | ***M***<sub>**r**</sub> |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>2</sub>O | C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>4</sub> | 180.0 |
| **B** | C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>3</sub>O | C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>4</sub> | 184.0 |
| **C** | C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>4</sub> | C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>4</sub> | 184.0 |
| **D** | C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>4</sub> | C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>4</sub> | 180.0 |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Count the atoms from the skeletal formula:

  - 9 carbon atoms
  - 8 hydrogen atoms
  - 4 oxygen atoms

- Molecular formula = C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>4</sub>

- C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>4</sub> is already the simplest whole number ratio of atoms, so the empirical formula is also C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>4</sub>.

- Calculate *M*<sub>r</sub>:

*M*<sub>r</sub> = (9 x 12.0) + (8 x 1.0) + (4 x 16.0)

*M*<sub>r</sub> = 180.0

**A** is incorrect as the empirical formula C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>2</sub>O does not reduce from C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>4</sub> (the ratio 9:8:4 shares no common factor greater than 1).

**B** is incorrect as the molecular formula C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>4</sub> gives the wrong hydrogen count. The four substituted carbons on the benzene ring are each bonded to a substituent and carry no hydrogen atoms.

**C** is incorrect as the hydrogen count is wrong for the same reason as B, and C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>4</sub> is not the simplest ratio so it cannot be the empirical formula.

parts.problemMd:
An element, **X**, has a relative atomic mass of *A*<sub>r</sub> and exists as a diatomic molecule, **X**<sub>2</sub>.

Which expression represents the total number of atoms present in *m* grams of the gas?

(Where *L* represents the Avogadro constant.)
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- The relative molecular mass of **X**<sub>2</sub> is **2***A*<sub>r</sub>.

- The number of moles of **X**<sub>2</sub> in *m* grams is:

$\frac{m}{2A_{r}}$

- Each molecule of **X**<sub>2</sub> contains 2 atoms, so the number of moles of atoms is:

$2 \times \frac{m}{2A_{r}} = \frac{m}{A_{r}}$

- Multiplying by the Avogadro constant *L* gives the total number of atoms:

$\frac{mL}{A_{r}}$

**B** is incorrect as $\frac{mL}{2A_{r}}$ gives the number of **molecules**, not atoms and it misses the step of multiplying by 2 for the diatomic molecule.

**C** is incorrect as $\frac{2mL}{A_{r}}$ results from using *A*<sub>r</sub> (not 2*A*<sub>r</sub>) as the molar mass of **X**<sub>2</sub>, then multiplying by 2 again for the diatomic molecule.

**D** is incorrect as $\frac{mA_{r}}{L}$ results from multiplying mass by molar mass rather than dividing, and dividing by *L* rather than multiplying.

parts.problemMd: What is the mass of 0.56 moles of potassium dichromate (VI), K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Calculate the relative formula mass of K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>:

(2 x 39.1) + (2 x 52.0) + (7 x 16.0) = 294.2

- Calculate the mass:

mass = moles x *M*<sub>r</sub>

= 0.56 x 294.2

= **164.75 g**

**A** is incorrect as this uses atomic numbers instead of relative atomic masses in the *M*<sub>r</sub> calculation.

**C** is incorrect as this is from incorrectly dividing *M*<sub>r</sub> by moles to calculate mass.

**D** is incorrect as this is from missing out one oxygen atom in the relative formula mass calculation.

parts.problemMd:
Ethane has the formula C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>.

What is the mass in grams of one molecule of ethane? (*A*<sub>r</sub>: C = 12.0; H = 1.0)

(the Avogadro constant *L* = 6.02 x 10<sup>23</sup>)
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Calculate the relative formula mass of ethane:

*M*<sub>r</sub> = (12.0 x 2) + (1.0 x 6) = 30.0

- Divide by the Avogadro constant to find the mass of one molecule:

mass of one molecule = $\frac{30.0}{6.02\times10^{23}}$

mass of one molecule = **4.98 x 10**<sup>**-23**</sup> g

**A** is incorrect as this multiplies the molar mass by the Avogadro constant rather than dividing, giving a very large number.

**C** is incorrect as this is the relative formula mass of ethane, not the mass of one molecule.

**D** is incorrect as this uses a relative formula mass of 18.0, meaning one carbon atom has been omitted from the calculation.

parts.problemMd:
What is the number of molecules of nitrogen gas in 4.00 g?

(the Avogadro constant *L* = 6.02 x 10<sup>23</sup>)
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- Calculate the *M*<sub>r</sub> of N<sub>2</sub>:

*M*<sub>r</sub> of N<sub>2</sub> = 14.0 x 2 = 28.0

- Calculate the moles of N<sub>2</sub>:

moles = $\frac{\mathrm{mass}}{M_{r}}$

moles = $\frac{4.00}{28.0}$

moles = 0.143 mol

- Calculate the number of molecules:

0.143 x 6.02 x 10<sup>23</sup> = **8.61 x 10**<sup>**22**</sup>

**B** is incorrect as this shows a student mixing up the mole calculation, dividing *M*<sub>r</sub> by mass rather than mass by *M*<sub>r</sub>.

**C** is incorrect as this is from calculating moles = mass x *M*<sub>r</sub> and multiplying by Avogadro's constant.

**D** is incorrect as this is from using the relative atomic mass of nitrogen (14) rather than the relative formula mass of N<sub>2</sub> (28).

> **[exam-tip]**
> The question asks for the number of nitrogen molecules in 4.00 g, not atoms. Make sure you calculate the relative formula mass of N<sub>2</sub> (28.0), not the relative atomic mass of N (14.0).

parts.problemMd:
The mass of a coin is 20% nickel. The coin has a mass of 10.0 g.

How many nickel atoms are in the coin?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Find the mass of nickel in the coin:

10.0 x 0.2 = 2.0 g

- Find the moles of nickel:

moles = $\frac{mass}{M_{r}}$

moles = $\frac{2.0}{58.7}$

moles = 0.034 mol

- Find the number of nickel atoms (*L* = 6.02 x 10<sup>23</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>):

0.034 x 6.02 x 10<sup>23</sup> =** **2.05 x 10<sup>22</sup>

**A** is incorrect as this uses the atomic number of nickel (28) instead of the relative atomic mass (58.7): 2.0 / 28 x 6.02 x 10<sup>23</sup> = 4.30 x 10<sup>22</sup>.

**B** is incorrect as this uses the total coin mass (10.0 g) rather than just the nickel content (2.0 g): 10.0 / 58.7 x 6.02 x 10<sup>23</sup> = 1.03 x 10<sup>23</sup>.

**C** is incorrect as this uses the mass of nickel (2.0 g) directly as the number of moles without dividing by the molar mass: 2.0 x 6.02 x 10<sup>23</sup> = 1.20 x 10<sup>24</sup>.

parts.problemMd:
A coin with a mass of 9.97 g contains 5.921% nickel by mass.

How many nickel atoms are in the coin?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- Find the mass of nickel in the coin:

9.97 x 0.05921 = 0.590 g

- Find the moles of nickel:

moles = $\frac{mass}{M_{r}}$

moles = $\frac{0.590}{58.7}$

moles = 0.01006 mol

- Find the number of nickel atoms (*L* = 6.02 x 10<sup>23</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>):

0.01006 x 6.02 x 10<sup>23</sup> = 6.05 x 10<sup>21</sup>

**B** is incorrect because it uses the atomic number of nickel (28) instead of its relative atomic mass (58.7): 0.590 ÷ 28 × 6.02 × 10<sup>23</sup>

**C** is incorrect because it ignores the percentage and uses the mass of the whole coin: 9.97 ÷ 58.7 × 6.02 × 10<sup>23</sup>

**D** is incorrect because it multiplies the mass of nickel by the relative atomic mass instead of dividing: 0.590 × 58.7 × 6.02 × 10<sup>23</sup>

parts.problemMd: Which sample contains the greatest number of molecules?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- 1 g of methanal contains:

$\frac{1}{30}$ = 0.0333 moles

- 2 g of carbon dioxide contains:

$\frac{2}{44}$ = 0.04545 moles

- 3 g of sulfur, S<sub>8</sub>, contains:

$\frac{3}{256.8}$ = 0.01168 moles

- 4 g of bromine contains:

$\frac{4}{159.8}$ = 0.02503 moles

- Therefore, the number of molecules in 2 g of carbon dioxide will be the highest as this contains the most moles.

**A**, **C** & **D** are incorrect as these do not have the highest number of moles and therefore the greatest number of molecules.

parts.problemMd:
When heated, calcium nitrate, Ca(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>, will decompose to a white solid and a mixture of gases. One of the gases released is an oxide of nitrogen,**Y**.

8.2 g of anhydrous calcium nitrate is heated until no further reaction takes place.

What is the mass of **Y** produced?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Write a balanced equation for the thermal decomposition of calcium nitrate and identify gas **Y**:

2Ca(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> (s) → 2CaO (s) + 4NO<sub>2</sub> (g) + O<sub>2</sub> (g)

- Gas **Y** is nitrogen dioxide, NO<sub>2</sub>.
- Calculate the molar mass of the reactant and of gas **Y**:

*M*<sub>r</sub>[Ca(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>] = 40.1 + 2[14.0 + 3 x 16.0] = 164.1 g mol<sup>-1</sup>

*M*<sub>r</sub>[NO<sub>2</sub>] = 14.0 + 2 x 16.0 = 46.0 g mol<sup>-1</sup>

- Calculate the number of moles of calcium nitrate:

*n*(Ca(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>) = $\frac{\mathrm{mass}}{M_{r}}$

*n*(Ca(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>) = $\frac{8.2}{164.1}$

*n*(Ca(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>) = 0.050 mol

- Use the stoichiometric ratio to find the moles of NO<sub>2</sub> produced:

2 mol Ca(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> produces 4 mol NO<sub>2</sub>, so the molar ratio is 1 : 2

*n*(NO<sub>2</sub>) = 2 x 0.050 = 0.10 mol

- Calculate the mass of gas **Y**:

mass = *n* x *M*<sub>r</sub>

mass = 0.10 x 46.0

mass = 4.6 g

**A** is incorrect as this uses a 1:1 molar ratio between Ca(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> and NO<sub>2</sub> instead of the correct 1:2 ratio: 0.050 x 1 x 46.0 = 2.3 g.

**B** is incorrect as this uses the molar mass of N<sub>2</sub> (28.0 g mol<sup>-1</sup>) instead of NO<sub>2</sub> (46.0 g mol<sup>-1</sup>) for gas **Y**: 0.10 x 28.0 = 2.8 g.

**D** is incorrect as this applies a 4:1 molar ratio (n(NO<sub>2</sub>) = 4 x n(Ca(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>)) rather than the correct 1:2 ratio: 0.050 x 4 x 46.0 = 9.2 g.

parts.problemMd: Which substance has the greatest number of atoms?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Convert mass of CH<sub>4</sub> from kg to g:

1.69 x 10<sup>-4</sup> x 1000 = 0.169 g

- Calculate moles of CH<sub>4</sub>:

moles = $\frac{0.169}{16.0}$ = 0.01056 mol

- Calculate number of molecules of CH<sub>4</sub>:

0.01056 x 6.02 x 10<sup>23</sup> = 6.36 x 10<sup>21</sup>

- Calculate number of atoms:

5 x 6.36 x 10<sup>21</sup> = **3.18 x 10**<sup>**22**</sup>

**A** is incorrect as the number of atoms for chlorine is 1.92 x 10<sup>21</sup>.

- Convert mass from mg to g: 113 mg / 1000 = 0.113 g
- Calculate moles of chlorine: 0.113 / 71.0 = 0.00159 mol
- Calculate molecules of chlorine: 0.00159 x 6.02 x 10<sup>23</sup> = 9.58 x 10<sup>20</sup> molecules
- Calculate atoms of chlorine: 2 x 9.58 x 10<sup>20</sup> = 1.92 x 10<sup>21</sup> atoms

**B** is incorrect as the number of atoms for sulfur is 2.48 x 10<sup>21</sup>.

- Convert mass from kg to g: 1.32 x 10<sup>-4</sup> kg x 1000 = 0.132 g
- Calculate moles of sulfur: 0.132 / 32.1 = 0.00411 mol
- Calculate atoms of sulfur: 0.00411 x 6.02 x 10<sup>23</sup> = 2.48 x 10<sup>21</sup> atoms

**C** is incorrect as the number of atoms of ammonia is 1.30 x 10<sup>22</sup>.

- Convert mass from mg to g: 92 mg / 1000 = 0.092 g
- Calculate moles of ammonia: 0.092 / 17.0 = 0.00541 mol
- Calculate molecules of ammonia: 0.00541 x 6.02 x 10<sup>23</sup> = 3.26 x 10<sup>21</sup> molecules
- Calculate atoms of ammonia: 4 x 3.26 x 10<sup>21</sup> = 1.30 x 10<sup>22</sup> atoms

> **[exam-tip]**
> Always convert units to grams before calculating moles:
> 
> - mg → g: divide by 1000
> - kg → g: multiply by 1000

parts.problemMd:
A gas cylinder for a portable heater contains 13 kg of butane.

How many butane molecules are in the gas cylinder?

The Avogadro’s constant,* L* = 6.022 x 10<sup>23</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- Calculate the relative formula mass of butane:

C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub> = 58.0

- Calculate the moles of butane:

moles = $\frac{13000}{58.0}$ = 224.14 mol

- Calculate the number of molecules of butane:

224.14 x 6.02 x 10<sup>23</sup> = **1.35 x 10**<sup>**26**</sup>

**B** is incorrect as the mass has not been converted from kg to g: using 13 instead of 13 000 gives 13 / 58.0 x 6.02 x 10<sup>23</sup> = 1.35 x 10<sup>23</sup>.

**C** is incorrect as C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub> was used to work out the relative formula mass instead of C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub> for butane.

**D** is incorrect as the number of molecules of butane was divided by the Avogadro constant rather than multiplied.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Remember to convert kg to g when calculating the number of moles:
> 
> 13 kg x 1000 = 13 000 g

parts.problemMd: Which mass of substance contains the greatest number of atoms?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- **A**, 3.00 g of ammonia:
- Calculate the number of *M*<sub>r</sub>:

14.0 + (3 x 1.0) = 17.0

- Calculate the number of moles:

moles = $\frac{\mathrm{mass}}{M_{r}}$

moles = $\frac{3.00}{17.0}$

moles = 0.18 mol

- Calculate the number of moles of atoms:

0.18 x 4 = 0.72 mol of atoms

- **B**, 3.00 g of chloromethane:

*M*<sub>r</sub> = 12.0 + (3 x 1.0) + 35.5 = 50.5

moles = $\frac{3.00}{50.5}$ = 0.059 mol

0.059 x 5 = 0.30 mol of atoms

- **C**, 4.00 g of hydrogen sulfide:

*M*<sub>r</sub> = (2 x 1.0) + 32.1 = 34.1

moles= $\frac{4.00}{34.1}$ = 0.12 mol

0.12 x 3 = 0.36 mol of atoms

- **D**, 4.00 g of hydrogen chloride:

*M*<sub>r</sub> = 1.0 + 35.5 = 36.5

moles= $\frac{4.00}{36.5}$ = 0.11 mol

0.11 x 2 = 0.22 mol of atoms

- Option **A** contains the greatest number of moles of atoms and, therefore, the greatest number of atoms.

**B**, **C** & **D** are incorrect as they do not contain the greatest number of moles of atoms.

> **[exam-tip]**
> There is no need to use the Avogadro constant to answer this question. The option with the greatest number of moles of atoms has the greatest number of atoms, so comparing moles directly is sufficient.

parts.problemMd:
The equation for a reaction is shown.

Mg<sub>3</sub>N<sub>2</sub> (s) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l) → Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub> (aq) + NH<sub>3</sub> (aq)

Which row gives the smallest whole-number coefficients required to balance the equation?

|   | **Mg**<sub>3</sub>**N**<sub>2</sub> | **H**<sub>2</sub>**O** | **Mg(OH)**<sub>2</sub> | **NH**<sub>3</sub> |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | 1 | 6 | 3 | 2 |
| **B** | 1 | 3 | 3 | 1 |
| **C** | 2 | 6 | 2 | 2 |
| **D** | 2 | 6 | 3 | 2 |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- Starting with 1 Mg<sub>3</sub>N<sub>2</sub>:

  - 3 Mg and 2 N on the left
  - So, 3 Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub> and 2 NH<sub>3</sub> are needed on the right
- 3 Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub> contains 6 OH groups (6 O, 6 H)
- 2 NH<sub>3</sub> contains 6 H

  - Total H on the right = 12
  - So, 6 H<sub>2</sub>O are needed on the left
- Balanced equation:

Mg<sub>3</sub>N<sub>2</sub> (s) + 6H<sub>2</sub>O (l) → 3Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub> (aq) + 2NH<sub>3</sub> (aq)

**B**, **C** and **D** are incorrect as these options do not give the correctly balanced equation.

parts.problemMd: Which ionic equation represents the reaction between aqueous calcium chloride and aqueous silver nitrate?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Ionic equations show only the species that participate in the reaction; spectator ions are omitted
- Ca<sup>2+</sup> (aq) and NO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> (aq) are the spectator ions in this reaction
- Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq) reacts with Cl<sup>-</sup> (aq) to form the insoluble precipitate AgCl (s):

Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq) + Cl<sup>-</sup> (aq) → AgCl (s)

**A** is incorrect as AgNO<sub>3</sub> is written in molecular form; as a soluble ionic compound it must be shown as separate ions.

**B** is incorrect as CaCl<sub>2</sub> must be written as Ca<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + 2Cl<sup>-</sup> (aq), retaining the spectator ion Ca<sup>2+</sup>.

**C** is incorrect as Ca<sup>2+</sup> (aq) and NO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> (aq) are spectator ions that do not react.

parts.problemMd: Which ionic equation represents the reaction between aqueous sodium ethanoate and aqueous hydrochloric acid?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Sodium ethanoate (CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>Na) fully dissociates in solution: Na<sup>+</sup> (aq) + CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>2</sub><sup>-</sup> (aq)
- HCl is a strong acid that fully dissociates: H<sup>+</sup> (aq) + Cl<sup>-</sup> (aq); Na<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>-</sup> are spectator ions
- Ionic equation:

CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>2</sub><sup>-</sup> (aq) + H<sup>+</sup> (aq) → CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H (aq)

**A** is incorrect as HCl must be written as H<sup>+</sup> (aq) and Cl<sup>-</sup> (aq), as it is a strong acid that fully dissociates in solution.

**C** is incorrect as Na<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>-</sup> are spectator ions that do not react.

**D** is incorrect as CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>Na is an ionic compound that must be written as separate ions in solution.

parts.problemMd:
A compound contains 52.2% carbon, 13.0% hydrogen and 34.8% oxygen by mass.

What is the empirical formula of this compound?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Assume 100 g of compound:

  - C = 52.2 g
  - H = 13.0 g
  - O = 34.8 g
- Divide by relative atomic mass (data booklet):

C = $\frac{52.2}{12.0}$ = 4.35

H = $\frac{13.0}{1.0}$ = 13.0

O = $\frac{34.8}{16.0}$ = 2.18

- Divide by the smallest value (2.18):

C = $\frac{4.35}{2.18}$ = 2

H = $\frac{13.0}{2.18}$ ≈ 6

O = $\frac{2.18}{2.18}$ = 1

- Empirical formula: C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O

**A** is incorrect as CH<sub>2</sub>O would require the percentage composition to be in the ratio C:H:O = 1:2:1.

**B** is incorrect as C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>13</sub>O<sub>2</sub> does not give the correct ratio of atoms.

**D** is incorrect as C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>2</sub>O does not give the correct ratio of atoms.

parts.problemMd:
A sample of hydrated calcium sulfate, CaSO<sub>4</sub>**∙***x*H<sub>2</sub>O, has a relative formula mass of 172.2.

What is the value of *x*?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Relative formula mass of CaSO<sub>4</sub>:

40.1 + 32.1 + (4 × 16.0) = 136.2

- Relative formula mass of H<sub>2</sub>O = 18.0
- Mass of water of crystallisation:

172.2 − 136.2 = 36.0

- Calculate *x*:

*x* = $\frac{36.0}{18.0}$ = 2

**A** is incorrect as *x* = 1 gives a relative formula mass of 154.2.

**C** is incorrect as *x* = 3 gives a relative formula mass of 190.2.

**D** is incorrect as *x* = 4 gives a relative formula mass of 208.2.

parts.problemMd:
A hydrated carbonate of an unknown Group 1 metal, **X**, has the formula **X**<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>**∙**10H<sub>2</sub>O and a relative formula mass of 286.

What is the identity of **X**?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Set up an equation:

2A<sub>r</sub>(**X**) + 12.0 + 3(16.0) + 10(2.0 + 16.0) = 286

- Simplify:

2A<sub>r</sub>(**X**) + 240 = 286

- Solve:

A<sub>r</sub>(**X**) = (286 − 240) ÷ 2 = 23

- Relative atomic mass 23 corresponds to sodium (Na) from the data booklet

**A** is incorrect as Li has a relative atomic mass of 6.9.

**C** is incorrect as K has a relative atomic mass of 39.1.

**D** is incorrect as Rb has a relative atomic mass of 85.5.

parts.problemMd:
The skeletal formula of phenazine is shown.

![Skeletal formula of phenazine](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/2-atoms-molecules-and-stoichiometry/2-3-formulas/assets/001-skeletal-formula-of-phenazine.png)

What is the empirical formula of phenazine?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- The empirical formula is the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms in a compound
- Phenazine has the molecular formula C<sub>12</sub>H<sub>8</sub>N<sub>2</sub> (two benzene rings fused to a central pyrazine ring)
- Dividing by the highest common factor of 2: C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>4</sub>N

**B** is incorrect as C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub>N would require 6 hydrogen atoms per unit, not 4.

**C** is incorrect as C<sub>12</sub>H<sub>8</sub>N<sub>2</sub> is the molecular formula of phenazine, not the empirical formula.

**D** is incorrect as C<sub>12</sub>H<sub>12</sub>N<sub>2</sub> does not match the molecular formula of phenazine.

parts.problemMd:
An additive in leaded petrol is composed of lead, carbon and hydrogen only. The compound contains 6.19% hydrogen and 29.7% carbon by mass.

What is the value of *x* in the empirical formula PbC<sub>8</sub>H<sub>x</sub>?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Assume 100 g:

  - C = 29.7 g
  - H = 6.19 g
- Moles (data booklet):

C = $\frac{29.7}{12.0}$ = 2.475 mol

H = $\frac{6.19}{1.0}$ = 6.19 mol

- Divide by the smallest (2.475):

C = $\frac{2.475}{2.475}$ = 1

H = $\frac{6.19}{2.475}$ = 2.5

- Scale to match 8 carbon atoms in the formula:

H = 2.5 × 8 = 20

- Therefore *x* = 20

**A** is incorrect as *x* = 5 gives a H:C mole ratio of 0.625:1.

**B** is incorrect as *x* = 6 gives a H:C mole ratio of 0.75:1.

**C** is incorrect as *x* = 16 gives a H:C mole ratio of 2:1.

parts.problemMd:
Hydrated copper(II) sulfate, CuSO<sub>4</sub>**∙***x*H<sub>2</sub>O, has a relative formula mass of 231.6.

What is the value of *x*?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Relative formula mass of CuSO<sub>4</sub>:

63.5 + 32.1 + (4 × 16.0) = 159.6

- Relative formula mass of H<sub>2</sub>O = 18.0
- Mass of water of crystallisation:

231.6 − 159.6 = 72.0

- Calculate *x*:

*x* = $\frac{72.0}{18.0}$ = 4

**A** is incorrect as CuSO<sub>4</sub>**∙**2H<sub>2</sub>O would have a relative formula mass of 195.6.

**B** is incorrect as CuSO<sub>4</sub>**∙**3H<sub>2</sub>O would have a relative formula mass of 213.6.

**D** is incorrect as CuSO<sub>4</sub>**∙**5H<sub>2</sub>O would have a relative formula mass of 249.6.

parts.problemMd:
An organic compound has the following composition by mass: C, 53.33%; H, 11.11%; O, 35.56%.

What is the empirical formula of the compound?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Assume 100 g:

  - C = 53.33 g
  - H = 11.11 g
  - O = 35.56 g
- Divide by relative atomic mass (data booklet):

C = $\frac{53.33}{12.0}$ = 4.44

H = $\frac{11.11}{1.0}$ = 11.11

O = $\frac{35.56}{16.0}$ = 2.22

- Divide by the smallest value (2.22):

C = $\frac{4.44}{2.22}$ = 2

H = $\frac{11.11}{2.22}$ = 5

O = $\frac{2.22}{2.22}$ = 1

- Empirical formula: C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>O

**A** is incorrect as C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>O would require the H:C ratio to be 2:1, not 5:2.

**C** is incorrect as C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>2</sub> is not in its simplest whole-number ratio, as it simplifies to C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>O.

**D** is incorrect as C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O<sub>2</sub> is not in its simplest whole-number ratio, as it simplifies to C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>O.

parts.problemMd:
A compound has the following composition by mass: H, 5.00%; N, 35.00%; O, 60.00%.

What is the identity of the compound?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Assume 100 g:

  - H = 5.00 g
  - N = 35.00 g
  - O = 60.00 g
- Divide by relative atomic mass (data booklet):

H = $\frac{5.00}{1.0}$ = 5.00

N = $\frac{35.00}{14.0}$ = 2.50

O = $\frac{60.00}{16.0}$ = 3.75

- Divide by the smallest value (2.50):

H = $\frac{5.00}{2.50}$ = 2

N = $\frac{2.50}{2.50}$ = 1

O = $\frac{3.75}{2.50}$ = 1.5

- Scale to whole numbers (× 2):

H = 4

N = 2

O = 3

- Empirical formula H<sub>4</sub>N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> corresponds to NH<sub>4</sub>NO<sub>3</sub>

**A** is incorrect as HNO<sub>2</sub> has the composition H:N:O = 1:1:2.

**B** is incorrect as HNO<sub>3</sub> has the composition H:N:O = 1:1:3.

**C** is incorrect as NH<sub>2</sub>OH has the composition H:N:O = 3:1:1.

parts.problemMd:
A sample of compound **M** contains 1.46 g of carbon, 0.482 g of hydrogen and 1.69 g of nitrogen.

What is the empirical formula of **M**?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Moles of each element (data booklet):

C = $\frac{1.46}{12.0}$ = 0.122 mol

H = $\frac{0.482}{1.0}$ = 0.482 mol

N = $\frac{1.69}{14.0}$ = 0.121 mol

- Divide by the smallest value (0.121):

C = $\frac{0.122}{0.121}$ ≈ 1

H = $\frac{0.482}{0.121}$ ≈ 4

N = $\frac{0.121}{0.121}$ = 1

- Empirical formula: CH<sub>4</sub>N

**A** is incorrect as CH<sub>2</sub>N would require the H:C ratio to be 2:1, not 4:1.

**C** is incorrect as C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>N does not match the calculated ratio of atoms.

**D** is incorrect as C<sub>4</sub>HN<sub>4</sub> does not match the calculated ratio of atoms.

> **[exam-tip]**
> A common mistake is to use a relative atomic mass of 16.0 for nitrogen, presumably from an expectation that the third element is oxygen.

parts.problemMd: What is the number of molecules in 500 cm<sup>3</sup> of oxygen at room temperature and pressure (r.t.p.)?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- Convert volume to dm<sup>3</sup>:

500 cm<sup>3</sup> = 0.500 dm<sup>3</sup>

- Calculate moles of O<sub>2</sub>:

moles = $\frac{\mathrm{volume}}{\mathrm{molar} \mathrm{volume}}$

moles = $\frac{0.500}{24.0}$

moles = 0.0208 mol

- Calculate number of molecules:

number of molecules = moles x L

number of molecules = 0.0208 x 6.02 x 10<sup>23</sup>

number of molecules = 1.25 x 10<sup>22</sup>

**B** is incorrect as 1.34 x 10<sup>22</sup> uses the molar volume at s.t.p. (22.4 dm<sup>3</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>) rather than r.t.p. (24.0 dm<sup>3</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>).

**C** is incorrect as 2.51 x 10<sup>22</sup> counts oxygen atoms rather than molecules. O<sub>2</sub> has 2 atoms per molecule, giving double the correct value.

**D** is incorrect as 1.25 x 10<sup>25</sup> uses 500 dm<sup>3</sup> rather than the correct 0.500 dm<sup>3</sup> (500 cm<sup>3</sup> ÷ 1000).

parts.problemMd:
A 5.62 g sample of anhydrous sodium sulfate, Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, is dissolved in water and the solution made up to 250 cm<sup>3</sup> in a volumetric flask.

What is the concentration in mol dm<sup>-3</sup> of the sodium sulfate solution?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Calculate *M*<sub>r</sub> of Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>:

*M*<sub>r</sub> = (2 x 23.0) + 32.1 + (4 x 16.0) = 142.1 g mol<sup>-1</sup>

- Calculate moles of Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>:

moles = $\frac{\mathrm{mass}}{M_{r}}$

moles = $\frac{5.62}{142.1}$

moles = 0.0395 mol

- Convert volume to dm<sup>3</sup>:

250 cm<sup>3</sup> = 0.250 dm<sup>3</sup>

- Calculate concentration:

concentration = $\frac{\mathrm{moles}}{\mathrm{volume}}$

concentration = $\frac{0.0395}{0.250}$

concentration = 0.158 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>

**A** is incorrect as 1.6 x 10<sup>-4</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup> results from dividing moles by 250 cm<sup>3</sup> without first converting to dm<sup>3</sup>.

**B** is incorrect as 0.016 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> results from using 2.50 dm<sup>3</sup> instead of 0.250 dm<sup>3</sup> as the volume.

**D** is incorrect as 0.61 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> results from inverting the moles calculation, dividing *M*<sub>r</sub> by mass rather than mass by *M*<sub>r</sub>.

parts.problemMd:
Methane and steam can be used to prepare hydrogen and carbon monoxide as shown by the equation below.

CH<sub>4</sub> (g) + H<sub>2</sub>O (g) → 3H<sub>2</sub> (g) + CO (g)

200 g of methane was reacted with an excess of steam to produce 642 dm<sup>3</sup> of hydrogen gas at r.t.p.

What is the percentage yield of hydrogen?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Calculate moles of CH<sub>4</sub>:

moles = $\frac{\mathrm{mass}}{M_{r}}$

moles = $\frac{200}{16.0}$

moles = 12.5 mol

- From the equation, 1 mol CH<sub>4</sub> produces 3 mol H<sub>2</sub>:

theoretical yield = 12.5 x 3 = 37.5 mol

- Calculate actual yield of H<sub>2</sub>:

actual yield = $\frac{\mathrm{volume}}{\mathrm{molar} \mathrm{volume}}$

actual yield = $\frac{642}{24.0}$

actual yield = 26.75 mol

- Calculate percentage yield:

percentage yield = $\frac{\mathrm{actual} \mathrm{yield}}{\mathrm{theoretical} \mathrm{yield}}$ x 100

percentage yield = $\frac{26.75}{37.5}$ x 100

percentage yield = 71.3%

**A** is incorrect as 33.3% divides the moles of CH<sub>4</sub> (12.5 mol) by the theoretical yield of H<sub>2</sub> (37.5 mol), confusing the two quantities.

**B** is incorrect as 46.7% uses a 1:1 ratio of CH<sub>4</sub> to H<sub>2</sub> (theoretical yield = 12.5 mol) and then inverts the percentage yield formula, dividing theoretical by actual.

**D** is incorrect as 140.2% inverts the percentage yield formula, dividing the theoretical yield by the actual yield rather than actual by theoretical.

parts.problemMd:
A volume of nitrogen gas, 2.00 dm<sup>3</sup> measured at room temperature and pressure (r.t.p.), was reacted with a large volume of hydrogen gas to produce ammonia. Only 15.0% of the nitrogen gas reacted to produce ammonia.

What mass of ammonia was produced?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Calculate moles of N<sub>2</sub> at r.t.p.:

moles = $\frac{\mathrm{volume}}{\mathrm{molar} \mathrm{volume}}$

moles = $\frac{2.00}{24.0}$

moles = 0.0833 mol

- Apply the 15.0% yield to find moles that react:

moles of N<sub>2</sub> that react = 0.0833 x 0.150 = 0.0125 mol

- From N<sub>2</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub> → 2NH<sub>3</sub>, calculate moles of NH<sub>3</sub>:

moles of NH<sub>3</sub> = 0.0125 x 2 = 0.0250 mol

- Calculate mass of NH<sub>3</sub>:

mass = moles x *M*<sub>r</sub>

mass = 0.0250 x 17.0

mass = 0.425 g

**A** is incorrect as 0.213 g uses a 1:1 molar ratio of N<sub>2</sub> to NH<sub>3</sub> rather than the correct 1:2 ratio from the equation.

**C** is incorrect as 0.455 g uses the molar volume at s.t.p. (22.4 dm<sup>3</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>) instead of r.t.p. (24.0 dm<sup>3</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>).

**D** is incorrect as 2.83 g does not apply the 15.0% yield, instead it assumes all of the nitrogen reacts to form ammonia.

parts.problemMd:
Excess aqueous cold sodium hydroxide is reacted with 0.125 mol of chlorine gas, Cl<sub>2</sub>. One of the products is a compound of sodium, oxygen and chlorine.

What mass of the product is formed?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- Balanced equation:

2NaOH (aq) + Cl<sub>2</sub> (g) → NaClO (aq) + NaCl (aq) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l)

- From the equation, 1 mol Cl<sub>2</sub> produces 1 mol NaClO:

moles of NaClO = 0.125 mol

- Calculate *M*<sub>r</sub> of NaClO:

*M*<sub>r</sub> = 23.0 + 35.5 + 16.0 = 74.5 g mol<sup>-1</sup>

- Calculate mass of NaClO:

mass = moles x *M*<sub>r</sub>

mass = 0.125 x 74.5

mass = 9.31 g

**B** is incorrect as 13.3 g uses the molar mass of NaClO<sub>3</sub> (106.5 g mol<sup>-1</sup>), the product of the reaction with hot concentrated NaOH, rather than NaClO from the cold reaction.

**C** is incorrect as 18.6 g doubles the moles of product to 0.250 mol, treating the ratio as 2 mol NaOH producing 2 mol NaClO rather than the correct 2:1 ratio.

**D** is incorrect as 26.6 g combines both errors: using the molar mass of NaClO<sub>3</sub> (106.5 g mol<sup>-1</sup>) and double the moles (0.250 mol).

parts.problemMd:
When heated magnesium nitrate, Mg(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>, will decompose to a white solid and a mixture of gases. One of the gases released is an oxide of nitrogen, **X**.

7.4 g of anhydrous magnesium nitrate is heated until no further reaction takes place.

What is the mass of **X** produced?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Balanced equation:

2Mg(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> (s) → 2MgO (s) + 4NO<sub>2</sub> (g) + O<sub>2</sub> (g)

- Calculate moles of Mg(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>:

moles = $\frac{\mathrm{mass}}{M_{r}}$

moles = $\frac{7.4}{148.3}$

moles = 0.0499 mol

- From the equation, the ratio of Mg(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> to NO<sub>2</sub> is 1:2:

moles of NO<sub>2</sub> = 0.0499 x 2 = 0.0998 mol

- Calculate mass of NO<sub>2</sub>:

mass = moles x *M*<sub>r</sub>

mass = 0.0998 x 46.0

mass = 4.6 g

**A** is incorrect as 1.5 g uses the molar mass of NO (30 g mol<sup>-1</sup>) instead of NO<sub>2</sub> (46 g mol<sup>-1</sup>), and applies a 1:1 mole ratio instead of 1:2.

**B** is incorrect as 2.3 g applies a 1:1 mole ratio of Mg(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> to NO<sub>2</sub> rather than the correct 1:2 ratio from the equation.

**C** is incorrect as 3.0 g uses the molar mass of NO (30 g mol<sup>-1</sup>) instead of NO<sub>2</sub> (46 g mol<sup>-1</sup>), though the 1:2 mole ratio is applied correctly.

parts.problemMd:
Excess water and 0.144 g of an aluminium compound **X** were reacted to form a gas. The gas burns completely in O<sub>2</sub> to form H<sub>2</sub>O and 72 cm<sup>3</sup> of CO<sub>2</sub> only. The volume of CO<sub>2</sub> was measured at room temperature and pressure.

What is the formula for **X**?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- The compound reacts with water to give Al(OH)<sub>3</sub> and CH<sub>4</sub>.

  - The methane burns completely to give CO<sub>2</sub>.

- Convert volume and calculate moles of CO<sub>2</sub>:

volume of CO<sub>2</sub> = 72 ÷ 1000 = 0.072 dm<sup>3</sup>

moles = $\frac{\mathrm{volume}}{\mathrm{molar} \mathrm{volume}}$

moles = $\frac{0.072}{24.0}$

moles of CO<sub>2</sub> = 0.003 mol

- Moles of C in the original compound = moles of CO<sub>2</sub> = 0.003 mol

- Calculate mass of C:

mass of C = 0.003 x 12.0 = 0.036 g

- Calculate mass of Al:

mass of Al = 0.144 − 0.036 = 0.108 g

- Calculate moles of Al:

moles = $\frac{\mathrm{mass}}{M_{r}}$

moles = $\frac{0.108}{27.0}$

moles of Al = 0.004 mol

- Determine the ratio Al : C:

Al : C = 0.004 : 0.003 = 4 : 3

- The formula is Al<sub>4</sub>C<sub>3</sub>

**A** is incorrect as Al<sub>2</sub>C<sub>3</sub> has a ratio of 2:3, which does not match the calculated Al to C mole ratio of 4:3.

**B** is incorrect as Al<sub>3</sub>C<sub>4</sub> inverts the mole ratio, placing the smaller value (C) as the Al subscript and the larger value (Al) as the C subscript.

**D** is incorrect as Al<sub>5</sub>C<sub>3</sub> does not correspond to the calculated mole ratio and results from an error in determining the mass of aluminium in the compound.

parts.problemMd:
A metal element of mass 1.15 g reacted with 300 cm<sup>3</sup> of oxygen at room conditions to form an oxide which contains O<sup>2-</sup> ions.

Which one of these is the metal?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Calculate moles of O<sub>2</sub>:

moles = $\frac{\mathrm{volume}}{\mathrm{molar} \mathrm{volume}}$

moles = $\frac{0.300}{24.0}$

moles of O<sub>2</sub> = 0.0125 mol

- Test Group 1 (oxide M<sub>2</sub>O): 4M + O<sub>2</sub> → 2M<sub>2</sub>O, so moles of metal = 4 x moles of O<sub>2</sub>:

moles of metal = 4 x 0.0125 = 0.050 mol

- Calculate *M*<sub>r</sub> of metal:

*M*<sub>r</sub> = $\frac{\mathrm{mass}}{\mathrm{moles}}$

*M*<sub>r</sub> = $\frac{1.15}{0.050}$

*M*<sub>r</sub> = 23 → sodium (Group 1)

- Test Group 2 (oxide MO): 2M + O<sub>2</sub> → 2MO, so moles of metal = 2 x moles of O<sub>2</sub>:

moles of metal = 2 x 0.0125 = 0.025 mol

*M*<sub>r</sub> = 1.15 ÷ 0.025 = 46 → no matching Group 2 element

- The metal is sodium, *M*<sub>r</sub> = 23

**A** is incorrect as calcium has *M*<sub>r</sub> = 40, which does not match either calculated value (23 for Group 1 or 46 for Group 2).

**B** is incorrect as magnesium has *M*<sub>r</sub> = 24, which does not match the Group 2 calculated value of 46.

**C** is incorrect as potassium has *M*<sub>r</sub> = 39, which does not match the Group 1 calculated value of 23.

parts.problemMd:
Solid fertilisers often contain the elements N, P and K in a ratio of 15 g : 30 g : 15 g per 100 g of fertiliser. It is recommended that the fertiliser is used at 28 g of fertiliser per 5 dm<sup>3</sup> of water.

What is the concentration of nitrogen atoms in the solution?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Calculate mass of nitrogen in 28 g of fertiliser:

mass of N = 28 x $\frac{15}{100}$

mass of N = 4.2 g

- Calculate moles of nitrogen:

moles = $\frac{\mathrm{mass}}{M_{r}}$

moles = $\frac{4.2}{14.0}$

moles = 0.30 mol

- Calculate concentration of nitrogen:

concentration = $\frac{\mathrm{moles}}{\mathrm{volume}}$

concentration = $\frac{0.30}{5}$

concentration = 0.060 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>

**A** is incorrect as 0.030 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> uses the molar mass of N<sub>2</sub> (28 g mol<sup>-1</sup>) instead of N atoms (14 g mol<sup>-1</sup>) when converting mass to moles.

**C** is incorrect as 0.40 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> misses out the 15% mass fraction. Instead, it divides the total fertiliser mass directly by *M*<sub>r</sub>(N) and the volume without accounting for the nitrogen content.

**D** is incorrect as 0.84 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> reports a mass concentration rather than a molar concentration, i.e. the mass of nitrogen (4.2 g) is divided by volume without first converting to moles.

choices.label: B
choices.textMd: The percentage by mass of each element present in the compounds.

choices.label: C
choices.textMd: Their molecular formulae are formed by multiplying the empirical formula by the same integer

choices.label: D
choices.textMd: The total number of atoms present in one mole of each compound.

parts.problemMd:
Two distinct organic compounds, **X** and **Y**, are found to have the same empirical formula.

Which of the following **must** be identical for both compounds?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Compounds with the same empirical formula share the same simplest ratio of atoms.
- This means the percentage by mass of each element must be identical, regardless of the molecular formula.

**A** is incorrect as compounds with the same empirical formula can have different molecular formulae and therefore different *M*<sub>r</sub> values.

**C** is incorrect as the integer multiplier used to convert an empirical formula to a molecular formula does not have to be the same for different compounds.

**D** is incorrect as different molecular formulae contain different numbers of atoms per molecule, so one mole of each compound contains a different total number of atoms.

parts.problemMd:
1.00 g of carbon is combusted in a limited supply of oxygen. 0.50 g of the carbon combusts to form CO<sub>2</sub> and 0.50 g of the carbon combusts to form CO.

These were passed through excess NaOH (aq) and the remaining gas then dried and collected.

Assuming that all gas volumes were taken at room conditions, what is the volume of gas at the end of the reaction?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- Combustion reactions:

C + O<sub>2</sub> → CO<sub>2</sub>

2C + O<sub>2</sub> → 2CO

- CO<sub>2</sub> is absorbed by excess NaOH:

CO<sub>2</sub> + 2NaOH → Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O

- CO does not react with NaOH, so only CO remains after passing through the solution
- Calculate moles of CO produced:

moles = $\frac{\mathrm{mass}}{M_{r}}$

moles = $\frac{0.50}{12.0}$

moles of CO = 0.0417 mol

- Calculate volume of CO remaining:

volume = moles x molar volume

volume = 0.0417 x 24.0

volume = 1.0 dm<sup>3</sup>

**B** is incorrect as 1.5 dm<sup>3</sup> arises from incorrectly including part of the CO<sub>2</sub> volume. Only the CO that remains after absorption should be counted.

**C** is incorrect as 2 dm<sup>3</sup> is the total volume of CO and CO<sub>2</sub> produced before passing through NaOH, without accounting for the absorption of CO<sub>2</sub>.

**D** is incorrect as 3 dm<sup>3</sup> results from including oxygen gas volumes alongside the carbon oxide products in the final calculation.

parts.problemMd:
The eggshell of a chicken egg makes up 5% of the total egg mass.

The average egg has a mass of 50 g.

Assume that chicken eggshell is pure calcium carbonate.

What is the number of eggshells needed to neutralise 50 cm<sup>3</sup> of 2.0 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> ethanoic acid?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Balanced equation:

2CH<sub>3</sub>COOH + CaCO<sub>3</sub> → (CH<sub>3</sub>COO)<sub>2</sub>Ca + CO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O

- Calculate moles of CaCO<sub>3</sub> per eggshell (*M*<sub>r</sub> of CaCO<sub>3</sub> = 100):

mass of eggshell per egg = 5% x 50 = 2.5 g

moles of CaCO<sub>3</sub> = $\frac{2.5}{100}$ = 0.025 mol per eggshell

- Calculate moles of ethanoic acid:

moles = concentration x volume

moles = 2.0 x $\frac{50}{1000}$

moles of CH<sub>3</sub>COOH = 0.10 mol

- From the 2:1 ratio, calculate moles of CaCO<sub>3</sub> needed:

moles of CaCO<sub>3</sub> = $\frac{0.10}{2}$ = 0.050 mol

- Calculate number of eggshells:

number of eggshells = $\frac{0.050}{0.025}$ = 2

**A** is incorrect as 1 eggshell results from using the full egg mass (50 g) as if it were entirely CaCO<sub>3</sub>, greatly underestimating the moles of carbonate per shell.

**C** is incorrect as 3 eggshells results from an error in applying the 2:1 acid-to-carbonate mole ratio, leading to an overestimate of the CaCO<sub>3</sub> required.

**D** is incorrect as 4 eggshells results from using a 1:1 ratio of ethanoic acid to CaCO<sub>3</sub> rather than the correct 2:1 ratio, doubling the moles of carbonate required.

parts.problemMd:
When a sample of potassium oxide, K<sub>2</sub>O, is dissolved in 250 cm<sup>3</sup> of distilled water, 25 cm<sup>3</sup> of this solution is titrated against sulfuric acid with a concentration of 2.00 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>. Complete neutralisation takes place with 15 cm<sup>3</sup> of sulfuric acid.

What is the mass of the original sample of potassium oxide dissolved in 250 cm<sup>3</sup> of distilled water?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Reactions:

K<sub>2</sub>O + H<sub>2</sub>O → 2KOH and 2KOH + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → K<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O

- Calculate moles of H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>:

moles = concentration x volume

moles = 2.00 x $\frac{15}{1000}$

moles of H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> = 0.030 mol

- From the 2:1 ratio (KOH : H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>), calculate moles of KOH in the 25 cm<sup>3</sup> aliquot:

moles of KOH = 0.030 x 2 = 0.060 mol

- Scale up to the full 250 cm<sup>3</sup> solution:

moles of KOH = 0.060 x $\frac{250}{25}$ = 0.60 mol

- From K<sub>2</sub>O + H<sub>2</sub>O → 2KOH (ratio 1:2), calculate moles of K<sub>2</sub>O:

moles of K<sub>2</sub>O = $\frac{0.60}{2}$ = 0.30 mol

- Calculate mass of K<sub>2</sub>O:

mass = moles x *M*<sub>r</sub>

mass = 0.30 x 94.2

mass = 28.3 g

**A** is incorrect as 2.83 g uses only the 25 cm<sup>3</sup> titration aliquot without scaling up to the full 250 cm<sup>3</sup> solution.

**C** is incorrect as 47.1 g results from an error in the stoichiometric ratio between K<sub>2</sub>O and KOH in the dissolving step, leading to an incorrect number of moles of K<sub>2</sub>O.

**D** is incorrect as 56.6 g treats the K<sub>2</sub>O to KOH ratio as 1:1 rather than 1:2, using 0.60 mol K<sub>2</sub>O directly in the mass calculation.

parts.problemMd:
Excess acidified aqueous potassium dichromate(VI) was mixed with 2.76 g of ethanol. The reaction mixture was then boiled under reflux for one hour. The organic product was collected by distillation.

The yield of the product was 75.0%

What is the mass of the product collected?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Reaction:

CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH → CH<sub>3</sub>COOH (oxidation using excess acidified K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>)

- Calculate moles of ethanol:

moles = $\frac{\mathrm{mass}}{M_{r}}$

moles = $\frac{2.76}{46.0}$

moles of ethanol = 0.0600 mol

- 1:1 molar ratio, so theoretical moles of ethanoic acid = 0.0600 mol
- Calculate theoretical mass of ethanoic acid:

theoretical mass = moles x *M*<sub>r</sub>

theoretical mass = 0.0600 x 60.0

theoretical mass = 3.60 g

- Apply the 75.0% yield:

actual mass = 3.60 x 0.750

actual mass = 2.70 g

**A** is incorrect as 1.98 g uses the molar mass of partial oxidation product ethanal (CH<sub>3</sub>CHO, *M*<sub>r</sub> = 44) rather than the full oxidation product ethanoic acid (*M*<sub>r</sub> = 60).

**B** is incorrect as 2.07 g multiplies the starting mass of ethanol directly by the percentage yield, without first converting to moles and calculating the theoretical product mass.
