> - Nuclear charge increases (one extra proton per element).
> - Atomic radius decreases (electrons added to the same shell are pulled closer by the greater nuclear charge).
> - Shielding stays similar (no new inner shell is added).
> 
> The combined effect is a stronger attraction between the nucleus and the bonding pair of electrons, so electronegativity increases.
> 
> A common error is to state only 'more protons' without linking to the attraction for the bonding electrons. The mark scheme rewards the cause-and-effect: greater nuclear charge plus smaller atomic radius plus similar shielding lead to stronger attraction.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The electronegativities of some elements are shown in Table 3.1.

**Table 3.1**

| **Element** | **Electronegativity** |
| --- | --- |
| Li | 1.0 |
| H | 2.1 |
| C | 2.5 |
| N | 3.0 |
| Cl | 3.0 |

Explain how the carbon-hydrogen bond (such as in CH<sub>4</sub>) differs from the nitrogen-hydrogen bond (such as in NH<sub>3</sub>) in terms of the bond polarity.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The N-H bond is more polar than the C-H bond because:
> 
> - The N-H bond is more polar than the C-H bond; **[1 mark]**
> - The difference in electronegativity in C-H is smaller / 0.4
> **OR**
> The difference in electronegativity in N-H is larger / 0.9; **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A 2-mark 'explain' question on bond polarity needs both a comparison and a reason. The comparison alone is not enough.
> 
> Use Table 3.1 to calculate:
> 
> - C-H: ΔEN = 2.5 − 2.1 = 0.4
> - N-H: ΔEN = 3.0 − 2.1 = 0.9
> 
> The larger electronegativity difference (0.9 > 0.4) means the bonding pair of electrons is more strongly drawn towards the nitrogen atom in N-H, making it the more polar bond.
> 
> A common pitfall is to quote the individual electronegativity values without taking the difference. Examiners want the comparison of ΔEN, not just '2.5 vs 3.0'.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The electronegativities of some elements are shown in Table 3.1.

**Table 3.1**

| **Element** | **Electronegativity** |
| --- | --- |
| Li | 1.0 |
| H | 2.1 |
| C | 2.5 |
| N | 3.0 |
| Cl | 3.0 |

Explain, in terms of electronegativity, why the bonding in ammonia (NH<sub>3</sub>) is covalent but the bonding in lithium chloride (LiCl) is ionic.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The bonding in NH<sub>3</sub> is covalent but the bonding in LiCl is ionic because:
> 
> For NH<sub>3</sub>:
> 
> - The difference in electronegativity between N and H is small; **[1 mark]**
> - (So) the electrons are shared (between the two atoms); **[1 mark]**
> 
> For LiCl:
> 
> - The difference in electronegativity between Li and Cl is large; **[1 mark]**
> - (So) the electron is transferred from Li to Cl (forming Li<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>-</sup> ions); **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Bonding type (covalent vs ionic) is determined by the electronegativity difference between the two atoms in the bond. Use Table 3.1 to anchor your reasoning:
> 
> - N-H: ΔEN = 3.0 − 2.1 = 0.9 (small difference, so the bonding pair is shared between the atoms, giving a covalent bond)
> - Li-Cl: ΔEN = 3.0 − 1.0 = 2.0 (large difference, so the electron is fully transferred from Li to Cl, giving an ionic bond)
> 
> The question says 'in terms of electronegativity', so do not score by reasoning from 'metals vs non-metals' alone. The marks are awarded for:
> 
> 1. Stating that the electronegativity difference is small (NH<sub>3</sub>) or large (LiCl).
> 2. Linking that difference to electron sharing (covalent) or transfer (ionic).
> 
> For the fourth mark, the direction of electron transfer matters: lithium loses an electron to chlorine. Stating 'electrons are transferred' without specifying which atom gains and which atom loses will not score the fourth mark.

parts.problemMd:
Chlorine (Cl) reacts with boron (B) to form boron trichloride (BCl<sub>3</sub>).

i) What type of bond is the B-Cl bond?

[1]

ii) How is this bond formed?

[1]

iii) The electronegativities of boron, chlorine and hydrogen are 2.0, 3.2 and 2.2 respectively. Is the B-Cl more or less polar than a B-H bond in borane (BH<sub>3</sub>)? Explain your answer.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The type of bond between B and Cl:
> 
> - Covalent; **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The B-Cl bond is formed from:
> 
> - A shared pair of electrons between the B and Cl atoms
> **OR**
> The sharing of one electron from B and one electron from Cl; **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The B-Cl bond is more polar than the B-H bond because:
> 
> - The B-H bond is less polar than the B-Cl bond; **[1 mark]**
> - The difference in electronegativity in B-H is smaller / 0.2
> **OR**
> The difference in electronegativity in B-Cl is larger / 1.2; **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part i), the answer is 'covalent'. Both B and Cl are non-metals, so they form a covalent bond by sharing electrons. The bond is polar (because of the electronegativity difference shown in part iii)), but the bond type is still classified as covalent.
> 
> For part ii), the sharing must be specified clearly. 'A shared pair of electrons' or 'one electron from each atom' both work; vague phrases like 'they share electrons' may not score.
> 
> For part iii), a 2-mark explain question requires a comparison and a reason:
> 
> - Comparison: B-H is less polar OR B-Cl is more polar
> - Reason: smaller (or larger) difference in electronegativity, with the calculated values where possible
> 
> The calculated electronegativity differences are:
> 
> - B-H: ΔEN = 2.2 − 2.0 = 0.2
> - B-Cl: ΔEN = 3.2 − 2.0 = 1.2
> 
> The larger difference (1.2 vs 0.2) means the B-Cl bond is more polar. Citing the numerical values is the safest way to secure the second mark.

parts.problemMd:
Molecules and separate atoms (such as noble gases) are attracted to one another by intermolecular forces.

i) What is the strongest type of intermolecular force that takes place between water (H<sub>2</sub>O) molecules?

[1]

ii) Draw a diagram that illustrates the interaction between two water molecules. Indicate any lone pairs of electrons and partial charges in your diagram.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The strongest type of intermolecular force between water molecules:
> 
> - Hydrogen bonding; **[1 mark]**

ii) The completed diagram is:

![Diagram of two water molecules showing δ− oxygen with two lone pairs, δ+ hydrogens, and a dotted line labelled hydrogen bond between them](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/3-chemical-bonding/3-1-electronegativity-and-bonding/assets/002-diagram-of-two-water-molecules-showing-oxygen-wi.jpg)

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a hydrogen bond (clearly labelled) going from a hydrogen atom in one molecule to an oxygen atom in another molecule.
> 
> 1 mark for a partial positive (δ<sup>+</sup>) charge on all hydrogen atoms AND a partial negative (δ<sup>-</sup>) charge on both oxygen atoms.
> 
> 1 mark for two lone pairs on each oxygen atom, with the hydrogen bond clearly starting at a lone pair.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Hydrogen bonding only occurs when a hydrogen atom is covalently bonded to a very electronegative atom (F, O or N), leaving the H electron-deficient.
> 
> In water, the more electronegative oxygen carries a δ<sup>-</sup> charge while the hydrogen atoms carry δ<sup>+</sup> charges. The hydrogen bond forms between the δ<sup>+</sup> hydrogen of one molecule and a lone pair on the δ<sup>-</sup> oxygen of another.
> 
> Common diagram errors include:
> 
> - Drawing the hydrogen bond starting at the oxygen atom itself rather than at a lone pair.
> - Forgetting to label δ<sup>+</sup> / δ<sup>-</sup> on all atoms.
> - Showing only one lone pair on each oxygen atom (oxygen has two).
> 
> The hydrogen bond is conventionally drawn as a dashed line between the H of one molecule and a lone pair on the O of another.

parts.problemMd:
The boiling point of tetrachloromethane (CCl<sub>4</sub>) is 77 °C whereas the boiling point of water (H<sub>2</sub>O) is 100 °C.

i) Suggest why the boiling point of H<sub>2</sub>O is higher than that of CCl<sub>4</sub>.

[2]

ii) Predict whether the boiling point of methane (CH<sub>4</sub>) is higher or lower than the boiling point of CCl<sub>4</sub>. Explain your answer.

[4]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The boiling point of H<sub>2</sub>O is higher than that of CCl<sub>4</sub> because:
> 
> - There are stronger intermolecular forces / hydrogen bonds between the H<sub>2</sub>O molecules (in addition to the other intermolecular forces); **[1 mark]**
> - More energy is required to break the intermolecular forces between the H<sub>2</sub>O molecules; **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The boiling point of CH<sub>4</sub>:
> 
> - Will be lower than that of CCl<sub>4</sub>; **[1 mark]**
> - (Because) there are more electrons in CCl<sub>4</sub>; **[1 mark]**
> - (Therefore) there are more / stronger Van der Waals' forces in CCl<sub>4</sub>; **[1 mark]**
> - (So) more energy is required to break the intermolecular forces between the CCl<sub>4</sub> molecules; **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Boiling point depends on the strength of the intermolecular forces between molecules, NOT on the strength of the covalent bonds within molecules. The covalent bonds stay intact on boiling; only the intermolecular forces break.
> 
> For part i), the key fact is that H<sub>2</sub>O has hydrogen bonds (because each H is bonded to a very electronegative O, leaving the H electron-deficient), whereas CCl<sub>4</sub> has only Van der Waals' forces. Although the C-Cl bonds are polar, the tetrahedral symmetry of CCl<sub>4</sub> means the bond dipoles cancel and the molecule has no permanent dipole. Hydrogen bonds are much stronger than Van der Waals' forces, so H<sub>2</sub>O boils at the higher temperature.
> 
> For part ii), CCl<sub>4</sub> molecules have far more electrons (74 in total) than CH<sub>4</sub> molecules (10), so the Van der Waals' forces between CCl<sub>4</sub> molecules are stronger.
> 
> A common slip is to compare the strengths of C-H and C-Cl bonds. These are covalent bonds within the molecule and do not affect boiling point.
> 
> For full marks, work through the cause-and-effect chain explicitly: more electrons in CCl<sub>4</sub> → stronger Van der Waals' forces → more energy needed to break IMFs → higher boiling point for CCl<sub>4</sub> (so CH<sub>4</sub> has the lower boiling point).

parts.problemMd: Define the term *electronegativity*.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Electronegativity is:
> 
> - The ability of an atom to attract a pair of electrons / a bonding pair of electrons towards itself in a covalent bond; **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> This is a high-frequency exam definition, so learn it precisely.
> 
> The definition packs three ideas into a single mark: an atom (the agent), attracting a pair of electrons (the action), in a covalent bond (the context). All three must be present to score the mark.
> 
> A common slip is to omit 'in a covalent bond', which leaves the definition incomplete. Another is to write 'attract atoms' or 'attract electrons' without specifying that it is a pair (or bonding pair) of electrons. Be precise about each of the three elements.

parts.problemMd: State and explain the general trend in electronegativity across a period.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The general trend in electronegativity across a period:
> 
> - (Electronegativity) shows a general increase; **[1 mark]**
> 
> Explanation:
> 
> - (Across the period) there is a greater / increased nuclear charge
> **OR**
> There are more protons in the nucleus; **[1 mark]**
> - The electrons are added to the same shell
> **OR**
> The shielding is the same / shielding does not change
> **OR**
> There are no additional shells of electrons (added); **[1 mark]**
> - (Therefore,) there is a stronger attraction between the (bonding) electrons and the nucleus; **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The 'state and explain' command requires both the trend and the underlying reasoning. A one-word answer ('increases') will only score the first mark.
> 
> Anchor the explanation to the three factors that affect electronegativity. Across a period:
> 
> - Nuclear charge increases (one extra proton per element)
> - Atomic radius decreases (electrons added to the same shell are pulled closer by the greater nuclear charge)
> - Shielding stays roughly the same (no new inner shell)
> 
> The combined effect is a stronger attraction between the nucleus and the bonding pair of electrons, so electronegativity increases.
> 
> A common error is to state only that 'there are more protons' without linking this to the attraction for the bonding electrons. The fourth mark is awarded for connecting the cause (greater nuclear charge, same shielding) to the consequence (stronger attraction).

parts.problemMd:
The Pauling electronegativity values of different elements are shown in Fig. 3.1.

![electronegativity-values](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/3-chemical-bonding/3-1-electronegativity-and-bonding/assets/003-electronegativity-values.png)

**Fig. 3.1**

A compound formed from magnesium and oxygen has a different structure to a compound formed from phosphorus and oxygen.

Predict the type of bonds that will occur in each compound. Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The type of bonds in each compound:
> 
> - The bond between Mg and O is ionic; **[1 mark]**
> - The difference in electronegativity is greater than 1.7; **[1 mark]**
> - The bond between P and O is polar covalent / covalent with some ionic character; **[1 mark]**
> - The difference in electronegativity is between 0.4 and 1.7; **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The presence of Pauling electronegativity values in the figure is your cue to use them. A response based only on 'magnesium is a metal and oxygen is a non-metal, while phosphorus and oxygen are both non-metals' will not score at this level. You must reference the electronegativity differences explicitly.
> 
> Use these threshold values to decide bond type:
> 
> - ΔEN ≈ 0.0 to 0.4: non-polar covalent
> - ΔEN ≈ 0.4 to 1.7: polar covalent (or 'covalent with some ionic character')
> - ΔEN ≳ 1.7: predominantly ionic
> 
> For Mg-O, ΔEN ≈ 3.5 − 1.2 = 2.3, which is greater than 1.7, so the bond is ionic. For P-O, ΔEN ≈ 3.5 − 2.1 = 1.4, which sits between 0.4 and 1.7, so the bond is polar covalent.
> 
> A common slip is to give the bond type without the supporting electronegativity reasoning. Each bond type and its justification is awarded as a separate mark, so state the rule and the calculation explicitly.

parts.problemMd: Explain why the melting point of phosphorus(III) oxide, P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>6</sub>, is lower than that of magnesium oxide in terms of their bonding and structure.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The melting point of phosphorus(III) oxide is lower than that of magnesium oxide because:
> 
> - MgO has a giant ionic lattice with strong ionic bonds
> **AND**
> P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>6</sub> has a simple molecular / covalent structure with weak intermolecular forces; **[1 mark]**
> - More energy is required to break the (ionic) bonds in MgO than to overcome the weak intermolecular forces in P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>6</sub>; **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The key distinction here is between bonding within molecules (intramolecular) and bonding between molecules (intermolecular). P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>6</sub> has strong intramolecular covalent bonds, but it is the weak intermolecular forces between P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>6</sub> molecules that are overcome on melting.
> 
> A common error is to compare 'covalent bonds' against 'ionic bonds' directly and conclude that ionic must be stronger. The comparison is between ionic bonds and intermolecular forces, not ionic bonds and covalent bonds.
> 
> Acceptable terms for the intermolecular forces in P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>6</sub> include:
> 
> - London dispersion forces
> - Van der Waals' forces
> - Permanent dipole-permanent dipole forces
> 
> State explicitly that MgO has a giant ionic lattice and P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>6</sub> has a simple molecular structure to secure the first mark. Describing the bonding alone is not enough.

parts.problemMd:
Phosphorus(III) oxide, P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>6</sub>, contains no P–P or O–O bonds.

In the P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>6</sub> molecule, all oxygen atoms are bonded to two other atoms and all phosphorus atoms are bonded to three other atoms.

Sketch a structure for P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>6</sub>.
parts.solutionMd:
A structure for P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>6</sub> is:

![Two schematic phosphorus–oxygen cage structures, left undetailed, right with several P=O double bonds, illustrating different polyphosphate arrangements.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/3-chemical-bonding/3-1-electronegativity-and-bonding/assets/004-two-schematic-phosphorus-oxygen-cage-structures-.bin)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a structure where each P atom is bonded to three O atoms AND each O atom is bonded to two atoms (a P=O double bond counts as the O being divalent in the alternative structure).

> **[exam-tip]**
> The first diagram is the canonical P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>6</sub> cage structure: four phosphorus atoms at the corners of a tetrahedron, with six oxygen atoms bridging the P-P edges. The second diagram is also accepted, with two of the oxygen atoms forming P=O double bonds (treated as divalent in this counting).
> 
> Check your structure has the correct bond count: each P with three bonds and each O with two bonds (or one double bond), giving six P-O linkages in total.
> 
> Common errors are drawing P=O bonds in positions that leave a P with only two bonds, or omitting one or more of the six oxygen atoms.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The Pauling electronegativity values of different elements are shown in Fig. 3.1.

![electronegativity-values](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2023/03/electronegativity-values.png)

{align=center} **Fig. 3.1**

Explain the difference in electronegativity shown in Fig. 3.1 between magnesium and calcium.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The difference in electronegativity between magnesium and calcium is because:
> 
> - Calcium has more shielding (than magnesium); **[1 mark]**
> - Calcium has a larger atomic radius (than magnesium); **[1 mark]**
> - (Therefore) there is less attraction between the calcium nucleus and the bonding pair of electrons; **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Magnesium and calcium are in the same group (Group 2), so the key factors that change down the group are atomic radius and shielding, not nuclear charge. Although calcium has a greater nuclear charge than magnesium, the increase is more than offset by the larger atomic radius and additional inner shells of shielding electrons.
> 
> When explaining electronegativity differences, anchor your reasoning to the attraction between the nucleus and the bonding pair of electrons:
> 
> - Down a group: atomic radius and shielding both increase, weakening the attraction. Electronegativity decreases.
> - Across a period: nuclear charge increases while shielding stays similar, strengthening the attraction. Electronegativity increases.
> 
> The third mark requires you to state the consequence explicitly: less attraction for the bonding pair means lower electronegativity. Listing only the two factors (shielding and radius) without the attraction outcome will score 2 of the 3 marks.
> 
> You can also gain credit by reversing the comparison. For example, 'magnesium has less shielding than calcium' scores the same mark as 'calcium has more shielding than magnesium'.

parts.problemMd:
Sodium is a metal in the Periodic Table.

Draw a labelled diagram to show the arrangement of particles in a crystal of sodium.

In your answer, include at least six particles of each type.
parts.solutionMd:
A labelled diagram showing the arrangement of particles in a crystal of sodium:

![Diagram showing 6 positive metal ions (indicated with a + sign inside each of them). The ions are in two rows of three. Each ion has a dot representing an electron next to it.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/3-chemical-bonding/3-2-ionic-bonding/assets/002-diagram-showing-6-positive-metal-ions-indicated-.bin)

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a regular arrangement / lattice of (at least six) positive metal ions.
> 
> 1 mark for the positive charge shown on each metal ion, e.g. a + sign inside each ion / labelled as Na<sup>+</sup> / labelled as 'positive metal ions' or 'cations'.
> 
> 1 mark for at least six electrons drawn between the ions AND labelled as 'delocalised electrons' (or described as a 'sea of delocalised electrons').

> **[exam-tip]**
> A metallic crystal should be drawn as a regular lattice of positive metal ions surrounded by a 'sea' of delocalised electrons.
> 
> Show the structure clearly:
> 
> - Each sodium ion must have a + sign inside the circle (or be explicitly labelled Na<sup>+</sup>) to indicate the loss of its outer electron.
> - The electrons drawn between the ions MUST be labelled as 'delocalised electrons' (or shown as a 'sea of delocalised electrons'). CIE examiner reports (Nov 2022) flag this as a frequent reason for losing the mark. A bare dot, a − sign, or 'e<sup>-</sup>' on its own is not enough.
> - Arrange the ions in a regular pattern (rows and columns) to show that ions can slide past one another, which explains why metals are malleable.
> 
> The question specifies 'at least six particles of each type', so draw at least six ions AND at least six electrons. Drawing fewer ions will cost you the first marking point.

parts.problemMd:
Sodium can react with chlorine to produce sodium chloride.

Sodium chloride is ionically bonded.

State the meaning of the term ‘ionic bond’.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The term 'ionic bond' means:
> 
> - Electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions / between cations and anions / between positive and negative ions; **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> This is a high-frequency CIE definition. Learn the syllabus wording word-for-word.
> 
> The two key elements:
> 
> - 'Electrostatic attraction' (not just 'attraction' or 'force')
> - 'Between oppositely charged ions' (also accepted as 'between cations and anions' or 'between positive and negative ions')
> 
> CIE accepts variations on the polarity wording but NOT on 'electrostatic'. Saying 'ions are attracted to each other' is too vague to score.
> 
> A common slip is to describe ionic bonding as 'electron transfer'. While electron transfer forms the ions, the bond itself is the electrostatic attraction between the ions formed.
> 
> For context: in sodium chloride, sodium loses one electron to become Na<sup>+</sup> and chlorine gains one electron to become Cl<sup>-</sup>. The ionic bond is the electrostatic attraction between Na<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>-</sup> in the giant ionic lattice.

parts.problemMd: Draw the 'dot and cross' diagram to show the ions formed by sodium chloride.
parts.solutionMd:
The 'dot and cross' diagram of the ions in sodium chloride:

![Electron diagrams of sodium and chloride ions showing electron shells, charge symbols and brackets, illustrating electron transfer in ionic bonding.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/3-chemical-bonding/3-2-ionic-bonding/assets/003-electron-diagrams-of-sodium-and-chloride-ions-sh.png)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for sodium ion shown as [Na]<sup>+</sup> with square brackets around the ion, an empty outer shell, and a single + charge as superscript outside the bracket.
> 
> 1 mark for chloride ion shown as [Cl]<sup>-</sup> with square brackets, 8 electrons in the outer shell (7 of one symbol AND 1 of the other to show electron transfer from sodium), and a single − charge as superscript outside the bracket.
> 
> Inner shells are not required, but if drawn must be correct. Missing brackets, missing charges, undifferentiated dots/crosses, or an incomplete outer shell on Cl<sup>-</sup> are not accepted.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The mark in CIE dot-and-cross questions is awarded for the DIAGRAM, not for written electronic configuration. To secure both marks:
> 
> - Use square brackets [ ] around each ion.
> - Place the charge as a superscript outside the brackets, e.g. [Na]<sup>+</sup> and [Cl]<sup>-</sup>.
> - Show only the OUTER shell of each ion (inner shells are optional but must be correct if drawn).
> - Use dots for one ion's electrons and crosses for the other to show that one electron has transferred from sodium to chlorine.
> 
> For Na<sup>+</sup>, the outer shell is empty because the 3s<sup>1</sup> electron has transferred away, so the bracket contains an empty outer circle.
> 
> For Cl<sup>-</sup>, the outer shell has 8 electrons in total. Show 7 of one symbol (Cl's own electrons) and 1 of the other (the electron transferred from Na). This visually demonstrates the transfer.
> 
> Charge notation:
> 
> - CIE uses '+' and '−' for single charges (never '+1', '1+', or just '1').
> - For multiple charges (e.g. Mg<sup>2+</sup>), the number goes before the sign and both go as superscript outside the bracket.
> 
> Common mistakes that cost marks:
> 
> - Forgetting the square brackets.
> - Showing all 8 electrons on Cl<sup>-</sup> as the same symbol (this fails to show electron transfer).
> - Drawing only 7 electrons on Cl<sup>-</sup> (forgetting the transferred electron).
> - Missing the charge entirely.

parts.problemMd:
Both lithium and lithium chloride contain ions of lithium. However, the structure bonding and properties of these substances are very different.

State how the ions are held together in solid lithium and in solid lithium chloride.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The ions are held together in solid lithium and solid lithium chloride by:
> 
> - Lithium: (strong) electrostatic attraction between (positive) lithium ions / Li<sup>+</sup> and delocalised electrons; **[1 mark]**
> - Lithium chloride: (strong) electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions / Li<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>-</sup>; **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> This question tests two distinct types of bonding side-by-side:
> 
> - Metallic bonding (in lithium): a regular lattice of Li<sup>+</sup> ions held together by their electrostatic attraction to delocalised outer electrons (often described as a 'sea' of electrons in textbooks, though the CIE mark scheme just says 'delocalised electrons').
> - Ionic bonding (in lithium chloride): a giant ionic lattice of Li<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>-</sup> ions held together by the electrostatic attraction between the oppositely charged ions.
> 
> For both marks, the words 'electrostatic attraction' (or 'electrostatic forces') are what the mark scheme rewards. Saying just 'attraction' or 'force' will not score.
> 
> A common slip is to describe ionic bonding as 'electron transfer'. While the ions are formed by electron transfer, the bond itself is the electrostatic attraction between the ions formed.

parts.problemMd:
Table 4.1 below shows the melting and boiling points of lithium and lithium chloride.

**Table 4.1**

|   | **Melting point (°C)** | **Boiling point (°C)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Lithium** | 180.5 | 1342 |
| **Lithium chloride** | 605.0 | 1382 |

Explain what can be deduced from the information in Table 4.1.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> What can be deduced from Table 4.1:
> 
> - Lithium chloride has higher melting and boiling points than lithium
> **OR**
> The ionic bonding (in LiCl) is stronger than the metallic bonding (in Li); **[1 mark]**
> - More energy is needed to overcome the (stronger) electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions (in LiCl) than between Li<sup>+</sup> and delocalised electrons (in Li); **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The question says 'explain what can be deduced from the information in Table 4.1', so you must:
> 
> - Make a comparison from the data (e.g. LiCl mp 605 °C vs Li mp 180.5 °C).
> - Link that comparison to the relative strengths of the bonding types AND the energy needed to overcome the forces.
> 
> The mark scheme gives credit in two parts. The first mark is for noticing that LiCl has the higher mp / bp (or that ionic bonding is stronger than metallic bonding). The second mark is for the explicit energy link: more energy is required to overcome the stronger attraction in LiCl. Stating only 'stronger forces' without the energy-to-overcome step will only score 1 of 2 marks.
> 
> Note: the boiling points (1342 °C vs 1382 °C) are very close, so most of the contrast comes from the melting points. Either or both pairs of values can be cited.

parts.problemMd:
Two students, **A** and **B**, are comparing the properties of lithium and lithium chloride.

Student **A** states that both lithium and lithium chloride will conduct electricity, but Student **B **states that **only** lithium will conduct electricity. 

State whether Student **A**, Student **B**, or neither student is correct. Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Whether Student A, Student B, or neither is correct:
> 
> - Student B is incorrect AND Student A is partly correct
> **OR**
> Both Student A and Student B are incorrect; **[1 mark]**
> 
> Lithium:
> 
> - Lithium will conduct electricity (at all times); **[1 mark]**
> - Lithium has delocalised electrons that move (through the metal structure) and carry charge; **[1 mark]**
> 
> Lithium chloride:
> 
> - Lithium chloride conducts electricity when molten / dissolved (in solution), but not when solid; **[1 mark]**
> - When solid the ions are in fixed positions / cannot move
> **AND**
> When molten / dissolved the ions are free to move / mobile (and carry charge); **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For a substance to conduct electricity, charged particles (electrons or ions) must be free to move.
> 
> Lithium (a metal):
> 
> - Has delocalised outer electrons that move through the metallic lattice at all times.
> - Conducts electricity in both solid and molten states.
> 
> Lithium chloride (an ionic compound):
> 
> - Solid: ions are locked in position in the giant ionic lattice and cannot move, so it does NOT conduct electricity.
> - Molten or aqueous: the lattice has broken apart, so the Li<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>-</sup> ions are free to move and carry charge.
> 
> The trick is that BOTH students are wrong. Student A is wrong because LiCl does not conduct as a solid. Student B is wrong because LiCl does conduct when molten or dissolved (so 'only lithium will conduct' is too strong).
> 
> CIE wording note: use 'free to move' or 'mobile' (CIE's standard phrase), not 'can flow'. Say 'carry charge' not 'carry the charge'.
> 
> Marking note: stating just 'they are wrong' without justification will not score the explanation marks. You need to explicitly cover (i) lithium conducts via delocalised electrons and (ii) LiCl conducts only when molten or dissolved because the ions are then mobile.

parts.problemMd:
Student **A** and **B** then went on to discuss the bonding in another substance, CaF<sub>2</sub>.

Explain, in terms of electrons, how CaF<sub>2</sub> is formed from its atoms.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> CaF<sub>2</sub> is formed from its atoms by:
> 
> - 1 Ca atom loses 2 electrons (to form Ca<sup>2+</sup>); **[1 mark]**
> - 2 F atoms (each) gain 1 electron (to form F<sup>-</sup>); **[1 mark]**
> - Forming Ca<sup>2+</sup> AND 2 F<sup>-</sup> (correct charges and ratio); **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The 'in terms of electrons' command means you must describe the loss and gain of electrons explicitly. You must:
> 
> - State which atom loses electrons and how many.
> - State which atom gains electrons and how many.
> - Identify the resulting ions (with correct charges and ratio).
> 
> For CaF<sub>2</sub>:
> 
> - Calcium (Group 2) loses its 2 outer electrons to achieve a full outer shell, forming Ca<sup>2+</sup>.
> - Each fluorine (Group 17) gains 1 electron to achieve a full outer shell, forming F<sup>-</sup>.
> - The formula tells you there are TWO fluoride ions per calcium ion, so 2 fluorine atoms each gain 1 electron (not 'fluorine gains 2 electrons', which would form F<sup>2-</sup> and is incorrect).
> 
> CIE convention: use digits ('2 electrons') rather than words ('two electrons'). The third mark is for stating the resulting ions clearly with correct charges and the 1:2 ratio.

parts.problemMd:
Table 2.1 shows the properties of four substances.

**Table 2.1**

| **Substance** | **Boiling point** | **Electrical** **conductivity of solid** | **Electrical conductivity** **when molten** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Copper** | high | conducts | conducts |
| **Lithium bromide** | high | does not conduct | conducts |
| **Sulfur** | low | does not conduct | does not conduct |

State the meaning of the term ionic bonding.
parts.solutionMd:
The term ionic bonding refers to:

- The strong force of attraction; **[1 mark]**
- Between + and – ions / oppositely charged ions; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *You need to know this standard definition*

  - *An ionic bond is the strong electrostatic force of attraction between oppositely charged ions*
  - *Using the word particles instead of ions will sometimes get the second mark but this is not guaranteed *

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Table 2.1 shows the properties of four substances.

**Table 2.1**

| **Substance** | **Boiling point** | **Electrical** **conductivity of solid** | **Electrical conductivity** **when molten** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Copper** | high | conducts | conducts |
| **Lithium bromide** | high | does not conduct | conducts |
| **Sulfur** | low | does not conduct | does not conduct |

Identify the information in the table that shows that lithium bromide is an ionic compound.
parts.solutionMd:
The information in which shows lithium bromide is an ionic compound is:

- Does not conduct electricity when solid but conducts when molten; **[1 mark]**
- Higher boiling point; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *Ionic compounds cannot conduct electricity when they are solid as the ions are not able to move*

  - *Ionic compounds can conduct electricity when they are melted / molten or dissolved as the ions can now move*
- *The boiling point of ionic compounds is high as the strong (electrostatic) forces of attraction require a large amount of energy to overcome*

parts.problemMd:
Lithium bromide dissolves in organic solvents, whereas potassium fluoride is insoluble in organic solvents.

Suggest a reason for the difference in solubility in organic solvents.
parts.solutionMd:
A reason for the difference in solubility in organic solvents:

- The lithium ion is small and highly charged; **[1 mark]**
- Bromide ion is polarised;** [1 mark]**
- Therefore lithium bromide has covalent character;** [1 mark] **
- Potassium fluoride does not have covalent character / potassium ion does not polarise the fluoride ion;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *The lithium ion is small compared to the potassium ion*
- *They also have the same charge*
- *Therefore the lithium ion can pull electron density from the large bromide ion towards itself and this creates covalent character which means it can interact with the organic solvent*
- *Any fully ionic compound can not interact with the organic solvent*

parts.problemMd:
Strontium nitride reacts with water to form strontium hydroxide and ammonia.

Write the balanced symbol equation for this reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
The balanced symbol equation is:

Sr<sub>3</sub>N<sub>2</sub> + 6H<sub>2</sub>O → 3Sr(OH)<sub>2</sub> + 2NH<sub>3</sub>

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct formulae of all reactants and products.
> 
> 1 mark for correctly balanced equation.
> 
> State symbols are not required.

> **[exam-tip]**
> First write the formulae using the charges on the ions, then balance the atoms.
> 
> Step 1: write the formulae.
> 
> - Strontium nitride: Sr<sup>2+</sup> and N<sup>3-</sup>. Use the swap-and-drop method to get Sr<sub>3</sub>N<sub>2</sub>.
> - Strontium hydroxide: Sr<sup>2+</sup> and OH<sup>-</sup>. Swap-and-drop gives Sr(OH)<sub>2</sub>. Note the brackets, because the hydroxide is a polyatomic ion.
> - Ammonia: NH<sub>3</sub> (covalent, not ionic).
> - Water: H<sub>2</sub>O.
> 
> Step 2: balance the atoms.
> 
> - 3 Sr on the left → 3 Sr(OH)<sub>2</sub> on the right.
> - 6 OH on the right → 6 H<sub>2</sub>O on the left (each provides one OH).
> - 2 N on the left → 2 NH<sub>3</sub> on the right.
> - Check H: 12 on the left (6 × H<sub>2</sub>O) and 12 on the right (3 × 2 + 2 × 3 = 12). Balanced.
> 
> A common slip is to forget the brackets around (OH) in strontium hydroxide. Without brackets, Sr(OH)<sub>2</sub> becomes SrOH<sub>2</sub>, which has the wrong stoichiometry.

parts.problemMd:
Strontium nitride has a melting point of 1200 °C.

i) Explain why its melting point is high.

[1]

ii) State and explain the conditions under which strontium nitride will act as an electrical conductor.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The melting point of strontium nitride is high because:
> 
> - The strong electrostatic forces of attraction between the oppositely charged ions require a large amount of energy to overcome; **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) Strontium nitride will act as an electrical conductor when:
> 
> - It is molten / liquid; **[1 mark]**
> - It is dissolved (in water) / aqueous; **[1 mark]**
> 
> Explanation:
> 
> - The ions are free to move / mobile (and carry charge); **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part i), the question asks why the melting point is HIGH. The mark scheme requires three elements:
> 
> - 'Strong' attraction (just 'attraction' is not enough)
> - 'Electrostatic' attraction (the specific force type)
> - 'Between oppositely charged ions' (the particles involved)
> 
> Drop any one element and you risk losing the mark.
> 
> For part ii), strontium nitride is an ionic compound, so:
> 
> - As a SOLID, the ions are fixed in the giant ionic lattice and cannot move. No charge flow, no conduction.
> - When MOLTEN or in AQUEOUS solution, the ions are free to move and can carry charge.
> 
> The third explanation mark is for linking the mobility of the ions to charge flow. CIE wording note: use 'free to move' or 'mobile' (CIE's canonical phrase). Do NOT add 'when a potential difference is applied'. This clause is not in the CIE mark scheme.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Strontium nitride has a melting point of 1200 °C.

The melting point of magnesium nitride is 1500 °C. Explain the difference between the melting point for strontium nitride and magnesium nitride.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The melting points are different because:
> 
> - Mg<sup>2+</sup> is smaller than Sr<sup>2+</sup> / Mg<sup>2+</sup> has (a) higher charge density; **[1 mark]**
> - Stronger electrostatic attraction between Mg<sup>2+</sup> and N<sup>3-</sup> than between Sr<sup>2+</sup> and N<sup>3-</sup>
> **AND**
> More energy is needed to overcome the attraction; **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Magnesium and strontium are both Group 2 metals, so their ions both carry a 2+ charge. The difference in melting points is therefore controlled by ion SIZE (or charge density), not the magnitude of the charge.
> 
> Smaller ions can pack more closely in the lattice, so:
> 
> - The distance between the centres of the cation and anion is shorter.
> - The electrostatic attraction between Mg<sup>2+</sup> and N<sup>3-</sup> is therefore stronger than between Sr<sup>2+</sup> and N<sup>3-</sup>.
> - More energy is needed to break the lattice on melting, so magnesium nitride has the higher melting point (1500 °C vs 1200 °C for strontium nitride).
> 
> CIE wording note: use 'higher charge density'. This is the canonical CIE phrase and appears in 9701/41 May/June 2024 mark schemes. Charge density combines ion size and charge, so it is more precise than 'smaller ion' alone.
> 
> For full marks in M2, include the energy-to-overcome link. Stating only 'stronger attraction' without 'more energy needed to break' may only score the first mark.

parts.problemMd:
Magnesium is a lightweight metal used for the manufacturing of car seats.

Describe the structure and bonding present in solid magnesium.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The structure and bonding present in solid magnesium:
> 
> - A regular (lattice) arrangement of metal ions / positive ions / cations / Mg<sup>2+</sup> ions; **[1 mark]**
> - (Surrounded by) delocalised electrons; **[1 mark]**
> - (Strong) electrostatic attraction between the positive ions and delocalised electrons; **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Three distinct ideas earn the three marks:
> 
> 1. **The arrangement of cations.** A regular lattice of positive metal ions (Mg<sup>2+</sup>).
> 2. **The presence of delocalised electrons.** Outer electrons that are not associated with any single ion. Often described as a 'sea' of electrons in textbooks, but the CIE mark scheme just says 'delocalised electrons'.
> 3. **The bonding force itself.** The electrostatic attraction between the positive ions and the delocalised electrons.
> 
> A common slip is to describe only the structure (the lattice of ions) without mentioning the delocalised electrons, or to describe only the bonding without locating the ions in a lattice. All three points are independently marked.
> 
> You can support your written answer with a labelled diagram of a metallic lattice showing positive ions, delocalised electrons, and the electrostatic attraction. Some examiners look for marking points within supporting diagrams.

parts.problemMd: Explain why magnesium has a considerably higher boiling point than sodium.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Magnesium has a higher boiling point than sodium because:
> 
> - Mg forms Mg<sup>2+</sup> ions
> **AND**
> Na forms Na<sup>+</sup> ions / Mg has more delocalised electrons per atom than Na (2 vs 1); **[1 mark]**
> - (This results in) stronger electrostatic attraction between the positive ions and delocalised electrons in magnesium; **[1 mark]**
> - (Therefore) more energy is required to overcome the (stronger) attraction in magnesium than in sodium; **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The strength of metallic bonding is determined by three factors:
> 
> - Charge on the cation (higher = stronger).
> - Number of delocalised electrons per atom (more = stronger).
> - Size of the cation (smaller = stronger).
> 
> For Mg vs Na:
> 
> - Mg forms Mg<sup>2+</sup> (vs Na<sup>+</sup>), giving twice the cation charge.
> - Mg releases 2 outer electrons per atom into the 'sea' (vs 1 for Na).
> - Mg<sup>2+</sup> has a smaller ionic radius than Na<sup>+</sup>.
> 
> All three factors point the same way: Mg has stronger metallic bonding, so more energy is required to overcome the electrostatic attraction between the cations and delocalised electrons.
> 
> For full marks, link the factor (charge / delocalised electrons / size) to the strength of attraction AND to the energy needed to overcome it. Stating only 'stronger forces' will not score the third mark.

parts.problemMd: Explain why metals are suitable for manufacturing shaped objects such as railings.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Metals are suitable for manufacturing shaped objects because:
> 
> - Metals are malleable (can be hammered / shaped without breaking); **[1 mark]**
> - The layers of positive ions can slide over each other (when force is applied); **[1 mark]**
> - The positive ions are attracted to delocalised electrons in all directions
> **OR**
> The metallic bonding is non-directional; **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Metals are malleable (can be shaped under force) because of two structural features:
> 
> - The layers of positive ions in the metallic lattice can slide past one another when a force is applied.
> - The metallic bond is non-directional. The delocalised electrons are equally attracted to all surrounding positive ions, so the electrostatic attraction is maintained even when the layers move.
> 
> This is what allows metals to be hammered, rolled, or extruded into shapes (railings, sheets, wires) without the metallic bonding breaking.
> 
> By contrast, ionic and covalent solids are brittle because their bonds ARE directional. When layers slide in an ionic solid, like charges meet and the lattice shatters; in a covalent solid, the directional bonds are broken irreversibly.
> 
> A common slip is to say only 'metals are malleable' without explaining the underlying reason. The mark scheme expects you to explain both WHAT the property is (malleability) and WHY (sliding layers + non-directional bonding).

parts.problemMd: Describe metallic bonding.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Metallic bonding is:
> 
> - The (strong) electrostatic attraction between positively charged metal ions / cations
> **AND**
> Delocalised electrons; **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> This is a 1-mark CIE definition. Both elements must be present to score:
> 
> - 'Electrostatic attraction' (not just 'attraction' or 'force')
> - 'Between positive ions / cations / metal ions' AND 'delocalised electrons'
> 
> Saying only 'attraction between ions and electrons' is too vague. Specify that the ions are positive AND that the electrons are delocalised.
> 
> A common slip is to describe metallic bonding as 'sharing of electrons' (covalent) or 'transfer of electrons' (ionic). Metallic bonding is neither. The outer electrons become delocalised across the metallic lattice.

parts.problemMd:
In terms of ions and electrons, complete Table 2.1 to identify **one **similarity and **one **difference between metallic bonding and other types of bonding.

**Table 2.1**

| ** ** | **Similarities with metallic bonding** | **Differences to metallic bonding** |
|---|---|---|
| **Covalent bonding** |   |   |
| **Ionic bonding** |   |   |
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> For each row of Table 2.1:
> 
> Covalent bonding:
> 
> - Similarity: electrons are shared / both involve electrostatic attraction; **[1 mark]**
> - Difference: covalent bonding shares electrons between atoms
> **AND**
> metallic bonding has electrons delocalised between (positive) ions; **[1 mark]**
> 
> Ionic bonding:
> 
> - Similarity: involves the (transfer of) electrons / involves positively charged ions / both involve electrostatic attraction; **[1 mark]**
> - Difference: ionic bonding forms positive AND negative ions
> **AND**
> metallic bonding forms positive ions only; **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> This is a comparison question, so each response needs a similarity AND a difference. The mark scheme expects you to fill all four cells of Table 2.1.
> 
> Each type of bonding involves an electrostatic attraction:
> 
> - Metallic: between positive ions and delocalised electrons.
> - Ionic: between oppositely charged ions.
> - Covalent: between nuclei and the shared bonding electrons.
> 
> Similarities to metallic:
> 
> - Covalent: both involve sharing of electrons (delocalised electrons in metallic CAN be thought of as 'shared' between cations).
> - Ionic: both involve transfer of electrons to form ions (the outer electrons in metallic atoms are 'transferred' to the delocalised pool, leaving cations).
> 
> Differences from metallic:
> 
> - Covalent: localised between two specific atoms (vs delocalised across the whole lattice).
> - Ionic: forms BOTH positive and negative ions (vs only positive ions in metallic).
> 
> A common slip is to give a similarity that applies to all three bonding types ('all involve electrostatic attraction'). This is true but very generic. Be specific about HOW each type differs from metallic.

parts.problemMd: State **two** factors that affect the strength of metallic bonding in metals.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Two factors that affect the strength of metallic bonding:
> 
> Any **two** from (1 mark for each point):
> 
> - The number of delocalised / outer / valence electrons per atom
> **OR**
> The charge of the metal ion
> - The size of the metal ion / ionic radius / charge density
> - The arrangement of atoms in the metallic lattice / packing efficiency
> 
> **[2 marks]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The strength of metallic bonding (which determines properties like melting point, boiling point, and hardness) depends on three main factors:
> 
> 1. **Number of delocalised electrons.** More outer electrons released per atom means a higher concentration of delocalised electrons, giving stronger attraction. Mg<sup>2+</sup> (2 electrons released) gives stronger bonding than Na<sup>+</sup> (1 electron released).
> 2. **Cation charge.** Closely related to the first factor. A higher charge on the cation gives stronger electrostatic attraction to the delocalised electrons.
> 3. **Cation size / charge density.** Smaller cations pack more closely and have higher charge density, giving stronger attraction. Mg<sup>2+</sup> is smaller than Na<sup>+</sup>, contributing to Mg's higher melting point.
> 
> Any two of these factors will score the marks. CIE accepts 'higher charge density' as a single descriptor that combines size and charge.

parts.problemMd: Draw a diagram showing the structure of magnesium.
parts.solutionMd:
The diagram showing the structure of magnesium:

![Diagram of the giant metallic lattice of magnesium showing regularly arranged 2+ positive ions with delocalised electrons (e⁻) between them](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/3-chemical-bonding/3-3-metallic-bonding/assets/002-diagram-of-the-giant-metallic-lattice-of-magnesi.png)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a regular (lattice) arrangement of metal ions / positive ions / cations AND each ion shown with a 2+ charge.
> 
> 1 mark for delocalised electrons drawn between the ions AND labelled (as 'delocalised electrons' or shown as a 'sea of delocalised electrons').

> **[exam-tip]**
> A magnesium metallic lattice diagram needs three features for full marks:
> 
> - A regular array of cations (rows and columns).
> - A 2+ charge clearly shown on each ion (Mg loses 2 outer electrons, so ions are Mg<sup>2+</sup>, not Mg<sup>+</sup>).
> - Delocalised electrons shown between the ions AND labelled. CIE examiner reports flag unlabelled electrons as a frequent reason for losing marks.
> 
> Common errors specific to magnesium:
> 
> - Showing the charge as just '+' (this would be sodium). Mg<sup>2+</sup> requires '2+'.
> - Drawing a single isolated ion. The lattice arrangement must show multiple ions in a regular pattern.
> - Drawing electrons inside the ion circles instead of between them. Delocalised electrons sit in the gaps between the cations.

parts.problemMd:
Identify the highest energy orbital which contains electrons in a magnesium atom.

Sketch the shape of this orbital.
parts.solutionMd:
The highest energy orbital in Mg is the 3s orbital.

![Diagram showing a circle to represent the shape of an s-orbital](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/3-chemical-bonding/3-3-metallic-bonding/assets/003-diagram-showing-a-circle-to-represent-the-shape-.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for identification as 3s AND a correct spherical sketch (representing an s-orbital).

> **[exam-tip]**
> Magnesium's electron configuration is 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup> 3s<sup>2</sup>, so the highest energy occupied orbital is 3s.
> 
> The s-orbital is spherical (a single sphere centred on the nucleus). Don't draw a 'p-orbital' shape (figure-of-eight / dumbbell). That's wrong for an s-orbital.
> 
> Quick electron-configuration check for Mg:
> 
> - Period 3, Group 2, so 2 electrons in the third shell.
> - Both electrons go into the 3s subshell (3s<sup>2</sup>).
> - 3s is higher in energy than 2p, which fills first.
> 
> Both halves of the answer are required for the single mark: state '3s' AND draw a sphere.

parts.problemMd:
Mg reacts with Si to form the ionic compound magnesium silicide, Mg<sub>2</sub>Si

Draw the dot-cross structure of Mg<sub>2</sub>Si.
parts.solutionMd:
The dot-and-cross diagram for Mg<sub>2</sub>Si:

![Dot-and-cross diagram showing two Mg²⁺ ions each with a full outer shell and one Si⁴⁻ ion with eight electrons, illustrating ionic bonding and charge.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/3-chemical-bonding/3-3-metallic-bonding/assets/004-dot-and-cross-diagram-showing-two-mg-ions-each-w.png)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for two [Mg]<sup>2+</sup> ions, each with empty outer shells (or 8 electrons shown if the second shell is drawn as the outermost), with a 2+ charge as superscript outside the bracket.
> 
> 1 mark for one [Si]<sup>4-</sup> ion with 8 electrons in the outer shell (4 of one symbol AND 4 of the other, showing electron transfer from the two Mg atoms) and a 4- charge as superscript outside the bracket.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Mg<sub>2</sub>Si is an ionic compound formed by complete electron transfer:
> 
> - Each Mg atom loses 2 electrons (the 3s<sup>2</sup> pair), forming Mg<sup>2+</sup> (electron configuration 2,8).
> - One Si atom gains 4 electrons (the 4 electrons released by the 2 Mg atoms), forming Si<sup>4-</sup> (electron configuration 2,8,8).
> 
> For full marks:
> 
> - Use square brackets around each ion.
> - Show charges as superscripts outside the brackets, e.g. [Mg]<sup>2+</sup> and [Si]<sup>4-</sup> (use '2+' and '4-', not '+2' or '-4').
> - For Si<sup>4-</sup>, show 8 electrons in the outer shell with 4 dots (Si's own electrons) and 4 crosses (the electrons from the two Mg atoms) to demonstrate electron transfer.
> - For Mg<sup>2+</sup>, the outer shell is empty because the 3s electrons have transferred away. The second shell is now the outermost shell shown, with 8 electrons.
> 
> A common slip is to draw all 8 electrons on Si<sup>4-</sup> as the same symbol. This fails to show the electron transfer and loses the mark.

parts.problemMd:
The reaction between an ammonia molecule and a hydrogen ion forms an ammonium ion.

The structure of an ammonium ion is shown.

![Structural formula of the ammonium ion: central nitrogen bonded to four hydrogens in a tetrahedral arrangement, enclosed in brackets with a positive charge.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/3-chemical-bonding/3-4-covalent-bonding-and-coordinate-dative-covalent-bonding/assets/014-structural-formula-of-the-ammonium-ion-central-n.png)

i) State the type of bond represented in the diagram by N—H.

[1]

ii) State the type of bond represented in the diagram by N→H.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The type of bond represented in the diagram by N—H:
> 
> - Covalent **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The type of bond represented in the diagram by N→H:
> 
> - Dative (covalent) / coordinate **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The two bond types differ in HOW the shared pair of electrons is supplied:
> 
> - A single covalent bond (N—H): one electron donated from each atom (one from N, one from H).
> - A dative (covalent) / coordinate bond (N→H): both electrons in the pair come from the same atom. In this case, both come from the nitrogen atom.
> 
> The arrow notation N→H shows the direction in which the electrons have been donated. Once formed, the bond itself behaves identically to a normal covalent bond.
> 
> For the ammonium ion (NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>):
> 
> - 3 of the 4 N—H bonds are normal covalent bonds (carried over from NH<sub>3</sub>).
> - The 4th bond is a dative covalent bond formed when NH<sub>3</sub> donates its lone pair to H<sup>+</sup>.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The reaction between an ammonia molecule and a hydrogen ion forms an ammonium ion.

The structure of an ammonium ion is shown.

i) State the type of bond represented in the diagram by N—H.

ii) State the type of bond represented in the diagram by N→H.

The type of bond represented in the diagram by N→H:
- Dative (covalent) / coordinate

Explain how the N→H bond is formed.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The coordinate (dative covalent) N→H bond forms because:
> 
> - Both electrons in the bonding pair come from nitrogen
> **OR**
> A lone pair of electrons from N is donated to H<sup>+</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> In the ammonium ion (NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>), the H<sup>+</sup> that joined NH<sub>3</sub> to form the ion has no electrons of its own. It is a bare proton. The nitrogen atom in NH<sub>3</sub> has a lone pair and donates BOTH electrons of that lone pair to the H<sup>+</sup> to form the new N—H bond.
> 
> Once formed, the coordinate bond is indistinguishable from the other three N—H bonds in terms of length and strength.
> 
> A common slip is to describe dative covalent bond formation as 'electron transfer from N to H'. That would be ionic bonding. In a dative covalent bond, both electrons in the bonding pair come from one atom. The electrons are shared between both atoms once the bond forms.

parts.problemMd: Explain why the bond angles in the NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> ion are all 109.5°.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The bond angles in the NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> ion are all 109.5° because:
> 
> - There are four bonding pairs of electrons (around the central N atom) **[1 mark]**
> - They repel each other / repel as far apart as possible (giving a tetrahedral shape) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> VSEPR (Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion) theory says that electron pairs around a central atom arrange themselves to minimise repulsion (i.e. as far apart as possible).
> 
> For NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>:
> 
> - 4 bonding pairs (the four N—H bonds, including the dative one) and 0 lone pairs around the central N.
> - 4 bonding pairs arrange themselves tetrahedrally, with bond angles of 109.5°.
> - All four pairs are bonding pairs, so the repulsion is symmetrical, giving a regular tetrahedral shape.
> 
> Compare with the parent molecule NH<sub>3</sub>:
> 
> - 3 bonding pairs + 1 lone pair around N.
> - The lone pair repels more strongly than the bonding pairs, compressing the H—N—H bond angle to 107°.
> 
> When NH<sub>3</sub> donates its lone pair to form NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>, that lone pair becomes a bonding pair, removing the unequal repulsion and opening the bond angle from 107° to 109.5°.
> 
> The order of repulsion strengths is:
> 
> - lone pair / lone pair > lone pair / bonding pair > bonding pair / bonding pair

parts.problemMd:

Complete the diagram to show, in terms of orbital overlap, how the σ bond and the π bond are formed in a C=C double bond. Label each bond.

![Two bold black letter C shapes spaced widely apart on a plain white background.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/3-chemical-bonding/3-4-covalent-bonding-and-coordinate-dative-covalent-bonding/assets/018-two-bold-black-letter-c-shapes-spaced-widely-apa.png)
parts.solutionMd:
The diagram showing the orbital overlap for each bond:

![Diagram of a carbon–carbon double bond, showing central sigma bond between two C atoms and shaded pi bond regions above and below the bond axis](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/3-chemical-bonding/3-4-covalent-bonding-and-coordinate-dative-covalent-bonding/assets/019-diagram-of-a-carbon-carbon-double-bond-showing-c.png)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correctly drawn **AND** labelled σ bond (showing direct/end-on overlap of orbitals between the two carbon atoms).
> 
> 1 mark for correctly drawn **AND** labelled π bond (showing sideways overlap of p orbitals above **AND** below the carbon–carbon bond axis).
> 
> If both bonds are drawn correctly but the labels are swapped, award 1 mark only.

> **[exam-tip]**
> A C=C double bond consists of:
> 
> - 1 σ bond, formed from end-on (direct) overlap of sp<sup>2</sup> hybrid orbitals between the two carbon atoms. The electron density is concentrated along the line connecting the two nuclei.
> - 1 π bond, formed from sideways overlap of the unhybridised p orbitals on each carbon. The electron density forms two lobes, one above and one below the plane of the σ bond.
> 
> Important diagram conventions:
> 
> - The two lobes above and below the C=C bond represent ONE π bond, not two.
> - Only ONE of the lobes needs to be labelled as π for the mark.

parts.problemMd:
Use the data in Table 5.1 to explain why ethene contains stronger covalent bonds between carbon atoms than ethane.

**Table 5.1**

| **Bond** | **Bond Length** |
|---|---|
| C-C | 150 pm |
| C=C | 134 pm |
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The covalent bond between carbon atoms in ethene is stronger than in ethane because:
> 
> - The C=C bond is shorter (134 pm) than the C-C bond (150 pm) **[1 mark]**
> - (Because) there is greater electron density between the carbon atoms (in ethene) **[1 mark]**
> - There is more attraction between the (bonding) electrons and the atomic nuclei **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The question requires you to use the data in Table 5.1, so talk about the bond lengths in your answer.
> 
> Why C=C is stronger than C-C:
> 
> - A double bond contains 1 σ + 1 π bond (vs 1 σ for a single bond), so there is twice as much electron density between the nuclei in C=C.
> - Greater electron density between the nuclei pulls the atoms closer together, so C=C is shorter (134 pm) than C-C (150 pm).
> - The closer the nuclei, the stronger the electrostatic attraction between the bonding electrons and both nuclei, so the bond is stronger and harder to break.
> 
> A common slip is to state only 'C=C is shorter' or 'there is more electron density' without linking these to the increased attraction. The mark scheme awards three independent marks for:
> 
> 1. The bond-length comparison
> 2. The electron-density observation
> 3. The attraction-strength conclusion.

parts.problemMd:
Describe and explain the relative thermal stabilities of HCl, HBr and HI, using the data in Table 5.2.

**Table 5.2**

|   | **Bond energy / kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> | **Bond length / pm** |
|---|---|---|
| HCl | 431 | 127 |
| HBr | 366 | 141 |
| HI | 299 | 161 |
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The relative thermal stabilities of HCl, HBr and HI:
> 
> - HCl is the most thermally stable and HI is the least thermally stable
> **OR**
> The order of thermal stability, from most to least stable, is HCl > HBr > HI **[1 mark]**
> - (Because) HI has the largest bond length and the lowest bond energy **[1 mark]**
> - Less energy is needed to break the H–I bond / HI decomposes more readily because there is less attraction between the nucleus and the bonding electrons (due to the larger atomic radius / longer bond going down the group) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> You must use the data from Table 5.2 to score full marks. Identify the trend, explain the cause, and link to thermal stability.
> 
> Trend in Table 5.2 (going down the group H-Cl → H-Br → H-I):
> 
> - Bond energy decreases (431 → 366 → 299 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>).
> - Bond length increases (127 → 141 → 161 pm).
> 
> Why this happens:
> 
> - The halogen atom gets larger going down Group 17, so the bonding pair of electrons is further from the halogen nucleus.
> - The attraction between the H-X bonding electrons and the halogen nucleus weakens.
> - Less energy is needed to break the bond, so the hydrogen halide decomposes more readily and is less thermally stable.
> 
> A common pitfall is to confuse thermal stability with the reactivity of elemental halogens. Going down Group 17, elemental halogens become less reactive as oxidising agents, but the hydrogen halides become less thermally stable. HI has the weakest H-I bond and decomposes most readily. Always use the data in the table.

parts.problemMd:
The boiling points of the hydrogen halides are shown in Table 5.3.

**Table 5.3**

| **Hydrogen halide** | **Boiling point / K** |
|---|---|
| HF | 293 |
| HCl | 188 |
| HBr | 207 |
| HI | 238 |

i) Explain why hydrogen halides have relatively low boiling points despite having strong covalent bonds.

[2]

ii) Explain why HF has a higher boiling point than HCl.

[4]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) Hydrogen halides have relatively low boiling points despite having strong covalent bonds because:
> 
> - Only the weak (van der Waals' / id–id / pd–pd) intermolecular forces between molecules are broken at the boiling point, NOT the (strong) covalent bonds within molecules **[1 mark]**
> - The intermolecular forces are weaker than the covalent bonds **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) HF has a higher boiling point than HCl because:
> 
> - Both have instantaneous dipole–induced dipole (id–id) forces **[1 mark]**
> - HCl has permanent dipole–permanent dipole (pd–pd) forces (in addition to id–id forces) **[1 mark]**
> - HF has hydrogen bonding (in addition to id–id forces) **[1 mark]**
> - Hydrogen bonds are stronger than pd–pd forces, so more energy is required to break them **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Two ideas underpin both sub-parts:
> 
> - Boiling point depends on the strength of the INTERMOLECULAR forces, NOT the covalent bonds within the molecules.
> - Stronger intermolecular forces require more energy to overcome, giving a higher boiling point.
> 
> For part i), the trick is recognising that 'strong covalent bonds' is irrelevant. The covalent bonds stay intact on boiling. Only the (relatively weak) intermolecular forces break.
> 
> For part ii), according to the specification van der Waals' forces is a generic term covering BOTH:
> 
> - Instantaneous dipole–induced dipole (id–id) forces (formerly called London dispersion forces): present in ALL molecules.
> - Permanent dipole–permanent dipole (pd–pd) forces: present in molecules with a permanent dipole (polar covalent bonds with no symmetric cancellation).
> 
> The hierarchy of intermolecular forces, from weakest to strongest:
> 
> - id–id < pd–pd < hydrogen bonding
> 
> For HF vs HCl:
> 
> - HCl has pd–pd forces (Cl is more electronegative than H, but not enough to form hydrogen bonds).
> - HF has hydrogen bonding (F is one of the three elements F, O, N that allow hydrogen bonding because F is highly electronegative AND has a lone pair).
> - Hydrogen bonding is stronger than pd–pd, so HF has a higher boiling point despite both molecules being similar in size.
> 
> A common slip is to conflate van der Waals' forces with hydrogen bonding. Hydrogen bonding is a SEPARATE, STRONGER type of intermolecular force, present only when H is bonded to F, O, or N.

parts.problemMd:
The structure of a molecule is shown in Fig. 2.1.

![Skeletal formula of an organic molecule containing multiple carbon-carbon single bonds, double bonds, and one triple bond.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/3-chemical-bonding/3-4-covalent-bonding-and-coordinate-dative-covalent-bonding/assets/015-skeletal-formula-of-an-organic-molecule-containi.png)

**Fig. 2.1**

State the number of σ bonds and π bonds in one molecule of this compound.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The number of sigma and pi bonds in the molecule:
> 
> - 21 sigma bonds **[1 mark]**
> - 5 pi bonds **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Bond-counting rules:
> 
> - Single bond = 1 σ bond
> - Double bond = 1 σ + 1 π bond
> - Triple bond = 1 σ + 2 π bonds
> 
> For Fig. 2.1, count each type of bond first, then convert to σ and π totals.

parts.problemMd:
Fig. 2.2 shows the structure of ethanol.

![Displayed formula of ethanol with one carbon atom marked for hybridisation identification.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/3-chemical-bonding/3-4-covalent-bonding-and-coordinate-dative-covalent-bonding/assets/016-displayed-formula-of-ethanol-with-one-carbon-ato.png)

**Fig. 2.2**

State the hybridisation of the carbon atom marked in Fig. 2.2.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The hybridisation of the carbon atom marked in Fig. 2.2:
> 
> - sp<sup>3</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Quick hybridisation check by counting bonds at the atom:
> 
> - 4 single bonds (or equivalent: e.g. 3 single bonds + 1 lone pair) → sp<sup>3</sup>
> - 1 double bond + 2 single bonds → sp<sup>2</sup>
> - 1 triple bond + 1 single bond OR 2 double bonds → sp
>

parts.problemMd: Sketch a labelled diagram to show, in terms of orbital overlap, how the bonds are formed in methanol, CH<sub>3</sub>OH. Your diagram should include any lone pairs of electrons.
parts.solutionMd:
The diagram showing the orbital overlap in methanol:

![Diagram showing orbital overlap in methanol: 
- sp3 orbitals on C overlapping with 1s on H atoms and sp3 on O
- sp3 orbital on O overlapping with 1s on H
- two lone pairs shown on O in sp3 orbitals](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/3-chemical-bonding/3-4-covalent-bonding-and-coordinate-dative-covalent-bonding/assets/017-diagram-showing-orbital-overlap-in-methanol-sp3-.png)

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct C-H overlap (sp<sup>3</sup> on C with 1s on H) **AND** correct C-O bond (sp<sup>3</sup> on C with sp<sup>3</sup> on O).
> 
> 1 mark for correct O-H bond (sp<sup>3</sup> on O with 1s on H).
> 
> 1 mark for two lone pairs on the oxygen (in sp<sup>3</sup> orbitals).
> 
> A generic 'correct overlap' without labelled orbital types is not accepted.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Methanol has the formula CH<sub>3</sub>OH, with all single bonds. All bonds are σ bonds, formed from end-on overlap of orbitals.
> 
> For the diagram, label each overlap with the specific orbital types:
> 
> - Each C-H bond: end-on overlap between an sp<sup>3</sup> hybrid orbital on C and the 1s orbital on H.
> - The C-O bond: end-on overlap of an sp<sup>3</sup> hybrid orbital on C with an sp<sup>3</sup> hybrid orbital on O.
> - The O-H bond: end-on overlap of an sp<sup>3</sup> hybrid orbital on O with the 1s orbital on H.
> - The oxygen atom has two lone pairs in its remaining sp<sup>3</sup> orbitals. These must be drawn explicitly.
> 
> Common errors:
> 
> - Drawing p orbitals (figure-of-eight shape) instead of sp<sup>3</sup> hybrids (asymmetric lobes) on C and O.
> - Forgetting to label orbital types (the mark scheme requires sp<sup>3</sup> and 1s labels explicitly).

parts.problemMd: Describe how the carbon-carbon triple bond forms in propyne, CH<sub>3</sub>C≡CH. Refer to orbital overlap and hybridisation in your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The carbon-carbon triple bond in propyne forms as follows:
> 
> - The two carbon atoms (in the triple bond) are sp hybridised **[1 mark]**
> - The σ bond is formed from end-on / head-on overlap of sp hybrid orbitals (one from each carbon) **[1 mark]**
> - Two π bonds are formed from sideways overlap of unhybridised p orbitals (one pair on each carbon) **[1 mark]**
> 
> The third mark requires explicit reference to two π bonds.

> **[exam-tip]**
> A triple bond consists of 1 σ bond + 2 π bonds.
> 
> Hybridisation determines the geometry around each carbon and the bonds formed:
> 
> - **sp** hybridisation: 2 sp hybrid orbitals + 2 unhybridised p orbitals. Forms 1 σ + 2 π bonds (triple bond, linear geometry).
> - **sp**<sup>**2**</sup> hybridisation: 3 sp<sup>2</sup> hybrid orbitals + 1 unhybridised p orbital. Forms 1 σ + 1 π bond (double bond, trigonal planar).
> - **sp**<sup>**3**</sup> hybridisation: 4 sp<sup>3</sup> hybrid orbitals. Forms 4 σ bonds only (single bonds, tetrahedral).
> 
> For propyne (CH<sub>3</sub>C≡CH):
> 
> - The two triple-bonded carbons are sp hybridised.
> - The σ bond between them comes from end-on (head-on) overlap of one sp orbital from each carbon.
> - The two π bonds come from sideways overlap of two pairs of unhybridised p orbitals (one pair in the y-direction, one in the z-direction, both perpendicular to the bond axis).
> 
> A common slip is to mention only ONE π bond. The mark scheme explicitly requires TWO π bonds. This is what distinguishes a triple bond from a double bond.

parts.problemMd:
Fig. 3.1 shows the structure of an organic molecule.

![Skeletal formula of an organic molecule containing multiple carbon-carbon double bonds and carbon-carbon single bonds.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/3-chemical-bonding/3-4-covalent-bonding-and-coordinate-dative-covalent-bonding/assets/013-skeletal-formula-of-an-organic-molecule-containi.png)

> 
> - 6 **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Quick rule of thumb for hybridisation in organic molecules:
> 
> - C in a triple bond → sp
> - C in a double bond → sp<sup>2</sup>
> - C in single bonds only → sp<sup>3</sup>

> Only the carbon atoms involved in C=C double bonds are sp<sup>2</sup>. Count each carbon at the end of a double bond, not the bonds themselves.

parts.problemMd:
Phosphorus reacts with chlorine to form PCl<sub>5</sub>.

| bond angles in PCl<sub>5</sub> |   |

parts.solutionMd:
i) The shape and bond angles in a molecule of PCl<sub>5</sub> are:

| shape of PCl<sub>5</sub> | trigonal bipyramidal / trigonal bipyramid |

>

ii) The dot-and-cross diagram of a molecule of PCl<sub>5</sub> (showing outer electrons only) is:

![Dot-and-cross diagram of PCl5 showing 5 P–Cl bonding pairs (one dot and one cross each) and 3 lone pairs on each Cl atom; P has no lone pairs and an expanded octet of 10 electrons.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/3-chemical-bonding/3-4-covalent-bonding-and-coordinate-dative-covalent-bonding/assets/008-dot-and-cross-diagram-of-pcl5-showing-5-p-cl-bon.png)

> **[exam-tip]**
> PCl<sub>5</sub> is an example of a molecule where the central atom expands its octet. It has 10 electrons in its outer shell instead of 8.
> 
> Phosphorus has 5 outer electrons (3s<sup>2</sup> 3p<sup>3</sup>). Each pairs with one electron from a chlorine atom to form 5 covalent bonds, so P ends up with 10 outer-shell electrons.
> 
> Shape and bond angles:
> 
> - 5 bonding pairs around P, no lone pairs.
> - Trigonal bipyramidal arrangement: 3 atoms in a triangular plane (120° between them) + 2 atoms above and below (90° to the plane).
> - The two distinct bond angles are 120° (between the three equatorial Cl atoms) and 90° (between equatorial and axial Cl atoms).
> 
> For the dot-and-cross diagram:
> 
> - Show only the outer-shell electrons (the question specifies this).
> - Each P-Cl bond contains 1 electron from P (dot) and 1 from Cl (cross).
> - Each Cl atom has 3 lone pairs in addition to the bonding pair. Show all three.
> - The P expands its octet, so 10 electrons around P is correct (not 8).

parts.problemMd:
In the solid state, phosphorus(V) chloride exists as an ionic lattice containing [PCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>+</sup> and [PCl<sub>6</sub>]<sup>–</sup> ions.

Draw three-dimensional diagrams to show the shapes of the [PCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>+</sup> and [PCl<sub>6</sub>]<sup>–</sup> ions.

parts.solutionMd:
The shapes of [PCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>+</sup> and [PCl<sub>6</sub>]<sup>–</sup> are:

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct tetrahedral shape of [PCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>+</sup>.

> Three-dimensional shapes should be shown using wedges and dotted lines.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Apply VSEPR theory to each ion by counting the bonding pairs and lone pairs around the central P atom:
> 
> - [PCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>+</sup>: 4 bonding pairs (4 P-Cl bonds), 0 lone pairs. Tetrahedral shape, bond angle 109.5°.

> Drawing tips:
> 
> - Use wedges (solid triangles) for bonds coming out of the page, dotted lines for bonds going behind, and plain lines for bonds in the plane of the page.
