parts.problemMd: A student suggests that the PCl<sub>5</sub> molecule has sp<sup>3</sup> hybridisation. Explain why the student is incorrect.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The student is incorrect because:
> 
> - sp<sup>3</sup> hybridisation produces only 4 (hybrid) orbitals (from one s + three p orbitals) **[1 mark]**
> - But PCl<sub>5</sub> has 5 covalent / sigma / σ bonds, so requires 5 hybrid orbitals (sp<sup>3</sup>d hybridisation) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The number of hybrid orbitals needed equals the number of σ bonds + lone pairs around the central atom.
> 
> For PCl<sub>5</sub>:
> 
> - 5 σ bonds (P-Cl) and 0 lone pairs = 5 electron domains.
> - 5 hybrid orbitals are required.
> - sp<sup>3</sup> hybridisation only generates 4 hybrid orbitals (1 s + 3 p), so it cannot account for the 5 bonds.
> 
> PCl<sub>5</sub> actually has sp<sup>3</sup>d hybridisation (1 s + 3 p + 1 d = 5 hybrid orbitals), but you are not expected to know this in detail. The specification doesn't require you to name the hybridisation in PCl<sub>5</sub>. You only need to explain why sp<sup>3</sup> isn't enough.
> 
> A common slip is to focus on the shape (trigonal bipyramidal) rather than the orbital count. The mark scheme awards marks for the orbital-counting argument, not the geometry.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

In the solid state, phosphorus(V) chloride exists as an ionic lattice containing [PCl~4~]^+^ and [PCl~6~]^–^ ions.

Antimony(V) chloride is another Group 15 chloride. Under standard conditions, it is a liquid made from SbCl<sub>5</sub> molecules.

Use your answer to (b) to explain why phosphorus(V) chloride, in its solid form, has a higher melting point than antimony(V) chloride.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Phosphorus(V) chloride in its solid form has a higher melting point than antimony(V) chloride because:
> 
> - Solid PCl<sub>5</sub> has strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions ([PCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>+</sup> and [PCl<sub>6</sub>]<sup>-</sup>) **[1 mark]**
> - SbCl<sub>5</sub> has only weak van der Waals' / intermolecular forces between SbCl<sub>5</sub> molecules **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> This question requires you to apply the structure information from earlier parts:
> 
> - Solid PCl<sub>5</sub> exists as ionic [PCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>+</sup>[PCl<sub>6</sub>]<sup>-</sup> (from part b's equilibrium). It has a giant ionic lattice with strong electrostatic forces of attraction between cations and anions.
> - SbCl<sub>5</sub> exists as discrete SbCl<sub>5</sub> molecules. It has a simple molecular structure with weak van der Waals' / intermolecular forces (id–id and pd–pd) between molecules.
> 
> Strong ionic bonds require much more energy to break than weak intermolecular forces, so PCl<sub>5</sub> has the higher melting point.
> 
> Mark scheme strictness:
> 
> - The first mark requires the full long form 'electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions'. Saying 'PCl<sub>5</sub> has stronger forces' or just 'ionic' will not score.
> - The second mark requires reference to weak van der Waals' / intermolecular forces in SbCl<sub>5</sub>. Acceptable terms: van der Waals' forces, intermolecular forces, id–id, pd–pd.
> - Do NOT refer to 'breaking covalent bonds' in either case. Boiling and melting break intermolecular forces (or the ionic lattice), NOT covalent bonds.

parts.problemMd:
Under the right conditions, molecules of SbCl<sub>5</sub> join together to form Sb<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>10</sub>.

Complete Fig. 4.1 to show the bonding in Sb<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>10</sub>. Include the coordinate (dative covalent) bonds.

![Two diagrams of antimony pentachloride showing trigonal bipyramidal geometry with five Cl atoms around central Sb, illustrating different 3D bond orientations](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/3-chemical-bonding/3-4-covalent-bonding-and-coordinate-dative-covalent-bonding/assets/011-two-diagrams-of-antimony-pentachloride-showing-t.png)

**Fig. 4.1**
parts.solutionMd:
The bonding in Sb<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>10</sub> is:

![Two antimony pentachloride molecules with trigonal bipyramidal geometry, with arrows indicating coordinate bonds interaction between the SbCl₅ units](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/3-chemical-bonding/3-4-covalent-bonding-and-coordinate-dative-covalent-bonding/assets/012-two-antimony-pentachloride-molecules-with-trigon.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for two coordinate bonds shown as arrows from (bridging) Cl to Sb (the arrow direction must be Cl → Sb, indicating Cl as the donor and Sb as the acceptor).

> **[exam-tip]**
> Sb is in Group 15 (like P), so SbCl<sub>5</sub> can also expand its octet. Just as P can accept a lone pair from a Cl<sup>-</sup> to form [PCl<sub>6</sub>]<sup>-</sup>, Sb can accept a lone pair from a Cl atom on a neighbouring SbCl<sub>5</sub> molecule to form Sb<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>10</sub>.
> 
> For each coordinate (dative covalent) bond:
> 
> - The lone pair of electrons comes from the Cl atom on one molecule.
> - The lone pair is donated to the Sb atom on the neighbouring molecule.
> - The arrow must point FROM the donor (Cl) TO the acceptor (Sb). Direction is checked.
> 
> In Sb<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>10</sub>, two such bridging coordinate bonds form between the two SbCl<sub>5</sub> units, giving a dimeric structure with each Sb now bonded to 6 Cl atoms (octahedral around Sb).
> 
> Examiners comment that many students are not familiar with the arrow convention for coordinate bonds. Make sure you draw the arrowheads clearly and pointing from Cl (donor) to Sb (acceptor).

parts.problemMd:
The other Group 15 elements also form pentachlorides with the exception of nitrogen.

Suggest a reason why nitrogen does not form NCl<sub>5</sub>.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Nitrogen does not form NCl<sub>5</sub> because:
> 
> Any **one** from:
> 
> - Nitrogen has no (accessible) d orbitals (in the valence / 2nd shell)
> - Nitrogen cannot expand its octet (only 8 electrons in valence shell)
> - Nitrogen is too small (to bond to 5 chlorine atoms)
> - The repulsion between electron pairs would be too great
> 
> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Period 2 elements (Li to Ne) cannot expand their octets. They are limited to a maximum of 8 electrons in their outer shell. Two reasons:
> 
> - They have no available d orbitals in the second shell. (2d orbitals don't exist; 3d is too high in energy.)
> - Their atoms are too small to physically accommodate more than 4 substituent atoms around the central atom.
> 
> Period 3 elements (Na to Ar) and below CAN expand their octets because they have available 3d orbitals (or 4d, 5d, etc.) and are physically larger.
> 
> This is why P, As, Sb form pentachlorides (PCl<sub>5</sub>, AsCl<sub>5</sub>, SbCl<sub>5</sub>) but N does not form NCl<sub>5</sub>.
> 
> The most commonly credited answers are 'no d orbitals' and 'cannot expand octet'. 'Too small' is also accepted; 'repulsion too great' is rarely the prime answer in mark schemes.
> 
> Examiner reports note that this type of question is often poorly answered. Students forget that the octet rule has limits and that Period 2 elements cannot exceed it.

parts.problemMd:
Sulfur can form bonds with six fluorine atoms to form sulfur hexafluoride, SF<sub>6</sub>.

i) State the number of electrons in the outer shell of the sulfur atom in SF<sub>6</sub>.

[1]

ii) State the reason why the sulfur atom is able to accommodate this number of electrons.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The number of electrons in the outer shell of the sulfur atom in SF<sub>6</sub>:
> 
> - 12 **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The reason the sulfur atom can accommodate this number of electrons:
> 
> - Sulfur has available empty 3d orbitals / can use its 3d orbitals to expand its octet **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Period 2 elements such as carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen cannot accommodate more than 8 electrons in their outer shell because the second shell contains only s and p subshells.
> 
> Sulfur is in Period 3. The third shell contains 3s, 3p, and 3d subshells. The 3d orbitals are empty in ground-state sulfur and are energetically accessible for bonding, allowing sulfur to form 6 bonds in SF<sub>6</sub> and accommodate 12 electrons in its outer shell.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Sulfur can form bonds with six fluorine atoms to form sulfur hexafluoride, SF~6~.

State the shape of a molecule of SF<sub>6</sub>.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The shape of a molecule of SF<sub>6</sub>:
> 
> - Octahedral **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> In SF<sub>6</sub>, sulfur forms 6 bonds with 6 fluorine atoms and has no lone pairs. Six bonding domains with no lone pairs gives an octahedral arrangement.

parts.problemMd: State the F-S-F bond angles in SF<sub>6</sub>.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The F-S-F bond angles in SF<sub>6</sub>:
> 
> - 90° **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> In an octahedral molecule, the six bonding domains point towards the vertices of a regular octahedron. All adjacent bond angles are 90°. Because there are no lone pairs to distort the geometry, all F-S-F angles in SF<sub>6</sub> are exactly 90°.
> 
> Do not confuse with trigonal bipyramidal molecules such as PF<sub>5</sub>, which have two different bond angles: 90° (axial-equatorial) and 120° (equatorial-equatorial).
> 
> The molecules listed in the CIE 9701 syllabus with their shapes and bond angles are:
> 
> - BF<sub>3</sub>: trigonal planar, 120°
> - CO<sub>2</sub>: linear, 180°
> - CH<sub>4</sub>: tetrahedral, 109.5°
> - NH<sub>3</sub>: pyramidal, 107°
> - H<sub>2</sub>O: non-linear, 104.5°
> - SF<sub>6</sub>: octahedral, 90°
> - PF<sub>5</sub>: trigonal bipyramidal, 90° and 120°

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Sulfur can form bonds with six fluorine atoms to form sulfur hexafluoride, SF~6~.

The shape of a molecule of SF~6~: Octahedral

Sulfur has an electronegativity value of 2.58 and fluorine has an electronegativity value of 3.98.

i) Deduce whether the S-F bond is polar.

[1]

ii) Deduce whether the SF<sub>6</sub> molecule is polar. Explain your answer.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The polarity of the S-F bond:
> 
> - The S-F bond is polar **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The polarity of SF<sub>6</sub>:
> 
> - SF<sub>6</sub> is non-polar / has no net dipole moment **[1 mark]**
> - The six polar S-F bonds are arranged symmetrically / the bond dipoles cancel **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A bond is polar when there is a significant electronegativity difference between the bonded atoms, generally 0.5 or more on the Pauling scale. The electronegativity difference for S-F is 3.98 - 2.58 = 1.40, so each S-F bond is strongly polar, with fluorine as δ- and sulfur as δ+.
> 
> A molecule can contain polar bonds but still be non-polar overall if the bond dipoles cancel due to symmetry. In SF<sub>6</sub>, the octahedral geometry means the six S-F bond dipoles point outward along three perpendicular axes in opposing pairs. The dipoles cancel exactly, giving no net dipole.
> 
> Contrast with H<sub>2</sub>O: two polar O-H bonds at 104.5° do not cancel, so H<sub>2</sub>O is polar.

parts.problemMd:
The shapes of the molecules BH<sub>3</sub> and NH<sub>3</sub> are shown in Fig. 1.1.

![Structural diagrams showing the trigonal planar shape of BH3 with 120° bond angles and the pyramidal shape of NH3.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/3-chemical-bonding/3-5-shapes-of-molecules/assets/011-structural-diagrams-showing-the-trigonal-planar-.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

Explain why each bond angle in BH<sub>3</sub> is 120°.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The bond angle in BH<sub>3</sub> is 120° because:
> 
> - BH<sub>3</sub> has 3 bonding pairs of electrons and no lone pairs **[1 mark]**
> - The bonding pairs repel each other equally and arrange as far apart as possible to minimise repulsion **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> VSEPR theory states that electron pairs in the outer shell repel each other and arrange to minimise repulsion. Boron (Group 3) has 3 outer-shell electrons, all used to form the 3 B-H bonds. With 3 bonding pairs and no lone pairs, all repulsions are equal.
> 
> In a planar arrangement, equal repulsion between 3 pairs gives 360° / 3 = 120° bond angles. BH<sub>3</sub> is trigonal planar.
> 
> Note: bond angles are 120° due to repulsion between electron pairs, not between hydrogen atoms.

parts.problemMd: State the H-N-H bond angle in a molecule of NH<sub>3</sub>.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The H-N-H bond angle in NH<sub>3</sub>:
> 
> - 107° **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> NH<sub>3</sub> has 3 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair on nitrogen = 4 electron domains. Four electron domains give approximately 109.5° (tetrahedral), but the lone pair exerts greater repulsion than a bonding pair, compressing the H-N-H angles to approximately 107°.
> 
> The H-N-H bond angle in NH<sub>3</sub> (107°) is smaller than the H-B-H angle in BH<sub>3</sub> (120°) because NH<sub>3</sub> has a lone pair on nitrogen whereas BH<sub>3</sub> does not.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The shapes of the molecules BH~3~ and NH~3~ are shown in Fig. 1.1.

The bond angle in BH~3~ is 120°.

The H-N-H bond angle in NH~3~: 107°

Explain this difference in bond angles.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The bond angle in NH<sub>3</sub> is smaller than in BH<sub>3</sub> because:
> 
> - NH<sub>3</sub> has a lone pair of electrons on the central nitrogen atom, whereas BH<sub>3</sub> has no lone pairs **[1 mark]**
> - Lone pair–bonding pair repulsion is greater than bonding pair–bonding pair repulsion, reducing the H-N-H bond angle **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The order of electron pair repulsion strength is:
> 
> - lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bonding pair > bonding pair–bonding pair
> 
> In BH<sub>3</sub>, all three bonding pairs repel equally, giving 120°. In NH<sub>3</sub>, the lone pair exerts extra repulsion on the bonding pairs, compressing them and reducing the H-N-H angle from the ideal tetrahedral value (109.5°) to approximately 107°.

parts.problemMd: State the basic principles of the Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion (VSEPR) theory used to predict the shapes of molecules.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The basic principles of VSEPR theory:
> 
> - Electron pairs / electron domains in the outer shell of the central atom repel each other **[1 mark]**
> - Electron pairs arrange as far apart as possible to minimise repulsion **[1 mark]**
> - Lone pair–lone pair repulsion > lone pair–bonding pair repulsion > bonding pair–bonding pair repulsion **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> VSEPR theory is based on three key ideas:
> 
> 1. Electron pairs in the outer shell are negatively charged and repel each other.
> 2. To minimise repulsion, electron pairs arrange as far apart as possible in space. The arrangement determines the shape.
> 3. Not all electron pairs repel equally. Lone pairs are concentrated closer to the central atom and exert more repulsion than bonding pairs.
> 
> The repulsion hierarchy explains why molecules with lone pairs have bond angles smaller than the ideal value. For example, H<sub>2</sub>O has 2 lone pairs and a H-O-H angle of 104.5°, compared to the tetrahedral ideal of 109.5°.

parts.problemMd: State the shape of, and the F-O-F bond angle in, a molecule of OF<sub>2</sub>. Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The shape and F-O-F bond angle of OF<sub>2</sub>:
> 
> - Non-linear / V-shaped / bent **[1 mark]**
> - F-O-F bond angle in the range 97° to 109° **[1 mark]**
> - Oxygen has 4 electron domains: 2 bonding pairs and 2 lone pairs
> **OR**
> Oxygen has a tetrahedral arrangement of electron pairs **[1 mark]**
> 
> Lone pair–bonding pair repulsion is greater than bonding pair–bonding pair repulsion, reducing the F-O-F bond angle below 109.5°.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Oxygen in OF<sub>2</sub> has 6 outer-shell electrons: 2 used in the two O-F bonds and 4 remaining as 2 lone pairs. Four electron domains give a tetrahedral electron geometry, but the shape is named by bonding domains only: 2 bonding pairs + 2 lone pairs = non-linear / V-shaped.
> 
> Fluorine is more electronegative than hydrogen, which slightly increases the F-O-F bond angle compared to H<sub>2</sub>O (104.5°). A value in the range 97° to 109° is accepted.
> 
> The rough rule of thumb is that each lone pair reduces the bond angle by approximately 2.5° from the ideal tetrahedral value of 109.5°.

parts.problemMd:
State the shape of, and the bond angle in, each of the following molecules.

i) BF<sub>3</sub>

[2]

ii) NBr<sub>3</sub>

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The shape and bond angle in BF<sub>3</sub>:
> 
> - Trigonal planar **[1 mark]**
> - 120° **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The shape and bond angle in NBr<sub>3</sub>:
> 
> - Trigonal pyramidal **[1 mark]**
> - 107° **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For BF<sub>3</sub>: boron (Group 3) has 3 outer-shell electrons, all used in bonding. BF<sub>3</sub> has 3 bonding pairs and no lone pairs: trigonal planar, 120°.
> 
> For NBr<sub>3</sub>: nitrogen (Group 5) has 5 outer-shell electrons. Three are used in bonding, leaving 1 lone pair. Four electron domains (3 bonding pairs + 1 lone pair): trigonal pyramidal, approximately 107°.
> 
> The identity of the substituent (F vs Br) does not change the shape. What matters is the electron domain count around the central atom.

parts.problemMd: State and explain the H-C-H bond angle in ethene, C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>, and the H-N-H bond angle in hydrazine, N<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The bond angles are:
> 
> - H-C-H bond angle in ethene: any angle in the range 118° to 122° **[1 mark]**
> - H-N-H bond angle in hydrazine: any angle in the range 104° to 108° **[1 mark]**
> 
> Explanation:
> 
> - Each carbon atom in ethene has 3 electron domains: 1 C=C double bond and 2 C-H single bonds / 3 bonding regions and no lone pairs **[1 mark]**
> - Each nitrogen atom in hydrazine has 4 electron domains: 3 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair **[1 mark]**
> - Lone pair–bonding pair repulsion is greater than bonding pair–bonding pair repulsion, reducing the H-N-H angle below 109.5° **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For ethene (C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>): each carbon forms a C=C double bond and two C-H single bonds. For VSEPR, the C=C double bond counts as one electron domain. Each carbon has 3 electron domains, no lone pairs: trigonal planar geometry, approximately 120°.
> 
> For hydrazine (N<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>): each nitrogen has 3 N-H bonds and 1 lone pair = 4 electron domains. The ideal tetrahedral angle of 109.5° is compressed to approximately 107° by the lone pair's extra repulsion.

parts.problemMd:
Hydrazine can be oxidised to form diimide, HN=NH.

State the shape around each nitrogen atom in diimide and predict the H-N-N bond angle.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The shape and H-N-N bond angle in diimide:
> 
> - Non-linear / V-shaped / bent around each nitrogen atom **[1 mark]**
> - H-N-N bond angle in the range 115° to 120° **[1 mark]**
> 
> An answer of exactly 120° is not accepted as the lone pair on nitrogen reduces the angle below 120°.

> **[exam-tip]**
> In diimide (HN=NH), each nitrogen forms one N=N double bond and one N-H single bond, and has one lone pair. A double bond counts as one electron domain in VSEPR, so each nitrogen has 3 electron domains: 2 bonding domains and 1 lone pair.
> 
> ![Lewis structure of diimide, HN=NH, showing a nitrogen–nitrogen double bond, lone pairs on each nitrogen and single bonds to hydrogen atoms](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/3-chemical-bonding/3-5-shapes-of-molecules/assets/013-lewis-structure-of-diimide-hn-nh-showing-a-nitro.png)
> 
> Three electron domains give a trigonal planar electron geometry (ideal 120°), but the lone pair exerts additional repulsion, reducing the H-N-N angle to slightly below 120°.
> 
> Since both nitrogen atoms are bent symmetrically (HN=NH), the molecule is planar overall.

parts.problemMd:
Hydrazine forms a cation with an ethane-like structure called hydrazinediium, N<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub><sup>2+</sup>.

Predict the H-N-H bond angle in the N<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub><sup>2+</sup> cation.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The H-N-H bond angle in N<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub><sup>2+</sup>:
> 
> - 109.5° / 109° **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> In the N<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub><sup>2+</sup> cation, each nitrogen has accepted a proton, similar to how ammonia (NH<sub>3</sub>) becomes ammonium (NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>). Each nitrogen now has 4 bonding pairs and no lone pairs.
> 
> ![Lewis structure of N2H6(2+): two bonded N+ atoms, each attached to three H atoms with wedge and dash bonds indicating 3D geometry](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/3-chemical-bonding/3-5-shapes-of-molecules/assets/014-lewis-structure-of-n2h6-2-two-bonded-n-atoms-eac.png)
> 
> Four bonding domains with no lone pairs gives a tetrahedral arrangement with bond angles of 109.5°.
> 
> The structure is analogous to ethane: each carbon in ethane has 4 bonding pairs, no lone pairs, and bond angles of 109.5°.

parts.problemMd:
Methanamide, HCONH<sub>2</sub>, is the simplest aliphatic amide.

Draw a dot-and-cross diagram to show the bonding in a molecule of methanamide.

Show outer shell electrons only.
parts.solutionMd:
The dot-and-cross diagram for methanamide, HCONH<sub>2</sub> is:

![Dot-and-cross diagram of methanamide showing a C=O double bond, a C-N single bond, a C-H bond, two N-H bonds, with lone pairs on O and N, outer shell electrons only.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/3-chemical-bonding/3-5-shapes-of-molecules/assets/012-dot-and-cross-diagram-of-methanamide-showing-a-c.jpeg)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct bonding pairs: C=O double bond, C-H single bond, C-N single bond, two N-H single bonds shown as shared electron pairs.
> 
> 1 mark for correct non-bonding pairs: two lone pairs on oxygen, one lone pair on nitrogen.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Methanamide (HCONH<sub>2</sub>) contains 1 C, 1 O, 1 N, and 3 H atoms. Typical bonding in uncharged covalent molecules:
> 
> - Carbon forms 4 bonds
> - Oxygen forms 2 bonds (2 lone pairs remaining)
> - Nitrogen forms 3 bonds (1 lone pair remaining)
> - Hydrogen forms 1 bond
> 
> In methanamide: carbon forms a C=O double bond, a C-N single bond, and a C-H single bond (4 bonds total). Nitrogen forms the C-N bond and two N-H bonds (3 bonds, 1 lone pair). Oxygen forms the C=O double bond (2 bonds, 2 lone pairs).

parts.problemMd: State and explain the H-C-N and C-N-H bond angles around the C and N atoms in HCONH<sub>2</sub>.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> H-C-N bond angle:
> 
> - Any angle in the range 117° to 120° **[1 mark]**
> - Carbon has 3 electron domains: 2 single bonds (C-H and C-N) and 1 double bond (C=O) / 3 bonding regions and no lone pairs **[1 mark]**
> - The electron domains arrange to minimise repulsion / repel each other equally **[1 mark]**
> 
> C-N-H bond angle:
> 
> - Any angle in the range 104° to 108° **[1 mark]**
> - Nitrogen has 4 electron domains: 3 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair **[1 mark]**
> - Lone pair–bonding pair repulsion is greater than bonding pair–bonding pair repulsion, reducing the C-N-H bond angle below 109.5° **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For the carbon atom in HCONH<sub>2</sub>: carbon forms a C=O double bond, a C-N single bond, and a C-H single bond. For VSEPR, the double bond counts as one electron domain. Carbon has 3 electron domains, no lone pairs: trigonal planar geometry, approximately 120°.
> 
> For the nitrogen atom: nitrogen forms a C-N bond and two N-H bonds, with one lone pair remaining. Four electron domains (3 bonding + 1 lone pair): ideal tetrahedral 109.5° compressed to approximately 107° by the lone pair's greater repulsion.

parts.problemMd: State the shape around each of the C and N atoms in HCONH<sub>2</sub>.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The shapes around C and N in HCONH<sub>2</sub>:
> 
> - Around C: trigonal planar; **[1 mark]**
> - Around N: trigonal pyramidal / pyramidal; **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The shape around an atom is determined by its bonding domains only — lone pairs affect bond angles but are not counted when naming the shape.
> 
> Around C: 3 bonding domains, no lone pairs: trigonal planar.
> 
> Around N: 3 bonding domains and 1 lone pair: trigonal pyramidal / pyramidal.
> 
> Note: at A Level, the lone pair on nitrogen in amides can be delocalised into the C=O pi bond, making the geometry around N closer to trigonal planar in reality. For a straightforward VSEPR question at this level, trigonal pyramidal / pyramidal is the expected answer.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Methanamide, HCONH~2~, is the simplest aliphatic amide.

State, with a reason, whether HCONH<sub>2</sub> is a polar molecule.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The polarity of HCONH<sub>2</sub>:
> 
> - Methanamide is polar; **[1 mark]**
> - It contains polar bonds (C=O / N-H); **[1 mark]**
> - The bond dipoles do not cancel / there is an unsymmetrical distribution of charge / there is a net dipole moment; **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For a molecule to be polar, it must contain polar bonds AND those bonds must be arranged unsymmetrically so their dipoles do not cancel.
> 
> Methanamide contains a strongly polar C=O bond (oxygen is much more electronegative than carbon) and polar N-H bonds (nitrogen is more electronegative than hydrogen).
> 
> The geometry of methanamide is not symmetrical, which means that the C=O and N-H dipoles point in a similar direction, giving a resultant net dipole. Methanamide is therefore polar.
> 
> Contrast with SF<sub>6</sub>, which has polar S-F bonds but is non-polar because the six bonds are arranged symmetrically and the dipoles cancel exactly.

parts.problemMd: State the three main types of intermolecular force and place them in ascending order of strength.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The three main types of intermolecular force, in ascending order of strength:
> 
> - Instantaneous dipole-induced dipole (id-id) forces / London dispersion forces, permanent dipole-permanent dipole (pd-pd) forces, and hydrogen bonding **[1 mark]**
> - (In ascending order of strength) instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces < permanent dipole-permanent dipole forces < hydrogen bonding **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Van der Waals' forces is a generic term that covers all intermolecular forces except hydrogen bonding. It does not distinguish between id-id and pd-pd forces, so use the specific syllabus terms above to be precise.
> 
> You must know the order of strength: id-id forces are the weakest, pd-pd forces are intermediate, and hydrogen bonding is the strongest.

parts.problemMd:
Draw a diagram to show hydrogen bonding between two molecules of methanol, CH<sub>3</sub>OH.

Your diagram should include all relevant lone pairs of electrons and dipoles.
parts.solutionMd:
A diagram showing hydrogen bonding between two molecules of methanol is:

![Diagram of two methanol molecules showing partial charges, lone pairs and a dotted hydrogen bond between the δ+ hydrogen of one and δ− oxygen of the other](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/3-chemical-bonding/3-6-intermolecular-forces-electronegativity-and-bond-properties/assets/010-diagram-of-two-methanol-molecules-showing-partia.png)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for two lone pairs on at least one oxygen atom **AND** correct dipoles (δ- on O and δ+ on H) on at least one O-H bond
> 
> 1 mark for a dotted line shown between a lone pair on one oxygen and the correct O-H hydrogen on another molecule

> **[exam-tip]**
> It is good practice to draw lone pairs on every oxygen atom, but showing at least one is sufficient for the mark.
> 
> Hydrogen bonding forms between an electronegative atom with a lone pair (O, N, or F) as the acceptor and a hydrogen atom bonded directly to O, N, or F as the donor. For methanol, the relevant hydrogen is the O-H hydrogen (δ+). The C-H hydrogens are not involved, as C-H bonds are not significantly polar.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The three main types of intermolecular force, in ascending order of strength:
- Instantaneous dipole-induced dipole (id-id) forces / London dispersion forces, permanent dipole-permanent dipole (pd-pd) forces, and hydrogen bonding
- (In ascending order of strength) instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces < permanent dipole-permanent dipole forces < hydrogen bonding

Methanol, CH<sub>3</sub>OH, can be oxidised to methanal, CH<sub>2</sub>O, and then to methanoic acid, HCOOH.

State the strongest type of intermolecular force present between:

i) Methanal molecules

[1]

ii) Methanoic acid molecules

[1]

iii) A molecule of water and a molecule of methanal

[1]

iv) A molecule of water and a molecule of methanoic acid

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The strongest type of intermolecular force in each case:
> 
> i) Methanal molecules:
> 
> - Permanent dipole-permanent dipole (pd-pd) forces **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) Methanoic acid molecules:
> 
> - Hydrogen bonding **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) A molecule of water and a molecule of methanal:
> 
> - Hydrogen bonding **[1 mark]**
> 
> iv) A molecule of water and a molecule of methanoic acid:
> 
> - Hydrogen bonding / ion-dipole forces **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Methanal has a polar C=O bond (δ- on O, δ+ on C) but no O-H, N-H, or F-H bond, so it cannot act as a hydrogen bond donor. Its strongest self-interaction is permanent dipole-permanent dipole (pd-pd) forces.
> 
> All these molecules can form hydrogen bonds with water because water has both O-H bonds (hydrogen bond donors, δ+) and lone pairs on oxygen (hydrogen bond acceptors, δ-). The lone pair on the C=O oxygen in methanal accepts a hydrogen bond from the δ+ H of water.
> 
> Methanoic acid partially ionises in water as it is a weak acid, so ion-dipole interactions can also form between the resulting ions and water molecules.

parts.problemMd:
Methanoic acid reacts with sodium hydroxide to form sodium methanoate:

HCOOH + NaOH → HCOONa + H<sub>2</sub>O

Explain why sodium methanoate is a solid at room temperature and methanoic acid is a liquid.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Sodium methanoate is a solid and methanoic acid is a liquid at room temperature because:
> 
> - Sodium methanoate is ionic / contains Na<sup>+</sup> and HCOO<sup>-</sup> / is a giant ionic lattice **[1 mark]**
> - Methanoic acid is a simple molecular / covalent substance / has hydrogen bonds between molecules **[1 mark]**
> - Ionic bonds are stronger than hydrogen bonds / require more energy to overcome / require a higher temperature to break (or reverse argument) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> This reaction is an acid-base neutralisation using an organic acid, producing a salt (sodium methanoate) and water. Salts are ionic, so sodium methanoate has a giant ionic lattice structure with strong ionic bonds between Na<sup>+</sup> and HCOO<sup>-</sup> ions.
> 
> Although methanoic acid has the strongest type of intermolecular force (hydrogen bonding), hydrogen bonds are still far weaker than ionic bonds. This is why the melting point of sodium methanoate is much higher, making it a solid while methanoic acid remains a liquid at room temperature.

The lone pair repels bonding pairs more strongly, compressing the H-N-H angle to 107° and giving a pyramidal shape. parts.problemMd:
Ammonia is a polar molecule whereas methane is non-polar.

i) Explain what is meant by the term *bond polarity*, using the N-H bond as an example.

[2]

ii) Explain why the ammonia molecule is polar.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) Bond polarity, using the N-H bond as an example:
> 
> - Nitrogen and hydrogen have different electronegativities
> **OR**
> The N-H bond has a dipole **[1 mark]**
> - The bonding electrons are more attracted to nitrogen (N<sup>δ-</sup>-H<sup>δ+</sup>)
> **OR**
> The bonding electrons are unequally shared **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The ammonia molecule is polar because:
> 
> - The molecule is asymmetrical / the bond dipoles do not cancel out **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> You must reference the N-H bond or ammonia in your answer to part i) or you may not score the marks.
> 
> Electronegativity is the ability of an atom to attract electrons in a covalent bond. Nitrogen (electronegativity 3.0) is more electronegative than hydrogen (electronegativity 2.1), so the bonding electrons are pulled towards nitrogen, giving the N-H bond a permanent dipole (N<sup>δ-</sup>-H<sup>δ+</sup>).
> 
> For part ii): a molecule is polar only when its bond dipoles do not cancel. In NH<sub>3</sub>, the three N-H dipoles all point towards nitrogen and the lone pair adds to the asymmetry, so the dipoles do not cancel and ammonia has a net dipole moment.

parts.problemMd: State the strongest type of intermolecular force present in liquid ammonia.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The strongest type of intermolecular force present in liquid ammonia is:
> 
> - Hydrogen bonding **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Ammonia, NH<sub>3</sub>, has a lone pair on nitrogen and N-H bonds where the H is δ+ (due to nitrogen's high electronegativity). This allows hydrogen bonds to form between the lone pair on one nitrogen and the δ+ hydrogen of an adjacent NH<sub>3</sub> molecule.
> 
> All simple molecular substances also have instantaneous dipole-induced dipole (id-id) forces, but hydrogen bonding is the strongest type present and has the greatest influence on ammonia's physical properties.

parts.problemMd:
Ammonia gas reacts with hydrogen chloride gas to form solid ammonium chloride, NH<sub>4</sub>Cl.

State the three types of bonding present in solid ammonium chloride.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The three types of bonding present in solid ammonium chloride are:
> 
> - Covalent bonding (between N and H in the NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> ion) **[1 mark]**
> - Co-ordinate / dative covalent bonding (one N-H bond formed using the lone pair on N) **[1 mark]**
> - Ionic bonding (between NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>-</sup>) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When NH<sub>3</sub> reacts with HCl, the HCl donates H<sup>+</sup> (a proton with no electrons). The nitrogen in NH<sub>3</sub> uses its lone pair to form a co-ordinate (dative covalent) bond with this H<sup>+</sup>, creating the ammonium ion, NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>.
> 
> Once the NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> ion is formed, all four N-H bonds are identical in length and strength. It is not possible to distinguish the original covalent bonds from the co-ordinate bond in the final ion. This question tests your understanding of how the bond forms, not the final structure.
> 
> The NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> ion then forms an ionic bond with the Cl<sup>-</sup> ion, giving solid ammonium chloride its giant ionic lattice structure.

parts.problemMd:
The structural formulae of water, methanol and methoxymethane, CH<sub>3</sub>OCH<sub>3</sub>, are given below.

![Three structural formulas: water (O bonded to two H), methanol (O bonded to CH₃ and H), and dimethyl ether (O bonded to two CH₃ groups), left to right](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/3-chemical-bonding/3-6-intermolecular-forces-electronegativity-and-bond-properties/assets/013-three-structural-formulas-water-o-bonded-to-two-.png)

i) State the number of lone pairs of electrons around the oxygen atom in a molecule of methoxymethane.

[1]

ii) Suggest a value for the C-O-C bond angle in methoxymethane.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The number of lone pairs of electrons around the oxygen atom in methoxymethane:
> 
> - 2 **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) A value for the C-O-C bond angle in methoxymethane:
> 
> - Between 104° and 105° **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The oxygen atom in methoxymethane has two bonding pairs (one to each carbon) and two lone pairs, giving four electron domains. The question asks for the number of lone pairs, not the total number of electrons.
> 
> The four electron domains give a tetrahedral electron geometry, but the lone pairs repel the bonding pairs more strongly, compressing the C-O-C bond angle below the ideal tetrahedral value of 109.5° to approximately 104-105°. This is the same reasoning as for water (H-O-H angle ~104.5°).

parts.problemMd:
The physical properties of covalent compounds depend on the intermolecular forces between their molecules.

|   | Type of intermolecular force |
|---|---|
| **A** | Permanent dipole-permanent dipole (pd-pd) forces |
| **B** | Instantaneous dipole-induced dipole (id-id) forces |
| **C** | Hydrogen bonding |

Using the letters A, B, or C, state the strongest intermolecular force present in each of the following compounds.

| Compound | Formula | Strongest intermolecular force |
|---|---|---|
| ethanal | CH<sub>3</sub>CHO |   |
| ethanol | CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH |   |
| methoxymethane | CH<sub>3</sub>OCH<sub>3</sub> |   |
| 2-methylpropane | (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCH<sub>3</sub> |   |
parts.solutionMd:
The strongest intermolecular force in each compound:

| Compound | Formula | Strongest intermolecular force |
|---|---|---|
| ethanal | CH<sub>3</sub>CHO | **Final answer:** **A** |
| ethanol | CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH | **Final answer:** **C** |
| methoxymethane | CH<sub>3</sub>OCH<sub>3</sub> | **Final answer:** **A** |
| 2-methylpropane | (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCH<sub>3</sub> | **Final answer:** **B** |

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for ethanal = A (pd-pd forces)
> 
> 1 mark for ethanol = C (hydrogen bonding)
> 
> 1 mark for methoxymethane = A (pd-pd forces)
> 
> 1 mark for 2-methylpropane = B (id-id forces)

> **[exam-tip]**
> The order of strength is: C (hydrogen bonding) > A (pd-pd forces) > B (id-id forces). Identify the strongest force that can be present in each molecule.
> 
> Hydrogen bonding (C) requires an O-H, N-H, or F-H bond as the donor. Ethanol has an -OH group, so C applies.
> 
> Permanent dipole-permanent dipole forces (A) require a net molecular dipole. Ethanal has a polar C=O bond; the dipoles do not cancel, giving pd-pd forces. Methoxymethane has two polar C-O bonds in a bent arrangement; the dipoles do not fully cancel, so pd-pd forces apply. Neither has an O-H bond, so hydrogen bonding is not possible.
> 
> 2-methylpropane is a non-polar hydrocarbon. Only id-id forces (B) are present.

parts.problemMd:
Ethoxyethane, C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OC<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>, and water are immiscible.

Explain why ethoxyethane does not dissolve in water.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Ethoxyethane does not dissolve in water because:
> 
> - Hydrogen bonds exist between H<sub>2</sub>O molecules **[1 mark]**
> - Ethoxyethane has no O-H bonds and cannot form hydrogen bonds with water / the interactions between ethoxyethane and water are insufficient to compensate for breaking water-water hydrogen bonds **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> To dissolve in water, hydrogen bonds between water molecules must be broken and new intermolecular interactions must form between the solute and water. If these new interactions are not strong enough to compensate, the substance is immiscible.
> 
> Ethoxyethane has a lone pair on oxygen, so it can accept a hydrogen bond from water. However, it has no O-H bond, so it cannot donate hydrogen bonds. The large non-polar C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub> groups also disrupt the water hydrogen bonding network. The net interaction between ethoxyethane and water is insufficient to overcome the extensive water-water hydrogen bonding.

parts.problemMd: Explain why butan-1-ol has a higher boiling point than butanal.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Butan-1-ol has a higher boiling point than butanal because:
> 
> - Butan-1-ol contains hydrogen bonding
> **AND**
> Butanal contains permanent dipole-permanent dipole (pd-pd) forces **[1 mark]**
> - Hydrogen bonding is stronger than pd-pd forces, requiring more energy to overcome **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> It can be helpful to draw out the structures of both molecules to identify the relevant functional groups.
> 
> Butan-1-ol:
> 
> ![Structural formula of an alcohol: four-carbon chain with single bonds, terminal carbon attached to an OH group showing two lone electron pairs](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/3-chemical-bonding/3-6-intermolecular-forces-electronegativity-and-bond-properties/assets/007-structural-formula-of-an-alcohol-four-carbon-cha.png)
> 
> Butan-1-ol has an -OH group: the O-H bond is polar (δ- on O, δ+ on H) and oxygen has lone pairs, allowing hydrogen bonding between butan-1-ol molecules.
> 
> Butanal:
> 
> ![Structural formula of an aldehyde: four-carbon chain with single bonds, terminal aldehyde group with the oxygen showing two lone electron pairs](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/3-chemical-bonding/3-6-intermolecular-forces-electronegativity-and-bond-properties/assets/008-structural-formula-of-an-aldehyde-four-carbon-ch.png)
> 
> Butanal has a C=O group but no O-H bond, so it cannot donate hydrogen bonds. Its strongest intermolecular force is permanent dipole-permanent dipole (pd-pd) forces from the polar C=O bond.
> 
> Hydrogen bonding is stronger than pd-pd forces, so butan-1-ol requires more energy to overcome its intermolecular forces and has a higher boiling point.

parts.problemMd:
Ethane, C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>, and disilane, Si<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>, are hydrides of Group 14 elements.

Explain why disilane has a higher boiling point than ethane.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Disilane has a higher boiling point than ethane because:
> 
> - Disilane has stronger instantaneous dipole-induced dipole (id-id) / London dispersion forces **[1 mark]**
> - (Due to) more electrons
> **OR**
> A stronger instantaneous dipole **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Both ethane and disilane are non-polar molecules, so the only intermolecular forces present are instantaneous dipole-induced dipole (id-id) forces, also called London dispersion forces.
> 
> The strength of id-id forces depends on how easily the electron cloud can be polarised, which in turn depends on the number of electrons. Si<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub> contains more electrons than C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub> (silicon is one period below carbon and has more electron shells), giving it a more polarisable electron cloud. This produces stronger id-id forces and a higher boiling point.

parts.problemMd:
Ethanol is soluble in water, whereas ethane is insoluble.

Explain this difference.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Ethanol is soluble but ethane is insoluble because:
> 
> - Ethane has only non-polar C-H bonds / no polar bonds **[1 mark]**
> - Ethanol forms hydrogen bonds with water (due to the -OH group) **[1 mark]**
> - The energy released forming ethanol-water hydrogen bonds is sufficient to overcome the hydrogen bonds between water molecules / ethanol-water interactions compensate for breaking water-water hydrogen bonds **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Ethane contains only C-H bonds, which are non-polar due to the small electronegativity difference between carbon and hydrogen. Non-polar substances cannot form hydrogen bonds with water, so the energy released when ethane interacts with water (only id-id forces form) is insufficient to break the water-water hydrogen bonds.
> 
> Ethanol has an -OH group with a highly electronegative oxygen bonded to hydrogen. This allows ethanol to form hydrogen bonds with water, both as a donor (via O-H) and as an acceptor (via the lone pair on O).
> 
> ![Diagram of ethanol molecules showing partial charges and a dotted hydrogen bond between the oxygen atom and a hydrogen on a neighbouring water molecule](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/3-chemical-bonding/3-6-intermolecular-forces-electronegativity-and-bond-properties/assets/009-diagram-of-ethanol-molecules-showing-partial-cha.png)
> 
> The energy released by these new hydrogen bonds is sufficient to overcome the water-water hydrogen bonds, so ethanol dissolves.

parts.problemMd:
Water has a relatively high surface tension compared to most liquids.

Explain this anomalous property of water.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Water has a high surface tension because:
> 
> - Water molecules form strong hydrogen bonds with each other **[1 mark]**
> - Molecules at the surface are only attracted inward / downward by hydrogen bonds, creating a strong net cohesive force at the surface **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Whenever you need to explain an anomalous property of water, think about hydrogen bonding first.
> 
> Molecules in the bulk liquid are surrounded by water molecules on all sides and experience hydrogen bonding in all directions, so the net force is zero. Molecules at the surface have no water molecules above them, so they experience a net inward pull. This makes the surface resistant to being broken or stretched, giving water its unusually high surface tension.

parts.problemMd:
Ammonia, NH<sub>3</sub>, is highly soluble in water.

Draw diagrams to show the **two** different ways a hydrogen bond can form between one molecule of water and one molecule of ammonia. Your diagrams should include all relevant dipoles and lone pairs of electrons.
parts.solutionMd:
The two ways a hydrogen bond can form between water and ammonia are:

| ![Diagram of a hydrogen bond between water and ammonia, showing partial charges, lone pairs and three‑dimensional bond wedges and dashes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/3-chemical-bonding/3-6-intermolecular-forces-electronegativity-and-bond-properties/assets/003-diagram-of-a-hydrogen-bond-between-water-and-amm.png) | ![Diagram of a hydrogen bond between ammonia and water showing partial charges, N–H and O–H bonds, and lone pairs on nitrogen and oxygen](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/3-chemical-bonding/3-6-intermolecular-forces-electronegativity-and-bond-properties/assets/004-diagram-of-a-hydrogen-bond-between-ammonia-and-w.png) |
|---|---|

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for δ- on O and at least one δ+ H shown correctly in a water molecule
> 
> 1 mark for δ- on N and at least one δ+ H shown correctly in an ammonia molecule
> 
> 1 mark for one diagram showing a hydrogen bond between the H of an ammonia molecule (N-H) and the O atom of a water molecule
> 
> 1 mark for one diagram showing a hydrogen bond between the H of a water molecule (O-H) and the N atom of an ammonia molecule

> **[exam-tip]**
> There are two distinct hydrogen bonds that can form between NH<sub>3</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O:
> 
> - Way 1: The δ+ H on ammonia (N-H bond) forms a hydrogen bond with the lone pair on the δ- O of water
> - Way 2: The δ+ H on water (O-H bond) forms a hydrogen bond with the lone pair on the δ- N of ammonia
> 
> Represent hydrogen bonds as dashed lines. Show partial charges (δ+ and δ-) and lone pairs clearly in both diagrams.

parts.problemMd:
Ammonia, NH<sub>3</sub>, hydrogen chloride, HCl, and fluorine, F<sub>2</sub>, all exist as gases at room temperature and pressure. The boiling point of NH<sub>3</sub> is −33 °C.

Predict which gas, HCl or F<sub>2</sub>, has the lowest boiling point. Explain the relative boiling points of all three gases in terms of the intermolecular forces present.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> - F<sub>2</sub> has the lowest boiling point **[1 mark]**
> - F<sub>2</sub> has only instantaneous dipole-induced dipole (id-id) / London dispersion forces **[1 mark]**
> - HCl also has permanent dipole-permanent dipole (pd-pd) forces (in addition to id-id forces) **[1 mark]**
> - F<sub>2</sub> and HCl have the same number of electrons (18 each), so their id-id forces are similar in strength **[1 mark]**
> - HCl therefore has stronger overall intermolecular forces than F<sub>2</sub>, requiring more energy to overcome
> **OR**
> F<sub>2</sub> has weaker overall intermolecular forces, requiring less energy to overcome **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The key to this question is recognising that F<sub>2</sub> and HCl are isoelectronic (both have 18 electrons), so their id-id forces are approximately equal in strength. The additional pd-pd forces in HCl (from the polar H-Cl bond) give it stronger overall intermolecular forces and a higher boiling point than F<sub>2</sub>.
> 
> NH<sub>3</sub> has the highest boiling point of the three because it forms hydrogen bonds (the strongest type of intermolecular force), which require significantly more energy to overcome than either pd-pd or id-id forces.
> 
> Always identify all types of intermolecular forces present in each substance before comparing their relative boiling points.

parts.solutionMd:
i) Hydrogen cyanide (HCN):

![Completed dot-and-cross diagram of hydrogen cyanide showing H bonded to C by a single bond and C triple-bonded to N, with a lone pair on nitrogen](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/3-chemical-bonding/3-7-dot-and-cross-diagrams/assets/018-completed-dot-and-cross-diagram-of-hydrogen-cyan.png)

**[1 mark]**

ii) Carbon dioxide (CO<sub>2</sub>):

![Completed dot-and-cross diagram of carbon dioxide showing two double bonds from the central carbon to each oxygen atom, with two lone pairs on each oxygen](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/3-chemical-bonding/3-7-dot-and-cross-diagrams/assets/019-completed-dot-and-cross-diagram-of-carbon-dioxid.png)

**[1 mark]**

iii) Boron trifluoride (BF<sub>3</sub>):

![Completed dot-and-cross diagram of boron trifluoride showing three single bonds from the central boron to each fluorine atom, with three lone pairs on each fluorine](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/3-chemical-bonding/3-7-dot-and-cross-diagrams/assets/020-completed-dot-and-cross-diagram-of-boron-trifluo.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct HCN diagram: H single-bonded to C; C triple-bonded to N; lone pair on N only; correct electron counts throughout
> 
> 1 mark for correct CO<sub>2</sub> diagram: O=C=O with double bonds to each oxygen; 2 lone pairs on each O; no lone pairs on C; correct electron counts
> 
> 1 mark for correct BF<sub>3</sub> diagram: central B with 3 single bond pairs to three F atoms; 3 lone pairs on each F; incomplete octet on B (only 6 electrons around B)

> **[exam-tip]**
> Each of these three molecules tests a different aspect of covalent bonding:
> 
> - HCN:
> 
>   - Carbon forms a triple bond with nitrogen (1 sigma + 2 pi bonds).
>   - Only nitrogen has a lone pair in the completed structure.
> - CO<sub>2</sub>:
> 
>   - Carbon forms two double bonds.
>   - Each oxygen has 2 lone pairs.
>   - Carbon has no lone pairs and a complete octet.
> - BF<sub>3</sub>:
> 
>   - Boron is in Group 13 and only has 3 outer electrons.
>   - After bonding to three fluorines, boron has only 6 electrons (an incomplete octet).
>   - This is why BF<sub>3</sub> acts as a Lewis acid and can accept a lone pair to form a coordinate bond.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Draw dot-and-cross diagrams for the following molecules.

Show outer shell electrons only.

i) Hydrogen cyanide, HCN.

ii) Carbon dioxide, CO~2~.

iii) Boron trifluoride, BF~3~.

Use your diagrams in (a) to deduce which of the three molecules is most likely to form a coordinate (dative covalent) bond. Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The molecule from (a) most likely to form a coordinate (dative covalent) bond is:
> 
> - Boron trifluoride (BF<sub>3</sub>) **[1 mark]**
> 
> Explanation:
> 
> - Boron's outer shell has space for two more electrons
> **OR**
> Boron only has six outer shell electrons / boron has an incomplete outer shell **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> In HCN and CO<sub>2</sub>, the central carbon atom has a complete outer shell (8 electrons). It cannot accept an electron pair from a donor and so cannot form a coordinate bond.
> 
> In BF<sub>3</sub>, the central boron atom has only 6 outer shell electrons. This incomplete octet means boron can accept a lone pair from a donor molecule such as NH<sub>3</sub>, making BF<sub>3</sub> a Lewis acid. The coordinate bond forms when a lone pair is donated into boron's vacant orbital.

parts.problemMd:

The molecule from (a) most likely to form a coordinate (dative covalent) bond is:

- Boron trifluoride (BF~3~)

Explanation:

OR

Boron only has six outer shell electrons / boron has an incomplete outer shell

Show outer shell electrons only.

[1]

ii) Explain how the coordinate (dative covalent) bond forms between the boron trifluoride and ammonia molecules.

parts.solutionMd:
i) The dot-and-cross diagram for the product of boron trifluoride and ammonia is:

![Completed dot-and-cross diagram of the BF3-NH3 adduct showing a coordinate bond between the nitrogen atom of ammonia and the boron atom of BF3, with all outer shell electrons shown](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/3-chemical-bonding/3-7-dot-and-cross-diagrams/assets/021-completed-dot-and-cross-diagram-of-the-bf3-nh3-a.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct BF<sub>3</sub>-NH<sub>3</sub> adduct: coordinate bond between N and B shown with both electrons from nitrogen using the same symbol (both dots or both crosses); correct lone pairs on all atoms
> 
> ii) The coordinate (dative covalent) bond forms because:
> 
> - Ammonia has a lone pair of electrons on nitrogen
> **AND**
> Boron trifluoride has an incomplete outer shell / only 6 electrons around B **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> In the dot-and-cross diagram of the product, the coordinate bond must be shown with both electrons from the same atom. Use two dots (from nitrogen's lone pair) between the N and B atoms, while the other N-H bonds each have one dot and one cross.

> NH<sub>3</sub> acts as the electron pair donor (Lewis base) and BF<sub>3</sub> acts as the electron pair acceptor (Lewis acid). The lone pair from nitrogen fills the vacant orbital on boron to form the coordinate bond.

parts.problemMd:
Phosphorus tribromide and sulfur tetrafluoride are two colourless compounds which both react with water to form toxic products.

Draw diagrams to show the arrangement of outer electrons in both compounds.
parts.solutionMd:
The dot-and-cross diagrams for phosphorus tribromide and sulfur tetrafluoride are:

Phosphorus tribromide (PBr<sub>3</sub>):

![Diagram of a phosphorus tribromide (PBr3) molecule, showing a central phosphorus atom bonded to three bromine atoms, with electron dot structures.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/3-chemical-bonding/3-7-dot-and-cross-diagrams/assets/012-diagram-of-a-phosphorus-tribromide-pbr3-molecule.bin)

Sulfur tetrafluoride (SF<sub>4</sub>):

![Dot-and-cross diagram of sulfur tetrafluoride showing a central sulfur atom bonded to four fluorine atoms, with one lone pair on sulfur and three lone pairs on each fluorine atom, demonstrating an expanded octet](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/3-chemical-bonding/3-7-dot-and-cross-diagrams/assets/013-dot-and-cross-diagram-of-sulfur-tetrafluoride-sh.jpg)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a correct dot-and-cross diagram of PBr<sub>3</sub>: central P atom with 3 bond pairs (one to each Br), 1 lone pair on P; 3 lone pairs on each Br atom
> 
> 1 mark for a correct dot-and-cross diagram of SF<sub>4</sub>: central S atom with 4 bond pairs (one to each F), 1 lone pair on S; 3 lone pairs on each F atom (expanded octet on S)

> **[exam-tip]**
> Both PBr<sub>3</sub> and SF<sub>4</sub> have central atoms from Period 3, so they can accommodate more than 8 electrons in their outer shell (expanded octet). This is only possible for elements in Period 3 and beyond, because they have vacant d orbitals available.
> 
> For PBr<sub>3</sub>: phosphorus is in Group 15 (5 outer electrons) and each bromine is in Group 17 (7 outer electrons). Draw 3 bond pairs between P and each Br, plus 1 lone pair on P. Each Br has 3 lone pairs.
> 
> For SF<sub>4</sub>: sulfur is in Group 16 (6 outer electrons) and each fluorine is in Group 17 (7 outer electrons). Draw 4 bond pairs between S and each F, plus 1 lone pair on S (giving S 10 electrons in total). Each F has 3 lone pairs.

parts.problemMd: State the shape of, and the Br-P-Br bond angle in, a molecule of PBr<sub>3</sub>.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The shape and bond angle of PBr<sub>3</sub> are:
> 
> - Pyramidal / trigonal pyramidal **[1 mark]**
> - 107° / approximately 107° **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> PBr<sub>3</sub> has 3 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair around the central phosphorus atom. The lone pair exerts greater repulsion than a bonding pair, pushing the three P-Br bonds downward and reducing the bond angle from the ideal tetrahedral value of 109.5° to approximately 107°.
> 
> This is the same electron arrangement as NH<sub>3</sub>, PCl<sub>3</sub>, and NF<sub>3</sub>: all have a pyramidal shape and a bond angle of approximately 107°.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Phosphorus tribromide and sulfur tetrafluoride are two colourless compounds which both react with water to form toxic products.

Explain why molecules of PBr<sub>3</sub> and SF<sub>4</sub> are polar.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> PBr<sub>3</sub> and SF<sub>4</sub> are polar because:
> 
> - P-Br and S-F bonds are polar / there is a difference in electronegativity between the bonded atoms **[1 mark]**
> - The molecules have non-symmetrical shapes so the bond dipoles do not cancel **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Both PBr<sub>3</sub> (pyramidal) and SF<sub>4</sub> (see-saw) have unsymmetrical shapes due to the lone pair(s) on the central atom. Even though each individual P-Br or S-F bond is polar, the key point is that the bond dipoles do not point in equal and opposite directions, so they cannot cancel.
> 
> Compare this with a non-polar molecule such as BF<sub>3</sub> (trigonal planar, no lone pairs). In BF<sub>3</sub> the three equal B-F dipoles cancel exactly because the molecule is perfectly symmetrical. The absence of lone pairs on the central atom is what allows full cancellation.

parts.problemMd: Construct an equation for the reaction of ammonia, NH<sub>3</sub>, with a hydrogen ion.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The equation for the reaction is:
> 
> - NH<sub>3</sub> + H<sup>+</sup> → NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are not required

> **[exam-tip]**
> The ammonium ion, NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>, forms because the lone pair on the nitrogen atom in NH<sub>3</sub> is donated to the hydrogen ion. This forms a coordinate (dative covalent) bond between nitrogen and H<sup>+</sup>.
> 
> Note the → arrow: H<sup>+</sup> has no lone pairs to donate back, so this reaction does not proceed in reverse under these conditions.

parts.problemMd: Predict the shapes of an ammonia molecule and an ammonium ion.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The shapes are:
> 
> - Ammonia: Pyramidal / trigonal pyramidal **[1 mark]**
> - Ammonium ion: Tetrahedral **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> NH<sub>3</sub> has 3 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair around the nitrogen atom. The lone pair repels bonding pairs more strongly, compressing the H-N-H bond angle to approximately 107° and giving a pyramidal shape.
> 
> NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> has 4 bonding pairs and no lone pairs around nitrogen. All four pairs repel equally, giving a tetrahedral shape with a bond angle of 109.5°. The fourth N-H bond is a coordinate bond, but once formed it is identical to the other three.

parts.problemMd:
Draw a dot-and-cross diagram to show the bonding in the ammonium ion.

Show outer shell electrons only.
parts.solutionMd:
The dot-and-cross diagram for the ammonium ion is:

![Dot-and-cross diagram of the ammonium ion showing a central nitrogen atom bonded to four hydrogen atoms, with three ordinary covalent bonds and one coordinate bond, enclosed in square brackets with a 1+ charge](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/3-chemical-bonding/3-7-dot-and-cross-diagrams/assets/014-dot-and-cross-diagram-of-the-ammonium-ion-showin.jpg)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for 1 central nitrogen atom surrounded by 4 hydrogen atoms, with 3 shared pairs of electrons **AND** 1 coordinate bond shown with both electrons from nitrogen
> 
> 1 mark for square brackets **AND** 1+ charge outside the brackets

> **[exam-tip]**
> Two features are essential in this diagram:
> 
> - The coordinate bond:
> 
>   - Show both electrons using the same symbol (both dots or both crosses), donated from the lone pair on nitrogen.
>   - This distinguishes the dative bond from the three ordinary covalent bonds.
> - The ionic notation:
> 
>   - Draw square brackets around the complete ion and write the 1+ charge as a superscript outside.
>   - Without both of these, you will lose the second mark.

parts.problemMd:
Draw a dot-and-cross diagram for the nitrate(V) ion, NO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup>.

Show outer shell electrons only.
parts.solutionMd:
The dot-and-cross diagram for the NO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> ion is:

![Dot-and-cross diagram of the nitrate ion showing a central nitrogen atom bonded to three oxygen atoms with one single covalent bond, one double covalent bond, and one coordinate bond, enclosed in square brackets with a 1- charge](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/3-chemical-bonding/3-7-dot-and-cross-diagrams/assets/022-dot-and-cross-diagram-of-the-nitrate-ion-showing.png)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct bonding around N: one single covalent bond, one double covalent bond, and one coordinate bond to the three oxygen atoms; correct electron counts for each atom
> 
> 1 mark for square brackets **AND** 1- charge outside the brackets

> **[exam-tip]**
> The NO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> ion has three different types of N-O bond. To construct the diagram:
> 
> 1. Start with nitrogen: 5 outer electrons.
> 2. Double bond: 2 electrons from N, 2 from O — this oxygen now has a complete octet.
> 3. Single bond: 1 from N, 1 from O — this oxygen needs 1 extra electron to complete its octet. That extra electron accounts for the 1- charge on the ion.
> 4. Coordinate bond: both electrons donated from N's lone pair to the third O atom.
> 5. Complete the lone pairs on each oxygen.
> 6. Enclose in square brackets and place the 1- charge as a superscript outside.
> 
> Without the square brackets and charge, you will lose the second mark.

parts.problemMd:
An ionic compound has the empirical formula H<sub>4</sub>N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>.

Suggest the formulae of the ions present in this compound.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The ions present in H<sub>4</sub>N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> are:
> 
> - NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> **[1 mark]**
> - NO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> H<sub>4</sub>N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> is the empirical formula of ammonium nitrate, NH<sub>4</sub>NO<sub>3</sub>. One NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> ion and one NO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> ion give the combined formula H<sub>4</sub>N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>, confirming the match.
> 
> Learn the formulae and charges of all common polyatomic ions as CIE will not provide them. Key ions to know: NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>, NO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup>, SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup>, CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2-</sup>, OH<sup>-</sup>, and PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3-</sup>.
> 
> Always include the correct charge on each ion in your answer. Both the formula and the charge are required for each mark.

parts.problemMd:
Draw a dot-and-cross diagram for the CN<sup>-</sup> ion.

Show outer shell electrons only.
parts.solutionMd:
The dot-and-cross diagram for the CN<sup>-</sup> ion is:

![Dot-and-cross diagram of the cyanide ion showing a triple bond between carbon and nitrogen, with a lone pair on carbon and a lone pair on nitrogen, enclosed in square brackets with a 1- charge](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/3-chemical-bonding/3-7-dot-and-cross-diagrams/assets/023-dot-and-cross-diagram-of-the-cyanide-ion-showing.png)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct bonding: C≡N triple bond with correct electron distribution
> 
> 1 mark for the complete structure: lone pairs on both C and N **AND** square brackets **AND** 1- charge outside the brackets

> **[exam-tip]**
> The CN<sup>-</sup> ion has 10 outer electrons in total: 4 from carbon, 5 from nitrogen, and 1 extra for the 1- charge.
> 
> Distribute them as follows:
> 
> - Form a C≡N triple bond using 6 of the 10 electrons (3 shared pairs).
> - The remaining 4 electrons form 2 lone pairs: one on carbon and one on nitrogen.
> 
> Remember the ionic notation: square brackets around the complete structure with the 1- charge as a superscript outside. This is required for the second mark.

parts.problemMd:
Compare the C≡N bond energy and bond length in the cyanide ion, CN<sup>-</sup>, with the C-N bond energy and bond length in methylamine, CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>.

Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Comparing the C≡N bond in the cyanide ion with the C-N bond in methylamine:
> 
> - The bond energy of C≡N in CN<sup>-</sup> is greater than the bond energy of C-N in methylamine **[1 mark]**
> - The bond length of C≡N in CN<sup>-</sup> is shorter than the bond length of C-N in methylamine **[1 mark]**
> - CN<sup>-</sup> contains a triple bond whereas methylamine contains a single bond; a triple bond has greater electron density between the nuclei, requiring more energy to break **AND** pulling the nuclei closer together **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Bond energy and bond length are inversely related: the stronger the bond (higher bond energy), the shorter it is. Both trends have the same cause. More shared electron pairs between two nuclei means stronger electrostatic attraction, which pulls the atoms closer together and makes the bond harder to break.
> 
> The CIE 9701 definitions to know:
> 
> - Bond energy: the energy required to break one mole of a particular covalent bond in the gaseous state
> - Bond length: the internuclear distance between two covalently bonded atoms
> 
> CIE 9701 uses the term bond energy (not bond enthalpy). Use the correct term in your answer.

name: The Gaseous State: Ideal & Real Gases & pV = nRT

parts.problemMd: Which diagram shows the graph of *p*V against *n* for an ideal gas at constant pressure and temperature?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- The ideal gas equation *pV = nRT* rearranges to:

*pV* = (*RT*) × *n*

- At constant *p* and *T*, this is in the form *y = mx*: a straight line through the origin with gradient *RT*.
- **D** shows a straight line through the origin, showing a directly proportional relationship between *pV* and *n*.

**A** is incorrect as the line does not pass through the origin, implying *pV* is non-zero when *n* = 0.

**B** is incorrect as the line is curved, inconsistent with *pV* being directly proportional to *n*.

**C** is incorrect as a horizontal line implies *pV* is constant as *n* increases. This would mean adding more moles at constant *p* and *T* does not change the volume, which contradicts *pV = nRT*.

parts.problemMd:
The *M*<sub>*r*</sub>* *value of a gas can be calculated from the general gas equation.

Which expression will give the value of *M*<sub>r</sub> for a sample of a gas of mass *m *grams?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- The molar mass of a gas can be derived from the ideal gas law, *pV = nRT*.
- The definition of molar mass is used to replace *n* in the equation.
- The *M*<sub>r</sub> of a substance is the mass of 6.02 x 10<sup>23</sup> molecules (one mole), therefore:

*n* = $\frac{m}{M_{r}}$

- Substituting for *n* in the ideal gas law equation:

*pV* = $\frac{m}{M_{r}} \times R T$

- Rearranging for *M*<sub>r</sub>:

*M*<sub>r</sub> = $\frac{mRT}{pV}$

parts.problemMd: Which gas least resembles an ideal gas at room temperature?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- Ideal behaviour is seen with identical particles with no internal structure, no volume, random motion, no intermolecular forces and elastic collisions (no loss of momentum).
- Ammonia has strong intermolecular forces (hydrogen bonding), so it deviates most from ideal behaviour.

**B** is incorrect as carbon dioxide only experiences instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces, which are weaker than hydrogen bonds.

**C** is incorrect as helium behaves most like an ideal gas at room temperature due to its weak instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces and small atomic radius.

**D** is incorrect as hydrogen only experiences instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces, which are weaker than hydrogen bonds.

choices.label: A
choices.textMd: Intermolecular forces of attraction exist between gas molecules.

choices.label: B
choices.textMd: Ideal gas molecules collide inelastically upon impact with each other.

choices.label: C
choices.textMd: One mole of an ideal gas occupies the same volume under the same conditions of temperature and pressure.

choices.label: D
choices.textMd: The volume of a given mass of an ideal gas is doubled if its temperature is raised from 25℃ to 50 ℃.

parts.problemMd:
The ideal gas equation below summarises the gas laws.

*pV = nRT*

Which statement below is correct?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- The ideal gas equation is:

*pV = nRT*

- Where *p* is pressure (Pa), *V* is the volume (m<sup>3</sup>), *n* is the number of moles, *R* is the gas constant (8.31 J K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>), and *T* is the temperature (K).
- **Avogadro's law**:

  - For a confined gas, the volume (*V*) and the number of moles (*n*) are directly proportional if the pressure and temperature both remain constant.

**A** is incorrect as the presence of intermolecular forces is not a gas law. An ideal gas will have no intermolecular forces between the molecules.

**B** is incorrect as in an ideal gas particles need to collide elastically (i.e. not lose momentum).

**D** is incorrect as the temperature is in °C, not kelvin. **Charles's law** states that the volume of a given amount of gas is directly proportional to its temperature on the kelvin scale when the pressure is held constant.

parts.problemMd:
Which conditions of pressure and temperature give the most accurate value of *M*<sub>r</sub>?

|   | **Pressure** | **Temperature** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | Low | High |
| **B** | Low | Low |
| **C** | High | High |
| **D** | High | Low |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- For *pV = nRT* to give an accurate *M*<sub>r</sub>, the gas must behave as close to ideal as possible.

- At **low pressure**, molecules are widely spaced, which means that molecular volume is negligible relative to the container volume, and intermolecular forces are negligible.

- At **high temperature**, kinetic energy far outweighs intermolecular forces between molecules, so the gas approximates ideal behaviour.

**B** is incorrect as low temperature means kinetic energy is small relative to intermolecular forces, causing greater deviation from ideal behaviour.

**C** is incorrect as high pressure causes significant molecular volume and intermolecular force effects.

**D** is incorrect as high pressure and low temperature both promote non-ideal behaviour.

parts.problemMd:
0.96 g of hydrogen gas is contained in a sealed vessel of volume of 7.0 × 10<sup>−3</sup> m<sup>3</sup> at a temperature of 303 K.

Assume the gas behaves as an ideal gas.

What is the pressure of the vessel?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- The ideal gas equation is *pV = nRT*

- Rearranged for pressure:

p = $\frac{nRT}{V}$

- Number of moles of hydrogen (H<sub>2</sub>, *M*<sub>r</sub> = 2):

n = $\frac{0.96}{2}$ = 0.48 mol

- Known quantities:

  - Number of moles; 0.48 mol
  - Volume; 7.0 × 10<sup>−3</sup> m<sup>3</sup>
  - Temperature; 303 K
- Substitution into the equation:

p = $\frac{0.48\times8.31\times303}{7.0\times10^{-3}}$

p = 172700 Pa ≈ 173 kPa

**A** is incorrect as 172.7 Pa results from using the volume as 7.0 m<sup>3</sup> rather than 7.0 × 10<sup>−3</sup> m<sup>3</sup>, a factor-of-1000 error.

**C** is incorrect as 345 kPa results from using the relative atomic mass of hydrogen (*A*<sub>r</sub> = 1) rather than the molecular mass of H<sub>2</sub> (*M*<sub>r</sub> = 2), doubling the number of moles and the pressure.

**D** is incorrect as 691.1 kPa results from using *A*<sub>r</sub> = 1 for hydrogen combined with a further factor-of-two error in the moles calculation.

parts.problemMd:
A 5370 cm<sup>3</sup> sample of oxygen is measured at a temperature of 60 °C. The pressure measured was 103 kPa.

Assume the gas behaves as an ideal gas.

What is the mass of the sample of oxygen?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- The ideal gas equation is:

*pV = nRT*

- Rearranged for number of moles:

n = $\frac{pV}{RT}$

- Known quantities:

  - Pressure; 103 kPa = 103000 Pa
  - Volume; 5370 cm<sup>3</sup> = 0.00537 m<sup>3</sup>
  - Temperature; 60 °C = 333 K
- Substitution into the equation:

n = $\frac{103000\times0.00537}{8.31\times333}$

n = 0.1999 mol

- Mass of oxygen (O<sub>2</sub>, *M*<sub>r</sub> = 32):

*mass = n × M*<sub>r</sub> = 0.1999 × 32 = 6.4 g

**A** is incorrect as 1.8 g results from using *M*<sub>r</sub> = 18 (for water) instead of *M*<sub>r</sub> = 32 for oxygen.

**B** is incorrect as 3.2 g results from using the relative atomic mass of oxygen (*A*<sub>r</sub> = 16) rather than the molecular mass of O<sub>2</sub> (*M*<sub>r</sub> = 32), giving half the correct mass.

**C** is incorrect as 3.6 g results from an error in the volume unit conversion.

parts.problemMd:
A sample of chlorine gas with a mass of 5.35 g has a volume of 1.247 × 10<sup>−3</sup> m<sup>3</sup> at a pressure of 1.00 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa.

Assuming the gas acts as an ideal gas, what is the temperature of the gas?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- The ideal gas equation is *pV = nRT*

- Rearranged for temperature:

*T* = $\frac{pV}{nR}$

- Number of moles of Cl<sub>2</sub> (*M*<sub>r</sub> = 71):

n = $\frac{5.35}{71}$ = 0.075 mol

- Known quantities:

  - Pressure; 1.00 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa.
  - Volume; 1.247 × 10<sup>−3</sup> m<sup>3</sup>.
  - Number of moles; 0.075 mol.
- Substitution into the equation:

*T* = `\frac{\left(\right. 1 . 0 \times 10^{5} \left.\right) \times \left(\right. 1 . 247 \times 10^{- 3} \left.\right)}{0 . 075 \times 8 . 31}`

*T* = 200 K

**A** is incorrect as 100 K results from using the relative atomic mass of chlorine (*A*<sub>r</sub> = 35.5) rather than the molecular mass of Cl<sub>2</sub> (*M*<sub>r</sub> = 71), doubling the number of moles and halving the temperature.

**C** is incorrect as 250 K results from an error in the moles calculation.

**D** is incorrect as 300 K results from a molar mass error in the calculation.

parts.problemMd:
A bubble rose from the sea bed to the surface. The bubble had a volume of 200 cm<sup>3</sup> at a pressure of 101 kPa just below the surface. The temperature at the sea bed and the surface are the same.

The pressure at the sea bed is 2020 kPa. Assume the gas behaves as an ideal gas.

What is the volume of the bubble at the sea bed?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- At constant temperature, Boyle's Law applies.

  - Since both pressures are in kPa, no unit conversion is needed:

*P*<sub>1</sub>*V*<sub>1</sub> = *P*<sub>2</sub>*V*<sub>2</sub>

*V*<sub>2</sub> = $\frac{P_{1}}{P_{2}}$ × *V*<sub>1</sub> = $\frac{101}{2020}$ × 200 = **10 cm**<sup>**3**</sup>

**B** is incorrect as 200 cm<sup>3</sup> would imply no change in volume, requiring equal pressures.

**C** is incorrect as 100 cm<sup>3</sup> results from an arithmetic error in the pressure ratio.

**D** is incorrect as 4000 cm<sup>3</sup> results from applying the ratio in the wrong direction: *P*<sub>2</sub>/*P*<sub>1</sub> × *V*<sub>1</sub> = 2020/101 × 200 = 4000 cm<sup>3</sup>.

parts.problemMd:
Sodium reacts with water in the equation below.

2Na (s) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l) → 2NaOH (aq) + H<sub>2</sub> (g)

Which mass of sodium reacts with water to produce 960 cm<sup>3</sup> of hydrogen gas at r.t.p.?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- At r.t.p., 1 mol of gas occupies 24.0 dm<sup>3</sup>, so n(H<sub>2</sub>) = 0.960 ÷ 24.0 = 0.0400 mol
- From the equation, 2 mol Na produces 1 mol H<sub>2</sub>, so n(Na) = 2 × 0.0400 = 0.0800 mol
- Mass of sodium = 0.0800 × 23.0 = 1.84 g

**A** is incorrect because it halves the amount of hydrogen instead of doubling it: 0.0200 × 23.0

**B** is incorrect because it assumes a 1 : 1 ratio of Na to H<sub>2</sub>: 0.0400 × 23.0

**D** is incorrect because it treats sodium as Na<sub>2</sub> and uses 46.0: 0.0800 × 46.0

parts.problemMd: At 298 K and 101 kPa, which is the only compound that exists as a gas?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- A temperature of 298 K is room temperature (25 °C) and a pressure of 101 kPa is 1 atmosphere.
- Chloroethane has a polar C–Cl bond, giving rise to permanent dipole-permanent dipole forces and instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces.

  - These are weaker than hydrogen bonds.
- So, chloroethane has a boiling point below 298 K and is a gas at room temperature.

**A** is incorrect as 1-aminopropane has an N–H bond which allows hydrogen bonding between molecules, making it a liquid at 298 K.

**C** is incorrect as ethane-1,2-diol has two O–H bonds and forms extensive hydrogen bonding, so it is a liquid at 298 K.
