parts.problemMd:
The diagram shows a Hess's law cycle for the conversion of graphite to diamond.

![Hess's law enthalpy cycle for the conversion of graphite to diamond, showing ΔH~1~ for combustion of graphite, ΔH~2~ for combustion of diamond, and ΔH~r~ for the graphite to diamond conversion](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/5-chemical-energetics/5-2-hesss-law/assets/001-hess-s-law-enthalpy-cycle-for-the-conversion-of-.png)

Which equation represents ΔH<sub>r</sub>?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B because:**

- To calculate Δ*H*<sub>r</sub> using Hess's law, find an alternative route through the cycle:
- Travel along Δ*H*<sub>1</sub> in the same direction = add Δ*H*<sub>1</sub>
- Travel along Δ*H*<sub>2</sub> in the opposite direction = subtract Δ*H*<sub>2</sub>
- This gives Δ*H*<sub>r</sub> = Δ*H*<sub>1</sub> − Δ*H*<sub>2</sub>

**A **is incorrect as it adds both enthalpy changes rather than subtracting Δ*H*<sub>2</sub>.

**C **is incorrect as the signs of Δ*H*<sub>1</sub> and Δ*H*<sub>2</sub> are reversed. It is Δ*H*<sub>1</sub> − Δ*H*<sub>2</sub>, not Δ*H*<sub>2</sub> − Δ*H*<sub>1</sub>.

**D **is incorrect as it reverses both arrows, giving a negative sum. Only Δ*H*<sub>2</sub> is reversed in the correct route.

parts.problemMd:
What is the standard enthalpy change of formation, Δ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup>, of propan-1-ol, C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O?

| **Substance** | Δ*H*<sub>c</sub><sup>θ</sup>** / kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> |
|---|---|
| C (s) | −394 |
| H<sub>2</sub> (g) | −286 |
| C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O (l) | −1816 |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Known quantities:

  - Δ*H*<sub>c</sub><sup>θ</sup>(C (s)) = −394 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>
  - Δ*H*<sub>c</sub><sup>θ</sup>(H<sub>2</sub> (g)) = −286 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>
  - Δ*H*<sub>c</sub><sup>θ</sup>(C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O (l)) = −1816 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>
- Formula C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O requires 3 mol C and 4 mol H<sub>2</sub> as elements (O<sub>2</sub> has Δ*H*<sub>c</sub><sup>θ</sup> = 0)
- Calculate Δ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup>(C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O):

Δ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup> = ΣΔ*H*<sub>c</sub><sup>θ</sup>(elements) − Δ*H*<sub>c</sub><sup>θ</sup>(compound)

ΣΔ*H*<sub>c</sub><sup>θ</sup>(elements) = 3(−394) + 4(−286) = −1182 + (−1144) = −2326 kJ

Δ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup> = −2326 − (−1816) = −2326 + 1816 = **−510 kJ mol**<sup>**−1**</sup>

**A** is incorrect as it inverts the formula and uses only 1 mol each of C and H<sub>2</sub>: (−1816) − [(−394) + (−286)] = −1816 + 680 = −1136 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>.

**C** is incorrect as it inverts the formula with the correct stoichiometry: (−1816) − (−2326) = +510 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>.

**D** is incorrect as it uses only 1 mol each of C and H<sub>2</sub> with the correct formula: [(−394) + (−286)] − (−1816) = −680 + 1816 = +1136 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>.

parts.problemMd:
The first stage in the industrial production of nitric acid from ammonia can be represented by the following equation.

4NH<sub>3</sub> (g) + 5O<sub>2</sub> (g) ⇌ 4NO (g) + 6H<sub>2</sub>O (g)

Using the following standard enthalpy change of formation data, what is the standard enthalpy change of reaction, Δ*H*<sub>r</sub><sup>θ</sup>, for this reaction?

| **Compound** | ***∆H***<sub>**f**</sub><sup>**θ**</sup>** /kJ mol**<sup>**–1**</sup> |
|---|---|
| NH<sub>3</sub> (g) | −51.3 |
| NO (g) | +92.2 |
| H<sub>2</sub>O (g) | −239.6 |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Known quantities:

  - Δ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup>(NH<sub>3</sub> (g)) = −51.3 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>
  - Δ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup>(NO (g)) = +92.2 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>
  - Δ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup>(H<sub>2</sub>O (g)) = −239.6 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>
  - Δ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup>(O<sub>2</sub> (g)) = 0 (element in standard state)
- Calculate Δ*H*<sub>r</sub><sup>θ</sup> for 4NH<sub>3</sub> (g) + 5O<sub>2</sub> (g) ⇌ 4NO (g) + 6H<sub>2</sub>O (g):

Δ*H*<sub>r</sub><sup>θ</sup> = ΣΔ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup>(products) − ΣΔ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup>(reactants)

ΣΔ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup>(products) = 4(+92.2) + 6(−239.6) = +368.8 + (−1437.6) = −1068.8 kJ

ΣΔ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup>(reactants) = 4(−51.3) + 5(0) = −205.2 kJ

Δ*H*<sub>r</sub><sup>θ</sup> = −1068.8 − (−205.2) = −1068.8 + 205.2 = **−863.6 kJ mol**<sup>**−1**</sup>

**A** is incorrect as it gives +863.6 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>, which has the correct magnitude but the wrong sign. This is caused by reversing the products and reactants in the formula: (−205.2) − (−1068.8) = +863.6 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>.

**B** is incorrect as it gives −1601.2 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>. This is caused by an error in the stoichiometric coefficients applied to the product enthalpies.

**D** is incorrect as it gives −1274.0 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>. This is caused by from treating Δ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup>(NH<sub>3</sub>) as positive (+51.3) instead of negative: −1068.8 − (+205.2) = −1274.0 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>.

parts.problemMd:
Titanium occurs naturally as the mineral rutile, TiO<sub>2</sub>. One possible method of extraction of titanium is to reduce it by heating with carbon.

TiO<sub>2</sub> (s) + 2C (s) → Ti (s) + 2CO (g)

The standard enthalpy changes of formation of TiO<sub>2</sub> (s) and CO (g) are –890 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup> and –105 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup> respectively.

What is the standard enthalpy change of reaction, Δ*H*<sub>r</sub><sup>θ</sup>, for this reaction?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Known quantities:

  - Δ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup>(TiO<sub>2</sub> (s)) = −890 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>
  - Δ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup>(CO (g)) = −105 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>
  - Δ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup>(C (s)) = 0 and Δ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup>(Ti (s)) = 0 (elements in standard state)
- Calculate Δ*H*<sub>r</sub><sup>θ</sup> for TiO<sub>2</sub> (s) + 2C (s) → Ti (s) + 2CO (g):

Δ*H*<sub>r</sub><sup>θ</sup> = ΣΔ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup>(products) − ΣΔ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup>(reactants)

ΣΔ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup>(products) = 0 + 2(−105) = −210 kJ

ΣΔ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup>(reactants) = (−890) + 2(0) = −890 kJ

Δ*H*<sub>r</sub><sup>θ</sup> = (−210) − (−890) = −210 + 890 = **+680 kJ mol**<sup>**−1**</sup>

**A** is incorrect as it gives −785 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>. This is caused by using only 1 mol of CO instead of 2 mol and then reversing the sign: (−105) − (−890) = +785, taken as −785 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>.

**B** is incorrect as it gives −680 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>, which is the correct magnitude with the wrong sign. This is caused by reversing the products and reactants in the formula: (−890) − (−210) = −680 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>.

**D** is incorrect as it gives +785 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>. This is caused by using only 1 mol of CO instead of the correct 2 mol: (−105) − (−890) = +785 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>.

parts.problemMd:
The combustion of ethanol is increasingly being used to fuel cars.

| **Substance** | Δ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup>** / kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> |
|---|---|
| CO<sub>2</sub> (g) | −382 |
| H<sub>2</sub>O (g) | −275 |
| C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH (l) | −266 |

What is the standard enthalpy change of combustion, Δ*H*<sub>c</sub><sup>θ</sup>, of ethanol?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- Known quantities:

  - Δ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup>(CO<sub>2</sub> (g)) = −382 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>
  - Δ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup>(H<sub>2</sub>O (g)) = −275 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>
  - Δ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup>(C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH (l)) = −266 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>
  - Δ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup>(O<sub>2</sub> (g)) = 0 (element in standard state)
- Combustion equation:

C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH (l) + 3O<sub>2</sub> (g) → 2CO<sub>2</sub> (g) + 3H<sub>2</sub>O (g)

- Calculate Δ*H*<sub>c</sub><sup>θ</sup>(C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH):

Δ*H*<sub>c</sub><sup>θ</sup> = ΣΔ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup>(products) − ΣΔ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup>(reactants)

ΣΔ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup>(products) = 2(−382) + 3(−275) = −764 + (−825) = −1589 kJ

ΣΔ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup>(reactants) = (−266) + 3(0) = −266 kJ

Δ*H*<sub>c</sub><sup>θ</sup> = (−1589) − (−266) = −1589 + 266 = **−1323 kJ mol**<sup>**−1**</sup>

**B** is incorrect as it uses 1 mol of CO<sub>2</sub> and 1 mol of H<sub>2</sub>O instead of the correct 2 and 3: [(−382) + (−275)] − (−266) = −657 + 266 = −391 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>.

**C** is incorrect as it inverts the formula and uses 1 mol of each product: (−266) − [(−382) + (−275)] = −266 + 657 = +391 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>.

**D** is incorrect as it inverts the formula with the correct stoichiometry: (−266) − (−1589) = +1323 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>.

parts.problemMd:
The equations for the formation of two sulfur oxides are shown.

S (s) + O<sub>2 </sub>(g) → SO<sub>2</sub> (g)     *∆H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup> = –297 kJ mol<sup>–1</sup>

S (s) + 1.5O<sub>2</sub> (g) → SO<sub>3</sub> (g)    *∆H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup> = –395 kJ mol<sup>–1</sup>

What is the standard enthalpy change of reaction, Δ*H*<sub>r</sub><sup>θ</sup>, for 2SO<sub>2</sub> (g) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) → 2SO<sub>3</sub> (g)?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- Known quantities:

  - Δ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup>(SO<sub>2</sub>) = −297 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>
  - Δ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup>(SO<sub>3</sub>) = −395 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>
  - Stoichiometry from the target equation: 2 mol of each
- Calculate Δ*H*<sub>r</sub><sup>θ</sup>:

Δ*H*<sub>r</sub><sup>θ</sup> = ΣΔ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup>(products) − ΣΔ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup>(reactants)

ΣΔ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup>(2SO<sub>3</sub>) = 2 × (−395) = −790 kJ

ΣΔ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup>(2SO<sub>2</sub>) = 2 × (−297) = −594 kJ

Δ*H*<sub>r</sub><sup>θ</sup> = (−790) − (−594) = **−196 kJ mol**<sup>**−1**</sup>

**B** is incorrect as it uses a coefficient of 1 for both sulfur oxides instead of 2: (−395) − (−297) = −98 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>.

**C** is incorrect as it uses a coefficient of 1 and reverses the products and reactants: (−297) − (−395) = +98 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>.

**D** is incorrect as it reverses the products and reactants with the correct stoichiometric coefficients: 2(−297) − 2(−395) = +196 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>.

parts.problemMd:
A student calculated the standard enthalpy change of formation of propane, C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub>, using the standard enthalpy changes of combustion shown.

| **Substance** | Δ*H*<sub>*c*</sub><sup>θ</sup>** / kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> |
|---|---|
| C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub> (g) | −2220 |
| H<sub>2</sub> (g) | −286 |
| C (s) | Y |

The student used an incorrect value, Y, for the standard enthalpy change of combustion of carbon but performed the calculation correctly. The final answer obtained was −158 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>.

What value did the student use for the standard enthalpy change of combustion of carbon?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Known quantities:

  - Δ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup>(C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub>) = −158 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup> (the student's calculated answer)
  - Δ*H*<sub>c</sub><sup>θ</sup>(C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub>) = −2220 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>
  - Δ*H*<sub>c</sub><sup>θ</sup>(H<sub>2</sub>) = −286 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>
  - Δ*H*<sub>c</sub><sup>θ</sup>(C) = Y kJ mol<sup>−1</sup> (unknown)
- Calculate Y using the Hess's law formation expression:

Δ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup>(C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub>) = ΣΔ*H*<sub>c</sub><sup>θ</sup>(elements) − Δ*H*<sub>c</sub><sup>θ</sup>(compound)

−158 = [3Y + 4 × (−286)] − (−2220)

−158 = 3Y − 1144 + 2220

−158 = 3Y + 1076

3Y = −1234

Y = −1234 ÷ 3 = **−411 kJ mol**<sup>**−1**</sup>

**A** is incorrect as it gives −1234 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>, which is the value of 3Y before dividing by the stoichiometric coefficient of carbon.

**B** is incorrect as it uses only 1 mol of H<sub>2</sub> instead of 4 mol in the combustion equation for propane: [3Y + 1 × (−286)] − (−2220) = −158 gives Y = −697 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>.

**D** is incorrect as it inverts the Hess cycle expression, subtracting the element combustion enthalpies from the compound combustion enthalpy: (−2220) − [3Y + 4(−286)] = −158 gives Y = −306 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>.

parts.problemMd:
Given the following standard enthalpy changes,

I<sub>2</sub> (s) → I<sub>2</sub> (g)   ∆H<sup>Ɵ</sup> = +38 kJ mol<sup>–1</sup>

I<sub>2</sub> (g) + 3Cl<sub>2</sub> (g) → 2ICl<sub>3</sub> (s)   ∆H<sup>Ɵ</sup> = –214 kJ mol<sup>–1</sup>

What is the standard enthalpy change of formation, Δ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup>, of ICl<sub>3</sub> (s)?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Known quantities:
- I<sub>2</sub> (s) → I<sub>2</sub> (g): Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> = +38 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>
- I<sub>2</sub> (g) + 3Cl<sub>2</sub> (g) → 2ICl<sub>3</sub> (s): Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> = −214 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>
- Target: Δ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup>(ICl<sub>3</sub> (s)) for 1 mol, from I<sub>2</sub> (s) and Cl<sub>2</sub> (g)

- Both equations produce 2 mol of ICl<sub>3</sub> (s); halve each to give 1 mol

![Hess's law cycle for the formation of 1 mol of ICl~3~ (s) from I~2~ (s) and Cl~2~ (g), showing the sublimation of I~2~ and the reaction of I~2~ (g) with Cl~2~ (g)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/5-chemical-energetics/5-2-hesss-law/assets/005-hess-s-law-cycle-for-the-formation-of-1-mol-of-i.jpg)

- Halved sublimation step:

½ × (+38) = +19 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>

- Halved reaction step:

½ × (−214) = −107 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>

- Calculate Δ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup>(ICl<sub>3</sub>):

Δ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup>(ICl<sub>3</sub>) = +19 + (−107) = **−88 kJ mol**<sup>**−1**</sup>

**A** is incorrect as it uses the full enthalpy of the second equation without halving: −214 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup> is the enthalpy for forming 2 mol of ICl<sub>3</sub> (s), not 1 mol.

**B** is incorrect as it uses both equations at full scale without halving: +38 + (−214) = −176 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>.

**C** is incorrect as it halves the second equation correctly but omits the sublimation step, starting from I<sub>2</sub> (g) rather than I<sub>2</sub> (s): ½ × (−214) = −107 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>.

parts.problemMd:
The following standard enthalpy changes are given.

CO (g) + $\frac{1}{2}$ O<sub>2</sub> (g)   → CO<sub>2</sub> (g)   ∆*H*<sup>θ</sup>  = –283 kJ mol<sup>–1</sup>

H<sub>2</sub> (g) + $\frac{1}{2}$ O<sub>2</sub> (g)   → H<sub>2</sub>O (I)   ∆*H*<sup>θ</sup>  = –286 kJ mol<sup>–1</sup>

H<sub>2</sub>O (g)   → H<sub>2</sub>O (I)   ∆*H*<sup>θ</sup> = –44 kJ mol<sup>–1</sup>

What is the standard enthalpy change, Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup>, for the following reaction?

CO<sub>2</sub> (g) + H<sub>2</sub> (g) → CO (g) + H<sub>2</sub>O (g)
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Known quantities:

  - CO (g) + ½O<sub>2</sub> (g) → CO<sub>2</sub> (g): Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> = −283 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup> (equation 1)
  - H<sub>2</sub> (g) + ½O<sub>2</sub> (g) → H<sub>2</sub>O (l): Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> = −286 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup> (equation 2)
  - H<sub>2</sub>O (g) → H<sub>2</sub>O (l): Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> = −44 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup> (equation 3)
- Target reaction:

CO<sub>2</sub> (g) + H<sub>2</sub> (g) → CO (g) + H<sub>2</sub>O (g)

- Reverse equation 1 (CO<sub>2</sub> → CO + ½O<sub>2</sub>): +283 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>
- Use equation 2 as written (H<sub>2</sub> + ½O<sub>2</sub> → H<sub>2</sub>O (l)): −286 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>
- Reverse equation 3 (H<sub>2</sub>O (l) → H<sub>2</sub>O (g)): +44 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup> ![Hess's law cycle showing the route from CO~2~ (g) and H~2~ (g) to CO (g) and H~2~O (g) via CO~2~, H~2~O (l), and the three given equations](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/5-chemical-energetics/5-2-hesss-law/assets/002-hess-s-law-cycle-showing-the-route-from-co-2-g-a.jpg)
- Calculate Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> by combining the three equations:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> = +283 + (−286) + 44 = **+41 kJ mol**<sup>**−1**</sup>

**A** is incorrect as it gives the enthalpy change for the reverse of the target reaction: −(+41) = −41 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>.

**B** is incorrect as it omits the H<sub>2</sub>O vaporisation step (equation 3): +283 + (−286) = −3 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>.

**C** is incorrect as it omits equation 3 and uses equation 1 in the forward direction rather than reversed: (−283) + (+286) = +3 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>.

parts.problemMd:
Iodine trichloride, ICl<sub>3</sub>, is made by reacting iodine with chlorine.

I<sub>2</sub> (s) + Cl<sub>2</sub> (g) → 2ICl (s)   Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> = +14 kJ mol<sup>–1</sup>

ICl (s) + Cl<sub>2</sub> (g) → ICl<sub>3</sub> (s)   Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> = –88 kJ mol<sup>–1</sup>

What is the standard enthalpy change of formation, Δ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup>, of solid iodine trichloride?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Known quantities:

  - I<sub>2</sub> (s) + Cl<sub>2</sub> (g) → 2ICl (s): Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> = +14 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup> (equation 1)
  - ICl (s) + Cl<sub>2</sub> (g) → ICl<sub>3</sub> (s): Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> = −88 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup> (equation 2)
- Target:

  - Δ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup>(ICl<sub>3</sub> (s)) for 1 mol, from I<sub>2</sub> (s) and Cl<sub>2</sub> (g)
- Equation 1 produces 2 mol of ICl (s); halve it to give 1 mol of ICl (s) as intermediate ![Hess's law cycle for the formation of 1 mol of ICl~3~ (s) from I~2~ (s) and Cl~2~ (g), showing the intermediate formation of ICl (s) via two steps](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/5-chemical-energetics/5-2-hesss-law/assets/003-hess-s-law-cycle-for-the-formation-of-1-mol-of-i.jpg)
- Halved equation 1:

½ × (+14) = +7 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>

- Equation 2 as written:

−88 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>

- Calculate Δ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup>(ICl<sub>3</sub>):

Δ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup>(ICl<sub>3</sub>) = +7 + (−88) = **−81 kJ mol**<sup>**−1**</sup>

**A** is incorrect as it uses the full first equation and applies equation 2 twice: +14 + 2(−88) = −162 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>.

**C** is incorrect as it uses the full first equation without halving: +14 + (−88) = −74 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>.

**D** is incorrect as it gives −60 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>, arising from an incorrect combination of the two equations without the required halving adjustment.

parts.problemMd:
Standard enthalpy changes include enthalpy of formation, enthalpy of combustion and enthalpy of neutralisation.

i) Define the term standard enthalpy change of formation.

[2]

ii) Construct an equation that represents the standard enthalpy change of formation of ammonia, NH<sub>3</sub>. Include state symbols.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The standard enthalpy change of formation is:
> 
> - The enthalpy change when one mole of a compound is formed from its elements **[1 mark]**
> - In their standard states, under standard conditions (298 K and 100 kPa) **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The equation representing the standard enthalpy change of formation of ammonia is:
> 
> - ½N<sub>2</sub> (g) + 1½H<sub>2</sub> (g) → NH<sub>3</sub> (g) **[1 mark]**
> 
> Equations using integers (e.g. N<sub>2</sub> (g) + 3H<sub>2</sub> (g) → 2NH<sub>3</sub> (g)) are not accepted as they do not represent the formation of one mole of NH<sub>3</sub>

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part i), both marking points must be included to score both marks. The enthalpy change involves forming one mole of a compound from its elements, and the elements must be in their standard states — the most stable form of each element at 298 K and 100 kPa. For example, the standard state of carbon is graphite (not diamond), and the standard state of bromine is liquid Br<sub>2</sub> (not gas).
> 
> For part ii), CIE accepts fractional coefficients in enthalpy of formation equations. The equation must produce exactly one mole of NH<sub>3</sub>. Using N<sub>2</sub> (g) + 3H<sub>2</sub> (g) → 2NH<sub>3</sub> (g) does not score the mark because it represents the formation of two moles.

parts.problemMd: State what is meant by standard conditions in enthalpy measurements.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Standard conditions in enthalpy measurements are:
> 
> - A temperature of 298 K
> **AND**
> A pressure of 100 kPa **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A common error is to give the temperature in degrees Celsius (25 °C) rather than kelvin. CIE requires the temperature in kelvin (298 K) and the pressure in kPa (100 kPa).

parts.problemMd:
The equation for the reaction between dilute sulfuric acid and aqueous sodium hydroxide is shown.

H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (aq) + 2NaOH (aq) → Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (aq) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l)

Explain why the enthalpy change for this reaction does not represent the standard enthalpy change of neutralisation.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The enthalpy change does not represent the standard enthalpy change of neutralisation because:
> 
> - The standard enthalpy change of neutralisation is defined as the enthalpy change when one mole of water is formed from the reaction of an acid and a base **[1 mark]**
> - This reaction produces two moles of water / the equation must be halved so that only one mole of water is produced **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The key criterion for the standard enthalpy change of neutralisation is that exactly one mole of water must be formed. The identity of the acid and base does not matter.
> 
> Always check the coefficient of water in any neutralisation equation. If it is not 1, the equation does not directly represent the standard enthalpy change of neutralisation.

parts.problemMd:
Freon 21 is a hydrochlorofluorocarbon that was used as a propellant and refrigerant but later withdrawn from use because of its effect on ozone depletion. The formula is CHCl<sub>2</sub>F.

Freon 21 is produced by reacting hydrogen fluoride with trichloromethane in the following reaction:

CHCl<sub>3</sub> (g) + HF (g) → CHCl<sub>2</sub>F (g) + HCl (g)

Use the data in Table 2.1 to calculate the standard enthalpy change of reaction, Δ*H*°<sub>r</sub>, for this reaction. Show your working.

| Compound | Standard enthalpy change of formation, Δ*H*°<sub>f</sub> / kJ mol<sup>–1</sup> |
|---|---|
| CHCl<sub>3</sub> (g) | –103.2 |
| CHCl<sub>2</sub>F (g) | –284.1 |
| HF (g) | –273.3 |
| HCl (g) | –92.3 |

**Table 2.1**
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the standard enthalpy change of reaction, Δ*H*°<sub>r</sub>:

- State the relationship:

Δ*H*°<sub>r</sub> = ΣΔ*H*°<sub>f</sub> (products) − ΣΔ*H*°<sub>f</sub> (reactants)

- Substitute the values from Table 2.1:

Δ*H*°<sub>r</sub> = [(–284.1) + (–92.3)] − [(–103.2) + (–273.3)] **[1 mark]**

Δ*H*°<sub>r</sub> = –376.4 − (–376.5)

Δ*H*°<sub>r</sub> = **+0.1 kJ mol**<sup>**–1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct substitution: [(–284.1) + (–92.3)] − [(–103.2) + (–273.3)]
> 
> 1 mark for correct final answer: +0.1 kJ mol<sup>–1</sup> (allow 0.1 kJ mol<sup>–1</sup>)

> **[exam-tip]**
> The formula for calculating the standard enthalpy change of reaction using standard enthalpies of formation is:
> 
> Δ*H*°<sub>r</sub> = ΣΔ*H*°<sub>f</sub> (products) − ΣΔ*H*°<sub>f</sub> (reactants)
> 
> All four values in the table are negative. Be careful with the signs when subtracting a group of negative values — use brackets around each set of products and reactants to avoid sign errors.
> 
> The answer is very close to zero (+0.1 kJ mol<sup>–1</sup>), meaning the reaction is approximately thermoneutral. This affects how you draw the reaction pathway diagram in part (b): the two horizontal lines should be at almost the same height.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Freon 21 is a hydrochlorofluorocarbon that was used as a propellant and refrigerant but later withdrawn from use because of its effect on ozone depletion. The formula is CHCl₂F.

Freon 21 is produced by reacting hydrogen fluoride with trichloromethane in the following reaction:

CHCl₃ (g) + HF (g) → CHCl₂F (g) + HCl (g)

Use the data in Table 2.1 to calculate the standard enthalpy change of reaction, Δ*H*°r, for this reaction.

On Fig. 2.1, sketch a reaction pathway diagram for this reaction. Label the diagram to show the enthalpy change of reaction, Δ*H*°<sub>r</sub>, and the activation energy, *E*<sub>a</sub>.

**Fig. 2.1**
parts.solutionMd:
The completed reaction pathway diagram is:

![Reaction pathway diagram showing reactants and products at almost the same energy level with a curved hump above; ΔH°r labelled as a near-zero energy difference between reactants and products, and Ea labelled as an upward arrow from the reactants level to the peak of the curve](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/5-chemical-energetics/5-1-enthalpy-change-h/assets/018-reaction-pathway-diagram-showing-reactants-and-p.png)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a correctly drawn reaction profile with reactants and products labelled and at approximately the same energy level (Δ*H*°<sub>r</sub> ≈ 0), with a smooth curve showing a hump
> 
> 1 mark for activation energy *E*<sub>a</sub> correctly labelled as an upward arrow from the reactants energy level to the peak of the curve

> **[exam-tip]**
> Since the standard enthalpy change of reaction from part (a) is +0.1 kJ mol<sup>–1</sup>, which is very close to zero, the reactants and products should be drawn at almost identical heights. If you draw them far apart, you have not correctly applied the calculated value.
> 
> The activation energy is always shown as an arrow from the energy level of the reactants up to the peak of the curve. It represents the minimum energy that reactant particles must have to react.

parts.problemMd: Define the term activation energy.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The definition of activation energy is:
> 
> - The minimum energy required for a reaction to occur / the minimum energy that colliding particles must possess for a successful collision **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The activation energy, *E*<sub>a</sub>, is shown on a reaction pathway diagram as an arrow from the energy level of the reactants to the peak of the curve. It represents the energy barrier that reacting particles must overcome for the reaction to proceed.

parts.problemMd: Define the term bond energy.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The definition of bond energy is:
> 
> - The energy required to break one mole of a specified bond **[1 mark]**
> - In a gaseous molecule, averaged over a range of similar compounds **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The definition must include both marking points:
> 
> - Bond energy relates to breaking one mole of a specific bond
> - It is an average value taken from a variety of gaseous molecules.
> 
> The average is necessary because the exact energy depends on the molecular environment. A C–H bond in methane has a slightly different energy from a C–H bond in ethanol. Bond energies are always positive (endothermic) because breaking bonds always requires an input of energy.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The definition of bond energy is:

- The energy required to break one mole of a specified bond
- In a gaseous molecule, averaged over a range of similar compounds

Suggest why the value of Δ*H*<sub>r</sub> calculated using bond energies may differ from the value obtained by experiment.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The calculated value may differ from the experimental value because:
> 
> - Bond energies are average values (taken over a range of compounds and molecular environments) and not exact values for the specific bonds in the molecules **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Bond energy data tables list average values calculated from many different compounds. For example, the C–H bond energy is an average of the C–H bond energy in methane, ethane, ethanol, and many other molecules. The actual C–H bond energy in a specific molecule may differ slightly from this average, introducing a small error into the calculated enthalpy change.

parts.problemMd:
Use the data given in Table 3.1 to calculate the enthalpy change for the hydration of ethene to form ethanol. Show your working.

CH<sub>2</sub>=CH<sub>2</sub> (g) + H<sub>2</sub>O (g) → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH (l)

**Table 3.1**

| Bond | Bond energy / kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> |
|---|---|
| C–C | 346 |
| C=C | 614 |
| C–H | 414 |
| C–O | 358 |
| O–H | 463 |
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the enthalpy change for the hydration of ethene:

- List the bonds broken (endothermic) in the reactants:

E(C=C) = 1 x 614 = 614 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

E(C–H) = 4 x 414 = 1656 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

E(O–H) = 2 x 463 = 926 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

Total bonds broken = 614 + 1656 + 926 = 3196 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> **[1 mark]**

- List the bonds formed (exothermic) in the products:

E(C–C) = 1 x 346 = 346 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

E(C–H) = 5 x 414 = 2070 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

E(C–O) = 1 x 358 = 358 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

E(O–H) = 1 x 463 = 463 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

Total bonds formed = 346 + 2070 + 358 + 463 = 3237 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the enthalpy change:

Δ*H*<sub>r</sub> = total bonds broken − total bonds formed

Δ*H*<sub>r</sub> = 3196 − 3237

Δ*H*<sub>r</sub> = **−41 kJ mol**<sup>**−1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct total bonds broken: 3196 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for correct total bonds formed: 3237 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for correct final answer: −41 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

> **[exam-tip]**
> Drawing out the full structural formulae of the reactants and products helps you identify every bond.
> 
> ![Structural equation showing ethene reacting with water to form ethanol, with carbon–carbon double bond becoming single and –OH group added](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/5-chemical-energetics/5-1-enthalpy-change-h/assets/016-structural-equation-showing-ethene-reacting-with.jpeg)
> 
> In ethene (CH<sub>2</sub>=CH<sub>2</sub>), there are four C–H bonds and one C=C bond. Water (H<sub>2</sub>O) has two O–H bonds.
> 
> In ethanol (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH), there are five C–H bonds, one C–C bond, one C–O bond, and one O–H bond.

parts.problemMd:
Molecules of NO<sub>2</sub> can be formed by the reaction between N<sub>2</sub> and O<sub>2</sub>. The bond between the N and O atoms in NO<sub>2</sub> is a double covalent bond.

The enthalpy change of reaction for this reaction is +497 kJ mol<sup>–1</sup>. Calculate the bond energy, in kJ mol<sup>–1</sup>, of the N=O bond.

Show your working.

Use relevant data from **Table 3.2**.

**Table 3.2**

| **Bond** | **Bond energy / kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> |
|---|---|
| N≡N | 941 |
| O=O | 495 |

Bond energy of the N=O bond = ............................. kJ mol<sup>–1</sup>
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the bond energy of the N=O bond:

- The equation for the reaction is:

N<sub>2</sub> (g) + 2O<sub>2</sub> (g) → 2NO<sub>2</sub> (g)

- Calculate the total energy for bonds broken:

1 × N≡N = 941 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

2 × O=O = 2 × 495 = 990 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

Total bonds broken = +1931 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Set up the Δ*H*<sub>r</sub> equation:

Δ*H*<sub>r</sub> = Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed)

+497 = +1931 − 4(N=O) **[1 mark]**

- Solve for the bond energy of N=O:

4(N=O) = 1931 − 497

4(N=O) = 1434

N=O = $\frac{1434}{4}$

N=O = **358.5 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The reaction equation is N<sub>2</sub> (g) + 2O<sub>2</sub> (g) → 2NO<sub>2</sub> (g), so 1 N≡N bond and 2 O=O bonds are broken, and 4 N=O bonds are formed.
> 
> Work step by step:
> 
> - Find the total bond energy for bonds broken
> - Set up the Δ*H*<sub>r</sub> equation
> - Solve for the N=O bond energy

parts.problemMd:
The boiling points of carbon dioxide and nitrogen dioxide are -78.5 <sup>o</sup>C and 21 <sup>o</sup>C respectively.

Suggest a reason for the difference.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> A reason for the difference in boiling points between carbon dioxide and nitrogen dioxide:
> 
> - The van der Waals / intermolecular forces are (much) stronger in NO<sub>2</sub> / weaker in CO<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**
> 
> Plus, any **one** from:
> 
> - NO<sub>2</sub> has permanent dipole-dipole attractions between molecules; CO<sub>2</sub> does not
> - NO<sub>2</sub> is polar but CO<sub>2</sub> is not
> - In CO<sub>2</sub> the molecule is symmetrical and the dipoles cancel out / there is no net dipole
> 
> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The C=O bond is actually more polar than the N=O bond (greater electronegativity difference), but NO<sub>2</sub> has a lone pair on nitrogen that makes it a bent molecule, whereas CO<sub>2</sub> is linear.
> 
> The linear shape of CO<sub>2</sub> causes the bond dipoles to cancel, giving no net dipole. So, CO<sub>2</sub> only has weaker dispersion (London) forces, resulting in a much lower boiling point.

parts.problemMd:
Propane gas is used widely as a fuel which can be used in camping gas stoves. The enthalpy of combustion for propane is −2219.2 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>.

Calculate the minimum mass of fuel needed to bring 150 cm<sup>3</sup> of water from 25.0°C to its boiling point of 100.0°C.

Show your working.

................... g
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the minimum mass of propane needed:

- Calculate the energy required to heat the water:

*q* = *mc*Δ*T*

*q* = 150 x 4.18 x 75

*q* = 47025 J

- Convert from J to kJ:

*q* = $\frac{47025}{1000}$

*q* = 47.025 kJ **[1 mark]**

- Rearrange the Δ*H* equation for *n*:

Δ*H* = $\frac{q}{n}$

*n* = $\frac{q}{ΔH}$

- Calculate the moles of propane required:

*n* = $\frac{47.025}{2219.2}$

*n* = 0.02119 mol **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the *M*<sub>r</sub> of propane:

*M*<sub>r</sub> of propane = (3 × 12) + (8 × 1)

*M*<sub>r</sub> of propane = 44.0 g mol<sup>-1</sup>

- Calculate the mass of propane:

mass = moles × *M*<sub>r</sub>

mass of propane = 0.02119 x 44.0

mass of propane = **0.93 g** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Allow error carried forward if method is correct

> **[exam-tip]**
> *q* is calculated in J, so you must divide by 1000 to convert to kJ before using the enthalpy of combustion value (in kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>).

parts.problemMd:
The enthalpy change of solution for ammonium chloride can be measured using calorimetry. 12.04 g of ammonium chloride is dissolved in 125.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of water at 19.5 °C.

The standard enthalpy change of solution of ammonium chloride is +15.1 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>. Calculate the energy change, *q*, in J, when 12.04 g of ammonium chloride is dissolved in 125.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of water.

Show your working.

*q* = ................................. J
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the energy change, *q*, in J:

- Calculate the moles of ammonium chloride:

moles = $\frac{\mathrm{mass}}{M_{r}}$

*n*(NH<sub>4</sub>Cl) = $\frac{12.04}{53.5}$

*n*(NH<sub>4</sub>Cl) = 0.2250 mol **[1 mark]**

- Convert Δ*H*<sub>sol</sub> from kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> to J mol<sup>-1</sup>:

Δ*H*<sub>sol</sub> = 15.1 x 1000

Δ*H*<sub>sol</sub> = 15100 J mol<sup>-1</sup>

- Calculate the energy change:

*q* = *n* x Δ*H*<sub>sol</sub>

*q* = 0.2250 x 15 100

*q* = **3397.5 J** (to 3 s.f.) **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> The final answer must be given to 2 or more significant figures
> 
> Δ*H*<sub>sol</sub> must be converted from kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> to J mol<sup>-1</sup> (×1000) to score the second mark

> **[exam-tip]**
> Work backwards from Δ*H*<sub>sol</sub> to find the energy change for the actual amount used (0.225 mol, not 1 mol).

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The enthalpy change of solution for ammonium chloride can be measured using calorimetry. 12.04 g of ammonium chloride is dissolved in 125.0 cm^3^ of water at 19.5 °C.

The standard enthalpy change of solution of ammonium chloride is +15.1 kJ mol^-1^.

Use your answer to part (a) to calculate the final temperature, in °C, of the solution.

The specific heat capacity of the solution is 4.18 J g<sup>-1</sup> K<sup>-1</sup>.

Show your working.

Final temperature = ................................. °C
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the final temperature of the solution:

- Calculate the temperature change:

*q* = *mc*Δ*T*

Δ*T* = $\frac{q}{mc}$

Δ*T* = $\frac{3398}{125.0\times4.18}$

Δ*T* = 6.5 °C **[1 mark]**

- The dissolution is endothermic, so the temperature decreases:

*T*<sub>final</sub> = 19.5 °C − 6.5 °C

*T*<sub>final</sub> = **13.0 °C** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Allow error carried forward from part (a) if method is correct

> **[exam-tip]**
> The positive enthalpy of solution (+15.1 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>) tells you that dissolution is endothermic. Heat is absorbed from the surroundings, so the temperature of the solution decreases.
> 
> Subtract the temperature change from the initial temperature to find the final temperature.

parts.problemMd:
Use the data in Table 2.1 to calculate the enthalpy change of reaction for the hydrogenation of propene.

Show your working.

**Table 2.1**

| **Bond** | **Bond energy / kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> |
|---|---|
| H–H | 435 |
| C–H | 413 |
| C–C | 347 |
| C=C | 619 |

Enthalpy of hydrogenation, Δ*H*<sub>r</sub> = ................................. kJ mol<sup>–1</sup>
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the enthalpy change of reaction for the hydrogenation of propene:

- Construct the equation for the hydrogenation:

CH<sub>3</sub>CH=CH<sub>2</sub> (g) + H<sub>2</sub> (g) → C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub> (g)

**[1 mark]**

- Identify and calculate bonds broken:

Bonds broken = 1 × C=C + 1 × H–H

Bonds broken = 619 + 435

Bonds broken = +1054 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

- Identify and calculate bonds formed:

Bonds formed = 1 × C–C + 2 × C–H

Bonds formed = 347 + 2(413)

Bonds formed = −1173 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate Δ*H*<sub>r</sub>:

Δ*H*<sub>r</sub> = +1054 + (−1173)

Δ*H*<sub>r</sub> = **−119 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup>

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct hydrogenation equation: CH<sub>3</sub>CH=CH<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub> → C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub>
> 
> 1 mark for bonds broken = +1054 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> (C=C + H–H) **AND** bonds formed = −1173 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> (C–C + 2 × C–H)
> 
> 1 mark for Δ*H*<sub>r</sub> = −119 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> Allow the full bond energy approach (using all bonds in propene and propane) for full marks if method and answer are correct

> **[exam-tip]**
> Only bonds that change in the reaction need to be counted. In the hydrogenation of propene, the C=C becomes C–C and H–H is broken while two new C–H bonds form. Bonds in CH<sub>3</sub> groups are identical on both sides and cancel out.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

**Table 2.1**

| **Bond** | **Bond energy / kJ mol**^**-1**^ |
| :---: | :---: |
| H–H | 435 |
| C–H | 413 |
| C–C | 347 |
| C=C | 619 |

Use the data in Table 2.1 to suggest, with a reason, whether the polymerisation of propene is exothermic or endothermic
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The polymerisation of propene is
> 
> - Exothermic 
> **OR**
> There is a net release of energy **[1 mark]**
> - One C=C bond is broken and two C–C bonds are formed
> **OR**
> One C=C bond is weaker than two C–C bonds (619 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> vs 2 × 347 = 694 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For each repeat unit of the polymer, one C=C bond breaks and two new C–C bonds form.
> 
> The energy released in forming two C–C bonds (2 × 347 = 694 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>) is greater than the energy required to break one C=C bond (619 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>), giving a net release of energy.

parts.problemMd:
Carbon, hydrogen and ethene each undergo complete combustion in oxygen.

| Equation | Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>c</sub> / kJ mol<sup>–1</sup> |
|---|---|
| C (s) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) → CO<sub>2</sub> (g) | −393.7 |
| H<sub>2</sub> (g) + ½O<sub>2</sub> (g) → H<sub>2</sub>O (l) | −285.9 |
| C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub> (g) + 3O<sub>2</sub> (g) → 2CO<sub>2</sub> (g) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l) | −1411.0 |

Use the data to calculate the standard enthalpy change of formation, Δ*H*<sup>*θ*</sup><sub>f</sub>, in kJ mol<sup>–1</sup>, of ethene at 298 K.

Show your working.

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub> = ................................. kJ mol<sup>–1</sup>
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the standard enthalpy change of formation, Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub>, of ethene:

- Apply Hess’s Law:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub> = 2Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>c</sub>(C) + 2Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>c</sub>(H<sub>2</sub>) − Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>c</sub>(C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>) **[1 mark]**

- Substitute values and calculate:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub> = 2(−393.7) + 2(−285.9) − (−1411.0)

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub> = −787.4 − 571.8 + 1411.0

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub> = **+51.8 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for applying Hess’s Law correctly: Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub> = 2Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>c</sub>(C) + 2Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>c</sub>(H<sub>2</sub>) − Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>c</sub>(C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>)
> 
> Allow 1 mark for a correctly labelled Hess cycle showing the correct route
> 
> ![Diagram of Hess’s law: 2C(s) + 2H₂(g) → C₂H₄(g), arrows to 2CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l) with enthalpy values −393.7×2, −285.9×2 and −1411.0 kJ](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/5-chemical-energetics/5-1-enthalpy-change-h/assets/015-diagram-of-hess-s-law-2c-s-2h-g-c-h-g-arrows-to-.png)
> 
> 1 mark for a final positive Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub> value = +51.8 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

> **[exam-tip]**
> Use Hess’s Law: the enthalpy change for the direct route (formation of ethene from its elements) equals the enthalpy change via combustion.
> 
> Construct the formation equation from the definition. 1 mole of compound formed from its elements in their standard states:
> 
> 2C (s) + 2H<sub>2</sub> (g) → C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub> (g)
> 
> Remember to multiply the combustion values by the stoichiometric coefficients in the formation equation before combining them.

parts.problemMd:
Compound **A** is a liquid containing carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. Quantitative analysis shows that **A** has the empirical formula CH<sub>2</sub>O.

A sample of **A** with a mass of 0.240 g is vaporised. At 80.0 °C and 101 kPa, the vapour occupies a volume of 116 cm<sup>3</sup>.

Calculate the relative molecular mass, *M*<sub>r</sub>, of **A**.

Show your working.

*M*<sub>r</sub> = .............
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the relative molecular mass, *M*<sub>r</sub>, of **A**:

- Convert units to SI:

*V* = 116 cm<sup>3</sup> = 116 × 10<sup>-6</sup> m<sup>3</sup>

*T* = 80.0 °C = 353 K

*p* = 101 kPa = 101 000 Pa

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate the number of moles, *n*, using *pV* = *nRT*:

*n* = $\frac{pV}{RT}$

*n* = $\frac{101000\times(116\times10^{-6})}{8.31\times353}$

*n* = 3.99 × 10<sup>-3</sup> mol

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate *M*<sub>r</sub>:

*M*<sub>r</sub> = $\frac{\mathrm{mass}}{\mathrm{moles}}$

*M*<sub>r</sub> = $\frac{0.240}{3.99\times10^{-3}}$

*M*<sub>r</sub> = **60.1 (to 3 s.f.)**

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct conversions of volume, temperature **AND **pressure to SI units
> 
> Answers given to more than 3 significant figures are accepted, if supported by workings

> **[exam-tip]**
> Watch units carefully.
> 
> If you use *R* = 8.31, you must use SI units. This means converting **kPa to Pa**, **cm**<sup>**3**</sup>** to m**<sup>**3**</sup>, and **°C to K** before substituting into *pV* = *nRT*.
> 
> A missed conversion (especially pressure or volume) is the most common reason these questions lose marks.

parts.problemMd:
Methyl methanoate, HCOOCH<sub>3</sub>, is a liquid ester.

i) Define the term standard enthalpy change of formation.

[2]

ii) The standard enthalpy changes of combustion, Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>c</sub>, in **Table 2.1** are for complete combustion to CO<sub>2</sub> (g) and H<sub>2</sub>O (l) under standard conditions.

**Table 2.1**

| Substance | Standard enthalpy change of combustion, Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>c</sub> / kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> |
|---|---|
| C (s) | –394 |
| H<sub>2</sub> (g) | –286 |
| HCOOCH<sub>3</sub> (l) | –975 |

The enthalpy of formation of methyl methanoate refers to the reaction:

2C (s) + 2H<sub>2</sub> (g) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) → HCOOCH<sub>3</sub> (l)

Use the data in Table 2.1 to calculate the standard enthalpy change of formation, Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub>, of liquid methyl methanoate.

Show your working.

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub> = ........................ kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) Standard enthalpy change of formation is:
> 
> - The enthalpy change when one mole / 1 mol of a compound is formed from its elements **[1 mark]**
> - In their standard states under standard conditions **[1 mark]**

ii) To calculate the standard enthalpy change of formation, Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub>, of liquid methyl methanoate:

- State the relationship used:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub> + Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>c</sub>(compound) = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>c</sub>(reactants)  **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the total enthalpy of combustion of the reactants:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>c</sub>(reactants) = (2 x C) + (2 x H<sub>2</sub>)

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>c</sub>(reactants) = (2 x -394) + (2 x -286)

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>c</sub>(reactants) = −1360 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Calculate Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub>:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub> = −1360 − (−975)

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub> = **−385 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub> + Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>c</sub>(compound) = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>c</sub>(reactants)
> 
> 1 mark for Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>c</sub>(reactants) = (2 x C) + (2 x H<sub>2</sub>) **OR** Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>c</sub>(reactants) = (2 x 394) + (2 x -286) **OR** Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>c</sub>(reactants) = −1360 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for a final negative Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub> value = −385 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> 3 marks can be awarded for a correct final answer with or without working
> 
> Only 1 mark is awarded for a final answer of +385 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

> **[exam-tip]**
> In formation definitions, do not forget the two precision points:
> 
> 1. One mole / 1 mol
> 2. Standard states under standard conditions.
> 
> In the Hess calculation, the most common error is missing the stoichiometry from the formation equation. Multiply the combustion values by the coefficients first (here, 2 for C and 2 for H<sub>2</sub>) before combining them with the ester’s combustion value.

parts.problemMd:
The equation for the formation of gaseous methyl methanoate from gaseous atoms is shown.

2C (g) + 4H (g) + 2O (g) → HCOOCH<sub>3</sub> (g)

Use bond energy data from the Data Booklet to calculate the enthalpy change for this reaction.

Show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the enthalpy change for this reaction:

- The reactants are gaseous atoms, so there are no bonds to break

Δ*H*<sub>(bonds broken)</sub> = 0

- Identify the bonds formed in HCOOCH<sub>3</sub> (g):

1 × C=O

2 × C–O

4 × C–H

**[1 mark]**

- Use bond energies from the Data Booklet to calculate the total energy of the bonds formed:

Δ*H*<sub>(bonds formed)</sub> = - (C=O + (2 x C–O) + (4 x C–H))

Δ*H*<sub>(bonds formed)</sub> = - ((740) + (2 x 360) + (4 x 410))

Δ*H*<sub>(bonds formed)</sub> = **- 3100 (kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup>**)**

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for Identify the bonds formed in HCOOCH<sub>3</sub> (g)
> 
> 1 mark for a final negative Δ*H*<sub>(bonds formed)</sub> value = - 3100 (kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>)
> 
> 2 marks can be awarded for a correct final answer with or without working

> **[exam-tip]**
> Since the reactants are gaseous atoms, this is a bond formation only question as there are no bonds to break. The enthalpy change is the negative of the total bond energies for all bonds formed.
> 
> The most common mistakes are:
> 
> - Treating it like a normal bond energy cycle and trying to “break” bonds in the reactants
> - Missing one of the C–O bonds in the ester group
> - Forgetting the negative sign

parts.problemMd:
A student investigates the rate of reaction of methyl methanoate with dilute hydrochloric acid.

parts.problemMd:
Complete the following Hess's law energy cycle relating butane to its standard enthalpy change of formation, Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>f</sub>, and standard enthalpy change of combustion, Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>c</sub>.

On your diagram:

- include the relevant species in the two empty boxes
- label each enthalpy change with its appropriate symbol
- complete the remaining two arrows to show the correct direction of enthalpy change

![Incomplete Hess's law energy cycle for butane showing two empty boxes and unlabelled arrows](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/5-chemical-energetics/5-2-hesss-law/assets/006-incomplete-hess-s-law-energy-cycle-for-butane-sh.png)
parts.solutionMd:
The completed Hess's law energy cycle for butane is:

![Completed Hess's law energy cycle for butane, with correct species in both boxes and arrows labelled with standard enthalpy change symbols in the correct directions](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/5-chemical-energetics/5-2-hesss-law/assets/007-completed-hess-s-law-energy-cycle-for-butane-wit.png)

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct species **AND **correct balancing / coefficients in both boxes
> 
> 1 mark for correct enthalpy change labels on all arrows
> 
> 1 mark for both arrows shown in the correct direction

> **[exam-tip]**
> Include state symbols on all species as they are part of the standard enthalpy change definitions.
> 
> The formation of oxides from their elements in standard states is equivalent to the combustion of those elements, so Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>f</sub> and Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>c</sub> labels may both appear on the same section of the cycle.

parts.problemMd:
Use the data in Table 1.1 to calculate the standard enthalpy change of combustion of butane, Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>c</sub>. Show your working.

**Table 1.1**

| **Substance** | **Standard enthalpy change of formation, **Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>f</sub>** / kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> |
|---|---|
| CO<sub>2</sub> (g) | −393.5 |
| C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub> (g) | −125 |
| H<sub>2</sub>O (l) | −286 |

Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>c</sub> (C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>) = .........................................kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the standard enthalpy change of combustion of butane, Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>c</sub>:

- Apply the Hess's law expression:

Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>c</sub> = −Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>f</sub> [C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub> (g)] + 4Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>f</sub> [CO<sub>2</sub> (g)] + 5Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>f</sub> [H<sub>2</sub>O (l)] **[1 mark]**

- Substitute values from Table 1.1:

Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>c</sub> = −(−125) + 4(−393.5) + 5(−286)

Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>c</sub> = **−2879 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct expression with correct stoichiometric coefficients
> 
> 1 mark for −2879 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

> **[exam-tip]**
> The balanced combustion equation for butane is:
> 
> C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub> (g) + 6.5O<sub>2</sub> (g) → 4CO<sub>2</sub> (g) + 5H<sub>2</sub>O (l)
> 
> Use the stoichiometric coefficients from this equation when applying the Hess's law expression. Oxygen is not included because Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>f</sub> [O<sub>2</sub> (g)] = 0.
> 
> Take care with signs. Subtracting the enthalpy of formation of the reactant means subtracting a negative value, making it positive: −(−125) = +125.

parts.problemMd:
Use the bond energies given in Table 1.2 to calculate the standard enthalpy change of combustion of butane. Show your working.

**Table 1.2**

| **Bond** | **Bond energy / kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> |
|---|---|
| C−C | 348 |
| C−H | 410 |
| C=O | 743 |
| H−O | 463 |
| O=O | 495 |

Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>c</sub> (C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>) = .........................................kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the standard enthalpy change of combustion of butane using bond energies:

- Identify and total the bonds broken (in reactants):

3 x C−C: 3 x 348 = +1044 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

6.5 x O=O: 6.5 x 495 = +3217.5 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

Total bonds broken = +8361.5 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Identify and total the bonds formed (in products):

8 x C=O: 8 x 743 = −5944 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

10 x H−O: 10 x 463 = −4630 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

Total bonds formed = −10574 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the enthalpy change:

Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>c</sub> = (+8361.5) + (−10574)

Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>c</sub> = **−2212.5 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> 
> 1 mark for total bonds formed = −10574 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> (8 x C=O, 10 x H−O with correct values)

>

parts.problemMd:

parts.solutionMd:
The equation for the formation of propane from propyne is:

> **[exam-tip]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Propane gas is commonly used as a fuel for outdoor cooking. It can be produced in a number of ways, including from the addition reaction of propyne gas with hydrogen. Propyne has the formula CHCCH3 and includes a triple bond.

The equation for the formation of propane from propyne is:

CHCCH3 (g) + 2H2 (g) → CH3CH2CH3 (g)

Table 2.1 lists the relevant standard enthalpy change of combustion data for the formation of propane from propyne.

**Table 2.1**

|   | **Standard enthalpy change of combustion, **Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>c</sub>** / kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> |
|---|---|
| **Hydrogen** | −285.8 |
| **Propane** | −2220 |
| **Propyne** | −1940 |

Calculate the standard enthalpy change of reaction, Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>r</sub>, for the formation of propane from propyne. Show your working.

Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>r</sub> = .........................................kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the standard enthalpy change of reaction, Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>r</sub>, for the formation of propane from propyne:

- Apply the Hess's law expression using combustion data:

Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>r</sub> = ΣΔ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>c</sub>(reactants) − ΣΔ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>c</sub>(products) **[1 mark]**

- Substitute values from Table 2.1:

Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>r</sub> = [Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>c</sub>(propyne) + 2 x Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>c</sub>(H<sub>2</sub>)] − Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>c</sub>(propane)

Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>r</sub> = [(−1940) + 2(−285.8)] − (−2220) **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the result:

Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>r</sub> = −2511.6 + 2220

Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>r</sub> = **−291.6 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct expression: ΣΔ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>c</sub>(reactants) − ΣΔ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>c</sub>(products), or equivalent Hess cycle approach
> 
> 1 mark for correct substitution with x2 multiplier for H<sub>2</sub>
> 
> 1 mark for −291.6 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

> **[exam-tip]**
> When combustion data is provided, the Hess's law expression is:
> 
> Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>r</sub> = ΣΔ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>c</sub>(reactants) − ΣΔ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>c</sub>(products)
> 
> This is the reverse of the formation data expression (Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>r</sub> = ΣΔ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>f</sub>(products) − ΣΔ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>f</sub>(reactants)). Take care not to confuse the two.
> 
> The stoichiometry from part (a) matters here. The balanced equation shows 2 mol H<sub>2</sub> are consumed, so Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>c</sub>(H<sub>2</sub>) must be multiplied by 2.

For example, the C−H bond energy is derived from many different molecules, so it does not represent any one C−H bond exactly. This is why a calculated bond energy value is only an approximation.

Fig. 3.1 shows the equipment used to determine the standard enthalpy change of combustion, Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>c</sub>, of 2-methylpropan-2-ol, C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9</sub>OH, using a calorimeter containing 75.0 g of water.

![Spirit burner calorimetry experiment setup showing a spirit burner beneath a metal can containing water](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/5-chemical-energetics/5-2-hesss-law/assets/010-spirit-burner-calorimetry-experiment-setup-showi.png)

**Fig. 3.1**

Table 3.1 shows the results of the experiment.

**Table 3.1**

|   | **Initial** | **Final** | **Change** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Mass of spirit burner / g** | 267.35 | 266.78 |   |
| **Temperature of water / °C** | 19.5 | 65.3 |   |

Calculate the standard enthalpy change of combustion, Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>c</sub>, of 2-methylpropan-2-ol. Include the sign and units. Show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the standard enthalpy change of combustion, Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>c</sub>, of 2-methylpropan-2-ol:

- Calculate the mass of 2-methylpropan-2-ol burned and the temperature change of the water:

mass burned = 267.35 − 266.78 = 0.57 g
**AND**
temperature change = 65.3 − 19.5 = 45.8 °C

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate the heat energy transferred to the water using *q* = *mc*Δ*T*:

*q* = 75.0 x 4.18 x 45.8

*q* = 14 358 J **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the *M*<sub>r</sub> of 2-methylpropan-2-ol, C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9</sub>OH:

*M*<sub>r</sub> = (4 x 12.0) + (10 x 1.0) + 16.0 = 74.0 **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the moles of 2-methylpropan-2-ol burned:

moles = $\frac{0.57}{74.0}$

moles = 7.703 x 10<sup>-3</sup> mol **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the standard enthalpy change of combustion:

Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>c</sub> = $\frac{-14358}{7.703\times10^{-3}}$

Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>c</sub> = **−1864 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for both mass change = 0.57 g **AND **temperature change = 45.8 °C
> 
> 1 mark for q = 14 358 J
> 
> 1 mark for *M*<sub>r</sub> = 74.0 g mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for moles = 7.703 x 10<sup>-3</sup> mol
> 
> 1 mark for −1864 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

> **[exam-tip]**
> The mass used in *q* = *mc*Δ*T* is the mass of water (75.0 g), not the mass of 2-methylpropan-2-ol burned. The mass of the spirit burner decreases because fuel is consumed.
> 
> The combustion reaction is exothermic, so the enthalpy change is negative.
> 
> To find the moles burned, use:
> 
> moles = $\frac{\mathrm{mass} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{fuel} \mathrm{burne}d}{M_{r}}$ =$\frac{0.57}{74.0}$

parts.problemMd: Define the term *standard enthalpy of combustion, *Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>c</sub>*.*

> - With all reactants and products in their standard states

> 
> If you are not using fractions to balance the equation, you must double the number of moles of all other chemicals.
> 
> Double-check your balancing once you have written your equation.
> 
> Many chemical calculations work from a balanced symbol equation, so if your equation is incorrect, any subsequent calculations will also contain errors.
