> To deduce the formula from a systematic name, use the Roman numeral as the oxidation number of the metal, then find the ratio of ions that balances the charges to zero:
> 
> - copper(I) oxide: Cu is +1, O is -2. Need 2 Cu (+2) for 1 O (-2), so the formula is Cu<sub>2</sub>O
> - iron(III) chloride: Fe is +3, Cl is -1. Need 3 Cl (-3) for 1 Fe (+3), so the formula is FeCl<sub>3</sub>
> - tin(IV) chloride: Sn is +4, Cl is -1. Need 4 Cl (-4) for 1 Sn (+4), so the formula is SnCl<sub>4</sub>
> - vanadium(II) oxide: V is +2, O is -2. Charges balance 1:1, so the formula is VO

parts.problemMd: Describe what is meant by a *disproportionation reaction*.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> A disproportionation reaction is one in which:
> 
> - A single species is simultaneously oxidised **AND **reduced **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Both parts of the definition must be present for the mark: the same species must be both oxidised and reduced, and this must happen simultaneously. Stating only that oxidation and reduction occur is not enough. You must specify that it is the same species involved in both processes.

parts.problemMd:
State whether the displacement reaction between copper(II) ions and magnesium is an example of a disproportionation reaction. Explain your answer in terms of changes in oxidation numbers.

Cu<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + Mg (s) → Mg<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + Cu (s)
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> For the displacement reaction between copper(II) ions and magnesium:
> 
> - This is not a disproportionation reaction **[1 mark]**
> - The oxidation number of Cu<sup>2+</sup> decreases from +2 to 0 (reduction) and Mg increases from 0 to +2 (oxidation), so different species are oxidised and reduced
> **OR**
> Reduction and oxidation do not happen to the same species **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For a reaction to be a disproportionation reaction, the same species must be both oxidised and reduced. In this reaction, Cu<sup>2+</sup> is reduced (oxidation number +2 → 0) and Mg is oxidised (oxidation number 0 → +2), but these are two different species. Because reduction and oxidation happen to different species, this is not disproportionation.
> 
> Be careful not to confuse *dis*placement with *dis*proportionation as they are unrelated terms.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A disproportionation reaction is one in which a single species is simultaneously oxidised AND reduced.

i) Construct an equation for the disproportionation reaction of sulfuric acid with copper(I) oxide to form copper, copper(II) sulfate and water.

[1]

ii) Identify which element, in this reaction, undergoes disproportionation.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The equation for the reaction of copper(I) oxide with sulfuric acid is:
> 
> - H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + Cu<sub>2</sub>O → Cu + CuSO<sub>4</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The element that undergoes disproportionation is:
> 
> - Copper / Cu **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The only element that could undergo disproportionation is copper:
> 
> - In copper(I) oxide, Cu has oxidation number +1
> - In copper (the product), Cu has oxidation number 0 (reduced from +1 to 0)
> - In copper(II) sulfate, Cu has oxidation number +2 (oxidised from +1 to +2)
> 
> Copper is simultaneously reduced and oxidised from the same starting oxidation number (+1), confirming it undergoes disproportionation.

parts.problemMd:
i) Construct an equation for the reaction of nitrogen dioxide with water to form nitric acid and nitrous acid, HNO<sub>2</sub>.

[1]

ii) Identify which element undergoes disproportionation.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The equation for the reaction of nitrogen dioxide with water is:
> 
> - 2NO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O → HNO<sub>3</sub> + HNO<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The element that undergoes disproportionation is:
> 
> - Nitrogen / N **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Nitrogen is the only element that could undergo disproportionation in this reaction:
> 
> - In nitrogen dioxide (NO<sub>2</sub>), N has oxidation number +4
> - In nitric acid (HNO<sub>3</sub>), N has oxidation number +5 (oxidised from +4 to +5)
> - In nitrous acid (HNO<sub>2</sub>), N has oxidation number +3 (reduced from +4 to +3)
> 
> Nitrogen is simultaneously oxidised and reduced from the same starting oxidation number (+4), confirming this is a disproportionation reaction.

parts.problemMd:
This question is about redox reactions.

When calcium reacts with Fe(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>, a redox reaction occurs.

Ca (s) + Fe(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> (aq) → Ca(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> (aq) + Fe (s)

Explain, in terms of electron transfer and oxidation numbers, which species has been oxidised and which has been reduced. Hence identify the reducing agent.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> In terms of electron transfer and oxidation numbers, the oxidised and reduced species, and the reducing agent:
> 
> - Ca / calcium has been oxidised; it loses electrons and its oxidation number increases from 0 to +2 **[1 mark]**
> - Fe<sup>2+</sup> / iron has been reduced; it gains electrons and its oxidation number decreases from +2 to 0 **[1 mark]**
> - Ca / calcium is the reducing agent **[1 mark]**
> - Its oxidation number increases from 0 to +2
> **OR**
> it loses 2 electrons **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> In a redox reaction, oxidation and reduction always occur simultaneously. Use OIL RIG to remember:
> 
> - Oxidation Is Loss of electrons; the oxidation number increases
> - Reduction Is Gain of electrons; the oxidation number decreases
> 
> The reducing agent is the species that is itself oxidised as it causes reduction in another species by donating electrons.
> 
> In this reaction, Ca loses electrons (oxidation number 0 → +2) and acts as the reducing agent, while Fe<sup>2+</sup> gains electrons (oxidation number +2 → 0) and acts as the oxidising agent.

parts.problemMd: State the systematic name of Fe(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The systematic name of Fe(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> is:
> 
> - Iron(II) nitrate(V) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Roman numerals in systematic names indicate the oxidation number of the element:
> 
> - Fe is +2 in Fe(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>: two NO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> ions each carry a −1 charge, so Fe must be +2 for the compound to be neutral
> - N is +5 in NO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup>: N + (3 × −2) = −1, so N = +5, shown by the Roman numeral (V)
> 
> The Roman numeral for nitrate is often omitted in everyday language, but when asked for the systematic name it must be included.

parts.problemMd:
Another redox reaction occurs between cobalt(III) oxide, Co<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>, and hydrochloric acid, HCl.

Co<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> (s) + 6HCl (aq) → 2CoCl<sub>2</sub> (aq) + 3H<sub>2</sub>O (l) + Cl<sub>2</sub> (g)

i) Explain, in terms of oxidation numbers, what has been reduced.

[2]

ii) A student describes this reaction as a disproportionation reaction. State whether the student is correct. Explain your answer using oxidation numbers.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The species that has been reduced:
> 
> - Co has been reduced **[1 mark]**
> - From +3 (in Co<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>) to +2 (in CoCl<sub>2</sub>) **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) Whether the student is correct:
> 
> - The student is not correct; disproportionation requires the same species to be simultaneously oxidised and reduced **[1 mark]**
> - Cl is only oxidised (from −1 in HCl to 0 in Cl<sub>2</sub>); the Cl in CoCl<sub>2</sub> remains at −1 and is not reduced **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part (i), give the oxidation number of the species in both the reactant and product to show the change. A bare statement like "Co is reduced" without the oxidation numbers will not score the second mark.
> 
> For part (ii), disproportionation requires the same element to be both oxidised and reduced in the same reaction. To gain both marks:
> 
> 1. State whether the reaction is disproportionation
> 2. Justify using oxidation numbers
> 
> In this reaction, chlorine goes from −1 in HCl to 0 in Cl<sub>2</sub> (oxidised only — it is not reduced anywhere in the equation). Cobalt is reduced, not the same element as the one oxidised, so the reaction is not disproportionation.

parts.problemMd:
Magnesium oxide, MgO, reacts with nitric acid, HNO<sub>3</sub>, when heated.

MgO (s) + 2HNO<sub>3</sub> (aq) → Mg(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> (aq) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l)

i) State the oxidation numbers of magnesium and nitrogen in the reactants and products by completing the table.

|   | MgO | HNO<sub>3</sub> | Mg(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mg |   | – |   |
| N | – |   |   |

[2]

ii) Explain whether the reaction between magnesium oxide and nitric acid is a redox reaction.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The completed table is:

|   | MgO | HNO<sub>3</sub> | Mg(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mg | **Final answer:** **+2** | – | **Final answer:** **+2** |
| N | – | **Final answer:** **+5** | **Final answer:** **+5** |

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for Mg = +2 in MgO **AND** Mg = +2 in Mg(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>
> 
> 1 mark for N = +5 in HNO<sub>3</sub> **AND** N = +5 in Mg(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>
> 
> ii) Whether the reaction is a redox reaction:
> 
> - It is not a redox reaction; the oxidation numbers of all species remain unchanged
> **OR**
> Neither Mg nor N changes oxidation number **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part (i), use the charge neutrality rule to work out each oxidation number:
> 
> - In MgO: O is −2 and the compound is neutral, so Mg = +2
> - In HNO<sub>3</sub>: H is +1, each O is −2, so N + 1 + (3 × −2) = 0, giving N = +5
> - In Mg(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>: Mg is always +2 in its compounds; the NO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> group retains the same structure, so N = +5
> 
> For part (ii), a redox reaction requires at least one element to change oxidation number. Since both Mg and N have identical oxidation numbers in the reactants and products, no electron transfer has occurred and this is not a redox reaction.

parts.problemMd:
Under suitable conditions, SCl<sub>2</sub> reacts with water to produce a yellow precipitate of sulfur and a solution **A**. Solution **A** contains a mixture of SO<sub>2</sub> (aq) and compound **B**.

State the oxidation number of sulfur in SCl<sub>2</sub>.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The oxidation number of sulfur in SCl<sub>2</sub> is:
> 
> - +2 **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> To find the oxidation number of S in SCl<sub>2</sub>, use the rules:
> 
> - Cl has oxidation number −1 in compounds
> - The sum of oxidation numbers in a neutral compound = 0
> 
> S + (2 × −1) = 0, so S = +2

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Under suitable conditions, SCl~2~ reacts with water to produce a yellow precipitate of sulfur and a solution **A**. Solution **A** contains a mixture of SO~2~ (aq) and compound **B**.

i) Deduce how the oxidation number of sulfur changes during the reaction of SCl<sub>2</sub> with water. Show your working.

[2]

ii) Identify the type of reaction that occurs when SCl<sub>2</sub> reacts with water. Explain your answer in terms of changes in oxidation numbers.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) How the oxidation number of sulfur changes:
> 
> - (Half the) sulfur goes from +2 to 0 (a decrease of 2) **[1 mark]**
> - (The other half of the) sulfur goes from +2 to +4 (an increase of 2) **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The type of reaction and explanation:
> 
> - Disproportionation **[1 mark]**
> - The same species (sulfur) is both oxidised and reduced; its oxidation number both increases (from +2 to +4) and decreases (from +2 to 0) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Disproportionation is a specific type of redox reaction in which the same element is simultaneously oxidised and reduced in a single reaction.
> 
> In this reaction, sulfur in SCl<sub>2</sub> has oxidation number +2. After the reaction:
> 
> - Some sulfur goes to 0 in the yellow precipitate of elemental S — this is reduction (decrease in oxidation number)
> - Some sulfur goes to +4 in SO<sub>2</sub> — this is oxidation (increase in oxidation number)
> 
> Since the same element (S) is both oxidised and reduced, this is disproportionation.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Under suitable conditions, SCl~2~ reacts with water to produce a yellow precipitate of sulfur and a solution **A**. Solution **A** contains a mixture of SO~2~ (aq) and compound **B**.

i) Suggest the identity of compound **B**.

[1]

ii) Construct an equation for the reaction between SCl<sub>2</sub> and water.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The identity of compound **B**:
> 
> - HCl **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The equation for the reaction between SCl<sub>2</sub> and water:
> 
> - 2SCl<sub>2</sub> (aq) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l) → S (s) + SO<sub>2</sub> (g) + 4HCl (aq) **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are not required.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The question provides most of the information needed:
> 
> - Reactants: SCl<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O (water)
> - Products: yellow precipitate of sulfur (S), SO<sub>2</sub>, and compound **B**
> 
> The remaining elements in the products are H and Cl from the reactants, so compound **B** must be HCl. Once you identify HCl, write the unbalanced equation and then balance it by inspection:
> 
> 2SCl<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O → S + SO<sub>2</sub> + 4HCl
> 
> Note: identifying HCl in part (i) directly gives you the key product needed for the equation in part (ii).

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Under suitable conditions, SCl2 reacts with water to produce a yellow precipitate of sulfur and a solution A. Solution A contains a mixture of SO2 (aq) and compound B.

i) Separate samples of solution **A** are tested with different reagents. Complete the table to describe what is observed when each reagent is added to solution **A**.

| Reagent | Observation |
|---|---|
| AgNO<sub>3</sub> (aq) |   |
| acidified K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> (aq) |   |

[2]

ii) State the systematic name of KMnO<sub>4</sub>.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) Observations when each reagent is added to solution **A**:
> 
> - AgNO<sub>3</sub> (aq): white precipitate / ppt forms **[1 mark]**
> - Acidified K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> (aq): (turns from) orange to green **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The systematic name of KMnO<sub>4</sub>:
> 
> - Potassium manganate(VII) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part (i):
> 
> - Solution **A** contains SO<sub>2</sub> (aq) and HCl (aq). The AgNO<sub>3</sub> reacts with Cl<sup>-</sup> ions to form a white precipitate of AgCl: Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq) + Cl<sup>-</sup> (aq) → AgCl (s)
> - Acidified K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> is an oxidising agent. SO<sub>2</sub> is a reducing agent that reduces the orange Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2-</sup> ions to green Cr<sup>3+</sup> ions. This colour change from orange to green is also seen when K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> is used to oxidise alcohols.
> 
> For part (ii): in MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup>, the oxidation number of Mn is found from: Mn + (4 × −2) = −1, so Mn = +7, shown by the Roman numeral (VII).

parts.problemMd:
For each of the equations below, complete the table to show the initial and final oxidation numbers of the elements printed in **bold**, and balance the equation.

i) ...... **Mn**O<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> + ...... **S**O<sub>2</sub> + ...... H<sub>2</sub>O → ...... **Mn**<sup>2+</sup> + ...... **S**O<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup> + ...... H<sup>+</sup>

| Element | Initial oxidation number | Final oxidation number |
|---|---|---|
| **Mn** |   |   |
| **S** |   |   |

[2]

ii) ...... **Cr**<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2-</sup> + ...... **N**O<sub>2</sub> + ...... H<sup>+</sup> → ...... **Cr**<sup>3+</sup> + ...... **N**O<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> + ...... H<sub>2</sub>O

| Element | Initial oxidation number | Final oxidation number |
|---|---|---|
| **Cr** |   |   |
| **N** |   |   |

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The completed table and balanced equation are:

| Element | Initial oxidation number | Final oxidation number |
|---|---|---|
| **Mn** | **Final answer:** **+7** | **Final answer:** **+2** |
| **S** | **Final answer:** **+4** | **Final answer:** **+6** |

2**Mn**O<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> + 5**S**O<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O → 2**Mn**<sup>2+</sup> + 5**S**O<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup> + 4H<sup>+</sup>

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for Mn = +7 and +2 **AND** S = +4 and +6 (all four oxidation numbers correct)
> 
> 1 mark for the correctly balanced equation: 2MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> + 5SO<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O → 2Mn<sup>2+</sup> + 5SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup> + 4H<sup>+</sup>

ii) The completed table and balanced equation are:

| Element | Initial oxidation number | Final oxidation number |
|---|---|---|
| **Cr** | **Final answer:** **+6** | **Final answer:** **+3** |
| **N** | **Final answer:** **+4** | **Final answer:** **+5** |

**Cr**<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2-</sup> + 6**N**O<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sup>+</sup> → 2**Cr**<sup>3+</sup> + 6**N**O<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>O

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for Cr = +6 and +3 **AND** N = +4 and +5 (all four oxidation numbers correct)
> 
> 1 mark for the correctly balanced equation: Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2-</sup> + 6NO<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sup>+</sup> → 2Cr<sup>3+</sup> + 6NO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>O

> **[exam-tip]**
> To balance a redox equation using oxidation numbers, follow these steps:
> 
> 1. Assign oxidation numbers to the redox-active elements
> 2. Identify which element is oxidised and which is reduced, and by how much
> 3. Multiply coefficients to balance total electron transfer (total oxidation = total reduction)
> 4. Balance remaining atoms using H<sub>2</sub>O (for O) and H<sup>+</sup> (for H)
> 5. Check that charge is balanced on both sides
> 
> For part (i): Mn gains 5 electrons (+7 → +2); S loses 2 electrons (+4 → +6). To balance: 2 × Mn (10 electrons gained) and 5 × S (10 electrons lost). Then balance O and H.
> 
> For part (ii): Each Cr gains 3 electrons (+6 → +3), but Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2-</sup> contains 2 Cr atoms (6 electrons gained total). N loses 1 electron (+4 → +5), so 6 NO<sub>2</sub> are needed to balance the 6 electrons gained.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> What is observed during the reaction in (a)(ii):
> 
> - (Solution turns from) orange **[1 mark]**
> - To green **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The dichromate ion, Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2-</sup>, is orange. In the reaction, it is reduced to Cr<sup>3+</sup> ions, which are green. This colour change (orange to green) is the characteristic observation whenever an acidified dichromate solution acts as an oxidising agent — you will also see this colour change when K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> is used to oxidise alcohols in organic chemistry.

parts.problemMd:
Zinc will displace copper from copper(II) sulfate solution.

i) Construct an equation for this reaction. Include state symbols.

[1]

ii) Explain, using oxidation numbers, why this is a redox reaction.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The equation for the reaction between zinc and copper(II) sulfate:
> 
> - Zn (s) + CuSO<sub>4</sub> (aq) → ZnSO<sub>4</sub> (aq) + Cu (s) **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) Why this is a redox reaction, using oxidation numbers:
> 
> - The oxidation number of Zn increases from 0 (in Zn) to +2 (in ZnSO<sub>4</sub>); Zn is oxidised **[1 mark]**
> - The oxidation number of Cu decreases from +2 (in CuSO<sub>4</sub>) to 0 (in Cu); Cu is reduced **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The equation is a standard displacement reaction — Zn displaces Cu, so the products are ZnSO<sub>4</sub> and Cu metal.
> 
> When explaining why a reaction is a redox reaction, always give:
> 
> 1. Which element is oxidised and its oxidation number change (increase)
> 2. Which element is reduced and its oxidation number change (decrease)
> 
> A bare statement like "oxidation numbers change" will not score full marks — you must identify the specific elements and show the before and after values.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Zinc will displace copper from copper(II) sulfate solution.

i) Construct an equation for this reaction. Include state symbols.

The equation for the reaction between zinc and copper(II) sulfate:

- Zn (s) + CuSO~4~ (aq) → ZnSO~4~ (aq) + Cu (s)

Identify the oxidising agent in the reaction in **(c)(i)**. Construct a half-equation to support your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The oxidising agent and supporting half-equation:
> 
> - Cu<sup>2+</sup> / CuSO<sub>4</sub> is the oxidising agent **[1 mark]**
> - Cu<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>-</sup> → Cu **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The oxidising agent is the species that is itself reduced — it oxidises another species by accepting electrons.
> 
> In this reaction:
> 
> - Cu<sup>2+</sup> accepts 2 electrons and is reduced to Cu (the oxidising agent)
> - Zn donates 2 electrons and is oxidised to Zn<sup>2+</sup> (the reducing agent)
> 
> The half-equation for the oxidising agent shows reduction: Cu<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>-</sup> → Cu.

parts.problemMd:
Household bleach contains NaClO as its active ingredient.

NaClO can be produced from the reaction between chlorine and aqueous sodium hydroxide.

i) State the conditions required for NaClO to be produced from this reaction.

[1]

ii) State the systematic name of NaClO.

[1]

iii) When chlorine and sodium hydroxide react under different conditions, sodium chlorate(V) is produced. Deduce the formula of sodium chlorate(V).

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The conditions required for NaClO to be produced:
> 
> - Cold / 15 °C **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The systematic name of NaClO:
> 
> - Sodium chlorate(I) **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The formula of sodium chlorate(V):
> 
> - NaClO<sub>3</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> NaClO and NaClO<sub>3</sub> are both produced when Cl<sub>2</sub> reacts with NaOH, but under different conditions:
> 
> - Cold / dilute NaOH (approximately 15 °C) → NaClO (sodium chlorate(I))
> - Hot / concentrated NaOH (approximately 70 °C) → NaClO<sub>3</sub> (sodium chlorate(V))
> 
> The Roman numerals indicate the oxidation number of chlorine:
> 
> - In NaClO: Na = +1, O = −2, so Cl = +1, shown by (I)
> - In NaClO<sub>3</sub>: Na = +1, three O = −6, so Cl = +5, shown by (V)
> 
> To deduce the formula of sodium chlorate(V): chlorate(V) means the ClO<sub>x</sub><sup>n-</sup> ion with Cl in oxidation state +5. With Cl = +5 and three O atoms (3 × −2 = −6), the ion charge is +5 − 6 = −1, giving ClO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup>. Combined with Na<sup>+</sup>: NaClO<sub>3</sub>.

parts.problemMd:
The balanced symbol equation showing the reaction of chlorine and sodium hydroxide to form NaClO is shown below.

Cl<sub>2</sub> (aq) + 2NaOH (aq) → NaClO (aq) + NaCl (aq) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l)

i) Construct an ionic equation for this reaction.

[1]

ii) Explain, in terms of changes in oxidation numbers, why this is an example of a disproportionation reaction.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The ionic equation for this reaction is:
> 
> - Cl<sub>2</sub> + 2OH<sup>-</sup> → Cl<sup>-</sup> + ClO<sup>-</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are not required.
> 
> ii) This is a disproportionation reaction because:
> 
> - The same species / element is both oxidised and reduced **[1 mark]**
> - Cl is oxidised from 0 (in Cl<sub>2</sub>) to +1 (in ClO<sup>-</sup>)
> **AND**
> Cl is reduced from 0 (in Cl<sub>2</sub>) to −1 (in NaCl / Cl<sup>-</sup>) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part (i), to write the ionic equation:
> 
> 1. Replace all soluble ionic compounds with their separated ions
> 2. Cancel spectator ions (those unchanged on both sides)
> 
> Na<sup>+</sup> is a spectator ion and cancels out, giving:
> 
> Cl<sub>2</sub> + 2OH<sup>-</sup> → Cl<sup>-</sup> + ClO<sup>-</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>O
> 
> For part (ii), the two marks require:
> 
> 1. A statement that the same element (Cl) is both oxidised and reduced
> 2. Specific oxidation number evidence for both the oxidation AND the reduction
> 
> Both the oxidation and reduction with their oxidation number values must be stated to score the second mark.

parts.problemMd:
The concentration of NaClO in bleach can be found by reacting it with hydrogen peroxide, H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>.

NaClO (aq) + H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> (aq) → NaCl (aq) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l)

Explain, using oxidation numbers, why chlorine has been reduced in this reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Chlorine has been reduced in this reaction because:
> 
> - The oxidation number of Cl decreases from +1 (in NaClO) to −1 (in NaCl) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> To show reduction using oxidation numbers, state:
> 
> 1. The oxidation number of the element in the reactant
> 2. The oxidation number of the element in the product
> 3. That the oxidation number has decreased (meaning the species has been reduced)
> 
> A decrease in oxidation number = reduction. In this case, Cl goes from +1 to −1 (a decrease of 2), confirming reduction. Note also that hydrogen peroxide is oxidised in this reaction: O goes from −1 in H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> to 0 in O<sub>2</sub> (an increase in oxidation number).

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The concentration of NaClO in bleach can be found by reacting it with hydrogen peroxide, H₂O₂.

NaClO (aq) + H₂O₂ (aq) → NaCl (aq) + O₂ (g) + H₂O (l)

A student reacted an excess of aqueous hydrogen peroxide with 10.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of a sample of bleach. They collected 108 cm<sup>3</sup> of oxygen gas. Assume that under the conditions used, the molar gas volume is 24.0 dm<sup>3</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>.

Calculate the concentration of NaClO in the bleach, in g per 100 cm<sup>3</sup>. Show your working.

concentration of NaClO = ................................. g per 100 cm<sup>3</sup>
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the concentration of NaClO in the bleach:

- List the known values:

- volume of O<sub>2</sub> collected = 108 cm<sup>3</sup>
- molar gas volume = 24.0 dm<sup>3</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup> = 24 000 cm<sup>3</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>
- volume of bleach = 10.0 cm<sup>3</sup> = 0.0100 dm<sup>3</sup>
- *M*<sub>r</sub> (NaClO) = 23.0 + 35.5 + 16.0 = 74.5 g mol<sup>-1</sup>

- Calculate the moles of O<sub>2</sub>:

*n*(O<sub>2</sub>) = V (cm<sup>3</sup>) ÷ 24 000

*n*(O<sub>2</sub>) = 108 ÷ 24 000

*n*(O<sub>2</sub>) = **4.50 x 10**<sup>**-3**</sup> mol **[1 mark]**

- Deduce the moles of NaClO from the 1:1 molar ratio in the equation:

*n*(NaClO) = *n*(O<sub>2</sub>)

*n*(NaClO) = **4.50 x 10**<sup>**-3**</sup> mol **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the concentration of NaClO in mol dm<sup>-3</sup>:

concentration = $\frac{n}{V}$

concentration = $\frac{4.50\times10^{-3}}{0.0100}$

concentration = **0.450 mol dm**<sup>**-3**</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the concentration in g dm<sup>-3</sup>:

concentration (g dm<sup>-3</sup>) = concentration (mol dm<sup>-3</sup>) x *M*<sub>r</sub>(NaClO)

= 0.450 x 74.5

= **33.5 g dm**<sup>**-3**</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Convert to g per 100 cm<sup>3</sup>:

concentration (g per 100 cm<sup>3</sup>) = 33.5 ÷ 10

= **3.35 g per 100 cm**<sup>**3**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for *n*(O<sub>2</sub>) = 4.50 × 10<sup>-3</sup> mol
> 
> 1 mark for *n*(NaClO) = 4.50 × 10<sup>-3</sup> mol
> 
> 1 mark for concentration = 0.450 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for mass concentration = 33.5 g dm<sup>-3</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for 3.35 g per 100 cm<sup>3</sup>
> 
> Allow error carried forward if an earlier calculation is incorrect.

> **[exam-tip]**
> This question requires several unit conversions:
> 
> - Volume of gas: divide by 24 000 (not 24) to convert from cm<sup>3</sup> to mol using the molar gas volume in dm<sup>3</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>; alternatively, divide by 1000 first to get dm<sup>3</sup>, then divide by 24.0
> - Volume of bleach: divide 10.0 cm<sup>3</sup> by 1000 to get 0.0100 dm<sup>3</sup> before calculating concentration in mol dm<sup>-3</sup>
> - Final conversion: 33.5 g dm<sup>-3</sup> means 33.5 g in 1000 cm<sup>3</sup>; divide by 10 to get g per 100 cm<sup>3</sup>
> 
> The molar ratio of NaClO to O<sub>2</sub> is 1:1 from the equation, so moles of NaClO equal moles of O<sub>2</sub> directly.

parts.problemMd:
The tetrathionate ion, S<sub>4</sub>O<sub>6</sub><sup>2–</sup>, is shown in Fig 1.1.

![Structural diagram of the tetrathionate ion showing four sulfur atoms bonded in a chain with six bridging oxygen atoms](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/6-electrochemistry/6-1-redox-processes-electron-transfer-and-changes-in-oxidation-number-oxidation-state/assets/005-structural-diagram-of-the-tetrathionate-ion-show.png)

**Fig 1.1**

Deduce the oxidation number of sulfur in the tetrathionate ion. Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The oxidation number of sulfur in S<sub>4</sub>O<sub>6</sub><sup>2–</sup>:
> 
> - +2.5 **[1 mark]**
> - This is an average value; the tetrathionate ion contains sulfur atoms with two different oxidation numbers
> **OR**
> The oxidation number is not a whole number because the sulfur atoms exist in different bonding environments **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> To calculate the oxidation number of S in S<sub>4</sub>O<sub>6</sub><sup>2–</sup>:
> 
> - Each oxygen atom has an oxidation number of −2, giving a total of −12
> - The overall charge on the ion is −2
> - The sum of the oxidation numbers of all atoms must equal the ionic charge, so the four sulfur atoms together contribute +10
> - Average oxidation number per sulfur = +10 ÷ 4 = +2.5
> 
> Non-integer oxidation numbers arise when an element exists in two different bonding environments within the same ion or molecule, giving an average value. Do not round to a whole number as +2.5 is the expected answer.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The tetrathionate ion, S~4~O~6~^2–^, is shown in Fig 1.1.

Sodium tetrathionate can be formed by reacting sodium thiosulfate, Na<sub>2</sub>S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>, with iodine.

i) Construct an equation for the reaction between sodium thiosulfate and iodine. Include state symbols.

[2]

ii) Identify the oxidising agent in this reaction.

[1]

iii) State the colour change that would be observed during this reaction.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The equation for the reaction between sodium thiosulfate and iodine is:

2Na<sub>2</sub>S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> (aq) + I<sub>2</sub> (aq) → Na<sub>2</sub>S<sub>4</sub>O<sub>6</sub> (aq) + 2NaI (aq)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct formula for sodium tetrathionate, Na<sub>2</sub>S<sub>4</sub>O<sub>6</sub>, **AND** NaI as the other product
> 
> 1 mark for correctly balanced equation **AND** all four correct state symbols
> 
> ii) The oxidising agent in this reaction:
> 
> - I<sub>2</sub> / iodine **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The colour change observed when this reaction goes to completion:
> 
> - Orange-brown / brown / red-brown to colourless **[1 mark]**
> 
> 'Red' is not accepted without 'brown'

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part (i): the formula of sodium tetrathionate is derived from the tetrathionate ion S<sub>4</sub>O<sub>6</sub><sup>2–</sup> in Part (a). Two Na<sup>+</sup> ions balance the 2− charge to give Na<sub>2</sub>S<sub>4</sub>O<sub>6</sub>. The other product, NaI, forms because iodine is reduced from I<sub>2</sub> (oxidation number 0) to I<sup>–</sup> (oxidation number −1), which combines with Na<sup>+</sup>.
> 
> For part (ii): the oxidising agent accepts electrons and is itself reduced. Iodine, I<sub>2</sub>, gains electrons to form I<sup>–</sup> ions (oxidation number decreases 0 → −1), so I<sub>2</sub> is the oxidising agent.
> 
> For part (iii): aqueous iodine (I<sub>2</sub>) is orange-brown. As iodine is consumed by the reaction with thiosulfate, the colour disappears and the solution becomes colourless. This is the same colour change used as an endpoint signal in iodine-thiosulfate titrations.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The tetrathionate ion, S~4~O~6~^2–^, is shown in Fig 1.1.

Deduce the oxidation number of sulfur in the tetrathionate ion. Explain your answer.

Sodium tetrathionate can also be made by reacting sodium hydrogensulfite, NaHSO<sub>3</sub>, with disulfur dichloride, S<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>.

2NaHSO<sub>3</sub> + S<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> → Na<sub>2</sub>S<sub>4</sub>O<sub>6</sub> + 2HCl

State whether this reaction is an example of a disproportionation reaction. Explain your answer in terms of changes in oxidation numbers.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Whether this reaction is a disproportionation reaction:
> 
> - This reaction is not a disproportionation reaction; disproportionation requires a single element in one reactant to be simultaneously oxidised and reduced **[1 mark]**
> - Oxidation number of S in NaHSO<sub>3</sub> = +4 and is reduced to +2.5; oxidation number of S in S<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> = +1 and is oxidised to +2.5; the sulfur species undergoing oxidation and reduction are in different reactants **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> To find the oxidation number of S in NaHSO<sub>3</sub>: Na = +1, H = +1, each O = −2; the compound is neutral, so S + 1 + 1 + (3 x −2) = 0, giving S = +4.
> 
> To find the oxidation number of S in S<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>: each Cl = −1; the compound is neutral, so 2S + 2(−1) = 0, giving S = +1.
> 
> The average oxidation number of S in Na<sub>2</sub>S<sub>4</sub>O<sub>6</sub> = +2.5 (from Part (a)).
> 
> In this reaction, sulfur from NaHSO<sub>3</sub> (S = +4) and sulfur from S<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> (S = +1) both change to +2.5 in the product. This is comproportionation — two species of the same element at different oxidation numbers converge to form a product at an intermediate oxidation number. Since oxidation and reduction occur in two different reactant species, this cannot be described as disproportionation.

parts.problemMd:
Photochromic glass contains an evenly distributed mixture of copper(I) chloride and silver(I) chloride. When ultraviolet light passes through the glass, the silver(I) chloride is separated into its ions. The chloride ions are then converted into chlorine atoms and the silver(I) ions into silver atoms. The silver atoms cluster together causing the lenses of photochromic glasses to darken.

Construct two ionic half-equations for the processes involved in the darkening of photochromic glasses. State whether each process is oxidation or reduction. Explain your answer in terms of electron transfer.
parts.solutionMd:
The two ionic half-equations for the processes involved in the darkening are:

Cl<sup>–</sup> (aq) → Cl (aq) + e<sup>–</sup>

Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq) + e<sup>–</sup> → Ag (s)

- The first reaction is oxidation; chloride ions lose electrons (oxidation number of Cl increases from −1 to 0)
- The second reaction is reduction; silver ions gain electrons (oxidation number of Ag decreases from +1 to 0)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for both ionic half-equations correct
> 
> 1 mark for correctly identifying the Cl<sup>–</sup> half-equation as oxidation (Cl<sup>–</sup> loses electrons / oxidation number increases from −1 to 0) **AND** the Ag<sup>+</sup> half-equation as reduction (Ag<sup>+</sup> gains electrons / oxidation number decreases from +1 to 0)
> 
> The dissociation AgCl → Ag<sup>+</sup> + Cl<sup>–</sup> is not a redox process and should not be included as a half-equation

> **[exam-tip]**
> Use OIL RIG to classify the half-equations:
> 
> - Oxidation Is Loss: Cl<sup>–</sup> loses one electron per ion (Cl<sup>–</sup> → Cl + e<sup>–</sup>); this is oxidation
> - Reduction Is Gain: Ag<sup>+</sup> gains one electron per ion (Ag<sup>+</sup> + e<sup>–</sup> → Ag); this is reduction
> 
> The dissociation of AgCl into ions (AgCl → Ag<sup>+</sup> + Cl<sup>–</sup>) is described in the stem but is not a redox process as there is no transfer of electrons and no change in oxidation numbers.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Photochromic glass contains an evenly distributed mixture of copper(I) chloride and silver(I) chloride. When ultraviolet light passes through the glass, the silver(I) chloride is separated into its ions. The chloride ions are then converted into chlorine atoms and the silver(I) ions into silver atoms. The silver atoms cluster together causing the lenses of photochromic glasses to darken.

Identify the oxidising agent in the darkening process described in part (a). Explain your answer in terms of changes in oxidation number.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The oxidising agent in the darkening process described in part (a):
> 
> - Ag<sup>+</sup> / silver(I) ions **[1 mark]**
> - The oxidation number of silver decreases from +1 in Ag<sup>+</sup> to 0 in Ag; a decrease in oxidation number indicates reduction, so Ag<sup>+</sup> gains electrons and acts as the oxidising agent **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The oxidising agent is the species that causes oxidation in another — it does so by accepting electrons and is itself reduced. In this reaction, Ag<sup>+</sup> ions are reduced (oxidation number +1 → 0, gaining electrons to form Ag atoms), so Ag<sup>+</sup> is the oxidising agent.
> 
> The reducing agent is Cl<sup>–</sup>, which loses electrons and is itself oxidised (oxidation number −1 → 0).

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Photochromic glass contains an evenly distributed mixture of copper(I) chloride and silver(I) chloride. When ultraviolet light passes through the glass, the silver(I) chloride is separated into its ions. The chloride ions are then converted into chlorine atoms and the silver(I) ions into silver atoms. The silver atoms cluster together causing the lenses of photochromic glasses to darken.

The two ionic half-equations for the processes involved in the darkening are:
Cl⁻ (aq) → Cl (aq) + e⁻
Ag⁺ (aq) + e⁻ → Ag (s)

The darkening process caused by the formation of silver atoms is reversible. Copper(I) chloride first reacts with the chlorine atoms from part (a) to form copper(II) chloride. Copper(II) chloride then reacts with the silver atoms from part (a) to reform silver(I) chloride.

Construct two equations to represent these reactions.
parts.solutionMd:
The two equations for the reactions that cause the lens to lighten are:

CuCl + Cl → CuCl<sub>2</sub>

CuCl<sub>2</sub> + Ag → CuCl + AgCl

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for CuCl + Cl → CuCl<sub>2</sub>
> **OR**
> Cu<sup>+</sup> + Cl → Cu<sup>2+</sup> + Cl<sup>–</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for CuCl<sub>2</sub> + Ag → CuCl + AgCl
> **OR**
> Cu<sup>2+</sup> + Ag → Cu<sup>+</sup> + Ag<sup>+</sup>
> 
> State symbols are not required

> **[exam-tip]**
> The available species are CuCl, Cl atoms (from Part (a)), and Ag atoms (from Part (a)).
> 
> - Step 1: CuCl reacts with Cl atoms. Cu<sup>+</sup> is oxidised to Cu<sup>2+</sup> and Cl atoms are reduced from 0 to −1, producing CuCl<sub>2</sub>.
> - Step 2: CuCl<sub>2</sub> reacts with Ag atoms. Cu<sup>2+</sup> is reduced to Cu<sup>+</sup> (accepting electrons from Ag), and Ag is oxidised from 0 to +1, producing AgCl.
> 
> Note: silver cannot displace copper from CuCl because copper is above silver in the reactivity series.

parts.problemMd:
Copper(I) chloride, similar to that used in photochromic glass, can be made in the laboratory by the following method:

- Warm 0.5 g copper(II) oxide with 5 cm<sup>3</sup> concentrated hydrochloric acid for 1 minute.
- Add 1.0 g of copper turnings.
- Gently boil for 5 minutes.
- Filter the solution into 250 cm<sup>3</sup> of deionised water.
- Allow the copper(I) chloride precipitate to settle.
- Decant the liquid.
- Allow the copper(I) chloride to dry.

i) Construct an equation for the reaction described. Include state symbols.

[1]

ii) A student states that the reaction in (i) is a disproportionation reaction. State whether the student is correct. Explain your answer in terms of changes in oxidation numbers.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The equation for the reaction, including state symbols:
> 
> - CuO (s) + Cu (s) + 2HCl (aq) → 2CuCl (s) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l) **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) Whether the student is correct:
> 
> - The student is not correct; this is not a disproportionation reaction **[1 mark]**
> - Disproportionation requires a single element in one reactant to be simultaneously oxidised and reduced; in this reaction, copper in CuO (+2) is reduced to +1 and copper in Cu (0) is oxidised to +1, but these are two different reactants **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part (i): HCl is aqueous, not liquid — include (aq) not (l) for hydrochloric acid. All state symbols are required by the question.
> 
> For part (ii): disproportionation is a type of redox reaction in which the same element in a single substance is simultaneously oxidised and reduced. In this reaction, Cu<sup>2+</sup> (from CuO, oxidation number +2) is reduced to +1 and Cu (copper turnings, oxidation number 0) is oxidised to +1. Since the two copper species come from two different reactants, this is comproportionation, not disproportionation.

Complete Table 3.1 by identifying, for each product, whether it is formed by oxidation, reduction, or neither oxidation nor reduction.

| SO<sub>2</sub> | **Final answer:** **Reduction** |

parts.problemMd:
Sulfur dioxide reacts with a solution of copper(II) chloride.

SO<sub>2</sub> (g) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l) + 2CuCl<sub>2</sub> (aq) → H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (aq) + 2HCl (aq) + 2CuCl (s)

Identify the reducing agent and oxidising agent in this reaction. Explain your answer in terms of changes in oxidation number.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The reducing agent and oxidising agent in this reaction:
> 
> - Reducing agent = sulfur dioxide / SO<sub>2</sub>; the oxidation number of sulfur increases from +4 in SO<sub>2</sub> to +6 in H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> **[1 mark]**
> - Oxidising agent = Cu<sup>2+</sup> ions / CuCl<sub>2</sub>; the oxidation number of copper decreases from +2 in CuCl<sub>2</sub> to +1 in CuCl **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Using oxidation numbers, only sulfur and copper change oxidation state in this reaction:
> 
> - Sulfur: +4 in SO<sub>2</sub> → +6 in H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (increase = oxidation)
> - Copper: +2 in CuCl<sub>2</sub> → +1 in CuCl (decrease = reduction)
> 
> The reducing agent is oxidised (it causes reduction in another species by donating electrons). Sulfur is oxidised, so SO<sub>2</sub> is the reducing agent.
> 
> The oxidising agent is reduced (it causes oxidation in another species by accepting electrons). Copper is reduced, so CuCl<sub>2</sub> / Cu<sup>2+</sup> is the oxidising agent.

parts.problemMd:
Sodium iodate is one of the main sources of iodine in the world. To extract the iodine, sodium iodate is reacted with aqueous sodium hydrogensulfite, NaHSO<sub>3</sub>, according to the following ionic equation.

2IO<sub>3</sub><sup>–</sup> (aq) + 5HSO<sub>3</sub><sup>–</sup> (aq) → 3HSO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> (aq) + 2SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2–</sup> (aq) + I<sub>2</sub> (aq) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l)

i) State the change in oxidation number of iodine in this reaction.

[1]

ii) Identify the role of the hydrogensulfite ion in this reaction. Explain your answer in terms of changes in oxidation numbers.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The change in oxidation number of iodine in this reaction:
> 
> - Decreases from +5 in IO<sub>3</sub><sup>–</sup> to 0 in I<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The role of the hydrogensulfite ion:
> 
> - Reducing agent / reductant **[1 mark]**
> - The oxidation number of sulfur increases from +4 in HSO<sub>3</sub><sup>–</sup> to +6 in HSO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> and SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2–</sup>; an increase in oxidation number indicates oxidation, so HSO<sub>3</sub><sup>–</sup> loses electrons and acts as the reducing agent **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part (i):
> 
> To find the oxidation number of I in IO<sub>3</sub><sup>–</sup>, O = −2 and the ion has a charge of −1. So I + 3(−2) = −1, giving I = +5. In I<sub>2</sub>, I = 0. The decrease from +5 to 0 indicates reduction of iodine.
> 
> For part (ii):
> 
> To find the oxidation number of S in HSO<sub>3</sub><sup>–</sup>, H = +1, O = −2, overall charge = −1. So 1 + S + 3(−2) = −1, giving S = +4. In both HSO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> and SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2–</sup>, S = +6. The increase in oxidation number of sulfur from +4 to +6 indicates oxidation. The species that is oxidised is the reducing agent, so HSO<sub>3</sub><sup>–</sup> acts as the reducing agent.

name: Chemical Equilibria: Reversible Reactions & Dynamic Equilibrium

parts.problemMd:
Nitrogen dioxide and dinitrogen tetroxide exist in equilibrium.

2NO<sub>2</sub> (g) ⇌ N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> (g)      ∆H = −57 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>

Which conditions give the greatest percentage of NO<sub>2</sub> in the equilibrium mixture?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- The **enthalpy change** of the forward reaction is **exothermic** (ΔH is negative), so the **reverse** reaction is **endothermic**.

- **Effect of temperature:**

  - An increase in temperature shifts the equilibrium to the **left** (the endothermic direction), increasing the percentage of NO<sub>2</sub> in the equilibrium mixture.

- **Effect of pressure:**

  - A decrease in pressure shifts the equilibrium to the side with **more moles of gas** (the left, 2 moles of NO<sub>2</sub> vs 1 mole of N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>), increasing the percentage of NO<sub>2</sub> in the equilibrium mixture.

**A** is incorrect as although high temperature correctly shifts the equilibrium to the left, high pressure shifts the equilibrium to the **right** (fewer moles of gas), decreasing the percentage of NO<sub>2</sub>.

**B** is incorrect as both high pressure and low temperature shift the equilibrium to the **right**: high pressure favours the side with fewer moles of gas, and low temperature favours the exothermic forward reaction. Both conditions decrease the percentage of NO<sub>2</sub>.

**D** is incorrect as although low pressure shifts the equilibrium to the left (increasing the percentage of NO<sub>2</sub>), low temperature shifts the equilibrium to the right (exothermic direction). The two conditions have opposing effects on the position of equilibrium.

choices.label: A

parts.problemMd:
Sulfuric acid is manufactured via a series of reactions in the Contact process. The equation for the main stage of this process is shown.

2SO<sub>2</sub> (g) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) ⇌ 2SO<sub>3</sub> (g)     ∆H = −197 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>

Which statement about this reaction is correct?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- The enthalpy change of the forward reaction is **exothermic** (ΔH is negative), so the **reverse** reaction is **endothermic**.

- The equilibrium will shift to the **left** when the temperature is raised to oppose the change, increasing the equilibrium amount of SO<sub>2</sub>.

  - This is in accordance with **Le Chatelier's principle**.

**A** is incorrect as the Contact process uses **vanadium(V) oxide** (V<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub>) as its catalyst. Iron is the catalyst used in the Haber process.

**C** is incorrect as increasing the temperature shifts the equilibrium to the **endothermic** (reverse) reaction, **lowering** the yield of SO<sub>3</sub>.

**D** is incorrect as increasing the pressure shifts the equilibrium to the side with **fewer moles of gas**. There are 3 moles of gas on the reactant side and 2 moles on the product side, so the equilibrium shifts to the right, **decreasing** the equilibrium amount of SO<sub>2</sub>.

choices.label: A
choices.textMd: The rate of the forward reaction is equal to the reverse reaction in a closed system, and the concentrations of the reactants and products are equal.

choices.label: B
choices.textMd: The rate of the forward reaction is equal to the reverse reaction in a closed system, and the concentrations of the reactants and products are constant.

choices.label: C
choices.textMd: The rate of the forward reaction is equal to the reverse reaction, and the concentrations of the reactants and products are constant.

choices.label: D

parts.problemMd: Which statement describes a dynamic equilibrium?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- The three conditions for a dynamic equilibrium are:

  1. The rate of the **forward reaction** equals the rate of the **reverse reaction**.
  2. The reaction takes place in a **closed system**.
  3. The concentrations of reactants and products are **constant** (not necessarily equal).

**A** is incorrect as the concentrations of reactants and products are **constant**, not necessarily equal. They can exist in any ratio (e.g. 50:50, 75:25) but remain unchanged once equilibrium is reached.

**C** is incorrect as it omits the requirement for a **closed system**. If the system is open, matter can escape and a dynamic equilibrium cannot be maintained.

**D** is incorrect as this describes a shift in equilibrium position in response to a change in conditions (Le Chatelier's principle), not the features of dynamic equilibrium itself.

parts.problemMd:
An equilibrium is set up in a closed container between equal amounts, in mol, of gaseous reactants A and B to form a gaseous product C.

The total pressure within the container at 50 °C is 3.0 atm.

A (g) + B (g) ⇌ 2C (g)

The equilibrium partial pressure of A at 50 °C is 0.50 atm.

What is the partial pressure of C, in atm, in the equilibrium mixture?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- As reactants A and B were added in equal amounts and react in a 1:1 molar ratio, their equilibrium mole fractions are identical.

  - Therefore, if p(A) = 0.50 atm, then **p(B) = 0.50 atm**.

- Applying Dalton's Law:

Total pressure = p(A) + p(B) + p(C)

3.0 = 0.50 + 0.50 + p(C)

**p(C) = 2.0 atm**

**A** is incorrect as this is obtained by multiplying p(A) by the stoichiometric coefficient of C: 0.50 × 2 = 1.0 atm. This approach does not apply Dalton's Law correctly.

**B** is incorrect as this is obtained by treating the mole fraction of C as 0.5 (based on stoichiometric coefficients), giving p(C) = 0.50 × 3.0 = 1.5 atm. The mole fraction must be calculated from equilibrium amounts, not stoichiometric coefficients.

**D** is incorrect as this is obtained by forgetting to account for gas B in the total pressure: 3.0 − 0.50 = 2.5 atm. The partial pressures of all three gases must sum to the total pressure.

choices.label: B

parts.problemMd:
The Haber process is used to produce ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen on an industrial scale. The diagram below represents the Haber process.

![Process flow diagram of ammonia synthesis showing N₂ and H₂ feed, heat exchanger, catalytic converter, condenser and NH₃ product stream with recycle lines](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/7-equilibria/7-1-chemical-equilibria-reversible-reactions-and-dynamic-equilibrium/assets/001-process-flow-diagram-of-ammonia-synthesis-showin.png)

What is the purpose of the heat exchanger?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- The **heat exchanger** transfers heat from the hot outgoing gas mixture to the **incoming nitrogen and hydrogen.**

- This gives the incoming molecules more **kinetic energy**, increasing the frequency of effective collisions.

- A higher collision frequency **increases the rate of reaction**, allowing equilibrium to be reached more quickly.

**A** is incorrect as separating ammonia from unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen is done by the **condenser**, not the heat exchanger.

**B** is incorrect as the forward reaction N<sub>2</sub> (g) + 3H<sub>2</sub> (g) ⇌ 2NH<sub>3</sub> (g) is **exothermic**. Increasing temperature shifts the equilibrium to the **left**, which **decreases** the yield of ammonia.

**D** is incorrect as the heat exchanger **warms** the incoming gases; it does not cool them.

parts.problemMd:
Ethanol is manufactured by reacting steam with ethene.

C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub> (g) + H<sub>2</sub>O (g) ⇌ C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH (g)     ΔH = −45 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>

Which pair of changes would both increase the equilibrium yield of ethanol?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- The equation C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub> (g) + H<sub>2</sub>O (g) ⇌ C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH (g) has **2 moles of gas on the left** and **1 mole on the right.**

- Increasing pressure shifts the equilibrium towards fewer moles of gas / the **right-hand side**, which increases the yield of ethanol.

- The forward reaction (ΔH = −45 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>) is **exothermic.** Decreasing temperature shifts the equilibrium to the **right** (the exothermic direction), further increasing the yield of ethanol.

**A** and **B** are incorrect as adding a catalyst increases the **rate** at which equilibrium is reached but has **no effect on the position of equilibrium** or yield.

**D** is incorrect as decreasing pressure shifts the equilibrium to the left (towards more moles of gas), and increasing temperature shifts the equilibrium to the left (suppressing the exothermic forward reaction), both **decreasing** the yield of ethanol.

parts.problemMd:
Propyl ethanoate is formed in an esterification reaction.

CH<sub>3</sub>COOH (l) + C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>7</sub>OH (l) ⇌ CH<sub>3</sub>COOC<sub>3</sub>H<sub>7</sub> (l) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l)     ΔH = −10 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>

What will increase the value of the equilibrium constant, *K*<sub>c</sub>?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- The esterification reaction has ΔH = −10 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>, so the forward reaction is **exothermic.**

- Decreasing temperature shifts the equilibrium to the right (the exothermic direction) to oppose the change, in accordance with Le Chatelier's principle.

- This increases the concentrations of propyl ethanoate and water relative to the reactants, so the value of *K*<sub>c</sub> **increases.**

**A** is incorrect as adding a catalyst increases the **rate** at which equilibrium is reached but has no effect on the position of equilibrium or the value of *K*<sub>c</sub>.

**C** is incorrect as all species in this reaction are **liquids**; pressure changes only affect gaseous equilibria and have no effect on *K*<sub>c</sub>.

**D** is incorrect as increasing temperature shifts the equilibrium to the left (the endothermic direction), decreasing the concentrations of propyl ethanoate and water relative to the reactants, which **decreases** the value of *K*<sub>c</sub>.

parts.problemMd:
Gaseous iodine reacts with hydrogen to establish an equilibrium at 450 °C.

H<sub>2</sub> (g) + I<sub>2</sub> (g) ⇌ 2HI (g)     ΔH = −9 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>

colourless + purple ⇌ colourless

Which change in conditions will cause the purple colour of the gas mixture to become paler?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- The forward reaction H<sub>2</sub> (g) + I<sub>2</sub> (g) ⇌ 2HI (g) is **exothermic** (ΔH = −9 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>).

  - The reverse reaction is therefore endothermic.

- Decreasing temperature shifts the equilibrium to the right (the exothermic direction) to oppose the change, in accordance with Le Chatelier's principle.

- This increases the yield of HI and decreases the concentration of I<sub>2</sub> (g), causing the gas mixture to become **paler.**

**A** & **C** are incorrect as there are **equal moles of gas on each side** of this equation (2 mol each). Pressure changes have no effect on the position of this equilibrium.

**D** is incorrect as increasing temperature shifts the equilibrium to the left (the endothermic direction), increasing the concentration of I<sub>2</sub> (g) and causing the gas mixture to become **darker**, not paler.

parts.problemMd:
Compounds A and B exist in equilibrium with compound C.

2A (g) +  B (g)  ⇌  2C (g)  ∆H = +6.5 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

What will increase the value of the equilibrium constant, *K*<sub>p</sub>?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Only **temperature** permanently changes the value of *K*<sub>p</sub>; the equilibrium shifts to oppose the temperature change, establishing a new equilibrium position with a different value of *K*<sub>p</sub>.

- No other change in conditions will affect the value of *K*<sub>p</sub>.

**A** is incorrect as adding a catalyst increases the **rate** at which equilibrium is reached but has no effect on the position of equilibrium or the value of *K*<sub>p</sub>.

**B** & **C** are incorrect as only temperature changes the value of *K*<sub>p</sub>. When pressure changes, all partial pressures change proportionally. The equilibrium shifts to maintain the same ratio and *K*<sub>p</sub> remains constant at the new equilibrium position.

parts.problemMd:
An equilibrium is established in the reaction.

AB (aq) + CD (aq) ⇌ AC (aq) + BD (aq)     ΔH = +180 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>

Which factor would affect the value of *K*<sub>c</sub> in this equilibrium?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Only **temperature** changes the value of *K*<sub>c</sub>

  - The equilibrium shifts to oppose the temperature change, establishing a new equilibrium position with a different value of *K*<sub>c</sub>.

- Any other change in conditions leaves *K*<sub>c</sub> constant.

**A** is incorrect as neither a change in pressure nor the presence of a catalyst affects the value of *K*<sub>c</sub>. All species are **aqueous**, so pressure changes have no effect; a catalyst only increases the **rate** at which equilibrium is reached without altering *K*<sub>c</sub>.

**C** & **D** are incorrect as changing the concentration of a reactant or product shifts the equilibrium, but the ratio of concentrations at the new equilibrium position remains the same and *K*<sub>c</sub> is unchanged.

parts.problemMd:
Ammonia is manufactured using the Haber process, which is represented by the following equation:

N<sub>2</sub> (g) + 3H<sub>2</sub> (g) ⇌ 2NH<sub>3</sub> (g)     ΔH = −93 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>

Which row describes what happens to the rates of the forward and reverse reactions when the temperature is increased?

|   | Rate of forward reaction | Rate of reverse reaction |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | no change | no change |
| **B** | no change | increases |
| **C** | increases | increases |
| **D** | increases | no change |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Increasing temperature gives all molecules more **kinetic energy**, increasing the frequency of effective collisions.

- Both the **forward and reverse rates** therefore increase.

- The **reverse reaction** (endothermic) is favoured by Le Chatelier's principle, so its rate increases more than the forward rate until a new equilibrium position is reached.

**A** is incorrect as both rates increase. Temperature always increases the rate of both forward and reverse reactions.

**B** is incorrect as the forward reaction rate also increases.

**D** is incorrect as the reverse reaction rate also increases.

parts.problemMd:
At 450<sup>o</sup>C, the value for *K*<sub>*c*</sub> for the below reaction is 60.

H<sub>2</sub> (g) + I<sub>2</sub> (g)  ⇌  2HI (g)

The equilibrium moles of H<sub>2</sub> and I<sub>2</sub> are 2 mol and 0.3 mol, respectively.

What is the number of moles of HI (g) present at equilibrium?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Known values:

  - *K*<sub>c</sub> = 60
  - n(H<sub>2</sub>) = 2 mol; n(I<sub>2</sub>) = 0.3 mol

- Write the *K*<sub>c</sub> expression:

`K_{c} = \frac{[\text{HI (g)}]^{2}}{[\text{H}_{2}\text{ (g)}][\text{I}_{2}\text{ (g)}]}`

- Rearrange to make [HI (g)] the subject:

`[\text{HI (g)}] = \sqrt{K_{c} \times [\text{H}_{2}\text{ (g)}] \times [\text{I}_{2}\text{ (g)}]}`

- Since there are equal moles of gas on each side (Δ*n* = 0), volume cancels and moles can be used directly:
- Substitute the known values:

n(HI) = $\sqrt{60\times2\times0.3}$

n(HI) = $\sqrt{36}$

n(HI) = **6 mol**

**A** is incorrect as 0.010 comes from inverting the *K*<sub>c</sub> expression and not taking the square root.

**B** is incorrect as 0.10 comes from inverting the *K*<sub>c</sub> expression.

**D** is incorrect as the square root has not been taken. The exponent of 2 on [HI] means you must take the square root to find n(HI).

parts.problemMd:
Ethyne and hydrogen are formed from methane, and a dynamic equilibrium is established.

2CH<sub>4</sub> (g)  ⇌  3H<sub>2</sub> (g) + C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>2</sub> (g)

What are the units for *K*<sub>c</sub>?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Write the *K*<sub>c</sub> expression for this reaction:

*K*<sub>c</sub> = `(left square bracket H _ 2 ( g ) right square bracket ^3 left square bracket C _ 2 H _ 2 ( g ) right square bracket)/(left square bracket CH _ 4 ( g ) right square bracket ^2)`

- The unit of each concentration term is mol dm<sup>-3</sup>:

*K*<sub>c</sub> = $\frac{[ \text{mol} dm^{ - } 3 ) ] ^{3} [ \text{mol} dm^{ - } 3 ]}{[ \text{mol} dm^{ - } 3 ] ^{2} }$

*K*<sub>c</sub> = $[ \text{mol} dm^{ - } 3 ) ] [ \text{mol} dm^{ - } 3 ]$

*K*<sub>c</sub> = mol<sup>2</sup> dm<sup>-6</sup>

**A, C & D **are incorrect as none of these units fit with the correct expression of *K*<sub>c</sub>.

parts.problemMd:
Upon heating, dinitrogen tetroxide will dissociate into nitrogen dioxide.

N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> (g)  ⇌  2NO<sub>2</sub> (g)

At a particular temperature, the equilibrium partial pressure of nitrogen dioxide was 0.67 atm and that of dinitrogen tetroxide was 0.33 atm.

What is the value of *K*<sub>p</sub> at this temperature?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Known values:

  - *p*(NO<sub>2</sub>) = 0.67 atm
  - *p*(N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>) = 0.33 atm

- Write the expression for *K*<sub>p</sub>:

$K_{p} = \frac{p(\text{NO}_{2})^{2}}{p(\text{N}_{2}\text{O}_{4})}$

- Substitute the equilibrium partial pressures:

$K_{p} = \frac{(0.67)^{2}}{0.33}$

$K_{p} = \frac{0.4489}{0.33}$

*K*<sub>p</sub> = **1.36**

**A** is incorrect as 0.49 comes from inverting the *K*<sub>p</sub> expression without applying the exponent: *p*(N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>) / *p*(NO<sub>2</sub>) = 0.33 / 0.67 = 0.49.

**B** is incorrect as 0.74 comes from inverting the *K*<sub>p</sub> expression: *p*(N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>) / *p*(NO<sub>2</sub>)<sup>2</sup> = 0.33 / (0.67)<sup>2</sup> = 0.74. The correct expression has products in the numerator.

**D** is incorrect as the stoichiometric coefficient of 2 for NO<sub>2</sub> has not been applied as an exponent: *p*(NO<sub>2</sub>) / *p*(N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>) = 0.67 / 0.33 = 2.03.

parts.problemMd:
Nitrogen monoxide and oxygen can be formed from the thermal decomposition of nitrogen dioxide.

2NO<sub>2</sub> (g) ⇌ 2NO (g) + O<sub>2</sub> (g)

In an experiment, 4 mol of nitrogen dioxide were put into a 1 dm<sup>3</sup> container and heated to a constant temperature. The equilibrium mixture contains 0.8 mol of oxygen.

Which expression gives the value of the equilibrium constant, *K*<sub>c</sub>, at the temperature of the experiment?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Known values:

  - n(NO<sub>2</sub>) initial = 4 mol
  - n(O<sub>2</sub>) at equilibrium = 0.8 mol
  - V = 1 dm<sup>3</sup>

- From the molar ratio NO<sub>2</sub> : NO : O<sub>2</sub> = 2 : 2 : 1, if 0.8 mol of O<sub>2</sub> forms:

  - change in NO<sub>2</sub> = −1.6 mol
  - change in NO = +1.6 mol

|   | 2NO<sub>2</sub> (g) ⇌ | 2NO (g) + | O<sub>2</sub> (g) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Initial moles | 4 | 0 | 0 |
| Change | −1.6 | +1.6 | +0.8 |
| Equilibrium moles | 2.4 | 1.6 | 0.8 |

- Since the volume is 1 dm<sup>3</sup>, equilibrium concentrations equal equilibrium moles numerically.
- Write the *K*<sub>c</sub> expression:

`K_{c} = \frac{[\text{NO (g)}]^{2}[\text{O}_{2}\text{ (g)}]}{[\text{NO}_{2}\text{ (g)}]^{2}}`

- Substitute equilibrium values:

*K*<sub>c</sub> = $\frac{1.6^{2}\times0.8}{2.4^{2}}$

**A** is incorrect as 0.8 mol has been used for NO (g) instead of 1.6 mol. The molar ratio 2:2:1 gives Δn(NO) = 2 × Δn(O<sub>2</sub>) = 2 × 0.8 = 1.6 mol.

**B** is incorrect as NO (g) has not been squared. The stoichiometric coefficient of 2 for NO becomes an exponent in the *K*<sub>c</sub> expression.

**C** is incorrect as NO<sub>2</sub> (g) has not been squared. The stoichiometric coefficient of 2 in the denominator also becomes an exponent in the *K*<sub>c</sub> expression.

choices.label: A
choices.textMd: In the first stage, a large excess of air under high pressure is used to improve the yield.

choices.label: B
