parts.problemMd: Which statement about the addition of a catalyst to a reversible reaction is correct?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- A catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy.
- This lowers the activation energy barrier for both the forward and reverse reactions equally, so the rate of both reactions increases.

**A** is incorrect as the average kinetic energy of the reacting particles is determined by the temperature of the system alone. A catalyst does not change the temperature and therefore has no effect on the average kinetic energy.

**B** is incorrect as a catalyst provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy but does not change the absolute energy levels of the reactants or products. The enthalpy change of the forward reaction is therefore unaffected.

**C** is incorrect as a catalyst is not consumed in the overall reaction. By definition, a catalyst is chemically unchanged at the end of the process, so its mass remains the same.

parts.problemMd:
Which row describes the effect of adding a catalyst to a reaction?

|   | activation energy of the alternative pathway | rate of reaction |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | higher | decreases |
| **B** | higher | increases |
| **C** | lower | decreases |
| **D** | lower | increases |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- A catalyst increases the rate of a chemical reaction by providing an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy than the uncatalysed route.
- Since the activation energy barrier is lower, a greater proportion of the reacting particles have energy greater than or equal to *E*<sub>a</sub>
- This increases the frequency of effective collisions and therefore the rate of reaction.

**A** and **B** are incorrect as a catalyst provides a pathway with a lower activation energy, not a higher one. A higher activation energy barrier would reduce the proportion of effective collisions and decrease the rate of reaction.

**C** is incorrect as a lower activation energy increases the proportion of molecules that can react, which increases the rate of reaction, not decreases it.

parts.problemMd:
Which row describes the catalyst used in the Haber process?

|   | type of catalysis | identity of catalyst |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | heterogeneous | iron |
| **B** | heterogeneous | vanadium(V) oxide |
| **C** | homogeneous | iron |
| **D** | homogeneous | vanadium(V) oxide |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- The Haber process uses finely divided iron as a catalyst.
- The reactants nitrogen and hydrogen are both gases, while the iron catalyst is a solid.
- Since the catalyst and reactants are in different physical states, this is an example of heterogeneous catalysis.

**C** is incorrect as iron is the correct catalyst identity, but the Haber process uses heterogeneous catalysis, not homogeneous. Homogeneous catalysis requires the catalyst to be in the same physical state as the reactants.

**B** and **D** are incorrect as vanadium(V) oxide is the catalyst for the Contact process (the industrial production of sulfuric acid), not the Haber process.

parts.problemMd:
The diagram shows the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution of molecular energies for a gaseous mixture. The peak is labelled Q, and the activation energy is marked as *E*<sub>a</sub>.

![Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution curve with peak Q marked at the top and activation energy Ea shown as a vertical line on the x-axis to the right of the peak](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/8-reaction-kinetics/8-3-homogeneous-and-heterogeneous-catalysts/assets/002-maxwell-boltzmann-distribution-curve-with-peak-q.png)

Which row describes the changes to the diagram when an effective catalyst is added?

|   | height of peak Q | position of *E*<sub>a</sub> |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | decreases | shifts to the left |
| **B** | decreases | shifts to the right |
| **C** | remains the same | shifts to the left |
| **D** | remains the same | shifts to the right |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- A catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy (*E*<sub>a</sub>).
- The height of peak Q is determined solely by the temperature and total number of molecules in the sample.

  - Adding a catalyst changes neither of these, so the height of peak Q remains the same.
- A lower *E*<sub>a</sub> corresponds to a position shifted to the left on the kinetic energy axis, as the activation energy has a smaller numerical value.

  - This is shown in the diagram below.

![Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution curve showing the original uncatalysed activation energy Ea and a second vertical line shifted to the left representing the lower activation energy of the catalysed pathway, with peak Q unchanged](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/8-reaction-kinetics/8-3-homogeneous-and-heterogeneous-catalysts/assets/003-maxwell-boltzmann-distribution-curve-showing-the.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as the height of peak Q only decreases when the temperature is raised, which causes the distribution to flatten and broaden. A catalyst does not change the temperature.

**B** is incorrect as a lower activation energy corresponds to a line shifted to the left on the kinetic energy axis (a smaller numerical value), not to the right.

**D** is incorrect as the height of peak Q remains the same (temperature is unchanged), and a lower *E*<sub>a</sub> shifts the line to the left, not to the right.

parts.problemMd:
Which row correctly describes the mechanism of a heterogeneous catalyst?

|   | phase of catalyst relative to reactants | way in which rate is increased |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | same phase | forms reactive intermediates |
| **B** | same phase | provides a surface for reactants to adsorb onto |
| **C** | different phase | forms reactive intermediates |
| **D** | different phase | provides a surface for reactants to adsorb onto |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- A heterogeneous catalyst is in a different physical state from the reactants.

  - For example, the iron catalyst in the Haber process is a solid, while the reactants nitrogen and hydrogen are gases.
- The mechanism involves reactant molecules adsorbing onto active sites on the solid catalyst surface.
- This weakens bonds in the adsorbed molecules and lowers the activation energy of the reaction, increasing the rate.

**A** and **B** are incorrect as a catalyst in the same physical state as the reactants is a homogeneous catalyst, not a heterogeneous one.

**C** is incorrect as forming reactive intermediates is characteristic of homogeneous catalysis, where the catalyst reacts with a reactant to form an intermediate compound before being regenerated. This is not the mechanism by which a heterogeneous catalyst operates.

parts.problemMd:
Photochromic glass is used for some glasses to enable them to work as sunglasses. The glass darkens when exposed to bright light and returns to transparent when the light is less bright. The darkness of the colour of the glass is related to the concentration of silver atoms.

The reactions involved are shown.

Reaction 1: Ag<sup>+</sup> + Cl<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Ag + Cl

Reaction 2: Cu<sup>+</sup> + Cl → Cu<sup>2+</sup> + Cl<sup>–</sup>

Reaction 3: Cu<sup>2+</sup> + Ag → Cu<sup>+</sup> + Ag<sup>+</sup>

Which statement about these reactions is correct?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Cu<sup>+</sup> and Cu<sup>2+</sup> ions act as catalysts because they are consumed and then regenerated across reactions 2 and 3.

  - They do not appear in the overall net equation.
- Adding reactions 2 and 3, the copper ions cancel out.

  - The net equation is Cl + Ag → Cl<sup>–</sup> + Ag<sup>+</sup>, which is the reverse reaction of reaction 1.
  - The copper ions therefore catalyse the reverse reaction, which returns the glass to transparent.

**A** is incorrect as Ag<sup>+</sup> ions are reduced in reaction 1. The oxidation number of silver decreases from +1 in Ag<sup>+</sup> to 0 in Ag. A decrease in oxidation number corresponds to reduction, not oxidation.

**C** is incorrect as Cu<sup>+</sup> ions are oxidised in reaction 2. The oxidation number of copper increases from +1 to +2, so Cu<sup>+</sup> is acting as a reducing agent, not an oxidising agent.

**D** is incorrect as the reaction that absorbs light must produce elemental silver, since the concentration of silver atoms determines the darkness of the glass. This occurs in the forward direction of reaction 1, not reaction 2.

parts.problemMd:
The stoichiometry of a catalysed reaction is shown.

*R* (g) + *S* (g) ⇌ *T* (g) + *U* (g)

Two experiments were carried out in which the amount of product *T* was measured against time. The results are shown in the diagram.

![Graph with amount of product T on the y-axis and time on the x-axis. Both curves begin at the origin and are steepest at time zero. Experiment 1 has a shallower initial gradient and reaches a higher plateau. Experiment 2 has a steeper initial gradient and reaches a lower plateau.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/8-reaction-kinetics/8-3-homogeneous-and-heterogeneous-catalysts/assets/001-graph-with-amount-of-product-t-on-the-y-axis-and.png)

Which row gives the changes to the conditions in experiment 1 that could produce the results for experiment 2?

|   | catalyst | initial amount of reactant *R* |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | less effective | decreased |
| **B** | less effective | increased |
| **C** | more effective | decreased |
| **D** | more effective | increased |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- In experiment 2, the initial gradient is steeper than in experiment 1, indicating a faster initial rate.

  - A more effective catalyst lowers the activation energy further, increasing the proportion of molecules with energy greater than or equal to *E*<sub>a</sub> and therefore increasing the rate.
- In experiment 2, the curve reaches a lower plateau, indicating a lower equilibrium yield of *T*.

  - A catalyst does not alter the equilibrium position; it only increases the rate at which equilibrium is reached.
  - The only way to lower the equilibrium yield of *T* at constant temperature and pressure is to begin with a decreased initial amount of reactant *R*.

**A** is incorrect as a less effective catalyst would produce a slower initial rate (shallower gradient), not a faster one.

**D** is incorrect as increasing the initial amount of reactant *R* would shift the equilibrium position to produce more *T*, giving a higher plateau, not a lower one.

**B** is incorrect as both variables are wrong: a less effective catalyst gives a slower rate, and more reactant *R* gives a higher equilibrium yield.

parts.problemMd: Which statement explains the effect of a catalyst using the Boltzmann distribution?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- A catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy (*E*<sub>a</sub>).
- On a Boltzmann distribution, the lower *E*<sub>a</sub> is represented by a vertical line shifted to the left on the kinetic energy axis.

  - This increases the area under the curve to the right of the *E*<sub>a</sub> line, meaning a greater proportion of molecules now have energy greater than or equal to the activation energy.
  - This leads to a higher frequency of effective collisions and an increased rate of reaction.

**A** is incorrect as the average kinetic energy of the reacting particles is determined by the temperature of the system alone. A catalyst does not alter the temperature and therefore has no effect on the average kinetic energy or the shape of the distribution curve.

**B** is incorrect as a catalyst does not increase the overall collision frequency between molecules. Collision frequency is increased by raising concentration or pressure. A catalyst only increases the proportion of collisions that are effective by lowering *E*<sub>a</sub>.

**D** is incorrect as a catalyst lowers *E*<sub>a</sub> equally for both the forward and reverse reactions. It increases the rate at which equilibrium is reached but does not alter the equilibrium position of the reaction.

parts.problemMd:
This question is about effective reactions and reaction rates.

According to collision theory, state **two **conditions that particles need for an effective collision to occur.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> According to collision theory, the two conditions for an effective collision are:
> 
> - Sufficient energy
> **OR**
> Energy greater than or equal to the activation energy / *E* ≥ *E*<sub>a</sub>; **[1 mark]**
> - (To be in the) correct orientation; **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For a chemical reaction to occur, the colliding particles must satisfy both conditions: correct orientation AND sufficient energy (*E* ≥ *E*<sub>a</sub>). A collision with the right orientation but insufficient energy will not result in a reaction, and vice versa.

parts.problemMd:
An increase in concentration means that there are more particles per unit volume.

In terms of collisions, explain how this increases the rate of reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> In terms of collisions, increasing the concentration increases the rate of reaction by:
> 
> - Increasing the frequency of (effective / successful) collisions per unit time
> **OR**
> Increasing the number of (effective / successful) collisions per unit time
> **OR**
> Having particles collide (effectively / successfully) more often **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The key phrase is "frequency of effective collisions", not just "more collisions." CIE mark schemes require both the frequency (per unit time) and the effectiveness aspect. Writing "more collisions" without "per unit time" or "effective" is unlikely to score the mark.
> 
> If the question describes a decrease in concentration, write "less frequent effective collisions". The logic reverses but the required terminology stays the same.

parts.problemMd:
Aqueous hydrogen peroxide, H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, decomposes to form oxygen and water.

2H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> (aq) → 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l) + O<sub>2</sub> (g)

A student investigates the decomposition of a hydrogen peroxide solution as outlined below.

- The student adds 25.00 cm<sup>3</sup> of H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> (aq) to a conical flask.
- The student adds a small spatula measure of manganese dioxide, MnO<sub>2</sub>.
- They quickly connect the flask to a gas syringe.
- The student measures the volume of oxygen every 100 seconds.

i) State the role of the manganese dioxide in this reaction.

[1]

The student obtained the following results.

| **Time / s** | 0 | 100 | 200 | 300 | 400 | 500 | 600 | 700 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Volume of O**~**2**~** / cm**^**3**^ | 0.0 | 7.0 | 13.5 | 18.0 | 21.0 | 22.5 | 23.0 | 23.0 |

ii) Calculate the average rate of reaction, in cm<sup>3</sup> s<sup>-1</sup>, for the first 100 seconds of the reaction.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The role of the manganese dioxide in this reaction is:
> 
> - Catalyst
> **OR**
> To increase the rate of reaction **[1 mark]**

ii) To calculate the average rate of reaction for the first 100 seconds:

average rate = $\frac{\mathrm{change} \mathrm{in} \mathrm{volume}}{\mathrm{change} \mathrm{in} \mathrm{time}}$

average rate = 7.0 ÷ 100

average rate = **0.07 cm**<sup>**3**</sup>** s**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Units required; answers without units are not accepted

> **[exam-tip]**
> The catalyst (manganese dioxide) is not consumed in the reaction. It speeds up the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide by providing an alternative reaction pathway of lower activation energy, so more particles have sufficient energy to react.

parts.problemMd:
The student plotted a graph of volume of O<sub>2</sub> against time.

![Graph showing volume of oxygen produced against time in the catalytic decomposition of hydrogen peroxide](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/8-reaction-kinetics/8-1-rate-of-reaction/assets/004-graph-showing-volume-of-oxygen-produced-against-.png)

Use the student's graph and tangent to find the rate of the reaction, in cm<sup>3</sup> s<sup>–1</sup>, at t = 300 s.

Show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
To find the rate of the reaction at t = 300 s:

- Read the coordinates of two points on the tangent at t = 300 s:

Volume at 200 s = 14.5 cm<sup>3</sup>

Volume at 400 s = 21.5 cm<sup>3</sup>

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate the change in volume:

change in volume = 21.5 − 14.5 = **7** cm<sup>3</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the rate of reaction:

rate = $\frac{7}{200}$

rate = **0.035 cm**<sup>**3**</sup>** s**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for tangent coordinates: volume at 200 s = 14.5 cm<sup>3</sup> **AND** volume at 400 s = 21.5 cm<sup>3</sup>
> 
> Other coordinate pairs read from the tangent are accepted if they lead to the correct gradient
> 
> Allow rates in the range 0.033–0.038 cm<sup>3</sup> s<sup>-1</sup> for the third mark
> 
> Correct units (cm<sup>3</sup> s<sup>-1</sup>) required for the third mark

> **[exam-tip]**
> The rate at a specific time equals the gradient of the tangent to the curve at that point:
> 
> rate = $\frac{ΔV}{Δt}$
> 
> When reading off the tangent, choose two points that are far apart on the line to reduce the percentage error in your readings. Extend the tangent as far as possible across the graph.
> 
> Note that the tangent is drawn at t = 300 s and the coordinates are read from the tangent line itself, not from the curve.

parts.problemMd:
A platinum-rhodium catalyst is used in the reaction forming nitrogen(II) oxide from ammonia.

4NH<sub>3</sub> (g) + 5O<sub>2</sub> (g) ⇌ 4NO (g) + 6H<sub>2</sub>O (g)

i) State what is meant by the term **heterogeneous catalyst**.

[1]

ii) Explain why a catalyst has no effect on the yield of the products in the reaction.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The term 'heterogeneous catalyst' means:
> 
> - (A catalyst that is in) a different phase / state to the reactants; **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) A catalyst has no effect on the yield of the products because:
> 
> - (A catalyst) increases the rate of both the forward and reverse reactions equally
> **OR**
> (A catalyst) does not shift the position of equilibrium; **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Heterogeneous catalysts are very common in industry. The platinum-rhodium catalyst in car catalytic converters and the iron catalyst in the Haber process are both heterogeneous, as they are solid catalysts with gaseous reactants.
> 
> A catalyst lowers the activation energy by the same amount for both the forward and reverse reactions. The proportion of molecules with sufficient energy increases equally in both directions, so the position of equilibrium is unchanged and the yield is unaffected.

parts.problemMd:
A group of students were completing a practical, investigating the factors which affect the rate of the following chemical reaction.

**A (s) + B (aq) → C (g)**

The students collected the gas produced and plotted the graph shown in Fig. 1.1.

![Graph showing volume of gas evolved over time for the original reaction, with a curve starting at the origin that rises and levels off at point R](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/8-reaction-kinetics/8-1-rate-of-reaction/assets/010-graph-showing-volume-of-gas-evolved-over-time-fo.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

i) State and explain what the letter **R** represents on the student's graph.

[1]

ii) In the original reaction above, the students used 0.5 g of **A** and 50 cm<sup>3</sup> of 1.0 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> of **B**. Sketch a curve on the graph in Fig 1.1 to show how the total volume of gas collected would change if the students still used 0.5 g of **A**, but used 50 cm<sup>3</sup> of 2.0 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> of **B**.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The letter **R** represents:
> 
> - The rate of reaction is zero at this point
> **OR**
> The reaction is complete / has stopped / no more product is produced
> **OR**
> All the reactants have been used up / reacted **[1 mark]**

ii) The sketch of the curve for 0.5 g of **A** and 50 cm<sup>3</sup> of 2.0 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> of **B** is:

![Graph showing the original curve and a new steeper curve that levels off at double the volume, representing the reaction with double the concentration of B](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/8-reaction-kinetics/8-1-rate-of-reaction/assets/011-graph-showing-the-original-curve-and-a-new-steep.png)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a curve steeper than the original that starts at the origin
> 
> 1 mark for the curve levelling off at double the height of the original curve

> **[exam-tip]**
> At point R, the gradient of the graph is zero because the rate of reaction is zero. At least one reactant has been fully consumed.
> 
> Doubling the concentration of B doubles the moles of B in the reaction mixture (since the volume is unchanged). B is the limiting reagent in the original reaction, so doubling its moles doubles the total volume of gas produced, i.e. the plateau is at double the original height.
> 
> The steeper initial gradient shows a faster rate because higher concentration of B means more particles per unit volume and more frequent effective collisions.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A group of students were completing a practical, investigating the factors which affect the rate of the following chemical reaction.

A (s) + B (aq) → C (g)

The students collected the gas produced and plotted the graph shown in Fig. 1.1.

Fig. 1.1

i) State and explain what the letter R represents on the student's graph.

Explain why the gradient of the curve in part **(b) **decreases as the time of the reaction progresses.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The gradient of the curve decreases as the reaction progresses because:
> 
> - The concentration of reactants decreases
> **OR**
> The reactants are used up; **[1 mark]**
> - The frequency of effective collisions decreases
> **OR**
> The rate of reaction / rate of formation of gas decreases; **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> As the reaction proceeds, reactant particles are consumed. Fewer reactant particles means fewer particles per unit volume, so collisions between A and B become less frequent. Since effective collisions decrease in frequency, the rate falls and the graph gradient decreases.
> 
> When all reactant particles have been consumed, the gradient reaches zero (point R on the graph from part (b)).

parts.problemMd:
Another way to increase the rate of reaction is to increase the temperature.

Explain why a small increase in temperature has a large effect on the initial rate of a chemical reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> A small increase in temperature causes a large increase in the rate of reaction because:
> 
> - A much higher proportion / many more molecules have energy greater than or equal to the activation energy (*E* ≥ *E*<sub>a</sub>); **[1 mark]**
> - The frequency of effective collisions (per unit time) increases significantly; **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> CIE mark schemes require reference to the proportion of molecules with energy greater than or equal to the activation energy (*E* ≥ *E*<sub>a</sub>). Simply stating "particles have more energy" or "kinetic energy increases" is not sufficient for the first mark.
> 
> The Boltzmann distribution curve is asymmetric, so even a small temperature rise shifts the curve so that the area to the right of *E*<sub>a</sub> increases disproportionately. This is why a small temperature increase produces such a large effect on the rate of reaction.

parts.problemMd:
This question is about how different factors affect the rate of a chemical reaction.

A reaction between reactant molecules can only occur when collisions between the reactant molecules are effective.

i) Explain what is meant by the term effective collision.

[1]

ii) State **two** factors that could cause an ineffective collision.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) An effective collision is:
> 
> - A collision that results in a reaction / products being formed **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) Two factors that could cause an ineffective collision are:
> 
> - The (reactant) particles do not collide in the correct orientation; **[1 mark]**
> - The (reactant) particles do not have energy greater than or equal to the activation energy (*E*<sub>a</sub>); **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> An effective collision requires two conditions simultaneously: correct orientation AND sufficient energy (*E* ≥ *E*<sub>a</sub>). An ineffective collision fails one or both conditions.
> 
> Note that most collisions are ineffective as particles collide constantly, but only a small fraction have both the right orientation and sufficient energy at the same moment.

A reaction between reactant molecules can only occur when collisions between the reactant molecules are effective.

i) An effective collision is a collision that results in a reaction / products being formed.

ii) Two factors that could cause an ineffective collision are:

A student made the following statement about factors that affect the rate of a chemical reaction.

'The rate of a reaction increases with temperature as there are more collisions'

Discuss why this statement is only true to an extent and what other factors need to be considered to fully explain how the rate of a reaction is affected by temperature.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Discussing the statement about temperature and rate:
> 
> - As temperature increases, there are more collisions (so the statement is partially correct) **[1 mark]**
> - The rate depends on the frequency of effective collisions, not just the total number of collisions **[1 mark]**
> - As temperature increases, the (average) kinetic energy / speed of the particles increases **[1 mark]**
> - This increases the frequency of collisions (per unit time) **[1 mark]**
> - A higher proportion of particles have energy ≥ *E*<sub>a</sub>, resulting in more frequent effective collisions **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The statement in the question is correct as far as it goes because higher temperature does produce more collisions. The error is in the reasoning: more collisions alone do not fully explain the increase in rate.
> 
> The critical distinction is between total collisions and effective collisions. Rate depends on effective collisions (those with *E* ≥ *E*<sub>a</sub> in the correct orientation). A small temperature rise causes a disproportionately large proportion of molecules to gain sufficient energy, amplifying the effect on rate well beyond what the collision frequency increase alone would predict.

parts.problemMd:
Hydrogen and oxygen can react to form water in an exothermic reaction.

2H<sub>2 </sub>(g) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) → 2H<sub>2</sub>O (g)

The rate of this reaction depends on the pressure as well as the temperature.

Describe and explain the effect of increasing the pressure on this reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The effect of increasing the pressure on the rate of reaction is:
> 
> - The rate increases; **[1 mark]**
> - There are more molecules / particles per unit volume / the molecules are closer together, so the frequency of (effective) collisions (per unit time) increases; **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When explaining concentration or pressure effects on rate, always include "per unit volume" when describing the particle density as stating "more molecules" alone is not sufficient. The key chain is:
> 
> - more particles per unit volume
> - → more frequent collisions
> - → more frequent effective collisions
> - → faster rate.
> 
> Avoid writing "there are more molecules" without specifying "per unit volume" or "per dm<sup>3</sup>" as this is a common reason marks are lost in this type of question.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Hydrogen and oxygen can react to form water in an exothermic reaction.

2H~2 ~(g) + O~2~ (g) → 2H~2~O (g)

If the rate of reaction increases suddenly, an explosion can occur.

A highly exothermic reaction, such as the reaction in **(c)**, is at more risk of exploding than a less exothermic reaction.

Suggest why.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> A highly exothermic reaction is at greater risk of exploding than a less exothermic reaction because:
> 
> - When the reaction starts, the temperature of the reactant particles increases more (than in a less exothermic reaction); **[1 mark]**
> - Many more particles have energy greater than or equal to the activation energy (*E* ≥ *E*<sub>a</sub>), so the rate increases more rapidly; **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> "Suggest" questions require you to apply your knowledge to an unfamiliar situation. Here, the chain of reasoning is:
> 
> - more exothermic
> - → more energy released
> - → greater temperature rise
> - → larger proportion of particles exceed *E*<sub>a</sub>
> - → rate increases more rapidly
> - → greater risk of a runaway reaction.
> 
> The key insight is that the temperature increase is self-reinforcing: as more particles react, more heat is released, which raises the temperature further. A positive feedback cycle that can lead to explosion.

**Fig. 3.1**

Draw curves on the graph in Fig 3.1 to show the results you would expect for Experiments **2** and **3**.

Label the curves **2** and **3**.

The curves for Experiments **2** and **3** drawn on Fig. 3.1 are:

![Graph showing three curves: Experiment 1 as the original curve, Experiment 2 steeper and reaching the same maximum mass loss, and Experiment 3 steeper and reaching double the maximum mass loss](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/8-reaction-kinetics/8-1-rate-of-reaction/assets/007-graph-showing-three-curves-experiment-1-as-the-o.png)

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A series of experiments was carried out to investigate the factors which affect the rate of reaction between calcium carbonate and dilute hydrochloric acid.

CaCO~3~ (s) + 2HCl (aq) → CaCl~2~ (aq) + H~2~O (l) + CO~2~ (g)

- 50.0 cm^3^ of hydrochloric acid was added to 10 g of small pieces of calcium carbonate (an excess) in a conical flask placed on an electronic balance.
- The loss in mass of the flask and its contents was recorded every 30 seconds for 10 minutes.
- The experiment was repeated using a different concentration of hydrochloric acid or a different temperature.
- The results are shown in Table 3.1

**Table 3.1**

| **Experiment** | **Concentration of hydrochloric acid / mol d**^**-3**^ | **Temperature / °C** |
| :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **1** | 0.50 | 20 |
| **2** | 0.50 | 60 |
| **3** | 1.00 | 20 |

Determine the initial rate of reaction for Experiment **1**.

You must show your working on the graph in Fig 3.2. Include units in your answer.

![Graph of mass lost in grams against time in seconds for Experiment 1, ready for a tangent to be drawn at t = 0 to determine the initial rate](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/8-reaction-kinetics/8-1-rate-of-reaction/assets/008-graph-of-mass-lost-in-grams-against-time-in-seco.png)

**Fig 3.2**
parts.solutionMd:
To determine the initial rate of reaction for Experiment **1:**

- Draw a tangent to the curve at t = 0:

![Graph of mass lost against time for Experiment 1, with a tangent line drawn at t = 0 to determine the initial rate of reaction](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/8-reaction-kinetics/8-1-rate-of-reaction/assets/009-graph-of-mass-lost-against-time-for-experiment-1.png)

- Calculate the gradient / initial rate:

initial rate = $\frac{change \text{in} \text{mass} \text{lost} ( \mathrm{g} )}{change \text{in} \text{time} ( \mathrm{s} )}$

initial rate = $\frac{1.0g}{312s}$

initial rate = **3.21 × 10**<sup>**-3**</sup>** g s**<sup>**-1**</sup>** **

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for tangent drawn to the curve at t = 0 AND tangent extends to at least 120 s
> 
> 1 mark for gradient calculation in the range 3.13 × 10<sup>-3</sup> to 3.53 × 10<sup>-3</sup> (e.g. gradient = 1.0 ÷ 312 = 3.21 × 10<sup>-3</sup>)
> 
> 1 mark for correct units: g s<sup>-1</sup> or g / s

> **[exam-tip]**
> For the initial rate, draw the tangent at t = 0 because the straight line should touch the curve at the very start, where the gradient is steepest.
> 
> Extend the tangent as far as possible across the graph to minimise reading errors.
> 
> Note that each small square on the x-axis is worth 12 s. Read the axis scale carefully before calculating the gradient. The units mark (g s<sup>-1</sup>) is independent of the numerical value, so always state units even if uncertain about the calculation.

**Extract:**

A series of experiments was carried out to investigate the factors which affect the rate of reaction between calcium carbonate and dilute hydrochloric acid.

CaCO~3~ (s) + 2HCl (aq) → CaCl~2~ (aq) + H~2~O (l) + CO~2~ (g)

- 50.0 cm^3^ of hydrochloric acid was added to 10 g of small pieces of calcium carbonate (an excess) in a conical flask placed on an electronic balance.
- The loss in mass of the flask and its contents was recorded every 30 seconds for 10 minutes.
- The experiment was repeated using a different concentration of hydrochloric acid or a different temperature.
- The results are shown in Table 3.1

**Table 3.1**

| **Experiment** | **Concentration of hydrochloric acid / mol d**^**-3**^ | **Temperature / °C** |
| :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **1** | 0.50 | 20 |
| **2** | 0.50 | 60 |
| **3** | 1.00 | 20 |

The results of Experiment **1** are shown in Fig. 3.1.

Calculate the average rate of reaction over the first 240 seconds of Experiment 1.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the average rate of reaction over the first 240 seconds of Experiment 1:

average rate = mass lost ÷ time

average rate = 0.5 ÷ 240

average rate = **0.0021 g s**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A series of experiments was carried out to investigate the factors which affect the rate of reaction between calcium carbonate and dilute hydrochloric acid.

CaCO~3~ (s) + 2HCl (aq) → CaCl~2~ (aq) + H~2~O (l) + CO~2~ (g)

- 50.0 cm^3^ of hydrochloric acid was added to 10 g of small pieces of calcium carbonate (an excess) in a conical flask placed on an electronic balance.
- The loss in mass of the flask and its contents was recorded every 30 seconds for 10 minutes.
- The experiment was repeated using a different concentration of hydrochloric acid or a different temperature.

The student repeated each experiment but used 10.0 g of larger sized pieces of calcium carbonate.

Suggest what effect this would have on the rate of reaction. Give your reasoning.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The effect of using larger pieces of calcium carbonate on the rate of reaction is:
> 
> - The rate would decrease; **[1 mark]**
> - Larger pieces have a smaller (total) surface area, so fewer (effective) collisions occur between the solid and acid per unit time; **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Surface area affects the rate because the reaction can only occur at the surface of the solid CaCO<sub>3</sub>, where it is in contact with the HCl (aq). Larger pieces have less surface area exposed per unit mass, so fewer collisions occur per second.
> 
> The total mass of calcium carbonate is unchanged (10.0 g), so the total amount of CO<sub>2</sub> produced (and the final mass loss) would be the same. Only the rate changes, not the total amount of product.

parts.problemMd:
A student is asked to investigate how the rate of reaction between sodium thiosulfate and hydrochloric acid depends on the concentration of sodium thiosulfate.

The reaction produces a precipitate of sulfur.

Na<sub>2</sub>S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> (aq) + 2HCl (aq) → 2NaCl (aq) + SO<sub>2</sub> (g) + S (s) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l)

The student is provided with:

- 0.10 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> sodium thiosulfate solution
- 1.0 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> hydrochloric acid
- distilled water
- standard laboratory apparatus

The reaction mixture must be maintained at 30.0 °C throughout the investigation.

i) Predict the relationship between the rate of reaction and the concentration of sodium thiosulfate.

[1]

ii) Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in this investigation.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The relationship between the rate of reaction and the concentration of sodium thiosulfate:
> 
> - The rate increases as concentration of sodium thiosulfate increases
> **OR**
> The rate is proportional to concentration **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The variables are:
> 
> - Independent variable: concentration of sodium thiosulfate
> **AND**
> Dependent variable: time for cross to disappear **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When asked to predict a relationship, don't just say "they are related." Be specific: "Rate increases as concentration increases." If you can, state whether it is directly proportional.
> 
> For the variables, remember:
> 
> **I**ndependent is what **I** change (Concentration).
> 
> **D**ependent is the **D**ata I collect (Time).
> 
> Rate is not an accepted answer for the dependent variable because it is calculated from time.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A student is asked to investigate how the rate of reaction between sodium thiosulfate and hydrochloric acid depends on the concentration of sodium thiosulfate.

The reaction produces a precipitate of sulfur.

Na~2~S~2~O~3~ (aq) + 2HCl (aq) → 2NaCl (aq) + SO~2~ (g) + S (s) + H~2~O (l)

The student is provided with:

- 0.10 mol dm^-3^ sodium thiosulfate solution
- 1.0 mol dm^-3^ hydrochloric acid
- distilled water
- standard laboratory apparatus

The reaction mixture must be maintained at 30.0 °C throughout the investigation.

Describe a method the student could use to investigate this relationship.

Your method should include:

- how to prepare at least five solutions of sodium thiosulfate with different concentrations
- how the reaction is carried out
- how the rate of reaction is determined
- how reliability of results is ensured
- appropriate safety precautions
parts.solutionMd:
To investigate how the rate depends on sodium thiosulfate concentration, prepare several dilutions of the sodium thiosulfate solution and measure the time taken for a sulfur precipitate to obscure a cross.

**Preparing at least five different concentrations**

- Keep the total volume of sodium thiosulfate + water the same each time (e.g. 50.0 cm<sup>3</sup>)
- Use a volumetric pipette or burette to measure the sodium thiosulfate accurately, then add distilled water to make the total up to 50.0 cm<sup>3</sup>
- Example set of five mixtures (all total 50.0 cm<sup>3</sup>):

- 10.0 cm<sup>3</sup> Na<sub>2</sub>S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> + 40.0 cm<sup>3</sup> water
- 20.0 cm<sup>3</sup> Na<sub>2</sub>S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> + 30.0 cm<sup>3</sup> water
- 30.0 cm<sup>3</sup> Na<sub>2</sub>S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> + 20.0 cm<sup>3</sup> water
- 40.0 cm<sup>3</sup> Na<sub>2</sub>S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> + 10.0 cm<sup>3</sup> water
- 50.0 cm<sup>3</sup> Na<sub>2</sub>S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> + 0.0 cm<sup>3</sup> water

**How the reaction is carried out**

- Place a conical flask over a paper cross
- Add one sodium thiosulfate dilution to the flask
- Measure a fixed volume of 1.0 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> HCl (same volume every time, so the acid is in excess)
- Add the acid to the flask, start the stopwatch immediately, swirl once to mix, then leave the flask on the cross

**Temperature control**

- Use a water bath to keep the reaction mixture at **30.0 °C**
- Check with a thermometer and allow solutions to reach **30.0 °C** before mixing

**How the rate is determined**

- Stop the stopwatch when the cross is no longer visible
- Record the time, *t*
- Compare rates using **1/*t*** (rate is proportional to 1/*t*)

**How reliability is ensured**

- Repeat each concentration at least three times
- Calculate a mean time (and then a mean 1/*t* if used)

**Safety precautions**

- Wear eye protection when handling acid
- Work in a well-ventilated area / fume cupboard
- Avoid inhaling sulfur dioxide

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - Preparation of different concentrations by mixing sodium thiosulfate solution with distilled water **[1 mark]**
> - Total volume of reaction mixture kept constant **[1 mark]**
> - Volume and/or concentration of hydrochloric acid kept constant and in excess **[1 mark]**
> - Temperature kept constant at 30.0 °C (e.g. water bath; solutions equilibrated before mixing) **[1 mark]**
> - Disappearing cross method described (flask over cross, timing until cross is obscured) **[1 mark]**
> - Repeats carried out and mean time calculated
> **OR**
> Results processed to rate using 1/*t* **[1 mark]**
> - Suitable precaution stated (e.g. work in a well-ventilated area / avoid inhaling SO<sub>2</sub> / eye protection) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Students often lose credit by changing concentration without keeping the total volume of sodium thiosulfate plus water constant.
> 
> It is also easy to forget reliability. Stating repeats and a mean is usually enough, but adding that you will compare rates using 1/*t* makes the processing step explicit.
> 
> Using volumetric apparatus helps because small volume errors change the concentration and make the comparison unfair.
> 
> If a temperature is specified (like 30.0 °C), you must say how you will keep it constant (water bath + thermometer), otherwise it looks like you ignored the constraint.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

i) Predict the relationship between the rate of reaction and the concentration of sodium thiosulfate.

The student processes the results and plots a graph.

i) State the quantities that should be plotted on the x-axis and y-axis.

[1]

ii) Sketch the line you would expect if the rate is directly proportional to the concentration of sodium thiosulfate.

Label both axes.

> i) The quantities that should be plotted on the x-axis and y-axis are:

> y-axis: rate of reaction **OR** 1/*t* **[1 mark]**

ii) The line you would expect if the rate is directly proportional to the concentration of sodium thiosulfate is:

![Graph with a linear upward trend showing the relationship between the rate of reaction on the y-axis and the concentration of sodium thiosulfate on the x-axis](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/8-reaction-kinetics/8-1-rate-of-reaction/assets/003-graph-with-a-linear-upward-trend-showing-the-rel.png)

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A student is asked to investigate how the rate of reaction between sodium thiosulfate and hydrochloric acid depends on the concentration of sodium thiosulfate.

The reaction produces a precipitate of sulfur.

Na~2~S~2~O~3~ (aq) + 2HCl (aq) → 2NaCl (aq) + SO~2~ (g) + S (s) + H~2~O (l)

Disappearing cross method described (flask over cross, timing until cross is obscured)

A second student performs the same investigation but measures the volume of sulfur dioxide gas produced over time instead of using the precipitation method.

State one advantage and one disadvantage of this alternative method compared with the disappearing cross method.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> **One** advantage of this alternative method is:
> 
> Any **one** from:
> 
> - There is a more objective endpoint than judging when a cross "disappears"
> - It is continuous data collection (volume vs time) rather than a single endpoint
> - It is possible to obtain an initial rate from the early gradient / a more detailed rate profile
> 
> **[1 mark]**
> 
> **One** disadvantage of this alternative method is:
> 
> Any **one** from:
> 
> - Sulfur dioxide is soluble in water so the measured volume is lower than the actual volume produced
> - It needs sealed apparatus (gas syringe) so leaks reduce the measured volume
> - There is a greater safety risk (handling toxic gas, pressure build-up)
> 
> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When evaluating gas collection methods involving SO<sub>2</sub> or CO<sub>2</sub>, remember that these gases are **soluble in water**. This is a classic disadvantage because the volume collected will be less than the actual volume produced.
> 
> While "toxic gas" is a valid disadvantage, examiners usually prefer points that affect the accuracy or reliability of the data (like solubility or leaks) rather than general lab safety, unless the question specifically asks about hazards.

parts.problemMd:
0.5 g of magnesium reacts with 50 cm<sup>3</sup> of 0.1 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> nitric acid. Magnesium is in excess.

A graph monitoring the volume of hydrogen gas produced is shown below:

![Graph showing volume of hydrogen gas produced over time as magnesium reacts with nitric acid, with volume rising steeply then levelling off](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/8-reaction-kinetics/8-1-rate-of-reaction/assets/005-graph-showing-volume-of-hydrogen-gas-produced-ov.png)

i) Calculate the average rate of reaction over the first 15 seconds of the reaction.

[1]

ii) Calculate the actual rate of reaction at 15 seconds.

[3]

iii) Explain the difference in values for rate.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
i) To calculate the mean rate of reaction over the first 15 seconds:

average rate = change in volume ÷ change in time

average rate = 50 ÷ 15

average rate = **3.3 cm**<sup>**3**</sup>** s**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) To calculate the actual rate of reaction at t = 15 s:
> 
> - Tangent drawn to the curve at t = 15 s with coordinates recorded correctly **[1 mark]**
> - Gradient of tangent calculated: gradient = Δ*V* ÷ Δ*t* **[1 mark]**
> - Rate in the range 1.5–2.0 cm<sup>3</sup> s<sup>-1</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The actual rate at t = 15 s is lower than the mean rate because:
> 
> - The rate is fastest at the very start of the reaction and has already decreased by t = 15 s
> **OR**
> The gradient of the curve is shallower at t = 15 s than at t = 0 / the curve has already started to level off **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The mean rate (part i) is calculated by dividing total volume produced by total time. It gives an average across the whole 15-second period. Since the rate is highest at t = 0 and decreases as reactants are consumed, the mean rate is higher than the actual rate at t = 15 s.
> 
> The actual rate at t = 15 s (part ii) is the gradient of the tangent drawn at that specific point. Extend the tangent as far as possible across the graph to minimise reading errors. Any rate in the range 1.5–2.0 cm<sup>3</sup> s<sup>-1</sup> is accepted.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

0.5 g of magnesium reacts with 50 cm³ of 0.1 mol dm⁻³ nitric acid. Magnesium is in excess.

A graph monitoring the volume of hydrogen gas produced is shown below:

Compare the expected rate and progress of the reaction if 25 cm<sup>3</sup> of 0.2 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> nitric acid was used instead of 50 cm<sup>3</sup> of 0.1 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> nitric acid.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Using 25 cm<sup>3</sup> of 0.2 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> nitric acid instead of 50 cm<sup>3</sup> of 0.1 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>:
> 
> - The initial rate of reaction would be higher / the initial gradient of the graph would be steeper; **[1 mark]**
> - The reaction would finish in less time; **[1 mark]**
> - The total / final volume of gas produced would remain the same (at 60 cm<sup>3</sup>); **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Both solutions contain the same number of moles of nitric acid:
> 
> 25 cm<sup>3</sup> x 0.2 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> = 0.005 mol HNO<sub>3</sub>
> 
> 50 cm<sup>3</sup> x 0.1 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> = 0.005 mol HNO<sub>3</sub>
> 
> Since the magnesium is in excess, the acid is the limiting reagent. The same moles of acid produce the same total volume of hydrogen gas in both cases, so the final volume is unchanged.
> 
> The more concentrated acid (0.2 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>) has more particles per unit volume, leading to more frequent effective collisions and a faster initial rate.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

0.5 g of magnesium reacts with 50 cm^3^ of 0.1 mol dm^-3^ nitric acid. Magnesium is in excess.

Suggest one change to the reaction that could be made to produce more hydrogen gas in total and explain your choice.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> One change that would produce more hydrogen gas in total is:
> 
> Any **one** from:
> 
> - Increase the concentration of the acid without decreasing the volume
> - Increase the volume of the acid without decreasing the concentration
> - Use more moles of acid
> 
> **[1 mark]**
> 
> The reasoning is:
> 
> - Increasing the moles of the limiting reagent (acid) increases the moles / volume of hydrogen gas produced; **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The magnesium is in excess, so the acid is the limiting reagent. The total volume of hydrogen produced is determined only by the moles of the limiting reagent. Changing the temperature, surface area of the magnesium, or adding a catalyst would affect the rate but not the total volume of gas.

parts.problemMd: Suggest why it is often better to study a slower reaction instead of a faster one.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Reasons why it is often better to study a slower reaction are:
> 
> Any **two** from (1 mark for each point):
> 
> - Shorter reaction times give a larger (percentage) error in timing
> - More readings can be taken in the initial part of the reaction, reducing the chance of anomalies being missed
> - The initial rate can be compared between reactions without the reaction needing to go to completion
> 
> **[2 marks]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For very fast reactions, the time interval is so short that even a small absolute error (e.g. ±0.5 s) represents a much larger percentage of the total time. This makes the calculated rate less accurate.
> 
> Slower reactions also allow more data points to be collected during the initial part of the reaction, making it easier to spot trends and anomalous results before the rate has changed significantly.

name: Effect of Temperature on Reaction Rates & the Concept of Activation Energy

parts.problemMd:
A reversible reaction is shown.

A + B ⇌ C + D

The reaction pathway diagram for this reaction is shown in Fig. 1.1.

![Reaction pathway diagram for A + B ⇌ C + D, with products C + D at a higher energy level than reactants A + B; activation energy Ea and enthalpy change ΔH are labelled](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/8-reaction-kinetics/8-2-effect-of-temperature-on-reaction-rates-and-the-concept-of-activation-energy/assets/035-reaction-pathway-diagram-for-a-b-c-d-with-produc.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

Use Fig. 1.1 to deduce whether the forward reaction is exothermic or endothermic. Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The forward reaction is endothermic:
> 
> - Endothermic **[1 mark]**
> - The energy level of the products is higher than / greater than / above the energy level of the reactants **[1 mark]**
> 
> 'Exothermic' is not accepted.

> **[exam-tip]**
> In an endothermic reaction, energy is taken in from the surroundings, so the products end up at a higher energy level than the reactants. In Fig. 1.1, C + D are at a higher energy level than A + B, confirming the forward reaction is endothermic.
> 
> Do not confuse the direction of Δ*H* with the direction of activation energy. The activation energy arrow always points upward from the reactants to the peak of the curve. The Δ*H* arrow shows the overall energy change between reactants and products.

parts.problemMd: Define the term activation energy, *E*<sub>a</sub>.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The activation energy, *E*<sub>a</sub>, is:
> 
> - The minimum energy required **[1 mark]**
> - For a collision to be effective / for a reaction to take place **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The syllabus defines activation energy as the minimum energy required for a collision to be effective. Both parts of the definition are required for full marks:
> 
> - The minimum energy threshold
> - The requirement that the collision is effective (not just any collision).
> 
> The activation energy of a reaction is not changed by temperature. It is only lowered by a catalyst, which provides an alternative reaction pathway of lower activation energy.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A reversible reaction is shown.

A + B ⇌ C + D

The reaction pathway diagram for this reaction is shown in Fig. 1.1.

Fig. 1.1

Use Fig. 1.1 to determine the activation energy for the forward reaction and for the reverse reaction.

activation energy of the forward reaction = .............................. kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

activation energy of the reverse reaction = .............................. kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>
parts.solutionMd:
To determine the activation energies from Fig. 1.1:

- Forward reaction:

activation energy = 150 + 180

activation energy = 330 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Reverse reaction:

activation energy = 180 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The activation energy of the forward reaction is the energy difference between the reactants (A + B) and the peak of the curve. Since the reaction is endothermic, the forward activation energy equals the enthalpy change Δ*H* plus the activation energy of the reverse reaction: 150 + 180 = 330 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>.
> 
> The activation energy of the reverse reaction is the energy difference between the products (C + D) and the peak of the curve: 180 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>. For an endothermic forward reaction, the reverse activation energy is always less than the forward activation energy.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The activation energy, *E*~a~, is:
- The minimum energy required
- For a collision to be effective / for a reaction to take place

Fig. 1.2 shows the reaction pathway diagram for the same reaction in the presence of a catalyst.

![Reaction pathway diagram showing the original reaction profile and a second catalysed reaction pathway with a lower activation energy peak, both curves sharing the same reactant and product energy levels](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/8-reaction-kinetics/8-2-effect-of-temperature-on-reaction-rates-and-the-concept-of-activation-energy/assets/036-reaction-pathway-diagram-showing-the-original-re.png)

**Fig. 1.2**

Use Fig. 1.2 to explain how the addition of a catalyst increases the rate of reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The addition of a catalyst increases the rate of reaction because:
> 
> - It provides an alternative pathway / route for the reaction **[1 mark]**
> - The alternative pathway has a lower activation energy / *E*<sub>a</sub> **[1 mark]**
> - A greater proportion of molecules have energy greater than or equal to *E*<sub>a</sub>, so there are more frequent effective collisions **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A catalyst does not change the energy levels of the reactants or products, or the shape of the Boltzmann distribution. It only provides an alternative reaction mechanism with a lower activation energy, as shown by the lower peak in Fig. 1.2.
> 
> The answer is:
> 
> - alternative pathway
> - → lower *E*<sub>a</sub>
> - → greater proportion of molecules with energy ≥ *E*<sub>a</sub>
> - → more frequent effective collisions
> - → faster rate.

parts.problemMd:
This question is about Boltzmann distribution curves.

The Boltzmann distribution curve of molecular energies for a general reaction at a given temperature is shown in **Fig. 2.1**.

![Boltzmann distribution curve showing number of molecules on the y-axis and energy on the x-axis, with the activation energy Ea marked as a vertical dashed line](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/8-reaction-kinetics/8-2-effect-of-temperature-on-reaction-rates-and-the-concept-of-activation-energy/assets/037-boltzmann-distribution-curve-showing-number-of-m.png)

**Fig. 2.1**

State what will happen to the curve when the temperature of the reaction is decreased.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> When the temperature is decreased:
> 
> - The curve shifts to the left
> **AND**
> The peak of the curve is higher / the maximum moves up **[1 mark]**
> - The curve finishes below the level of the original curve **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> At a lower temperature, molecules have less energy on average. The peak of the distribution shifts to the left (towards lower energy) and becomes higher because more molecules cluster around the lower most probable energy value.
> 
> The curve must also finish below the original at high energies, since fewer molecules have very high kinetic energies at a lower temperature.
> 
> ![Boltzmann distribution curves at two temperatures, showing that the lower temperature curve has a higher peak shifted to the left and finishes below the original curve at high energies](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/8-reaction-kinetics/8-2-effect-of-temperature-on-reaction-rates-and-the-concept-of-activation-energy/assets/038-boltzmann-distribution-curves-at-two-temperature.png)
> 
> Make sure you read the question carefully. Many students incorrectly describe the changes for an increase in temperature when the question asks about a decrease.

parts.problemMd: State how, if at all, the total area under a Boltzmann distribution curve changes with temperature.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> With changing temperature, the total area under the Boltzmann distribution:
> 
> - Does not change / remains the same **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The total area under the Boltzmann distribution curve represents the total number of molecules in the sample.
> 
> This number does not change with temperature, so the area under the curve remains constant regardless of the temperature.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

This question is about Boltzmann distribution curves.

The Boltzmann distribution curve of molecular energies for a general reaction at a given temperature is shown in **Fig. 2.1**.

{align=center} **Fig. 2.1**

State the effect of adding a catalyst on the activation energy, *E*<sub>a</sub>, of the reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> When a catalyst is added:
> 
> - The activation energy / *E*<sub>a</sub> decreases / is lower 
> **OR**
> The line for *E*<sub>a</sub> shifts to the left **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Adding a catalyst does not change the distribution of molecular energies or the Boltzmann distribution curve. It only provides an alternative reaction mechanism with a lower activation energy.
> 
> Since *E*<sub>a</sub> is lower, a greater proportion of molecules in the existing distribution now have sufficient energy to react, which increases the rate of reaction.

parts.problemMd:
The Boltzmann distribution of energies for a gas is shown in Fig. 2.2.

![Boltzmann distribution curve with a shaded region to the left of the activation energy Ea, representing molecules with energy less than or equal to Ea](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/8-reaction-kinetics/8-2-effect-of-temperature-on-reaction-rates-and-the-concept-of-activation-energy/assets/039-boltzmann-distribution-curve-with-a-shaded-regio.png)

**Fig. 2.2**

State what the shaded area of Fig. 2.2 represents.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The shaded area of Fig. 2.2 represents:
> 
> - The number of molecules that do not have enough energy to react
> **OR**
> The number of molecules with energy less than or equal to *E*<sub>a</sub>; **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Boltzmann distribution questions often focus on the unshaded area to the right of *E*<sub>a</sub>, which represents the molecules with sufficient energy to react. The shaded area is the complement: molecules with energy less than *E*<sub>a</sub> that cannot react.
> 
> Mark schemes often express the shaded region as *E* ≤ *E*<sub>a</sub>. If you are unsure about inequality symbols, describe them in words instead. For example, 'molecules with energy less than or equal to the activation energy'.

parts.problemMd:

parts.problemMd: Define the term *activation energy*, *E*<sub>a</sub>.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The activation energy, *E*<sub>a</sub>, is:
> 
> - The minimum energy required; **[1 mark]**
> - For a collision to be effective / for a reaction to take place; **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The syllabus defines activation energy as the minimum energy required for a collision to be effective. Both parts of the definition are required for full marks: the minimum energy threshold, and the requirement that the collision is effective.
> 
> Activation energy does not change with temperature. The Boltzmann distribution shifts with temperature, but the position of *E*<sub>a</sub> on the energy axis remains fixed.

parts.problemMd:
Two reactions involving aqueous sodium hydroxide, NaOH (aq), are given below.

CH<sub>3</sub>CHBrCH<sub>3</sub> + NaOH → CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>3</sub> + NaBr     **Reaction 1**

H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + 2NaOH → Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O     **Reaction 2**

The reagents in Reaction 1 must be heated together for some time for the reaction to occur. Reaction 2 is almost instantaneous at room temperature.

Suggest why these reactions occur at different rates.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Reactions 1 and 2 occur at different rates because:
> 
> - Reaction 1 requires energy to break covalent C–Br bonds / has a higher activation energy / greater *E*<sub>a</sub>; **[1 mark]**
> - Reaction 2 involves the reaction between oppositely charged ions (H<sup>+</sup> + OH<sup>-</sup> → H<sub>2</sub>O) / has a lower activation energy / *E*<sub>a</sub>; **[1 mark]**
> - At room temperature, a greater proportion of molecules have energy ≥ *E*<sub>a</sub> for Reaction 2, leading to more frequent effective collisions; **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The rate of a reaction depends on the activation energy.
> 
> Reaction 1 has a high activation energy because covalent C–Br bonds must be broken.
> 
> Reaction 2 is effectively H<sup>+</sup> (aq) + OH<sup>-</sup> (aq) → H<sub>2</sub>O (l), which has a very low activation energy because no strong bonds need to be broken and the ions are attracted to each other.

parts.problemMd:
Ammonia can be produced by the reaction of nitrogen and hydrogen in the presence of an iron catalyst.

N<sub>2</sub> (g) + 3H<sub>2</sub> (g) ⇌ 2NH<sub>3</sub> (g)          Δ*H* = −92 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

The activation energy for the forward catalysed reaction, *E*<sub>a,cat</sub>, is +109 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>.

Complete the reaction pathway diagram in Fig. 2.1 for the uncatalysed and the catalysed reaction between nitrogen and hydrogen.

You should label the following:

- products
- the enthalpy change of reaction, Δ*H*
- the activation energy of the forward uncatalysed reaction, *E*<sub>a</sub>
- the activation energy of the forward catalysed reaction, *E*<sub>a,cat</sub>

![Incomplete reaction pathway diagram showing energy on the y-axis and reaction coordinate on the x-axis, with the reactants N2 and 3H2 marked at the starting energy level; two unlabelled curve peaks are shown for the uncatalysed and catalysed pathways](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/8-reaction-kinetics/8-2-effect-of-temperature-on-reaction-rates-and-the-concept-of-activation-energy/assets/026-incomplete-reaction-pathway-diagram-showing-ener.png)

**Fig. 2.1**
parts.solutionMd:
The completed reaction pathway diagram is:

![Reaction pathway diagram showing the exothermic synthesis of ammonia, with reactants N2 + 3H2 at a higher energy level, products 2NH3 labelled at a lower energy level, a downward arrow for ΔH from reactants to products, and upward arrows from the reactants to the peaks of the uncatalysed curve labelled Ea and the catalysed curve labelled Ea,cat, with the catalysed peak lower than the uncatalysed peak](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/8-reaction-kinetics/8-2-effect-of-temperature-on-reaction-rates-and-the-concept-of-activation-energy/assets/027-reaction-pathway-diagram-showing-the-exothermic-.png)

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for exothermic profile with products (2NH<sub>3</sub>) correctly labelled **AND **at a lower energy level than the reactants
> 
> 1 mark for Δ*H* correctly labelled with an arrow from the energy level of the reactants to the energy level of the products
> 
> 1 mark for *E*<sub>a</sub> **AND ***E*<sub>a,cat</sub> both labelled with arrows from the reactants to the peak of each respective curve, with the *E*<sub>a,cat</sub> peak lower than the *E*<sub>a</sub> peak

If you draw an endothermic profile (reactants lower than products), you will lose the first mark but could still gain the remaining two.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Ammonia can be produced by the reaction of nitrogen and hydrogen in the presence of an iron catalyst.

N~2~ (g) + 3H~2~ (g) ⇌ 2NH~3~ (g)          Δ*H* = −92 kJ mol^-1^

The activation energy for the forward catalysed reaction, *E*~a,cat~, is +109 kJ mol^-1^.

Calculate the activation energy of the catalysed decomposition of ammonia into nitrogen and hydrogen. Show your working.

activation energy = ......................................................... kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the activation energy of the catalysed decomposition of ammonia:

- The decomposition of NH<sub>3</sub> is the reverse of the synthesis, so:

activation energy = *E*<sub>a,cat</sub> + Δ*H*(decomposition):

activation energy = 109 + 92 **[1 mark]**

activation energy = **201 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> The final mark is awarded for a correct value with correct units

> **[exam-tip]**
> The decomposition of ammonia (N<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub> → NH<sub>3</sub>) is the reverse of the synthesis reaction. On the reaction pathway diagram, the activation energy of the reverse catalysed reaction is measured from the energy level of the products (2NH<sub>3</sub>) to the peak of the catalysed curve.
> 
> Since the synthesis is exothermic (Δ*H* = −92 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>), the products are 92 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> lower in energy than the reactants. The activation energy of the reverse catalysed reaction is therefore: 109 + 92 = 201 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>.
> 
> ![Enthalpy profile for N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g), showing lower-energy products, −92 kJ mol⁻¹ enthalpy change and 201 kJ mol⁻¹ activation energy.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/8-reaction-kinetics/8-2-effect-of-temperature-on-reaction-rates-and-the-concept-of-activation-energy/assets/028-enthalpy-profile-for-n-g-3h-g-2nh-g-showing-lowe.png)

parts.solutionMd:

> An iron catalyst increases the rate of reaction because:
>

> - A greater proportion of molecules have energy greater than or equal to *E*<sub>a,cat</sub>; **[1 mark]**
> - So there are more frequent effective collisions; **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**

> 
> - lower *E*<sub>a,cat</sub>

parts.problemMd:
Platinum is used as a catalyst in catalytic converters, which are fitted to vehicle exhaust systems to remove nitrogen oxide from the exhaust gases.

2NO (g) + 2CO (g) → N<sub>2</sub> (g) + 2CO<sub>2</sub> (g)

i) State whether platinum acts as a homogeneous or heterogeneous catalyst in a catalytic converter.

[1]

ii) Deduce whether nitrogen is oxidised or reduced in this reaction. Explain your reasoning with reference to relevant oxidation numbers.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The type of catalyst is:
> 
> - Heterogeneous; **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The nitrogen is:
> 
> - Reduced; **[1 mark]**
> - The oxidation number of nitrogen decreases from +2 in NO to 0 in N<sub>2</sub>; **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Platinum is a solid catalyst; the reactants (NO and CO) are gases. Because the catalyst and reactants are in different phases, platinum is a heterogeneous catalyst.
> 
> When explaining whether an element is oxidised or reduced, always state both the initial and final oxidation numbers. A decrease in oxidation number indicates reduction; an increase indicates oxidation. Here, nitrogen decreases from +2 to 0, confirming reduction.

Fig. 3.1 below shows the Boltzmann distribution in a sample of a gas at a fixed temperature, *T*<sub>1</sub>.

> - x (horizontal) axis: Energy / Molecular energy / Kinetic energy
> **AND**
> y (vertical) axis: Number / proportion of molecules **[1 mark]**

ii) The sketch of the distribution at higher temperature *T*<sub>2</sub> is:

![Boltzmann distribution showing two curves at T1 and T2; the higher temperature T2 curve has a lower peak shifted to the right, immediately separates from T1, crosses T1 only once, and finishes above T1 at high energies](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/8-reaction-kinetics/8-2-effect-of-temperature-on-reaction-rates-and-the-concept-of-activation-energy/assets/034-boltzmann-distribution-showing-two-curves-at-t1-.jpg)

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

In any chemical reaction, the particles will all be moving in different directions, at different speeds and with different amounts of energy. Boltzmann distributions show the distribution of energy amongst particles in a chemical reaction.

State why a Boltzmann distribution curve always starts at the origin, and what the area under the curve represents.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> A Boltzmann distribution curve always starts at the origin because:
> 
> - There are no molecules with zero energy / all molecules have some energy / all molecules are moving **[1 mark]**
> 
> The area under the curve represents:
> 
> - The total number of molecules / particles in the sample **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The curve starts at (0, 0) because at zero energy there are zero molecules. All particles are in motion and therefore possess some kinetic energy.
> 
> The total area under the curve represents the total number of molecules. This does not change with temperature, which is why Boltzmann curves at different temperatures always enclose the same total area.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

In any chemical reaction, the particles will all be moving in different directions, at different speeds and with different amounts of energy. Boltzmann distributions show the distribution of energy amongst particles in a chemical reaction.

Fig. 3.1 below shows the Boltzmann distribution in a sample of a gas at a fixed temperature, *T*~1~.

Some changes were made individually to the reaction in part **(a)**.

Consider the Boltzmann distribution from Fig. 3.1. For each of the changes in parts (i), (ii) and (iii) below, state and explain the effect that the change would have on:

- The area under the curve
- The value at which the peak of the curve occurs (the most probable energy of the molecules)
- The proportion of molecules with energy greater than or equal to *E*<sub>a</sub>

i) The temperature of the original reaction is increased, but no other changes are made.

[2]

ii) The number of molecules in the original reaction mixture is increased, but no other changes are made.

[2]

iii) A catalyst is added to the original reaction mixture, but no other changes are made.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> For each of the following changes, the effects on the Boltzmann distribution are:
> 
> i) The temperature of the original reaction is increased:
> 
> - The area under the curve is unchanged, as the number of molecules is unchanged; **[1 mark]**
> - The most probable energy of the molecules / the position of the peak shifts to the right / increases
> **AND**
> The proportion of molecules with energy greater than or equal to *E*<sub>a</sub> increases; **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The number of molecules in the original reaction mixture is increased:
> 
> - The area under the curve increases, as the number of molecules increases; **[1 mark]**
> - The most probable energy of the molecules / the position of the peak does not change
> **AND**
> The proportion of molecules with energy ≥ *E*<sub>a</sub> remains the same / is unchanged (though the total number of molecules with energy ≥ *E*<sub>a</sub> increases); **[1 mark]**
>

> 1 mark for *E*<sub>a</sub> catalysed (reverse) = 157 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

> **[mark-scheme]**
> iii) Increasing the concentration of hydrogen iodide gas increases the rate of reaction because:
> 
> - More molecules are present in the same volume / molecules are closer together **[1 mark]**
> - The frequency of successful collisions increases **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part (i), make sure the catalysed and uncatalysed curves do not merge before reaching the products; each should have a distinct, separate peak.
> 
> For part (ii), to find the activation energy of the reverse reaction, add the magnitude of Δ*H* to the forward *E*<sub>a</sub>. The forward reaction is exothermic (Δ*H* = −52 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>), so the products are at a lower energy level than the reactants. Reversing the direction means starting from the products and climbing up to the transition state, so the reverse *E*<sub>a</sub> = forward *E*<sub>a</sub> + |Δ*H*|.
> 
> For part (iii), increasing the concentration places more molecules in the same volume, so collisions between reactant molecules are more frequent. More total collisions per unit time means more successful collisions (those with sufficient energy and the correct orientation), increasing the rate of reaction.

The activation energy when uncatalysed is +183 kJ mol^-1^ and when catalysed with gold it is +105 kJ mol^-1^.

Catalysts are often used in industrial processes and can be used in a variety of forms.

i) Explain why it is likely that the solid gold catalyst was used in powder form to catalyse the reaction mentioned in part **(b)**.

[1]

ii) Gold is a heterogeneous catalyst used in the formation of hydrogen iodide. State the difference between a homogeneous and heterogeneous catalyst.

[1]

iii) State how, if at all, the area under the curve of a Boltzmann distribution changes as a catalyst is introduced, without changing the temperature or the total number of molecules.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) Gold was used in powdered form because:
> 
> - (Powder form) increases the surface area (available for the reaction to occur on) **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) The difference between a homogeneous and heterogeneous catalyst is:
> 
> - A homogeneous catalyst is in the same physical state / phase as the reactants
> **AND**
> A heterogeneous catalyst is in a different physical state / phase from the reactants **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
