parts.problemMd:
When a hot platinum wire is plunged into a test tube of hydrogen chloride, no change occurs. However, if the experiment is repeated with hydrogen iodide, the gas is decomposed into its elements.

Which factor does **not** explain this observation?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Thermal stability depends on the strength of the H–X bond, which is determined by bond length and orbital overlap.

  - Electronegativity affects bond polarity, but polarity does not determine thermal stability.

- Thermal decomposition involves homolytic fission of the covalent bond.

  - This depends on bond enthalpy, not on the difference in electronegativity between the atoms.

**A** is incorrect as the activation energy for H–I decomposition is lower than for H–Cl, because the H–I bond is weaker. This does explain the observation.

**C** is incorrect as iodine has a larger atomic radius than chlorine, resulting in a longer H–I bond with less effective orbital overlap. The greater size of the iodine atom directly explains the lower thermal stability of HI.

**D** is incorrect as the H–Cl bond has a higher bond dissociation energy than H–I. The greater strength of the H–Cl bond means it does not break at the temperature of the platinum wire.

parts.problemMd:
Which row correctly describes the observations when aqueous silver nitrate, followed by aqueous ammonia, is added to the specified halide ion?

| Row | Halide ion | Colour of precipitate with AgNO<sub>3</sub> (aq) | Observation on adding aqueous ammonia |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | Cl<sup>−</sup> | white | dissolves in dilute aqueous ammonia |
| **B** | Br<sup>−</sup> | white | dissolves in concentrated aqueous ammonia only |
| **C** | I<sup>−</sup> | cream | remains insoluble in concentrated aqueous ammonia |
| **D** | Br<sup>−</sup> | cream | dissolves in dilute aqueous ammonia |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- When aqueous silver nitrate is added to a solution containing Cl<sup>−</sup> ions, a white precipitate of silver chloride (AgCl) forms.

- AgCl is the most soluble of the silver halides and dissolves in dilute aqueous ammonia to form a soluble complex ion.

**B** is incorrect as the colour of the AgBr precipitate is cream, not white. The solubility observation (concentrated aqueous ammonia only) is correct for Br<sup>−</sup>.

**C** is incorrect as the AgI precipitate is yellow, not cream. The insolubility in concentrated aqueous ammonia is correct for I<sup>−</sup>.

**D** is incorrect as AgBr does not dissolve in dilute aqueous ammonia. It only dissolves in concentrated aqueous ammonia.

parts.problemMd:
X, Y and Z represent different halogens. The table shows the results of nine experiments in which aqueous solutions of X<sub>2</sub>, Y<sub>2</sub> and Z<sub>2</sub> were added to separate aqueous solutions containing X<sup>−</sup>, Y<sup>−</sup> and Z<sup>−</sup> ions.

|   | X<sup>−</sup> (aq) | Y<sup>−</sup> (aq) | Z<sup>−</sup> (aq) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **X**<sub>**2**</sub>** (aq)** | no reaction | no reaction | no reaction |
| **Y**<sub>**2**</sub>** (aq)** | X<sub>2</sub> formed | no reaction | Z<sub>2</sub> formed |
| **Z**<sub>**2**</sub>** (aq)** | X<sub>2</sub> formed | no reaction | no reaction |

What is the correct order of decreasing strength of the ions X<sup>−</sup>, Y<sup>−</sup> and Z<sup>−</sup> as reducing agents?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- A stronger oxidising agent will displace a weaker oxidising agent from its halide solution.

  - Oxidising ability decreases down Group 17 as atomic radius increases and electron shielding increases.

- From the table:

  - Y<sub>2</sub> displaces both X<sup>−</sup> and Z<sup>−</sup>, so Y<sub>2</sub> is the strongest oxidising agent (Cl<sub>2</sub>).
  - Z<sub>2</sub> displaces only X<sup>−</sup>, so Z<sub>2</sub> is intermediate (Br<sub>2</sub>).
  - X<sub>2</sub> displaces nothing, so X<sub>2</sub> is the weakest oxidising agent (I<sub>2</sub>).

- The reducing power of halide ions is the inverse of the oxidising power of the parent halogen.
- The order of decreasing reducing strength is therefore:

X<sup>−</sup> (I<sup>−</sup>) > Z<sup>−</sup> (Br<sup>−</sup>) > Y<sup>−</sup> (Cl<sup>−</sup>).

**A** is incorrect as this order places Y<sup>−</sup> between X<sup>−</sup> and Z<sup>−</sup>, implying Cl<sup>−</sup> is more reducing than Br<sup>−</sup>. The reverse is true.

**C** is incorrect as this represents the order of oxidising ability of the parent halogens (Cl<sub>2</sub> > Br<sub>2</sub> > I<sub>2</sub>), which is the inverse of halide reducing power.

**D** is incorrect as Z<sup>−</sup> (Br<sup>−</sup>) is not the strongest reducing agent. X<sup>−</sup> (I<sup>−</sup>) is strongest because I<sub>2</sub> is the weakest oxidising agent.

parts.problemMd:
A dark red/brown solution is formed when a halide salt containing the halide ion **Y**<sup>**-**</sup> reacts with aqueous chlorine. This solution then forms a violet solution when shaken with a cyclohexane solution.

What is halogen, **Y**?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Chlorine (Cl<sub>2</sub>) is a stronger oxidising agent than iodine.

  - When aqueous chlorine reacts with iodide ions (**Y**<sup>**−**</sup>), it oxidises them to form aqueous iodine (I<sub>2</sub>), producing a dark red/brown solution:

Cl<sub>2</sub> (aq) + 2I<sup>−</sup> (aq) → 2Cl<sup>−</sup> (aq) + I<sub>2</sub> (aq).

- Iodine (I<sub>2</sub>) is a non-polar molecule and is much more soluble in non-polar solvents than in water.

  - When shaken with cyclohexane, iodine dissolves in the organic layer, producing a violet colour.

- The question asks for halogen **Y** (the neutral element), not the halide ion **Y**<sup>**−**</sup>.

  - The halogen is iodine.

**A** is incorrect as bromide is the ion (Br<sup>−</sup>), not the halogen. Bromine would also produce an orange/red colour in cyclohexane, not violet.

**B** is incorrect as fluorine is at the top of Group 17 and is a stronger oxidising agent than chlorine. Chlorine cannot remove electrons from fluoride ions because chlorine is the weaker oxidising agent. No reaction occurs between chlorine and a fluoride salt.

**C** is incorrect as iodide (I<sup>−</sup>) is the ion, not the neutral halogen. The question asks for halogen **Y**, which is the element iodine.

parts.problemMd: Which anion forms a white precipitate when tested with acidified aqueous silver nitrate?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Chloride ions react with acidified aqueous silver nitrate to form a white precipitate of silver chloride:

Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq) + Cl<sup>-</sup> (aq) → AgCl (s)

**A** is incorrect as carbonate ions are tested with dilute acid, which produces effervescence but no white precipitate with silver nitrate.

**B** is incorrect as sulfate ions are tested with acidified barium chloride solution, producing a white precipitate of barium sulfate (BaSO<sub>4</sub>).

**C** is incorrect as the acid removes any hydroxide ions from solution before silver nitrate is added. Even without acid, silver ions would react with hydroxide ions to form brown silver oxide (Ag<sub>2</sub>O), not a white precipitate.

Which row correctly identifies the chemical test and observation for an iodide ion?

|---|---|---|
| **A** | Acidified aqueous silver nitrate | Yellow precipitate insoluble in concentrated aqueous ammonia |
| **B** | Acidified barium chloride | White precipitate insoluble in hydrochloric acid |
| **C** | Acidified potassium nitrate | Yellow precipitate insoluble in concentrated aqueous ammonia |
| **D** | Bromine water | Brown solution changes to colourless solution |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- Acidified aqueous silver nitrate reacts with iodide ions to form a yellow precipitate of silver iodide (AgI).
- AgI is the least soluble of the silver halides and remains insoluble in both dilute and concentrated aqueous ammonia.

**B** is incorrect as acidified barium chloride is the test for sulfate ions, which produces a white precipitate of barium sulfate (BaSO<sub>4</sub>).

**C** is incorrect as potassium nitrate is not used to test for halide ions. All potassium and nitrate salts are soluble, so no precipitate would form.

**D** is incorrect as bromine water is the test for carbon-carbon double bonds in alkenes. Adding bromine water to iodide ions would cause bromine to oxidise the iodide, producing more brown iodine rather than a colourless solution.

parts.problemMd: Which observations are made when solid sodium bromide reacts with concentrated sulfuric acid?

**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

NaBr (s) + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (l) → NaHSO<sub>4</sub> (s) + HBr (g)

- Bromide ions are strong enough reducing agents to also reduce the sulfuric acid, producing bromine gas and sulfur dioxide:

2HBr (g) + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (l) → Br<sub>2</sub> (g) + SO<sub>2</sub> (g) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l)

- Bromine (Br<sub>2</sub>) is observed as a red-brown gas and SO<sub>2</sub> has a pungent, choking odour.

**A** is incorrect as steamy fumes only is the observation for solid sodium chloride reacting with concentrated sulfuric acid. The chloride ion is not a strong enough reducing agent to reduce the sulfuric acid.

**B** is incorrect as a yellow solid of sulfur is only produced in the reaction with sodium iodide, not sodium bromide. The iodide ion is a stronger reducing agent than bromide.

**C** is incorrect as a yellow solid indicates iodide chemistry, not bromide chemistry.

parts.problemMd:
A powder is known to be either a single sodium halide or a mixture of two different sodium halides.

An aqueous solution of the powder produces a pale yellow precipitate when tested with acidified aqueous silver nitrate. When concentrated aqueous ammonia is added, the precipitate partially dissolves, leaving a darker yellow precipitate.

What does the powder contain?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Adding acidified silver nitrate to a mixture of chloride and iodide ions produces white AgCl and yellow AgI.

  - The combined precipitate appears pale yellow.
- When concentrated aqueous ammonia is added, AgCl dissolves to form a soluble complex but AgI remains completely insoluble.
- The removal of the white AgCl leaves only the yellow AgI, making the remaining precipitate appear a darker yellow.

**A** is incorrect as pure sodium iodide would give a yellow precipitate of AgI that does not dissolve at all when concentrated aqueous ammonia is added.

**B** is incorrect as pure sodium bromide would give a cream precipitate of AgBr, not a pale yellow one. AgBr dissolves completely in concentrated aqueous ammonia, so no solid would remain.

**C** is incorrect as a mixture of sodium chloride and sodium bromide would give a pale to cream precipitate. Both AgCl and AgBr dissolve completely in concentrated aqueous ammonia, so the entire precipitate would dissolve rather than partially.

parts.problemMd:
Solid potassium halides react with concentrated sulfuric acid, according to the following equations.

Reaction 1:     2KCl + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → K<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + 2HCl

Reaction 2:     2KBr + 2H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → K<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + SO<sub>2</sub> + Br<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O

Reaction 3:     8KI + 5H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → 4K<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>S + 4I<sub>2</sub> + 4H<sub>2</sub>O

What is the largest change in the oxidation number of sulfur in each reaction?

|   | **Reaction 1** | **Reaction 2** | **Reaction 3** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | 0 | 0 | 4 |
| **B** | 0 | 2 | 4 |
| **C** | 0 | 2 | 8 |
| **D** | 0 | 4 | 8 |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- In H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, the oxidation number of sulfur is +6 (H = +1, O = −2).
- In reaction 1, the only sulfur-containing product is K<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, where sulfur is also +6, so the change is 0.
- In reaction 2, sulfur is reduced from +6 in H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> to +4 in SO<sub>2</sub>, so the largest change is 2.
- In reaction 3, sulfur is reduced from +6 in H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> to −2 in H<sub>2</sub>S, so the largest change is 6 − (−2) = 8.

**A** is incorrect as it gives 4 for reaction 3, which is the final oxidation state of sulfur in SO<sub>2</sub>, not the change in oxidation state from H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>.

**B** is incorrect as it gives 4 for reaction 3, confusing the final oxidation state of sulfur in SO<sub>2</sub> (+4) with the change in oxidation state to H<sub>2</sub>S, which is 8.

**D** is incorrect as it gives 4 for reaction 2. The change from +6 in H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> to +4 in SO<sub>2</sub> is 2, not 4.

parts.problemMd:
A student observed the reactions when solid sodium bromide and solid sodium fluoride were each reacted separately with concentrated sulfuric acid and concentrated phosphoric acid. The observations are recorded in the table below.

|   | **Sodium bromide** | **Sodium fluoride** |
|---|---|---|
| **Concentrated H**<sub>**2**</sub>**SO**<sub>**4**</sub> | Steamy fumes and brown vapour | Colourless acidic gas formed |
| **Concentrated H**<sub>**3**</sub>**PO**<sub>**4**</sub> | Colourless acidic gas formed | Colourless acidic gas formed |

Which deduction can be made from these observations?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Concentrated sulfuric acid can act both as an acid and as an oxidising agent
- When it acts as an acid, it produces the hydrogen halide; all halide salts react in this way
- The reactions of solid sodium fluoride with both acids are acid-base reactions only
- The reaction of solid sodium bromide with concentrated phosphoric acid is also an acid-base reaction only
- When concentrated sulfuric acid reacts with solid sodium bromide:

  - Bromide ions are strong enough reducing agents to reduce H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>
  - Bromide ions are oxidised to bromine:

2HBr (g) + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (l) → Br<sub>2</sub> (g) + SO<sub>2</sub> (g) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l)

- The brown vapour of bromine confirms that concentrated sulfuric acid is a stronger oxidising agent than bromine

**A** is incorrect as concentrated phosphoric acid only acts as an acid in these reactions. It is not an oxidising agent and is therefore a weaker oxidising agent than bromine

**B** is incorrect as concentrated sulfuric acid oxidises bromide ions but concentrated phosphoric acid does not. Concentrated sulfuric acid is therefore the stronger oxidising agent

**C** is incorrect as concentrated sulfuric acid is not a strong enough oxidising agent to oxidise fluoride ions. No redox reaction occurs with sodium fluoride under these conditions

parts.problemMd:
The following two experiments are carried out with anhydrous potassium chloride.

**Experiment 1:** Aqueous silver nitrate is added to an aqueous solution of potassium chloride, followed by an excess of aqueous ammonia - observation **X**.

**Experiment 2:** Concentrated sulfuric acid is added to solid potassium chloride, and the fumes produced are bubbled into aqueous potassium iodide solution - observation **Y**.

Which row correctly identifies observations **X** and **Y**?

|   | **X** | **Y** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | Colourless solution | Brown solution |
| **B** | Colourless solution | Colourless solution |
| **C** | White precipitate | Brown solution |
| **D** | White precipitate | Colourless solution |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- **Experiment 1 (Observation X):**

  - AgNO<sub>3</sub> reacts with Cl<sup>-</sup> ions to form a white precipitate of AgCl.
  - When aqueous ammonia is added, AgCl dissolves to form a soluble diamminesilver(I) complex, leaving a colourless solution

- **Experiment 2 (Observation Y):**

  - Concentrated sulfuric acid reacts with solid potassium chloride in an acid-base reaction:

KCl (s) + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (l) → KHSO<sub>4</sub> (s) + HCl (g)

- The HCl fumes dissolve in the aqueous potassium iodide to form hydrochloric acid
- HCl is not an oxidising agent and cannot remove electrons from iodide ions (I<sup>-</sup>), so no displacement reaction occurs and the solution remains colourless

**A** and **C** are incorrect as they suggest a brown solution for observation Y. You might assume that 'chloride fumes' entering a potassium iodide solution would displace iodide to form brown iodine, but this requires the elemental halogen (Cl<sub>2</sub>). HCl is an acid, not an oxidising agent, and does not displace I<sup>-</sup>

**C** and **D** are incorrect as they show a white precipitate for observation X. AgCl does form initially, but it dissolves completely in aqueous ammonia, leaving a colourless solution

parts.problemMd:
Element 85, astatine, is a halogen. When concentrated sulfuric acid is added to solid sodium astatide, the products are astatine, hydrogen astatide, hydrogen sulfide and sodium sulfate.

Which product is formed by the oxidation of one of the constituents of sodium astatide?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- When concentrated sulfuric acid reacts with solid sodium astatide, it acts as both an acid and an oxidising agent.
- The astatide ion (At<sup>-</sup>) is oxidised to elemental astatine (At<sub>2</sub>):

2At<sup>-</sup> → At<sub>2</sub> + 2e<sup>-</sup>

- Astatine (At<sub>2</sub>) is therefore the product formed by oxidation of At<sup>-</sup>, a constituent of sodium astatide.

**A** is incorrect as sodium sulfate is produced in the acid-base reaction between NaAt and H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>. Na<sup>+</sup> is not oxidised.

**B** is incorrect as hydrogen sulfide is formed when sulfur in H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> is reduced from +6 to −2. It is a reduction product of sulfuric acid, not an oxidation product of a constituent of NaAt.

**C** is incorrect as hydrogen astatide is formed in the acid-base step (At<sup>-</sup> + H<sup>+</sup> → HAt). The At<sup>-</sup> ion is not oxidised in this step.

parts.problemMd:
**Q** is a salt of one of the Group 17 elements chlorine, bromine, iodine, or astatine.

The reaction scheme shows a series of reactions using a solution of **Q** as the starting reagent.

**Q** (aq) `-> from AgNO _ 3 ( aq ) to HNO _ 3 ( aq ) of` precipitate $\xrightarrow{excess \text{dilute} NH_{3} ( \text{aq} )}$ colourless solution  $\xrightarrow{excess \text{dilute} HNO_{3} ( \text{aq} )}$ precipitate

What could **Q** be?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- Adding acidified silver nitrate to a halide solution gives precipitates of different colours:

  - Cl<sup>-</sup> forms white AgCl
  - Br<sup>-</sup> forms cream AgBr
  - I<sup>-</sup> forms yellow AgI
  - At<sup>-</sup> forms yellow AgAt
- Only AgCl dissolves in excess dilute aqueous ammonia to give a colourless solution.
- The colourless solution reforms a precipitate on addition of excess dilute nitric acid, confirming the halide ion present is Cl<sup>-</sup>.

**B** is incorrect as sodium bromide gives a cream precipitate with acidified silver nitrate that remains insoluble in excess dilute aqueous ammonia.

**C** is incorrect as potassium iodide gives a yellow precipitate with acidified silver nitrate that remains insoluble in excess dilute aqueous ammonia.

**D** is incorrect as potassium astatide gives a yellow precipitate with acidified silver nitrate that remains insoluble in excess dilute aqueous ammonia.

parts.problemMd:
Two students, R and S, were asked to draw bar charts to represent how some properties of the halogens and their compounds differ in magnitude. Their diagrams are shown.

![Two bar charts drawn by students R and S showing properties of halogens and their compounds. Student R's chart shows the enthalpy change for halogen reactions with hydrogen, with bar heights decreasing from Cl to Br to I indicating less exothermic reactions going down the group. Student S's chart shows the solubility of silver halides in ammonia, with bar heights increasing from AgCl to AgBr to AgI.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/11-group-17/11-3-some-reactions-of-the-halide-ions/assets/001-two-bar-charts-drawn-by-students-r-and-s-showing.png)

Which of the students' diagrams is correct?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Student R's bar chart shows the enthalpy change for X<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub> → 2HX becoming less exothermic going down Group 17.
- This is correct as H–X bond strength decreases down the group, so less energy is released in the reaction.

**A** is incorrect as Student S's bar chart shows the wrong trend for the solubility of silver halides in ammonia. Solubility decreases down the group (AgCl dissolves in dilute ammonia, AgBr and AgI remain insoluble), not increases.

**C** is incorrect as only Student R's bar chart is correct. Student S's chart shows the wrong solubility trend for silver halides in ammonia.

**D** is incorrect as Student R's bar chart correctly shows the enthalpy change for X<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub> → 2HX becoming less exothermic going down Group 17.

parts.problemMd:
Concentrated sulfuric acid is added to separate solid samples of sodium chloride and sodium bromide. In both reactions, steamy fumes are observed. However, in the reaction with sodium bromide, a brown gas is also produced.

Which statement correctly explains these observations?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- When concentrated sulfuric acid reacts with solid sodium chloride, it acts only as an acid, producing hydrogen chloride gas observed as steamy fumes.
- Br<sup>-</sup> ions are stronger reducing agents than Cl<sup>-</sup> ions because reducing power of halide ions increases down Group 17.
- When concentrated sulfuric acid reacts with solid sodium bromide, the Br<sup>-</sup> ions reduce the sulfuric acid, producing bromine (Br<sub>2</sub>) observed as a brown gas, along with SO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O.

**A** is incorrect as option A describes an acid oxide reacting with sodium hydroxide, which is unrelated to the reactions described.

**C** is incorrect as Br<sup>-</sup> ions are oxidised to bromine in this reaction, not reduced. Br<sup>-</sup> loses electrons and its oxidation state increases from −1 to 0.

parts.problemMd:
Chlorine is widely used in water treatment plants. When chlorine reacts with water, hydrochloric acid and another chlorine-containing acid are produced.

Which row describes this reaction?

|   | moles of Cl<sub>2</sub> reacting | moles of HCl produced | identity of the other acid |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | 1 | 1 | HClO |
| **B** | 2 | 3 | HClO<sub>2</sub> |
| **C** | 3 | 5 | HClO<sub>3</sub> |
| **D** | 4 | 7 | HClO<sub>4</sub> |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- When chlorine dissolves in water, it undergoes a reversible disproportionation reaction:

Cl<sub>2</sub> (aq) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l) ⇌ HCl (aq) + HClO (aq)

- 1 mole of Cl<sub>2</sub> produces 1 mole of HCl and 1 mole of HClO
- The equilibrium lies to the left in pure water, so only a small proportion of Cl<sub>2</sub> dissolves and reacts

**B** is incorrect as the 2:3 molar ratio does not match the balanced equation for the water reaction; HClO<sub>2</sub> is not formed here

**C** is incorrect as the 3:5 molar ratio matches the hot, concentrated NaOH reaction, not the water reaction; HClO<sub>3</sub> is not formed here

**D** is incorrect as HClO<sub>4</sub> is not formed when chlorine reacts with water

parts.problemMd:
When chlorine reacts with cold, dilute aqueous sodium hydroxide, the following reaction occurs.

Cl<sub>2</sub> (aq) + 2NaOH (aq) → NaCl (aq) + NaClO (aq) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l)

Which statement is correct?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- The oxidation numbers of chlorine change as follows in this reaction:

  - Cl<sub>2</sub>: oxidation number = 0
  - NaCl: oxidation number of Cl = −1 (decrease → chlorine is **reduced**)
  - NaClO: oxidation number of Cl = +1 (increase → chlorine is **oxidised**)
- The simultaneous oxidation and reduction of the same species in a single reaction is known as disproportionation

**A** is incorrect as chlorine is both oxidised and reduced in this reaction, not just oxidised

**B** is incorrect as the oxidation number of Cl in NaClO is +1, not 0: Na = +1, O = −2, so Cl must be +1 for the compound to be neutral

**D** is incorrect as Cl<sub>2</sub> is an uncombined element, so the oxidation number of chlorine is 0, not −1

parts.problemMd:
When chlorine reacts with hot, concentrated aqueous sodium hydroxide, the following reaction occurs.

3Cl<sub>2</sub> (g) + 6NaOH (aq) → 5NaCl (aq) + NaClO<sub>3</sub> (aq) + 3H<sub>2</sub>O (l)

Which row shows the oxidation state of chlorine in each substance?

|   | Cl<sub>2</sub> | NaCl | NaClO<sub>3</sub> |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | 0 | −1 | +5 |
| **B** | 0 | +1 | −5 |
| **C** | 0 | +1 | −3 |
| **D** | 0 | −1 | +3 |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- The oxidation state of chlorine in each substance:
- Cl<sub>2</sub> is an uncombined element, so the oxidation state = 0
- In NaCl: Na = +1, so Cl = −1
- In NaClO<sub>3</sub>: Na = +1, each O = −2 (total −6); overall charge = 0, so +1 + Cl + (−6) = 0, giving Cl = +5
- This is a disproportionation reaction: Cl<sub>2</sub> (oxidation state 0) is simultaneously reduced to −1 in NaCl and oxidised to +5 in NaClO<sub>3</sub>

**B** and **C** are incorrect as they assign +1 to Cl in NaCl; the sodium ion is always +1, making the chloride ion −1. The +1 oxidation state occurs in NaClO (the cold, dilute NaOH product), not in NaCl

**D** is incorrect as the oxidation state of Cl in NaClO<sub>3</sub> would be +3, not +5; the correct calculation gives Cl = +5 (not +3)

Cl<sub>2</sub> (aq) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l) ⇌ HCl (aq) + HClO (aq)

- Chlorine is simultaneously reduced to −1 in HCl and oxidised to +1 in HClO

**B** is incorrect as HClO is an acid, so universal indicator turns red (not blue) before the bleaching action of HClO turns it colourless

**C** is incorrect as chloric(I) acid is a weak acid that partially dissociates in water:

HClO (aq) ⇌ H<sup>+</sup> (aq) + ClO<sup>-</sup> (aq)

**D** is incorrect as chlorine reacts with cold, dilute aqueous sodium hydroxide to form three products:

parts.problemMd:
When the yellow liquid NCl<sub>3</sub> is stirred into aqueous sodium hydroxide, the reaction that occurs can be represented by the following equation.

2NCl<sub>3</sub> (l) + 6NaOH (aq) → N<sub>2</sub> (g) + 3NaCl (aq) + 3NaClO (aq) + 3H<sub>2</sub>O (l)

Which statement about this reaction is **not** correct?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Statement C is incorrect: nitrogen is reduced in this reaction, not oxidised
- In NCl<sub>3</sub>: each Cl = −1, so N + 3(−1) = 0, giving N = +3
- In N<sub>2</sub>: oxidation state = 0 (uncombined element)
- Decrease in oxidation state (+3 → 0): nitrogen gains electrons.

  - It has been **reduced**

**A** is incorrect as the reaction produces sodium chlorate(I), NaClO (aq), which acts as a bleaching and disinfecting agent. 'Sodium hypochlorite' is an outdated name as CIE uses the IUPAC systematic name. This statement is true.

**B** is incorrect as N<sub>2</sub> (g) is produced within an aqueous reaction mixture, producing effervescence. This statement is true.

**D** is incorrect as NaCl (aq) is produced, providing Cl<sup>-</sup> (aq) ions; adding acidified aqueous silver nitrate gives a white precipitate of AgCl. This statement is true.

parts.problemMd: Which equation represents the oxidation of chlorine in its reaction with hot, concentrated aqueous sodium hydroxide?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- The question asks for the oxidation half-equation, not the full balanced equation
- In the hot, concentrated NaOH reaction, Cl<sub>2</sub> is oxidised to ClO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup>:

  - Cl changes from 0 in Cl<sub>2</sub> to +5 in ClO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> (increase → oxidation)
  - Each Cl atom loses 5 electrons, so the half-equation shows 5e<sup>-</sup>

$\frac{1}{2}$Cl<sub>2</sub> + 6OH<sup>-</sup> → ClO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> + 3H<sub>2</sub>O + 5e<sup>-</sup>

**A** is incorrect as this is the full equation for the cold, dilute NaOH reaction (producing NaClO, where Cl = +1), not an oxidation half-equation for the hot, concentrated reaction

**B** is incorrect as this is the oxidation half-equation for the cold, dilute NaOH reaction; it produces ClO<sup>-</sup> where Cl = +1, not ClO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> where Cl = +5

**D** is incorrect as this is the correctly balanced full equation for the hot, concentrated NaOH reaction; however, the question asks for the oxidation half-equation only, not the full ionic equation

parts.problemMd: When chlorine gas is added to water during purification, which compound is the main disinfectant formed?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- When chlorine dissolves in water, it reacts reversibly to form chloric(I) acid and hydrochloric acid:

Cl<sub>2</sub> (aq) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l) ⇌ HClO (aq) + HCl (aq)

- Chloric(I) acid (HClO) is the main disinfectant, which kills bacteria in the water

**B** is incorrect as HCl is also produced in this reaction, but hydrochloric acid does not have disinfecting properties

**C** is incorrect as ClO<sub>2</sub> is not formed when chlorine reacts with water

**D** is incorrect as CHCl<sub>3</sub> is a disinfection byproduct that forms when chlorine reacts with organic matter in water, not from the direct reaction of Cl<sub>2</sub> with water

parts.problemMd:
When chlorine is bubbled through aqueous sodium hydroxide, different substances are formed depending on the conditions.

Which statement is **not **correct?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Statement C is incorrect:

- The two reactions are:

Cl<sub>2</sub> (g) + 2NaOH (aq) → NaCl (aq) + NaClO (aq) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l)

(cold, dilute NaOH: chlorine oxidised to +1 in NaClO)

3Cl<sub>2</sub> (g) + 6NaOH (aq) → 5NaCl (aq) + NaClO<sub>3</sub> (aq) + 3H<sub>2</sub>O (l)

(hot, concentrated NaOH: chlorine oxidised to +5 in NaClO<sub>3</sub>)

**A** is a correct statement: in hot, concentrated NaOH, chlorine is oxidised to +5 and ClO<sub>3</sub><sup>–</sup> ions are formed in sodium chlorate(V)

> **[exam-tip]**
> If you are asked for the conditions, always state both the temperature and the concentration as mark schemes require these. For example:
> 
> - 'cold, dilute NaOH'

parts.problemMd: Which statement describes the reaction of chlorine with water?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Chlorine undergoes a reversible disproportionation reaction when dissolved in water:

Cl<sub>2</sub> (aq) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l) ⇌ HCl (aq) + HClO (aq)

- In HCl, Cl has oxidation state −1 (decrease from 0 → chlorine is reduced)
- In HClO, Cl has oxidation state +1 (increase from 0 → chlorine is oxidised)
- The same element is simultaneously oxidised and reduced (disproportionation)
- The equilibrium lies to the left in pure water, so only a small proportion of Cl<sub>2</sub> reacts

  - Even a small equilibrium amount of HClO is sufficient to disinfect

**A** is incorrect as chlorine is not only oxidised; it is also simultaneously reduced to form HCl

**B** is incorrect as chlorine is not only reduced; it is also simultaneously oxidised to form HClO

**D** is incorrect as the products of chlorine reacting with water are HCl and HClO, not HClO<sub>3</sub>; HClO<sub>3</sub> (where Cl = +5) is formed in the hot, concentrated NaOH reaction, not the water reaction

> **[exam-tip]**
> A common mistake is to confuse the products of chlorine reacting with water (HCl and HClO, molecular acids) with the products of chlorine reacting with cold, dilute NaOH (NaCl and NaClO, ionic salts). In water, the products are weak acids, while in alkali, they are ionic compounds.

parts.problemMd:
Aqueous sodium chlorate(I) is added to aqueous potassium bromide. A brown solution is produced along with aqueous sodium chloride.

Which statement is correct?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- The ionic equation for this reaction is:

ClO<sup>-</sup> (aq) + 2Br<sup>-</sup> (aq) + 2H<sup>+</sup> (aq) → Br<sub>2</sub> (aq) + Cl<sup>-</sup> (aq) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l)

- The chlorate(I) ion oxidises bromide ions to bromine:

2Br<sup>-</sup> → Br<sub>2</sub> + 2e<sup>-</sup>

- Bromine has an oxidation state of −1 in Br<sup>-</sup> and 0 in Br<sub>2</sub>.

  - An increase in oxidation state indicates oxidation has occurred

**A** is incorrect as the oxidation state of chlorine in NaClO is +1, not +5; +5 belongs to NaClO<sub>3</sub>, which is formed from the reaction of chlorine with hot, concentrated sodium hydroxide

**B** is incorrect as the brown solution is aqueous bromine, Br<sub>2</sub> (aq). Chlorine gas would appear as a pale green gas, not a brown solution. A 'red-brown gas' describes bromine vapour above the liquid, whereas in aqueous reactions, the observation is always the colour of the solution

**D** is incorrect as NaClO is the oxidising agent, not the reducing agent; the chlorate(I) ion is itself reduced (Cl changes from +1 in ClO<sup>-</sup> to −1 in Cl<sup>-</sup>) and causes the oxidation of the bromide ions

name: Physical Properties of the Group 17 Elements

parts.problemMd:
The elements of Group 17 of the Periodic Table show trends in their properties.

Explain why bromine is a liquid at room temperature, but fluorine and chlorine are gases.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Bromine is a liquid at room temperature while fluorine and chlorine are gases because:
> 
> - Bromine has a higher boiling point than fluorine and chlorine **[1 mark]**
> - Bromine molecules have more electrons than fluorine or chlorine molecules **[1 mark]**
> - The instantaneous dipole-induced dipole (id-id) forces between Br<sub>2</sub> molecules are stronger, so more energy is required to separate the molecules **[1 mark]**
> 
> The reverse argument (fluorine and chlorine have fewer electrons, weaker id-id forces, lower boiling points, so exist as gases) is also accepted.

> **[exam-tip]**
> You must be able to state and explain the trend in boiling points down Group 17.
> 
> The key reasoning chain:
> 
> - More electrons per molecule
> - → stronger instantaneous dipole-induced dipole (id-id) forces
> - → more energy needed to overcome these forces
> - → higher boiling point
> - → liquid or solid state at room temperature.
> 
> Going down Group 17, fluorine and chlorine are gases, bromine is a liquid, and iodine is a solid. This reflects the increasing strength of id-id forces as the molecules get larger.

parts.problemMd: The bond enthalpy of the halogen molecules generally decreases down Group 17. Explain why the bond enthalpy of F<sub>2</sub> is lower than that of Cl<sub>2</sub>.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The bond enthalpy of F<sub>2</sub> is lower than that of Cl<sub>2</sub> because:
> 
> - The fluorine atom is very small / the F–F bond is very short, so the lone pairs on adjacent fluorine atoms are very close together **[1 mark]**
> - This causes strong repulsion between the lone pairs, which weakens the bond **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Bond enthalpy is the energy needed to break one mole of a given covalent bond. The higher the bond enthalpy, the stronger the bond.
> 
> The general trend down Group 17 is for bond enthalpy to decrease as the atoms get larger and bonds get longer. However, fluorine is an exception because its bond enthalpy is lower than chlorine's despite being at the top of the group.
> 
> This is because fluorine atoms are so small that the lone pairs on the two F atoms in F<sub>2</sub> are unusually close together. The lone pair repulsion partially counteracts the bonding attraction and makes the F–F bond weaker than expected.

parts.problemMd: State the trend in volatility of chlorine, bromine and iodine. Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:

> The trend in volatility of the halogens is:
> 
> - Volatility decreases (down the group / from Cl<sub>2</sub> to I<sub>2</sub>) **[1 mark]**
> - (The number of) electrons in the molecules increases **[1 mark]**
> - Resulting in stronger id-id forces between molecules **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Volatility refers to how easily a substance is converted into a gas
> - Cl<sub>2</sub> has the fewest electrons, the weakest id-id forces, and the highest volatility. So, it is a gas at room temperature
> - Br<sub>2</sub> has more electrons, stronger id-id forces, and lower volatility. So, it is a liquid at room temperature
> - I<sub>2</sub> has the most electrons, the strongest id-id forces, and the lowest volatility. So, it is a solid at room temperature

> - Chlorine atoms are smaller / the outer electrons of Cl are closer to the nucleus, so the nuclear attraction for electrons is greater in Cl than in Br **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Both Cl<sub>2</sub> and Br<sub>2</sub> can displace iodide ions from solution, but Cl<sub>2</sub> does so more vigorously
> - Going down Group 17, oxidising ability decreases
> 
>   - Cl<sub>2</sub> is a stronger oxidising agent than Br<sub>2</sub> because its outer electrons are in a shell closer to the nucleus

parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The equation for the reaction of bromine with hydrogen:
> 
> - Br<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub> → 2HBr **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are not required.
> 
> ii) The trend in thermal stability of the hydrogen halides:
> 
> - Trend: decreases (down the group) **[1 mark]**
> 
> Explanation:
> 
> - Atomic radius of the halogens increases (down the group) **[1 mark]**
> - Bond length of the H–X bond increases **[1 mark]**
> - Less energy is required to break the bond / bond strength decreases / bond dissociation energy decreases **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> State symbols are not required for the equation in part i), so focus on getting the formula and balancing correct.

This involves breaking the H–X bond within the molecule, not the forces between molecules. Answers mentioning van der Waals' forces, hydrogen bonding, or boiling points will not gain marks here.

parts.problemMd:
In the reaction outlined in part **(a)**, bromine, Br<sub>2</sub>, is acting as an oxidising agent.

Order the halogens below from the weakest to strongest oxidising agent.

Bromine, Br<sub>2</sub>

Chlorine, Cl<sub>2</sub>

Iodine, I<sub>2</sub>
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The correct order from weakest to strongest oxidising agent:
> 
> - Iodine < bromine < chlorine **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Oxidising power decreases going down Group 17. As the atomic radius increases, the outer electron shells move further from the nucleus. An incoming electron experiences more shielding from the nuclear charge, so the attraction between the nucleus and the gained electron decreases. This means halogens lower in the group are less effective at gaining electrons and acting as oxidising agents.

parts.problemMd: Explain why an iodide ion, I<sup>–</sup>, is a better reducing agent than a bromide ion, Br<sub> </sub><sup>–</sup>.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Iodide ions are better reducing agents than bromide ions because:
> 
> - An iodide ion / I<sup>–</sup> is larger than a bromide ion / Br<sup>–</sup> / has a larger ionic radius than a bromide ion **[1 mark]**
> - The outermost electrons of I<sup>–</sup> are more shielded by inner electron shells **[1 mark]**
> - The outermost electrons are less strongly held / more easily lost / more easily donated **[1 mark]**
> 
> Answers must make a comparison between I<sup>–</sup> and Br<sup>–</sup>. Stating properties of iodide alone without reference to bromide is not accepted.

> **[exam-tip]**
> A reducing agent donates electrons, so it will itself be oxidised in the process.
> 
> This question asks you to compare two ions, so your answer must be comparative. Saying "I<sup>–</sup> has a large atomic radius" alone will not gain marks. You must say "I<sup>–</sup> is larger than Br<sup>–</sup>" or "I<sup>–</sup> has a larger ionic radius."
> 
> The reasoning follows from size: I<sup>–</sup> is lower in Group 17, so it is larger. Its outermost electrons are further from the nucleus and more shielded by inner electron shells. This means the nucleus has a weaker hold on the outer electrons, so they are more easily donated, which makes I<sup>–</sup> a better reducing agent.

parts.problemMd:
A group of students are asked to determine the order of reactivity of the halogens and are provided with solutions of potassium chloride, potassium bromide and potassium iodide, as well as aqueous samples of each of the halogens.

i) Describe how the students would use the reagents named above to determine the trend in reactivity down Group 17 and give expected observations.

[3]

ii) Suggest the trend that the students would find from their results.

[2]

iii) Explain your answer to part **(a)(ii)**, using relevant ionic equations.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) Students would use displacement reactions to determine the trend in reactivity down Group 17:
> 
> - React chlorine with / bubble chlorine into / add chlorine solution to potassium bromide solution
> **AND**
> The solution turns orange / red-brown in colour **[1 mark]**
> - React chlorine with / bubble chlorine into / add chlorine solution to potassium iodide solution
> **AND**
> The solution turns brown / dark brown in colour **[1 mark]**
> - React bromine with / add bromine solution to potassium iodide solution
> **AND**
> The solution turns brown / dark brown in colour **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The trend found from the results:
> 
> - Reactivity decreases down Group 17 **[1 mark]**
> - Chlorine is the most reactive because it displaces bromide and iodide ions
> **AND**
> Iodine is the least reactive because iodide will not displace chloride or bromide ions **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The relevant ionic equations are:
> 
> - Cl<sub>2</sub> + 2Br<sup>–</sup> → 2Cl<sup>–</sup> + Br<sub>2</sub>
> **AND**
> Cl<sub>2</sub> + 2I<sup>–</sup> → 2Cl<sup>–</sup> + I<sub>2</sub>
> **AND**
> Br<sub>2</sub> + 2I<sup>–</sup> → 2Br<sup>–</sup> + I<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**
> 
> All three ionic equations must be correct for the mark. Spectator ions (K<sup>+</sup>, Na<sup>+</sup>) are not included in ionic equations.
> 
> State symbols are not required.

> **[exam-tip]**
> A more reactive halogen can displace a less reactive one from solution because it is a stronger oxidising agent, which means that it removes electrons from the halide ion more readily.
> 
> For the equations in part iii), only include the halogen and the halide ion that reacts. Spectator ions such as K<sup>+</sup> are not shown. Write ionic equations unless the question specifically allows full equations.
> 
> When describing observations, be specific about colour: bromine gives an orange solution, and iodine gives a brown solution in water. Do not describe the observation for iodine as a black precipitate. In aqueous solution, iodine gives a brown colour.

parts.problemMd:
Halogens react with hydrogen gas to form hydrogen halides. Chlorine reacts with hydrogen when exposed to ultraviolet light to form hydrogen chloride.

i) Write an equation for the reaction of chlorine and hydrogen.

[1]

ii) Explain why the thermal stability of the hydrogen halides decreases down the group.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The equation for the reaction of chlorine and hydrogen:
> 
> - H<sub>2</sub> + Cl<sub>2</sub> → 2HCl **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The thermal stability of the hydrogen halides decreases down the group because:
> 
> - The atomic radius of the halogens increases (down the group) **[1 mark]**
> - Resulting in a longer H–X bond length **[1 mark]**
> - The longer the bond, the weaker it is
> **AND**
> Less energy is required to break it / bond dissociation energy decreases **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Do not confuse thermal stability with boiling point. The hydrogen halides show an interesting boiling point pattern: HF has an anomalously high boiling point due to hydrogen bonding, and boiling points increase from HCl to HI due to stronger van der Waals' forces. Thermal stability is a separate concept that is about breaking the H–X covalent bond, not the forces between molecules.
> 
> The explanation here is about bond length and bond strength: as the halogen gets larger going down the group, the H–X bond gets longer. Longer bonds are weaker, so less energy is needed to break them, and the hydrogen halides decompose more easily when heated.

parts.problemMd:
The hydrogen halides do not show perfect periodicity. A bar chart of boiling points, as seen in Fig. 2.1, shows that the boiling point of hydrogen fluoride, HF, is much higher than periodic trends would indicate.

![Bar chart showing the boiling points of hydrogen halides HF, HCl, HBr and HI, where HF has an anomalously high boiling point compared to the increasing trend seen for HCl, HBr and HI](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/11-group-17/11-2-the-chemical-properties-of-the-halogen-elements-and-the-hydrogen-halides/assets/001-bar-chart-showing-the-boiling-points-of-hydrogen.png)

Fig. 2.1

Explain why the boiling point of HF is much higher than the boiling point of the other hydrogen halides.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The boiling point of HF is anomalously high because:
> 
> - HF has hydrogen bonding (between molecules) **[1 mark]**
> - The other hydrogen halides (HCl, HBr, HI) only have van der Waals' forces, which are weaker than hydrogen bonds **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> All the hydrogen halides (HX) have a permanent dipole because of the difference in electronegativity between H and X. This gives them permanent dipole–permanent dipole forces. However, only HF forms hydrogen bonds, because fluorine is highly electronegative, has a small atomic radius, and acts as a hydrogen bond acceptor.
> 
> Hydrogen bonds are stronger than the van der Waals' forces in the other hydrogen halides, so more energy is needed to separate HF molecules giving it a much higher boiling point.
> 
> Note that "van der Waals' forces" is an umbrella term covering both instantaneous dipole–induced dipole (id-id) forces and permanent dipole–permanent dipole (pd-pd) forces.

parts.problemMd:
There is an increase in boiling point moving from HCl to HI.

Explain this trend in boiling points of the hydrogen halides.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The increase in boiling points from HCl to HI is due to:
> 
> - Increasing mass / size / number of electrons of the halogen atom **[1 mark]**
> - Results in stronger van der Waals' forces / London forces / instantaneous dipole–induced dipole forces **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Two types of intermolecular forces are present in all the hydrogen halides:
> 
> 1. Permanent dipole–permanent dipole (pd-pd) forces
> 2. Instantaneous dipole–induced dipole (id-id) forces
> 
> Going from HCl to HI, the halogen becomes less electronegative, so the H–X bond becomes less polar and pd-pd forces decrease. However, the atoms get larger and have more electrons, which strengthens the id-id forces. The increase in id-id forces outweighs the decrease in pd-pd forces, so the overall intermolecular forces increase and boiling points rise.
> 
> For these 2 marks, stating that larger atoms have stronger van der Waals' forces is sufficient. You do not need to explain the full interplay between both force types.

parts.problemMd: Explain why HF is more thermally stable than HI.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> HF is more thermally stable than HI because:
> 
> - The H–F bond is shorter than the H–I bond / fluorine has a smaller atomic radius than iodine, giving a shorter bond **[1 mark]**
> - A shorter bond is a stronger bond, so more energy is required to break the H–F bond / the H–F bond has a higher bond dissociation energy **[1 mark]**
> 
> The reverse argument (starting from HI being less thermally stable) is also acceptable.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Thermal stability describes how well a substance resists breaking down when heated. A thermally stable substance requires more energy to decompose.
> 
> Do not confuse this with electronegativity. While fluorine is more electronegative than iodine, electronegativity affects oxidising power, not thermal stability. The key factor here is bond length: fluorine is smaller, so the H–F bond is shorter, and shorter bonds are stronger.
> 
> A common error is to state that "HF has a longer bond than HI", which is incorrect. Fluorine is above iodine in the group and has a smaller atomic radius, so it forms a shorter H–X bond.
> 
> shorter bond = stronger bond = more thermally stable

parts.problemMd:
This question is about the reactions and properties of the elements in Group 17 of the Periodic Table.

Define the term electronegativity and explain the trend in electronegativity seen down Group 17.

explanation:

> **[exam-tip]**

Electronegativity is about attracting electrons in a bond, so saying "the nucleus has weaker attraction for the outer electrons" would earn marks for an ionisation energy question but will not be credited here. parts.problemMd:

> - Add chlorine solution / aqueous chlorine / Cl<sub>2</sub> (aq) to each solution **[1 mark]**

> **OR**
> Cl<sub>2</sub> + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **OR**
> Cl<sub>2</sub> + 2KI → 2KCl + I<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
