parts.problemMd:
Ammonia, NH<sub>3</sub>, is synthesised from its elements in the Haber process.

i) Construct an equation for this process.

[1]

ii) State the three usual operating conditions of the Haber process.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) An equation for the Haber process:
> 
> - N<sub>2</sub> (g) + 3H<sub>2</sub> (g) ⇌ 2NH<sub>3</sub> (g) **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are not required
> 
> ii) Three usual operating conditions of the Haber process:
> 
> - Temperature: approximately 450 °C (accept 400–500 °C) **[1 mark]**
> - Pressure: approximately 200 atm (accept 150–300 atm) **[1 mark]**
> - Catalyst: iron **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The conditions for the Haber process represent a compromise between equilibrium yield, rate of reaction, and economic cost. A lower temperature gives a higher yield but a slower rate; very high pressure improves yield but is expensive and technically demanding. Both must be balanced for the process to be industrially viable.

parts.problemMd:
Ammonia can act as a Brønsted–Lowry base.

Explain why.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Ammonia acts as a Brønsted–Lowry base because:
> 
> - It accepts a proton / H<sup>+</sup> ion **[1 mark]**
> - To form the ammonium ion / NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Acids are proton donors and bases are proton acceptors. When ammonia accepts a proton, the ammonium ion is formed:
> 
> NH<sub>3</sub> (aq) + H<sup>+</sup> (aq) → NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> (aq)

parts.problemMd:
1.50 dm<sup>3</sup> of ammonia gas were dissolved in water to form 300 cm<sup>3</sup> of aqueous alkali at room conditions.

i) Calculate the amount, in mol, of NH<sub>3</sub>(g) dissolved.

Show your working.

[1]

ii) Construct an equation for the neutralisation of aqueous ammonia by dilute sulfuric acid.

[1]

iii) Calculate the volume of 0.80 mol dm<sup>–3</sup> sulfuric acid that is required to neutralise the 300 cm<sup>3</sup> of aqueous ammonia.

Show your working.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
i) To calculate the amount, in mol, of NH<sub>3</sub>(g) dissolved:

- List the known values:

  - Volume of NH<sub>3</sub> = 1.50 dm<sup>3</sup>
  - Molar gas volume at room conditions = 24.0 dm<sup>3</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>
- Calculate the amount of NH<sub>3</sub>:

n(NH<sub>3</sub>) = $\frac{\text{volume}}{\text{molar gas volume}}$

n(NH<sub>3</sub>) = $\frac{1.50}{24.0}$

n(NH<sub>3</sub>) = **0.0625 mol** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) An equation for the neutralisation of aqueous ammonia by dilute sulfuric acid:
> 
> - 2NH<sub>3</sub> (aq) + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (aq) → (NH<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (aq) **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are not required

iii) To calculate the volume of 0.80 mol dm<sup>–3</sup> sulfuric acid required:

- From the equation in (ii), n(H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>) = n(NH<sub>3</sub>) ÷ 2:

n(H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>) = $\frac{0.0625}{2}$ = 0.03125 mol **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the volume:

V(H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>) = $\frac{n}{c}$ = $\frac{0.03125}{0.80}$

V(H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>) = 0.0391 dm<sup>3</sup> = **39.1 cm**<sup>**3**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Allow error carried forward from (i) for the volume calculation in (iii)

> **[exam-tip]**
> The molar gas volume at room conditions is 24.0 dm<sup>3</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup> and is provided in the data booklet. Note that the neutralisation of ammonia with sulfuric acid produces the ammonium salt (NH<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, but no water is produced as a product.

parts.problemMd:
i) Draw a three-dimensional diagram of each species below to show its shape. Clearly show the bond angles.

[4]

| **Ammonia** | **Ammonium ion** |
|---|---|
|   |   |

ii) State the name of the shape of an ammonia molecule and an ammonium ion.

Ammonia molecule ................................................................................

Ammonium ion .........................................................................................

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
i) Three-dimensional diagrams showing the shape and bond angles:

| **Ammonia** | **Ammonium ion** |
|---|---|
| ![Diagram of an ammonia molecule showing nitrogen with a lone pair and three hydrogens, with a marked H–N–H bond angle of 107 degrees](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/12-nitrogen-and-sulfur/12-1-nitrogen-and-sulfur/assets/003-diagram-of-an-ammonia-molecule-showing-nitrogen-.png) | ![Diagram of ammonium ion showing tetrahedral N–H bonds, 109.5° bond angle marked, wedge and dash notation, in square brackets with positive charge](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/12-nitrogen-and-sulfur/12-1-nitrogen-and-sulfur/assets/004-diagram-of-ammonium-ion-showing-tetrahedral-n-h-.png) |

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a correct three-dimensional diagram of an ammonia molecule
> 
> 1 mark for a H–N–H bond angle of 107° shown on the ammonia diagram
> 
> 1 mark for a correct three-dimensional diagram of an ammonium ion
> 
> 1 mark for a H–N–H bond angle of 109.5° shown on the ammonium ion diagram
> 
> ii) Names of the shapes:
> 
> - Ammonia molecule: (trigonal) pyramidal **[1 mark]**
> - Ammonium ion: tetrahedral **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> In ammonia, the lone pair on nitrogen repels the three N–H bonding pairs more strongly than bonding pairs repel each other, compressing the bond angle to 107° and giving a trigonal pyramidal shape.
> 
> In the ammonium ion, the lone pair is used to form a dative covalent bond with a proton, leaving four equivalent bonding pairs arranged tetrahedrally with a bond angle of 109.5°.

parts.problemMd:
Ammonia gas can also be prepared by heating a mixture of ammonium chloride and calcium hydroxide.

Construct an equation for this reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
An equation for the reaction of ammonium chloride with calcium hydroxide is:

- 2NH<sub>4</sub>Cl (s) + Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub> (s) → CaCl<sub>2</sub> (s) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (g) + 2NH<sub>3</sub> (g) **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> State symbols are not required

> **[exam-tip]**
> Ammonia is prepared in the laboratory by heating an ammonium salt with a base. The ammonium ion (NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>) acts as an acid (proton donor) and the hydroxide ion (OH<sup>−</sup>) acts as a base (proton acceptor).

parts.problemMd:
The high temperatures reached in an internal combustion engine cause nitrogen and oxygen from the air to react, forming nitrogen monoxide.

i) Construct an equation for this reaction.

[1]

ii) Deduce the oxidation number of nitrogen in N<sub>2</sub> and NO to show that nitrogen is oxidised in this reaction.

[1]

iii) Nitrogen monoxide reacts further with oxygen to form nitrogen dioxide.

Construct an equation for this reaction.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) An equation for the formation of nitrogen monoxide:
> 
> - N<sub>2</sub> (g) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) → 2NO (g) **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are not required
> 
> ii) Oxidation numbers of nitrogen:
> 
> - Oxidation number of N in N<sub>2</sub> = 0
> **AND**
> Oxidation number of N in NO = +2
> **AND**
> An increase in oxidation number shows nitrogen has been oxidised **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) An equation for the further oxidation of nitrogen monoxide:
> 
> - 2NO (g) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) → 2NO<sub>2</sub> (g) **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are not required

> **[exam-tip]**
> When explaining oxidation or reduction using oxidation numbers, always state the oxidation number of the element in both the reactant and product and note whether it has increased (oxidation) or decreased (reduction). You must know the equations for the formation of NO and NO<sub>2</sub> from their elements.

parts.problemMd: Nitrogen oxides play a role in the formation of photochemical smog. Explain how.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Nitrogen oxides contribute to the formation of photochemical smog by:
> 
> - Reacting with unburnt hydrocarbons / VOCs in the presence of sunlight **[1 mark]**
> - To form photochemical oxidants / pollutants such as PAN (peroxyacetyl nitrate, CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>NO<sub>2</sub>) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Photochemical smog forms when nitrogen oxides react with unburnt hydrocarbons in the presence of sunlight, hence the term photochemical. You are not required to know the equations for these reactions; knowing that PAN is one pollutant produced is sufficient.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Nitrogen oxides contribute to the formation of photochemical smog by:
- Reacting with unburnt hydrocarbons / VOCs in the presence of sunlight
- To form photochemical oxidants / pollutants such as PAN (peroxyacetyl nitrate, CH₃CO₃NO₂)

The brown haze associated with photochemical smog is typically worse in cities in the afternoons of hot sunny days.

Suggest why.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Any **two** from (1 mark for each point):
> 
> - In cities: higher traffic density / more cars means greater concentrations of nitrogen oxides and unburnt hydrocarbons
> - In afternoons: pollutants accumulate throughout the day as traffic builds up
> - On hot sunny days: greater light intensity drives the photochemical reactions more rapidly
> 
> **[2 marks]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The 'suggest' command word means you should apply your knowledge to a novel context. Consider the three aspects separately: cities (sources of emissions), afternoons (time for accumulation), and hot sunny days (energy for photochemical reactions). Two marks means two distinct points.

parts.problemMd:
Catalytic converters are fitted to exhaust systems to reduce the pollutants emitted by car engines. Nitrogen monoxide, NO, and carbon monoxide, CO, are removed in a catalytic converter, forming nitrogen and carbon dioxide.

i) Construct an equation for the removal of NO and CO.

[1]

ii) Identify the reducing agent in this reaction. Explain your answer using changes in oxidation numbers.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) An equation for the removal of NO and CO in a catalytic converter:
> 
> - 2CO (g) + 2NO (g) → 2CO<sub>2</sub> (g) + N<sub>2</sub> (g) **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are not required
> 
> ii) The reducing agent:
> 
> - Carbon monoxide / CO **[1 mark]**
> - Oxidation number of C increases from +2 (in CO) to +4 (in CO<sub>2</sub>), showing CO is oxidised and therefore the reducing agent
> **OR**
> Oxidation number of N decreases from +2 (in NO) to 0 (in N<sub>2</sub>), showing NO is reduced by CO **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A reducing agent reduces another species and is itself oxidised in the process.
> 
> To identify the reducing agent, track oxidation number changes:
> 
> - Carbon in CO increases from +2 to +4 (oxidised), so CO is the reducing agent.
> - Alternatively, nitrogen in NO decreases from +2 to 0 (reduced), confirming that CO causes the reduction.

parts.problemMd:
Nitrogen dioxide, NO<sub>2</sub>, is a pollutant gas produced in the combustion of fuels in motor vehicles and power stations.

Construct an equation for the formation of NO<sub>2</sub> from its elements.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The equation for the formation of NO<sub>2</sub> from its elements is:
> 
> - N<sub>2</sub> + 2O<sub>2</sub> → 2NO<sub>2</sub>
> **OR**
> 2NO + O<sub>2</sub> → 2NO<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> You can either give the equation for the direct formation of nitrogen dioxide from nitrogen and oxygen in the air, or show the oxidation of nitrogen monoxide to nitrogen dioxide.

parts.problemMd:
i) State how NO<sub>2</sub> is removed from the exhaust gases of motor vehicles.

[1]

ii) Construct an equation for this process.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) NO<sub>2</sub> is removed from the exhaust gases of motor vehicles by:
> 
> - A catalytic converter
> **AND**
> Passing the exhaust gases over a (hot) catalyst / Pt / Rh **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The equation for this process is:
> 
> - NO<sub>2</sub> + 2CO → ½N<sub>2</sub> + 2CO<sub>2</sub>
> **OR**
> 2NO<sub>2</sub> + CH<sub>4</sub> → CO<sub>2</sub> + N<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Sometimes a question asks only that a catalytic converter removes NO<sub>2</sub>; other times it also asks for the catalyst type or reaction equation. Give all available information to maximise your marks.
> 
> The most commonly expected equation uses carbon monoxide as the reductant.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Nitrogen dioxide, NO~2~, is a pollutant gas produced in the combustion of fuels in motor vehicles and power stations.

The equation for the formation of NO~2~ from its elements is:
N~2~ + 2O~2~ → 2NO~2~

Suggest whether the production of the pollutant NO<sub>2</sub> in motor vehicles would be reduced if fossil fuels were replaced by hydrogen as a fuel for combustion. Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Whether the production of NO<sub>2</sub> would be reduced:
> 
> - No, it would not be reduced
> **AND**
> NO<sub>2</sub> is formed from N<sub>2</sub> and O<sub>2</sub> in the air at high temperature, not from the fuel itself **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The fuel used for combustion has no impact on the formation of nitrogen dioxide. Both nitrogen and oxygen come from the air, not the fuel. It is the high temperatures in the combustion engine that cause them to react, regardless of the fuel type.

parts.problemMd:
In the atmosphere, NO<sub>2</sub> acts as a homogeneous catalyst for the oxidation of SO<sub>2</sub> to SO<sub>3</sub>.

SO<sub>2</sub> (g) + ½ O<sub>2</sub> (g) $\overset{NO_{2}}{\rightarrow}$ SO<sub>3</sub> (g)

i) State one environmental consequence of the formation of SO<sub>3</sub> in the atmosphere.

[1]

The oxidation takes place in two steps. The initial reaction is between NO<sub>2</sub> and SO<sub>2</sub>.

reaction **1**     NO<sub>2</sub> (g) + SO<sub>2</sub> (g) $\rightleftharpoons$ NO (g) + SO<sub>3</sub> (g)     Δ*H* = −42 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>

ii) Construct an equation to show how the NO<sub>2</sub> catalyst is regenerated in the second step.

[1]

iii) The temperature of the atmosphere decreases with height from the ground.

Suggest how the position of the equilibrium in reaction **1** changes as height increases. Explain your answer.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) One environmental consequence of the formation of SO<sub>3</sub> in the atmosphere is:
> 
> - SO<sub>3</sub> dissolves in rainwater to form sulfuric acid / SO<sub>3</sub> contributes to acid rain **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The equation for regeneration of the NO<sub>2</sub> catalyst is:
> 
> - NO + ½O<sub>2</sub> → NO<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The position of the equilibrium in reaction 1 as height increases:
> 
> - The equilibrium shifts to the right (towards products) **[1 mark]**
> - Because the reaction is exothermic (ΔH = −42 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>), a decrease in temperature favours the forward reaction **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When SO<sub>3</sub> dissolves in rainwater, dilute sulfuric acid is formed:
> 
> SO<sub>3</sub> (g) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l) → H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (aq)
> 
> When explaining how equilibrium is affected by changing conditions, always state the direction the equilibrium shifts **AND** give a reason.
> 
> As height increases, temperature decreases. A decrease in temperature always favours the exothermic direction.
> 
> In this reaction, the forward reaction has a negative Δ*H*. So, a decrease in temperature increases the yield of NO and SO<sub>3</sub>.

parts.problemMd:
Ammonia gas can be prepared from ammonium chloride and calcium hydroxide.

i) Explain how ammonia can be prepared from these reagents.

[2]

ii) Describe a test and the expected observation to confirm the presence of ammonia gas.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) Ammonia can be prepared from ammonium chloride and calcium hydroxide by:
> 
> - Mixing and heating (ammonium chloride and calcium hydroxide) **[1 mark]**
> - Drying (the ammonia) with calcium oxide **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) A test and expected observation to confirm the presence of ammonia gas:
> 
> - Hold damp red litmus paper near the gas; the paper turns blue **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Ammonium chloride and calcium hydroxide are both solids. The ammonia gas produced is typically passed through a U-tube containing calcium oxide, which acts as a drying agent to absorb any water.

parts.problemMd: Explain, using the Brønsted–Lowry theory, why the reaction between ammonium chloride and calcium hydroxide is an example of an acid-base reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Using the Brønsted–Lowry theory, this is an acid-base reaction because:
> 
> - NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> acts as a Brønsted–Lowry acid as it is a proton donor **[1 mark]**
> - OH<sup>–</sup> acts as a Brønsted–Lowry base as it is a proton acceptor **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> You must identify which species is acting as an acid and which as a base, and explain why in terms of proton donation and acceptance.

parts.problemMd:
i) Draw a dot-and-cross diagram to show the bonding in an ammonium ion.

Show outer-shell electrons only.

[2]

ii) All four N-H bonds in the ammonium ion are equal in length. Explain why.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The dot-and-cross diagram of the ammonium ion is:

![Diagram of the ammonium ion: nitrogen bonded to four hydrogens, with one N–H shown as a dative bond using an arrow, enclosed in brackets with a plus sign](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/12-nitrogen-and-sulfur/12-1-nitrogen-and-sulfur/assets/005-diagram-of-the-ammonium-ion-nitrogen-bonded-to-f.png)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for an arrow pointing from N to an H atom (showing the dative covalent bond)
> 
> 1 mark for the rest of the structure including square brackets and + charge
> 
> ii) All four N-H bonds in the ammonium ion are equal in length because:
> 
> - All four covalent bonds are equivalent (the dative bond is indistinguishable from the other bonds once formed)
> **OR**
> The positive charge is spread evenly around the ion **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The ammonium ion has a coordinate (dative covalent) bond shown by an arrow pointing from N (which donates the lone pair) to the H<sup>+</sup> ion. Once formed, this bond is completely indistinguishable from the other three N-H bonds in terms of length and strength.

parts.problemMd:
Nitrogen gas, N<sub>2</sub>, is very unreactive.

i) Explain the lack of reactivity of the nitrogen molecule.

[2]

ii) State the number of σ (sigma) and π (pi) bonds in a nitrogen molecule.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The nitrogen molecule is unreactive because:
> 
> - It has a strong N≡N triple bond / high bond enthalpy **[1 mark]**
> - N<sub>2</sub> is a non-polar molecule **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The nitrogen molecule contains:
> 
> - 1 σ bond **AND** 2 π bonds **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> As nitrogen is made from two identical nitrogen atoms, electrons are shared equally and the molecule is non-polar. This means it is not attracted to or likely to react with other molecules.
> 
> The triple bond consists of one sigma bond (end-on overlap of sp hybrid orbitals) and two pi bonds (sideways overlap of p orbitals at right angles to each other).

parts.problemMd:
In an internal combustion engine, nitrogen reacts with oxygen to form nitrogen monoxide, NO. In the atmosphere, NO is further oxidised to nitrogen dioxide, NO<sub>2</sub>. Nitrogen dioxide then reacts with oxygen and water in the atmosphere to form dilute nitric acid, HNO<sub>3</sub>.

i) Construct equations for these three reactions. Include state symbols.

[3]

ii) Identify the change in oxidation number of nitrogen in each reaction, and state whether nitrogen is oxidised or reduced.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The three equations are:
> 
> - Step 1: N<sub>2</sub> (g) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) → 2NO (g) **[1 mark]**
> - Step 2: 2NO (g) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) → 2NO<sub>2</sub> (g) **[1 mark]**
> - Step 3: 4NO<sub>2</sub> (g) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) → 4HNO<sub>3</sub> (aq) **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The changes in oxidation number of nitrogen and whether it is oxidised or reduced:
> 
> - Step 1: 0 to +2 **AND** oxidised **[1 mark]**
> - Step 2: +2 to +4 **AND** oxidised **[1 mark]**
> - Step 3: +4 to +5 **AND** oxidised **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Nitrogen in NO has oxidation number +2, and in NO<sub>2</sub> has oxidation number +4 (oxygen is always −2, overall compound is 0).
> 
> In nitric acid, HNO<sub>3</sub>: H = +1, three O atoms = −6 total, so N = +5.
> 
> In each reaction the oxidation number of nitrogen increases, so nitrogen is oxidised in all three steps.

parts.problemMd:
A car travelled one kilometre and released 0.23 g of an oxide of nitrogen, N~*x*<sub>O</sub>*y*~, which occupies 120 cm<sup>3</sup> at room conditions.

Calculate the values of *x* and *y*. Show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the values of *x* and *y*:

- Calculate the moles of N<sub>x</sub>O<sub>y</sub>:

n = $\frac{120}{24000}$

n = 0.005 mol **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the relative molecular mass, *M*<sub>r</sub>:

*M*<sub>r</sub> = $\frac{0.23}{0.005}$

*M*<sub>r</sub> = 46 g mol<sup>−1</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Deduce *x* and *y* from the *M*<sub>r</sub>:

*x* = **1**
**AND**
*y* = **2** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Allow error carried forward throughout.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Make sure the volume and the molar gas volume are in the same units before dividing: 120 ÷ 24 000 (both in cm<sup>3</sup>) or 0.120 ÷ 24 (both in dm<sup>3</sup>). The molar gas volume (24.0 dm<sup>3</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup> at room conditions) is given in the Data Booklet.
> 
> Once you have the *M*<sub>r</sub>, find the formula by trial and error: 14 + 32 = 46, so *x* = 1 (one nitrogen atom) and *y* = 2 (two oxygen atoms).

name: Formulas, Functional Groups & the Naming of Organic Compounds
section: 13. An Introduction to AS Level Organic Chemistry

parts.problemMd:
What is the correct formula for 1-fluoro-3-methylbut-2-ene?

| **A** | Displayed | ![Displayed formula of 1-fluoro-3-methylbut-2-ene with the methyl group incorrectly placed on carbon 2](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-1-formulas-functional-groups-and-the-naming-of-organic-compounds/assets/008-displayed-formula-of-1-fluoro-3-methylbut-2-ene-.jpg) |
|---|---|---|
| **B** | Empirical | C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>9</sub>F |
| **C** | Skeletal | ![Incorrect skeletal formula omitting the fluorine atom and double bond with the branch on the wrong carbon](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-1-formulas-functional-groups-and-the-naming-of-organic-compounds/assets/009-incorrect-skeletal-formula-omitting-the-fluorine.jpg) |
| **D** | Structural | CH<sub>2</sub>FCH<sub>2</sub>C(CH<sub>3</sub>)CH<sub>3</sub> |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- The name 1-fluoro-3-methylbut-2-ene identifies the parent chain, double bond, and substituents:

  - Parent chain: but-2-ene — a four-carbon chain with a C=C double bond at C2
  - 1-fluoro: fluorine atom on C1
  - 3-methyl: methyl group (–CH<sub>3</sub>) on C3
- The molecular formula is C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>9</sub>F
- The ratio 5:9:1 cannot be simplified further, so the empirical formula equals the molecular formula: C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>9</sub>F

![Structural formulas showing the molecular and empirical formula derivation for 1-fluoro-3-methylbut-2-ene](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-1-formulas-functional-groups-and-the-naming-of-organic-compounds/assets/010-structural-formulas-showing-the-molecular-and-em.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as the displayed formula shown places the methyl group on the wrong carbon.

**C** is incorrect as the skeletal formula shown omits the fluorine atom and the C=C double bond, and places the branch on the wrong carbon.

**D** is incorrect as CH<sub>2</sub>FCH<sub>2</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> has no C=C double bond. It is the structural formula for 1-fluoro-3-methylbutane, the saturated compound.

parts.problemMd:
Which row correctly identifies the hydrocarbon molecules?

![Four molecules labelled 1 to 4: molecules 1 and 2 contain only carbon and hydrogen; molecules 3 and 4 contain additional elements](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-1-formulas-functional-groups-and-the-naming-of-organic-compounds/assets/018-four-molecules-labelled-1-to-4-molecules-1-and-2.jpg)

|   | **1** | **2** | **3** | **4** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | **✓** | **✓** | **✓** | **✓** |
| **B** | **✓** | **✓** | **✓** | **⨯** |
| **C** | **✓** | **✓** | **⨯** | **⨯** |
| **D** | **⨯** | **⨯** | **⨯** | **✓** |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- A hydrocarbon is a compound containing carbon and hydrogen only
- Molecule 1 is represented by a skeletal formula; no heteroatoms are shown, so it contains only carbon and hydrogen
- Molecule 2 shows a displayed formula with only C–C and C–H bonds, confirming it is also a hydrocarbon
- Molecules 3 and 4 both contain elements other than carbon and hydrogen, so they are not hydrocarbons

**A** and **B** are incorrect as they include a tick for molecule 3, which contains a heteroatom and is not a hydrocarbon.

**D** is incorrect as it marks molecule 4 as the only hydrocarbon. Molecule 4 contains a heteroatom. Molecules 1 and 2 are the hydrocarbons.

parts.problemMd:
What is the name of the circled functional group?

![Structural formula of an organic molecule with a C=O carbonyl group bonded to two carbon atoms, with the carbonyl group circled](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-1-formulas-functional-groups-and-the-naming-of-organic-compounds/assets/015-structural-formula-of-an-organic-molecule-with-a.jpg)
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- The circled group contains a C=O bond bonded to two other carbon atoms, making it a ketone
- In the molecule shown, one carbon is a –CH<sub>3</sub> group and the other is a –CH<sub>2</sub>– group

**A** is incorrect as an aldehyde also contains a C=O, but the carbonyl carbon is bonded to at least one hydrogen atom (–CHO), not two carbon atoms.

**B** is incorrect as an alkene contains a C=C double bond, not a C=O bond.

**C** is incorrect as a carboxylic acid contains a –COOH group, where the carbonyl carbon is bonded to a hydroxyl group (–OH).

parts.problemMd:
What is the systematic name of the molecule shown?

![Displayed formula of a branched pentane chain with a chloro group and a methyl group as substituents](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-1-formulas-functional-groups-and-the-naming-of-organic-compounds/assets/006-displayed-formula-of-a-branched-pentane-chain-wi.jpg)
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Identify the longest carbon chain: five carbons, so the parent chain is pentane

![Displayed formula of the molecule with the longest five-carbon chain highlighted](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-1-formulas-functional-groups-and-the-naming-of-organic-compounds/assets/007-displayed-formula-of-the-molecule-with-the-longe.jpg)

- Number the chain from the end that gives the lowest values:

  - The chloro group at C2
  - The methyl group at C3 (combination 2,3) is lower than 3,4
- The –CH<sub>3</sub> group is named methyl; the –Cl is named chloro
- Substituents are listed alphabetically: chloro before methyl
- Systematic name: 2-chloro-3-methylpentane

**A** is incorrect as the longest chain is five carbons (pentane), not four (butane). The –CH<sub>3</sub> branch is part of the longest chain, not an ethyl substituent.

**C** is incorrect as the longest chain is five carbons (pentane), not four (butane). The substituents are also listed in the wrong order.

**D** is incorrect as numbering from the wrong end of the chain gives positions 3 and 4, not the lowest possible 2 and 3.

parts.problemMd:
Compound A, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, is produced by the oxidation of compound B, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>14</sub>O.

Which functional group is present in compound B?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Compound B (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>14</sub>O) fits the general formula C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+2</sub>O, which corresponds to an alcohol

  - Alcohols contain a hydroxyl (–OH) functional group
- Compound A (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>2</sub>) is produced by oxidation of compound B, confirming B is a primary alcohol

C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>14</sub>O → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>2</sub>

C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>13</sub>OH → C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>11</sub>COOH

![Reaction scheme showing the oxidation of hexan-1-ol (a primary alcohol) to hexanoic acid (a carboxylic acid)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-1-formulas-functional-groups-and-the-naming-of-organic-compounds/assets/022-reaction-scheme-showing-the-oxidation-of-hexan-1.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as the carbonyl group (C=O) is present in compound A, not B.

**B** is incorrect as the carboxyl group (–COOH) is present in compound A, not B.

**C** is incorrect as an ester (general formula C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n</sub>O<sub>2</sub>) also matches compound A, but esters are formed by condensation reactions, not by simple oxidation of an alcohol.

parts.problemMd:
What is the systematic name of the molecule shown?

![Skeletal formula of a branched hexane chain with three methyl substituents at positions 2, 4 and 4](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-1-formulas-functional-groups-and-the-naming-of-organic-compounds/assets/004-skeletal-formula-of-a-branched-hexane-chain-with.png)
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Identify the longest carbon chain: six carbons, so the parent chain is hexane
- There are three –CH<sub>3</sub> methyl substituents: prefix trimethyl

![Skeletal formula with the longest six-carbon chain highlighted and methyl groups at C2, C4 and C4 labelled](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-1-formulas-functional-groups-and-the-naming-of-organic-compounds/assets/005-skeletal-formula-with-the-longest-six-carbon-cha.png)

- Number from the end that gives the lowest values:

  - Methyl groups at C2, C4, and C4 (combination 2,4,4) is lower than 3,3,5
- Systematic name: 2,4,4-trimethylhexane

**A** is incorrect as 2,3,3-tetramethylpentane is a different isomer; it has four methyl groups on a five-carbon chain.

**C** is incorrect as the longest continuous carbon chain contains six carbons (hexane), not five. A common mistake is to mistake the end of the chain for an ethyl branch on a pentane, giving the false name 2-ethyl-2,4-dimethylpentane.

**D** is incorrect as numbering from the wrong end of the chain places the methyl groups at C3, C3, and C5 instead of the lower C2, C4, C4.

parts.problemMd: Which molecule contains an aldehyde functional group?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- An aldehyde contains a carbonyl carbon (–C=O) bonded to at least one hydrogen atom
- In condensed structural formulas this is written as –CHO or CHO– (at the start of a chain)
- Molecule D contains a CHO– group at C1, confirming it is an aldehyde (specifically 3-hydroxypentanal)

![Displayed structural formula of an aldehyde group showing the carbonyl carbon bonded to one hydrogen and one carbon chain](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-1-formulas-functional-groups-and-the-naming-of-organic-compounds/assets/021-displayed-structural-formula-of-an-aldehyde-grou.png)

**A** is incorrect as CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COCH<sub>3</sub> contains a –CO– group flanked by two carbon chains, making it a ketone (pentan-2-one).

**B** is incorrect as CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOH contains a –COOH group. The similar notation –CHO (aldehyde) and –COOH (carboxylic acid) is a common source of confusion. In a carboxylic acid the carbonyl carbon is bonded to a hydroxyl group, not a hydrogen atom.

**C** is incorrect as CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOCH<sub>3</sub> contains a –COO– linkage, which represents an ester (methyl propanoate).

parts.problemMd:
Xylitol is an artificial sweetener used in toothpaste.

![Structural formula of xylitol showing a five-carbon chain with five hydroxyl groups, two at the terminal carbons (primary alcohols) and three on the internal carbons (secondary alcohols)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-1-formulas-functional-groups-and-the-naming-of-organic-compounds/assets/020-structural-formula-of-xylitol-showing-a-five-car.png)

Which functional groups are formed when xylitol is oxidised?

|   | **alkene** | **aldehyde** | **carboxylic acid** | **ketone** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | ⨯ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| **B** | ⨯ | ✓ | ⨯ | ✓ |
| **C** | ⨯ | ✓ | ⨯ | ⨯ |
| **D** | ✓ | ⨯ | ⨯ | ⨯ |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- Xylitol contains two primary alcohol groups at the ends of the carbon chain and three secondary alcohol groups on the internal carbons
- Primary alcohols oxidise to aldehydes (under limited oxidation) and to carboxylic acids (under complete oxidation with excess oxidising agent)
- Secondary alcohols oxidise to ketones
- All three of these functional groups (aldehyde, carboxylic acid, ketone) could therefore be produced

**B** is incorrect as it excludes carboxylic acid. Primary alcohols can be fully oxidised to carboxylic acids under suitable conditions.

**C** is incorrect as it excludes both carboxylic acid and ketone. Secondary alcohols oxidise to ketones.

**D** is incorrect as an alkene cannot be produced by oxidation of an alcohol. Alkene formation requires an elimination (dehydration) reaction, not oxidation.

parts.problemMd:
Which row identifies the functional groups and structural formula of 4-hydroxybutanenitrile?

|   | **group 1** | **group 2** | **structural formula** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | carboxyl | amide | HOOCCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CONH<sub>2</sub> |
| **B** | hydroxyl | amine | HOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> |
| **C** | hydroxyl | nitrile | CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>2</sub>CN |
| **D** | hydroxyl | nitrile | HOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CN |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- The prefix hydroxy– indicates a hydroxyl group (–OH)
- The suffix –nitrile indicates a nitrile group (–C≡N)
- In a nitrile, the carbon of the –C≡N group is always C1 of the parent chain
- But– indicates a four-carbon chain including the nitrile carbon: C1(–C≡N)–C2–C3–C4
- 4-hydroxy places the –OH on C4, the far end of the chain, giving HOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CN

**A** is incorrect as it contains a carboxyl group (–COOH) and an amide group (–CONH<sub>2</sub>); neither matches the functional groups in 4-hydroxybutanenitrile.

**B** is incorrect as it contains an amine group (–NH<sub>2</sub>) rather than a nitrile group (–C≡N). The –nitrile suffix specifies –C≡N, not –NH<sub>2</sub>.

**C** is incorrect as it contains –OH and –C≡N but the structural formula CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>2</sub>CN places the hydroxyl group on C3, making it 3-hydroxybutanenitrile, not 4-hydroxybutanenitrile.

parts.problemMd: How many stereoisomers does 3-chloropent-2-ene have?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Check for geometrical (E/Z) isomerism

  - The molecule contains a C=C double bond at position 2
  - Each carbon of the double bond is bonded to two different groups:
  
    - C2: CH<sub>3</sub> and H
    - C3: Cl and CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>
  - Therefore, E/Z isomerism is possible.
  - This gives 2 geometrical isomers (E and Z)

![Structural formulas of Z-3-chloropent-2-ene and E-3-chloropent-2-ene, showing different spatial arrangements of chlorine and ethyl groups.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-1-formulas-functional-groups-and-the-naming-of-organic-compounds/assets/001-structural-formulas-of-z-3-chloropent-2-ene-and-.bin)

- Check for chiral centres

  - No carbon atom is bonded to four different groups.
  - The alkene carbons are sp<sup>2</sup>, so cannot be chiral.
  - No additional stereoisomerism arises.
- Therefore, the total number of stereoisomers is *2*.

Limonene is found in the peel of citrus fruits.

| **D** | C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>16</sub> | C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>16</sub> |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- Empirical formula is the simplest whole number ratio of atoms in a chemical formula
- Molecular formula is the actual number and type of atoms in a formula
- Counting up the number of C and H atoms in limonene and taking into account the two double bonds, gives a molecular formula of C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>16</sub> and an empirical formula of C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>8</sub>

**B** is incorrect as the double bonds have been ignored, resulting in two extra hydrogens in the molecular formula, which also gives an incorrect empirical formula

parts.problemMd: Which pair of homologous series does **not** have the same C:H ratio in their general formulae?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- A homologous series is a group with the same functional group and similar chemical properties.
- Alkanes and alkenes are different homologous series as they have different functional groups.
- Alkanes have single carbon-carbon bonds and the general formula C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+2</sub>
- Alkenes have a double carbon-carbon bond and the general formula C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n</sub>

![Structural diagrams of an alkane (C–C single bond) and an alkene (C=C double bond) illustrating the different bonding in these two homologous series](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-2-characteristic-organic-reactions/assets/003-structural-diagrams-of-an-alkane-c-c-single-bond.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as aldehydes and ketones both have the general formula C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n</sub>O, giving a C:H ratio of 1:2.

**C** is incorrect as aldehydes (C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n</sub>O) and alkenes (C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n</sub>) both have a C:H ratio of 1:2.

**D** is incorrect as carboxylic acids and esters both have the general formula C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, giving a C:H ratio of 1:2.

parts.problemMd:
The following mechanism shows hydrogen cyanide reacting with propanone.

![Two-step nucleophilic addition mechanism showing CN- attacking the carbonyl carbon of propanone to form a tetrahedral intermediate, followed by proton transfer from HCN to give 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile and regenerate CN-](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-2-characteristic-organic-reactions/assets/002-two-step-nucleophilic-addition-mechanism-showing.jpg)

Which statement is **not** correct?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- The reaction between hydrogen cyanide and propanone is a nucleophilic addition reaction.
- A nucleophile is an electron-pair donor.
- An electrophile is an electron-pair acceptor.
- In this reaction, CN<sup>-</sup> is donating a pair of electrons (as shown by the arrow) and the carbon in propanone is accepting them.

**B** is incorrect as this is heterolytic bond breaking. Only one atom receives both electrons from the covalent bond, making this heterolytic.

**C** is incorrect as propanone is a ketone, so this statement is true.

**D** is incorrect as this is an example of a nucleophilic addition reaction.

choices.label: A
choices.textMd: The organic molecule acts as an electrophile and becomes less saturated.

choices.label: B
choices.textMd: The organic molecule acts as an electrophile and becomes more saturated.

choices.label: C
choices.textMd: The organic molecule acts as a nucleophile and becomes less saturated.

choices.label: D
choices.textMd: The organic molecule acts as a nucleophile and becomes more saturated.

parts.problemMd: Which statement describes an electrophilic addition reaction?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- If a reaction is electrophilic, the inorganic reagent is acting as an electrophile (electron-pair acceptor).
- Therefore, the organic reactant acts as a nucleophile (electron-pair donor). This is usually because the organic molecule is an alkene, and one of the electron pairs in the double bond is donated to the inorganic reagent, e.g. HBr.
- In an addition reaction, the organic molecule gains atoms.
- In an electrophilic addition reaction, an alkene is converted to a halogenoalkane and therefore becomes more saturated.

**A** is incorrect as the inorganic reagent (e.g. HBr) acts as the electrophile, not the organic molecule. In addition reactions the organic molecule gains atoms, becoming more saturated.

**B** is incorrect as the inorganic reagent acts as the electrophile, not the organic molecule. In electrophilic addition, the organic molecule acts as the nucleophile.

**C** is incorrect as addition reactions result in the organic molecule gaining atoms, making it more saturated, not less saturated.

parts.problemMd: Which species acts as a nucleophile?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- A nucleophile is an electron-pair donor; it is either a negative ion or has a lone pair of electrons capable of being donated.

- OH<sup>-</sup> has three lone pairs of electrons and a negative charge, making it a nucleophile.

**A** is incorrect as ethane has no lone pairs and will not act as a nucleophile.

**B** is incorrect as a free radical has an unpaired electron and reacts via homolytic (radical) mechanisms. It does not donate or accept electron pairs, so it is neither a nucleophile nor an electrophile.

**C** is incorrect as a hydrogen ion has no electrons. It accepts electron pairs and is therefore an electrophile, not a nucleophile.

parts.problemMd: What type of reaction occurs when 1-chloroethane reacts with aqueous sodium hydroxide?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- When a halogenoalkane reacts with aqueous sodium or potassium hydroxide, the OH<sup>-</sup> ion replaces the halogen, forming an alcohol.
- The hydroxide ion is a **nucleophile** (an electron-pair donor).
- The hydroxide ion takes the place of the halogen in the compound, so this is a **substitution** reaction.
- The overall mechanism is nucleophilic substitution.

  - The reaction can be summarised as:

![Nucleophilic substitution mechanism showing OH- attacking the delta-positive carbon of 1-chloroethane, displacing Cl- to give ethanol](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-2-characteristic-organic-reactions/assets/001-nucleophilic-substitution-mechanism-showing-oh-a.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as electrophilic addition involves an electrophile attacking a C=C double bond. 1-chloroethane has no double bond, and OH<sup>-</sup> is a nucleophile, not an electrophile.

**B** is incorrect as electrophilic substitution involves an electrophile. OH<sup>-</sup> is a nucleophile, not an electrophile.

**C** is incorrect as nucleophilic addition adds atoms across a double bond. 1-chloroethane has no C=C double bond. Instead, the halogen is replaced by OH<sup>-</sup> in a substitution reaction.

parts.problemMd:
Which row gives correct statements about a homologous series?

|   | **same general formula** | **similar chemical properties** | **gradual change in physical properties** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| **B** | ✓ | ⨯ | ✓ |
| **C** | ⨯ | ✓ | ✓ |
| **D** | ✓ | ✓ | ⨯ |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- A homologous series is a family of carbon compounds that all contain the same functional group.
- All members can be represented by the same general formula, e.g. C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+2</sub> for alkanes.
- Since all members contain the same functional group, they have similar chemical properties and undergo the same types of reactions.
- As successive members increase in size by one –CH<sub>2</sub>– unit, their intermolecular forces increase.

  - This results in a gradual change in physical properties, such as increasing boiling points and densities.

**B** is incorrect as members of a homologous series do have similar chemical properties, because they all contain the same functional group and undergo the same types of reactions.

**C** is incorrect as all members of a homologous series share the same general formula by definition (e.g. C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+2</sub> for alkanes).

**D** is incorrect as the gradual increase in chain length does produce a gradual change in physical properties, such as increasing boiling points and densities.

parts.problemMd: Which diagram correctly shows the heterolytic fission of the C–Cl bond in 1-chloropropane?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Heterolytic fission involves the movement of a pair of electrons.
- This means that a double-headed arrow is required.
- To form a chloride ion, Cl<sup>-</sup>, the double-headed arrow should go from the centre of the bond to the chlorine atom.

**A** is incorrect as the electron pair (double-headed arrow) is going to the carbon atom, which would result in a CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub><sup>-</sup> ion and a Cl<sup>+</sup> ion.

**C** is incorrect as there are 2 double-headed arrows, which would suggest the movement of 4 electrons from a single covalent bond that contains only 2 electrons.

**D** is incorrect as this is the correct diagram for homolytic fission of the C–Cl bond, which forms a CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub><sup>•</sup> radical and a Cl<sup>•</sup> radical.

parts.problemMd:
The reaction sequence below shows a pair of reaction types.

CH<sub>3</sub>CH=CHCH<sub>3</sub> $\overset{\mathrm{HI} \mathrm{in} \mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{COOH}}{\rightarrow}$ CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHICH<sub>3</sub> $\xrightarrow{NaOH ( \text{aq} )}$ CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>3</sub>

Which row in the table identifies reaction 1 and reaction 2?

|   | **Reaction 1** | **Reaction 2** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | Nucleophilic addition | Nucleophilic substitution |
| **B** | Electrophilic addition | Electrophilic substitution |
| **C** | Nucleophilic addition | Electrophilic substitution |
| **D** | Electrophilic addition | Nucleophilic substitution |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- The first reaction is electrophilic addition because:

  - HI is acting as an electrophile and is accepting a bonding pair of electrons from the alkene double bond; therefore the reaction is electrophilic.

  - The resulting organic molecule contains 2 more atoms than the initial organic molecule; therefore it is an addition reaction.

![Electrophilic addition mechanism of HI to but-2-ene, showing overall equation, polarisation of HI and attack on the double bond forming a carbocation intermediate, and nucleophilic capture by I- to give 2-iodobutane](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-2-characteristic-organic-reactions/assets/004-electrophilic-addition-mechanism-of-hi-to-but-2-.jpg)

- The second reaction is nucleophilic substitution because:

  - The OH<sup>-</sup> ion from NaOH is acting as a nucleophile and is donating a bonding pair of electrons to the organic molecule; therefore the reaction is nucleophilic.

  - In the resulting organic molecule, the hydroxyl (OH) group has replaced the iodine; therefore it is a substitution reaction.

![Nucleophilic substitution mechanism showing OH- attacking the delta-positive carbon of 2-iodobutane, displacing iodide ion to give 2-butanol](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-2-characteristic-organic-reactions/assets/005-nucleophilic-substitution-mechanism-showing-oh-a.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as the first reaction is not nucleophilic addition. HI acts as the electrophile by accepting electrons from the alkene double bond, making reaction 1 electrophilic addition.

**B** is incorrect as the second reaction is not electrophilic substitution. OH<sup>-</sup> is a nucleophile that replaces the iodine atom, making reaction 2 nucleophilic substitution.

**C** is incorrect as the first reaction is not nucleophilic addition. HI acts as the electrophile, not as a nucleophile, making reaction 1 electrophilic addition.

parts.problemMd:
The methyl group, CH<sub>3</sub>, can exist as an anion, a cation or a free radical. The CH<sub>3</sub> species can act as a nucleophile, an electrophile or a free radical depending on the number of outer shell electrons on the methyl carbon atom.

How many outer shell electrons must be present for CH<sub>3</sub> to act in these different ways?

|   | **nucleophile** | **electrophile** | **free radical** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | 6 | 8 | 7 |
| **B** | 8 | 6 | 7 |
| **C** | 6 | 7 | 8 |
| **D** | 8 | 7 | 6 |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- A nucleophile is a species that donates a pair of electrons.

  - The CH<sub>3</sub> species has a lone pair of electrons when it has 8 outer shell electrons.

- An electrophile is a species that accepts a pair of electrons.

  - An electron-deficient CH<sub>3</sub> species has 6 outer shell electrons.

- To act as a free radical, the CH<sub>3</sub> species must have an unpaired electron, giving 7 outer shell electrons.

**A** is incorrect as the nucleophile and electrophile values are swapped. The nucleophile (lone pair, electron donor) requires 8 outer shell electrons and the electrophile (electron-deficient) requires 6.

**C** is incorrect as the free radical requires 7 outer shell electrons (unpaired electron), not 8. The electrophile requires 6 outer shell electrons, not 7.

**D** is incorrect as the free radical requires 7 outer shell electrons (unpaired electron), not 6. The electrophile requires 6 outer shell electrons, not 7.

parts.problemMd:
Which row correctly describes a nucleophile and an electrophile?

|   | **nucleophile** | **electrophile** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | Has a lone pair of electrons | Accepts a pair of electrons |
| **B** | Is a negative ion | Is a positive ion |
| **C** | Attacks double bonds | Is only involved in substitution reactions |
| **D** | Accepts a pair of electrons | Has a lone pair of electrons |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- Nucleophiles have a lone pair of electrons and are electron-pair donors.
- Electrophiles accept electron pairs and are electron-pair acceptors.

**B** is incorrect as both nucleophiles and electrophiles can be covalently bonded molecules or atoms. For example, the double bond in alkenes makes them nucleophiles, and the permanent dipole in HBr makes it an electrophile.

**C** is incorrect as nucleophiles react with many functional groups, not just molecules with double bonds. Electrophiles are involved in both addition reactions (e.g. electrophilic addition to alkenes) and substitution reactions (e.g. electrophilic substitution in benzene).

**D** is incorrect as nucleophiles are electron-pair donors and electrophiles are electron-pair acceptors.

name: Shapes of Organic Molecules; σ & π Bonds
section: 13. An Introduction to AS Level Organic Chemistry

parts.problemMd: How many π bonds are present in one molecule of ethene?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- π bonds are formed by the sideways overlap of adjacent p orbitals
- Ethene contains one carbon-carbon double bond (C=C)
- The C=C double bond consists of one σ bond, formed by head-on orbital overlap, and one π bond, formed by sideways overlap of p orbitals

**A** is incorrect as 0 would suggest ethene contains only single bonds with no π bonds present.

**C** is incorrect as 2 would suggest the C=C double bond consists of two π bonds. A double bond consists of one σ bond and one π bond only.

**D** is incorrect as 3 π bonds would require multiple double or triple bonds, which are not present in ethene.

parts.problemMd: Which type of bond is formed by the sideways overlap of p orbitals?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- A π bond is formed by the sideways overlap of adjacent p orbitals above and below the internuclear axis

**A** is incorrect as a dative covalent bond is formed when one atom donates both electrons to a shared pair. It is not formed by the sideways overlap of p orbitals.

**B** is incorrect as a hydrogen bond is an intermolecular force of attraction between an electron-deficient hydrogen atom (bonded to N, O, or F) and a lone pair on a neighbouring electronegative atom. It is not formed by orbital overlap.

**D** is incorrect as a σ bond is formed by the head-on (end-to-end) overlap of atomic orbitals along the internuclear axis, not by sideways overlap.

parts.problemMd:
How many σ bonds and π bonds are present in a double bond?

|   | **σ bonds** | **π bonds** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | 0 | 2 |
| **B** | 1 | 1 |
| **C** | 1 | 2 |
| **D** | 2 | 0 |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- A double bond consists of one σ bond, formed by the head-on overlap of atomic orbitals, and one π bond, formed by the sideways overlap of p orbitals

**A** is incorrect as a combination of 0 σ bonds and 2 π bonds is not possible. The internuclear axis between two bonded atoms must always be occupied by a σ bond before any π bonds can form.

**C** is incorrect as a combination of 1 σ bond and 2 π bonds is the composition of a triple bond, not a double bond.

**D** is incorrect as a combination of 2 σ bonds and 0 π bonds would suggest a double bond consists of two σ bonds. A double bond always consists of one σ bond and one π bond.

parts.problemMd: What is the hybridisation of the carbon atom in methane?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Methane contains four σ bonds between the central carbon atom and four hydrogen atoms
- To form four equivalent bonds, the carbon atom hybridises one s orbital and three p orbitals to give four identical sp<sup>3</sup> hybrid orbitals
- Four sp<sup>3</sup> hybrid orbitals arrange themselves tetrahedrally to minimise repulsion

**A** is incorrect as sp hybridisation involves mixing one s orbital and one p orbital, producing two hybrid orbitals. This is associated with triple bonds, such as in ethyne.

**B** is incorrect as sp<sup>2</sup> hybridisation involves mixing one s orbital and two p orbitals, producing three hybrid orbitals. This is associated with double bonds, such as in ethene.

**D** is incorrect as sp<sup>4</sup> hybridisation is not possible. The p subshell contains only three orbitals (p<sub>x</sub>, p<sub>y</sub>, p<sub>z</sub>), so a maximum of three p orbitals can participate in hybridisation with one s orbital.

parts.problemMd: Which molecule is a straight-chain hydrocarbon?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- A straight-chain hydrocarbon consists of a continuous series of carbon atoms without any branches or ring structures
- Propane (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>) contains a continuous, unbranched chain of three carbon atoms

**A** is incorrect as 2-methylpropane is a branched aliphatic hydrocarbon. The longest continuous chain contains three carbon atoms with a methyl group branching off the central carbon atom.

**B** is incorrect as benzene is an aromatic hydrocarbon. It consists of a planar, cyclic ring of six carbon atoms, not an open chain.

**C** is incorrect as cyclopentane is an alicyclic hydrocarbon. The five carbon atoms form a closed ring rather than an open chain.

parts.problemMd:
Methyl isocyanate, CH<sub>3</sub>NCO, is a toxic liquid which is used in the production of adhesives.

The sequence of atoms in a methyl isocyanate molecule is H<sub>3</sub>C—N=C=O.

What is the approximate angle between the bonds formed by the N atom?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- From the sequence H<sub>3</sub>C—N=C=O, the nitrogen atom forms a single bond with the methyl group and a double bond with the isocyanate carbon
- Nitrogen has 5 valence electrons; after forming these bonds, one lone pair remains
- The nitrogen atom therefore has three regions of electron density: two bonding regions and one lone pair

![Dot-and-cross diagram of the nitrogen atom in methyl isocyanate showing three regions of electron density in a trigonal planar arrangement](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-3-shapes-of-organic-molecules--and--bonds/assets/004-dot-and-cross-diagram-of-the-nitrogen-atom-in-me.jpg)

- Three regions of electron density arrange in a trigonal planar geometry, giving an approximate bond angle of 120° (slightly less than 120° due to the greater repulsion from the lone pair)

**A** is incorrect as 107° is the bond angle in ammonia (NH<sub>3</sub>), where nitrogen has three bonding pairs and one lone pair giving a tetrahedral electron geometry. In methyl isocyanate, the nitrogen has three regions of electron density, not four.

**B** is incorrect as 109.5° is the bond angle for a perfect tetrahedral geometry with four bonding pairs and no lone pairs. The nitrogen in methyl isocyanate has three regions of electron density, giving a trigonal planar geometry.

**D** is incorrect as 180° is the bond angle for a linear geometry with only two regions of electron density. The carbon atom in the isocyanate group (—N=C=O) has a 180° bond angle, not the nitrogen atom.

parts.problemMd:
The diagram shows part of the structure of cysteine, an amino acid, with three bond angles labelled.

![Chemical structure of the amino acid cysteine, with bond angles labelled x, y and z ](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-3-shapes-of-organic-molecules--and--bonds/assets/002-chemical-structure-of-the-amino-acid-cysteine-wi.png)

What is the correct order of the bond angles *x*, *y* and *z*, from smallest to largest?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Angle *y*:

  - The central carbon atom has four bond pairs and no lone pairs, giving a tetrahedral geometry with a bond angle of 109.5°
- Angle *x*:

  - The nitrogen atom in the amine group has three bond pairs and one lone pair, giving a trigonal pyramidal geometry with a bond angle of 107°
- Angle *z*:

  - The oxygen atom has two bond pairs and two lone pairs, giving a bent geometry with a bond angle of 104.5°
- The correct size order from smallest to largest is *z* (104.5°) < *x* (107°) < *y* (109.5°)
- All three central atoms have a base tetrahedral electron geometry. Lone pairs repel more strongly than bond pairs, compressing the bond angle by approximately 2.5° per lone pair.

**A** is incorrect as *x* < *y* < *z* would place the oxygen atom as having the largest bond angle. Oxygen has two lone pairs, which cause greater repulsion and produce a smaller bond angle than either carbon or nitrogen.

**B** is incorrect as *x* < *z* < *y* incorrectly assigns a smaller angle to oxygen than to nitrogen. Oxygen has two lone pairs (giving 104.5°), which produce a smaller bond angle than the single lone pair on nitrogen (107°).

**D** is incorrect as *z* < *y* < *x* would suggest the nitrogen atom has the largest bond angle. The tetrahedral carbon atom, with no lone pairs, has the largest bond angle of 109.5°.

parts.problemMd: What is the minimum number of carbon atoms required to form a chiral acyclic alkane?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- For a carbon atom to be a chiral centre, it must be bonded to four different groups
- In an acyclic alkane, the four substituents are limited to hydrogen atoms and alkyl chains
- The four smallest different substituents are: H (0 additional carbons), methyl (1 carbon), ethyl (2 carbons), and propyl (3 carbons)
- Minimum total: 1 (central chiral carbon) + 0 + 1 + 2 + 3 = 7 carbon atoms

![Structural formula of 3-methylhexane showing the chiral centre at carbon 3, bonded to four different groups: a hydrogen atom, a methyl group, an ethyl group, and a propyl group](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-3-shapes-of-organic-molecules--and--bonds/assets/003-structural-formula-of-3-methylhexane-showing-the.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as 6 carbon atoms is not sufficient. After the central chiral carbon, only 5 remain. The three smallest different alkyl groups (methyl, ethyl, propyl) require 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 carbons, but only 5 are available. Any valid distribution of 5 carbons among three groups requires two identical groups, which destroys the chiral centre.

**C** is incorrect as 9 carbon atoms, while sufficient, is not the minimum. The smallest chiral acyclic alkane (3-methylhexane) requires only 7 carbon atoms.

**D** is incorrect as 11 carbon atoms, while sufficient, is not the minimum required to form a chiral acyclic alkane.

parts.problemMd: What is the bond angle around an sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised carbon atom?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- An sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised carbon atom has three regions of electron density (three σ bonds and no lone pairs)
- Three regions of electron density arrange in a trigonal planar geometry to minimise repulsion
- A trigonal planar geometry gives bond angles of 120°

**A** is incorrect as 104.5° is the bond angle associated with a central atom having two bond pairs and two lone pairs, such as the oxygen atom in water (H<sub>2</sub>O). Carbon does not have two lone pairs in any stable organic molecule.

**B** is incorrect as 109.5° is the bond angle for a perfect tetrahedral geometry, corresponding to sp<sup>3</sup> hybridisation with four σ bonds and no lone pairs, such as in methane (CH<sub>4</sub>).

**D** is incorrect as 180° is the bond angle for a linear geometry, corresponding to sp hybridisation with only two regions of electron density, such as in ethyne.

parts.problemMd:
The structure of the amino acid cysteine is shown.

![Structural formula of cysteine showing three carbon atoms: the carboxyl carbon with a C=O double bond, the alpha-carbon bonded to four different groups, and the beta-carbon bonded to the thiol group](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-3-shapes-of-organic-molecules--and--bonds/assets/001-structural-formula-of-cysteine-showing-three-car.png)

How many carbon atoms in a molecule of cysteine are sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- An atom is sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised when it is surrounded by three regions of electron density, as a double bond counts as one region
- In cysteine, only the carboxyl carbon (-COOH) is bonded to three groups: a hydroxyl (-OH) group, the adjacent carbon, and a C=O double bond
- The alpha-carbon and beta-carbon each form four σ bonds with no double bonds, so both are sp<sup>3</sup> hybridised

**A** is incorrect as there is one sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised carbon atom in cysteine (the carboxyl carbon). A value of 0 would suggest no carbon atom in the molecule contains a double bond.

**C** is incorrect as only one carbon atom (the carboxyl carbon) is sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised. The alpha-carbon has four different single-bond groups attached and is sp<sup>3</sup> hybridised.

**D** is incorrect as only one carbon atom is sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised. The alpha-carbon and beta-carbon each form four σ bonds with no double bonds and are therefore sp<sup>3</sup> hybridised.

parts.problemMd:
Limonene is found in the peel of citrus fruits.

![Skeletal formula of limonene showing a six-membered carbon ring with an isopropenyl substituent and one endocyclic double bond, giving two C=C double bonds in total](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-3-shapes-of-organic-molecules--and--bonds/assets/005-skeletal-formula-of-limonene-showing-a-six-membe.png)

How many σ and π bonds are present in this molecule?

|   | **σ** | **π** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | 12 | 2 |
| **B** | 22 | 4 |
| **C** | 24 | 4 |
| **D** | 26 | 2 |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Limonene has the molecular formula C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>16</sub>

![Displayed formula of limonene](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-3-shapes-of-organic-molecules--and--bonds/assets/006-displayed-formula-of-limonene.png)

- Every covalent bond contains one σ bond

  - The carbon skeleton contains 10 C-C σ bonds and 16 C-H σ bonds
  - This gives 26 σ bonds in total
- Each C=C double bond consists of one σ bond and one π bond:

  - Limonene contains two C=C double bonds
  - This gives 2 π bonds

**A** is incorrect as 12 σ bonds accounts only for the visible bonds in the carbon skeleton and does not include the C-H σ bonds to implicit hydrogen atoms. Each CH, CH<sub>2</sub>, or CH<sub>3</sub> group contains additional σ bonds that must be counted.

**B** is incorrect as 4 π bonds would suggest each double bond contains two π bonds. A C=C double bond consists of one σ bond and one π bond only, giving 2 π bonds for a molecule with two double bonds.

**C** is incorrect as 24 σ bonds and 4 π bonds reflects an undercount of σ bonds and an overcount of π bonds. Not all C-H σ bonds have been included in the total, and each double bond contributes only one π bond.

name: Isomerism: Structural Isomerism & Stereoisomerism
section: 13. An Introduction to AS Level Organic Chemistry

parts.problemMd: Which compound exhibits both optical and geometrical isomerism?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Optical isomers are isomers that have the same atoms and bonds but different spatial arrangements of the atoms.

  - The isomers are mirror images of each other and cannot be superimposed over one another (they are enantiomers).

- These are formed when a molecule has a chiral centre.

  - A chiral centre is identified by a carbon atom with 4 different groups/atoms bonded to it.
- Two types of geometric isomers are possible due to the restriction surrounding the C=C double bond.

  - Cis isomers have the functional groups on the same side of the carbon chain.
  - Trans isomers have the functional groups on opposite sides of the carbon chain.

![Structural diagrams showing cis isomers with identical groups on the same side of the C=C double bond, and trans isomers with identical groups on opposite sides](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-4-isomerism-structural-isomerism-and-stereoisomerism/assets/010-structural-diagrams-showing-cis-isomers-with-ide.webp)

**A** is incorrect as this has cis-trans but no chiral carbons, therefore no optical isomerism.

**B** is incorrect as this has cis-trans but no chiral carbons and therefore no optical isomerism.

**D** is incorrect as this doesn't have cis-trans isomerism.

parts.problemMd:
Which labelled carbon atom is a chiral centre?

![Skeletal structure of an organic compound with four carbon atoms labelled A, B, C and D](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-4-isomerism-structural-isomerism-and-stereoisomerism/assets/011-skeletal-structure-of-an-organic-compound-with-f.png)
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- This carbon has four different atoms / groups of atoms:

  - A hydrogen atom.
  - A CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> group.
  - A chlorine atom.
  - A COCH<sub>2</sub>Cl group.

**A** is incorrect as this carbon has two hydrogen atoms attached.

**B** is incorrect as this carbon does not have four groups attached due to the C=O carbonyl group.

**D** is incorrect as this carbon has two hydrogen atoms attached.

parts.problemMd:
Pentane and 2,2-dimethylpropane are isomers.

Which type of isomerism exists between these two molecules?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- Chain isomers have the same molecular formula but a different length carbon chain due to branching.
- 2,2-dimethylpropane has the same molecular formula as pentane (C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub>), but the longest carbon chain is three carbons long in 2,2-dimethylpropane and five carbons long in pentane.

![Structural diagrams comparing pentane with a five-carbon chain and 2,2-dimethylpropane with a three-carbon longest chain, illustrating chain isomerism](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-4-isomerism-structural-isomerism-and-stereoisomerism/assets/008-structural-diagrams-comparing-pentane-with-a-fiv.jpg)

**B** is incorrect as there is not a different functional group in 2,2-dimethylpropane compared to pentane, so it cannot be a functional group isomer.

**C** is incorrect as position isomers have the same carbon skeleton with a substituent at a different position. The carbon chain length changes between pentane and 2,2-dimethylpropane, so they are chain isomers, not position isomers.

**D** is incorrect as 2,2-dimethylpropane does not show stereoisomerism. It has no chiral centre and no restricted double bond.

choices.label: A
choices.textMd: A compound that contains a different molecular formula and the atoms are arranged differently in space

choices.label: B
choices.textMd: A compound that contains the same molecular formula but the atoms are arranged differently in space

choices.label: C
choices.textMd: A compound with the same empirical formula but different structural formula
