parts.problemMd: Which statement defines **structural isomers**?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Structural isomers include chain isomers, positional isomers and functional group isomers.
- All of which have the same molecular formula but different structural formula.

**A** is incorrect as this is an incorrect definition. Isomers must have the same molecular formula, not a different one.

**B** is incorrect as this is the definition for stereoisomers, which have the same molecular and structural formula but atoms arranged differently in space.

**C** is incorrect as empirical formula is the smallest whole number ratio of atoms in a compound. Molecular formula is the actual number of atoms of elements in a compound.

parts.problemMd:
Gamma-linolenic acid is an active compound found in evening primrose oil.

CH<sub>3</sub>(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>4</sub>CH=CHCH<sub>2</sub>CH=CHCH<sub>2</sub>CH=CH(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>4</sub>COOH

What is the maximum number of stereoisomers of gamma-linolenic acid?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Stereoisomers are compounds only different by the **spatial arrangement** of the atoms in the molecule.
- One type of stereoisomerism is **optical isomerism.**

  - These are non-superimposable mirror images of each other around a chiral carbon.
  - A chiral carbon is one with 4 different bonds attached.
  - No carbon atoms in this molecule are chiral.
- Another type of stereoisomerism is **geometric.**

  - This is shown below showing examples of ***cis-trans isomers*** of gamma-linolenic acid.
  - In **trans** isomers, the groups on either side of the double bond are on **different** sides of the double bond plane.
  - In **cis** isomers, the groups on either side of the double bond are on the **same** side of the double bond plane.

![Skeletal structures showing examples of cis and trans isomers at the three C=C double bonds in gamma-linolenic acid](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-4-isomerism-structural-isomerism-and-stereoisomerism/assets/004-skeletal-structures-showing-examples-of-cis-and-.jpg)

- The maximum number of stereoisomers of gamma-linolenic acid is 8, as the configuration at each double bond can be as follows:

  1. cis, cis, cis
  2. cis, cis, trans
  3. cis, trans, trans
  4. cis, trans, cis
  5. trans, cis, cis
  6. trans, cis, trans
  7. trans, trans, cis
  8. trans, trans, trans

**A** is incorrect as 3 is the number of C=C double bonds in gamma-linolenic acid, not the number of stereoisomers. Each double bond can independently adopt a cis or trans configuration, giving 2<sup>3</sup> = 8 stereoisomers in total.

**B** is incorrect as 4 would result from considering only 2 of the 3 double bonds as sources of geometric isomerism (2<sup>2</sup> = 4). All three double bonds in gamma-linolenic acid produce cis/trans isomers.

**C** is incorrect as 6 is not the correct count. The number of stereoisomers is 2<sup>n</sup>, where n is the number of double bonds giving geometric isomerism. With 3 such double bonds, there are 2<sup>3</sup> = 8 stereoisomers.

parts.problemMd: How many structural isomers have the molecular formula C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>5</sub>Br<sub>3</sub>?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Structural isomers have the atoms arranged in a completely different order.
- These can be:

  - Chain isomers (branched chains)
  - Position isomers (groups moved on the carbon skeleton)
  - Functional group isomerism (different functional groups and a member of a different homologous series).
- The 5 structural isomers of C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>5</sub>Br<sub>3</sub> are shown below:

![Five structural isomers of C3H5Br3: 1,1,1-tribromopropane; 1,1,2-tribromopropane; 1,1,3-tribromopropane; 1,2,2-tribromopropane; and 1,2,3-tribromopropane](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-4-isomerism-structural-isomerism-and-stereoisomerism/assets/009-five-structural-isomers-of-c3h5br3-1-1-1-tribrom.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as there are more than 4 structural isomers of C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>5</sub>Br<sub>3</sub>. Systematically placing the three bromine atoms at all possible positions on the propane chain gives 5 unique structures.

**C** is incorrect as 6 would involve counting the same structure twice when numbered from opposite ends of the chain. For example, 1,2,2-tribromopropane and 2,2,3-tribromopropane are the same compound. There are only 5 unique structural isomers.

**D** is incorrect as 7 significantly overcounts the structural isomers of C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>5</sub>Br<sub>3</sub>. A systematic approach to placing three bromine atoms at all positions on the propane chain gives only 5 unique structures.

parts.problemMd: How many structural isomers with the molecular formula C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O<sub>2</sub> are esters?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Structural isomers have the atoms arranged in a completely different order.

  - Isomeric esters are esters with a different location of the functional group or different carbon chain arrangement.
- The 9 possible ester structural isomers of C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O<sub>2</sub> are shown below:

![Nine structural isomers of C5H10O2 that are esters, including methyl butanoate, ethyl propanoate, propyl ethanoate, butyl methanoate, and their branched-chain equivalents](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-4-isomerism-structural-isomerism-and-stereoisomerism/assets/001-nine-structural-isomers-of-c5h10o2-that-are-este.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as 4 accounts for only the methanoate ester isomers of C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O<sub>2</sub>. The ethanoate, propanoate, and butanoate ester groups must also be considered, giving 9 structural isomers in total.

**B** is incorrect as 5 does not account for all structural isomers of C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O<sub>2</sub>. Both branched and unbranched carbon chains must be considered for each ester group, giving 9 structural isomers in total.

**C** is incorrect as 7 does not include all possible branched-chain arrangements. A systematic approach considering all combinations of ester group and alkyl group, including chain branching in both R and R' groups, gives 9 structural isomers.

parts.problemMd:
11-*cis* retinal, C<sub>20</sub>H<sub>28</sub>O, is found in the retina of animal eyes and is required for vision. The molecule contains an aldehyde group, a cyclohexene ring and an aliphatic side chain. Within the side chain, there is a double bond between carbons 11 and 12.

Which row shows the correct information for 11-*cis* retinal?

|   | **Arrangement of atoms around the adjacent carbons 11 and 12 ** | **Total number of carbon-carbon double bonds** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | ![Structural diagram showing a trans arrangement of substituents around the C11=C12 double bond](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-4-isomerism-structural-isomerism-and-stereoisomerism/assets/012-structural-diagram-showing-a-trans-arrangement-o.jpg) | 5 |
| **B** | ![Structural diagram showing a trans arrangement of substituents around the C11=C12 double bond](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-4-isomerism-structural-isomerism-and-stereoisomerism/assets/013-structural-diagram-showing-a-trans-arrangement-o.jpg) | 6 |
| **C** | ![Structural diagram showing the cis arrangement of substituents around the C11=C12 double bond](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-4-isomerism-structural-isomerism-and-stereoisomerism/assets/014-structural-diagram-showing-the-cis-arrangement-o.jpg) | 5 |
| **D** | ![Structural diagram showing the cis arrangement of substituents around the C11=C12 double bond](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-4-isomerism-structural-isomerism-and-stereoisomerism/assets/015-structural-diagram-showing-the-cis-arrangement-o.jpg) | 6 |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- The question states that it is a *cis* isomer. In a *cis* isomer, the substituents are on the **same** side of the double bond, as shown below.

![Structural diagram showing the cis arrangement of substituents around the C=C double bond between C11 and C12, with both substituent groups on the same side of the double bond](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-4-isomerism-structural-isomerism-and-stereoisomerism/assets/016-structural-diagram-showing-the-cis-arrangement-o.jpg)

- The cyclohexene ring contains one C=C double bond. There are 4 further C=C double bonds on the aliphatic chain, giving 5 carbon-carbon double bonds in total.

**A** is incorrect as the image shows a *trans* arrangement of substituents around the C11=C12 double bond. 11-*cis* retinal has a *cis* arrangement at this position.

**B** is incorrect as the image shows a *trans* arrangement at C11=C12, and 6 incorrectly includes the C=O double bond of the aldehyde group. Only carbon-carbon double bonds are counted, giving 5.

**D** is incorrect as 6 includes the C=O double bond of the aldehyde group in the count. The question specifies carbon-carbon double bonds only, of which there are 5.

parts.problemMd: Which compound is both chiral and acidic?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- The question asks for a molecule that is both chiral and acidic.
- Molecule **D** is acidic due to the carboxylic acid group (COOH).
- Molecule **D** is chiral because the highlighted carbon is bonded to 4 different groups:

![Skeletal structure of molecule D with the chiral carbon highlighted, showing four different substituent groups](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-4-isomerism-structural-isomerism-and-stereoisomerism/assets/002-skeletal-structure-of-molecule-d-with-the-chiral.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as this is 1-methylcyclohexanol, an alcohol, and it is achiral (no carbon atoms with 4 different groups attached to it).

**B** is incorrect as it is acidic but not chiral due to the double bond.

**C** is incorrect as this is chiral but not acidic.

parts.problemMd:
Cholesterol is a biological molecule used in the production of steroid hormones.

![Skeletal structure of cholesterol (C27H46O) showing the fused four-ring steroid system with a hydroxyl group at C3 and an aliphatic side chain](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-4-isomerism-structural-isomerism-and-stereoisomerism/assets/005-skeletal-structure-of-cholesterol-c27h46o-showin.png)

How many chiral centres are there in one molecule of cholesterol?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- The following **8** carbons are chiral centres:

  - C3 (OH, C4, C2, H).
  - C8 (C9, C14, C7, H).
  - C9 (C10, C8, C11, H).
  - C10 (C5, C9, C1, C19).
  - C13 (C14, C17, C12, C18).
  - C14 (C13, C8, C15, H).
  - C17 (C13, C20, C16, H).
  - C20 (C17, C22, C21, H).

- The 4 different groups that each carbon is bonded to are shown in brackets.

![Skeletal structure of cholesterol with 8 chiral centres highlighted at C3, C8, C9, C10, C13, C14, C17, and C20](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-4-isomerism-structural-isomerism-and-stereoisomerism/assets/006-skeletal-structure-of-cholesterol-with-8-chiral-.jpg)

- A chiral centre is an atom that has four different groups bonded to it. Each chiral centre gives rise to 2 optical isomers.
- When trying to find chiral centres, remember the following:

  - Hydrogens are not shown in skeletal drawings, but hydrogens often determine if the carbon is chiral. If a carbon has more than one hydrogen attached, you can dismiss it as a potential chiral centre.
  - Carbons on double or triple bonds cannot be chiral centres because they can't have bonds to 4 **different** groups.
  - Within complex cyclic molecules, each carbon in a ring can be considered as a different group if the overall group it is attached to is different.

**A** is incorrect as there are more than 5 chiral centres in cholesterol. This answer arises from identifying only the most visually obvious stereocentres and missing the ring junction carbons.

**B** is incorrect as one of the tertiary ring junction carbons (C8, C9, or C14) has been missed. These carbons have an implicit hydrogen atom that is not drawn in the skeletal structure.

**D** is incorrect as this overcounts the chiral centres. Carbons in the C=C double bond are sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised and cannot be chiral, and C25 at the end of the tail is bonded to two identical methyl groups.

parts.problemMd: How many isomeric alkenes, including stereoisomers, are produced when 2-bromobutane is heated with ethanolic NaOH?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- When a halogenoalkane reacts with ethanolic NaOH (elimination conditions), dehydrohalogenation occurs.
- Secondary halogenoalkanes undergo both substitution and elimination; the ethanolic solvent favours elimination.
- The following elimination reactions can occur, producing 3 isomeric alkenes:

![Reaction scheme showing the elimination reactions of 2-bromobutane with ethanolic NaOH, producing but-1-ene, cis-but-2-ene, and trans-but-2-ene](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-4-isomerism-structural-isomerism-and-stereoisomerism/assets/007-reaction-scheme-showing-the-elimination-reaction.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as only one product (the major alkene) has been identified, without considering elimination in both directions.

**B** is incorrect as this identifies but-1-ene and but-2-ene as structural isomers but misses that but-2-ene exists as cis and trans stereoisomers.

**D** is incorrect as but-1-ene cannot show cis-trans isomerism. The terminal alkene carbon (=CH<sub>2</sub>) is bonded to two identical hydrogen atoms, so no geometric isomerism is possible.

parts.problemMd: How many isomers, including structural and stereoisomers, with the molecular formula C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub> contain a π bond?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- There are 6 different isomers of C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub> that contain a π bond (have a C=C double bond).

![Six isomers of C5H10 that contain a C=C double bond: pent-1-ene, cis-pent-2-ene, trans-pent-2-ene, 2-methylbut-1-ene, 2-methylbut-2-ene, and 3-methylbut-1-ene](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-4-isomerism-structural-isomerism-and-stereoisomerism/assets/003-six-isomers-of-c5h10-that-contain-a-c-c-double-b.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as there are more than 3 isomers of C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub> that contain a π bond. All 5 alkene structural isomers must be identified, and cis-pent-2-ene and trans-pent-2-ene must be counted as separate stereoisomers, giving a total of 6.

**B** is incorrect as 4 is an undercount of the structural isomers of C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub> that are alkenes. Five structural isomers exist; including cis- and trans-pent-2-ene as separate stereoisomers gives a total of 6.

**C** is incorrect as 5 represents only the number of structural isomers of C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub> that are alkenes. Cis-pent-2-ene and trans-pent-2-ene are two distinct stereoisomers, so the total is 6.

parts.problemMd:
**X**, **Y** and **Z** are all organic compounds.

**X** can be manufactured by the oxidation of propene.

CH<sub>3</sub>CH=CH<sub>2</sub> + O<sub>2</sub> → CH<sub>2</sub>=CHCHO + H<sub>2</sub>O

Name **X** and name all the functional groups present in **X**.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The name and functional groups of **X** are:
> 
> - Name: propenal **[1 mark]**
> - Functional groups: alkene
> **AND**
> aldehyde / carbonyl **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> To name **X** (CH<sub>2</sub>=CHCHO), identify the longest carbon chain and the principal functional group:
> 
> - Three carbons = prop-
> - The aldehyde group (-CHO) has the highest priority and gives the suffix -al
> - The double bond gives the infix -en-
> - Combining these: prop + en + al = propenal
> 
> The compound contains two functional groups: an aldehyde (the -CHO group) and an alkene (the C=C bond).

parts.problemMd:
**Z** is a saturated hydrocarbon that is a structural isomer of pentene.

Draw the skeletal formula of **Z**.
parts.solutionMd:
The skeletal formula of **Z** is:

![Skeletal formula of cyclopentane showing a regular five-membered ring](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-1-formulas-functional-groups-and-the-naming-of-organic-compounds/assets/025-skeletal-formula-of-cyclopentane-showing-a-regul.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct skeletal formula of cyclopentane (a five-membered ring with no substituents or double bonds)

> **[exam-tip]**
> Pentene has the molecular formula C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>. A saturated hydrocarbon with this molecular formula cannot be a straight-chain alkane (alkanes have the general formula C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+2</sub>, which would give C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub> for five carbons). The only saturated cyclic hydrocarbon with five carbons is cyclopentane, drawn as a regular pentagon in skeletal form.

parts.problemMd: Crotonic acid has the molecular formula C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O<sub>2</sub>. Deduce the empirical formula of crotonic acid.

> **[mark-scheme]**

> Compound 1 (3-bromo-2-methylpropan-1-ol) has molecular formula C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9</sub>BrO. The subscripts 4, 9, 1 and 1 share no common factor greater than 1.
> 
> Compound 2 (2-chloropropanal) has molecular formula C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>5</sub>ClO. The subscripts 3, 5, 1 and 1 share no common factor greater than 1.
> 
> Compound 3 (2-chlorobut-2-en-1-ol) has molecular formula C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>7</sub>ClO. The subscripts 4, 7, 1 and 1 share no common factor greater than 1.
> 
> Compound 4 (but-2-enoic acid) has molecular formula C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O<sub>2</sub>. The subscripts 4, 6 and 2 share a common factor of 2, so the empirical formula is C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>3</sub>O, which differs from the molecular formula.

parts.problemMd:
Terpenes are a class of organic compounds widely used as fragrances in products such as perfumes. Nerol is a terpene found in many essential oils such as lemongrass and hops. The structure of nerol is shown in Fig. 1.1.

![Skeletal formula of nerol, a 10-carbon unsaturated alcohol with a hydroxyl group](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-1-formulas-functional-groups-and-the-naming-of-organic-compounds/assets/030-skeletal-formula-of-nerol-a-10-carbon-unsaturate.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

i) Deduce the molecular formula of nerol.

[1]

ii) Calculate the relative molecular mass, *M*<sub>r</sub>, of nerol. Show your working.

[1]

iii) Deduce the empirical formula of nerol.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The molecular formula of nerol is:
> 
> - C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>18</sub>O **[1 mark]**

ii) To calculate the relative molecular mass of nerol:

*M*<sub>r</sub> = (10 x 12.0) + (18 x 1.0) + 16.0

*M*<sub>r</sub> = 154.0 **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> iii) The empirical formula of nerol is:
> 
> - C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>18</sub>O **[1 mark]**
> 
> The empirical formula is the same as the molecular formula for nerol.

> **[exam-tip]**
> When counting atoms in a skeletal formula, trace each line end and vertex systematically to avoid missing any carbon or hydrogen atoms.
> 
> To find the empirical formula, find the highest common factor (HCF) of all subscripts in the molecular formula. For C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>18</sub>O, the HCF of 10, 18, and 1 is 1, so the empirical formula is the same as the molecular formula: C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>18</sub>O.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Terpenes are a class of organic compounds widely used as fragrances in products such as perfumes. Nerol is a terpene found in many essential oils such as lemongrass and hops. The structure of nerol is shown in Fig. 1.1.

Deduce whether molecules of nerol show geometrical (cis-trans) isomerism and whether they show optical isomerism. Explain your answers.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Geometrical (cis-trans) isomerism:
> 
> - Nerol does show geometrical (cis-trans) isomerism
> **AND**
> there are two different groups attached to each carbon of one of the C=C bonds **[1 mark]**
> - The C=C adjacent to the CH<sub>2</sub>OH group shows geometrical isomerism; the terminal C=C does not (one carbon of the terminal C=C has two identical methyl groups attached) **[1 mark]**
> 
> Optical isomerism:
> 
> - Nerol does not show optical isomerism
> **AND**
> there are no chiral centres / no carbon atom with four different groups attached **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Geometrical (cis-trans) isomerism requires restricted rotation around a C=C bond AND two different groups on each of the two carbons forming that bond.
> 
> Nerol has two C=C bonds. The terminal C=C has two methyl groups on one carbon; having identical groups on one carbon means this bond cannot show geometrical isomerism. The other C=C, adjacent to the CH<sub>2</sub>OH group, has two different groups on each carbon and does show geometrical isomerism. Nerol and geraniol are geometrical isomers of each other.
> 
> Optical isomerism requires a chiral centre: a carbon atom bonded to four different groups. There is no such carbon in nerol, so it does not show optical isomerism.

The completed skeletal formulae are:

Linalool (3,7-dimethylocta-1,6-dien-3-ol):

![Skeletal formula of linalool showing an 8-carbon chain with methyl groups at C3 and C7, double bonds at C1 and C6, and a hydroxyl group at C3](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-1-formulas-functional-groups-and-the-naming-of-organic-compounds/assets/031-skeletal-formula-of-linalool-showing-an-8-carbon.png)

**[1 mark]**

Geraniol (3,7-dimethylocta-2,6-dien-1-ol):

![Skeletal formula of geraniol showing an 8-carbon chain with methyl groups at C3 and C7, double bonds at C2 and C6, and a hydroxyl group at C1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-1-formulas-functional-groups-and-the-naming-of-organic-compounds/assets/032-skeletal-formula-of-geraniol-showing-an-8-carbon.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct skeletal formula of linalool: hydroxyl at C3, double bonds at C1 and C6, methyl groups at C3 and C7
> 
> 1 mark for correct skeletal formula of geraniol: hydroxyl at C1, double bonds at C2 and C6, methyl groups at C3 and C7

> **[exam-tip]**
> To draw skeletal formulae from IUPAC names, work through the name systematically:
> 
> 1. Identify the parent chain:
> 
>   - "octa" = 8 carbons.
> 2. Identify the principal functional group:
> 
>   - "-ol" = alcohol (OH).
>   - This determines the numbering direction as the OH carbon gets the lowest possible locant.
> 3. Locate the double bonds:
> 
>   - "1,6-dien" (linalool) means double bonds between C1 and C2, and between C6 and C7.
>   - "2,6-dien" (geraniol) means double bonds between C2 and C3, and between C6 and C7.
> 4. Add the substituents:
> 
>   - "3,7-dimethyl" means methyl groups at C3 and C7 for both isomers.

parts.problemMd:
i) Define the term *hydrocarbon*.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:

> i) The term *hydrocarbon* means:
>

> 
> - C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+2</sub> **[1 mark]**
>

> - C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub> **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd: State **two** characteristics of a homologous series.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Two characteristics of a homologous series are:
> 
> Any **two** from (1 mark for each point):
> 
> - Same general formula
> - Each successive member differs by a –CH<sub>2</sub>– group
> - Same functional group / similar chemical properties
> - Gradual trend in physical properties (e.g. boiling point)
> 
> **[2 marks]**

> **[exam-tip]**

parts.problemMd: State the names of the three steps involved in a free radical substitution reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**

parts.problemMd:
A molecule of chlorine, Cl<sub>2</sub>, undergoes bond fission when exposed to UV light.

i) Construct an equation for this reaction.

ii) State the type of bond fission involved.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:

> i) The equation for this reaction is:
> 
> - Cl<sub>2</sub> $\overset{\mathrm{UV} \mathrm{light}}{\rightarrow}$ 2Cl• **[1 mark]**
> 
> UV light should be shown above the arrow (or equivalent notation)
> 
> ii) The type of bond fission is:
> 
> - Homolytic (bond fission) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> In homolytic fission, one electron from the covalent bond goes to each atom, forming two radicals.
> 
> A single-headed curly arrow shows the movement of one electron; a double-headed arrow shows a pair of electrons.

parts.problemMd:
Fig 2.1 shows the breaking of a covalent bond.

parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The name of this type of bond fission is:
> 
> - Heterolytic (fission) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> In heterolytic fission, one atom takes both electrons from the bond, forming a positive ion and a negative ion.
> 
> The more electronegative atom takes both electrons, forming the anion; the other atom becomes the cation.
> 
> A double-headed curly arrow shows the movement of an electron pair to one atom.

parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Three other types of reaction mechanism are:
> 
> Any **three** from (1 mark for each point):

> - Electrophilic addition
> - Nucleophilic substitution

> - Nucleophilic addition
> - Electrophilic substitution
>

> Free radical substitution is not accepted as it was given in part (a).

> The curly arrow mechanisms covered at AS Level are electrophilic addition, nucleophilic substitution, and elimination.

> - Nucleophilic substitution: an atom or group is replaced by another (e.g. bromoethane + OH<sup>-</sup> → ethanol + Br<sup>-</sup>)

parts.problemMd: By reference to the hybridisation of the carbon atoms and orbital overlap, describe how the σ and π bonds are formed in the triple bond of propyne.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The σ and π bonds in the triple bond of propyne are formed as follows:
> 
> - The carbon atoms forming the triple bond are sp hybridised **[1 mark]**
> - The σ bond is formed from the head-on overlap of sp orbitals (from each carbon atom) **[1 mark]**
> - Two π bonds are formed from the sideways overlap of unhybridised p orbitals (on each carbon atom) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A triple bond consists of one σ bond and two π bonds. To form a triple bond, the two carbon atoms must be sp hybridised.
> 
> The σ bond forms from the head-on (direct) overlap of one sp orbital from each carbon atom. The two π bonds are formed from the sideways overlap of the two unhybridised p orbitals on each carbon.

parts.problemMd: Explain why the ring of carbon atoms in cyclohexane, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>, is non-planar. In your answer, refer to the hybridisation of the carbon atoms and the C–C–C bond angles.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Cyclohexane has a non-planar ring of carbon atoms because:
> 
> - The carbon atoms are sp<sup>3</sup> hybridised **[1 mark]**
> - Each carbon has a tetrahedral arrangement of bonds
> **AND**
> The C–C–C bond angles are 109.5° **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Hybridisation determines the geometry around each atom:
> 
> - sp<sup>3</sup> hybridised carbon ↔ tetrahedral geometry ↔ bond angles of 109.5°
> - sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised carbon ↔ trigonal planar geometry ↔ bond angles of 120°
> - sp hybridised carbon ↔ linear geometry ↔ bond angles of 180°
> 
> In cyclohexane, the 109.5° tetrahedral bond angles prevent the ring from being flat:
> 
> ![Skeletal formula of cyclohexane showing six linked carbon atoms, each bonded to hydrogen atoms, illustrating a non-planar branched hydrocarbon structure](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-3-shapes-of-organic-molecules--and--bonds/assets/007-skeletal-formula-of-cyclohexane-showing-six-link.png)
> 
> A flat ring would require 120° bond angles, which would require sp<sup>2</sup> hybridisation and double bonds. The puckered shape allows each carbon to maintain its preferred tetrahedral geometry.

![Displayed formula of ethanol with one carbon atom labelled](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-3-shapes-of-organic-molecules--and--bonds/assets/009-displayed-formula-of-ethanol-with-one-carbon-ato.png)

**Fig. 3.2**

State the hybridisation of the carbon atom marked in Fig. 3.2.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The hybridisation of the carbon atom marked in Fig. 3.2 is:
> 
> - sp<sup>3</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Both carbon atoms in ethanol form only single bonds and have no lone pairs, giving 4 electron domains around each carbon. This means both are sp<sup>3</sup> hybridised, with a tetrahedral arrangement and bond angles of approximately 109.5°. The oxygen atom is also sp<sup>3</sup> hybridised.

parts.problemMd:
The structure of ibuprofen is shown in Fig. 1.1.

![Skeletal structure of ibuprofen showing benzene ring, carboxylic acid, and isobutyl chain](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-3-shapes-of-organic-molecules--and--bonds/assets/010-skeletal-structure-of-ibuprofen-showing-benzene-.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

State the number of pi (π) bonds and the number of chiral centres in a molecule of ibuprofen.

number of π bonds ..............................

number of chiral centres ..............................
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The number of pi (π) bonds and chiral centres in ibuprofen is:
> 
> - π bonds = 4 **[1 mark]**
> - chiral centres = 1 **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> To count π bonds: each double bond contains one π bond. In ibuprofen, the benzene ring has 3 (shown in the Kekulé structure) and the carboxylic acid has 1 C=O, giving 4 π bonds total.
> 
> A chiral centre is a carbon atom bonded to four different groups. In ibuprofen, the carbon bearing the methyl group, the carboxylic acid group, the isobutyl chain, and a hydrogen atom is the only chiral centre (1 total).

parts.solutionMd:

> **[exam-tip]**

> ![Diagram of a ibuprofen molecule showing sp2 (green) and sp3 (blue) hybridised carbon atoms, with labelled CH3 side groups and a carboxylic acid](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-3-shapes-of-organic-molecules--and--bonds/assets/011-diagram-of-a-ibuprofen-molecule-showing-sp2-gree.png)

> When counting, look for double bonds and aromatic ring carbons first, these are sp<sup>2</sup>. Any carbon with only single bonds is sp<sup>3</sup>.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The structure of ibuprofen is shown in Fig. 1.1.

![Skeletal structure of ibuprofen showing benzene ring, carboxylic acid, and isobutyl chain](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2022/06/ibuprofen-structure-ib-hl-sq-h-14-2-q1a.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

Describe and explain the shape of the benzene ring in ibuprofen.

In your answer, include:

- the bond angle between carbon atoms
- the hybridisation of the carbon atoms
- how orbital overlap forms σ and π bonds between the carbon atoms
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The shape of the benzene ring in ibuprofen is:
> 
> - Bond angle between carbon atoms is 120° **[1 mark]**
> - All carbon atoms in the ring are sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised **[1 mark]**
> - The sp<sup>2</sup> orbitals overlap head-on to form σ bonds between adjacent carbons; the unhybridised p orbitals overlap sideways to form a delocalised π system above and below the ring **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> All carbons in the benzene ring are sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised, giving a trigonal planar arrangement around each carbon with bond angles of 120°. This forces all six carbons into the same plane, making the ring planar.
> 
> The sp<sup>2</sup> hybrid orbitals form sigma bonds between adjacent carbon atoms (head-on overlap). Each carbon also has one unhybridised p orbital perpendicular to the ring; these overlap sideways with neighbouring p orbitals to form a delocalised π system above and below the plane of the ring.

name: Isomerism: Structural Isomerism & Stereoisomerism
section: 13. An Introduction to AS Level Organic Chemistry

parts.problemMd: State the **three **different types of structural isomerism.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The three types of structural isomerism are:
> 
> - Chain (isomerism) **[1 mark]**
> - Positional (isomerism) **[1 mark]**
> - Functional group (isomerism) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Structural isomers are compounds that have the same molecular formula but different structural formulae.
> 
> You should know the three different types and be prepared to determine the possible structural formulae of an organic molecule given its molecular formula.

parts.problemMd:
State the type of **structural** isomerism that occurs between the following pairs of compounds.

i) 2-methylpentane and 2,3-dimethylbutane.

[1]

ii) butan-1-ol and butan-2-ol

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The type of structural isomerism shown by 2-methylpentane and 2,3-dimethylbutane is:
> 
> - Chain (isomerism) **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The type of structural isomerism shown by butan-1-ol and butan-2-ol is:
> 
> - Positional (isomerism) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Chain isomers have the same molecular formula but different longest carbon chain lengths because a section of the chain has been branched off.
> 
> Positional isomers arise from differences in the position of a functional group along the carbon chain. Both butan-1-ol and butan-2-ol are C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O alcohols but the –OH group is on a different carbon.

Compounds **A** to **F** are shown in **Fig 1.1**.

**Fig 1.1**

i) State the systematic name of compound **B**.

[1]

ii) State the type of structural isomerism shown by compounds **A** and **D**.

[1]

iii) State the type of structural isomerism shown by compounds **C** and **E**.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The systematic name of compound **B** is:
> 
> - Butanoic acid **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The type of structural isomerism shown by compounds **A** and **D** is:
> 
> - Functional group isomerism **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The type of structural isomerism shown by compounds **C** and **E** is:
> 
> - Chain isomerism **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Compound **B** has four carbons (but–), single carbon–carbon bonds (–an–) and a carboxylic acid functional group (–oic acid). This gives the systematic name butanoic acid.
> 
> Compounds **A** (a ketone) and **D** (an aldehyde) are functional group isomers. Both have the molecular formula C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O but the C=O group has moved from within the chain to the terminal position, changing the functional group.
> 
> Compounds **C** and **E** are chain isomers. Both are C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O alcohols but one has a branched carbon chain and the other is straight-chain.

parts.problemMd: State the two types of stereoisomerism.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The two types of stereoisomerism are:
> 
> - Geometrical (cis/trans)
> **AND**
> Optical **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Stereoisomers are molecules with the same structural formula but a different arrangement of atoms in 3D space.

parts.problemMd: Explain what is meant by the term *chiral centre*.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> A chiral centre is:
> 
> - A carbon atom that has four different atoms / groups of atoms attached to it **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Defining a chiral centre is not a common question as the focus is usually on identifying and drawing them. However, you cannot identify or draw chiral centres without knowing this definition.

> - The -an- portion tells you the main chain contains only single bonds
> - The -al suffix tells you carbon-1 is an aldehyde (CHO) group
> - The 2-chloro portion tells you there is a chlorine atom attached to carbon-2
> - A common mistake when drawing the skeletal formula of any aldehyde is to forget the hydrogen atom attached to the carbonyl (C=O) bond
> 
> For compound 3 (3-bromo-2-methylpropan-1-ol):
> 
> - The main carbon chain is 3 carbons with single bonds, so the name is propane-based
> - There is an alcohol group, a methyl group and a bromine group
> - The alcohol is highest priority, so it is on carbon-1: propan-1-ol
> - The methyl group is second highest priority: 2-methylpropan-1-ol
> - The bromine group is lowest priority: 3-bromo-2-methylpropan-1-ol
> - For the skeletal formula: re-draw the displayed formula, remove the carbon symbols (angling the chain to show structure clearly), then remove all hydrogen atoms except the one attached to the oxygen
> 
> For compound 4 (3-methylbut-2-enoic acid):
> 
> - The longest carbon chain is 4 carbons, so the name is but-based
> - The carboxylic acid group is automatically carbon-1: butanoic acid
> - There is a C=C double bond at carbon-2: but-2-enoic acid
> - There is a methyl group on carbon-3: 3-methylbut-2-enoic acid
> - For the displayed formula: re-draw the skeletal formula, place carbon symbols at each junction and chain end, then add the correct number of hydrogen atoms to each carbon — take care around double bonds as carbon has a maximum of 4 bonds

Explain why compound **1** shows geometrical (cis/trans) isomerism but compound **4** does not.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Compound **1** shows geometrical (cis/trans) isomerism but compound **4** does not because:
> 
> - There is no free rotation about the C=C / carbon-carbon double bond **[1 mark]**
> - Due to the presence of a π bond **[1 mark]**
> - The C=C of compound **1** has different atoms / groups on each carbon **[1 mark]**
> - The C=C of compound **4** has two identical groups / methyl groups on one carbon **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For an alkene to show geometrical (cis/trans) isomerism, each carbon of the C=C double bond must have two different atoms or groups attached.
> 
> Compound 1 has a hydrogen atom and a methyl group at one end of the C=C, and a chlorine atom and a CH<sub>2</sub>OH group at the other end. Both ends have two different groups, so compound 1 shows geometrical isomerism.
> 
> Compound 4 has two methyl groups at one end of the C=C. Because this end has two identical groups, geometrical isomerism is not possible.
> 
> The isomerism arises because the π bond system above and below the σ bond prevents free rotation about the C=C.

[1]

[1]
parts.solutionMd:

>

> 
> ii) The type of structural isomerism shown is:
> 
> - Chain / branched chain **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The three types of structural isomerism are chain isomerism, positional isomerism and functional group isomerism.
> 
> A straight-chain alkane cannot show functional group isomerism because the molecule is saturated. This means you are looking for chain or positional isomerism.

> Methane, ethane and propane cannot have chain or positional isomers as their chains are too short. Butane is the first straight-chain alkane long enough to rearrange:

parts.problemMd: Which equation represents a valid propagation step in the free radical reaction between ethane and chlorine?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- A propagation step involves a free radical reacting with a stable molecule to produce a new radical and a new stable molecule, keeping the chain reaction going.
- **A** shows how a chlorine radical abstracts a hydrogen from chloroethane, producing a chloroethyl radical and HCl.

  - The number of free radicals is unchanged, so this is a valid propagation step.
- The standard propagation steps for the ethane and chlorine reaction are:

C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub> + Cl• → C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>• + HCl

C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>• + Cl<sub>2</sub> → C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>Cl + Cl•

- Further substitution of the product C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>Cl is also a valid propagation step.

**B** is incorrect as it shows two radicals combining to form one stable molecule, which is a termination step (net destruction of radicals).

**C** is incorrect as it produces an H• radical. Hydrogen radicals are not formed in this mechanism; Cl• abstracts H to form HCl, not H•.

**D** is incorrect as the equation is unbalanced. Chlorine appears in the product (HCl) but not in the reactants.

parts.problemMd:
One of the reactions taking place in a catalytic converter in a car exhaust system is between nitrogen oxide and octane (unburned petrol). The products of this reaction are non-toxic.

Which is the correct equation for the reaction?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub> is the correct formula for octane.
- Carbon dioxide (CO<sub>2</sub>), nitrogen gas (N<sub>2</sub>) and water (H<sub>2</sub>O) are all non-toxic products.

**A** and **B** are incorrect as octane is an alkane with formula C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub>, whereas **A** and **B** show C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>16</sub>, which is octene.

**C** is incorrect as CO is carbon monoxide, which is a toxic gas.

parts.problemMd:
The hydrocarbon C<sub>17</sub>H<sub>36</sub> can be cracked.

Which compound is the **least** likely to be produced in this reaction?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Cracking is a reaction in which larger alkane molecules are broken down into smaller alkane and alkene molecules.
- For C<sub>16</sub>H<sub>34</sub> to be produced from C<sub>17</sub>H<sub>36</sub>, the remaining fragment would be CH<sub>2</sub>:

C<sub>17</sub>H<sub>36</sub> → C<sub>16</sub>H<sub>34</sub> + CH<sub>2</sub>

- CH<sub>2</sub> cannot exist as a stable molecule.
- The minimum stable alkene requires at least two carbon atoms to form a C=C double bond (ethene, C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>).
- Therefore, C<sub>16</sub>H<sub>34</sub> cannot be produced by cracking.

**A**, **B** and **C** are incorrect as these compounds can all be produced by valid cracking equations that leave a stable alkane or alkene as the other fragment:

C<sub>17</sub>H<sub>36</sub> → C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub> + C<sub>14</sub>H<sub>28</sub> (alkane + alkene)

C<sub>17</sub>H<sub>36</sub> → C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub> + C<sub>13</sub>H<sub>28</sub> (alkene + alkane)

C<sub>17</sub>H<sub>36</sub> → C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>16</sub> + C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>20</sub> (alkene + alkane)

parts.problemMd:
In the presence of ultraviolet light, ethane and chlorine react to give a mixture of products.

Which compound could be present in the mixture of products?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Initiation = net formation of radicals
- In the initiation step, free radical Cl• atoms are formed:

Cl<sub>2</sub> → 2Cl•

- Propagation = no change in the number of free radicals
- These free radical Cl• atoms remove a hydrogen from the ethane making an ethyl free radical, C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>•:

C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub> + Cl• → C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>• + HCl

- Termination = net destruction of free radicals
- Two of these radicals can then pair up in a termination step to form butane, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> (C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>):

C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>• + C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>• → C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>

- Therefore, option **C** is the only compound that could be present in the mixture.

**A** is incorrect as CH<sub>3</sub>Cl cannot be formed from the reaction between ethane and chlorine. All carbon-containing products must retain the two-carbon skeleton of ethane; a one-carbon product such as chloromethane is not possible.

**B** is incorrect as CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Cl (1-chloropropane) contains three carbon atoms and cannot be formed from ethane and chlorine. No three-carbon products can arise from a two-carbon starting material.

**D** is incorrect as CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> (pentane) contains five carbon atoms. The termination step joining two ethyl radicals (C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>•) produces butane (four carbons), not pentane.

parts.problemMd:
The cracking of a single hydrocarbon molecule, C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+2</sub>, produces two hydrocarbon molecules only. Each hydrocarbon product contains the same number of carbon atoms in one molecule.  Each hydrocarbon product has non-cyclic structural isomers.

What is the value of n?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Cracking an alkane to produce exactly two molecules with the same number of carbon atoms yields one alkane and one alkene.

  - For n = 8, C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub> cracks to give C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub> (butane) and C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub> (butene).

- Both products must have non-cyclic structural isomers:

  - C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub> has two non-cyclic structural isomers: butane and methylpropane
  - C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub> has three non-cyclic structural isomers: but-1-ene, but-2-ene, and 2-methylpropene
  - Cis-but-2-ene and trans-but-2-ene are E/Z stereoisomers of but-2-ene, not separate structural isomers.
- Both products satisfy the condition, so n = 8.

**A** is incorrect as when n = 4, cracking gives ethane (C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>) and ethene (C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>). Neither 2-carbon compound has any structural isomers.

**B** is incorrect as when n = 6, cracking gives propane (C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub>) and propene (C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>). Propane has no structural isomers, and propene's only structural isomer is cyclopropane, which is cyclic. Neither product satisfies the condition.

**D** is incorrect as n = 9 is odd. It is not possible to split an odd number of carbon atoms into two products with the same number of carbons each.

parts.problemMd:
Which hydrocarbon would **not** be collected in the inverted tube by heating pentane, CH<sub>3</sub>(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, in the apparatus shown?

![Diagram of cracking apparatus: a horizontal tube containing pentane on mineral fibre and aluminium oxide heated strongly, connected by a delivery tube to an inverted test tube submerged in water for gas collection](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-1-alkanes/assets/001-diagram-of-cracking-apparatus-a-horizontal-tube-.png)
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Heating pentane over an aluminium oxide catalyst cracks the molecule.
- Cracking breaks down larger alkane molecules into smaller alkanes and alkenes.
- So, for pentane, the cracking process will produce alkanes and alkenes of five or fewer carbons.
- Therefore, CH<sub>3</sub>(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>8</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> would not be produced in this reaction as it contains 10 carbons, which is more than the original pentane (5 carbons).

**A** is incorrect as methane (CH<sub>4</sub>) is a gas at room temperature and pressure and could be produced by cracking pentane, for example:

C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub> → CH<sub>4</sub> + C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>

Gases are collected in the inverted tube by displacement of water.

**B** is incorrect as ethane (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>) is a gas at room temperature and pressure and could be produced by cracking pentane, for example:

C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub> → C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub> + C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>

It would be collected in the inverted tube.

**C** is incorrect as but-1-ene (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH=CH<sub>2</sub>) is a gas at room temperature and pressure and could be produced by cracking pentane, for example:

C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub> → C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub> + CH<sub>4</sub>

It would be collected in the inverted tube.

parts.problemMd:
0.200 mol of a hydrocarbon undergoes complete combustion to give 35.2 g of carbon dioxide and 14.4 g of water as the only products.

What is the molecular formula of the hydrocarbon?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- List the known values:

  - mass of CO<sub>2</sub> = 35.2 g, *M*<sub>r</sub>(CO<sub>2</sub>) = 44
  - mass of H<sub>2</sub>O = 14.4 g, *M*<sub>r</sub>(H<sub>2</sub>O) = 18
  - moles of hydrocarbon = 0.200 mol
- Calculate the moles of CO<sub>2</sub>:

moles = $\frac{m}{M_{r}}$

moles = 35.2 / 44

moles of CO<sub>2</sub> = 0.800 mol

- Calculate the moles of H<sub>2</sub>O:

moles = $\frac{m}{M_{r}}$

moles = 14.4 / 18

moles of H<sub>2</sub>O = 0.800 mol

- Scale to per mole of hydrocarbon to find the molecular formula:

C atoms per molecule = 0.800 / 0.200 = 4

H atoms per molecule = (2 x 0.800) / 0.200 = 8

- The molecular formula is C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>.

**A** is incorrect as C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub> has the same empirical formula (CH<sub>2</sub>) as C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>. This traps candidates who calculate only the simplest ratio without using the 0.200 mol value to scale to the molecular formula.

**B** is incorrect as C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub> would give a CO<sub>2</sub> to H<sub>2</sub>O mole ratio of 2:3, not 1:1.

**C** is incorrect as C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>4</sub> would give only 0.400 mol H<sub>2</sub>O from 0.200 mol of compound, not 0.800 mol.

parts.problemMd: Which statement about the free-radical substitution of ethane with chlorine is correct?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- In free-radical substitution of ethane with chlorine, the reaction begins with an initiation step.
- Ultraviolet light provides the energy needed to break the Cl–Cl bond by homolytic fission.
- This produces chlorine radicals, which are required to start the chain reaction.

**A** is incorrect as the collision of two radicals to form a stable molecule occurs in the termination step, not propagation.

**B** is incorrect as the final mixture also contains unreacted ethane, unreacted chlorine, and further substituted products such as dichloroethane.

**C** is incorrect as the initiation step involves homolytic, not heterolytic, fission of the Cl–Cl bond, not the C–H bond.

parts.problemMd:
Samples of 10 cm<sup>3</sup> of each of the first four members of the alkane series are separately mixed with 70 cm<sup>3</sup> of oxygen. Each is then burned and the total volume, *V*, of residual gas measured again at room temperature and pressure.

Which graph represents the results that would be obtained?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- The first four members of the alkane series are methane (CH<sub>4</sub>), ethane (C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>), propane (C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub>) and butane (C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>).
- At room temperature, water produced by combustion condenses to liquid and contributes negligible volume to the residual gas.
- Methane:

CH<sub>4</sub> + 2O<sub>2</sub> → CO<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O

O<sub>2</sub> consumed = 2 x 10 = 20 cm<sup>3</sup>; CO<sub>2</sub> produced = 10 cm<sup>3</sup>

Residual volume = (70 − 20) + 10 = 60 cm<sup>3</sup>

- Ethane:

C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub> + $\frac{7}{2}$O<sub>2</sub> → 2CO<sub>2</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub>O

O<sub>2</sub> consumed = 3.5 x 10 = 35 cm<sup>3</sup>; CO<sub>2</sub> produced = 20 cm<sup>3</sup>

Residual volume = (70 − 35) + 20 = 55 cm<sup>3</sup>

- Propane:

C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub> + 5O<sub>2</sub> → 3CO<sub>2</sub> + 4H<sub>2</sub>O

O<sub>2</sub> consumed = 5 x 10 = 50 cm<sup>3</sup>; CO<sub>2</sub> produced = 30 cm<sup>3</sup>

Residual volume = (70 − 50) + 30 = 50 cm<sup>3</sup>

- Butane:

C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub> + $\frac{13}{2}$O<sub>2</sub> → 4CO<sub>2</sub> + 5H<sub>2</sub>O

O<sub>2</sub> consumed = 6.5 x 10 = 65 cm<sup>3</sup>; CO<sub>2</sub> produced = 40 cm<sup>3</sup>

Residual volume = (70 − 65) + 40 = 45 cm<sup>3</sup>

- The four values (60, 55, 50, 45 cm<sup>3</sup>) decrease linearly by 5 cm<sup>3</sup> per member, as shown in graph **B**.

parts.problemMd:
The petrol additive tetraethyl-lead (IV), Pb(C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>)<sub>4</sub>, is now banned in many countries. When it is completely burned in air, lead (II) oxide, CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O are formed.

How many moles of oxygen are required to burn one mole of Pb(C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>)<sub>4</sub>?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Expand the formula Pb(C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>)<sub>4</sub>:

1 Pb, 4 x 2 = 8 C, 4 x 5 = 20 H

- The balanced equation for complete combustion is:

Pb(C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>)<sub>4</sub> + $\frac{27}{2}$O<sub>2</sub> → PbO + 8CO<sub>2</sub> + 10H<sub>2</sub>O

- Count the total oxygen atoms required on the right-hand side:

1 (in PbO) + 16 (in 8CO<sub>2</sub>) + 10 (in 10H<sub>2</sub>O) = 27 oxygen atoms

- Calculate the moles of O<sub>2</sub>:

moles of O<sub>2</sub> = 27 / 2

moles of O<sub>2</sub> = 13.5

**A** (9.5) is incorrect and results from failing to multiply the carbon count by 4 when expanding the bracket, giving only 4 CO<sub>2</sub> molecules instead of 8.

**B** (11) is incorrect and results from failing to multiply the hydrogen count by 4 when expanding the bracket, giving only 5 H<sub>2</sub>O molecules instead of 10.

**D** (27) is incorrect as 27 is the total number of oxygen atoms required, not the number of moles of O<sub>2</sub> molecules. Dividing by 2 is required since oxygen is diatomic.

parts.problemMd:
The cracking of eicosane, C<sub>20</sub>H<sub>42</sub>, produces a hydrocarbon that is in very high demand for transportation and also three consecutive members of the same homologous series of hydrocarbons.

What are the correct products of cracking for the given reaction?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- The highest demand hydrocarbon for transportation is octane (C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub>).
- Subtract octane from eicosane to find the remaining fragment:

C<sub>20</sub>H<sub>42</sub> - C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub> = C<sub>12</sub>H<sub>24</sub>

- C<sub>12</sub>H<sub>24</sub> has the general formula C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n</sub>, so the remaining three products are alkenes.
- Let the smallest alkene have n carbons.

  - Three consecutive alkenes total 12 carbons:

n + (n + 1) + (n + 2) = 12

3n + 3 = 12

n = 3

- The three consecutive alkenes are propene (C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>), butene (C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>) and pentene (C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>).
- Overall cracking equation:
- C<sub>20</sub>H<sub>42</sub> → C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub> + C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub> + C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub> + C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>

**A** is incorrect as the carbon count of the products (4 + 4 + 6 + 8 = 22) exceeds the 20 carbons in eicosane, so it is stoichiometrically impossible.

**C** is incorrect as ethane is not a hydrocarbon in high demand for transportation (it is a gas at room temperature, not a liquid fuel). The remaining alkenes in this option are also not consecutive members of the same homologous series.

**D** is incorrect as ethene is not a hydrocarbon in high demand for transportation, and the three alkenes (ethene, pentene, heptene) are not consecutive members of the same homologous series.

parts.problemMd:
Ethene reacts with steam in the presence of sulfuric acid.

C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>  +  H<sub>2</sub>O  $\rightarrow$ CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH

What type of reaction is this?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- In an addition reaction, two compounds come together to form one larger compound.
- There are no other products produced.
- Therefore, the reaction between ethene and steam is an addition reaction.

**A** is incorrect as an acid-base reaction involves an acid and a base as reactants.

**C** is incorrect as in a hydrolysis reaction, chemical bonds are broken by the addition of water, however that is not the case here.

**D** is incorrect as in a substitution reaction, an atom or functional group is replaced by another similar species.

> **[exam-tip]**
> This reaction is also known as hydration, which is the addition of water across the C=C double bond. Do not confuse hydration with hydrolysis:
> 
> - Hydration forms a single product with no bonds broken by water
> - Hydrolysis uses water to break a bond in the substrate (e.g. ester → carboxylic acid + alcohol).

parts.problemMd: What is the mechanism for the reaction between propene and bromine in an organic solvent?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- In an addition reaction, two compounds come together to form one larger compound with no other products, as shown:

![Equation showing the addition of bromine to propene to form 1,2-dibromopropane](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-2-alkenes/assets/005-equation-showing-the-addition-of-bromine-to-prop.jpg)

- As Br<sub>2</sub> approaches the electron-rich C=C double bond in propene, the Br<sub>2</sub> molecule is polarised: the nearer Br atom develops a δ+ charge and acts as an electrophile.
- The π electrons from the C=C double bond attack the δ+ Br atom, and the Br–Br bond breaks heterolytically.
- A Br atom becomes attached to each carbon.
- Therefore, it is an electrophilic addition reaction.

![Curly arrow mechanism showing electrophilic addition of bromine to propene, forming 1,2-dibromopropane](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-2-alkenes/assets/006-curly-arrow-mechanism-showing-electrophilic-addi.jpg)

**B** is incorrect as electrophilic substitution involves an electrophile replacing an existing atom or group. No atoms are replaced here.

**C** is incorrect as nucleophilic addition involves a nucleophile attacking an electrophilic carbon. Br<sub>2</sub> acts as an electrophile, not a nucleophile.

**D** is incorrect as nucleophilic substitution involves a nucleophile replacing a leaving group. There is no leaving group in this reaction.

parts.problemMd:
A molecule of a polymer contained the sequence shown.

![Structural formula of a linear hydrocarbon chain with alternating hydrogen and chlorine atoms bonded to carbon atoms along the backbone](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-2-alkenes/assets/008-structural-formula-of-a-linear-hydrocarbon-chain.jpg)

Which monomer could produce this polymer by addition polymerisation?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

1. Identify the monomers in the displayed diagram

![Polymer chain with each repeating monomer unit highlighted to show the two-carbon, one-chlorine repeating structure](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-2-alkenes/assets/009-polymer-chain-with-each-repeating-monomer-unit-h.jpg)

2. Break the bond between these monomers

![Polymer chain with the single bond between adjacent repeating units broken to show individual monomer units](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-2-alkenes/assets/010-polymer-chain-with-the-single-bond-between-adjac.jpg)

3. Add in the double bond between the carbon atoms

![Monomer unit with C=C double bond re-introduced between the two backbone carbon atoms](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-2-alkenes/assets/011-monomer-unit-with-c-c-double-bond-re-introduced-.jpg)

4. Convert the structural formula to the condensed formula

![Condensed structural formula of chloroethene CH2=CHCl, the monomer for this polymer](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-2-alkenes/assets/012-condensed-structural-formula-of-chloroethene-ch2.jpg)

**B** is incorrect as CHCl=CHCl (1,2-dichloroethene) would produce a polymer in which every backbone carbon carries a Cl atom, giving two Cl atoms per repeating unit. This is inconsistent with the structure shown.

**C** is incorrect as CH<sub>3</sub>CCl=CH<sub>2</sub> is a three-carbon monomer. Polymerisation would give a three-carbon backbone repeating unit, not a two-carbon one.

**D** is incorrect as CH<sub>3</sub>CCl=CHCl is also a three-carbon monomer. Polymerisation would give a three-carbon backbone with two Cl atoms per repeating unit.
