choices.textMd: Both products can be hydrolysed to form the same organic compound.

choices.label: D
choices.textMd: Both products can form hydrogen bonds with water.

parts.problemMd:
Ethene reacts with aqueous bromine to give two products, CH<sub>2</sub>BrCH<sub>2</sub>Br and CH<sub>2</sub>BrCH<sub>2</sub>OH.

Which statement about these products is correct?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Bromine is an electrophile (electron-accepting species) and reacts with ethene via electrophilic addition.

![Mechanism of electrophilic addition of bromine to ethene, showing formation of both 1,2-dibromoethane and 2-bromoethanol](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-2-alkenes/assets/003-mechanism-of-electrophilic-addition-of-bromine-t.jpg)

- Both products, CH<sub>2</sub>BrCH<sub>2</sub>Br (1,2-dibromoethane) and CH<sub>2</sub>BrCH<sub>2</sub>OH (2-bromoethanol), can be hydrolysed using hot aqueous NaOH to give the same organic compound, ethane-1,2-diol.

![Equations showing hydrolysis of 1,2-dibromoethane and 2-bromoethanol both giving ethane-1,2-diol](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-2-alkenes/assets/004-equations-showing-hydrolysis-of-1-2-dibromoethan.jpg)

**A** and **B** are incorrect as both products are formed by electrophilic addition, not electrophilic substitution or nucleophilic addition.

**D** is incorrect as 1,2-dibromoethane (CH<sub>2</sub>BrCH<sub>2</sub>Br) has no N–H, O–H, or F–H bonds, so it cannot form hydrogen bonds with water. Only 2-bromoethanol (CH<sub>2</sub>BrCH<sub>2</sub>OH) can form hydrogen bonds via its –OH group.

parts.problemMd:
Pent-2-ene, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH=CHCH<sub>3</sub>, reacts in a similar way to ethene.

Pent-2-ene is reacted with cold, dilute, acidified manganate (VII) ions.

What will be produced in the greatest amount?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- When ethene reacts with cold, dilute, acidified manganate(VII) ions, ethane-1,2-diol is produced.

![Equation showing ethene reacting with cold dilute acidified KMnO4 to form ethane-1,2-diol](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-2-alkenes/assets/021-equation-showing-ethene-reacting-with-cold-dilut.jpg)

- In a similar way, pent-2-ene reacts with cold, dilute, acidified manganate(VII) ions to form pentan-2,3-diol:

CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH=CHCH<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O + [O] → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(OH)CH(OH)CH<sub>3</sub>

**B** is incorrect as CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COCOCH<sub>3</sub> (pentane-2,3-dione) cannot be synthesised from pent-2-ene by mild oxidation with cold, dilute manganate(VII) ions.

**C** is incorrect as CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> (pentan-3-ol) and CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>3</sub> (pentan-2-ol) are the products of hydration of pent-2-ene, not mild oxidation with manganate(VII) ions.

**D** is incorrect as CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOH (propanoic acid) and CH<sub>3</sub>COOH (ethanoic acid) are produced only by oxidative cleavage using hot, concentrated, acidified manganate(VII) ions.

parts.problemMd:
Isomers **X** and **Y** both react with HBr.

![Structural formulae of isomers X and Y, both containing C=C double bonds that react with HBr by electrophilic addition](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-2-alkenes/assets/019-structural-formulae-of-isomers-x-and-y-both-cont.jpg)

A mixture of **X** and **Y** is reacted with HBr.

Which three structures represent three **different** possible products of this reaction?

| **A** | (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCBr<sub>3</sub> | (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CBrCHBr<sub>2</sub> | CH<sub>3</sub>CHBrCHBrCH<sub>3</sub> |
|---|---|---|---|
| **B** | (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCBr<sub>3</sub> | (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CBrCHBr<sub>2</sub> | CH<sub>3</sub>CBr<sub>2</sub>CHBrCH<sub>3</sub> |
| **C** | (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CBrCBr<sub>3</sub> | (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCBr<sub>3</sub> | CH<sub>3</sub>CBr<sub>2</sub>CHBrCH<sub>3</sub> |
| **D** | (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CBrCHBr<sub>2</sub> | CHBr<sub>2</sub>CBr(CH<sub>3</sub>)CH<sub>3</sub> | CH<sub>3</sub>CHBrCBr<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- In the electrophilic addition of HBr to an alkene, the H end of HBr acts as the electrophile.

  - The δ+ H is attracted to the electron-rich C=C double bond.
- H adds to one carbon and Br adds to the other, breaking the C=C double bond.
- Drawing out the structural formula of each product from X and Y is the clearest approach:

![Structural formulae showing all possible products from electrophilic addition of HBr to isomers X and Y](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-2-alkenes/assets/020-structural-formulae-showing-all-possible-product.jpg)

- The three different products from the reaction of HBr with isomers **X** and **Y** are:

  1. (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCBr<sub>3</sub>
  2. (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CBrCHBr<sub>2</sub>
  3. CH<sub>3</sub>CBr<sub>2</sub>CHBrCH<sub>3</sub>

**A** is incorrect as the third product listed (CH<sub>3</sub>CHBrCHBrCH<sub>3</sub>) is not formed from this reaction. This product would arise from addition of Br<sub>2</sub>, not HBr.

**C** is incorrect as the first product listed ((CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CBrCBr<sub>3</sub>) is not formed; HBr addition to these isomers cannot produce a CBr<sub>3</sub> group at that position.

**D** is incorrect as none of the three products in that row correctly reflects the regiochemistry of HBr addition to isomers X and Y.

parts.problemMd:
What is the major product formed when compound Q is warmed with excess HBr?

![Structural formula of compound Q, an organic molecule containing a C=C double bond and one or more hydroxyl groups](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-2-alkenes/assets/027-structural-formula-of-compound-q-an-organic-mole.jpg)
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Each –OH group in compound Q reacts with HBr to undergo nucleophilic substitution, replacing –OH with Br.
- The C=C double bond also reacts with HBr by electrophilic addition, adding H to one carbon and Br to the other.
- With excess HBr, both types of reaction proceed fully, giving the product shown in option **C**.

**A** is incorrect as it does not show complete substitution of all –OH groups or full addition across the C=C double bond.

**B** is incorrect as it shows an incorrect or incomplete transformation of compound Q with excess HBr.

**D** is incorrect as it shows incorrect regiochemistry or an incomplete reaction with excess HBr.

parts.problemMd:
The oxidative cleavage of an alkene using hot, concentrated, acidified potassium manganate(VII) results in the complete rupture of the carbon–carbon double bond.

Which row correctly identifies the final products formed from the specified structural groups?

|   | Structural group in alkene | Final products formed |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | R–CH=CH–R′ | Two different aldehydes |
| **B** | CH₂=C(R)₂ | Carbon dioxide and a ketone |
| **C** | R–CH=CH₂ | A carboxylic acid and methanoic acid |
| **D** | R–CH=C(R)₂ | A carboxylic acid and an alcohol |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Hot, concentrated, acidified KMnO<sub>4</sub> causes oxidative cleavage, meaning the C=C bond breaks and each carbon is oxidised as far as possible.
- In CH<sub>2</sub>=C(R)<sub>2</sub>, the CH<sub>2</sub> end is terminal, so it is fully oxidised to CO<sub>2</sub> (and H<sub>2</sub>O).
- The other carbon is disubstituted (no H attached to that double-bond carbon), so it forms a ketone, which is not oxidised further under these conditions.
- Therefore, the final products are carbon dioxide and a ketone.

**A** is incorrect because R–CH=CH–R’ gives two monosubstituted alkene carbons. Each –CH= fragment is oxidised to a carboxylic acid, not an aldehyde as aldehydes are intermediate products that are further oxidised.

**C** is incorrect because the terminal =CH<sub>2</sub> end in R–CH=CH<sub>2</sub> is fully oxidised to CO<sub>2</sub> (and H<sub>2</sub>O), not methanoic acid.

**D** is incorrect because oxidative cleavage produces carbonyl compounds (carboxylic acids or ketones), not alcohols.

parts.problemMd:
A polymer has the repeating unit

![Chemical structure of polyisobutylene, showing a repeating unit with a methyl group branch on a carbon chain.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-2-alkenes/assets/001-chemical-structure-of-polyisobutylene-showing-a-.png)

Which monomer would produce this polymer by addition polymerisation?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- The repeating unit shows a two-carbon backbone, indicating addition polymerisation of an alkene.
- One backbone carbon has one H atom and one CH<sub>3</sub> group; the other has two H atoms.
- This corresponds to propene, CH<sub>2</sub>=CH–CH<sub>3</sub>, which gives the repeating unit –[–CH<sub>2</sub>–CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)–]–.

**A** is incorrect as ethene would produce a –[–CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>–]– backbone with no CH<sub>3</sub> side groups.

**C** is incorrect as butane is a saturated alkane and cannot undergo addition polymerisation.

**D** is incorrect as but-2-ene would give a repeating unit in which both backbone carbons carry a CH<sub>3</sub> group, not just one.

parts.problemMd:
Limonene is an oil formed in the peel of citrus fruits.

![Structural formula of limonene, a cyclic terpene containing a six-membered ring with one endocyclic C=C double bond and an isopropenyl side chain containing a second C=C double bond](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-2-alkenes/assets/013-structural-formula-of-limonene-a-cyclic-terpene-.png)

Which product is formed when an excess of bromine, Br<sub>2</sub> (l), reacts with limonene at room temperature in the dark?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Limonene contains two C=C double bonds

  - One in the six-membered ring
  - One in the isopropenyl side chain.
- The reaction is carried out at room temperature in the dark.

  - In the dark, only electrophilic addition occurs.
  - UV light would initiate free-radical substitution instead.
- When reacted with excess Br<sub>2</sub>, electrophilic addition occurs across both double bonds.
- Each double bond reacts with one molecule of Br<sub>2</sub>, adding two Br atoms across each bond, giving four Br atoms in total.

![Structural diagram showing electrophilic addition of excess bromine to both double bonds in limonene, producing a tetrabromo product](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-2-alkenes/assets/014-structural-diagram-showing-electrophilic-additio.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as it shows bromine added across only one of the two double bonds. Excess Br<sub>2</sub> ensures both double bonds react fully.

**B** is incorrect as it shows an incomplete or incorrect bromination product of limonene.

**C** is incorrect as it shows addition to only one double bond or addition in the wrong positions.

parts.problemMd: Which isomer of C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>13</sub>OH gives the greatest number of different alkenes when it is dehydrated?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Alcohols can be dehydrated to form alkenes by losing a water molecule across adjacent carbons to form a C=C double bond.
- CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> (hexan-3-ol) can lose H from either C2 or C4, giving two constitutional isomers, each with E/Z stereoisomers:

  - hex-2-ene: (E)-hex-2-ene and (Z)-hex-2-ene
  - hex-3-ene: (E)-hex-3-ene and (Z)-hex-3-ene
- That gives 4 different alkenes in total (more than any other option).

![Structural formulae of the four alkenes formed by dehydration of hexan-3-ol, showing both constitutional isomers and their E/Z stereoisomers](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-2-alkenes/assets/002-structural-formulae-of-the-four-alkenes-formed-b.jpg)

**A** and **D** are incorrect as these are primary alcohols. Elimination can only occur in one direction, giving fewer alkene isomers than a secondary alcohol.

**C** is incorrect as CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>C(CH<sub>3</sub>)(OH)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> (3-methylpentan-3-ol) gives 3 different alkenes on dehydration: (E)-3-methylpent-2-ene, (Z)-3-methylpent-2-ene and 2-ethylbut-1-ene, which is fewer than the 4 from option **B**.

choices.label: A
choices.textMd: Both bond angles x and y are approximately 120°.

choices.label: C
choices.textMd: It gives an orange precipitate with 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine reagent.

choices.label: D
choices.textMd: It reacts with an alcohol to give an ester.

parts.problemMd:
Acrylic acid is produced from propene, a gaseous product of oil refineries.

![Structural formula of acrylic acid (prop-2-enoic acid, CH2=CHCOOH), with bond angles x and y labelled at the sp2 carbon atoms](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-2-alkenes/assets/007-structural-formula-of-acrylic-acid-prop-2-enoic-.jpg)

Which statement about acrylic acid is **not** correct?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- 2,4-Dinitrophenylhydrazine (2,4-DNPH) reacts with the C=O bond in aldehydes and ketones to give an orange precipitate.
- Although acrylic acid contains a C=O bond (as part of the –COOH group), 2,4-DNPH does not react with carboxylic acids.
- Therefore, acrylic acid does not produce an orange precipitate with 2,4-DNPH.

**A** is incorrect as each sp<sup>2</sup> carbon in acrylic acid has 3 bonding groups and no lone pairs, giving bond angles x and y of approximately 120°.

**B** is incorrect as acrylic acid contains a C=C double bond, which undergoes electrophilic addition with aqueous bromine and decolourises it.

**D** is incorrect as acrylic acid is a carboxylic acid, which reacts with alcohols in an esterification reaction to form an ester.

parts.problemMd: Which compound has an *M*<sub>r</sub> of 84 and will react with HBr to give a product with an *M*<sub>r</sub> of 164.9?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- HBr undergoes electrophilic addition with alkenes only: H adds to one carbon and Br adds to the other across the C=C double bond. Only alkenes react with HBr, so only **B** and **D** are candidates.
- Check compound **D** (hex-3-ene, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>):
- Calculate the *M*<sub>r</sub> of hex-3-ene:

*M*<sub>r</sub> = (6 x 12) + (12 x 1)

*M*<sub>r</sub> = 72 + 12

*M*<sub>r</sub> = 84

- In electrophilic addition, HBr adds across the C=C bond. The *M*<sub>r</sub> of the product equals *M*<sub>r</sub>(alkene) + *M*<sub>r</sub>(HBr):

*M*<sub>r</sub>(product) = 84 + 80.9

*M*<sub>r</sub>(product) = 164.9

- Both conditions are satisfied, confirming compound **D**.

![Structural diagram confirming hex-3-ene reacting with HBr to form 3-bromohexane with the correct molecular masses](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-2-alkenes/assets/022-structural-diagram-confirming-hex-3-ene-reacting.jpg)

**A** and **C** are incorrect as these compounds are not alkenes and do not react with HBr by electrophilic addition.

**B** is incorrect as although it is an alkene with *M*<sub>r</sub> = 84, its product with HBr does not have *M*<sub>r</sub> = 164.9.

parts.problemMd:
Alkane **X** has molecular formula C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>.

**X** reacts with Cl<sub>2</sub> (g) in the presence of ultraviolet light to produce only two different monochloroalkanes, C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9</sub>Cl. Both of these monochloroalkanes produce the same alkene **Y**, and no other organic products, when they are treated with hot ethanolic KOH.

What is produced when **Y** is treated with hot concentrated acidified KMnO<sub>4</sub>?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Alkane **X** (C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>) must be branched for two different monochloroalkanes to both give the same alkene on dehydrohalogenation.

  - Alkane **X** is therefore 2-methylpropane, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>CH.
- Free radical substitution of 2-methylpropane with Cl<sub>2</sub> in sunlight gives 1-chloro-2-methylpropane and 2-chloro-2-methylpropane.
- Both undergo dehydrohalogenation with hot ethanolic KOH to give the same alkene, **Y** = 2-methylprop-1-ene (CH<sub>2</sub>=C(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>).

![Structural diagram showing pathways from 2-methylpropane through both monochloroalkanes to 2-methylprop-1-ene, then oxidative cleavage products](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-2-alkenes/assets/028-structural-diagram-showing-pathways-from-2-methy.jpg)

- Hot concentrated acidified KMnO<sub>4</sub> cleaves the C=C bond by vigorous oxidation:

  - The terminal =CH<sub>2</sub> end is fully oxidised to CO<sub>2</sub> (and H<sub>2</sub>O).
  - The C(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> end is disubstituted (no H on that carbon) and forms a ketone: CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>3</sub> (propanone).

**A** is incorrect as propanoic acid (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H) would require a –CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> fragment on the double bond, which is not present in 2-methylprop-1-ene.

**C** is incorrect as methanoic acid (HCO<sub>2</sub>H) comes from a –CH= fragment. The terminal =CH<sub>2</sub> in 2-methylprop-1-ene is fully oxidised to CO<sub>2</sub>, not methanoic acid.

**D** is incorrect as ethanoic acid (CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H) alone would result from oxidative cleavage of a symmetric alkene such as but-2-ene, not 2-methylprop-1-ene.

choices.label: B
choices.textMd: Polymerise ethene followed by oxidation with cold acidified KMnO<sub>4</sub>.

choices.label: D
choices.textMd: Polymerise 1,2-dichloroethene followed by oxidation with cold acidified KMnO<sub>4</sub>.

parts.problemMd:
The following diagram represents the structure of a possible polymer.

![Structural diagram of a polymer repeating unit in which each backbone carbon atom carries a hydroxyl group](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-2-alkenes/assets/029-structural-diagram-of-a-polymer-repeating-unit-i.jpg)

Which sequence of reactions could be used to produce this polymer?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

1. Draw the monomer structural formula

![Structural formula of 1,2-dichloroethene (CHCl=CHCl), the monomer](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-2-alkenes/assets/030-structural-formula-of-1-2-dichloroethene-chcl-ch.jpg)

2. Break the C=C double bond to form the polymer backbone unit

![Polymer repeating unit from 1,2-dichloroethene, with each backbone carbon bonded to one Cl](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-2-alkenes/assets/031-polymer-repeating-unit-from-1-2-dichloroethene-w.jpg)

3. Replace each –Cl with –OH by hydrolysis

![Polymer repeating unit after hydrolysis, showing both Cl groups replaced by OH groups](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-2-alkenes/assets/032-polymer-repeating-unit-after-hydrolysis-showing-.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as polymerising ethene gives a saturated poly(ethene) backbone with no substituents. Hydrating a saturated polymer does not introduce –OH groups along the chain.

**B** and **D** are incorrect as oxidation with cold acidified KMnO<sub>4</sub> converts C=C double bonds into diol groups. Once polymerised, the backbone is saturated and has no C=C bonds to oxidise. In option **D**, the –Cl groups in poly(1,2-dichloroethene) cannot be replaced by cold KMnO<sub>4</sub> oxidation because hydrolysis is the correct method.

parts.problemMd:
Oxidation of an alkene **Y** gives a diol; further oxidation gives a diketone.

What could be **Y**?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Mild oxidation with cold dilute KMnO<sub>4</sub> converts the C=C double bond into a diol, adding an –OH group to each alkene carbon.
- For the diol to undergo further oxidation to a diketone, both –OH groups must be secondary, i.e. each carbon bearing –OH must also carry at least one H atom.

  - A secondary alcohol oxidises to a ketone.
  - A tertiary alcohol (no H on that carbon) cannot be oxidised further.
- In option **C** (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH=CHC<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>), each alkene carbon carries one H and one C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub> group. After diol formation, both –OH groups are secondary and are oxidised to C=O, giving a diketone.

![Structural diagram showing the oxidation of C6H5CH=CHC6H5 first to the diol then to the diketone product](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-2-alkenes/assets/015-structural-diagram-showing-the-oxidation-of-c6h5.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as CH<sub>3</sub>CH=C(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> gives a diol in which the right-hand C bears no H atoms (tertiary). This –OH group cannot be oxidised further, so a diketone cannot form.

![Structural diagram showing the diol from CH3CH=C(CH3)2, with the tertiary C-OH group that cannot be further oxidised](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-2-alkenes/assets/016-structural-diagram-showing-the-diol-from-ch3ch-c.jpg)

**B** is incorrect as (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCH=CH<sub>2</sub> gives a diol in which the terminal C has a primary –OH group. A primary alcohol oxidises to a carboxylic acid, not a ketone, so a diketone is not formed.

![Structural diagram showing the diol from (CH3)2CHCH=CH2, with the primary C-OH group highlighted](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-2-alkenes/assets/017-structural-diagram-showing-the-diol-from-ch3-2ch.jpg)

**D** is incorrect as (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C=CHCH<sub>3</sub> gives a diol in which the left-hand C carries two C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub> groups and no H atoms (tertiary). This –OH group cannot be further oxidised.

![Structural diagram showing the diol from (C6H5)2C=CHCH3, with the tertiary C-OH group that cannot be further oxidised](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-2-alkenes/assets/018-structural-diagram-showing-the-diol-from-c6h5-2c.jpg)

parts.problemMd:
Ethene is prepared by adding ethanol dropwise to heated reagent **Y**. To purify the ethene, it is bubbled through solution **Z** and then collected.

Which row identifies reagent **Y** and solution **Z**?

|   | **Reagent Y** | **Solution Z** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | Acidified K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> | Dilute NaOH |
| **B** | Concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> | Dilute H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> |
| **C** | Concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> | Dilute NaOH |
| **D** | Ethanolic NaOH | Concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Ethanol undergoes dehydration to form ethene.

  - Concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (heated) is the correct reagent for this reaction, eliminating options **A** and **D**.
- The ethene produced contains acidic impurities, principally SO<sub>2</sub> formed by oxidation of ethanol by hot concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>.

  - These must be removed before the gas is collected.
- In option **C**, passing the gas through dilute NaOH neutralises the acidic SO<sub>2</sub> impurity, giving purified ethene.

**A** is incorrect as acidified K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> oxidises ethanol to ethanal rather than dehydrating it to ethene.

**B** is incorrect as passing the gas through dilute H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> adds more acid rather than removing it.

**D** is incorrect as ethanolic NaOH promotes elimination of HX from haloalkanes, not dehydration of alcohols.

parts.problemMd: Explain why alkanes are generally unreactive.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Alkanes are generally unreactive because:
> 
> - The C–H and C–C bonds have high bond enthalpies / bond strengths **[1 mark]**
> - The C–H bonds are non-polar / have very low polarity **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The two marking points are the strength of the bonds and their lack of polarity.
> 
> The C–H bond has a bond enthalpy of 411 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> and the C–C bond has a bond enthalpy of 346 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>. These high values mean a large amount of energy is needed to break them.
> 
> Carbon and hydrogen have very similar electronegativities, so C–H bonds have very low polarity. There is no significant dipole to attract ionic reagents or nucleophiles.

parts.problemMd:
Methane reacts with chlorine to produce chloromethane, CH<sub>3</sub>Cl. The reaction is initiated by the formation of chlorine free radicals.

i) Explain what is meant by the term *free radical*.

[1]

ii) State the condition required to form chlorine free radicals from Cl<sub>2</sub>.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) A free radical is:
> 
> - A species with an unpaired electron **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The condition required to form chlorine free radicals from Cl<sub>2</sub> is:
> 
> - Ultraviolet / UV light **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A free radical is represented as X<sup>•</sup>, where the dot indicates the unpaired electron.
> 
> In CIE A Level Chemistry, always use the full term "free radical" rather than just "radical".

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Methane reacts with chlorine to produce chloromethane, CH~3~Cl. The reaction is initiated by the formation of chlorine free radicals.

Name the type of bond fission that occurs in the initiation step.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The type of bond fission in the initiation step is:
> 
> - Homolytic fission **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> In homolytic fission, the covalent bond breaks symmetrically: each atom receives one electron from the shared pair, forming two radicals. This is shown by single-headed (fish-hook) curly arrows in mechanism diagrams.
> 
> ![Diagram showing homolytic fission of Cl2 producing two chlorine radicals](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-1-alkanes/assets/002-diagram-showing-homolytic-fission-of-cl2-produci.png)
> 
> Compare with heterolytic fission, where both electrons go to one atom, forming a positive ion and a negative ion. Alkanes undergo homolytic fission with halogens because the Cl–Cl bond breaks equally due to the identical electronegativities of the two atoms.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Methane reacts with chlorine to produce chloromethane, CH~3~Cl. The reaction is initiated by the formation of chlorine free radicals.

i) Construct two equations to show the propagation steps in this mechanism.

[2]

ii) Ethane is produced as a by-product in this reaction.

Construct an equation for the termination step that forms ethane.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The two propagation steps are:
> 
> - Cl<sup>•</sup> + CH<sub>4</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub><sup>•</sup> + HCl **[1 mark]**
> - CH<sub>3</sub><sup>•</sup> + Cl<sub>2</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>Cl + Cl<sup>•</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are not required.
> 
> ii) The termination step that forms ethane is:
> 
> - CH<sub>3</sub><sup>•</sup> + CH<sub>3</sub><sup>•</sup> → C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub> / CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are not required.

> **[exam-tip]**
> In each propagation step, a free radical reacts with a molecule to generate a new free radical. The chlorine radical consumed in step 1 is regenerated in step 2, keeping the chain reaction going.
> 
> Ethane forms in a termination step, where two methyl radicals combine. This illustrates a key limitation of free radical substitution: unwanted by-products are produced alongside the desired product.
> 
> Other valid termination steps are:
> 
> Cl<sup>•</sup> + Cl<sup>•</sup> → Cl<sub>2</sub>
> 
> Cl<sup>•</sup> + CH<sub>3</sub><sup>•</sup> → CH<sub>3</sub>Cl.

parts.problemMd:
Describe the difference in conditions between the complete and incomplete combustion of octane.

Construct one equation for the complete combustion and one equation for the incomplete combustion of octane.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The difference in conditions and equations are:
> 
> - Complete combustion occurs with an excess / plentiful supply of oxygen
> **AND**
> Incomplete combustion occurs with a limited / insufficient supply of oxygen **[1 mark]**
> - C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub> + 12.5O<sub>2</sub> → 8CO<sub>2</sub> + 9H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**
> - C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub> + 8.5O<sub>2</sub> → 8CO + 9H<sub>2</sub>O
> **OR**
> C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub> + 4.5O<sub>2</sub> → 8C + 9H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**
> 
> Fractional coefficients are accepted.
> 
> Allow doubled coefficients (e.g. 2C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub> + 25O<sub>2</sub> → 16CO<sub>2</sub> + 18H<sub>2</sub>O for complete combustion).

> **[exam-tip]**
> The key difference between complete and incomplete combustion is the oxygen supply. Complete combustion requires excess oxygen and produces only carbon dioxide and water. Incomplete combustion occurs when oxygen is limited and produces carbon monoxide (and/or carbon) and water.
> 
> To balance the complete combustion equation for octane (C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub>): balance C first (8CO<sub>2</sub>), then H (9H<sub>2</sub>O), then O (12.5O<sub>2</sub>). Fractional coefficients are acceptable in CIE exams, or you can double all coefficients to give whole numbers.

parts.problemMd:
Carbon monoxide is an atmospheric pollutant produced in the internal combustion engines of motor vehicles.

i) State one adverse effect of carbon monoxide on human health.

[1]

ii) Identify one other pollutant produced in internal combustion engines. State the environmental consequence of this pollutant.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) One adverse effect of carbon monoxide on human health is:
> 
> Any **one** from:
> 
> - It is toxic / poisonous
> - It binds irreversibly to haemoglobin, reducing the blood's ability to carry oxygen
> - It prevents oxygen being delivered to cells / organs
> - It forms carboxyhaemoglobin instead of oxyhaemoglobin
> 
> **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) A pollutant and its environmental consequence:
> 
> Any **one** of the following (1 mark for each point):
> 
> Set 1
> 
> - Pollutant: oxides of nitrogen / NO<sub>x</sub> / nitrogen monoxide / nitrogen dioxide
> - Consequence: reacts with water to form nitric acid / causes acid rain
> **OR**
> Reacts with unburnt hydrocarbons to form photochemical smog / peroxyacetyl nitrate (PAN)
> 
> **OR**
> 
> Set 2
> 
> - Pollutant: unburnt hydrocarbons / volatile organic compounds / VOCs
> - Consequence: reacts with oxides of nitrogen to form photochemical smog / peroxyacetyl nitrate (PAN)
> 
> **[2 marks]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Carbon monoxide is toxic because it binds to haemoglobin more strongly than oxygen. This prevents oxygen from being transported to cells.
> 
> For part ii), you need to name a specific pollutant AND give its environmental consequence. The two main pollutants tested at CIE A Level are oxides of nitrogen and unburnt hydrocarbons. One mark is for correctly identifying the pollutant, one mark is for stating its environmental consequence.

parts.problemMd:
Octane can be cracked to form pentane and one other product.

i) Construct an equation for this reaction.

[1]

ii) State the reagent and conditions required for this cracking reaction.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The equation for the reaction is:
> 
> - C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub> → C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub> + C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub> **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The reagent and conditions required are:
> 
> - Reagent: aluminium oxide / Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> / zeolite / aluminosilicate **[1 mark]**
> - Conditions: high temperature **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are not required.

> **[exam-tip]**
> For the cracking equation, balance carbon and hydrogen atoms on both sides.
> 
> - Octane (C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub>) → pentane (C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub>) + propene (C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>).
> - Check:
> 
>   - 8C = 5 + 3 ✓
>   - 18H = 12 + 6 ✓
> 
> For the conditions, "heat" alone is not sufficient, you must specify "high temperature".

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Octane can be cracked to form pentane and one other product.

i) Construct an equation for this reaction.

The equation for the reaction is:

C~8~H~18~ → C~5~H~12~ + C~3~H~6~

Describe a chemical test and the expected observations to distinguish between the two organic products formed in (c).
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> A chemical test to distinguish between pentane and propene:
> 
> - Add aqueous bromine / bromine water / Br<sub>2</sub> (aq) **[1 mark]**
> - Pentane / C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub>: the bromine water remains orange / no change **[1 mark]**
> - Propene / C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>: the bromine water turns colourless / decolourises **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> This test works because propene (an alkene) contains a C=C double bond, which reacts with bromine by electrophilic addition. Bromine is used up, so the orange colour disappears.
> 
> Pentane (an alkane) does not react with bromine water under these conditions, so the orange colour remains.
> 
> You need to state the reagent clearly (bromine water, not just "bromine") and give distinct observations for both products to score all three marks.

parts.problemMd:
A reaction scheme involving cyclohexane is shown in Fig. 1.1.

![Reaction scheme: cyclohexane converted by reaction 1 to chlorocyclohexane, then by reaction 2 to cyclohexene with a double bond in the ring](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-1-alkanes/assets/003-reaction-scheme-cyclohexane-converted-by-reactio.png)

**Fig. 1.1.**

Reaction **1** involves a free radical substitution mechanism.

State the essential condition required for reaction **1** to occur.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The essential condition required for reaction **1** to occur is:
> 
> - Ultraviolet / UV light **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Reaction **1** is a free-radical substitution. UV light provides the energy needed to break the Cl–Cl bond homolytically, generating two chlorine radicals that initiate the chain reaction.
> 
> Without UV light, the Cl–Cl bond cannot break, so no free radicals form and the reaction does not proceed. Alkanes are too unreactive to react with Cl<sub>2</sub> in the dark.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Reaction 1 involves a free radical substitution mechanism.

Complete Table 1.1 to give details of the mechanism in reaction **1**. Include curly arrows to show the movement of electrons occurring in the termination step.

**Table 1.1**

![Incomplete table showing free radical chlorination of cyclohexane, with initiation, propagation and termination steps containing incomplete equations](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-1-alkanes/assets/004-incomplete-table-showing-free-radical-chlorinati.png)
parts.solutionMd:
The completed Table 1.1 is:

![Completed table showing initiation, propagation, and termination steps for the free-radical substitution of cyclohexane with chlorine](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-1-alkanes/assets/005-completed-table-showing-initiation-propagation-a.png)

**[5 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for naming the initiation step
> 
> 1 mark for HCl as a product in the first propagation step
> 
> 1 mark for naming the propagation step
> 
> 1 mark for correct species in the termination step
> 
> 1 mark for correct single-headed (fish-hook) curly arrows in the termination step

> **[exam-tip]**
> Free-radical substitution has three stages. Make sure you know the names and equations for each:
> 
> - Initiation: Cl<sub>2</sub> → 2Cl<sup>•</sup> (one molecule gives two radicals)
> - Propagation (two steps): radicals react with molecules to produce new radicals, keeping the chain going
> - Termination: two radicals combine to give a molecule (the chain ends)
> 
> For the curly arrows in the termination step, use single-headed (fish-hook) arrows to show movement of single electrons. These are different from the double-headed arrows used in ionic mechanisms.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A reaction scheme involving cyclohexane is shown in Fig. 1.1.

Reaction scheme: cyclohexane converted by reaction 1 to chlorocyclohexane, then by reaction 2 to cyclohexene with a double bond in the ring

Deduce the type of reaction that occurs in reaction **2.**
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The type of reaction that occurs in reaction **2** is:
> 
> - Elimination **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> In reaction **2**, chlorocyclohexane loses HCl to form cyclohexene. The removal of a small molecule (HCl) from adjacent carbon atoms to form a C=C double bond is called elimination.
> 
> The conditions for this reaction are heat with ethanolic sodium hydroxide (NaOH in ethanol). Compare this with aqueous NaOH, which gives nucleophilic substitution to form cyclohexanol instead.

parts.problemMd:
Hex-3-ene is an isomer of cyclohexane. Hex-3-ene can be converted into propanoic acid.

hex-3-ene $\overset{\mathrm{reaction}3}{\rightarrow}$ propanoic acid

Deduce the reagents and conditions for reaction **3.**
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The reagents and conditions for reaction **3** are:
> 
> - Reagent: potassium manganate(VII) / KMnO<sub>4</sub>
> **AND**
> Acid / acidified / acidic conditions **[1 mark]**
> - Conditions: hot
> **AND**
> Concentrated **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Reaction **3** is an oxidative cleavage of the C=C double bond in hex-3-ene to form propanoic acid. This requires hot, concentrated acidified KMnO<sub>4</sub>.
> 
> Be careful with the conditions. Cold, dilute KMnO<sub>4</sub> opens the double bond to form a diol rather than cleaving it to form carboxylic acids.
> 
> Hex-3-ene is a symmetrical internal alkene, so oxidative cleavage produces two identical molecules of propanoic acid.

parts.problemMd:
i) Explain what is meant by the term *cracking*.

[1]

ii) Suggest why cracking is a useful process in the petroleum industry.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) Cracking is:
> 
> - The breaking down of large hydrocarbon molecules into smaller, more useful ones **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) Cracking is useful in the petroleum industry because:
> 
> - Smaller hydrocarbons are more useful / in greater demand (as fuels and chemical feedstocks)
> **OR**
> Alkenes produced can be used to make polymers / other useful chemicals **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Crude oil contains a large proportion of long-chain hydrocarbons, which are less in demand. Cracking breaks these down into shorter-chain alkanes (useful as fuels) and alkenes (useful for making plastics and other chemicals).
> 
> "Cracking" specifically means the decomposition of long-chain hydrocarbons into shorter chains. Do not describe it simply as "breaking bonds". The answer must make clear that large molecules are converted into smaller, more useful ones.

parts.problemMd:
i) State the reagent and conditions required for the cracking of alkanes.

[2]

ii) Construct an equation for the cracking of tetradecane, C<sub>14</sub>H<sub>30</sub>, to form heptane, C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>16</sub>, and two other organic products.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The reagent and conditions required are:
> 
> - Reagent: aluminium oxide / Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> / zeolite / aluminosilicate **[1 mark]**
> - Conditions: high temperature **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) An equation for the cracking of tetradecane to form heptane and two other products:
> 
> - C<sub>14</sub>H<sub>30</sub> → C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>16</sub> + C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub> + C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>
> **OR**
> C<sub>14</sub>H<sub>30</sub> → C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>16</sub> + C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub> + C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>
> **OR**
> C<sub>14</sub>H<sub>30</sub> → C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>16</sub> + 2C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub> + C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub> **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are not required.
> 
> The equation must show exactly two other organic products in addition to heptane.
> 
> The equation C<sub>14</sub>H<sub>30</sub> → C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>16</sub> + C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>14</sub> is not accepted because it gives only one other product.

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part i), be specific. "Heat" alone is not sufficient, you must say "high temperature".
> 
> For part ii), balance the carbon and hydrogen atoms on both sides. Heptane uses 7 of the 14 carbons, so the remaining 7 carbons must be distributed across two other products. Remember that cracking produces a mixture of alkanes and alkenes.

parts.problemMd:
The combustion of octane, C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub>, in internal combustion engines produces a mixture of pollutants, including carbon monoxide, nitrogen monoxide and unburnt hydrocarbons.

i) State one adverse effect of carbon monoxide on human health.

[1]

ii) State one environmental consequence of releasing nitrogen monoxide / oxides of nitrogen into the atmosphere.

[1]

iii) State one environmental consequence of releasing unburnt hydrocarbons into the atmosphere.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) One adverse effect of carbon monoxide on human health is:
> 
> Any **one** from:
> 
> - It is toxic / poisonous
> - It binds irreversibly to haemoglobin, preventing oxygen from being carried in the blood
> - It prevents oxygen being delivered to cells / organs
> 
> **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) One environmental consequence of nitrogen monoxide / oxides of nitrogen is:
> 
> Any **one** from:
> 
> - It causes acid rain (by reacting with water to form nitric acid)
> - It damages / kills aquatic life
> - It causes respiratory problems
> 
> **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) One environmental consequence of unburnt hydrocarbons is:
> 
> Any **one** from:
> 
> - They react with nitrogen oxides in sunlight to form photochemical smog / peroxyacetyl nitrate (PAN)
> - They contribute to global dimming
> 
> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Carbon monoxide is toxic because it binds to haemoglobin more strongly than oxygen, preventing oxygen transport to cells.
> 
> Oxides of nitrogen react with water in the atmosphere to form nitric acid, which contributes to acid rain. This damages ecosystems, particularly lakes and rivers.
> 
> Unburnt hydrocarbons react with nitrogen oxides in sunlight to produce photochemical smog, a complex mixture of pollutants including peroxyacetyl nitrate (PAN), which is harmful to human health and vegetation.

parts.problemMd: Construct an equation to demonstrate how a catalytic converter removes carbon monoxide and nitrogen monoxide from exhaust gases.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The equation for the catalytic converter reaction is:
> 
> - 2CO + 2NO → 2CO<sub>2</sub> + N<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> In a catalytic converter, carbon monoxide is oxidised to carbon dioxide and nitrogen monoxide is reduced to nitrogen. This single reaction removes both pollutants simultaneously.
> 
> The catalyst (typically platinum, palladium, or rhodium) lowers the activation energy for this reaction, allowing it to occur at the relatively low temperatures found in exhaust gases.

parts.problemMd:
Methane reacts with chlorine gas under suitable conditions to form chloromethane.

i) Name the mechanism that occurs in this reaction.

[1]

ii) Two test tubes are set up, each containing a small amount of methane and pale green chlorine gas. One test tube is left in the dark, whereas the other is placed in direct sunlight.

State and explain the observations in each test tube.

[3]

iii) Construct an equation for the overall reaction that occurs in the sunlight.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The mechanism is:
> 
> - Free-radical substitution **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The observations in each test tube are:
> 
> In the dark:
> 
> - No change / the mixture remains pale green **[1 mark]**
> 
> In sunlight:
> 
> - The pale green colour disappears / the mixture becomes colourless
> **OR**
> Misty / steamy fumes of hydrogen chloride (HCl) are produced **[1 mark]**
> 
> Explanation:
> 
> - UV light is required to initiate the reaction / to cause homolytic fission of the Cl–Cl bond **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The equation for the overall reaction in sunlight is:
> 
> - CH<sub>4</sub> + Cl<sub>2</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>Cl + HCl **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Free-radical substitution is a three-stage chain reaction: initiation, propagation, and termination. Only the initiation step requires UV light.
> 
> The pale green colour of the reaction mixture is due to chlorine gas. When UV light causes homolytic fission of the Cl–Cl bond, the reaction proceeds and the chlorine is consumed, so the pale green colour disappears.
> 
> Misty or steamy fumes in the test tube placed in sunlight are hydrogen chloride (HCl) gas produced during the reaction.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Methane reacts with chlorine gas under suitable conditions to form chloromethane.

The mechanism for this reaction involves an initiation step.

i) Name the type of bond breaking that occurs in the initiation step. Explain what happens to the electrons in the bond.

[2]

ii) Explain what is meant by the term *free radical*.

[1]

iii) Suggest why the Cl–Cl bond is broken in the initiation step rather than the C–H bond.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The type of bond breaking is:
> 
> - Homolytic fission **[1 mark]**
> - Each atom in the covalent bond receives one electron when the bond breaks **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) A free radical is:
> 
> - A species with an unpaired electron **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The Cl–Cl bond is broken in preference to the C–H bond because:
> 
> - The C–H bond requires more energy to break than is available from UV light
> **OR**
> UV light does not provide enough energy to break the C–H bond **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Bonds can break in two ways.
> 
> 1. In homolytic fission, the covalent bond splits equally and each atom receives one electron, forming two free radicals.
> 2. In heterolytic fission, the bond splits unequally and one atom receives both electrons, forming a positive ion and a negative ion.
> 
> Free radicals are highly reactive because of their unpaired electron. They can also be called radicals, without the word "free".
> 
> The bond enthalpy of C–H is higher than that of Cl–Cl, so UV light provides sufficient energy to break the Cl–Cl bond but not the C–H bond.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Methane reacts with chlorine gas under suitable conditions to form chloromethane.

i) Name the mechanism that occurs in this reaction.

The mechanism is:
- Free-radical substitution

iii) Construct an equation for the overall reaction that occurs in the sunlight.

The equation for the overall reaction in sunlight is:
- CH~4~ + Cl~2~ → CH~3~Cl + HCl

The mechanism also involves propagation and termination steps.

i) Construct two equations to show the propagation steps in this mechanism.

[2]

ii) Construct an equation to show one possible termination step.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The two propagation steps are:

CH<sub>4</sub> + Cl<sup>•</sup> → CH<sub>3</sub><sup>•</sup> + HCl

CH<sub>3</sub><sup>•</sup> + Cl<sub>2</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>Cl + Cl<sup>•</sup>

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for each correct propagation equation (in any order)

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) One possible termination step is:
> 
> - CH<sub>3</sub><sup>•</sup> + CH<sub>3</sub><sup>•</sup> → C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>
> **OR**
> Cl<sup>•</sup> + Cl<sup>•</sup> → Cl<sub>2</sub>
> **OR**
> Cl<sup>•</sup> + CH<sub>3</sub><sup>•</sup> → CH<sub>3</sub>Cl **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> In each propagation step, one free radical is consumed and another is produced. This keeps the chain reaction going. The two propagation steps must be given in the correct stoichiometric form.
> 
> In termination steps, two free radicals combine to form a stable, non-radical molecule. Any one of the three possible termination steps is acceptable unless the question specifies otherwise.

parts.problemMd:
1,2-dibromoethane reacts with bromine in the presence of ultraviolet light to produce a mixture of further substituted halogenoalkanes.

i) Construct an equation for the initiation step of this reaction.

[1]

ii) Explain why the bond breaking in the initiation step is described as homolytic fission.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The initiation step is:
> 
> - Br<sub>2</sub> → 2Br<sup>•</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The bond breaking is described as homolytic fission because:
> 
> - Each bromine atom receives one electron from the Br–Br covalent bond / shared pair of electrons **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> In homolytic fission, the bond breaks symmetrically: each atom takes one electron from the shared pair. This produces two radicals (species with unpaired electrons) rather than ions.
> 
> This is different from heterolytic fission, where both electrons go to one atom, forming a positive ion and a negative ion.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

1,2-dibromoethane reacts with bromine in the presence of ultraviolet light to produce a mixture of further substituted halogenoalkanes.

Construct two equations to show the propagation steps in this mechanism that produce 1,1,2-tribromoethane.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The two propagation steps are:
> 
> - CH<sub>2</sub>BrCH<sub>2</sub>Br + Br<sup>•</sup> → CH<sub>2</sub>BrCHBr<sup>•</sup> + HBr **[1 mark]**
> - CH<sub>2</sub>BrCHBr<sup>•</sup> + Br<sub>2</sub> → CH<sub>2</sub>BrCHBr<sub>2</sub> + Br<sup>•</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> In each propagation step, a free radical reacts with a molecule to produce a new free radical. The bromine radical consumed in step 1 is regenerated in step 2, allowing the chain to continue.
> 
> In step 1, the bromine radical removes a hydrogen atom from 1,2-dibromoethane to form HBr, leaving a carbon radical on C-2. In step 2, this carbon radical reacts with Br<sub>2</sub> to form 1,1,2-tribromoethane and regenerate a Br<sup>•</sup>.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

1,2-dibromoethane reacts with bromine in the presence of ultraviolet light to produce a mixture of further substituted halogenoalkanes.

The two propagation steps are:
- CH₂BrCH₂Br + Br• → CH₂BrCHBr• + HBr
- CH₂BrCHBr• + Br₂ → CH₂BrCHBr₂ + Br•

Traces of 1,2,3,4-tetrabromobutane are found in the reaction mixture.

i) Construct an equation for the termination step that forms 1,2,3,4-tetrabromobutane.

[1]

ii) Construct an equation to show the overall reaction for the formation of hexabromoethane from 1,1,2-tribromoethane.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The termination step that forms 1,2,3,4-tetrabromobutane is:
> 
> - CH<sub>2</sub>BrCHBr<sup>•</sup> + CH<sub>2</sub>BrCHBr<sup>•</sup> → CH<sub>2</sub>BrCHBrCHBrCH<sub>2</sub>Br **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The overall equation for the formation of hexabromoethane is:
> 
> - CHBr<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br + 3Br<sub>2</sub> → CBr<sub>3</sub>CBr<sub>3</sub> + 3HBr **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> 1,2,3,4-Tetrabromobutane forms when two CH<sub>2</sub>BrCHBr<sup>•</sup> radicals combine in a termination step. Two free radicals combine to form one molecule with no unpaired electrons, ending the chain reaction.
> 
> For the overall equation, count the hydrogen atoms on 1,1,2-tribromoethane (3 H atoms). Each H removed requires one Br<sub>2</sub>, so 3Br<sub>2</sub> are needed and 3HBr are produced.

parts.problemMd: Suggest two reasons why free-radical substitution is not a good method for producing a single, pure halogenoalkane.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Free-radical substitution is not a good method for producing a single, pure halogenoalkane because:
> 
> Any **two** from (1 mark for each point):
> 
> - Further substitution can occur, producing a mixture of mono-, di-, and tri-substituted products
> - The halogen can be substituted at different positions in the carbon chain, forming structural isomers
> - Termination steps produce unexpected by-products (e.g. longer-chain hydrocarbons)
> - The reaction is difficult to control
> 
> **[2 marks]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The main limitations are:
> 
> - Further substitution (once one H is replaced, the product can react again)
> - Positional isomers (for chains with more than one type of H atom, different structural isomers form)
> - Unexpected by-products from termination steps.
> 
> These limitations mean free-radical substitution produces a mixture of products rather than a single pure compound.

parts.problemMd:
A sample of pent-1-ene, with a mass of 1.33 g, is warmed to 60°C in a sealed container. The volume of the container is 500 cm<sup>3</sup>.

Calculate the pressure inside the container.

Include units and give your answer to an appropriate number of significant figures. [molar gas constant (*R*) = 8.31 J mol<sup>−1</sup> K<sup>−1</sup>]
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the pressure inside the container:

- Calculate the moles of pent-1-ene:

moles = $\frac{1.33}{70.0}$

moles = 0.0190 mol

**[1 mark]**

- Convert the volume and temperature to SI units:

volume = 500 x 10<sup>-6</sup> m<sup>3</sup>

temperature = 60 + 273 = 333 K

**[1 mark]**

- Rearrange the ideal gas equation and substitute:

*p* = $\frac{nRT}{V}$

*p* = $\frac{0.0190\times8.31\times333}{500\times10^{-6}}$

*p* = 105 154 Pa

**[1 mark]**

- Round to an appropriate number of significant figures and state units:

*p* = **105 000 Pa**

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for moles of pent-1-ene = 0.019 mol (M<sub>r</sub> of C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub> = 70.0)
> 
> 1 mark for volume = 500 x 10<sup>-6</sup> m<sup>3</sup> **AND** temperature = 333 K (both required)
> 
> 1 mark for correct substitution into *pV* = *nRT*
> 
> 1 mark for final answer to 2 or 3 sf with correct units
> 
> Allow 1.05 x 10<sup>5</sup> Pa or 1.1 x 10<sup>5</sup> Pa. Allow N m<sup>-2</sup> in place of Pa or answer expressed in kPa (105 kPa).

> **[exam-tip]**
> The molar mass of pent-1-ene (C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>) = (5 x 12.0) + (10 x 1.0) = 70.0 g mol<sup>-1</sup>.
> 
> The ideal gas equation *pV* = *nRT* requires SI units throughout: pressure in Pa, volume in m<sup>3</sup>, temperature in K, and amount in mol. Divide the volume in cm<sup>3</sup> by 10<sup>6</sup> to convert to m<sup>3</sup>, and add 273 to convert °C to K.
> 
> A correct final answer with units and no working shown still scores 4 marks, but showing your working allows error-carried-forward credit if an earlier step is wrong.
