parts.problemMd:
This question is about alkenes.

One method of preparing ethene in a school or college laboratory is from ethanol by using the apparatus shown below in Fig. 3.1.

![Diagram of ethanol vapour passed over heated pumice to form ethene, collected as gas in an inverted test tube over water in a trough.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-2-alkenes/assets/044-diagram-of-ethanol-vapour-passed-over-heated-pum.png)

**Fig. 3.1**

i) Write a balanced equation for this reaction.

[1]

ii) What type of reaction is this?

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) A balanced equation for this reaction is:
> 
> - C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH → C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The type of reaction is:
> 
> - Elimination / Dehydration **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> You should know the formulae for ethanol (C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH) and ethene (C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>) and be able to construct the balanced equation. The reaction is called elimination because a small molecule (water) is eliminated from the organic compound, and dehydration because water is lost. Both terms are accepted.
> 
> The catalyst shown in the apparatus (pumice) acts as a surface catalyst. Aluminium oxide (Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>) and concentrated acids (H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> or H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub>) are also used as catalysts for this reaction.

parts.problemMd:
Ethene is bubbled into two separate test-tubes, one containing aqueous hydrogen bromide and the other containing cold, dilute acidified potassium manganate(VII).

In each case, complete Table 3.1** **to describe any colour changes you would see and give the structural formula of the organic product.

**Table 3.1**

|   | aqueous hydrogen bromide | cold, dilute acidified potassium manganate(VII) |
|---|---|---|
| colour at start |   |   |
| colour after reaction |   |   |
| structural formula of organic product |   |   |
parts.solutionMd:
The completed table is:

|   | aqueous hydrogen bromide | cold, dilute acidified potassium manganate(VII) |
|---|---|---|
| colour at start | **Final answer:** **colourless** | **Final answer:** **purple** |
| colour after reaction | **Final answer:** **colourless** | **Final answer:** **colourless / decolourised** |
| structural formula of organic product | **Final answer:** **CH**<sub>**3**</sub>**CH**<sub>**2**</sub>**Br** | **Final answer:** **HOCH**<sub>**2**</sub>**CH**<sub>**2**</sub>**OH** |

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for both correct colour entries for aqueous hydrogen bromide (colourless at start and colourless after reaction)
> 
> 1 mark for the correct structural formula of the product with aqueous hydrogen bromide: CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br
> 
> 1 mark for both correct colour entries for potassium manganate(VII) (purple at start, colourless / decolourised after reaction)
> 
> 1 mark for the correct structural formula of the product with cold dilute acidified potassium manganate(VII): HOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH
> 
> "Clear" is not accepted in place of "colourless". Both colour entries must be correct to score each mark.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Aqueous HBr is a colourless solution and the product bromoethane (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br) is also colourless, so no colour change is observed in the HBr reaction.
> 
> KMnO<sub>4</sub> is purple. When ethene reacts with cold, dilute acidified KMnO<sub>4</sub>, the alkene is oxidised to a diol (ethane-1,2-diol: HOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH) and the purple manganate(VII) ion is reduced, so the solution decolourises.
> 
> Alkenes also react with hot concentrated acidified KMnO<sub>4</sub>, but the product and conditions are different — learn both reactions.

parts.problemMd:
Cyclohexene has the following structural formula.

![Simple line drawing of a six‑sided cyclohexene ring, showing one double bond on the right side against a plain white background](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-2-alkenes/assets/045-simple-line-drawing-of-a-six-sided-cyclohexene-r.png)

What is the molecular formula of cyclohexene?
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The molecular formula of cyclohexene is:
> 
> - C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>10</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The molecular formula gives the actual number of atoms of each element. Cyclohexene has a six-membered ring with one C=C double bond. The two carbons in the double bond each have one H atom; the remaining four ring carbons each have two H atoms. This gives a total of 6 carbons and 10 hydrogens: C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>10</sub>.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Cyclohexene has the following structural formula.

![Simple line drawing of a six‑sided cyclohexene ring, showing one double bond on the right side against a plain white background](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2023/01/cyclohexene.png)

Cyclohexene can react with bromine.

i) Draw the structural formula of the compound formed when cyclohexene is reacted with bromine.

[1]

ii) State what type of mechanism is involved in forming this product.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The structural formula of the compound formed when cyclohexene reacts with bromine is:

![Structural formula of 1,2-dibromocyclohexane with bromine atoms added across the former double bond](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-2-alkenes/assets/046-structural-formula-of-1-2-dibromocyclohexane-wit.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct structure of 1,2-dibromocyclohexane, with both bromine atoms on adjacent carbons that previously formed the double bond
> 
> ii) The type of mechanism is:
> 
> - Electrophilic **[1 mark]**
> - Addition **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Cycloalkenes undergo the same electrophilic addition reactions as straight-chain alkenes — do not be put off by the ring structure. Bromine adds across the C=C bond: the two bromine atoms go onto the two carbons that previously formed the double bond.
> 
> The mechanism is electrophilic addition: the C=C bond acts as a nucleophile (electron-rich), attracting the electrophile Br<sub>2</sub> (which becomes polarised as it approaches). The first step forms a cyclic bromonium ion intermediate; the bromide ion then attacks from the opposite face, giving the trans-addition product.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Cyclohexene has the following structural formula.

![Simple line drawing of a six‑sided cyclohexene ring, showing one double bond on the right side against a plain white background](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2023/01/cyclohexene.png)

Draw the structural formula of the compound formed when cyclohexene is reacted with hot concentrated acidified potassium manganate(VII).
parts.solutionMd:
The structural formula of the compound formed is:

![Structural formula of hexanedioic acid (adipic acid): HOOC-(CH2)4-COOH, the product of cyclohexene oxidative cleavage](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-2-alkenes/assets/047-structural-formula-of-hexanedioic-acid-adipic-ac.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct structural formula of hexanedioic acid: HOOC(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>4</sub>COOH
> 
> The –COOH group may be written as –CO<sub>2</sub>H. Accept any unambiguous structural formula for hexanedioic acid.

> **[exam-tip]**
> When hot concentrated acidified KMnO<sub>4</sub> reacts with cyclohexene, the C=C bond is completely broken. Each carbon in the double bond is bonded to an H atom and an alkyl group (the rest of the ring), so both carbons are oxidised to carboxylic acid groups (–COOH). This opens the ring to give hexanedioic acid: HOOC(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>4</sub>COOH.
> 
> The product depends on the substituents on the C=C carbons: if a carbon has one H atom and one alkyl group, oxidation gives –COOH; if a carbon has no H atoms (two alkyl groups), oxidation gives a ketone (C=O) instead.

parts.problemMd:
Compound **B** contains carbon, hydrogen and oxygen only.

It has the following percentage composition by mass: C 54.5%, H 9.1%, O 36.4%.

Calculate the empirical formula of **B**.

Show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the empirical formula of **B**:

- Convert the percentages to moles:

moles of C = $\frac{54.5}{12.0}$ = 4.5417

moles of H = $\frac{9.1}{1.0}$ = 9.1

moles of O = $\frac{36.4}{16.0}$ = 2.275

**[1 mark]**

- Divide each value by the smallest (2.275…) to get the ratio:

C = $\frac{4.5417}{2.275}$ $\approx$ 2

H = $\frac{9.1}{2.275}$ = 4

O = $\frac{2.275}{2.275}$ = 1

State the empirical formula:

**Final answer:** **C**<sub>**2**</sub>**H**<sub>**4**</sub>**O**

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct calculation of moles for C, H and O
> 
> 1 mark for correct simplest whole-number ratio leading to C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>O

> **[exam-tip]**
> Keep several significant figures during the mole calculations, then simplify the ratio at the end. Rounding too early is a common reason students end up with the wrong whole-number ratio.

parts.problemMd:
Compound **C** is the secondary alcohol, butan-2-ol, CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>.

i) Butan-2-ol can be converted into but-2-ene by dehydration.

State the reagent and conditions required for this reaction.

[2]

ii) Butan-2-ol is heated under reflux with acidified potassium dichromate(VI).

State the colour change observed.

[1]

iii) Name the organic product formed in (b)(ii).

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The reagent and conditions for the dehydration of butan-2-ol are:
> 
> - Concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>
> **OR**
> H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub> **[1 mark]**
> - Heat / around 170 °C **[1 mark]**
> 
> Sulfuric acid must be concentrated for the first mark.
> 
> Heated vapour over Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> scores **[2 marks]**
> 
> ii) The colour change is:
> 
> - Orange to green **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The organic product is:
> 
> - Butanone / butan-2-one **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> In (i), you need both parts for full marks: a dehydrating agent (often concentrated sulfuric acid) and heating. Writing “sulfuric acid” without “concentrated”, or missing the heat/temperature, is usually not enough.
> 
> In (ii), “orange to green” is specific to dichromate(VI). Answers like “decolourised” often show confusion with other oxidising agents.
> 
> In (iii), remember that secondary alcohols oxidise to ketones only, so the product is butanone (butan-2-one), not an aldehyde or carboxylic acid.

parts.problemMd:
But-2-ene shows geometrical (cis/trans) isomerism.

i) Explain the term geometrical isomerism.

In your answer, refer to the features of the double bond and the groups attached to it.

[2]

ii) Draw the displayed formula of trans-but-2-ene.

[1]

iii) Describe a chemical test to show the presence of the C=C double bond in but-2-ene.

Reagent: …………………………………………

Observation: …………………………………

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) Geometrical (cis/trans) isomerism arises because:
> 
> - There is restricted rotation about the C=C double bond due to the presence of a π bond **[1 mark]**
> - There are two different groups attached to each carbon of the C=C double bond **[1 mark]**

ii) The displayed formula of trans-but-2-ene is:

![Displayed formula of trans-but-2-ene showing methyl groups on opposite sides of the double bond](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-2-alkenes/assets/033-displayed-formula-of-trans-but-2-ene-showing-met.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct displayed formula of trans-but-2-ene with methyl groups on opposite sides of the C=C bond
> 
> iii) To test for the C=C double bond in but-2-ene:
> 
> - Reagent: Bromine water / aqueous bromine **[1 mark]**
> - Observation: Orange/brown to colourless (decolourised) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For (i), avoid vague phrases such as "different spatial arrangement" on their own. You must refer specifically to restricted rotation due to the presence of the π bond and the requirement for two different groups on each carbon of the C=C bond.
> 
> For (ii), make sure the cis/trans arrangement is unambiguous. The key mark is for showing the methyl groups on opposite sides of the double bond. All bonds must be shown as the question asks for the displayed formula.
> 
> For (iii), always pair the reagent with a clear observable change. Writing "reacts" or "no change" without specifying the colour change will not gain credit.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Compound **C** is the secondary alcohol, butan-2-ol, CH~3~CH(OH)CH~2~CH~3~.

ii) Butan-2-ol is heated under reflux with acidified potassium dichromate(VI).

State the colour change observed.

iii) Name the organic product formed in (b)(ii).

Infrared spectroscopy is used to identify functional groups.

Use the Data Booklet to identify the bond responsible for the following absorption peaks found in organic spectra.

i) A strong absorption peak at 1700 cm⁻¹.

[1]

ii) A broad absorption peak in the range 3200–3600 cm⁻¹.

[1]

iii) State how the infrared spectrum of the product formed in (b)(iii) would differ from the spectrum of butan-2-ol.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The bond responsible for a strong absorption peak at 1700 cm<sup>-1</sup> is:
> 
> - C=O / carbonyl **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The bond responsible for a broad absorption peak in the range 3200–3600 cm<sup>-1</sup> is:
> 
> - O–H (alcohol) / hydroxyl **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The differences between the spectra are:
> 
> - The product does not have an O–H absorption at 3200–3600 cm<sup>-1</sup>
> **OR**
> The O–H absorption at 3200–3600 cm<sup>-1</sup> disappears or decreases **[1 mark]**
> - The product has a C=O absorption at about 1700 cm<sup>-1</sup>
> **OR**
> A C=O absorption at about 1700 cm<sup>-1</sup> appears **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For (i), be specific. The peak at around 1700 cm<sup>-1</sup> is characteristic of a carbonyl (C=O) group, not just a generic "double bond".
> 
> For (ii), the key clue is that the peak is broad. Sharp peaks in this region are not typical of alcohol O–H bonds.
> 
> For (iii), full marks require two clear comparisons: the loss of the O–H absorption from the alcohol and the appearance of the C=O absorption in the ketone.

parts.problemMd:
This question is about hydrocarbons.

10 cm<sup>3 </sup>of a gaseous hydrocarbon, C<sub>*x*</sub>H<sub>*y*</sub>, was reacted with 100 cm<sup>3 </sup>of oxygen gas, an excess. The final volume of the gaseous mixture was 95 cm<sup>3</sup>.

This gaseous mixture was treated with concentrated, aqueous sodium hydroxide to absorb the carbon dioxide present. This reduced the gas volume to 75 cm<sup>3</sup>.

All gas volumes were measured at 298 K and 100 kPa.

i) Write an equation for the reaction between sodium hydroxide and carbon dioxide.

[1]

ii) Calculate the volume of carbon dioxide produced by the combustion of the hydrocarbon.

volume of CO<sub>2</sub> produced = ................. cm<sup>3</sup> [1]

iii) Calculate the volume of oxygen used up in the reaction with the hydrocarbon.

volume of O<sub>2</sub> used = ................. cm<sup>3</sup> [1]

iv) Use your answers to **(b)(ii)** and **(b)(iii)**, together with the initial volume of hydrocarbon, to balance the equation below.

............C<sub>*x*</sub>H<sub>*y*</sub> + ............O<sub>2</sub> → ............CO<sub>2</sub> + *z*H<sub>2</sub>O

[2]

v) Deduce the values of *x*, *y* and *z* in the equation in** (iv)**.

*x* = .............................
*y* = .............................
*z* = .............................

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) An equation for the reaction between sodium hydroxide and carbon dioxide is:
> 
> - 2NaOH + CO<sub>2</sub> → Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**

ii) The volume of carbon dioxide produced by the combustion of the hydrocarbon is:

volume of CO<sub>2</sub> = 95 − 75 = **20 cm**<sup>**3**</sup> **[1 mark]**

iii) The volume of oxygen used up in the reaction with the hydrocarbon is:

volume of O<sub>2</sub> used = 100 − 75 = **25 cm**<sup>**3**</sup> **[1 mark]**

iv) Using the volume ratio hydrocarbon : O<sub>2</sub> : CO<sub>2</sub> = 10 : 25 : 20, simplified to 2 : 5 : 4, the balanced equation is:

**2**C<sub>*x*</sub>H<sub>*y*</sub> + **5**O<sub>2</sub> → **4**CO<sub>2</sub> + *z*H<sub>2</sub>O

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 2 marks for all three correct balancing numbers (2, 5, and 4); allow 1 mark for exactly two correct balancing numbers
> 
> v) The values of *x*, *y* and *z* are:
> 
> - *x* = 2 **[1 mark]**
> - *y* = 2 **[1 mark]**
> - *z* = 2 **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> After combustion, the gaseous mixture (95 cm<sup>3</sup>) contains excess O<sub>2</sub> and CO<sub>2</sub>. Treating with NaOH absorbs the CO<sub>2</sub>, reducing the volume to 75 cm<sup>3</sup>, so the volume of CO<sub>2</sub> = 95 − 75 = 20 cm<sup>3</sup>. Since the initial O<sub>2</sub> was 100 cm<sup>3</sup> and 75 cm<sup>3</sup> remains, the O<sub>2</sub> used = 100 − 75 = 25 cm<sup>3</sup>.
> 
> The volume ratio is hydrocarbon : O<sub>2</sub> : CO<sub>2</sub> = 10 : 25 : 20, which simplifies to 2 : 5 : 4. This gives the balanced equation: 2C<sub>*x*</sub>H<sub>*y*</sub><sub> + </sub>5O<sub>2</sub> → 4CO<sub>2</sub> + *z*H<sub>2</sub>O.
> 
> To find *x*: 4 CO<sub>2</sub> means 4 C on the right; with 2 formula units of C~*x*<sub>H</sub>*y*~ on the left, *x* = 2. To find *z*: 10 O on the left (5O<sub>2</sub>), 8 in 4CO<sub>2</sub>, so 2 in *z*H<sub>2</sub>O, giving *z* = 2. To find *y*: 4 H on the right (2H<sub>2</sub>O) and 2 formula units of C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>y</sub>, so *y* = 2. The hydrocarbon is C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>2</sub> (ethyne).

parts.problemMd:
A branched-chain hydrocarbon, **W**, with the formula C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>, reacts with hydrogen bromide, HBr, to give two products **X** and **Y**.

**X** and **Y** are structural isomers of molecular formula C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9</sub>Br. More **X** is produced than **Y**.

i) Give the structural formulae **and** names of the compounds **W**, **X**, and **Y**.

[3]

ii) When **W** reacts with hydrogen bromide, more **X** than **Y** is produced. Explain why.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The structural formulae and names of **W**, **X**, and **Y** are:
> 
> - **W** = (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C=CH<sub>2</sub>
> **AND**
> 2-methylpropene **[1 mark]**
> - **X** = (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CBrCH<sub>3</sub>
> **AND**
> 2-bromo-2-methylpropane **[1 mark]**
> - **Y** = (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCH<sub>2</sub>Br
> **AND**
> 1-bromo-2-methylpropane **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) More **X** is produced than **Y** because:
> 
> Any **two** from (1 mark for each point):
> 
> - The halide bonds to the carbon with the most alkyl groups / most substituted carbon
> - A tertiary carbocation is more stable than a primary carbocation
> - Alkyl groups stabilise the carbocation through the inductive effect (+I)
> 
> **[2 marks]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> 2-methylpropene is the only branched-chain alkene with the formula C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>. When it reacts with HBr, the δ+H of H–Br acts as the electrophile and accepts electrons from the C=C bond. This forms a carbocation: either tertiary (positive charge on C2, attached to three alkyl groups) or primary (positive charge on C1, attached to one alkyl group).
> 
> The tertiary carbocation at C2 is more stable because three alkyl groups push electron density towards the positive carbon through the inductive effect. The bromide ion preferentially attacks this more stable intermediate, giving 2-bromo-2-methylpropane (**X**) as the major product.

parts.problemMd:
Pent-2-ene will react with HBr.

Draw the mechanism for the reaction of pent-2-ene with hydrogen bromide. You do not need to include any partial charges.
parts.solutionMd:
The mechanism for the reaction of pent-2-ene with hydrogen bromide is:

![Electrophilic addition mechanism showing pent-2-ene reacting with HBr to give a secondary carbocation intermediate and then a bromoalkane product](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-2-alkenes/assets/052-electrophilic-addition-mechanism-showing-pent-2-.png)

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from the C=C bond to the H atom of H–Br
> 
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from the H–Br bond to the Br atom, forming the carbocation intermediate
> 
> 1 mark for the correct carbocation intermediate drawn
> 
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from the lone pair on :Br<sup>–</sup> to the C<sup>+</sup> of the carbocation

> **[exam-tip]**
> This question specifies that you do not need to include partial charges (δ+ and δ–) on the H–Br molecule. Unless a question explicitly states this, you should always include the dipole to gain full marks.
> 
> Curly arrows must start from an area of high electron density (the C=C bond or a lone pair) and point to an area of low electron density. The major product is the bromoalkane formed via the more stable secondary carbocation intermediate.

parts.problemMd:
A student completed an investigation into the amount of C=C bonds in a molecule of cooking oil, with a density of 0.526 g cm<sup>-3</sup>, by titrating samples with 0.02 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> bromine water.

The student plans to use the following procedure for their investigation.

1. Measure 5.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of solvent into a conical flask.
2. Add five drops of cooking oil to the solvent, using a dropping pipette.
3. Swirl to ensure mixing.
4. Note the initial reading of the bromine water in the burette.
5. Add the 2.0 x 10<sup>-2</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup> bromine water from the burette to the solution in the conical flask slowly.

  - Shake vigorously after each addition until the bromine colour disappears.
6. As the bromine colour takes longer to fade with each addition, add less bromine water each time until there is just an excess of bromine in the flask.

  - This will be shown by a permanent yellow tint.
7. Note the final reading of the burette.

Suggest **two **improvements that the student could make to this procedure to obtain more consistent results.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Two improvements to obtain more consistent results are:
> 
> Any **two** from:
> 
> - Weigh out the oil (density is known, so volume can be calculated from mass)
> - Use a measured / known volume of cooking oil (e.g. with a graduated pipette)
> - Make a standard solution of the cooking oil and solvent
> - Titrate the bromine water against 25.0 cm<sup>3</sup> measured portions of the cooking oil / solvent mixture
> 
> **[2 marks]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Scientific titrations work with known volumes and concentrations to find an unknown quantity. Here, the concentration and volume of the bromine water are known, but "five drops" of cooking oil is not a precise or consistent volume. To calculate the number of C=C bonds per molecule, you need to know the amount (moles) of cooking oil used, which requires a precise mass or volume measurement.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A student completed an investigation into the amount of C=C bonds in a molecule of cooking oil, with a density of 0.526 g cm^-3^, by titrating samples with 0.02 mol dm^-3^ bromine water.

The student plans to use the following procedure for their investigation.

1. Measure 5.0 cm^3^ of solvent into a conical flask.
2. Add five drops of cooking oil to the solvent, using a dropping pipette.
3. Swirl to ensure mixing.
4. Note the initial reading of the bromine water in the burette.
5. Add the 2.0 x 10^-2^ mol dm^-3^ bromine water from the burette to the solution in the conical flask slowly.

- Shake vigorously after each addition until the bromine colour disappears.
6. As the bromine colour takes longer to fade with each addition, add less bromine water each time until there is just an excess of bromine in the flask.

- This will be shown by a permanent yellow tint.
7. Note the final reading of the burette.

The student’s titration results are shown in Table 2.1.

**Table 2.1**

| **Experiment ** | **Initial volume / cm**<sup>**3**</sup>** ** | **Final volume / cm**<sup>**3**</sup>** ** |
|---|---|---|
| Rough | 0.00 | 26.35 |
| 1 | 0.00 | 26.25 |
| 2 | 0.10 | 26.45 |
| 3 | 0.00 | 26.10 |

The approximate *M*<sub>r</sub> of the cooking oil is 1002 and its density is 0.526 g cm<sup>–3</sup>.

Assume each drop of cooking oil has a volume of 5.0 × 10<sup>–2 </sup>cm<sup>3</sup>.

The concentration of bromine water used was 2.0 × 10<sup>–2</sup> mol dm<sup>–3</sup>.

Use this data and the titration results from Table 3.1 to deduce the number of C=C double bonds in a molecule of the oil. Show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
To deduce the number of C=C bonds in the cooking oil:

- Calculate the mass of cooking oil used (5 drops):

mass = density x volume = 0.526 x (5.0 x 10<sup>-2</sup> x 5)

mass = 0.1315 g **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the moles of cooking oil:

moles of oil = $\frac{0.1315}{1002}$

moles of oil = 1.312 x 10<sup>-4</sup> mol **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the average titre (excluding rough):

average titre = $\frac{26.25+26.35}{2}$ = 26.30 cm<sup>3</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the moles of Br<sub>2</sub>:

moles of Br<sub>2</sub> = 2.0 x 10<sup>-2</sup> x $\frac{26.30}{1000}$

moles of Br<sub>2</sub> = 5.26 x 10<sup>-4</sup> mol **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the molar ratio of oil : Br<sub>2</sub>:

ratio = 1.312 x 10<sup>-4</sup> : 5.26 x 10<sup>-4</sup> = 1 : 4 **[1 mark]**

- State the conclusion:

number of C=C bonds per molecule = **4** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Rough titres are not used in titration calculations. The concordant titres are experiment 1 (26.25 cm<sup>3</sup>) and experiment 2 (26.35 cm<sup>3</sup>); allow ECF if the student uses a different concordant pair.
> 
> Each C=C bond reacts with one molecule of Br<sub>2</sub>, so the molar ratio of oil to bromine equals the number of C=C bonds per molecule of oil.

> **[exam-tip]**
> You have all the information needed to find the moles of cooking oil (mass and M<sub>r</sub>) and the moles of bromine (concentration and titre). Rough titres are never included in the average, even if they appear concordant with other results.
> 
> Once you have the molar ratio of oil to Br<sub>2</sub>, the key insight is that each C=C bond reacts with exactly one Br<sub>2</sub> molecule. A ratio of 1 : 4 therefore means 4 C=C bonds per molecule of oil.

parts.solutionMd:

> - Mono-unsaturated: (each carbon chain contains) one C=C bond / carbon-carbon double bond **[1 mark]**
> - Polyunsaturated: (each carbon chain contains) two or more / many C=C bonds / carbon-carbon double bonds **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
**X** and **Y** are the reagents required to convert 1-bromopropane into butanoic acid.

| **A** | NH<sub>3</sub> | HCl (aq) |
| **B** | KCN in C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH | NaOH (aq) |
| **C** | KCN in C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH | HCl (aq) |
| **D** | HCN | NaOH (aq) |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- If a halogenoalkane is heated under reflux with a solution of potassium cyanide in ethanol, the halogen is replaced by a -CN group and a nitrile is produced.

  - So, reagent X must be KCN in C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH.
- Next, to produce a carboxylic acid, the nitrile is heated under reflux with dilute hydrochloric acid.

parts.problemMd: Which reaction occurs when ethane and chlorine are mixed in diffused sunlight?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Ethane reacts with chlorine by free radical substitution in the presence of sunlight.
- In the presence of sunlight, Cl<sub>2</sub> breaks down to form two chlorine radicals:

Cl<sub>2</sub> → 2Cl•

- The generated chlorine radical can then react with ethane to give an ethane radical (C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>•) and HCl:

C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub> + Cl• → C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>• + HCl

- Therefore, the reaction is a free-radical substitution with hydrogen chloride produced.

**A** is incorrect as free radical substitution produces HCl, not H<sub>2</sub>.

**C** is incorrect as the reaction produces HCl gas; a gas is produced.

**D** is incorrect as the mechanism is free radical substitution, not nucleophilic substitution. Nucleophilic substitution requires a nucleophile attacking a carbon bonded to a leaving group, which does not apply here.

parts.problemMd:
Chlorofluoroalkanes, CFCs, can be used as refrigerants, aerosol propellants and fire extinguishers.

CFCs such as CCl<sub>3</sub>F and CCl<sub>2</sub>F<sub>2</sub> are more stable than chloroalkanes such as CCl<sub>4</sub>.

What is the reason for their greater stability?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- CFCs and chloroalkanes are similar as they both contain C–Cl bonds, but they differ in that CFCs contain C–F bonds.
- The bond energy of the C–F bond is larger than the C–Cl bond.
- So, it takes less energy to release Cl atoms than F atoms from CFCs.

  - This is why CFCs are more stable than chloroalkanes.

**A** and **B** are incorrect as the stability of a molecule comes from the strength of the bonds within the molecule, not the ionisation energy or stability of radicals.

**D** is incorrect as the polarity of a bond tells us how electronegative an atom is, which contributes to the strength of the bond, but is not the direct reason for the stability of the molecule overall.

parts.problemMd:
Light initiates the following reaction.

alkane + chlorine $\rightarrow$ chloroalkane + hydrogen chloride

What happens to the chlorine molecule during this photochemical reaction?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Homolytic fission = splitting a bond to produce two particles which both have a single unpaired electron (both are free radicals).

- Heterolytic fission = producing two particles which are different because one is a positive ion and the other is a negative ion.

- In this photochemical reaction, energy from sunlight causes chlorine molecules to split into two chlorine atoms, each with one unpaired electron.

- Free radicals are formed when a bond splits evenly, with each atom getting one of the two electrons.

- Hence, chlorine undergoes homolytic fission to give free radicals.

**A** is incorrect as heterolytic fission produces ions, not free radicals, and would give an electrophile (Cl<sup>+</sup>), not a radical.

**B** is incorrect as heterolytic fission does not occur here; the process is homolytic, producing radicals not electrophiles.

**C** is incorrect as homolytic fission does occur, but it produces free radicals, not electrophiles.

parts.problemMd:
High-energy irradiation in the stratosphere produces radicals from chlorofluoroalkanes, commonly known as CFCs.

Which radical could result from this irradiation of CHFC*l*CF<sub>2</sub>C*l*?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- In the given molecule above, there are:

C–H bonds, C–F bonds, C–Cl bonds and a C–C bond.

- In all the options the C–C bond remains intact.
- The order of bond strength of the remaining 3 bonds is:

C–F > C–H > C–Cl

- Therefore, a C–Cl bond will be broken since it requires the least energy – this only occurs in option **C**.

**A** is incorrect as the molecule loses an F atom, suggesting that a C–F bond is broken.

**B** is incorrect as the molecule loses a different F atom, yet still suggesting that a C–F bond is broken.

**D** is incorrect as the molecule loses an H atom, suggesting that a C–H bond is broken.

parts.problemMd: Which reaction is an example of nucleophilic substitution?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- A nucleophile is either a negatively charged species or a molecule with a lone pair of electrons, e.g. H<sub>2</sub>O.
- Nucleophilic substitution reactions involve substitution of a group or atom by a nucleophile.
- The only option which contains a nucleophile is water (H<sub>2</sub>O) in **C**, which acts via a lone pair on the oxygen atom.
- The mechanism for the reaction with bromopropane is as follows:

![Curly arrow mechanism for the SN2 nucleophilic substitution of 1-bromopropane with water, showing attack by the lone pair on oxygen and departure of bromide ion](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/15-halogen-compounds/15-1-halogenoalkanes/assets/012-curly-arrow-mechanism-for-the-sn2-nucleophilic-s.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as this is an elimination reaction; KOH in ethanolic solution removes HBr to form the alkene.

**B** is incorrect as this is an electrophilic addition reaction.

**D** is incorrect as this is a free radical substitution.

parts.problemMd:
Bromomethane, CH<sub>3</sub>Br, is used as a fumigant to destroy insect pests in grain that is to be stored. It can be made by reacting methanol with hydrogen bromide.

CH<sub>3</sub>OH  +  HBr  $\rightarrow$  CH<sub>3</sub>Br  + H<sub>2</sub>O

What type of reaction is this?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- A nucleophile is either a negatively charged species or a molecule with a lone pair of electrons.
- Nucleophilic substitution involves a nucleophile replacing a leaving group at a carbon atom.
- In this reaction, the Br<sup>–</sup> leaving group departs and is replaced by a nucleophile, as shown below:

![SN2 mechanism diagram for the reaction between methanol and hydrogen bromide to give bromomethane, showing curly arrows for bond breaking and forming](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/15-halogen-compounds/15-1-halogenoalkanes/assets/025-sn2-mechanism-diagram-for-the-reaction-between-m.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as condensation reactions involve the joining of two molecules with the loss of a small molecule (e.g. H<sub>2</sub>O); that does not occur here.

**B** is incorrect as electrophilic substitution requires an electrophile attacking an electron-rich centre (e.g. a benzene ring); OH<sup>–</sup> is a nucleophile, not an electrophile.

**C** is incorrect as free radical substitution involves homolytic fission and radical intermediates, initiated by UV light; no radicals are involved in this reaction.

parts.problemMd:
Dichlorodifluoromethane, CC*l*<sub>2</sub>F<sub>2</sub>, has been used in aerosol propellants and as a refrigerant.

Which statement helps to explain why dichlorodifluoromethane is chemically inert?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- In dichlorodifluoromethane, there are two C–F bonds and two C–Cl bonds.
- Both are strong bonds, and the C–F bond energy is the larger of the two.
- The C–F bond strength is the reason for the inertness of CCl<sub>2</sub>F<sub>2</sub> and CFCs in general.
- These bonds are so strong that they do not break under the energy of ordinary visible light.

  - UV light is required to break them.

**A** is incorrect as the non-flammability of fluorine compounds is a consequence of the inertness of CCl<sub>2</sub>F<sub>2</sub>, not a reason for it.

**B** is incorrect as the high electronegativity of fluorine contributes to the strength of the C–F bond, but electronegativity alone is not the direct reason for the inertness.

**D** is incorrect as the C–F bond is in fact highly polar; furthermore, bond polarity is not the direct reason for the inertness – bond energy is.

parts.problemMd:
The reaction of chlorine with methane is carried out in the presence of ultraviolet light.

What is the function of the ultraviolet light?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- This reaction is known as chlorination of methane and proceeds through the radical chain mechanism.
- The radical chain mechanism involves three steps: **initiation**, **propagation** and **termination**.
- Initiation requires an input of energy but after that the reaction is self-sustaining.
- This energy comes from the ultraviolet light source, which breaks the Cl–Cl bond homolytically to form two chlorine radicals.

**A** is incorrect as ultraviolet light does not break the C–H bonds in methane. It is the chlorine radical produced in initiation that abstracts a hydrogen atom in the propagation step.

**B** is incorrect as ultraviolet light causes homolytic fission of the Cl–Cl bond to give radicals, not ions.

**D** is incorrect as ultraviolet light provides the activation energy to form radicals, not heat for the mixture. The reaction proceeds at room temperature once initiated.

parts.problemMd:
Four drops of 1-chlorobutane, 1-bromobutane and 1-iodobutane were put separately into three test-tubes containing 1.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of aqueous silver nitrate at 60 °C.

A hydrolysis reaction occurred.

R represents the butane chain C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9–</sub> and *X* the halogen atom.

H<sub>2</sub>O (l) + R–*X* (l) + Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq) $\rightarrow$ R–OH (aq) + Ag*X* (s) + H<sup>+</sup> (aq)

The rate of formation of cloudiness in the tubes was in the order RCl < RBr < RI

Which statement explains this order of reactivity?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- The rate of formation of cloudiness (the order of reactivity) is related to the strength of the R–*X* bond.
- The carbon-iodine bond is the weakest and the carbon-chlorine bond is the strongest: C–Cl > C–Br > C–I
- So 1-iodobutane would react the quickest, followed by 1-bromobutane and then 1-chlorobutane.
- In order for a halide ion to be produced, the carbon-halogen bond must break – the weaker the bond, the more easily it breaks.
- Therefore, **bond energy** is the main factor deciding the relative rates of reaction.

**B** is incorrect as the ionisation energy of the halogen is a property of the isolated atom. It does not determine how easily the C–*X* bond breaks in solution.

**C** is incorrect as bond polarity is not the main factor here; although polarity contributes to bond strength, the dominant factor is bond energy.

**D** is incorrect as the solubility of the silver halide precipitate does not control the rate of the initial hydrolysis reaction.

parts.problemMd: What is involved in the mechanism of the reaction between aqueous sodium hydroxide and 1-bromobutane?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- Haloalkanes undergo nucleophilic substitution because the greater electronegativity of the halogen creates a partial positive charge (C<sup>δ+</sup>) on the carbon bonded to it.
- The nucleophile attacks the C<sup>δ+</sup> carbon while the C–Br bond breaks simultaneously.

  - This is a concerted, one-step process with no carbocation intermediate.
- This is an S<sub>N</sub>2 reaction.

  - **S**ubstitution **N**ucleophilic **b**imolecular, a reaction in which a bond is broken and a new bond formed simultaneously in one step.

![Curly arrow mechanism for the SN2 reaction of 1-bromobutane with hydroxide ion, showing simultaneous attack by OH⁻ on the δ+ carbon and departure of Br⁻](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/15-halogen-compounds/15-1-halogenoalkanes/assets/023-curly-arrow-mechanism-for-the-sn2-reaction-of-1-.jpg)

**B** is incorrect as, although the C–Br bond does break by heterolytic fission, S<sub>N</sub>2 has no discrete carbocation intermediate as the bond breaks and the new bond forms in the same step.

**C** is incorrect as the hydroxide ion (OH<sup>–</sup>) is a nucleophile, not an electrophile.

**D** is incorrect as the reaction does not involve homolytic fission. Homolytic fission produces two free radicals and is characteristic of radical chain reactions. Nucleophilic substitution proceeds by heterolytic fission of the C–Br bond, not radical combination.

parts.problemMd:
A reaction between chlorine and propane in the presence of ultraviolet light produces two isomeric monochloropropanes, C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>7</sub>Cl.

Which row identifies the type of bond fission in the initiation step and the expected ratio of 1-chloropropane to 2-chloropropane produced?

|   | **Type of bond fission in initiation step** | **Expected ratio of 1-chloropropane to 2-chloropropane produced** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | Heterolytic | 1:1 |
| **B** | Heterolytic | 3:1 |
| **C** | Homolytic | 1:1 |
| **D** | Homolytic | 3:1 |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Homolytic fission = splitting a bond to produce two free radicals (that are the same).
- Heterolytic fission = splitting a bond to produce a positive ion and a negative ion (that are different).
- Propane reacts with chlorine by free radical substitution in the presence of UV light.
- In the presence of UV, Cl<sub>2</sub> breaks down to form two chlorine radicals.

Cl<sub>2</sub> → 2Cl•

- This is an example of homolytic fission, which eliminates options **A** and **B**.
- In the next step, propane reacts with a chlorine radical to form the two isomers of chloropropane.

C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub> + Cl• → C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>7</sub>Cl

- For 1-chloropropane to form, the chlorine radical has 6 hydrogens it can react with – probability $\frac{6}{8}$
- For 2-chloropropane to form, the chlorine radical has 2 hydrogens it can react with – probability $\frac{2}{8}$
- Therefore, the expected ratio of 1-chloropropane to 2-chloropropane = 6 : 2 = **3 : 1**.

![Structural diagram of propane showing the six primary hydrogen atoms at C1 and C3 and two secondary hydrogen atoms at C2 for the statistical ratio calculation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/15-halogen-compounds/15-1-halogenoalkanes/assets/002-structural-diagram-of-propane-showing-the-six-pr.jpg)

choices.label: B
choices.textMd: It is more volatile than propene

parts.problemMd:
Bromine and propene undergo an addition reaction.

Which statement about the product is correct?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- When bromine and propene undergo an addition reaction, the double bond breaks, and a bromine atom becomes attached to each carbon.
- In this reaction with propene, 1,2-dibromopropane is formed.

![Displayed formula of 1,2-dibromopropane, product of electrophilic addition of Br₂ to propene, with bromine atoms on adjacent C1 and C2](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/15-halogen-compounds/15-1-halogenoalkanes/assets/021-displayed-formula-of-1-2-dibromopropane-product-.jpg)

- A chiral carbon atom is a carbon atom that is attached to four different types of atoms or groups of atoms.

![Structural formula of 1,2-dibromopropane with the chiral centre at C2 marked with an asterisk](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/15-halogen-compounds/15-1-halogenoalkanes/assets/022-structural-formula-of-1-2-dibromopropane-with-th.jpg)

- 1,2-dibromopropane possesses a chiral centre, so **C** is correct.

**A** is incorrect as haloalkanes don't contain a double bond, and hence don't exist as cis-trans isomers.

**B** is incorrect as 1,2-dibromopropane is less volatile than propene. Volatility depends on intermolecular forces, not covalent bond strength. 1,2-dibromopropane has a larger, more polarisable electron cloud, resulting in stronger London dispersion forces between molecules compared to propene.

**D** is incorrect as carbon-halogen bonds do not enable hydrogen bonding. Hydrogen bonding requires hydrogen to be directly bonded to a highly electronegative atom (N, O, or F).

parts.problemMd: Which compound undergoes an S<sub>N</sub>1 substitution reaction?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- S<sub>N</sub>1 reactions are nucleophilic substitutions, involving a nucleophile replacing a leaving group (just like in S<sub>N</sub>2).

  - However, S<sub>N</sub>1 reactions are unimolecular, so the rate of this reaction depends only on one species (the halogenoalkane).
- Tertiary halogenoalkanes tend to be the most reactive and tend to undergo nucleophilic substitution via the S<sub>N</sub>1 carbocation mechanism.
- Whereas, primary halogenoalkanes tend to be the least reactive and react via the S<sub>N</sub>2 mechanism.
- So, overall carbocation stability:

3º > 2º >> 1º

- Option **D**, 1-chloro-1-methylcyclohexane, is a tertiary halogenoalkane, hence it is the most likely option to undergo S<sub>N</sub>1 substitution.

**A** is incorrect as (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>CCH<sub>2</sub>I is a primary halogenoalkane (neopentyl iodide). Despite the bulky neopentyl group, the carbon bearing the iodine has no alkyl substituents, so this compound favours S<sub>N</sub>2.

**B** is incorrect as CH<sub>2</sub>=CHCl is a vinyl halide, where the halogen is directly attached to a C=C double bond, which delocalises electron density and makes nucleophilic substitution extremely unfavourable.

**C** is incorrect as CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br is a primary halogenoalkane, which favours S<sub>N</sub>2 nucleophilic substitution rather than S<sub>N</sub>1.

parts.problemMd:
CCl<sub>2</sub>FCClF<sub>2</sub> is converted to a fluorocarbon by the following route:

CCl<sub>2</sub>FCClF<sub>2</sub> $\overset{\text{step 1}}{\rightarrow}$ CCl<sub>3</sub>CF<sub>3</sub> $\overset{\text{step 2}}{\rightarrow}$ CCl<sub>2</sub>FCF<sub>3</sub>

What type of reaction is **step 2**?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- In the reaction CCl<sub>3</sub>CF<sub>3</sub> → CCl<sub>2</sub>FCF<sub>3</sub>
- A Cl atom is replaced with an F atom.
- F<sup>–</sup> (fluoride ion) is the nucleophile; hence it undergoes nucleophilic substitution:

![SN2 mechanism showing F⁻ acting as nucleophile displacing Cl⁻ from CCl₃CF₃ to give CCl₂FCF₃](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/15-halogen-compounds/15-1-halogenoalkanes/assets/018-sn2-mechanism-showing-f-acting-as-nucleophile-di.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as electrophilic substitution requires an electrophile attacking an electron-rich centre; F<sup>–</sup> is a nucleophile, not an electrophile.

**B** is incorrect as free-radical substitution involves homolytic fission and radical intermediates initiated by UV light; no radicals are involved in this halogen exchange reaction.

**C** is incorrect as isomerisation involves rearrangement of atoms within the same molecular formula; here a Cl atom is replaced by F, changing the formula.

parts.problemMd:
The presence of a halogen in an organic compound may be detected by warming the organic compound with aqueous ethanolic silver nitrate.

Which compound would be the quickest to produce a precipitate?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Heating the compounds causes the bonds to break, releasing the halide ions, which then react with the silver ions in AgNO<sub>3</sub> to form precipitates.
- The smaller the bond energy, the weaker the bond, the more quickly it breaks and the faster a precipitate is produced.
- Among F, Cl, Br and I, iodine has the largest atomic radius and the lowest electronegativity, so the C–I bond is the longest and least polar and therefore the weakest.
- Compound **C** is the only compound containing I, so it produces a precipitate most quickly.

**A** is incorrect as the compound shown contains Br. The C–Br bond is stronger than the C–I bond, so it reacts more slowly.

**B** is incorrect as the compound shown also contains Br. The same reasoning applies where C–Br breaks less easily than C–I.

**D** is incorrect as the compound shown contains Cl. The C–Cl bond has the highest bond energy of the three and is the slowest to break.

parts.problemMd:
In the hydrolysis of bromoethane by aqueous sodium hydroxide, which row correctly describes the attacking group and the leaving group?

|   | **Attacking group** | **Leaving group** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | Electrophile | Electrophile |
| **B** | Electrophile | Nucleophile |
| **C** | Nucleophile | Electrophile |
| **D** | Nucleophile | Nucleophile |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- The reaction between bromoethane and sodium hydroxide is **nucleophilic substitution**.
- The OH<sup>–</sup> ion uses a lone pair to attack the δ<sup>+</sup> carbon bonded to Br – OH<sup>–</sup> is the attacking nucleophile.
- The Br<sup>–</sup> ion departs with both bonding electrons – Br<sup>–</sup> has lone pairs and is the leaving nucleophile.
- Therefore, both the attacking group and the leaving group are nucleophiles.

![SN2 mechanism for the hydrolysis of bromoethane showing OH⁻ attacking the δ⁺ carbon and Br⁻ departing as the leaving nucleophile](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/15-halogen-compounds/15-1-halogenoalkanes/assets/011-sn2-mechanism-for-the-hydrolysis-of-bromoethane-.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as OH<sup>–</sup> is a nucleophile, not an electrophile; electrophiles accept electron pairs, whereas OH<sup>–</sup> donates them.

**B** is incorrect as the attacking group (OH<sup>–</sup>) is a nucleophile, not an electrophile.

**C** is incorrect as the leaving group (Br<sup>–</sup>) has lone pairs of electrons and acts as a nucleophile, not an electrophile.

parts.problemMd:
The table shows the time taken for a silver halide precipitate to appear when halogenoalkanes react with aqueous ethanolic silver nitrate at 50 <sup>o</sup>C.

| halogenoalkane | time for precipitate / s |
|---|---|
| 1-chlorobutane | >300 |
| 1-bromobutane | 120 |
| 1-iodobutane | 15 |

Which statement explains the differences in the times taken for the precipitate to appear?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- The table shows the reaction is slowest for 1-chlorobutane and fastest for 1-iodobutane.
- In this test, the rate depends mainly on how easily the C–X bond breaks to form ions.

  - C–I has the lowest bond enthalpy, so it breaks most easily → fastest precipitate.
  - C–Cl has the highest bond enthalpy, so it breaks least easily → slowest precipitate.
- This trend explains the observed order of reaction times.

**A** is incorrect as the C–I bond is the weakest of the carbon-halogen bonds, not the strongest.

**C** is incorrect as the oxidising power of the halogen is not the factor controlling the rate of this hydrolysis reaction.

parts.problemMd:
Bromoethane reacts with ammonia to form ethylamine.

Which set of conditions is required to maximise the yield of ethylamine and minimise further substitution products?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Bromoethane reacts with ammonia by nucleophilic substitution to form ethylamine.
- To maximise the yield of the primary amine, a large excess of ammonia is used.
- This reduces the chance of the ethylamine product acting as a nucleophile and undergoing further substitution to form secondary and tertiary amines.
- Ethanol is used as the solvent because it dissolves both the halogenoalkane and ammonia.
- A sealed tube is required to prevent volatile ammonia from escaping during heating.

**A** is incorrect as using excess bromoethane increases the likelihood of further substitution of the amine product, reducing the yield of ethylamine.

**B** is incorrect as, although heating bromoethane with excess ammonia in a sealed tube would form ethylamine, the solvent used is not ethanol. Without ethanol the halogenoalkane and ammonia are not in a suitable common solvent, reducing the yield of the primary amine.

**C** is incorrect as aqueous ammonia is a less effective solvent for the halogenoalkane and encourages competing reactions, reducing the yield of the primary amine.

parts.problemMd:
Consider the two-step synthesis:

ethane  $\overset{\mathrm{step}1}{\rightarrow}$ bromoethane $\overset{\mathrm{step}2}{\rightarrow}$ ethylamine

|   | step 1 reagents | step 2 reagents |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | Br<sub>2</sub>, UV light | NH<sub>3</sub>, ethanol, heat under pressure |
| **B** | HBr, room temperature | NH<sub>3</sub>, aqueous, reflux |
| **C** | Br<sub>2</sub>, UV light | KCN, ethanol, reflux |
| **D** | PBr<sub>3</sub>, reflux | HNO<sub>3</sub>, room temperature |

Which row shows the correct reagents and conditions?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

**Step 1: Ethane → bromoethane**

- Ethane is an alkane, so it reacts with bromine by free-radical substitution.
- This requires Br<sub>2</sub> and UV light to initiate homolytic fission of the Br–Br bond and form radicals.

**Step 2: Bromoethane → ethylamine**

- Bromoethane undergoes nucleophilic substitution with ammonia to form an amine.
- The conditions used are ethanolic ammonia, heat in a sealed tube, to prevent ammonia escaping and to increase the yield.

**B** is incorrect as HBr does not convert an alkane into a bromoalkane under these conditions.

**C** is incorrect as KCN would form a nitrile, not an amine.

**D** is incorrect as PBr<sub>3</sub> is used to convert alcohols to bromoalkanes, not alkanes, and HNO<sub>3</sub> is not used to make amines from halogenoalkanes.

parts.problemMd:
When an isomer **Y** of molecular formula C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9</sub>Br undergoes hydrolysis in aqueous sodium hydroxide to form an alcohol C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9</sub>OH, the rate of reaction is found to be independent of the concentration of OH<sup>–</sup> ions present.

Which is the most likely molecular structure of **Y**?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- The rate of reaction is independent of the concentration of OH<sup>–</sup>, which means the rate depends only on the concentration of the halogenoalkane, not the nucleophile.

  - This is characteristic of an S<sub>N</sub>1 reaction (**S**ubstitution **N**ucleophilic **u**nimolecular).
- In S<sub>N</sub>1, the C–Br bond breaks first (slow step) to form a carbocation intermediate, and then the nucleophile attacks (fast step).
- Tertiary carbocations are stabilised by the electron-donating inductive effect of three alkyl groups, making them more stable than secondary or primary carbocations.
- This stability lowers the activation energy of the first step and makes the S<sub>N</sub>1 pathway favourable.
- (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>CBr is a tertiary halogenoalkane, so it readily forms a stable tertiary carbocation and undergoes S<sub>N</sub>1 hydrolysis.

**A** is incorrect as (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCH<sub>2</sub>Br has Br on a primary carbon. Primary halogenoalkanes react by S<sub>N</sub>2, where the rate depends on the concentration of both the halogenoalkane and the nucleophile.

**B** is incorrect as CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br is a primary halogenoalkane and reacts by S<sub>N</sub>2. Its rate would be affected by changes in [OH<sup>–</sup>].

**D** is incorrect as CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHBrCH<sub>3</sub> is a secondary halogenoalkane. Secondary halogenoalkanes can undergo both S<sub>N</sub>1 and S<sub>N</sub>2, but the rate is not entirely independent of [OH<sup>–</sup>] as it would be for a tertiary compound.

parts.problemMd:
A tertiary bromoalkene, indicated here by      C–Br, reacts with aqueous NaOH. The mechanism has the reaction pathway below.

![3-3-cie-ial-chemistry-diagram-q4hard](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/15-halogen-compounds/15-1-halogenoalkanes/assets/009-3-3-cie-ial-chemistry-diagram-q4hard.png)

Which point in the diagram is correctly identified?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- A tertiary halogenoalkane reacts with a hydroxide ion by a two-step mechanism.
- This mechanism is known as an S<sub>N</sub>1 mechanism.

  - The '1' tells us that the rate of the reaction only depends on one reagent, in this case the concentration of the halogenoalkane, as shown in the first (slow) step of the mechanism.
- The first step in the mechanism is the breaking of the carbon-halogen bond – this forms a tertiary carbocation, as shown below:

![Two-step SN1 mechanism showing heterolytic C–Br bond breaking to form a tertiary carbocation intermediate, followed by OH⁻ attack](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/15-halogen-compounds/15-1-halogenoalkanes/assets/010-two-step-sn1-mechanism-showing-heterolytic-c-br-.jpg)

- Then, the tertiary carbocation is attacked immediately by the hydroxide ion.
- Reaction pathway diagrams display information about the energy changes during chemical reactions.
- The first bump corresponds to the slow step, as more energy is required here, and the second bump corresponds to the fast step, as less energy is required at this stage.
- Point X corresponds to the breaking of the C–Br bond (first transition state, energy maximum).
- Point Y corresponds to the intermediate step when the tertiary carbocation is formed (energy minimum between the two bumps).
- Therefore, option **C** is correct.

**A** is incorrect as it misidentifies point Y – in a two-step S<sub>N</sub>1 mechanism, Y is the energy minimum between the two transition states, corresponding to the tertiary carbocation intermediate, not a transition state.

**B** is incorrect as it misidentifies point X – X is at the first energy maximum (transition state for C–Br bond breaking), not at the carbocation intermediate.

**D** is incorrect as it misidentifies both points X and Y in the double-bump energy profile of the S<sub>N</sub>1 mechanism.

parts.problemMd: When a solution of potassium cyanide in ethanol is heated under reflux with 1-chloropropane, what is the organic product of the reaction?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- The cyanide ion CN<sup>–</sup> is a nucleophile and reacts with haloalkanes to produce a nitrile.
- This is a useful reaction for increasing the chain length by one carbon atom.

Potassium cyanide + 1-chloropropane → butanenitrile + potassium chloride

KCN + CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Cl → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CN + KCl

- Mechanism:

  - **Step 1:** The cyanide ion attacks at the partially positive carbon of the C–Cl dipole, leading to a high energy transition state.
  - **Step 2:** The chlorine atom leaves with its bonding electrons as a chloride ion.
  - **Step 3:** The final product is butanenitrile, a 4-carbon nitrile.

![SN2 mechanism showing CN⁻ attacking the δ⁺ carbon of 1-chloropropane via a transition state to form butanenitrile and Cl⁻](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/15-halogen-compounds/15-1-halogenoalkanes/assets/003-sn2-mechanism-showing-cn-attacking-the-carbon-of.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as the CN<sup>–</sup> replaces Cl and extends the chain. No chlorine remains in the organic product, so 1-chloropropanenitrile cannot form.

**C** is incorrect as ethanenitrile contains only 2 carbons. The product must contain the original 3-carbon chain plus the CN carbon, giving 4 carbons in total.

**D** is incorrect as propanenitrile contains only 3 carbons. The CN group adds one carbon to the chain, giving a 4-carbon nitrile, not a 3-carbon one.

parts.problemMd:
The compound 2-ethyl-3-methylbutanoic acid is used as a flavouring in some food.

![Structural formula of 2-ethyl-3-methylbutanoic acid showing a branched carbon chain with ethyl and methyl substituents on adjacent alpha and beta carbons and a carboxylic acid group](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/15-halogen-compounds/15-1-halogenoalkanes/assets/015-structural-formula-of-2-ethyl-3-methylbutanoic-a.jpg)

Which compound produces 2-ethyl-3-methylbutanoic acid when heated under reflux with potassium cyanide in ethanol, followed by acid hydrolysis of the reaction product?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- When halogenoalkanes are heated under reflux with ethanolic potassium cyanide, the CN<sup>–</sup> ion replaces the halogen and adds one carbon atom to the chain.
- 2-ethyl-3-methylbutanoic acid has a total of 7 carbon atoms.
- Therefore, the starting halogenoalkane must contain 6 carbon atoms.
- Compound **B** is a 6-carbon halogenoalkane; when heated with KCN in ethanol, the Br is substituted by CN:

![CN substitution step showing the reaction of the 6-carbon branched bromoalkane with KCN in ethanol to give the corresponding nitrile](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/15-halogen-compounds/15-1-halogenoalkanes/assets/016-cn-substitution-step-showing-the-reaction-of-the.jpg)

- Acid hydrolysis of the nitrile then gives the carboxylic acid:

![Acid hydrolysis step showing conversion of the nitrile intermediate to 2-ethyl-3-methylbutanoic acid under reflux with dilute acid](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/15-halogen-compounds/15-1-halogenoalkanes/assets/017-acid-hydrolysis-step-showing-conversion-of-the-n.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as it contains a different number of carbons or a different connectivity. Substitution with CN would not give the required branching pattern to produce 2-ethyl-3-methylbutanoic acid.

**C** is incorrect as its carbon skeleton does not match the structure needed. Even after CN substitution and hydrolysis, the product would not be 2-ethyl-3-methylbutanoic acid.

**D** is incorrect for the same reason that the carbon framework does not give the correct branching pattern in the target molecule.

parts.problemMd:
When phenacyl chloride, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>COCH<sub>2</sub>Cl, is reacted with aqueous NaOH, the substitution reaction follows an S<sub>N</sub>2 mechanism.

Which structure represents the transition state for this reaction?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- The structure of phenacyl chloride is:

![Structural formula of phenacyl chloride showing a benzene ring attached to a carbonyl group with a CH₂Cl group](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/15-halogen-compounds/15-1-halogenoalkanes/assets/013-structural-formula-of-phenacyl-chloride-showing-.jpg)

- In an S<sub>N</sub>2 mechanism, OH<sup>–</sup> attacks the carbon bonded to Cl, while the C–Cl bond breaks simultaneously, forming a pentacoordinate transition state.
- When reacted with aqueous NaOH, the reaction proceeds as follows:

![SN2 mechanism for phenacyl chloride with NaOH showing the pentacoordinate transition state with OH⁻ attacking and Cl⁻ departing simultaneously](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/15-halogen-compounds/15-1-halogenoalkanes/assets/014-sn2-mechanism-for-phenacyl-chloride-with-naoh-sh.jpg)

- Option **C** correctly represents the transition state for this S<sub>N</sub>2 reaction.

**A** is incorrect as the structure shown does not represent the correct transition state for S<sub>N</sub>2 attack on phenacyl chloride.

**B** is incorrect as the structure shown does not correspond to the transition state for the S<sub>N</sub>2 mechanism of this reaction.

**D** is incorrect as the structure shown does not correspond to the transition state formed during the S<sub>N</sub>2 reaction of phenacyl chloride with NaOH.

parts.problemMd:
Coniine is the major constituent of the poison 'oil of hemlock'.

![Structure of coniine showing a six-membered piperidine ring with a nitrogen atom and a propyl substituent](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/15-halogen-compounds/15-1-halogenoalkanes/assets/004-structure-of-coniine-showing-a-six-membered-pipe.jpg)

Coniine can be synthesised by reacting ammonia with a dibromo compound, **X,**C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>16</sub>Br<sub>2</sub> .

NH<sub>3</sub> + **X**$\rightarrow$ coniine + 2HBr

What is the name of compound **X**?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Coniine contains a six-membered ring with a nitrogen atom (a piperidine ring).
- To form a six-membered ring from NH<sub>3</sub> via two nucleophilic substitutions, the two Br atoms must be separated by four carbons (positions 1 and 5 of an octane chain).
- 1,5-dibromooctane has Br at C1 and C5, which allows NH<sub>3</sub> to displace both Br atoms and close into a six-membered ring.

![Structural formula of 1,5-dibromooctane showing bromine atoms at positions C1 and C5 of the octane chain with a propyl substituent at C5](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/15-halogen-compounds/15-1-halogenoalkanes/assets/005-structural-formula-of-1-5-dibromooctane-showing-.jpg)

![Step 1: NH₃ attacking the C1–Br bond of 1,5-dibromooctane by SN2 nucleophilic substitution to displace Br⁻](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/15-halogen-compounds/15-1-halogenoalkanes/assets/006-step-1-nh-attacking-the-c1-br-bond-of-1-5-dibrom.jpg)

- Ammonia attacks the C–Br bonds via nucleophilic substitution to form coniine.

![Step 2: intramolecular SN2 cyclisation forming the six-membered piperidine ring intermediate with a positive charge on nitrogen](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/15-halogen-compounds/15-1-halogenoalkanes/assets/007-step-2-intramolecular-sn2-cyclisation-forming-th.jpg)

![Step 3: deprotonation of the ammonium salt intermediate to give coniine, a piperidine ring with a propyl chain](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/15-halogen-compounds/15-1-halogenoalkanes/assets/008-step-3-deprotonation-of-the-ammonium-salt-interm.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as 1,1-dibromo-2-propylcyclopentane has both Br atoms on the same carbon (geminal dibromide). Two substitutions at the same carbon cannot form the required ring.

**B** is incorrect as 1,2-dibromo-2-propylcyclopentane has Br atoms on adjacent carbons. The two N–C bonds formed would be too close together to produce the six-membered ring of coniine.

**C** is incorrect as 1,4-dibromooctane has Br at C1 and C4, separated by only three carbons. Double substitution with NH<sub>3</sub> would give a five-membered ring, not the six-membered piperidine ring of coniine.

parts.problemMd:
A reaction pathway diagram is shown.

![Double-bump reaction pathway diagram with two transition state energy maxima and one intermediate energy minimum, characteristic of a two-step mechanism](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/15-halogen-compounds/15-1-halogenoalkanes/assets/019-double-bump-reaction-pathway-diagram-with-two-tr.jpg)

Which reaction does **not** have such a profile?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****B ****because:**

- Reaction pathway diagrams display information about the energy changes during chemical reactions.

- The reaction pathway diagram shows a tertiary halogenoalkane which undergoes the S<sub>N</sub>1 mechanism for nucleophilic substitution reactions.

- The first bump corresponds to the slow step, as more energy is required here, and the second bump corresponds to the fast step, as less energy is required at this stage.

- The halogenoalkane C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>Br in option **B** is a primary halogenoalkane which undergoes the S<sub>N</sub>2 mechanism for nucleophilic substitution.

- This kind of reaction can be represented on a reaction pathway by a single bump, as shown below:

![Energy profile diagram of a nucleophilic substitution, showing reactants, high transition state, and products C–O–H and Br⁻ with partial charges and bonds](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/15-halogen-compounds/15-1-halogenoalkanes/assets/020-energy-profile-diagram-of-a-nucleophilic-substit.jpg)

- The peak represents the formation of the transition state, where the outgoing Br and the incoming OH are half-bonded with the functional group carbon atom.

  - Therefore, option **B** is correct.

**A, C **&** D **are incorrect as these are all examples of S<sub>N</sub>1 reactions, and follow the double bump reaction pathway.

parts.problemMd: Which molecule has **no** permanent dipole?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- C<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>4</sub> (tetrachloroethene) is a symmetrical molecule: both carbon atoms carry two Cl atoms each.
- The C–Cl bond dipoles are arranged symmetrically and cancel exactly, so there is no net permanent dipole.

**A** is incorrect as CCl<sub>2</sub>F<sub>2</sub> contains both C–Cl and C–F bonds. These bonds have different dipole magnitudes because F and Cl have different electronegativities, so the bond dipoles do not cancel – there is a net permanent dipole.

**B** is incorrect as CHCl<sub>3</sub> contains three C–Cl bonds and one C–H bond. The molecule is not symmetrical, so the dipoles do not cancel – there is a net permanent dipole.

**D** is incorrect as C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>Cl contains a C–Cl bond and the molecule is not symmetrical, giving a net permanent dipole.

parts.problemMd:
Primary halogenoalkanes, such as RCH<sub>2</sub>X, and tertiary halogenoalkanes, such as R<sub>3</sub>CX, undergo hydrolysis with aqueous sodium hydroxide via different mechanisms.

i) Name the mechanism for the hydrolysis of a primary halogenoalkane.

Draw the structure of the transition state formed in this reaction.

[2]

ii) Name the mechanism for the hydrolysis of a tertiary halogenoalkane.

Draw the structure of the intermediate formed in this reaction.

[2]

iii) State one difference between these two mechanisms in terms of the species involved in the rate-determining step.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The mechanism for hydrolysis of RCH<sub>2</sub>X (primary) is:
> 
> - S<sub>N</sub>2 **[1 mark]**
> 
> The transition state is:
> 
> ![Transition state of RCH2X reacting with OH−](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/15-halogen-compounds/15-1-halogenoalkanes/assets/037-transition-state-of-rch2x-reacting-with-oh.png)
> 
> **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The mechanism for hydrolysis of R<sub>3</sub>CX (tertiary) is:
> 
> - S<sub>N</sub>1 **[1 mark]**
> 
> The structure of the intermediate formed in this reaction is:
> 
> ![Chemical diagram of a trigonal planar carbocation: central positively charged carbon atom bonded to three generic R groups at roughly 120 degrees apart](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/15-halogen-compounds/15-1-halogenoalkanes/assets/038-chemical-diagram-of-a-trigonal-planar-carbocatio.png)
> 
> **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) One difference between these two mechanisms in terms of the species involved in the rate-determining step is:
> 
> - In S<sub>N</sub>2 (primary), both RCH<sub>2</sub>X **AND** OH<sup>−</sup> are involved in the rate-determining step **[1 mark]**
> - In S<sub>N</sub>1 (tertiary), only R<sub>3</sub>CX is involved in the rate-determining step **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> S<sub>N</sub>2 (primary):
> 
> - One-step mechanism
> - OH<sup>−</sup> attacks as X<sup>−</sup> leaves simultaneously
> - Pentavalent transition state.
> 
> S<sub>N</sub>1 (tertiary):
> 
> - Two-step mechanism
> - C–X ionises first (slow, rate-determining)
> - OH<sup>−</sup> then attacks the carbocation (fast)
> 
> Both are nucleophilic substitution reactions.

parts.problemMd: Explain why concentrated sulfuric acid cannot be used to prepare iodoalkanes from potassium iodide.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Concentrated sulfuric acid cannot be used because:
> 
> - Concentrated sulfuric acid will oxidise I<sup>-</sup> ions to I<sub>2</sub> / iodide ions to iodine
> **OR**
> Iodide ions would be oxidised: 2I<sup>-</sup> → I<sub>2</sub> + 2e<sup>-</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> This question links to the reducing ability of halide ions. The reducing ability increases down Group 17:
> 
> F<sup>-</sup> < Cl<sup>-</sup> < Br<sup>-</sup> < I<sup>-</sup>.
> 
> In the reaction with concentrated sulfuric acid, iodide ions are strong enough reducing agents to reduce the sulfuric acid, which means the iodide ions are oxidised to iodine (I<sub>2</sub>) instead of forming HI. No HI is produced, so no iodoalkane can be formed.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Bromobutanes react with hot ethanolic potassium hydroxide solution to produce gaseous butenes.

0.0080 mol of liquid 1-bromobutane was injected into a round bottom flask containing hot ethanolic potassium hydroxide. After the reaction, the syringe was sealed using a clamp and removed from the apparatus. It was then allowed to cool to 25 °C.

The final volume of but-1-ene collected was 22.0 cm³.

Calculate the percentage of 1-bromobutane which was converted to but-1-ene. Show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the percentage of 1-bromobutane converted to but-1-ene:

- Calculate the theoretical volume of but-1-ene if all 1-bromobutane reacted:

theoretical volume = 0.0080 × 24 000 = 192 cm<sup>3</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the percentage converted:

percentage = $\frac{22.0}{192}$ × 100 = **11.5 %** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> A correct answer without working scores 2 marks.
> 
> Allow alternative method:
> 
> moles of but-1-ene = 22.0 ÷ 24 000 = 9.17 × 10<sup>-4</sup> mol
> 
> percentage = (9.17 × 10<sup>-4</sup> ÷ 0.0080) × 100 = 11.5%

> **[exam-tip]**
> As the reaction ratio is 1:1, 0.0080 mol of 1-bromobutane could produce a maximum of 0.0080 mol but-1-ene.
> 
> Method 1: calculate the theoretical volume (moles × 24 000), then find what percentage 22.0 cm<sup>3</sup> is of that volume.
> 
> Method 2: use moles = volume ÷ 24 000 to find the actual moles of but-1-ene, then calculate this as a percentage of 0.0080 mol.
> 
> Don't forget to multiply by 100 to convert to a percentage.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

0.0080 mol of liquid 1-bromobutane was injected into a round bottom flask containing hot ethanolic potassium hydroxide. After the reaction, the syringe was sealed using a clamp and removed from the apparatus. It was then allowed to cool to 25 °C.

The final volume of but-1-ene collected was 22.0 cm^3^.

Before cooling, the volume of but-1-ene in the gas syringe was 24.0 cm<sup>3</sup>.

Assuming constant pressure and that no but-1-ene is lost from the gas syringe during cooling, calculate the temperature of the gas in the syringe before cooling. Show your working.

Temperature = ...................... K
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the temperature of the gas in the syringe before cooling:

- At constant pressure and constant moles, V/T = constant:

$\frac{V_{1}}{T_{1}} = \frac{V_{2}}{T_{2}}$

$\frac{24.0}{T_{1}} = \frac{22.0}{298}$

$T_{1} = \frac{24.0\times298}{22.0}$ **[1 mark]**

Temperature = **325 K** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct substitution into V/T = V/T (or equivalent form)
> 
> 1 mark for correct final answer: 325 K (allow 325.1 K)
> 
> A correct answer without working scores 2 marks.

> **[exam-tip]**
> - At constant pressure and constant moles: V/T = constant, so V<sub>1</sub>/T<sub>1</sub> = V<sub>2</sub>/T<sub>2</sub>.
> - Remember to use temperature in kelvin: 25 °C = 298 K.

parts.problemMd: Which reagents could be used in the laboratory to convert propan-1-ol into 1-bromopropane?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Instead of using hydrobromic acid, propan-1-ol can be treated with a mixture of sodium or potassium bromide and concentrated sulfuric acid.

H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + 2KBr $\rightarrow$ K<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + 2HBr

- The hydrogen bromide then reacts with the alcohol.

parts.problemMd: Which skeletal formula represents 4-chloropentan-2-ol?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- The best approach to questions like this is to number the carbon chains.
- Generally, the lowest possible numbers want to be used, then groups are numbered in order of priority.
- The hydroxyl (OH) group is a higher priority group and therefore has a lower number, 2.
- Chlorine therefore takes the higher number, 4.

![Skeletal formula of 4-chloropentan-2-ol with carbons numbered showing OH on carbon 2 and Cl on carbon 4](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/16-hydroxy-compounds/16-1-alcohols/assets/011-skeletal-formula-of-4-chloropentan-2-ol-with-car.jpg)

- The compound is called 4-chloropentan-2-ol.

  - Pentane has 5 carbons, so draw and label this first.
  - Then, the -OH group will be on carbon 2, and the Cl will be on carbon 4.

**A** is incorrect as this compound has 6 carbons. It is 2-chlorohexan-4-ol.

**B** is incorrect as this compound is 2-chloropentan-3-ol.

**C** is incorrect as this compound is 3-chloropentan-2-ol.

parts.problemMd: Which alcohol has a chiral centre **and** can be oxidised to a ketone?

- A ketone is produced when a **secondary alcohol** is oxidised.

  - This eliminates options **C** (a primary alcohol) and **D** (a tertiary alcohol).
- A chiral centre is a carbon atom bonded to four different atoms or groups.
- The only compound with a chiral centre is pentan-2-ol:

![Skeletal formula of pentan-2-ol with the chiral centre highlighted](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/16-hydroxy-compounds/16-1-alcohols/assets/013-skeletal-formula-of-pentan-2-ol-with-the-chiral-.jpg)

- Therefore, **A** is correct.

**B** is incorrect as pentan-3-ol is a secondary alcohol, but it does not have a chiral centre.

**C** is incorrect as 3-methylhexan-1-ol is a primary alcohol.

**D** is incorrect as 3-methylhexan-3-ol is a tertiary alcohol.
