parts.problemMd:
When NaBH<sub>4</sub> is used as a reducing agent, carbonyl compounds are reduced to alcohols.

i) State the class of alcohol formed when each of the following is reduced by NaBH<sub>4</sub>:

an aldehyde (e.g. propanal)

a ketone (e.g. butanone)

[2]

ii) Explain why the reduction product of butanone can exhibit optical isomerism, but the reduction product of propanal cannot.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) Classes of alcohol formed:
> 
> - An aldehyde (e.g. propanal) is reduced to a primary alcohol **[1 mark]**
> - A ketone (e.g. butanone) is reduced to a secondary alcohol **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) Explanation:
> 
> - The reduction product of propanal is propan-1-ol: the alcoholic carbon has two H atoms attached, so it cannot have four different groups and cannot be a chiral centre **[1 mark]**
> - The reduction product of butanone is butan-2-ol: the alcoholic carbon has H, OH, CH<sub>3</sub>, and CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> attached / four different groups, giving a chiral centre and allowing optical isomers **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A chiral centre requires four different substituents on one carbon. Primary alcohols always have two H atoms on the alcoholic carbon, so a chiral centre is impossible. Whether a secondary alcohol has a chiral centre depends on whether the two groups on either side of the C–OH are different. For butan-2-ol they are (CH<sub>3</sub> and CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>), but for propan-2-ol they are not (both CH<sub>3</sub>).

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

When NaBH~4~ is used as a reducing agent, carbonyl compounds are reduced to alcohols.

i) State the class of alcohol formed when each of the following is reduced by NaBH~4~:

an aldehyde (e.g. propanal)

a ketone (e.g. butanone)

i) Classes of alcohol formed:

- An aldehyde (e.g. propanal) is reduced to a primary alcohol
- A ketone (e.g. butanone) is reduced to a secondary alcohol

Explain why the reduction product of a carbonyl compound, by NaBH<sub>4</sub> and acid, cannot be a tertiary alcohol.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The reduction product of a carbonyl compound cannot be a tertiary alcohol because:
> 
> - Tertiary alcohols have the formula R<sub>3</sub>COH, requiring three carbon groups on the alcoholic carbon
> **AND**
> Carbonyl compounds have the formula R<sub>2</sub>C=O, with only two carbon groups on the carbonyl carbon **[1 mark]**
> 
> - Reduction of a ketone (R<sub>2</sub>C=O) gives R<sub>2</sub>CHOH (secondary alcohol)
> **AND**
> Reduction of an aldehyde (RCHO) gives RCH<sub>2</sub>OH (primary alcohol), where the C–H bond formed means the product cannot be a tertiary alcohol **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A tertiary alcohol requires three carbon substituents on the alcoholic carbon. NaBH<sub>4</sub> adds a hydride ion (H<sup>–</sup>) to the carbonyl carbon, so the alcoholic carbon always retains at least one H, making the product primary or secondary, never tertiary.
> 
> The reverse logic also works: tertiary alcohols cannot be oxidised under normal conditions; the reverse of reduction of a carbonyl would therefore be impossible.

parts.problemMd:
This question is about the reactions of an organic compound **R**.

Analysis of 15.0 g of an organic compound, **R**, showed it to contain 69.8% carbon, 2.79 g of oxygen and the remaining mass was hydrogen.

i) Calculate the empirical formula of the organic compound **R**.

ii) Compound **R** has a molecular mass of 86.0 g mol<sup>-1</sup>, deduce the molecular formula of compound **R**.
parts.solutionMd:
i) To calculate the empirical formula of compound R:

- Calculate the mass of each element in the 15.0 g sample:

carbon: 15.0 x $\frac{69.8}{100}$ = 10.47 g

hydrogen: 15.0 – 10.47 – 2.79 = 1.74 g

**[1 mark]**

- Divide each mass by the relative atomic mass:

C = $\frac{10.47}{12.0}$ = 0.8725

H = $\frac{1.74}{1.0}$ = 1.74

O = $\frac{2.79}{16.0}$ = 0.174

**[1 mark]**

- Divide by the smallest value (0.174) to find the simplest ratio:

C : H : O = 5 : 10 : 1

Empirical formula = **C**<sub>**5**</sub>**H**<sub>**10**</sub>**O**

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct masses of carbon (10.47 g) **AND **hydrogen (1.74 g)
> 
> 1 mark for correct moles/ratios for all three elements
> 
> 1 mark for correct empirical formula (C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O)

ii) To deduce the molecular formula:

- Calculate the *M*<sub>r</sub> of the empirical formula:

(5 x 12.0) + (10 x 1.0) + 16.0 = 86.0

- This equals the given *M*<sub>r</sub>, so the molecular formula is:

**C**<sub>**5**</sub>**H**<sub>**10**</sub>**O** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Allow error carried forward from incorrect empirical formula

> **[exam-tip]**
> Alternative method for part i): convert all to percentages first (oxygen = 2.79/15.0 x 100 = 18.6%, hydrogen = 100 – 69.8 – 18.6 = 11.6%), then divide by *A*<sub>r</sub> to get ratios.
> 
> For part ii): if the empirical formula *M*<sub>r</sub> equals the given *M*<sub>r</sub>, the molecular formula is the same as the empirical formula.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Analysis of 15.0 g of an organic compound, **R**, showed it to contain 69.8% carbon, 2.79 g of oxygen and the remaining mass was hydrogen.

Compound **R** has a molecular mass of 86.0 g mol^-1^

Compound **R** is a straight chain organic compound. Compound **R** reacts with HCN, followed by dilute acid, to form compound **S**, which shows optical isomerism.

Compounds **R** and **S** were tested with acidified potassium dichromate(VI) and Tollens' reagent. The results are shown in **Table 2.1**.

**Table 2.1**

|   | **R** | **S** |
|---|---|---|
| Acidified potassium dichromate(VI) | Green solution | Green solution |
| Tollens' reagent | Silver mirror formed | No visible change |

Using this information and your answer from part **(a)**, deduce the identities of compounds **R** and **S**. Justify your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Deduction of the identities of R and S:
> 
> - Both R and S react with acidified K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>, therefore both could be an aldehyde, primary alcohol, or secondary alcohol **[1 mark]**
> 
> - Compound R forms a silver mirror with Tollens' reagent (positive test)
> **AND**
> Compound R has the formula C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O (from part (a)) and is a straight chain compound
> therefore compound R is pentanal **[1 mark]**
> 
> - Compound S reacts with acidified K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> but does not react with Tollens' reagent, therefore it is a primary or secondary alcohol **[1 mark]**
> 
> - Compound S is formed from compound R (pentanal) by reaction with HCN
> **AND**
> compound S is 2-hydroxyhexanenitrile **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Aldehydes give positive results with both acidified K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> and Tollens' reagent. The positive Tollens' result for R confirms it is an aldehyde. With formula C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O and a straight chain, the only possible aldehyde is pentanal.
> 
> The name of compound S must include the 'e': 2-hydroxyhexan**e**nitrile, not 2-hydroxyhexannitrile.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Compound **R** is a straight chain organic compound. Compound **R** reacts with HCN, followed by dilute acid, to form compound **S**, which shows optical isomerism.

Compound S is formed from compound R (pentanal) by reaction with HCN and compound S is 2-hydroxyhexanenitrile.

Draw the three-dimensional structures of the two optical isomers of compound **S**.
parts.solutionMd:
The three-dimensional structures of the two optical isomers of compound S are:

![Diagram comparing four stereoisomers of a chiral carbon bearing OH, CN, hydrogen and a butyl group, with mirror images separated by a dotted line](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/17-carbonyl-compounds/17-1-aldehydes-and-ketones/assets/029-diagram-comparing-four-stereoisomers-of-a-chiral.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct 3D representations of both optical isomers (both structures must be correct to gain the mark)

> **[exam-tip]**
> Compound S is 2-hydroxyhexanenitrile. The chiral centre is carbon 2, which is bonded to H, OH, CN, and CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> (four different groups).
> 
> Use wedge bonds (toward you) and dash bonds (away from you) to show the 3D arrangement. The two structures should be non-superimposable mirror images. Show at least one wedge and one dash in each structure; no bonds should be at 180° to each other.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Compound S is formed from compound R (pentanal) by reaction with HCN and compound S is 2-hydroxyhexanenitrile.

Draw the skeletal formulae of two straight-chain positional isomers of compound **S** that do not exhibit optical isomerism.
parts.solutionMd:
Two straight-chain positional isomers of compound S that do not exhibit optical isomerism are:

![Skeletal formulae of straight chain isomers of 2-hydroxyhexanenitrile](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/17-carbonyl-compounds/17-1-aldehydes-and-ketones/assets/030-skeletal-formulae-of-straight-chain-isomers-of-2.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for any two correct straight-chain positional isomers of compound S in which no carbon has four different groups attached

> **[exam-tip]**
> Compound S is 2-hydroxyhexanenitrile (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>11</sub>NO), containing –OH and –CN groups. Positional isomers place the same functional groups at different positions along the straight chain.
> 
> For the isomer to lack a chiral centre, no carbon should have four different groups attached. For example, placing –OH at the terminal carbon (which then has two H atoms) removes chirality.

parts.problemMd:
'Trans fats' can be found in some vegetable oils and are known to lead to increased blood cholesterol levels.

In the diagrams below, R<sub>1</sub> and R<sub>2</sub> are different hydrocarbon chains.

Which structure represents an optically active trans fatty acid?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- 'Trans fat' is a carboxylic acid with a long aliphatic chain that is unsaturated.

![Structural diagram of a trans fatty acid with a chiral carbon, showing R1 and R2 groups on opposite sides of the C=C double bond with a chiral centre marked with an asterisk](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-1-carboxylic-acids/assets/002-structural-diagram-of-a-trans-fatty-acid-with-a-.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as this compound is not optically active as it does not have a chiral carbon.

**B** and **D** are incorrect as they are not 'trans' in structure as the hydrogen atoms are on the same side of the double bond.

choices.label: A
choices.textMd: Heating propan-1-ol under reflux with acidified potassium dichromate(VI).

choices.label: B
choices.textMd: Heating propanal under reflux with acidified potassium dichromate(VI).

choices.label: C
choices.textMd: Heating propanenitrile under reflux with aqueous sodium hydroxide.

choices.label: D
choices.textMd: Heating propanenitrile under reflux with dilute sulfuric acid.

parts.problemMd: Which reaction does **not** produce propanoic acid?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- When propanenitrile is heated with aqueous sodium hydroxide under reflux, the products are sodium propanoate and ammonia.
- To produce the free carboxylic acid the products would need to be acidified.

**A**, **B** and **D** are incorrect as all of these reactions would produce propanoic acid.

parts.problemMd:
Propanenitrile, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>C$\equiv$N, is used to produce propanoic acid.

What are the conditions for this reaction?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- When propanenitrile is heated under reflux with dilute acid, an ammonium salt and propanoic acid are produced.

**B** is incorrect as acidified potassium dichromate(VI) is used to oxidise alcohols and aldehydes to carboxylic acids, not to hydrolyse nitriles.

**C** is incorrect as sodium borohydride is a mild reducing agent and will not reduce nitrile groups.

**D** is incorrect as while nitriles can be hydrolysed with alkali under reflux, the resulting solution would need to be acidified to produce the carboxylic acid.

parts.problemMd:
Sour milk contains a compound called lactic acid (2-hydroxypropanoic acid) which has the molecular formula CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)CO<sub>2</sub>H.

Which of the following reactions could lactic acid undergo?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Lactic acid has a secondary alcohol group and a carboxylic acid group.
- Reacting lactic acid with **methanoic acid** (HCO<sub>2</sub>H) produces an **ester** from the secondary alcohol group, as shown in reaction B.
- This is a condensation reaction and produces water alongside the ester.

![Diagram showing the esterification of lactic acid with methanoic acid, forming a lactate ester and water](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-1-carboxylic-acids/assets/003-diagram-showing-the-esterification-of-lactic-aci.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as Cl<sub>2</sub> does not substitute the –OH group of a secondary alcohol under normal conditions. The byproduct would also be HOCl, not OCl.

**C** is incorrect as methanol (CH<sub>3</sub>OH) would react with the **carboxylic acid** group in lactic acid, not the alcohol group, producing the methyl ester CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)CO<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>.

**D** is incorrect as NaHCO<sub>3</sub> reacts with the **carboxylic acid** group, not the alcohol group. The product would be CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)CO<sub>2</sub>Na, not CH<sub>3</sub>CH(ONa)CO<sub>2</sub>H as shown.

parts.problemMd:
Apples contain a compound called malic acid.

![Structural formula of malic acid (2-hydroxybutanedioic acid), showing two carboxylic acid groups and one secondary alcohol group](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-1-carboxylic-acids/assets/004-structural-formula-of-malic-acid-2-hydroxybutane.jpg)

Which substance will react with only one hydroxyl group in malic acid under suitable conditions?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- A 'hydroxyl' group is an '–OH' group, which in malic acid appears in both carboxylic acid groups and the alcohol group.
- If the substance only reacts with one hydroxyl group, this must be the alcohol group.

  - So, we must identify what does not react with a carboxylic acid group.
- The dichromate ion (Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2-</sup>), produced when K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> is dissolved in acidified aqueous solution, acts as an oxidising agent.
- Carboxylic acids are already at their highest oxidation state and therefore will not react with acidified dichromate ions.
- The secondary alcohol in malic acid is oxidised to a ketone, which is not oxidised further.

**B** is incorrect as sodium metal reacts with **both** the carboxylic acid groups and the alcohol group in redox reactions, producing a salt and hydrogen gas:

2RCOOH + 2Na $\rightarrow$ 2RCOONa + H<sub>2</sub>

2ROH + 2Na $\rightarrow$ 2RONa + H<sub>2</sub>

**C** is incorrect as sodium hydroxide reacts with **both** carboxylic acid groups in a neutralisation reaction:

RCOOH + NaOH $\rightarrow$ RCOONa + H<sub>2</sub>O

**D** is incorrect as PCl<sub>5</sub> reacts with **both** the carboxylic acid groups (producing an acyl chloride) and the alcohol group (producing a haloalkane):

RCOOH + PCl<sub>5</sub> $\rightarrow$ RCOCl + POCl<sub>3</sub> + HCl

ROH + PCl<sub>5</sub> $\rightarrow$ RCl + POCl<sub>3</sub> + HCl

parts.problemMd:
The natural bacterial fermentation of milk produces a compound called propanoic acid.

Propanoic acid is partly responsible for the flavour of Swiss cheese. Its structure is shown below:

![Structural formula of propanoic acid (CH3CH2COOH), showing the ethyl group attached to the carboxylic acid group](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-1-carboxylic-acids/assets/001-structural-formula-of-propanoic-acid-ch3ch2cooh-.png)

Which starting materials could be used to produce propanoic acid?

| ** ** | **CH**<sub>**3**</sub>**CH**<sub>**2**</sub>**CN** | **CH**<sub>**3**</sub>**CH**<sub>**2**</sub>**CHO** | **CH**<sub>**3**</sub>**CH**<sub>**2**</sub>**CH**<sub>**2**</sub>**OH** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | **✓** | **✓** | **✓** |
| **B** | **✓** | **✓** | **x** |
| **C** | **x** | **✓** | **✓** |
| **D** | **✓** | **x** | **x** |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- Compound 1, propanenitrile, can be hydrolysed to propanoic acid by heating with dilute hydrochloric acid.

- Compound 2, propanal, can be oxidised to propanoic acid by heating with acidified aqueous potassium dichromate(VI).

- Compound 3, propan-1-ol, can be oxidised to propanoic acid by heating under reflux with acidified aqueous potassium dichromate(VI).

**B**, **C** and **D** are incorrect as each is missing at least one valid reaction route to propanoic acid.

parts.problemMd:
*Sirolimus* is a drug used to treat patients after kidney transplants.

![Structural formula of sirolimus, a macrolide drug containing both ester and amide bonds](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-1-carboxylic-acids/assets/007-structural-formula-of-sirolimus-a-macrolide-drug.png)

*Sirolimus* produces an equimolar mixture of two organic products, on reaction with hot aqueous sodium hydroxide.

What is the structural formula of the product with the lower relative molecular mass?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- NaOH hydrolyses the ester and amide bonds in sirolimus.
- The carboxylic acid produced undergoes neutralisation with NaOH to produce a carboxylate salt (RCOO<sup>–</sup>Na<sup>+</sup>) and water.

![Diagram showing the two organic products of sirolimus hydrolysis with hot aqueous NaOH, with the lower Mr product highlighted](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-1-carboxylic-acids/assets/008-diagram-showing-the-two-organic-products-of-siro.jpg)

> **[exam-tip]**
> Amide bonds appear in Topic 28 of the syllabus and, like ester bonds, can be hydrolysed by hot aqueous sodium hydroxide. Being familiar with both bond types helps when analysing complex molecules such as sirolimus, which contains both.

parts.problemMd:
Compound **K**, C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O, is oxidised by acidified aqueous potassium dichromate(VI) to compound **L**.

Compound **L** reacts with butan-2-ol in the presence of a little concentrated sulfuric acid to give liquid **M**.

What could be the formula of liquid **M**?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O has zero degrees of unsaturation.

  - So, **K **must be a saturated compound.
  - It cannot be a ketone or aldehyde.
- Since **K **is oxidised to give a carboxylic acid, **K **must be a primary alcohol and **L **is a carboxylic acid.
- When a carboxylic acid reacts with an alcohol in the presence of a sulfuric acid catalyst, an ester is produced.
- The ester contains the butan-2-ol portion -OCH(CH<sub>3</sub>)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>

  - This is seen in **C**: CH<sub>3</sub>(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>

![Diagram showing the esterification of compound L with butan-2-ol to produce ester M, with the butan-2-ol portion of the ester highlighted](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-1-carboxylic-acids/assets/010-diagram-showing-the-esterification-of-compound-l.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as this would be the product if compound **L** reacted with 2-methylpropan-2-ol.

**B** is incorrect as this would be the product if compound **L** reacted with butan-1-ol.

**D** is incorrect as this would be the product if compound **L** reacted with 2-methylpropan-1-ol.

parts.problemMd:
Compound **X** can be made from 2-hydroxybutanoic acid.

![Structural formula of compound X, a cyclic diester formed from two molecules of 2-hydroxybutanoic acid condensing together](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-1-carboxylic-acids/assets/009-structural-formula-of-compound-x-a-cyclic-dieste.jpg)

What should be heated with 2-hydroxybutanoic acid in order to make compound **X**?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- 2-hydroxybutanoic acid has both an alcohol and carboxylic acid group
- Therefore, 2 molecules can react together in a condensation reaction, forming a diester (a molecule with two ester groups).
- Concentrated sulfuric acid acts as a catalyst in condensation reactions that result in esters.

**A** is incorrect as reacting 2-hydroxybutanoic acid with acidified aqueous potassium manganate(VII) would cause the secondary alcohol group to oxidise to a ketone, resulting in 2-oxobutanoic acid (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COCOOH).

**B** is incorrect as aluminium oxide (Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>) acts as a catalyst in the dehydration of alcohols to alkenes, therefore reacting 2-hydroxybutanoic acid with aluminium oxide would produce but-2-en-oic acid (CH<sub>3</sub>CH=CHCOOH).

**D** is incorrect as 2-hydroxybutanoic acid and sodium hydroxide would undergo a neutralisation reaction resulting in an organic salt CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(OH)COONa and water.

parts.problemMd:
Oxaloacetic acid can be synthesised from fumaric acid in a two-step process involving intermediate **Z**.

HO<sub>2</sub>CCH=CHCO<sub>2</sub>H $\overset{\mathrm{step}1}{\rightarrow}$ **Z** $\overset{\mathrm{step}2}{\rightarrow}$ HO<sub>2</sub>CCOCH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H

Each step involved can be achieved in the laboratory by using a single reagent.

Which row identifies intermediate **Z** and the reagent for step 2?

|   | **Z** | Reagent for step 2 |
|---|---|---|
| A | HO<sub>2</sub>CCH(OH)CH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H | Fehling's solution |
| B | HO<sub>2</sub>CCH(OH)CH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H | Acidified aqueous potassium manganate(VII), heat |
| C | HO<sub>2</sub>CCHBrCH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H | Acidified aqueous potassium manganate(VII), heat |
| D | HO<sub>2</sub>CCHBrCH(OH)CO<sub>2</sub>H | Warm NaOH (aq) |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Fumaric acid has an alkene functional group and oxaloacetic acid has a carbonyl functional group.
- Therefore, in step 1 the alkene group in fumaric acid is hydrated to produce an alcohol (**Z**) and in step 2 this alcohol group is oxidised to a ketone.
- The structure of **Z **is HO<sub>2</sub>CCH(OH)CH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H as there is an alcohol group on the 2nd carbon (which has the alkene group in fumaric acid).
- The reagent for step 2 is acidified aqueous potassium dichromate(VI), heated.

**A** is incorrect as Fehling's solution is an oxidising agent that converts aldehydes into carboxylic acids. Fehling's solution does not oxidise secondary alcohols as Cu<sup>2+</sup> is not a sufficiently strong oxidising agent.

**C** is incorrect as HO<sub>2</sub>CCHBrCH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H cannot be converted into oxaloacetic acid in a single step using acidified aqueous potassium manganate(VII).

**D** is incorrect as although the bromohydrin Z can be made in step 1 using Br<sub>2</sub> (aq), in step 2 NaOH would cause nucleophilic substitution of the C–Br bond and neutralise the carboxylic acid groups. It cannot produce the required ketone in a single step.

parts.problemMd:
Citric acid has the formula HO<sub>2</sub>CCH<sub>2</sub>C(OH)(CO<sub>2</sub>H)CH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H.

What is the volume of 0.2 mol dm<sup>–3</sup> aqueous sodium hydroxide required to neutralise a solution containing 0.008 mol of citric acid?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Calculate moles of NaOH required:

- Citric acid contains 3 carboxylic acid groups, each neutralised by one NaOH molecule.
- Therefore, for every 1 mole of citric acid, 3 moles of NaOH are required.
- 0.008 moles of citric acid is used.

0.008 x 3 = 0.024 moles of NaOH are required.

- Calculate volume of NaOH required:

moles = concentration x volume

volume = $\frac{\mathrm{moles}}{\mathrm{concentration}}$

volume = $\frac{0.024}{0.2}$

volume = 0.12 dm<sup>3</sup>

- Convert from dm<sup>3</sup> to cm<sup>3</sup>:

volume = 0.12 × 1000 = 120 cm<sup>3</sup>

**A** is incorrect as it assumes a 1:1 molar ratio between citric acid and NaOH, giving 40 cm<sup>3</sup>. The word "acid" does not always mean one acidic group.

**B** is incorrect as it assumes a 1:2 molar ratio. This occurs when only two of the three carboxylic acid groups are identified, giving 80 cm<sup>3</sup>. The most common mistake is missing the one written as CO<sub>2</sub>H in the central bracket

**D** is incorrect as it assumes a 1:4 molar ratio by incorrectly treating the alcohol –OH group as acidic. The –OH group is an alcohol, not a phenol, and does not react with NaOH. Counting all four –OH-containing groups gives 160 cm<sup>3</sup>.

parts.problemMd:
The compound 2-ethyl-3-methylbutanoic acid has the following structure:

![Structural formula of 2-ethyl-3-methylbutanoic acid, showing a branched 4-carbon chain with an ethyl group at C2 and methyl group at C3](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-1-carboxylic-acids/assets/005-structural-formula-of-2-ethyl-3-methylbutanoic-a.jpg)

Which compound will produce 2-ethyl-3-methylbutanoic acid by heating under reflux with ethanolic sodium cyanide and subsequent acid hydrolysis of the reaction product?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- Ethanolic sodium cyanide (NaCN) reacts with the halogenoalkane in option A via nucleophilic substitution, extending the carbon chain by one carbon to form a nitrile.
- Acid hydrolysis of the nitrile produces the corresponding carboxylic acid: 2-ethyl-3-methylbutanoic acid.

![Reaction scheme showing the two-step synthesis: halogenoalkane A reacts with ethanolic NaCN to form a nitrile intermediate, which is then hydrolysed under acidic conditions to give 2-ethyl-3-methylbutanoic acid](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-1-carboxylic-acids/assets/006-reaction-scheme-showing-the-two-step-synthesis-h.jpg)

**B**, **C** and **D** are incorrect as these halogenoalkanes would produce different carboxylic acids on reaction with ethanolic NaCN followed by acid hydrolysis.

parts.problemMd: Which compound requires the largest amount of cold aqueous sodium hydroxide for the complete neutralisation of 1 mole?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Malic acid has 2 carboxylic acid groups, so 1 mole of malic acid requires 2 moles of NaOH for complete neutralisation.
- Each of the compounds in **A**, **B **and **C **has only 1 carboxylic acid group, requiring only 1 mole of NaOH per mole of compound.

**A**, **B** and **C** are incorrect as lactic acid, gluconic acid and aspirin each have only 1 carboxylic acid group and therefore each require only 1 mole of NaOH per mole.

parts.problemMd: How many isomeric esters, including stereoisomers, can be synthesised from the reaction of methanoic acid with an alcohol of formula C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C**

- Methanoic acid has the formula HCOOH
- When an ester is formed:

  - The acid contributes the group HCOO–
  - The rest of the ester comes from the C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9</sub> alcohol
  - This gives an overall molecular formula of C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O<sub>2</sub>
- There are four different alcohols that can combine with methanoic acid to give four structural isomers of methanoate esters

  - One of these esters (butan-2-yl methanoate) contains a chiral centre, meaning it exists as two enantiomers
- This gives a total of 5 isomers (4 structural isomers, with 1 of them existing as a pair of optical isomers)

parts.problemMd:
The structure of ester **E** is shown in the diagram below.

![Structural formula of 3-methylbutan-1-yl ethanoate (ester E)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-2-esters/assets/008-structural-formula-of-3-methylbutan-1-yl-ethanoa.jpg)

**E** is hydrolysed in the presence of hydrochloric acid.

Which are the products of this hydrolysis?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Ester E is **3-methylbutan-1-yl ethanoate**.
- Acid hydrolysis (using dilute HCl and heat) breaks the ester bond by adding water across it.
- The ethanoate group produces **ethanoic acid**: CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H.
- The 3-methylbutan-1-yl group produces **3-methylbutan-1-ol**: (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH.

![Diagram showing the acid-catalysed hydrolysis of 3-methylbutan-1-yl ethanoate with H2O and H+ catalyst, producing ethanoic acid (labelled carboxylic acid) and 3-methylbutan-1-ol (labelled alcohol), with the ester bond highlighted in yellow](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-2-esters/assets/009-diagram-showing-the-acid-catalysed-hydrolysis-of.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as the alcohol product is incorrectly written as an aldehyde with an extra carbon. Acid hydrolysis of an ester produces an alcohol, not an aldehyde, and 3-methylbutan-1-ol has 5 carbons, not 6.

**C** is incorrect as chloride ions are spectator ions in acid hydrolysis and do not substitute into the ester. The reaction is a hydrolysis (addition of water across the ester bond), not a nucleophilic substitution by Cl<sup>-</sup>.

**D** is incorrect as CH<sub>3</sub>CHO is an aldehyde, not a carboxylic acid. Hydrolysis of an ester always produces a carboxylic acid, in this case ethanoic acid (CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H), not an aldehyde.

parts.problemMd:
The ester shown is responsible for the odour of bananas.

![Structural formula of 3-methylbutan-1-yl ethanoate, the ester responsible for the odour of bananas](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-2-esters/assets/012-structural-formula-of-3-methylbutan-1-yl-ethanoa.jpg)

Which pair of compounds reacts to form this ester?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- The ester in the question is **3-methylbutan-1-yl ethanoate**.
- To identify the reactants, the ester bond is broken:

  - The –C(=O)O– linkage shows the acid contributes –C(=O)–
  - The alcohol contributes –O–.
- The acid part is **ethanoic acid** (CH<sub>3</sub>COOH) as it is a straight-chain 2-carbon carboxylic acid.
- The alcohol part is **3-methylbutan-1-ol** as it is a branched 5-carbon alcohol with the methyl group at C3.
- **C** shows ethanoic acid and 3-methylbutan-1-ol, which is the correct pair.

**A** is incorrect as option A shows a branched carboxylic acid paired with an unbranched alcohol. The branching belongs on the alcohol (3-methylbutan-1-ol), not the acid. The acid in this ester is the straight-chain ethanoic acid.

**B** is incorrect as option B makes the same error as A. A branched carboxylic acid is shown paired with an unbranched alcohol, but the correct combination requires the straight-chain ethanoic acid and the branched 3-methylbutan-1-ol.

**D** is incorrect as option D shows ethanoic acid paired with an alcohol in which the methyl branch is on the wrong carbon. The correct alcohol is 3-methylbutan-1-ol (methyl at C3), not 2-methylbutan-1-ol (methyl at C2).

parts.problemMd:
Cetyl palmitate is a waxy solid and has the molecular formula C<sub>15</sub>H<sub>31</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>C<sub>16</sub>H<sub>33</sub>.

Which products are formed when cetyl palmitate is heated under reflux with an excess of aqueous sodium hydroxide?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- Step 1: the **ester**, C<sub>15</sub>H<sub>31</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>C<sub>16</sub>H<sub>33</sub>, is hydrolysed by dilute alkali under heat:

C<sub>15</sub>H<sub>31</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>C<sub>16</sub>H<sub>33</sub> + NaOH → C<sub>15</sub>H<sub>31</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H + C<sub>16</sub>H<sub>33</sub>OH

- Step 2: the carboxylic acid product, C<sub>15</sub>H<sub>31</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H, reacts with excess sodium hydroxide in a neutralisation reaction to produce C<sub>15</sub>H<sub>31</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>Na and water:

C<sub>15</sub>H<sub>31</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H + NaOH → C<sub>15</sub>H<sub>31</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>Na + H<sub>2</sub>O

- Therefore, the two organic products are C<sub>15</sub>H<sub>31</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>Na and C<sub>16</sub>H<sub>33</sub>OH.

**B** is incorrect as sodium does not replace hydrogen in alcohol groups, only in carboxylic acids.

**C** is incorrect as the structural formula C<sub>15</sub>H<sub>31</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>C<sub>16</sub>H<sub>33</sub> shows the carboxylic acid part of the ester before the ester bond and the alcohol part after. This option gets this the wrong way around.

**D** is incorrect as sodium does not replace hydrogen in alcohol groups, only in carboxylic acids. The structural formula also shows the carboxylic acid part before the ester bond and the alcohol part after, so this option reverses both.

parts.problemMd:
The diagram shows the structure of ethanedioic acid.

![Structural formula of ethanedioic acid: HOOC−COOH](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-2-esters/assets/002-structural-formula-of-ethanedioic-acid-hooc-cooh.jpg)

Ethanedioic acid reacts with ethanol in the presence of a few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid to form a diester. The molecular formula of the diester is C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O<sub>4</sub>.

What is the structural formula of the diester?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Ethanedioic acid has two –COOH groups, each of which undergoes esterification with one ethanol molecule to form one ester linkage.
- After both –COOH groups react, the product is the diester **diethyl oxalate**: CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>-O-CO-CO-O-CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>.
- The two adjacent carbonyl groups (–CO–CO–) come from the ethanedioic acid backbone, and each is linked to an ethyl group (–O–CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>) from ethanol.

![Structural formula of diethyl oxalate (option B): CH3CH2-O-CO-CO-O-CH2CH3](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-2-esters/assets/003-structural-formula-of-diethyl-oxalate-option-b-c.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as this structural formula shows two ester linkages joined directly (–CO<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>–), which places four oxygens consecutively and is not the structure of diethyl oxalate.

**C** is incorrect as the ester linkage atoms are in the wrong order (–O<sub>2</sub>C– instead of –CO<sub>2</sub>–). In a valid ester the carbonyl carbon must come before the ester oxygen when reading from the acid side.

**D** is incorrect as this structural formula represents the diester of ethane-1,2-diol with ethanoic acid (CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OCOCH<sub>3</sub>). This is a different combination of reactants, not the product of ethanedioic acid with ethanol.

parts.problemMd:
Lactic acid is a naturally occurring molecule.

![Structural formula of lactic acid (2-hydroxypropanoic acid), showing a hydroxyl group and a carboxylic acid group](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-2-esters/assets/013-structural-formula-of-lactic-acid-2-hydroxypropa.jpg)

What is a property of lactic acid?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Lactic acid (2-hydroxypropanoic acid) contains both an **alcohol** (–OH) and a **carboxylic acid** (–COOH) functional group in the same molecule.
- In the presence of concentrated sulfuric acid as a catalyst, the –OH group of one lactic acid molecule reacts with the –COOH group of another in a condensation reaction.
- An ester linkage (–CO–O–) forms and water is eliminated, producing a dimer ester.
- The product has the structure: HOOC–CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)–O–CO–CH(OH)–CH<sub>3</sub>.

![Structural formula of the ester product formed when two lactic acid molecules undergo self-esterification](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-2-esters/assets/014-structural-formula-of-the-ester-product-formed-w.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as aqueous bromine is decolourised by alkenes via electrophilic addition. Lactic acid contains no C=C double bond, so it does not react with bromine water.

**C** is incorrect as Fehling's solution is only reduced by aldehydes. Lactic acid does not contain an aldehyde group.

**D** is incorrect as lactic acid is soluble in water because the alcohol (–OH) and carboxylic acid (–COOH) groups both form hydrogen bonds with water molecules.

parts.problemMd: How many ester compounds have the molecular formula C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>2</sub>?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>2</sub> has one degree of unsaturation, consistent with the C=O group in an ester.
- By varying which part comes from the carboxylic acid and which from the alcohol, exactly 4 structural ester isomers are possible:

  - **Methyl propanoate**: CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> (propanoic acid + methanol)
  - **Ethyl ethanoate**: CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> (ethanoic acid + ethanol)
  - **Propan-1-yl methanoate**: HCO<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> (methanoic acid + propan-1-ol)
  - **Propan-2-yl methanoate**: HCO<sub>2</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> (methanoic acid + propan-2-ol)

![Structural formulae of the four ester isomers of C4H8O2: propan-1-yl methanoate, propan-2-yl methanoate, ethyl ethanoate, and methyl propanoate](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-2-esters/assets/001-structural-formulae-of-the-four-ester-isomers-of.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as 2 is an undercount. There are more structural isomers possible by varying both the acid and alcohol components.

**B** is incorrect as 3 is also an undercount. A common error is to overlook propan-2-yl methanoate (the branched-chain methanoate ester).

**D** is incorrect as 5 is an overcount. C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>2</sub> has two other isomers with this molecular formula (butanoic acid and 2-methylpropanoic acid) but these are carboxylic acids, not esters. Counting these as esters gives 5.

parts.problemMd:
Compound **Q** has the formula CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>.

Which row correctly shows the name of compound **Q** and how its boiling point compares with that of butanoic acid?

|   | **Name of Q** | **Boiling point compared to butanoic acid** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | Methyl propanoate | Lower |
| **B** | Propyl methanoate | Lower |
| **C** | Methyl propanoate | Higher |
| **D** | Propyl methanoate | Higher |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- Compound Q is an **ester** made from propanoic acid, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H, and methanol, CH<sub>3</sub>OH.
- The name of an ester starts with the alkyl group from the alcohol (in this case **methyl**), followed by the name of the carboxylic acid (in this case **propanoate**).
- Therefore, the name is **methyl propanoate**.
- The boiling point of methyl propanoate is **lower** than that of butanoic acid because it has only **dipole-dipole attractions** between molecules, whereas butanoic acid has stronger **hydrogen bonds**.

**B** is incorrect as propyl methanoate is the ester formed from methanoic acid and propan-1-ol, not propanoic acid and methanol. The name must reflect which compound provides the alkyl group (methanol → methyl) and which provides the acyl group (propanoic acid → propanoate).

**C** is incorrect as the name methyl propanoate is correct, but the boiling point comparison is wrong. Methyl propanoate has a lower boiling point than butanoic acid, not higher.

**D** is incorrect as both the name and the boiling point comparison are wrong. The correct name is methyl propanoate (not propyl methanoate) and the boiling point is lower than butanoic acid (not higher).

parts.problemMd:
In the presence of an H<sup>+</sup> catalyst, compound X reacts with ethanoic acid to produce the compound below.

![Displayed structural formula of the ester product, showing CH3-C(=O)-CH2-CH2-O-C(=O)-CH3: a 3-oxobutyl chain linked to an ethanoyl group via an ester bond](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-2-esters/assets/010-3-6-h-1.jpg)

What is the molecular formula of compound X?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- The ester shown is produced when compound X reacts with ethanoic acid, CH<sub>3</sub>COOH, in an esterification reaction.
- The -O-C(=O)-CH<sub>3</sub> group in the ester is the ethanoate part, contributed by ethanoic acid.
- The remaining part of the ester, CH<sub>3</sub>-C(=O)-CH<sub>2</sub>-CH<sub>2</sub>-, must come from compound X minus its -OH group.
- Compound X is therefore 1-hydroxybutan-3-one: HO-CH<sub>2</sub>-CH<sub>2</sub>-C(=O)-CH<sub>3</sub>.
- Its molecular formula is C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>2</sub>.

![Diagram showing the acid-catalysed hydrolysis of the ester, with the ester bond highlighted in yellow. Products are labelled 1-hydroxybutan-3-one (C4H8O2) and ethanoic acid (C2H4O2)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-2-esters/assets/011-3-6-h-1a.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O has only one oxygen atom. Compound X requires two oxygen atoms: one for the alcohol (-OH) group and one for the ketone (C=O) group.

**C** is incorrect as C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O<sub>2</sub> contains only two carbon atoms. The 3-oxobutyl chain in the ester requires compound X to have four carbon atoms.

**D** is incorrect as C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O<sub>3</sub> contains only two carbon atoms and three oxygen atoms, so neither the carbon count nor the oxygen count matches compound X.

parts.problemMd:
During a lesson, a teacher heated ethyl propanoate under reflux with aqueous sodium hydroxide. The mixture was then acidified, and the two organic products are then separated, purified and weighed.

Out of the total mass of products obtained, what is the percentage by mass of each product?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Alkaline hydrolysis of ethyl propanoate produces ethanol and sodium propanoate.
- After acidification, the sodium propanoate is converted to propanoic acid.
- The two organic products weighed are therefore **ethanol** and **propanoic acid**.
- Known values:

  - *M*<sub>r</sub>(ethanol, C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH) = (2 x 12) + (6 x 1) + 16 = 46 g mol<sup>-1</sup>
  - *M*<sub>r</sub>(propanoic acid, C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>COOH) = (3 x 12) + (6 x 1) + (2 x 16) = 74 g mol<sup>-1</sup>
- The two products are formed in a 1:1 molar ratio, so total *M*<sub>r</sub> = 46 + 74 = 120 g mol<sup>-1</sup>
- Calculate the percentage by mass of propanoic acid:

% propanoic acid = $\frac{74}{120}$ x 100

% propanoic acid = 61.7%

- Calculate the percentage by mass of ethanol:

% ethanol = $\frac{46}{120}$ x 100

% ethanol = 38.3%

**A** is incorrect as the two products have different molecular masses, so their percentage by masses cannot be equal.

**B** is incorrect as 57.7% and 42.3% arise from using incorrect molecular masses.

**D** is incorrect as 67.6% and 32.4% are obtained when sodium propanoate (*M*<sub>r</sub> = 96) is used instead of propanoic acid (*M*<sub>r</sub> = 74). The mixture was acidified before weighing, so the carboxylate salt is converted to the carboxylic acid.

parts.problemMd:
30 g of an alcohol and 30 g of a carboxylic acid are heated under reflux together to produce 33.2 g of propyl butanoate.

What is the yield of the ester?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- 1 mole of alcohol reacts with 1 mole of carboxylic acid to produce 1 mole of ester.
- Propyl butanoate is produced from propanol (C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>7</sub>OH) and butanoic acid (C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>7</sub>COOH).
- Known values:

  - mass of propanol = 30 g
  - *M*<sub>r</sub>(propanol) = (3 x 12) + (8 x 1) + 16 = 60 g mol<sup>-1</sup>
  - mass of butanoic acid = 30 g
  - *M*<sub>r</sub>(butanoic acid) = (4 x 12) + (8 x 1) + (2 x 16) = 88 g mol<sup>-1</sup>
  - *M*<sub>r</sub>(propyl butanoate) = (7 x 12) + (14 x 1) + (2 x 16) = 130 g mol<sup>-1</sup>
  - mass of propyl butanoate produced = 33.2 g
- Calculate the moles of each reactant:

moles of propanol = $\frac{30}{60}$

moles of propanol = 0.50 mol

moles of butanoic acid = $\frac{30}{88}$

moles of butanoic acid = 0.34 mol

- Butanoic acid provides fewer moles and is therefore the limiting reactant.

- Calculate the theoretical yield of propyl butanoate:

theoretical yield = 0.34 x 130

theoretical yield = 44.2 g

- Calculate the percentage yield:

% yield = $\frac{33.2}{44.2}$ x 100

% yield = 75 %

**A** is incorrect as 25% is obtained by dividing the mass of ester produced (33.2 g) by its *M*<sub>r</sub> (130 g mol<sup>-1</sup>) and treating the result as a percentage, rather than calculating the theoretical yield from the limiting reactant.

**B** is incorrect as 38% arises from dividing the actual mass of ester (33.2 g) by the *M*<sub>r</sub> of butanoic acid (88 g mol<sup>-1</sup>) rather than the theoretical yield (44.2 g).

**C** is incorrect as 50% arises from using propanol as the limiting reactant. Propanol provides 0.50 mol whereas butanoic acid provides only 0.34 mol, so butanoic acid is the limiting reactant, giving a theoretical yield of 44.2 g.

parts.problemMd:
30 g of an alcohol and 30 g of a carboxylic acid are heated under reflux together to produce 33 g of propyl butanoate.

What is the yield of the ester?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****D ****because:**

- 1 mole of alcohol reacts with 1 mole of carboxylic acid to produce 1 mole of ester.

- Propyl butanoate is produced from propanol and butanoic acid.

- **Known quantities:**

  - Mass of propanol; 30g
  - Molecular mass of propanol; 60 g mol<sup>-1</sup> *from periodic table*
  - Mass of butanoic acid; 30g
  - Molecular mass of butanoic acid; 88 g mol<sup>-1</sup> *from periodic table*
  - Mass of propyl butanoate produced; 33g
  - Molecular mass of propyl butanoate; 146 g mol<sup>-1</sup> *from periodic table*

- **Calculate the number of moles of each reactant:**

  - $moles=\frac{mass}{M_{r}}$
  - moles propanol = $\frac{30}{60}$ = 0.50 mol
  - moles butanoic acid = $\frac{30}{88}$ = 0.34 mol
  - *Therefore, butanoic acid is the limiting reactant – only 0.34 mol of each react.*

- **Calculate theoretical yield of propyl butanoate:**

  - moles × M<sub>r</sub> = mass
  - 0.34 mol × 146 g mol<sup>-1</sup> = 49.8 g

- **Calculate percentage yield of propyl butanoate:**

  - $\% y i e l d = \frac{a c t u a l y e i l d}{t h e o r e t i c a l y e i l d } \times 100 \%$
  - % yield = 33.0 g / 49.8 g × 100%
  - % yield = 66.26 % = **66 %**

choices.label: A
choices.textMd: Heating an ester with dilute acid under reflux produces a sodium carboxylate and an alcohol

choices.label: B
choices.textMd: Heating an ester with dilute alkali under reflux produces a carboxylic acid and an alcohol

choices.label: C
choices.textMd: Heating an ester with dilute acid under reflux produces a carboxylic acid and an alcohol in a reversible reaction.

choices.label: D
choices.textMd: Heating an ester with dilute alkali under reflux produces a carboxylic acid and an alcohol in a reversible reaction.

parts.problemMd: Which statement correctly describes the hydrolysis of an ester?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Acid hydrolysis of an ester (using dilute acid such as sulfuric acid) produces a carboxylic acid and an alcohol.
- This reaction is reversible, so an equilibrium mixture is formed.
- Rule of thumb:

  - Acid hydrolysis = reversible → carboxylic acid
  - Alkaline hydrolysis = irreversible → carboxylate salt

**A** is incorrect as sodium carboxylates are formed in alkaline, not acidic, hydrolysis.

**B** is incorrect as alkaline hydrolysis forms a carboxylate salt, not a carboxylic acid.

**D** is incorrect as alkaline hydrolysis is irreversible, not reversible.

parts.problemMd:
This question is about carboxylic acids.

State the general formula of a carboxylic acid
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The general formula of a carboxylic acid is:
> 
> - C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+1</sub>COOH **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The general formula can be understood by thinking about the carbon chain:
> 
> ![Hand-drawn structural formula of a carboxylic acid with a carbon chain and labelled hydrogens, showing an attached COOH group and notes “Above” and “Below”](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-1-carboxylic-acids/assets/023-hand-drawn-structural-formula-of-a-carboxylic-ac.png)
> 
> - For every carbon in the hydrocarbon chain, there is a hydrogen above and a hydrogen below, giving 2n hydrogens for n carbons
> - There is also one extra hydrogen at the end of the chain, giving 2n + 1 hydrogens in total
> - This gives the C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+1</sub> portion of the formula, with the carboxylic acid group (–COOH) added at the end

parts.problemMd:
State the systematic name of the carboxylic acid shown in Fig. 1.1.

![Displayed formula of a carboxylic acid, CH3CH(CH3)CH2COOH](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-1-carboxylic-acids/assets/024-displayed-formula-of-a-carboxylic-acid-ch3ch-ch3.png)

**Fig. 1.1**
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The systematic name of the carboxylic acid in Fig. 1.1 is:
> 
> - 3-methylbutanoic acid **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> To name a carboxylic acid systematically:
> 
> - Identify the longest carbon chain that includes the –COOH group — four carbons gives the stem "butan-"
> - The –COOH carbon is always carbon-1, so it does not need to be numbered in the name
> - Identify any substituents: there is a methyl group attached to carbon-3
> - Combine to give: 3-methylbutanoic acid

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

State the systematic name of the carboxylic acid shown in Fig. 1.1.

Displayed formula of a carboxylic acid, CH3CH(CH3)CH2COOH

Fig. 1.1

The systematic name of the carboxylic acid in Fig. 1.1 is: 3-methylbutanoic acid

i) Construct a balanced symbol equation to show the dissociation of the acid from part (b).

[1]

ii) State where the position of the equilibrium lies and what this says about the strength of the acid.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The balanced equation for the dissociation of 3-methylbutanoic acid is:
> 
> - CH<sub>3</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)CH<sub>2</sub>COOH ⇋ CH<sub>3</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)CH<sub>2</sub>COO<sup>-</sup> + H<sup>+</sup>
> **OR**
> C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9</sub>COOH ⇋ C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9</sub>COO<sup>-</sup> + H<sup>+</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> The equation must have a reversible arrow
> 
> ii) The position of the equilibrium and what this indicates:
> 
> - To the left **[1 mark]**
> - (This indicates it is a) weak acid **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Carboxylic acids are weak acids because they only partially dissociate in aqueous solution. The equilibrium lies to the left, meaning most molecules remain in the undissociated acid form.
> 
> Compare this with strong acids such as HCl, which fully dissociate and their equilibria lie completely to the right.
> 
> Always use the equilibrium symbol (⇋) rather than a forward arrow (→) when showing the dissociation of a weak acid, to reflect the reversible nature of the reaction.

parts.problemMd: Construct a balanced symbol equation, including state symbols, for the reaction of propanoic acid with sodium hydrogen carbonate powder.
parts.solutionMd:
The balanced symbol equation for the reaction of propanoic acid with sodium hydrogen carbonate is:

CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOH (aq) + NaHCO<sub>3</sub> (s) → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COONa (aq) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l) + CO<sub>2</sub> (g)

**OR**

C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>COOH (aq) + NaHCO<sub>3</sub> (s) → C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>COONa (aq) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l) + CO<sub>2</sub> (g)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a correct balanced equation with correct formulae for all species
> 
> Allow CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOH or C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>COOH for propanoic acid
> 
> 1 mark for correct state symbols: (aq) for propanoic acid and sodium propanoate, (s) for sodium hydrogen carbonate, (l) for water, and (g) for carbon dioxide

> **[exam-tip]**
> The reaction of a carboxylic acid with a hydrogen carbonate follows the pattern:
> 
> acid + hydrogen carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide
> 
> The salt formed is sodium propanoate (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COONa), which is soluble and has the state symbol (aq). The sodium hydrogen carbonate is a solid powder (s), the water produced is a liquid (l), and the carbon dioxide produced is a gas (g).

Construct an equation for reaction **1**, using [H] to represent one atom of hydrogen from the reducing agent.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> An equation for reaction 1, using [H] to represent one atom of hydrogen from the reducing agent:
> 
> - CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H + 4[H] → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH + H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Reaction 1 shows the reduction of propanoic acid to propan-1-ol. The [H] notation represents one atom of hydrogen from the reducing agent, so four [H] atoms are needed overall.

> The reduction of a carboxylic acid follows the pattern:

> R–COOH + 4[H] → R–CH<sub>2</sub>OH + H<sub>2</sub>O

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A series of reactions based on propanoic acid is shown.

i) Name the type of reaction for reaction **2**.

[1]

ii) State a suitable reagent and conditions for reaction **2**.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The type of reaction for reaction 2 is:
> 
> - Oxidation **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) A suitable reagent and conditions for reaction 2:
> 
> - Acidified potassium dichromate(VI) / acidified potassium manganate(VII) **[1 mark]**
> - Reflux **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Reaction 2 converts propan-1-ol to propanoic acid. Since the organic product gains oxygen compared to the reactant, this is oxidation.
> 
> The two standard oxidising agents for oxidising primary alcohols to carboxylic acids are:
> 
> - Acidified potassium dichromate(VI) (K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>): orange solution turns green as Cr(VI) is reduced to Cr(III)
> - Acidified potassium manganate(VII) (KMnO<sub>4</sub>): purple solution turns colourless as Mn(VII) is reduced
> 
> Reflux conditions are required to ensure complete oxidation to the carboxylic acid and to prevent any aldehyde intermediate from escaping as vapour.

parts.problemMd: Construct an equation for the reaction of propanoic acid with calcium carbonate, CaCO<sub>3</sub>.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> An equation for the reaction of propanoic acid with calcium carbonate:
> 
> - 2CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H + CaCO<sub>3</sub> → (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>)<sub>2</sub>Ca + H<sub>2</sub>O + CO<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Propanoic acid reacts with calcium carbonate in the same way as any acid reacts with a metal carbonate:
> 
> acid + metal carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide
> 
> The salt formed is calcium propanoate, (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>)<sub>2</sub>Ca. Two molecules of propanoic acid are needed to react with one molecule of CaCO<sub>3</sub> because calcium forms a 2+ ion, so two propanoate anions are required to balance the charge.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A series of reactions based on propanoic acid is shown.

![Flow chart of a series of reactions based on propanoic acid, showing reactions 1, 2, and 3 as arrows between structures](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2023/04/3-6-1a-m-3-6-reaction-of-carboxylic-acid-flow-chart.png)

i) State a suitable reagent and conditions for reaction **3**.

[2]

ii) Identify the other product of reaction **3**.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) A suitable reagent and conditions for reaction 3:
> 
> - CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H / ethanoic acid **[1 mark]**
> - Warm / heat / reflux
> **AND**
> Concentrated sulfuric acid **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The other product of reaction 3:
> 
> - Water **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Reaction 3 shows propan-1-ol reacting with ethanoic acid to form propyl ethanoate, which is an esterification reaction.
> 
> The name of the ester tells you the reagents: the first part of the name (propyl) comes from the alcohol (propan-1-ol), and the second part (ethanoate) comes from the carboxylic acid (ethanoic acid, CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H).
> 
> Esterification is a condensation reaction, where the two reactants join together and a small molecule (water) is eliminated. Concentrated sulfuric acid acts as a catalyst, and heating is required to achieve a reasonable rate of reaction.

parts.problemMd:
2-ethyl-3-methylbutanoic acid is present in fermented products such as rum.

i) Deduce the molecular formula of 2-ethyl-3-methylbutanoic acid.

[1]

ii) State the number of chiral carbon atoms in a molecule of 2-ethyl-3-methylbutanoic acid.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The molecular formula of 2-ethyl-3-methylbutanoic acid is:
> 
> - C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>14</sub>O<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The number of chiral carbon atoms:
> 
> - 1 / one **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> To deduce the molecular formula, count the atoms in the structural formula:
> 
> ![Structure of 2-ethyl-3-methylbutanoic acid](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-1-carboxylic-acids/assets/016-structure-of-2-ethyl-3-methylbutanoic-acid.png)
> 
> - Count carbons:
> 
>   - Main chain (4) + ethyl substituent (2) + methyl substituent (1) = 7 carbons
> - Saturated monocarboxylic acids follow C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n</sub>O<sub>2</sub>
> 
>   - For n = 7 this gives C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>14</sub>O<sub>2</sub>
> 
> To identify chiral carbons, use the displayed formula shown above and look for carbons bonded to four different groups:
> 
> - Carbon-2 is bonded to H, the ethyl group (–C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>), the carboxylic acid group (–CO<sub>2</sub>H), and the C3–C4 chain (–CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)CH<sub>3</sub>)
> 
>   - All four are different, so carbon-2 is chiral
> - Carbon-3 is bonded to H, the methyl substituent (–CH<sub>3</sub>), the terminal methyl (C4, also –CH<sub>3</sub>), and the C2 chain
> 
>   - It has two identical methyl groups, so it is not chiral

parts.problemMd:
A sample of 2-ethyl-3-methylbutanoic acid may be prepared in a school or college laboratory by the oxidation of:

**2-ethyl-3-methylbutan-1-ol** (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCH(C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>)CH<sub>2</sub>OH

i) State the reagent(s) that would be used for this oxidation.

reagent(s) .................................................................................................

colour change from .............................. to ..............................

[2]

ii) This reaction is carried out by heating the reacting chemicals together. What could be the main organic impurity present in the sample of the acid? Explain your answer.

[2]

iii) State whether a distillation apparatus or a reflux apparatus should be used.

Explain your answer.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The reagent and colour change for this oxidation:
> 
> - Acidified potassium dichromate(VI) / acidified K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>
> **OR**
> Acidified potassium manganate(VII) / acidified KMnO<sub>4</sub> **[1 mark]**
> - Orange to green (for K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>)
> **OR**
> Purple to colourless (for KMnO<sub>4</sub>) **[1 mark]**
> 
> The colour change must match the reagent chosen.
> 
> ii) The main organic impurity and reason:
> 
> - 2-ethyl-3-methylbutanal / (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCH(C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>)CHO **[1 mark]**
> - (Because) partial oxidation of the primary alcohol produces an aldehyde / the primary alcohol is not fully oxidised **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The apparatus and reason:
> 
> - Reflux **[1 mark]**
> - To ensure complete oxidation of the primary alcohol to the carboxylic acid / to prevent the intermediate aldehyde from escaping as vapour **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The two common oxidising agents both change colour as they are reduced:
> 
> - Acidified potassium dichromate(VI): orange turns green (Cr(VI) reduced to Cr(III))
> - Acidified potassium manganate(VII): purple turns colourless (Mn(VII) reduced to Mn(II))
> 
> Distillation is used when you want to collect the product as it forms and prevent further oxidation. For example, when stopping at the aldehyde stage. Reflux keeps the mixture in the flask to ensure complete oxidation all the way to the carboxylic acid.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

i) State the reagent(s) that would be used for this oxidation.

reagent(s) .................................................................................................

colour change from .............................. to ..............................

A structural isomer of 2-ethyl-3-methylbutan-1-ol is 2-ethyl-3-methylbutan-2-ol, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHC(OH)(C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>)CH<sub>3</sub>.

What colour change would be seen if this were heated with the reagents you have given in part **(b)(i)**?

Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The colour change observed when 2-ethyl-3-methylbutan-2-ol is heated with the oxidising agent from part (b)(i):
> 
> - No colour change **[1 mark]**
> - (Because) 2-ethyl-3-methylbutan-2-ol is a tertiary alcohol / the –OH group is bonded to a carbon bearing three alkyl groups **[1 mark]**
> 
> Tertiary alcohols cannot be oxidised by acidified dichromate(VI) or manganate(VII).

> **[exam-tip]**
> Classify the alcohol before predicting the outcome of oxidation:
> 
> - Primary alcohols (–OH on a carbon bonded to one alkyl group) can be oxidised to aldehydes, then to carboxylic acids
> - Secondary alcohols (–OH on a carbon bonded to two alkyl groups) can be oxidised to ketones only
> - Tertiary alcohols (–OH on a carbon bonded to three alkyl groups) cannot be oxidised
> 
> 2-ethyl-3-methylbutan-2-ol has the –OH group on a carbon bonded to three alkyl groups, making it a tertiary alcohol. No oxidation occurs and no colour change is observed.

parts.problemMd:
Propan-1-ol can be oxidised to propanoic acid using acidified potassium dichromate(VI).

State the systematic name of the intermediate formed during this oxidation.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The systematic name of the intermediate is:
> 
> - Propanal **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When a primary alcohol is oxidised, the reaction proceeds in two stages:
> 
> 1. Partial oxidation: primary alcohol → aldehyde (using distillation conditions to remove the aldehyde as it forms)
> 2. Full oxidation: primary alcohol → carboxylic acid (using excess oxidising agent under reflux)
> 
> Propan-1-ol oxidises to propanal as the intermediate, which then further oxidises to propanoic acid.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Propan-1-ol can be oxidised to propanoic acid using acidified potassium dichromate(VI).

i) State the final colour of the reaction mixture after the potassium dichromate(VI) has reacted.

[1]

ii) State the conditions to ensure that propanoic acid is obtained in a high yield.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The final colour of the reaction mixture after the potassium dichromate(VI) has reacted:
> 
> - Green **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The conditions to obtain propanoic acid in a high yield:
> 
> - Excess acidified potassium dichromate(VI) **[1 mark]**
> - Reflux **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When propan-1-ol is fully oxidised to propanoic acid:
> 
> - The potassium dichromate(VI) is reduced: the orange Cr(VI) solution turns green as it is converted to Cr(III)
> - Excess oxidising agent is needed to ensure all the aldehyde intermediate (propanal) is further oxidised to propanoic acid
> - Reflux prevents the volatile propanal from escaping as vapour and keeps it in contact with the oxidising agent until fully converted

parts.problemMd: Describe a chemical test and observation which confirms the presence of a carboxyl functional group.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> A chemical test and observation to confirm the presence of a carboxyl group:
> 
> - Add sodium carbonate (Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>) / potassium carbonate (K<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>)
> **OR**
> Add sodium hydrogen carbonate (NaHCO<sub>3</sub>) / potassium hydrogen carbonate (KHCO<sub>3</sub>) **[1 mark]**
> - Effervescence / fizzing / bubbling observed **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Carboxylic acids react with carbonates and hydrogen carbonates to produce carbon dioxide gas, which is observed as effervescence. This is a classic test for the carboxyl (–COOH) functional group.
> 
> Note that phenols do not react with sodium hydrogen carbonate, so NaHCO<sub>3</sub> in particular is useful for distinguishing carboxylic acids from other weakly acidic compounds.

parts.problemMd:
LiAlH<sub>4</sub> is a reducing agent.

LiAlH<sub>4</sub> cannot be used in aqueous solution because it reacts with water to produce LiOH(aq), H<sub>2</sub> (g) and a white precipitate which is soluble in excess sodium hydroxide. Identify the white precipitate.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The white precipitate is:
> 
> - Aluminium hydroxide / Al(OH)<sub>3</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> LiAlH<sub>4</sub> contains both lithium and aluminium. When it reacts with water:
> 
> - Lithium forms LiOH (given in the question)
> - Aluminium forms Al(OH)<sub>3</sub>, a white precipitate
> 
> Al(OH)<sub>3</sub> is amphoteric and it dissolves in excess NaOH to form the aluminate ion [Al(OH)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>-</sup>. This behaviour is a useful identifier: if a white precipitate dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide solution, aluminium ions are present.

parts.problemMd:
Butane-1,2-diol is oxidised to form compound **P** in reaction 1. Compound **P** is then reduced using LiAlH<sub>4</sub> in reaction 2 to give **Q**, and using NaBH<sub>4</sub> in reaction 3 to give **R**, as shown in Fig. 1.1.

![Reaction pathway diagram showing butane-1,2-diol oxidised to compound P, then P reduced by LiAlH4 to give Q and by NaBH4 to give R](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-1-carboxylic-acids/assets/020-reaction-pathway-diagram-showing-butane-1-2-diol.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

i) State the reagents and conditions required for reaction 1.

[2]

ii) Deduce whether **Q** or **R** is 2-hydroxybutanoic acid and explain the difference between reactions 2 and 3.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The reagents and conditions for reaction 1:
> 
> - Potassium dichromate(VI) (K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>) / potassium manganate(VII) (KMnO<sub>4</sub>) **[1 mark]**
> - Acidified (with dilute sulfuric acid)
> **AND**
> Heat under reflux **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) Which compound is 2-hydroxybutanoic acid and the difference between reactions 2 and 3:
> 
> - **R** is 2-hydroxybutanoic acid **[1 mark]**
> - NaBH<sub>4</sub> reduces only carbonyl (C=O) groups and cannot reduce carboxyl (–COOH) groups; LiAlH<sub>4</sub> reduces both **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Compound P contains both a ketone (C=O) and a carboxylic acid (–COOH) group, formed by oxidising both alcohol groups in butane-1,2-diol.
> 
> NaBH<sub>4</sub> is a mild reducing agent that selectively reduces aldehydes and ketones but cannot reduce the more stable carboxylic acid group. This gives R, which retains the –COOH group and is therefore 2-hydroxybutanoic acid.
> 
> LiAlH<sub>4</sub> is a stronger reducing agent that reduces both C=O and –COOH groups, converting the carboxylic acid to a primary alcohol. Q therefore has two alcohol groups rather than the required carboxylic acid.

parts.problemMd:
A third student prepares 2-hydroxybutanoic acid using propanal as the starting material as shown in Fig. 1.2. In step 1, propanal reacts with a mixture of NaCN and HCN.

![Reaction pathway diagram showing propanal reacting with NaCN and HCN to form S in step 1, then S reacting with HCl under reflux in step 2 to give 2-hydroxybutanoic acid](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-1-carboxylic-acids/assets/021-reaction-pathway-diagram-showing-propanal-reacti.png)

**Fig. 1.2**

Draw the mechanism for the reaction of propanal with the mixture of NaCN and HCN to form **S**.

In your mechanism, include:

- the identity of the ion that reacts with propanal
- the structure of the intermediate
- all charges, partial charges, lone pairs and curly arrows
parts.solutionMd:
The mechanism for the reaction of propanal with HCN / NaCN to form S is:

![Nucleophilic addition mechanism showing CN- attacking the carbonyl carbon of propanal, with curly arrows and the tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-1-carboxylic-acids/assets/022-nucleophilic-addition-mechanism-showing-cn-attac.png)

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for :CN<sup>-</sup> identified as the ion that reacts with propanal
> 
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from the lone pair on :CN<sup>-</sup> to the carbonyl carbon
> 
> 1 mark for correct partial charges (δ+ on carbonyl carbon, δ− on oxygen) AND a curly arrow from the C=O bond to the oxygen
> 
> 1 mark for a correct tetrahedral intermediate drawn

> **[exam-tip]**
> This is a nucleophilic addition mechanism. The cyanide ion (:CN<sup>-</sup>) is the nucleophile as it carries a lone pair on the carbon atom and attacks the δ+ carbonyl carbon.
> 
> In the NaCN / HCN mixture, NaCN provides the CN<sup>-</sup> ions and HCN provides the proton that converts the alkoxide intermediate to the hydroxyl group in product S.
> 
> When drawing the mechanism:
> 
> - The curly arrow from :CN<sup>-</sup> must originate from the lone pair on the cyanide carbon (not from the nitrogen end)
> - The curly arrow from C=O must come from the double bond, pushing electrons onto the oxygen to form O<sup>-</sup>
> - The intermediate must show a tetrahedral carbon with an O<sup>-</sup> charge

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A third student prepares 2-hydroxybutanoic acid using propanal as the starting material as shown in Fig. 1.2. In step 1, propanal reacts with a mixture of NaCN and HCN.

Fig. 1.2 shows: Reaction pathway diagram showing propanal reacting with NaCN and HCN to form S in step 1, then S reacting with HCl under reflux in step 2 to give 2-hydroxybutanoic acid

Construct a balanced equation for step 2, in which **S** is heated under reflux with dilute hydrochloric acid.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> A balanced equation for the acid hydrolysis of S in step 2:
> 
> - C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH(OH)CN + HCl + 2H<sub>2</sub>O → C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH(OH)COOH + NH<sub>4</sub>Cl **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The nitrile group (–C≡N) is hydrolysed to a carboxylic acid (–COOH) by heating under reflux with dilute acid. Both HCl and water are required as reactants, but the question may not make this obvious.
> 
> The same hydrolysis can also be carried out using an alkali, but this produces a carboxylate salt and ammonia rather than the free carboxylic acid and ammonium chloride.

parts.problemMd:
Lactic acid, 2-hydroxypropanoic acid, CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)COOH, occurs naturally in sour milk.

Lactic acid is chiral and shows stereoisomerism.

Draw the three-dimensional structures of the two optical isomers of lactic acid.

Use an asterisk (*) to identify the chiral carbon atom in one of the structures.
parts.solutionMd:
The three-dimensional structures of the two optical isomers of lactic acid are:

![Three-dimensional structures of the two optical isomers of lactic acid shown with wedge-and-dash bonds, with the chiral carbon atom marked with an asterisk](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-1-carboxylic-acids/assets/018-three-dimensional-structures-of-the-two-optical-.png)

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 marks for one correct three-dimensional structures with wedge-and-dash bonds shown
> 
> 1 mark for the non-superimposable mirror image
> 
> Allow 1 mark if the structures are drawn as displayed formulae without 3D representation but are otherwise correct
> 
> 1 mark for the chiral carbon atom correctly identified with an asterisk (*) in one of the structures

> **[exam-tip]**
> Optical isomers are non-superimposable mirror images of each other. To draw them correctly for lactic acid:
> 
> - Draw all bonds to the chiral carbon (the one bearing four different groups: H, OH, CH<sub>3</sub>, and COOH)
> - Use wedge bonds (solid triangle) for bonds coming towards you and dashed bonds for bonds going away
> - The second isomer is the mirror image of the first, with the arrangement of groups reversed
> 
> Note that the carbon atom in the COOH group is not chiral as it is bonded to only three different groups (=O, –OH, and the carbon chain), not four.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Step 1:
> 
> - Acidified potassium dichromate(VI) / acidified potassium manganate(VII) **[1 mark]**
> - Distillation **[1 mark]**
> 
> Step 2:
> 
> - HCN / mixture of HCN and NaCN
> **OR**
> KCN with dilute acid **[1 mark]**
> - Room temperature **[1 mark]**
> 
> Step 3:
> 
> - Dilute acid (e.g. HCl / H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>)
> **OR**
> Dilute alkali / NaOH **[1 mark]**
> - Heat under reflux **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The reaction pathway converts ethanol to lactic acid through three steps:
> 
> - Step 1: Ethanol (primary alcohol) → ethanal (aldehyde) by partial oxidation
> - Step 2: Ethanal → 2-hydroxypropanenitrile (hydroxynitrile) by nucleophilic addition of HCN
> - Step 3: 2-hydroxypropanenitrile → 2-hydroxypropanoic acid by hydrolysis of the nitrile group
> 
> In step 1, distillation is essential to remove ethanal as it forms and prevent further oxidation to ethanoic acid.
> 
> In step 3, acid hydrolysis gives the free carboxylic acid; alkali hydrolysis gives a carboxylate salt and ammonia. Both are accepted.

parts.problemMd:
Lactic acid, CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)COOH can be reduced by LiAlH<sub>4</sub>.

i) Construct an equation to show this reaction, using [H] to represent one atom of hydrogen from the reducing agent.

[1]

ii) State the systematic name of the organic product formed in this reaction.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) An equation for the reduction of lactic acid by LiAlH<sub>4</sub>:
> 
> - CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)COOH + 4[H] → CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>2</sub>OH + H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The systematic name of the organic product:
> 
> - Propane-1,2-diol **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> LiAlH<sub>4</sub> reduces the carboxylic acid group (–COOH) to a primary alcohol (–CH<sub>2</sub>OH). Four [H] atoms are needed overall: two to add across the C=O, one to protonate the O<sup>-</sup> to give –OH, and one is lost as part of the water molecule produced.
> 
> The product (propane-1,2-diol) has two alcohol groups:
> 
> ![Displayed formula of propane-1,2-diol showing two hydroxyl groups attached to carbons 1 and 2 of a three-carbon chain](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-1-carboxylic-acids/assets/019-displayed-formula-of-propane-1-2-diol-showing-tw.png)
> 
> - The secondary alcohol on carbon-2 was already present in the lactic acid molecule
> - The primary alcohol on carbon-1 is newly formed from reduction of the –COOH group
