Glycolic acid is added separately to each of the three reagents below.

Complete the table to show what you would observe. If a reaction occurs, state the functional group of glycolic acid responsible for the reaction.

| reagent | observation with glycolic acid | functional group |
|---|---|---|
| Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> |   |   |
| 2,4-DNPH |   |   |
| acidified K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> (aq) and heat |   |   |
parts.solutionMd:
The completed table is:

| reagent | observation with glycolic acid | functional group |
|---|---|---|
| Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> | **Final answer:** **Effervescence / fizzing / bubbling** | **Final answer:** **–COOH / carboxylic acid** |
| 2,4-DNPH | **Final answer:** **No visible reaction** | **Final answer:** **–** |
| acidified K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> (aq) and heat | **Final answer:** **Orange to green** | **Final answer:** **–OH / alcohol** |

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for effervescence / fizzing **AND** –COOH / carboxylic acid for Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>
> 
> 1 mark for no visible reaction for 2,4-DNPH (no functional group required)
>

> **[exam-tip]**
> Glycolic acid (HOCH<sub>2</sub>COOH) contains two functional groups: a primary alcohol (–OH) and a carboxylic acid (–COOH).

parts.problemMd:
All of the esters in part **(a)** are formed via a condensation reaction.

State the catalyst and conditions required to form an ester from a carboxylic acid and an alcohol.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The catalyst and conditions required for esterification are:
> 
> - Concentrated sulfuric acid catalyst **[1 mark]**
> - Heat / heat under reflux **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> This reaction is also called esterification. The concentrated sulfuric acid acts as a catalyst and speeds up the reaction without being consumed. Heating under reflux prevents volatile products from escaping while allowing the reaction to reach equilibrium.

parts.problemMd: State the reagents and conditions required for the acidic hydrolysis of an ester.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The reagents and conditions required for the acidic hydrolysis of an ester are:
> 
> - Dilute acid / dilute H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> / dilute HCl **[1 mark]**
> - Heat / heat under reflux **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Acidic hydrolysis is a reversible reaction that reforms the original carboxylic acid and alcohol. Because it is reversible, heating under reflux is used to keep reactants and products in contact.
> 
> Alkaline hydrolysis (using NaOH) is irreversible and produces a carboxylate salt rather than the free carboxylic acid. This question specifies acidic conditions, so only dilute acid and heat are needed.

> - Perfumes / fragrances
> - Solvents
> - Plasticisers
> 
> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Esters are widely used because of their pleasant fruity or floral smells and low toxicity. As well as food and fragrance applications, they are important industrial solvents and plasticisers used to soften polymers such as PVC.

parts.problemMd:
Two isomeric compounds are shown below in Fig. 1.1.

![Structural formulae of two isomeric hydroxy acids labelled A and B](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-2-esters/assets/015-structural-formulae-of-two-isomeric-hydroxy-acid.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

i) State the systematic name of each isomer.

[1]

ii) Suggest a chemical reagent to distinguish between these isomers and deduce the type of reaction taking place.

[2]

iii) State the observations made in each case.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The systematic names of the two isomers are:
> 
> - A = 3-hydroxy-3-methylbutanoic acid
> **AND**
> B = 2-hydroxy-3-methylbutanoic acid **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) A reagent to distinguish the isomers and the type of reaction:
> 
> - Acidified / H<sup>+</sup> / H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>
> **AND**
> (potassium) dichromate(VI) / K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> / Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2-</sup>
> **OR**
> Acidified / H<sup>+</sup> / H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>
> **AND**
> (potassium) manganate(VII) / KMnO<sub>4</sub> / MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> **[1 mark]**
> - Oxidation **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The observations in each case are:
> 
> - Isomer A: no change / no reaction
> - Isomer B: changes from orange to green
> 
> **OR**
> 
> - Isomer A: no change / no reaction
> - Isomer B: changes from purple to colourless
> 
> **[2 marks]**
> 
> The observations in part (iii) must match the reagent specified in part (ii)

> **[exam-tip]**
> Naming priority: when a molecule contains both a carboxylic acid and a hydroxyl group, the carboxylic acid takes priority as the principal characteristic group. The hydroxyl group is named as a prefix (hydroxy–) and the methyl branch is also a prefix (methyl–).
> 
> Isomer A is a tertiary alcohol where the –OH group is on a carbon bonded to three other carbon groups. Tertiary alcohols cannot be oxidised by dichromate(VI) or manganate(VII) under standard conditions, so isomer A gives no reaction.
> 
> Always state both the before and after colours for the oxidising agent test. 'The solution turns green' is not awarded because you must state it turns from orange to green (for dichromate) or from purple to colourless (for manganate(VII)).

3CH<sub>3</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)CH(OH)COOH (aq) + Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2-</sup> (aq) + 8H<sup>+</sup> (aq) → 3CH<sub>3</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)COCOOH (aq) + 2Cr<sup>3+</sup> (aq) + 7H<sub>2</sub>O (l)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**

> 
> 1 mark for correct balancing
> 
> State symbols are not required

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part (i):
> 
> - [O] represents one oxygen atom from the oxidising agent.
> - In the oxidation of a secondary alcohol –CHOH– to a ketone –C=O–, two hydrogen atoms are removed as H<sub>2</sub>O, so one [O] is needed.
> 
> For part (ii):
> 
> - The B→C half-equation shows 2 electrons transferred.
> - The dichromate half-equation shows 6 electrons.
> - Multiply the B→C half-equation by 3 (to give 6e<sup>–</sup>), add the two half-equations, then cancel the 6H<sup>+</sup> that appear on both sides:
> 
>   - 14H<sup>+</sup> − 6H<sup>+</sup> = 8H<sup>+</sup> on the left.

parts.problemMd:

parts.solutionMd:

**A** is incorrect as this is dimethylamine, a secondary amine with two methyl groups bonded to nitrogen.

parts.problemMd: Which type of reaction is used to synthesise ethylamine from bromoethane?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Bromoethane reacts with excess ethanolic ammonia under pressure.
- Ammonia acts as a nucleophile, donating a lone pair to the electron-deficient carbon bonded to bromine.
- Bromine is displaced as a bromide ion, forming ethylamine via nucleophilic substitution.
- The reaction mechanism is:

![Four-step SN2 nucleophilic substitution mechanism showing ammonia attacking 1-bromoethane, formation of intermediate, deprotonation by second ammonia molecule, and production of ethylamine and ammonium bromide](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/19-nitrogen-compounds/19-1-primary-amines/assets/002-four-step-sn2-nucleophilic-substitution-mechanis.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as electrophilic substitution requires an electrophile as the attacking species. Ammonia is a nucleophile, not an electrophile.

**C** is incorrect as oxidation of bromoethane replaces the C-Br bond with a C-OH bond, forming ethanol (an alcohol), not an amine.

**D** is incorrect as reduction of bromoethane replaces the C-Br bond with a C-H bond, forming ethane (an alkane), not an amine.

- Halogenoalkanes react with excess ethanolic ammonia under pressure via nucleophilic substitution to form a primary amine.
- Ammonia acts as the nucleophile, donating a lone pair to the electron-deficient carbon bonded to bromine, displacing bromide to form ethylamine.

![Four-step SN2 nucleophilic substitution mechanism showing ammonia attacking bromoethane to form ethylamine and ammonium bromide](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/19-nitrogen-compounds/19-1-primary-amines/assets/003-four-step-sn2-nucleophilic-substitution-mechanis.jpg)

**B** is incorrect as methanol reacts with bromoethane via nucleophilic substitution to form an ether (methoxyethane), not an ester.

**C** is incorrect as methylamine does react with bromoethane via nucleophilic substitution, but the product is a secondary amine (N-methylethanamine), not an amide.

**D** is incorrect as water reacts with bromoethane via hydrolysis (nucleophilic substitution) to form ethanol, which is an alcohol and not an acid.

choices.label: A
choices.textMd: A mixture of methylamine, dimethylamine and trimethylamine

parts.problemMd: Iodomethane is heated under pressure with ethanolic ammonia. The ammonia is not in excess. Which organic compounds are formed in the reaction mixture?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- When ammonia is not in excess, the primary amine formed (methylamine) can react further with iodomethane.
- Methylamine acts as a nucleophile and reacts with a second molecule of iodomethane to form dimethylamine (a secondary amine).
- Dimethylamine reacts with a third molecule of iodomethane to form trimethylamine (a tertiary amine).
- A mixture of all three amines is therefore produced.

![Reaction scheme showing iodomethane reacting with ammonia to give methylamine, then with further iodomethane to give dimethylamine and trimethylamine, labelled as primary, secondary, and tertiary amines respectively](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/19-nitrogen-compounds/19-1-primary-amines/assets/001-reaction-scheme-showing-iodomethane-reacting-wit.jpg)

**B** is incorrect as dimethylamine alone would only be produced if the reaction stopped after a single further substitution. In practice all three amines form when ammonia is not in excess.

**C** is incorrect as trimethylamine also forms when ammonia is not in excess. The cascade continues past dimethylamine.

**D** is incorrect as methylamine alone would only be the sole product if ammonia were in excess. Without excess ammonia the reaction cascade continues to give secondary and tertiary amines.

> **[exam-tip]**
> To produce only a primary amine, excess ethanolic ammonia under pressure should be used. The high concentration of ammonia suppresses further substitution, favouring formation of the primary amine only.

parts.problemMd:
1-chloropropane can be used to make propylamine.

Which row shows the correct reagent and type of reaction?

|   | **Reagent** | **Type of reaction** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | Aqueous ammonia | Electrophilic addition |
| **B** | Aqueous ammonia | Nucleophilic substitution |
| **C** | Ethanolic ammonia | Electrophilic addition |
| **D** | Ethanolic ammonia | Nucleophilic substitution |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- 1-chloropropane reacts with excess ethanolic ammonia under pressure via nucleophilic substitution.
- Ammonia acts as the nucleophile, attacking the electron-deficient carbon bonded to chlorine; the chlorine is displaced as a chloride ion to form propylamine.
- The overall equation is:

CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Cl + 2NH<sub>3</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> + NH<sub>4</sub>Cl

**A** is incorrect as electrophilic addition requires an electrophile as the attacking species and applies only to unsaturated molecules. 1-chloropropane is saturated and ammonia is a nucleophile, not an electrophile.

**B** is incorrect as aqueous ammonia hydrolyses 1-chloropropane via nucleophilic substitution to form propan-1-ol (an alcohol), not propylamine. Ethanolic ammonia is required to synthesise the amine.

**C** is incorrect as electrophilic addition applies only to unsaturated molecules. Even with ethanolic ammonia, the reaction type is nucleophilic substitution, not electrophilic addition.

parts.problemMd:
Chloroethane is heated under pressure with an excess of ethanolic ammonia.

Which compound is the main organic product?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- When a halogenoalkane is reacted with excess ethanolic ammonia under pressure, the main product is a primary amine.
- Ammonia acts as the nucleophile, displacing the chlorine atom from chloroethane via nucleophilic substitution to form ethylamine.
- Excess ammonia suppresses further substitution, so the primary amine is the main product.

**B** is incorrect as diethylamine is a secondary amine formed when ethylamine undergoes a further substitution with chloroethane. Excess ammonia suppresses this reaction.

**C** is incorrect as triethylamine is a tertiary amine that would form through a further cascade substitution. Again, excess ammonia prevents this from being the main product.

**D** is incorrect as tetraethylammonium chloride is a quaternary ammonium salt, not an amine, and would only form through extensive substitution in the absence of excess ammonia.

parts.problemMd:
Which row correctly identifies the reagents and conditions for the two reactions shown?

|   | **(CH**<sub>**3**</sub>**)**<sub>**2**</sub>**CO **$\rightarrow$** (CH**<sub>**3**</sub>**)**<sub>**2**</sub>**CHCN** | **CH**<sub>**3**</sub>**CHC*****l*****CH**<sub>**3**</sub>** **$\rightarrow$** CH**<sub>**3**</sub>**CH(NH**<sub>**2**</sub>**)CH**<sub>**3**</sub> |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | Ethanolic KCN, heat | Aqueous NH<sub>3</sub>, heat |
| **B** | Ethanolic KCN, heat | Excess ethanolic NH<sub>3</sub>, heat under pressure |
| **C** | KCN and dilute H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> | Aqueous NH<sub>3</sub>, heat |
| **D** | KCN and dilute H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> | Excess ethanolic NH<sub>3</sub>, heat under pressure |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- In the first reaction, propanone undergoes nucleophilic addition with acidified KCN (KCN and dilute H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>); CN<sup>-</sup> acts as the nucleophile, attacking the carbonyl carbon to form 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile.
- Dilute H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> is required to generate HCN in situ and maintain the acidic conditions needed for nucleophilic addition.

  - Ethanolic KCN alone does not give the cyanohydrin product reliably.
- In the second reaction, 2-chloropropane undergoes nucleophilic substitution with excess ethanolic ammonia under pressure.

  - Ammonia acts as the nucleophile, displacing chlorine to form propan-2-amine.
- Propan-2-amine (CH<sub>3</sub>CH(NH<sub>2</sub>)CH<sub>3</sub>) is a primary amine because the nitrogen carries only one carbon substituent, regardless of the class of the carbon it is bonded to.
- Excess ammonia suppresses further substitution and ensures the primary amine is the main product.

**A** is incorrect as ethanolic KCN does not provide the acidic conditions required for nucleophilic addition in reaction 1, and aqueous ammonia hydrolyses 2-chloropropane to give propan-2-ol (an alcohol) rather than the amine in reaction 2.

**B** is incorrect as ethanolic KCN is the wrong reagent for reaction 1. Dilute H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> is required to generate HCN in situ and promote cyanohydrin formation.

**C** is incorrect as aqueous ammonia hydrolyses 2-chloropropane via nucleophilic substitution to give propan-2-ol (an alcohol), not an amine. Ethanolic ammonia under pressure is required for amine synthesis.

parts.problemMd: Which amine can **not** be produced by the reduction of a nitrile?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Nitrile reduction always produces a primary amine with the -NH<sub>2</sub> group on a primary carbon.
- When a nitrile (-C≡N) is reduced, the nitrile carbon gains two hydrogen atoms and the nitrogen gains two more, giving a -CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> group.

  - The -NH<sub>2</sub> is always positioned on a primary carbon.
- Butan-2-amine has the -NH<sub>2</sub> group attached to C-2, a secondary carbon, which cannot arise from nitrile reduction.

**A** is incorrect as 2,2-dimethylpropan-1-amine can be produced by reducing 2,2-dimethylpropanenitrile. The -NH<sub>2</sub> group is on a primary carbon.

**B** is incorrect as 2-methylpropan-1-amine can be produced by reducing 2-methylpropanenitrile. The -NH<sub>2</sub> group is on a primary carbon.

**C** is incorrect as butan-1-amine can be produced by reducing butanenitrile. The -NH<sub>2</sub> group is on a primary carbon.

parts.problemMd:
What is the systematic name of the compound shown?

![Structural formula of a quaternary ammonium chloride salt showing nitrogen bonded to two methyl groups and two ethyl groups with a positive charge, paired with a chloride anion](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/19-nitrogen-compounds/19-1-primary-amines/assets/004-structural-formula-of-a-quaternary-ammonium-chlo.png)
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- The compound is a quaternary ammonium salt containing two ethyl groups and two methyl groups bonded to a positively charged nitrogen, with chloride as the counterion.
- Substituents are named in alphabetical order.

  - So, diethyl (e) comes before dimethyl (m).
- Each pair of identical groups requires the prefix 'di-'.
- The systematic name is therefore diethyldimethylammonium chloride.

![Annotated structural formula of diethyldimethylammonium chloride with labels identifying the two ethyl groups, two methyl groups, ammonium cation, and chloride anion](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/19-nitrogen-compounds/19-1-primary-amines/assets/005-annotated-structural-formula-of-diethyldimethyla.png)

**B** is incorrect as the compound contains two methyl groups; the 'di-' prefix is missing, giving 'diethylmethyl' instead of 'diethyldimethyl'.

**C** is incorrect as the groups are correct but placed in the wrong alphabetical order. Dimethyl appears before diethyl, whereas alphabetically diethyl (e) precedes dimethyl (m).

**D** is incorrect as both 'di-' prefixes are absent. The compound contains two ethyl and two methyl groups, requiring 'diethyldimethyl', not 'ethylmethyl'.

parts.problemMd: Hydrolysis of CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CN with dilute HCl produces which compound?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- **Hydrolysis** is the breakdown of a compound using water.
- When a nitrile is **refluxed** with dilute hydrochloric acid, **hydrolysis** occurs.
- The -CN group at the end of the hydrocarbon chain is converted into a -COOH group, forming a **carboxylic acid.**
- The ammonia in solution will act as a **base** and form an **ammonium salt** with Cl<sup>-</sup> (**NH**~<sub>**4**</sub>**Cl**).
- The reaction equation for this **hydrolysis** is:

CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CN + 2H<sub>2</sub>O + HCl → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOH + NH<sub>4</sub>Cl

**A** is incorrect as this is a primary amine which would have been formed if the nitrile group in CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CN was **reduced** instead of **hydrolysed**.

**B** is incorrect as this is an aldehyde and would not form upon hydrolysis of the nitrile.

**D** is incorrect as though a carboxylic acid is formed, the carbon chain is one carbon too short.

parts.problemMd:
The equation shows a chemical reaction

CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHClCH<sub>3</sub>  +  CN<sup>–</sup>  →  CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)CN  +  Cl<sup>–</sup>

What is the name for this type of reaction?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- A **nucleophilic substitution** reaction is one in which a **nucleophile** replaces another nucleophile.

  - A **nucleophile** is a species which can donate a pair of electrons.
- The cyanide ion (CN<sup>-</sup>) in this reaction is the **nucleophile** and replaces the **chlorine atom** in CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHClCH<sub>3</sub>.
- 2-chlorobutane is a **secondary halogenoalkane** so the nucleophilic substitution of 2-chlorobutane by the cyanide ion can follow an S<sub>N</sub>2 or S<sub>N</sub>1 reaction mechanism.
- The reaction of the halogenoalkane with cyanide ions (CN<sup>-</sup>) will add an extra carbon atom to the carbon chain.
- The reaction mechanism for this reaction via S<sub>N</sub>2 is as follows:

![SN2 mechanism: CN^-^ attacks the electrophilic carbon bearing the Cl leaving group in 2-chlorobutane, forming 2-methylbutanenitrile (CH~3~CH~2~CH(CH~3~)CN) and Cl^-^](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/19-nitrogen-compounds/19-2-nitriles-and-hydroxynitriles/assets/004-sn2-mechanism-cn-attacks-the-electrophilic-carbo.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as CN<sup>-</sup> is not an **electrophile**, which is an electron pair acceptor.

**B** is incorrect as a free radical substitution reaction is the reaction in which **halogen atoms** (not CN<sup>-</sup>) replace **hydrogen atoms** in alkanes.

**C** is incorrect as the reaction is a substitution reaction, **not** an addition reaction.

parts.problemMd: What are the reagents needed in the reaction of 1-bromopropane to butanenitrile?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- A **nucleophilic substitution** reaction is one in which a **nucleophile** replaces another nucleophile.

  - A **nucleophile** is a species which can **donate** a pair of electrons.
- The reaction of halogenoalkanes with cyanide ions, CN<sup>-</sup>, is an example of a **nucleophilic substitution** reaction.
- The cyanide ion (CN<sup>-</sup>) in this reaction is the **nucleophile** and **replaces** the **bromine atom** in bromopropane to give butanenitrile.
- The reaction of the halogenoalkane with cyanide ions (CN<sup>-</sup>) will add an extra carbon atom to the carbon chain.

  - '-**propane**' changes into '**butane**-' as there are now four carbon atoms in the carbon chain instead of three.
- The reaction should be carried out with KCN (to provide the **nucleophile** which is the cyanide ion) in ethanol (also known as **ethanolic solution of potassium cyanide**) which is then **heated** under reflux with the 1-bromopropane.

**A** is incorrect as ethanol and heat alone do not provide the cyanide ion (CN<sup>-</sup>) needed for the nucleophilic substitution reaction.

**B** is incorrect as KCN alone does not provide the correct conditions. Ethanol (as solvent) and heat under reflux are also required.

**C** is incorrect as KCN and ethanol are necessary but heat under reflux is also required to drive the nucleophilic substitution reaction.

parts.problemMd: What are the products when ethanenitrile is heated under reflux with dilute hydrochloric acid?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Hydrolysis is the breakdown of a compound using water.
- When a nitrile is refluxed with dilute hydrochloric acid, hydrolysis occurs.
- The -CN group at the end of the hydrocarbon chain is converted into a -COOH group, forming a carboxylic acid.
- The ammonia in solution will act as a base and form an ammonium salt with Cl<sup>-</sup> (NH<sub>4</sub>Cl).
- The reaction equation for this hydrolysis is:

CH<sub>3</sub>CN + 2H<sub>2</sub>O + HCl → CH<sub>3</sub>COOH + NH<sub>4</sub>Cl

**C** & **D** are incorrect as the number of carbons in the carbon chain remains unchanged. The carboxylic acid should therefore be ethanoic acid and not propanoic acid.

**A** is incorrect as the ammonia will react in solution to form an ammonium salt.

parts.problemMd: What are the products in the reaction of ethanenitrile and sodium hydroxide?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- Hydrolysis is the breakdown of a compound using water.
- When a nitrile is refluxed with sodium hydroxide solution, hydrolysis occurs.
- Instead of forming an ammonium salt (as seen in HCl reflux reactions), a sodium salt is formed, and ammonia gas is given off.
- The ammonia is formed from the reaction between ammonium (NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>) ions and hydroxide (OH<sup>-</sup>) ions.
- The reaction equation for this hydrolysis is:

CH<sub>3</sub>CN + H<sub>2</sub>O + NaOH → CH<sub>3</sub>COONa + NH<sub>3</sub>

- To form the free carboxylic acid the final solution has to be acidified with a strong acid such as dilute hydrochloric acid (HCl)

  - This means that the ethanoate ion in the sodium ethanoate salt will react with the hydrogen ions to form ethanoic acid.
  - Once reacted, ethanoic acid is a weak acid and holds onto the hydrogen rather than dissociating.

**C** & **D** are incorrect as the number of carbons in the carbon chain remain unchanged. The sodium salt should therefore be sodium ethanoate and not sodium propanoate.

**B** is incorrect as the ammonium salt is formed when a nitrile is refluxed with dilute hydrochloric acid, not sodium hydroxide.

parts.problemMd: Which one of the following reactants would **not** produce a nitrile in a one-step reaction?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Alkanes are very unreactive compounds due to their non-polar C-H bonds.
- They are therefore not likely to undergo reactions with nucleophiles and electrophiles.

  - Nucleophiles are species that can donate a pair of electrons.
  - Electrophiles are species that can accept a pair of electrons.
- The conversion of alkanes to nitriles is therefore a multi-step process.

**A **is incorrect as aldehydes can undergo a 1-step addition reaction with HCN at room temperature to form nitriles:

CH<sub>3</sub>CHO + HCN → CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)(CN)

**C **is incorrect as amides can undergo a 1-step dehydration reaction to form nitriles.

**D **is incorrect as halogenoalkanes undergo a 1-step substitution reaction with KCN in ethanol and heat to form nitriles:

CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br + CN<sup>-</sup> → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CN + Br<sup>-</sup>

parts.problemMd: Which of the following reactions would produce 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile is a hydroxynitrile.
- Hydroxynitriles can be formed from the nucleophilic addition reaction of aldehydes and ketones with HCN at room temperature.
- A nucleophilic addition is when a nucleophile is added to an unsaturated bond to form a single product.

  - A nucleophile is a species that donates a pair of electrons.
- Propanone (which is a ketone) and hydrogen cyanide are the correct reagents required for the conversion of propanone to 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile.
- The reaction mechanism is:

![Three-step nucleophilic addition mechanism: CN^-^ attacks the electrophilic carbonyl carbon of propanone, forming an alkoxide intermediate, which is protonated to give 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/19-nitrogen-compounds/19-2-nitriles-and-hydroxynitriles/assets/003-three-step-nucleophilic-addition-mechanism-cn-at.jpg)

**A, B** & **C** are incorrect as though these reactions contain the correct reactant (either an aldehyde or ketone), they do not contain the correct reagent (hydrogen cyanide, HCN).

parts.problemMd:
Which row does **not** identify a correct combination of reactant and reagent to produce a nitrile?

|   | **Reactant** | **Reagent** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | Halogenoalkane | Potassium cyanide and ethanol |
| **B** | Amide | Phosphorus(V) oxide |
| **C** | Aldehyde | Hydrogen cyanide |
| **D** | Ketone | Ammonia |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- To produce nitriles from aldehydes and ketones, **hydrogen cyanide** should be used.
- The reagent in option D should have been **hydrogen cyanide** and not ammonia.

**A, B** & **C** are incorrect as these are all correct combinations of reactants and reagents.

parts.problemMd: The following equations show reactions with nitrogen compounds. Which one correctly shows the hydrolysis of nitriles with dilute acid?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Hydrolysis is the breakdown of a compound using water.
- Nitriles can be hydrolysed either by refluxing it with dilute hydrochloric acid or with sodium hydroxide solution.
- When hydrolysed with a dilute acid the -CN group at the end of the hydrocarbon chain is converted into a -COOH group, forming a carboxylic acid.
- Ammonia in solution will act as a base to form ammonium salt with Cl<sup>-</sup> (NH<sub>4</sub>Cl).

  - Option **B **is therefore the only correct option.
- When a nitrile is refluxed with sodium hydroxide solution, hydrolysis can also occur.

  - Instead of forming an ammonium salt, now a sodium salt is formed, and ammonia gas is given off.
  - The ammonia is formed from the reaction between ammonium (NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>) ions and hydroxide (OH<sup>-</sup>) ions.
- The reaction equation for this hydrolysis is:

CH<sub>3</sub>CN + H<sub>2</sub>O + NaOH → CH<sub>3</sub>COONa + NH<sub>3</sub>

- To form the free carboxylic acid the final solution has to be acidified with a strong acid such as dilute hydrochloric acid (HCl).

  - This means that the ethanoate ion in the sodium ethanoate salt will react with the hydrogen ions to form ethanoic acid.
  - Once reacted, ethanoic acid is a weak acid and holds onto the hydrogen rather than dissociating.

**A** is incorrect as ammonium chloride (NH<sub>4</sub>Cl) is formed, not ammonia chloride (NH<sub>3</sub>Cl).

**C** is incorrect as ammonium chloride (NH<sub>4</sub>Cl) is formed, **not** ammonia (NH<sub>3</sub>). Ammonia would have been formed if the nitrile was hydrolysed by a sodium hydroxide solution.

**D** is incorrect as the water molecules are not correctly balanced in this reaction. 2 moles of water are needed for the reaction to become balanced.

parts.problemMd: The following equations show reactions with nitrogen compounds. Which one correctly shows the hydrolysis of nitriles with dilute sodium hydroxide?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- **Hydrolysis** is the breakdown of a compound using water.
- **Nitriles** can be hydrolysed either by **refluxing** it with **dilute hydrochloric acid** or with **sodium hydroxide solution.**
- When hydrolysed with **sodium hydroxide solution**, instead of forming an **ammonium salt**, now a **sodium salt** is formed, and **ammonia gas** is given off.
- The ammonia is formed from the reaction between **ammonium** (NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>) ions and **hydroxide** (OH<sup>-</sup>) ions.

  - Option **C** is therefore the correct option.
- To form the free carboxylic acid the final solution has to be acidified with a strong acid such as dilute hydrochloric acid (HCl).

  - This means that the ethanoate ion in the sodium ethanoate salt will react with the hydrogen ions to form ethanoic acid.
  - Once reacted, ethanoic acid is a weak acid and holds onto the hydrogen rather than dissociating.

**A** is incorrect as the water molecules are not correctly balanced in this reaction. 1 mole of water is needed for the reaction to become balanced.

**B** is incorrect as the water molecules are not correctly balanced in this reaction. 1 mole of water is needed for the reaction to become balanced and ammonium is not formed in the hydrolysis of nitriles by dilute aqueous hydroxide.

**D** is incorrect as ammonia (NH<sub>3</sub>) is formed, not ammonium (NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>). An ammonium salt would have been formed if the nitrile was hydrolysed by dilute hydrochloric acid solution.

parts.problemMd:
The reaction scheme shows a two-step synthesis starting from butanenitrile.

CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CN $\overset{\text{step 1}}{\rightarrow}$  **X**  $\overset{\text{step 2}}{\rightarrow}$ CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOH

Which row identifies the reagents and conditions for step 1 and step 2?

|   | Step 1 | Step 2 |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | Heat with dilute HCl under reflux | Neutralisation with NaOH |
| **B** | Heat with aqueous NaOH under reflux | Acidification with dilute HCl |
| **C** | Heat with LiAlH<sub>4</sub> in dry ether | Oxidation with acidified K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> |
| **D** | Heat with dilute H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> under reflux | Distillation |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Heating a nitrile with aqueous NaOH under reflux hydrolyses it to a carboxylate salt
- Acidification converts the carboxylate salt into the carboxylic acid
- This sequence correctly converts butanenitrile into butanoic acid

**A** is incorrect as acid hydrolysis already forms the acid and does not require neutralisation.

**C** is incorrect as LiAlH<sub>4</sub> reduces nitriles to primary amines, not acids.

**D** is incorrect as distillation is a separation technique, it does not change the functional group.

parts.problemMd:
The reaction sequence shows the two-step synthesis for the production of 2-hydroxybutanenitrile from propan-1-ol.

CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH $\overset{\text{step 1}}{\rightarrow}$  **X**  $\overset{\text{step 2}}{\rightarrow}$ CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHOHCN

Which set of reagents and conditions correctly completes **Step 1** and **Step 2**?

|   | Step 1 | Step 2 |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> / H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> under distillation | NaCN (aq) / H<sup>+</sup> (aq) |
| **B** | NaCl / H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> | NaCN / Ethanol |
| **C** | NaCN (aq) / H<sup>+</sup> (aq) | K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> / H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> under distillation |
| **D** | NaCN / Ethanol | NaCl / H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- 2-hydroxybutanenitrile is a hydroxynitrile.
- Hydroxynitriles can be formed from the nucleophilic addition reaction of aldehydes and ketones with HCN at room temperature.
- A nucleophilic addition is when a nucleophile is added to an unsaturated bond to form a single product — a nucleophile donates a pair of electrons.
- Since propan-1-ol is a primary alcohol it should be first oxidised to an aldehyde using acidified potassium dichromate under distillation to form propanal.
- The aldehyde propanal is then reacted with hydrogen cyanide (acidified NaCN) at room temperature to produce 2-hydroxybutanenitrile.

![Two-step synthesis: propan-1-ol is oxidised to propanal using acidified K~2~Cr~2~O~7~ under distillation; propanal then undergoes nucleophilic addition with NaCN (aq) / H^+^ (aq) to form 2-hydroxybutanenitrile](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/19-nitrogen-compounds/19-2-nitriles-and-hydroxynitriles/assets/001-two-step-synthesis-propan-1-ol-is-oxidised-to-pr.jpg)

parts.problemMd:
Butanone can undergo addition when mixed with NaCN (aq) / H<sup>+</sup> (aq), forming product **Z**. Product **Z** can then undergo hydrolysis when heated with dilute HCl, forming product **Y**.

Which compound is product Y?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- A nucleophilic addition is when a nucleophile is added to an unsaturated bond to form a single product.
- Hydroxynitriles are formed from the nucleophilic addition reaction of aldehydes and ketones with HCN at room temperature.
- Butanone is a ketone and will form 2-methyl-2-hydroxybutanenitrile.
- Hydrolysis is the breakdown of a compound using water.

  - Nitriles can be hydrolysed by refluxing it with dilute hydrochloric acid.
- The -CN group is converted into a -COOH group, forming a carboxylic acid.
- The ammonia in solution will act as a base and form an ammonium salt with Cl<sup>-</sup> (NH<sub>4</sub>Cl).

**A** & **B** are incorrect as these are amine products formed when the CN<sup>-</sup> group in Z is reduced rather than hydrolysed.

**C** is incorrect as this is the product if the reactant is an **aldehyde** rather than a **ketone.**

parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Propylamine has the formula CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>. The propyl- prefix tells you there is a three-carbon chain (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>–) and the -amine suffix tells you an NH<sub>2</sub> group is attached to it.
> 
> If you cannot recall the product, work backwards from the name. You know the product is an amine (contains N) and the three-carbon chain comes from 1-bromopropane. So the product is CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>.
>

parts.problemMd: State the reagents and conditions required to produce propylamine from 1-bromopropane.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The reagents and conditions required are:
> 
> - Excess ammonia / NH<sub>3</sub> in ethanol / ethanolic solution of ammonia **[1 mark]**
> - Heated under pressure / in a sealed tube **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Excess ammonia is used to prevent the newly formed propylamine from acting as a nucleophile and attacking another molecule of 1-bromopropane. If the ammonia is not in excess, a secondary amine (dipropylamine) would form as a by-product.
> 
> The reaction must be carried out under pressure because ammonia is a gas at room temperature. A sealed tube or pressurised vessel keeps the ammonia in contact with 1-bromopropane long enough to react.

parts.problemMd: Name the mechanism for the reaction of 1-bromopropane with ammonia.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The mechanism for this reaction is:
> 
> - Nucleophilic substitution **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The bromine atom in 1-bromopropane is more electronegative than carbon, so the C–Br bond is polarised (δ+C–δ–Br). The lone pair on the nitrogen atom of ammonia is attracted to this δ+C, making ammonia the nucleophile. The C–Br bond breaks and the bromide ion (Br<sup>–</sup>) leaves, so the overall process is nucleophilic substitution.

> 
> ii) The mechanism of this reaction is:
> 
> - Nucleophilic substitution **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The nitrogen atom in ammonia has a lone pair of electrons. The carbon of the C–Cl bond carries a partial positive charge (δ+C) because chlorine is more electronegative. The lone pair on N attacks this δ+C, making ammonia the nucleophile.

parts.problemMd: Use a chemical equation to explain why propylamine acts as a Brønsted-Lowry base when it dissolves in water.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Propylamine acts as a Brønsted-Lowry base because:
> 
> - It accepts a proton / H<sup>+</sup> from water / it has a lone pair of electrons that accepts a proton **[1 mark]**
> 
> The equation is:
> 
> - CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O ⇌ CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> + OH<sup>-</sup> 
> **OR**
> C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>7</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O ⇌ C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>7</sub>NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> + OH<sup>-</sup>**[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A Brønsted-Lowry base is a species that accepts a proton (H<sup>+</sup>). Propylamine has a lone pair on its nitrogen atom. When dissolved in water, this lone pair accepts a proton from H<sub>2</sub>O, forming the propylammonium ion (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>) and releasing a hydroxide ion (OH<sup>-</sup>).
> 
> The question asks you to explain, not just state. You must link the lone pair on nitrogen to the ability to accept a proton. Stating 'it accepts a proton' without reference to the lone pair will not score the first mark.
> 
> The equilibrium arrow (⇌) is required because propylamine is a weak base. Weak bases only partially ionise in water.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Propylamine can be produced by the reaction of 1-chloropropane with ammonia.

CH3CH2CH2Cl → CH3CH2CH2NH2

The reaction between 1-chloropropane and ammonia proceeds in two steps. Step 1 involves the formation of an intermediate. Step 2 forms the final propylamine product.

As the reaction proceeds, the bond angles around the nitrogen atom change. Explain these changes in the bond angles around the nitrogen atom.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> As the reaction proceeds, the bond angles around nitrogen change:
> 
> - Bond angle in ammonia **AND** propylamine = 107°
> **AND**
> Bond angle in the intermediate = 109.5° **[1 mark]**
> - Lone pair(s) on nitrogen in ammonia **AND** propylamine cause greater repulsion than bonding pairs
> **AND**
> The molecules have a pyramidal shape **[1 mark]**
> - All four bonds / bonding pairs around nitrogen in the intermediate
> **AND**
> The intermediate has a tetrahedral shape **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> In step 1, the lone pair on ammonia attacks the C–Cl bond. This forms an intermediate where nitrogen is bonded to four groups (no lone pairs remaining on N). Four bonding pairs with no lone pairs gives a tetrahedral shape with a bond angle of 109.5°.
> 
> In step 2, a proton is lost from the intermediate and the lone pair is restored on nitrogen in propylamine. One lone pair with three bonding pairs gives a pyramidal shape. The lone pair repels bonding pairs more strongly than bonding pairs repel each other, compressing the angle below the tetrahedral value to 107°.
> 
> Note that ammonia and propylamine have the same bond angle (107°) because both have one lone pair and three bonding pairs around nitrogen.

> Since ammonia is a neutral nucleophile, a proton (H<sup>+</sup>) must be lost from compound X to form the neutral amine product. Ammonia acts as a Brønsted-Lowry base in reaction 2 by accepting this proton to form NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> (compound Y). This is why excess ammonia is used.
> 
> The ammonium ion (NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>) combines with the chloride ion (Cl<sup>-</sup>) displaced in reaction 1 to form ammonium chloride (NH<sub>4</sub>Cl).
> 
> If a different halogenoalkane were used (for example 1-bromobutane), a Br<sup>-</sup> ion would be formed instead, combining with the ammonium ion to give ammonium bromide (NH<sub>4</sub>Br).

parts.problemMd:
Compound **X** is produced from cyclohexene by reaction with a hydrogen halide.

An amine which is a relatively weak base containing one nitrogen atom can be produced from compound **X** in one step.

Draw the mechanism for the formation of compound **X** from cyclohexene. Include charges, dipoles, lone pairs of electrons and curly arrows, as appropriate. State the hydrogen halide used in your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
The mechanism for the formation of compound **X** from cyclohexene using HBr is:

![Electrophilic addition mechanism showing HBr reacting with cyclohexene: curly arrow from C=C to H of HBr, dipoles on HBr, carbocation intermediate formed, then Br– attacks C+ to form bromocyclohexane](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/19-nitrogen-compounds/19-1-primary-amines/assets/008-electrophilic-addition-mechanism-showing-hbr-rea.png)

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from the C=C π bond to the H atom of H–Br / H–Cl / H–I
> 
> 1 mark for correct partial charges on the H–X bond (δ+H, δ–X) **AND** a curly arrow from the H–X bond to the X atom
> 
> 1 mark for the correct carbocation intermediate drawn
> 
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from the lone pair on X<sup>–</sup> to the positively charged carbon of the carbocation
> 
> Allow HBr, HCl, or HI as the hydrogen halide; compound **X** is then the corresponding halocyclohexane

> **[exam-tip]**
> This is an electrophilic addition mechanism. The π electrons of the C=C bond act as a nucleophile and are attracted to the δ+ hydrogen of H–Br. Two curly arrows are needed in the first step: one from the C=C to H, and one from the H–Br bond to Br. Both bonds must be shown breaking and forming simultaneously.
> 
> The carbocation intermediate has a positive charge on the carbon that did not bond to H. In the second step, Br<sup>–</sup> attacks this C<sup>+</sup> using its lone pair. The curly arrow must start from the lone pair on Br<sup>–</sup>, not from the Br<sup>–</sup> ion itself.
> 
> You can use HBr, HCl, or HI. The mechanism is the same for all three; compound **X** is the corresponding halocyclohexane (e.g. bromocyclohexane if HBr is used). Compound **X** is a halogenoalkane that can then undergo nucleophilic substitution with excess ethanolic ammonia to form cyclohexylamine.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Compound **X** is produced from cyclohexene by reaction with a hydrogen halide.

An amine which is a relatively weak base containing one nitrogen atom can be produced from compound **X** in one step.

Allow HBr, HCl, or HI as the hydrogen halide; compound **X** is then the corresponding halocyclohexane

Compound **X** reacts with ammonia to form cyclohexylamine.

i) State the reagents and conditions required for this reaction.

[2]

ii) Suggest why an excess of ammonia is used.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The reagents and conditions required are:
> 
> - Excess ammonia / NH<sub>3</sub> in ethanol / ethanolic solution of ammonia **[1 mark]**
> - Heated under pressure / in a sealed tube **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) An excess of ammonia is used to:
> 
> - Prevent the amine / cyclohexylamine from acting as a nucleophile and reacting with (another molecule of) compound **X** / the halogenoalkane
> **OR**
> Prevent the formation of secondary / tertiary amines **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The reaction must be carried out under pressure because ammonia is a gas at room temperature. A sealed tube or pressurised vessel keeps the ammonia in contact with compound **X** long enough to react.
> 
> If ammonia is not in excess, the newly formed cyclohexylamine can act as a nucleophile (it also has a lone pair on nitrogen) and attack another molecule of compound **X**. This produces a secondary amine as a by-product. Excess ammonia ensures the ammonia outcompetes the amine for the available halogenoalkane.

parts.problemMd:
Propylamine acts as a Brønsted-Lowry base when it dissolves in water.

Construct an equation to show this behaviour.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The equation is:
> 
> - CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O ⇌ CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> + OH<sup>-</sup> 
> **OR**
> C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>7</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O ⇌ C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>7</sub>NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> + OH<sup>-</sup>**[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A Brønsted-Lowry base is a species that accepts a proton (H<sup>+</sup>). Propylamine has a lone pair on its nitrogen atom. When dissolved in water, the lone pair accepts a proton from H<sub>2</sub>O, forming the propylammonium ion (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>) and releasing a hydroxide ion (OH<sup>-</sup>).
> 
> The equilibrium arrow (⇌) is required because propylamine is a weak base. Weak bases only partially ionise in water, so the forward and reverse reactions both occur simultaneously.

parts.problemMd:
When 1-chloropropane is heated under reflux with ethanolic potassium cyanide, KCN, the following reaction occurs.

CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Cl + KCN → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CN + KCl

i) Draw the displayed formula of the organic product formed in this reaction.

[1]

ii) State the systematic name of this organic product.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The displayed formula of the organic product is:

![Displayed formula of butanenitrile](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/19-nitrogen-compounds/19-2-nitriles-and-hydroxynitriles/assets/005-displayed-formula-of-butanenitrile.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) The systematic name of this organic product is:
> 
> - Butanenitrile **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When halogenoalkanes react with KCN, or NaCN, in ethanol, a nitrile is formed.
> 
> Nitriles have the organic functional group –CN.
> 
> Remember: there is a triple bond between the C and N atoms in the nitrile group.
> 
> When naming the organic product, don't forget the C atom in the nitrile group. The most common mistake is to give the name as propanenitrile.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

When 1-chloropropane is heated under reflux with ethanolic potassium cyanide, KCN, the following reaction occurs.

CH~3~CH~2~CH~2~Cl + KCN → CH~3~CH~2~CH~2~CN + KCl

Suggest why this reaction is useful to chemists during the synthesis of other organic compounds.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> This reaction is useful to chemists during the synthesis of other organic compounds because:
> 
> - It lengthens the carbon chain / forms a C–C bond **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> This reaction is of particular importance as it forms a carbon-carbon bond which can lengthen the carbon chain.
> 
> This is useful as new compounds can be synthesised which have more carbon atoms.
> 
> Sometimes, an organic compound may not be easily available as a raw material, but another organic compound with one less carbon atom may be readily available.
> 
> If this compound with one less carbon atom is made into a halogenoalkane and then refluxed with ethanolic KCN, a nitrile can be made with the desired number of carbon atoms which can undergo further synthesis.

parts.problemMd:
The CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CN can undergo hydrolysis.

i) Construct an equation for the acid hydrolysis of CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CN.

[2]

ii) Draw the displayed formula of the intermediate formed when CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CN is hydrolysed by sodium hydroxide.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The equation for the acid hydrolysis of CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CN is:
> 
> - CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CN + HCl + 2H<sub>2</sub>O → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOH + NH<sub>4</sub>Cl **[1 mark]**

ii) The displayed formula of the intermediate formed when CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CN is hydrolysed by sodium hydroxide is:

![Displayed formula of sodium butanoate](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/19-nitrogen-compounds/19-2-nitriles-and-hydroxynitriles/assets/006-displayed-formula-of-sodium-butanoate.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct displayed formula of sodium butanoate

> **[exam-tip]**
> Hydrolysis of nitriles can occur either by dilute acid or dilute alkali followed by acidification.
> 
> A carboxylic acid is the product in both cases, but when hydrolysed by dilute alkali, a carboxylate salt is the intermediate which requires acidification to form the carboxylic acid.
> 
> Alkali hydrolysis:
> 
> CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CN + NaOH + 2H<sub>2</sub>O → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COO<sup>–</sup>Na<sup>+</sup> + NH<sub>3</sub>
> 
> Acidification of sodium butanoate produces the carboxylic acid CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOH.
> 
> Unlike the formation of nitriles (which adds a carbon atom to the carbon chain), hydrolysis does not change the number of carbon atoms.

parts.problemMd:
Propanal undergoes nucleophilic addition with a mixture of HCN and NaCN to make 2-hydroxybutanenitrile, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(OH)CN.

The mechanism for this reaction occurs in two main steps. The first step involves a nucleophile attacking the carbonyl carbon of propanal.

Explain which species acts as the nucleophile during this reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The species which acts as the nucleophile during this reaction is:
> 
> - CN<sup>–</sup> / :CN<sup>–</sup> / the cyanide ion **[1 mark]**
> - (Because) it has a lone pair / is a lone pair donor **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Remember: a nucleophile is a species that is attracted to areas of (partial) positive charge.
> 
> This means they are an electron-rich species that is able to donate a pair of electrons.
> 
> The NaCN consists of Na<sup>+</sup> and CN<sup>–</sup> ions. The CN<sup>–</sup> ion has an available lone pair, which makes it the nucleophile in this reaction.

parts.problemMd:
Two students try to prepare butanoic acid from a halogenoalkane in the laboratory.

Both students perform a nucleophilic substitution reaction to form **P** in reaction 1 of **Fig. 2.1**.

They both form butanoic acid from **P** but student **A** uses a single reaction, while student **B** uses two reactions.

![Reaction scheme showing synthesis of butanoic acid from a halogenoalkane via intermediate compound P](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/19-nitrogen-compounds/19-2-nitriles-and-hydroxynitriles/assets/020-reaction-scheme-showing-synthesis-of-butanoic-ac.png)

i) State the reagents and conditions required for reaction 1.

[2]

ii) Student **A** uses 1-bromopropane to form **P**.

Student **B** uses a different halogenoalkane which forms **P** at a slower rate.

Suggest the identity of the halogenoalkane that student **B** uses. Explain your answer.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The reagents and conditions required for reaction 1 are:
> 
> - Heated under reflux **[1 mark]**
> - With a solution of sodium cyanide / NaCN in ethanol
> **OR**
> With a solution of potassium cyanide / KCN in ethanol **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The identity of the halogenoalkane that student **B** uses is:
> 
> - 1-chloropropane
> **OR**
> 1-fluoropropane **[1 mark]**

> **OR**
> (Because) the carbon-fluorine / C–F bond is stronger than the carbon-bromine / C–Br bond
> **OR**
> (Because) the reactivity of halogenoalkanes increases as you move down the halogens
> **OR**
> (Because) the halogenoalkanes above bromopropane are less reactive / react more slowly **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> You must state that the sodium cyanide (or potassium cyanide) is in ethanol / alcoholic conditions. If it is in water, a different reaction takes place (aqueous KCN gives an alcohol, not a nitrile).
> 
> The reactivity of halogenoalkanes increases as you move down the halogens because the carbon-halogen bond becomes weaker as the halogen becomes less electronegative.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Two students try to prepare butanoic acid from a halogenoalkane in the laboratory.

Both students perform a nucleophilic substitution reaction to form **P** in reaction 1 of **Fig. 2.1**.

They both form butanoic acid from **P** but student **A** uses a single reaction, while student **B** uses two reactions.

Explain why it is likely that student **A** will have a higher overall yield of butanoic acid from their halogenoalkane than student **B**.

For each reaction, give another solvent and the alternative product that will be formed.

reaction 1

alternative solvent ............................................................

alternative product............................................................

reaction 3

alternative solvent ............................................................

alternative product............................................................
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The alternative solvents and products for reactions 1 and 3 are:
> 
> Reaction 1:
> 
> - Alternative solvent: C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH / ethanol / alcohol **[1 mark]**
> - Alternative product: C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub> / ethene **[1 mark]**
>

>

>

> **[exam-tip]**
> It is easy to miss sigma bonds in this structure because some are not explicitly shown. They are contained within the CH<sub>3</sub> and OH groups, and there are 5 hidden hydrogen atoms in the phenyl ring.

parts.problemMd:
Poly(ethenol) is a polymer used to make dissolvable plastic bags. It can be made by addition polymerisation of CH<sub>2</sub>=CH(OH).

Which structure shows a polymer chain consisting of two monomer residues?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- In addition polymerisation, the C=C double bond in ethenol, CH<sub>2</sub>=CH(OH), opens to form the repeat unit −CH(OH)−CH<sub>2</sub>−:

![Diagram showing addition polymerisation of ethenol (CH₂=CH(OH)) to form poly(ethenol): ethenol monomer on the left with an arrow pointing to the bracketed repeat unit −CH(OH)−CH₂− with subscript n on the right](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/20-polymerisation/20-1-addition-polymerisation/assets/020-diagram-showing-addition-polymerisation-of-ethen.jpg)

- Structure A shows two of these repeat units joined together, which is the correct polymer chain section.

**B** is incorrect as while the first repeat unit is correctly drawn, the second is connected via a C−O ether linkage rather than a C−C bond. In addition polymerisation only carbon-carbon bonds join repeat units in the main chain.

**C** is incorrect as in **addition polymerisation** only C−C bonds connect repeat units in the main chain. Oxygen atoms within the backbone (as shown) are characteristic of condensation polymerisation, not addition polymerisation.

**D** is incorrect as in addition polymerisation the hydroxyl (−OH) group remains as a pendant side group throughout the chain. It does not react or appear as a terminal end group.

parts.problemMd:
Plastic waste can be incinerated to provide energy.

Which statement explains why poly(chloroethene), PVC, is removed from the waste before incineration?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- PVC, poly(chloroethene), is made by the addition polymerisation of chloroethene, H<sub>2</sub>C=CHCl:

![Diagram showing addition polymerisation of chloroethene (CH₂=CHCl) to form poly(chloroethene)/PVC: chloroethene monomer on the left with an arrow pointing to the bracketed repeat unit −CH₂−CHCl− with subscript n; below shows the expanded polymer chain −CH₂−CHCl−CH₂−CHCl−](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/20-polymerisation/20-1-addition-polymerisation/assets/015-diagram-showing-addition-polymerisation-of-chlor.jpg)

- When PVC is incinerated, **harmful gases** are produced, including **hydrogen chloride (HCl)**, **dioxins** and **carbon monoxide (CO)**, all of which are toxic to humans and animals.

**A** is incorrect as ozone layer destruction is caused by chlorine free radicals (Cl<sup>•</sup>) from CFC compounds, not by incinerating PVC. Burning PVC produces HCl gas, not chlorine radicals.

**B** is incorrect as while PVC has some flame-retardant properties due to its chlorine content, it can still be incinerated at high temperatures. The reason for its removal is the **toxic combustion products** (HCl, dioxins, CO), not difficulty in burning.

**C** is incorrect as PVC is **not** biodegradable. Synthetic polymers are not broken down by bacteria, so biodegradability is not relevant to the decision to remove it before incineration.

parts.problemMd:
The diagram below shows 2-methylpropene, C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>, a monomer used in the production of synthetic rubber.

![Displayed formula of 2-methylpropene: CH₂=C(CH₃)₂ with a C=C double bond, two hydrogen atoms on C1, and two methyl groups on C2](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/20-polymerisation/20-1-addition-polymerisation/assets/005-displayed-formula-of-2-methylpropene-ch-c-ch-wit.jpg)

What is the compound formed by 2-methylpropene when it undergoes addition polymerisation?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- When 2-methylpropene undergoes addition polymerisation its C=C **double bond breaks** to leave a single bond between the carbons, allowing each carbon to form a bond with adjacent monomer units.
- The compound's name indicates that the double bond is between carbons 1 and 2, and the methyl substituent is on carbon 2.
- Therefore, in the repeat unit the second carbon has two methyl groups (one from C3 of the main chain and one from the 2-methyl substituent):

![Diagram showing addition polymerisation of 2-methylpropene to poly(2-methylpropene): 2-methylpropene monomer with C1=C2 double bond and methyl branch at C2 on the left, arrow pointing to the bracketed repeat unit −CH₂−C(CH₃)₂− with subscript n on the right](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/20-polymerisation/20-1-addition-polymerisation/assets/006-diagram-showing-addition-polymerisation-of-2-met.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as repeat units in addition polymers have a **2-carbon backbone**. The 3-carbon backbone shown would require a different monomer or polymerisation mechanism.

**B** is incorrect as this is the repeat unit of **poly(but-2-ene)**, not poly(2-methylpropene). In poly(but-2-ene) each carbon in the repeat unit carries one methyl group.

**D** is incorrect as during addition polymerisation one bond in the C=C double bond breaks. The repeat unit contains only C−C single bonds in the main chain, not a retained double bond.

parts.problemMd: What is the repeat unit of PVC, poly(chloroethene)?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- In addition polymerisation, the C=C double bond in chloroethene, H<sub>2</sub>C=CHCl, breaks to form a C−C single bond, giving the repeat unit −CH<sub>2</sub>−CHCl−.
- PVC (polyvinylchloride) is more correctly named poly(chloroethene), made from the addition polymerisation of chloroethene.

**B** is incorrect as this is the repeat unit for poly(1,2-dichloroethene), which has one chlorine atom on each of the two adjacent carbons in the repeat unit.

**C** is incorrect as repeat units in addition polymers do **not** contain a C=C double bond. All C=C bonds break during addition polymerisation.

**D** is incorrect as repeat units in addition polymers do **not** contain a C=C double bond, and the repeat unit of PVC has only **one** chlorine atom, not two.

parts.problemMd:
But-2-en-1-ol, CH<sub>3</sub>CH=CHCH<sub>2</sub>OH, is a monomer that undergoes addition polymerisation.

Which structure is the repeat unit in poly(but-2-en-1-ol)?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- In but-2-en-1-ol:

  - 'but' = 4 carbons
  - '2-en' = C=C double bond between C2 and C3
  - '1-ol' = OH group on C1.
- In addition polymerisation, the C=C double bond breaks, forming a 2-carbon backbone in the repeat unit.

  - All other groups remain as pendant substituents:

![Diagram showing addition polymerisation of but-2-en-1-ol to poly(but-2-en-1-ol): displayed formula of but-2-en-1-ol with numbered carbons (C4−C3=C2−C1−OH) on the left with an arrow pointing to the bracketed repeat unit with subscript n on the right; below shows the simplified repeat unit −CH(CH₃)−CH(CH₂OH)−](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/20-polymerisation/20-1-addition-polymerisation/assets/016-diagram-showing-addition-polymerisation-of-but-2.jpg)

- The repeat unit is −CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)−CH(CH<sub>2</sub>OH)−:

  - C3 (bearing the methyl group) and C2 (bearing the hydroxymethyl group) form the 2-carbon backbone.

**A** is incorrect as repeat units in addition polymers do **not** contain C=C double bonds; all C=C bonds break during polymerisation.

**B** is incorrect as in addition polymerisation only the **two carbons** of the original double bond form the backbone. C1 (CH<sub>2</sub>OH) and C4 (CH<sub>3</sub>) remain as pendant groups, giving a 2-carbon rather than 4-carbon backbone.

**C** is incorrect as in addition polymerisation only the **two carbons** of the original double bond form the backbone. The OH group remains as a pendant substituent, not a terminal end group.
