parts.problemMd:
The infrared spectrum of a compound is shown below.

![IR spectrum showing a strong absorption at approximately 1720 cm-1 with no O-H absorption](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/22-analytical-techniques/22-1-infrared-spectroscopy/assets/001-ir-spectrum-showing-a-strong-absorption-at-appro.png)

Which compound is shown by the infrared spectrum?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Butanal contains a C=O (carbonyl) group, which gives the characteristic absorption between 1670 and 1740 cm<sup>-1</sup>.

**A** is incorrect as there is no absorption at 1500–1680 cm<sup>-1</sup> due to C=C, therefore the compound cannot be but-1-ene.

**B** is incorrect as there is no absorption at 3200–3600 cm<sup>-1</sup> due to O-H (alcohol), therefore the compound cannot be butan-1-ol.

**D** is incorrect as there is no absorption at 2500–3000 cm<sup>-1</sup> due to O-H (acid), therefore the compound cannot be butanoic acid.

parts.problemMd: Which class of compound does **not** contain the functional group responsible for the strong absorption between 1670 cm<sup>-1</sup> and 1740 cm<sup>-1</sup>?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- The absorption between 1670 and 1740 cm<sup>-1</sup> is characteristic of the C=O (carbonyl) bond, found in aldehydes, ketones, and carboxylic acids.
- Alcohols do not contain a C=O bond; the characteristic absorption of an alcohol is the O-H bond at 3200–3550 cm<sup>-1</sup>.

**B** is incorrect as aldehydes contain a C=O bond, which produces the characteristic absorption between 1670 and 1740 cm<sup>-1</sup>.

**C** is incorrect as carboxylic acids contain a C=O bond as part of the carboxyl group, which absorbs between 1670 and 1740 cm<sup>-1</sup>.

**D** is incorrect as ketones contain a C=O bond, which produces the characteristic absorption between 1670 and 1740 cm<sup>-1</sup>.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The three key infrared absorptions to learn for CIE IAL Chemistry are:
> 
> - O-H (alcohol): 3230–3550 cm<sup>-1</sup>.
> - C=O (aldehyde, ketone, carboxylic acid): 1670–1740 cm<sup>-1</sup>.
> - O-H (carboxylic acid, broad): 2500–3000 cm<sup>-1</sup>.

parts.problemMd: Which of the following corresponds to the base peak in a mass spectrum?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- The **base peak** is the most intense (tallest) peak in a mass spectrum.
- It corresponds to the ion with the greatest abundance in the sample.

**A** is incorrect as a fragment ion does not necessarily produce the base peak. The base peak is the most abundant ion regardless of how it is formed.

**B** is incorrect as the base peak is not necessarily produced by the ion with the lowest m/z ratio.

**C** is incorrect as the molecular ion peak does not necessarily correspond to the base peak. The molecular ion (M<sup>+</sup> or M<sub>●</sub><sup>+</sup>) is the unfragmented ionised molecule. It has the highest m/z ratio (excluding isotope peaks) but is not always the most abundant ion.

parts.problemMd:
The diagram shows the structural formula of ricinoleic acid.

![Structural formula of ricinoleic acid (12-hydroxyoctadec-9-enoic acid), an 18-carbon chain with a carboxylic acid group at C-1, a cis C=C double bond between C-9 and C-10, and a hydroxyl group at C-12](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/22-analytical-techniques/22-2-mass-spectrometry/assets/011-structural-formula-of-ricinoleic-acid-12-hydroxy.jpg)

The mass spectrum of ricinoleic acid shows a peak at m/z = 55.

Which fragment ion is responsible for this peak?

- A peak at m/z = 55 corresponds to a fragment ion with a mass of 55.
- [C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>7</sub>]<sup>+</sup> has m/z = (4 × 12) + (7 × 1) = 55.

**B** is incorrect as [CH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>]<sup>+</sup> has m/z = 58, not 55.

**C** is incorrect as [CH$\equiv$CHCHOH]<sup>+</sup> has m/z = 56, not 55.

parts.problemMd:
In a mass spectrometer, the ions are separated.

Which of the following species will be deflected to the greatest extent?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- In a mass spectrometer, ions with a smaller m/z ratio are deflected to a greater extent by the magnetic field.

  - <sup>35</sup>Cl<sup>+</sup> has m/z = 35
  - <sup>35</sup>Cl<sup>2+</sup> has m/z = $\frac{35}{2}$ = 17.5
  - <sup>37</sup>Cl<sup>+</sup> has m/z = 37
- <sup>35</sup>Cl<sup>2+</sup> has the smallest m/z ratio of the charged species and is therefore deflected to the greatest extent.

**A** is incorrect as <sup>35</sup>Cl<sup>+</sup> has m/z = 35, which is greater than the m/z of <sup>35</sup>Cl<sup>2+</sup>.

**C** is incorrect as <sup>37</sup>Cl carries no charge and is not deflected by the magnetic field.

**D** is incorrect as <sup>37</sup>Cl<sup>+</sup> has m/z = 37, which is the largest m/z of the charged species and is therefore deflected the least.

parts.problemMd:
A sample of silicon contains the following isotopes.

| **Isotope** | **Percentage abundance** |
|---|---|
| <sup>28</sup>Si | 81.21 |
| <sup>29</sup>Si | 14.10 |
| <sup>30</sup>Si | 4.69 |

Which is the relative atomic mass of silicon in this sample, to 1 dp?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- To calculate the relative atomic mass of silicon, multiply each isotopic mass by its percentage abundance, add the values, then divide by 100.

*A*<sub>r</sub>(Si) = $\frac{(28\times81.21)+(29\times14.10)+(30\times4.69)}{100}$

*A*<sub>r</sub>(Si) = $\frac{2823.48}{100}$

*A*<sub>r</sub>(Si) = 28.2

**A** is incorrect as 28.0 is the mass of the most abundant isotope (<sup>28</sup>Si), not the relative atomic mass.

**C** is incorrect as 29.0 is the simple mean of the three isotopic masses without weighting for abundance.

**D** is incorrect as 29.8 results from incorrectly mixing up the percentage abundances of the isotopes.

parts.problemMd:
Chlorine exists as two isotopes with mass numbers 35 and 37. A sample of chlorine contains 75.3% of chlorine-35 atoms.

Which is the relative atomic mass of chlorine in this sample, to 2 dp?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- To calculate the relative atomic mass of chlorine, multiply each isotopic mass by its percentage abundance, add the values, then divide by 100.

*A*<sub>r</sub>(Cl) = $\frac{(35\times75.3)+(37\times24.7)}{100}$

*A*<sub>r</sub>(Cl) = $\frac{2635.5+913.9}{100}$

*A*<sub>r</sub>(Cl) = $\frac{3549.4}{100}$

*A*<sub>r</sub>(Cl) = 35.49

**A** is incorrect as 35.00 is the mass of the more abundant isotope, <sup>35</sup>Cl, not the relative atomic mass.

**C** is incorrect as 36.00 is the simple mean of 35 and 37 without weighting for percentage abundance.

**D** is incorrect as 36.51 results from swapping the percentage abundances — using 75.3% for <sup>37</sup>Cl and 24.7% for <sup>35</sup>Cl instead.

parts.problemMd:
A sample of neon contains the following isotopes.

| **Isotope** | **Percentage abundance** |
|---|---|
| <sup>20</sup>Ne | 90.92 |
| <sup>21</sup>Ne | 0.26 |
| <sup>22</sup>Ne | 8.82 |

Which is the relative atomic mass of neon in this sample, to 2 dp?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- To calculate the relative atomic mass of neon, multiply each isotopic mass by its percentage abundance, add the values, then divide by 100.

*A*<sub>r</sub>(Ne) = $\frac{(20\times90.92)+(21\times0.26)+(22\times8.82)}{100}$

*A*<sub>r</sub>(Ne) = $\frac{1818.40+5.46+194.04}{100}$

*A*<sub>r</sub>(Ne) = $\frac{2017.90}{100}$

*A*<sub>r</sub>(Ne) = 20.18

**A** is incorrect as 20.00 is the mass of the most abundant isotope (<sup>20</sup>Ne), not the relative atomic mass.

**B** is incorrect as 20.09 results from mixing up the percentage abundances of <sup>21</sup>Ne and <sup>22</sup>Ne (using 0.26% for <sup>22</sup>Ne and 8.82% for <sup>21</sup>Ne).

**D** is incorrect as 21.00 is the simple mean of 20, 21 and 22 without weighting for percentage abundance.

parts.problemMd:
Nitrogen trichloride has the formula NCl<sub>3</sub>. A sample contains only <sup>14</sup>N atoms and chlorine atoms with mass numbers 35 and 37.

Which ion and m/z value in the table is **not** correct?

|   | **Ion** | **m/z** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | [<sup>14</sup>N(<sup>35</sup>Cl)<sub>3</sub>]<sup>+</sup> | 119 |
| **B** | [<sup>14</sup>N(<sup>35</sup>Cl)<sub>2</sub>(<sup>37</sup>Cl)]<sup>+</sup> | 121 |
| **C** | [<sup>14</sup>N(<sup>35</sup>Cl)(<sup>37</sup>Cl)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>+</sup> | 123 |
| **D** | [<sup>14</sup>N(<sup>37</sup>Cl)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>+</sup> | 125 |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****D**** because:**

- The question states that there are only nitrogen atoms with a mass of 14.
- All three Cl as <sup>35</sup>Cl:

[<sup>14</sup>N(<sup>35</sup>Cl)<sub>3</sub>]<sup>+</sup>, m/z = 14 + (3 × 35) = 119

- Two <sup>35</sup>Cl and one <sup>37</sup>Cl:

[<sup>14</sup>N(<sup>35</sup>Cl)<sub>2</sub>(<sup>37</sup>Cl)]<sup>+</sup>, m/z = 14 + (2 × 35) + 37 = 121

- One <sup>35</sup>Cl and two <sup>37</sup>Cl:

[<sup>14</sup>N(<sup>35</sup>Cl)(<sup>37</sup>Cl)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>+</sup>, m/z = 14 + 35 + (2 × 37) = 123

- All three Cl as <sup>37</sup>Cl:

[<sup>14</sup>N(<sup>37</sup>Cl)<sub>3</sub>]<sup>+</sup>, m/z = 14 + (3 × 37) = 125

- Therefore, ion **D** should be N(<sup>37</sup>Cl)<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>

**A**, **B** and **C** are incorrect as these are all valid molecular ions with correct m/z values.

parts.problemMd:
The mass spectrum of silicon is shown below.

![Mass spectrum of a silicon sample showing three peaks: the tallest at m/z = 28 (approximately 80% relative abundance), a medium peak at m/z = 29 (approximately 12%), and a small peak at m/z = 30 (approximately 8%)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/22-analytical-techniques/22-2-mass-spectrometry/assets/004-mass-spectrum-of-a-silicon-sample-showing-three-.jpg)

Which is the relative atomic mass of silicon in this sample, to 1 dp?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Reading relative abundances from the mass spectrum: m/z = 28 (80%), m/z = 29 (12%), m/z = 30 (8%).
- To calculate the relative atomic mass, multiply each isotopic mass by its relative abundance, add the values, then divide by 100.

*A*<sub>r</sub>(Si) = $\frac{(28\times80)+(29\times12)+(30\times8)}{100}$

*A*<sub>r</sub>(Si) = $\frac{2240+348+240}{100}$

*A*<sub>r</sub>(Si) = $\frac{2828}{100}$

*A*<sub>r</sub>(Si) = 28.3

**A** is incorrect as 28.0 is the mass of the most abundant isotope (<sup>28</sup>Si), not the relative atomic mass.

**C** is incorrect as 28.8 results from misreading the graph by swapping the relative abundances of the peaks at m/z = 28 and m/z = 29.

**D** is incorrect as 29.0 is the simple mean of 28, 29 and 30 without weighting for relative abundance.

parts.problemMd: Which alcohol does **not** have a fragment ion at m/z = 43 in its mass spectrum?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- A fragment ion at m/z = 43 corresponds to [C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>7</sub>]<sup>+</sup>, for example:

  - [CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>]<sup>+</sup>
  - [(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CH]<sup>+</sup>

- CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>3</sub> cannot produce a [C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>7</sub>]<sup>+</sup> fragment.

  - C−C cleavage on either side of the OH group gives at most a two-carbon fragment ([CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>]<sup>+</sup>, m/z = 29) or a one-carbon fragment ([CH<sub>3</sub>]<sup>+</sup>, m/z = 15).

**A** is incorrect as [CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>]<sup>+</sup> can be produced from CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH by C−C cleavage adjacent to the OH, giving m/z = 43.

**C** is incorrect as [CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>]<sup>+</sup> can be produced from CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> by cleavage of the bond between C-3 and C-4, giving m/z = 43.

**D** is incorrect as [(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CH]<sup>+</sup> can be produced from (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCH<sub>2</sub>OH by cleavage adjacent to the CH<sub>2</sub>OH group, giving m/z = 43.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Draw a vertical line through each C−C bond in turn to identify possible fragment ions. For m/z = 43, look for a three-carbon, seven-hydrogen fragment ([C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>7</sub>]<sup>+</sup>) on either side of each bond.

parts.problemMd: Which of the compounds below is not likely to have a fragment ion at *m/e* = 43 in its mass spectrum?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- A peak at m/z = 43 can arise from an ion with a mass of 43 for example:

  - [CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>]<sup>+</sup>
  - [CH<sub>3</sub>CO]<sup>+</sup>
  - [(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CH]<sup>+</sup>
- Propanoic acid (compound A) cannot produce any of these fragments:

  - It has no three-carbon hydrocarbon fragment .
  - It has no [CH<sub>3</sub>CO]<sup>+</sup> unit — the carbonyl is bonded to CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>, giving [CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CO]<sup>+</sup> at m/z = 57, not 43.

**B** is incorrect as it contains a [CH<sub>3</sub>CO]<sup>+</sup> unit, which produces [CH<sub>3</sub>CO]<sup>+</sup> at m/z = 43.

**C** is incorrect as it contains a (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CH unit, which produces [(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CH]<sup>+</sup> at m/z = 43.

**D** is incorrect as it contains a CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub> unit, which produces [CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>]<sup>+</sup> at m/z = 43.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Draw a vertical line through each C−C bond in turn to identify possible fragment ions. For m/z = 43, look for either a three-carbon hydrocarbon unit ([C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>7</sub>]<sup>+</sup>) or a CH<sub>3</sub>−C=O unit ([CH<sub>3</sub>CO]<sup>+</sup>) on either side of the bond.

parts.problemMd: Assuming chlorine exists as two isotopes and that carbon and hydrogen each exist as a single stable isotope only, how many molecular ion peaks are shown in the mass spectrum of C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>6</sub>Cl<sub>4</sub>?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Each Cl atom can be either <sup>35</sup>Cl or <sup>37</sup>Cl, giving 5 possible isotopologue combinations for a molecule with 4 Cl atoms.
- The 5 possible molecular ions for [C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>6</sub>Cl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>+</sup> are:

  - All four Cl atoms as <sup>35</sup>Cl → M (base mass)
  - Three <sup>35</sup>Cl and one <sup>37</sup>Cl → M+2
  - Two <sup>35</sup>Cl and two <sup>37</sup>Cl → M+4
  - One <sup>35</sup>Cl and three <sup>37</sup>Cl → M+6
  - All four Cl atoms as <sup>37</sup>Cl → M+8

**A** is incorrect as 2 is the number of chlorine isotopes, not the number of molecular ion peaks.

**B** is incorrect as 3 molecular ion peaks would be expected for a molecule containing two chlorine atoms (M, M+2 and M+4). C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>6</sub>Cl<sub>4</sub> contains four chlorine atoms, giving five molecular ion peaks.

**C** is incorrect as 4 peaks omits the M+8 peak (corresponding to all four chlorine atoms being <sup>37</sup>Cl). Five molecular ion peaks are expected.

parts.problemMd:
Bromine exists as two isotopes <sup>79</sup>Br and <sup>81</sup>Br, which are found in almost equal abundance.

Which of the following statements is correct?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- The peak representing the **molecular ion (M**<sup>**+**</sup>** or M•**<sup>**+**</sup>**)** is called the **molecular ion peak**.
- Excluding any peaks due to the presence of heavier isotopes, this is the peak with the highest m/z ratio.

  - This is the whole molecule that has lost one electron.
- Bromine has two isotopes, so there are two possible molecular ions:

  - M (<sup>79</sup>Br) m/z = 122
  - M+2 (<sup>81</sup>Br) m/z = 124

**A** is incorrect as isotopes have identical chemical reactivities.

**C** is incorrect as the differences in the number of neutrons do not affect atomic radii.

**D** is incorrect as the differences in the number of neutrons do not affect the first ionisation energy.

parts.problemMd: Which alcohol is likely to have a fragment ion at *m/z* = 31 in its mass spectrum?

**D** is incorrect as butan-2-ol does not contain a [CH<sub>2</sub>OH]<sup>+</sup> group and does not give a fragment ion at m/z = 31.

parts.problemMd:
Chlorine has two isotopes, <sup>35</sup>Cl and <sup>37</sup>Cl.

Which of the following is the number of molecular ion peaks in the mass spectrum of a sample of Cl<sub>2</sub>?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Chlorine exists as diatomic molecules.

  - When a sample of Cl<sub>2</sub> is ionised in the mass spectrometer, each molecule loses one electron to form the molecular ion, Cl<sub>2</sub><sup>•+</sup>.
- There are three possible Cl<sub>2</sub><sup>•+</sup> molecular ions, depending on which combination of isotopes is present:

  - <sup>35</sup>Cl<sub>2</sub><sup>•+</sup> at m/z = 70
  - <sup>35</sup>Cl<sup>37</sup>Cl<sup>•+</sup> at m/z = 72
  - <sup>37</sup>Cl<sub>2</sub><sup>•+</sup> at m/z = 74
- This gives three molecular ion peaks.
- Some Cl<sub>2</sub><sup>•+</sup> ions fragment further:

Cl<sub>2</sub><sup>•+</sup> → Cl<sup>•</sup> + Cl<sup>+</sup>

- The Cl<sup>+</sup> ions give additional fragment ion peaks at m/z = 35 and m/z = 37, but these are not molecular ion peaks.

![Mass spectrum of Cl2 showing three molecular ion peaks at m/z = 70, 72 and 74 from the three Cl2 isotope combinations (35Cl2, 35Cl37Cl and 37Cl2), and two fragment ion peaks at m/z = 35 and 37 from Cl+](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/22-analytical-techniques/22-2-mass-spectrometry/assets/010-mass-spectrum-of-cl2-showing-three-molecular-ion.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as 2 is the number of chlorine isotopes, not the number of molecular ion peaks.

**C** is incorrect as there are three possible Cl<sub>2</sub><sup>•+</sup> molecular ions (at m/z = 70, 72 and 74), not four.

**D** is incorrect as 5 is the total number of peaks in the mass spectrum, including two fragment ion peaks at m/z = 35 and 37, not just the molecular ion peaks.

parts.problemMd: Which of the following statements about the mass spectrum of CH<sub>3</sub>Br is correct?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- The mass spectrum of CH<sub>3</sub>Br shows three peaks:

1. Ionisation of CH<sub>3</sub><sup>79</sup>Br:

CH<sub>3</sub><sup>79</sup>Br → [CH<sub>3</sub><sup>79</sup>Br]<sup>•+</sup> + e<sup>−</sup> at m/z = 94

2. Ionisation of CH<sub>3</sub><sup>81</sup>Br:

CH<sub>3</sub><sup>81</sup>Br → [CH<sub>3</sub><sup>81</sup>Br]<sup>•+</sup> + e<sup>−</sup> at m/z = 96

3. Fragmentation:

[CH<sub>3</sub>Br]<sup>•+</sup> → [CH<sub>3</sub>]<sup>+</sup> + Br<sup>•</sup> at m/z = 15

- The two molecular ion peaks at m/z = 94 and 96 are of approximately equal size because <sup>79</sup>Br and <sup>81</sup>Br occur in approximately equal abundance.

![Mass spectrum of bromomethane showing two molecular ion peaks of approximately equal height at m/z = 94 and 96, and a fragment ion peak at m/z = 15](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/22-analytical-techniques/22-2-mass-spectrometry/assets/006-mass-spectrum-of-bromomethane-showing-two-molecu.jpg)

**B** is incorrect as the two molecular ion peaks at m/z = 94 and 96 are of approximately equal size, not in a 3:1 ratio. A 3:1 ratio is characteristic of compounds containing chlorine, not bromine.

**C** is incorrect as there is no molecular ion peak at m/z = 44 in the mass spectrum of CH<sub>3</sub>Br. The molecular ion peaks occur at m/z = 94 and 96.

**D** is incorrect as there is no single molecular ion peak at m/z = 95. Mass spectrometry separates isotopes, giving two distinct molecular ion peaks at m/z = 94 and 96.

parts.problemMd:
Two stable isotopes of bromine, <sup>79</sup>Br and <sup>81</sup>Br, exist in approximately equal abundance.

Which is the correct pattern of peaks in the mass spectrum of Br<sub>2</sub>?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Bromine is a diatomic molecule, so the mass spectrum of Br<sub>2</sub> shows peaks from both the molecular ion (Br<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>) and fragment ions (Br<sup>+</sup>).
- When Br<sub>2</sub> passes through the mass spectrometer, an electron is removed to form the molecular ion:

Br<sub>2</sub> → Br<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> + e<sup>−</sup>

- Br<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> can then fragment:

Br<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> → Br<sup>+</sup> + Br

- The Br<sup>+</sup> fragment ions give peaks at m/z = 79 and 81 in equal intensity.
- The unfragmented Br<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> ion exists in three isotopologue combinations:

  - <sup>79</sup>Br<sup>79</sup>Br<sup>+</sup>: m/z = 79 + 79 = 158 (relative probability 1)
  - <sup>79</sup>Br<sup>81</sup>Br<sup>+</sup>: m/z = 79 + 81 = 160 (relative probability 2)
  - <sup>81</sup>Br<sup>81</sup>Br<sup>+</sup>: m/z = 81 + 81 = 162 (relative probability 1)
- This gives five peaks in total: Br<sup>+</sup> at 79 and 81 (equal height), and Br<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> at 158, 160 and 162 in a 1:2:1 ratio.

**A** is incorrect as it shows only a single molecular ion peak, not three.

**B** is incorrect as it also shows only a single molecular ion peak, not three.

**D** is incorrect as it shows three molecular ion peaks at m/z = 158, 160 and 162 in a 9:6:1 ratio. The 9:6:1 pattern corresponds to Cl<sub>2</sub> (<sup>35</sup>Cl : <sup>37</sup>Cl ≈ 3:1), not Br<sub>2</sub> (<sup>79</sup>Br : <sup>81</sup>Br ≈ 1:1).

Which feature of the three mass spectra confirms that all three compounds have the molecular formula C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O?

- In all three mass spectra, the highest m/z peak (the molecular ion peak) appears at m/z = 74, confirming the molecular formula.

**A** is incorrect as m/z = 73 is a fragment ion peak ([M − H]<sup>+</sup>), not the molecular ion peak.

parts.problemMd:
Chlorine exists as two isotopes, <sup>35</sup>Cl and <sup>37</sup>Cl, in the ratio 3:1.

Which of the following statements about the molecular ion peaks in the mass spectrum of Cl<sub>2</sub> is correct?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Cl<sub>2</sub> is a diatomic molecule. When it passes through the mass spectrometer, an electron is removed to form the molecular ion:

Cl<sub>2</sub> → Cl<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> + e<sup>−</sup>

- Cl<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> can then fragment:

Cl<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> → Cl<sup>+</sup> + Cl

- The neutral Cl atom carries no charge and is not detected; the Cl<sup>+</sup> ions give peaks at m/z = 35 and 37.
- Three isotopologue combinations give three molecular ion peaks:

  - <sup>35</sup>Cl<sup>35</sup>Cl<sup>+</sup> at m/z = 70 — relative probability ∝ 3 × 3 = 9
  - <sup>35</sup>Cl<sup>37</sup>Cl<sup>+</sup> (two arrangements) at m/z = 72 — relative probability ∝ 2 × (3 × 1) = 6
  - <sup>37</sup>Cl<sup>37</sup>Cl<sup>+</sup> at m/z = 74 — relative probability ∝ 1 × 1 = 1
- The three molecular ion peaks at m/z = 70, 72 and 74 therefore appear in a 9:6:1 ratio.

![Mass spectrum of Cl2 showing Cl+ fragment ion peaks at m/z = 35 and 37, and molecular ion peaks at m/z = 70, 72 and 74 in a 9:6:1 ratio](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-chemistry-25/22-analytical-techniques/22-2-mass-spectrometry/assets/005-mass-spectrum-of-cl2-showing-cl-fragment-ion-pea.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as there are three molecular ion peaks (at m/z = 70, 72 and 74), not two. A 3:1 ratio applies to the individual chlorine isotopes, not to the molecular ion peaks.

**B** is incorrect as three molecular ion peaks exist. The peak at m/z = 72 from <sup>35</sup>Cl<sup>37</sup>Cl<sup>+</sup> is absent from this option.

**C** is incorrect as the middle peak arises from two arrangements (<sup>35</sup>Cl<sup>37</sup>Cl<sup>+</sup> and <sup>37</sup>Cl<sup>35</sup>Cl<sup>+</sup>), giving a relative probability of 2 × (3 × 1) = 6. The correct ratio is 9:6:1, not 9:3:1.

parts.problemMd:
A compound XF<sub>n</sub> is a fluoride of another halogen, X, and it is known that n > 1. The highest mass peak in the mass spectrum of XF<sub>n</sub> is assigned to the molecular ion and appears as a single peak at m/z = 222.

Which of the following statements is **not **correct?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- In mass spectrometry, peaks correspond to specific isotopic masses, not average relative atomic masses.
- Bromine has two stable isotopes:

  - <sup>79</sup>Br (mass 79)
  - <sup>81</sup>Br (mass 81)
- If X = <sup>79</sup>Br:

remaining mass for F atoms = 222 − 79 = 143

n = 143 ÷ 19 = 7.53 (not a whole number)

- If X = <sup>81</sup>Br:

remaining mass for F atoms = 222 − 81 = 141

n = 141 ÷ 19 = 7.42 (not a whole number)

- Neither bromine isotope gives a whole number of F atoms, so the compound cannot contain bromine.

**A** is incorrect as iodine has one stable isotope with mass 127. Substituting: 222 − 127 = 95; n = 95 ÷ 19 = 5 (a whole number), confirming IF<sub>5</sub>. This statement is correct.

**C** is incorrect as iodine fits all conditions. IF<sub>5</sub> has molecular mass = 127 + (5 × 19) = 222, consistent with the single molecular ion peak. This statement is correct.

**D** is incorrect as both <sup>19</sup>F and <sup>127</sup>I each exist as a single stable isotope, which explains why the molecular ion appears as a single unfragmented peak at m/z = 222 with no M+2 peak. This statement is correct.

choices.label: B
choices.textMd: CF<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H fragments by sequential loss of F atoms

choices.label: C
choices.textMd: Fluorine exists as a single stable isotope

parts.problemMd:
In the mass spectrum of trifluoroacetic acid, CF<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H, intense peaks are observed at m/z = 69 and 45 (base peak) in addition to other peaks.

The peak at m/z = 69 is accompanied by a peak at m/z = 70, which is about 1.1% the intensity of the peak at m/z = 69.

Which of the following statements is **not** supported by this information?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- If CF<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H fragmented by sequential loss of F atoms (mass 19 each time), peaks would be expected at m/z = 203, 184, 165, etc.
- The observed peaks at m/z = 69 ([CF<sub>3</sub>]<sup>+</sup>) and 45 ([HO<sub>2</sub>C]<sup>+</sup>) are consistent with a single C−C bond cleavage, not sequential F loss.
- The small peak at m/z = 70 (1.1% of m/z = 69) is consistent with the natural abundance of <sup>13</sup>C (~1.1%).

  - Since fluorine exists as a single stable isotope (<sup>19</sup>F only), this peak cannot arise from a heavier F isotope.

**A** is incorrect as this statement is supported. C−C bond cleavage is the fragmentation pathway, producing [CF<sub>3</sub>]<sup>+</sup> at m/z = 69 and [HO<sub>2</sub>C]<sup>+</sup> at m/z = 45.

**C** is incorrect as this statement is supported. <sup>19</sup>F is the only stable isotope of fluorine, which explains why the peak at m/z = 70 arises from <sup>13</sup>C and not from a heavier fluorine isotope.

**D** is incorrect as this statement is supported. [HO<sub>2</sub>C]<sup>+</sup> is a fragment ion at m/z = 45, which is the base peak formed by C−C bond cleavage.

parts.problemMd:
A sample is analysed by mass spectrometry and infrared spectroscopy. The data obtained are shown below.

| **Mass spectrometry** | **Infrared spectroscopy** |
|---|---|
| Molecular ion peak at m/z = 128 | Strong absorption at 1720 cm<sup>-1</sup> |
| Fragment ion peak at m/z = 15 | No broad absorption around 3200 cm<sup>-1</sup> |

Which compound is consistent with these spectroscopic data?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- A strong absorption at 1720 cm<sup>-1</sup> is consistent with a C═O (carbonyl) stretch.

  - Compound A contains a carbonyl group in the ketone wavenumber range (~1715–1725 cm<sup>-1</sup>).
- The molecular ion peak at m/z = 128 matches the relative molecular mass of compound A.
- The fragment ion at m/z = 15 corresponds to [CH<sub>3</sub>]<sup>+</sup>, consistent with a terminal methyl group in compound A.
- The absence of a broad absorption around 3200 cm<sup>-1</sup> confirms that no O−H group is present.

**B** is incorrect as compound B contains a hydroxyl (O−H) group, which would produce a broad absorption around 3200 cm<sup>-1</sup>. This absorption is absent from the data.

**C** is incorrect as compound C has a relative molecular mass of 129, not 128. A molecular ion at m/z = 129 does not match the data.

**D** is incorrect as compound D contains both a carbonyl group and a hydroxyl group. The O−H group would produce a broad absorption around 3200 cm<sup>-1</sup>, which is absent from the data.

parts.problemMd:
There are three possible isomers, **A**, **B** and **C**, with the molecular formula C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O.

Isomers **A** and **B** are positional isomers of each other.

Isomer **C** is a functional group isomer of **A** and **B**.

The percentage by mass of carbon in all three isomers is 60.0%.

Calculate the percentage by mass of hydrogen and oxygen in all three isomers.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the percentage by mass of hydrogen and oxygen in C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O:

- Calculate the *M*<sub>r</sub> of C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O:

*M*<sub>r</sub> = (3 x 12.0) + (8 x 1.0) + 16.0

*M*<sub>r</sub> = 60.0

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate the percentage by mass of each element:

% by mass = $\frac{\mathrm{total} \mathrm{mass} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{element}}{\mathrm{overall} \mathrm{mass} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{compound}}$ x 100

% by mass of H = $\frac{8.0}{60.0}$ x 100 = 13.3%

% by mass of O = $\frac{16.0}{60.0}$ x 100 = 26.7%

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for *M*<sub>r</sub> = 60.0
> 
> 1 mark for % H = 13.3% **AND** % O = 26.7%
> 
> Percentages given to 2 significant figures are accepted

> **[exam-tip]**
> All three isomers have the same molecular formula, so they all have the same percentage by mass for each element.
> 
> To find percentage by mass: divide the total mass of the element in one molecule by *M*<sub>r</sub>, then multiply by 100.
> 
> Check your answer:
> 
> 60.0 + 13.3 + 26.7 = 100.0

parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**

> 
> - Propan-1-ol **[1 mark]**
> 
> Explanation:
> 
> - The peak at *m*/*e* = 31 corresponds to the fragment ion CH<sub>2</sub>OH<sup>+</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> Propan-2-ol is not accepted.

> **[exam-tip]**
> To find which fragment has *m*/*e* = 31, calculate the mass of possible fragments from propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol:
> 
> - CH<sub>2</sub>OH: 12 + 2(1) + 16 + 1 = 31, which is CH<sub>2</sub>OH<sup>+</sup>
> 
> This fragment comes from propan-1-ol (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH) by cleavage of the C2−C3 bond, losing CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub> (mass 29) to give CH<sub>2</sub>OH<sup>+</sup> (mass 31).

> Propan-2-ol ((CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHOH) cannot produce *m*/*e* = 31. Breaking its C−C bonds gives CH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> (*m*/*e* = 15) or CH<sub>3</sub>CHOH<sup>+</sup> (*m*/*e* = 45).
> 
> Always include the <sup>+</sup> charge when writing fragment ion formulae.

parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Infrared spectroscopy could not be used to distinguish between **X** and **Y** because:
> 
> - They both contain the same key functional group
> **OR**
> They both contain a C=O bond and no other distinguishing functional group
> **OR**
> They are both carbonyl compounds **[1 mark]**
> - Both spectra would show an absorption at 1670–1740 cm<sup>-1</sup> due to the C=O bond, with no other key distinguishing absorption **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Compound **X** is a ketone (butan-2-one) and compound **Y** is an aldehyde (2-methylpropanal). Both functional groups contain a C=O bond that absorbs at 1670–1740 cm<sup>-1</sup>.
> 
> IR spectroscopy identifies functional groups by their characteristic absorptions. When two compounds share the same functional group and have no other distinguishing groups, their IR spectra look the same in the key regions above 1500 cm<sup>-1</sup>. This is why IR alone cannot distinguish between them.
> 
> To distinguish between an aldehyde and a ketone, chemical tests (such as Tollens' reagent or Fehling's solution) or mass spectrometry would be needed.

parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> A fragment ion present in compound **Y** but absent from compound **X** is:
> 
> - *m*/*e* = 28 **[1 mark]**
> - Formula: CO<sup>+</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Compound **Y** is an aldehyde (2-methylpropanal). Aldehydes produce a characteristic CHO<sup>+</sup> fragment at *m*/*e* = 29. This can lose a hydrogen atom to give CO<sup>+</sup> at *m*/*e* = 28.
> 
> Compound **X** is a ketone (butan-2-one). Ketones undergo α-cleavage to give acylium ions such as CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sup>+</sup> (*m*/*e* = 43), but do not readily produce CO<sup>+</sup> at *m*/*e* = 28.
> 
> This difference in fragmentation patterns allows mass spectrometry to distinguish between the two isomers even though they have the same *M*<sub>r</sub> and the same IR absorption region.

parts.problemMd:
Alcohol **A** can be prepared by hydrolysing the halogenoalkane C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CHBrCH<sub>3</sub> with aqueous sodium hydroxide. The melting and boiling point information of alcohol **A** and C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CHBrCH<sub>3</sub> are given in Table 1.1.

**Table 1.1**

|   | **melting point / K** | **boiling point / K** |
|---|---|---|
| alcohol **A** | 158 | 373 |
| C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CHBrCH<sub>3</sub> | 161 | 364 |

Construct an equation for the hydrolysis of C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CHBrCH<sub>3</sub> with aqueous sodium hydroxide. Include state symbols in your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
The equation for the hydrolysis of C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CHBrCH<sub>3</sub> with aqueous sodium hydroxide is:

C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CHBrCH<sub>3</sub> (l) + NaOH (aq) → C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CHOHCH<sub>3</sub> (l) + NaBr (aq)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct chemical formulae: C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CHBrCH<sub>3</sub> + NaOH → C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CHOHCH<sub>3</sub> + NaBr
> 
> 1 mark for all four correct state symbols: (l), (aq), (l), (aq)
> 
> C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CHOHCH<sub>3</sub> may also be written as CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>

> **[exam-tip]**
> This is a nucleophilic substitution reaction. The OH<sup>−</sup> ion from NaOH replaces the Br atom attached to the carbon chain.
> 
> To deduce the state symbols, use Table 1.1:
> 
> - The boiling points of C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CHBrCH<sub>3</sub> (364 K) and alcohol **A** (373 K) are both above room temperature (~298 K), so both are liquids (l)
> - NaOH is dissolved in water, so it is aqueous (aq)
> - NaBr is a soluble salt, so it forms an aqueous solution (aq)

parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Alcohol **A** can be separated using the following steps:
> 
> - Distil the reaction mixture
> **AND**
> To remove NaBr (aq) from the organic/aqueous mixture **[1 mark]**
> - Cool the distillate to approximately 0 °C
> **AND**
> Water freezes (mp 273 K) while alcohol **A** remains liquid (mp 158 K), using the data in Table 1.1 **[1 mark]**
> - Filter the cooled mixture
> **AND**
> To remove the solid ice, leaving liquid alcohol **A** **[1 mark]**
> 
> The separating funnel method is also accepted: add an organic solvent to dissolve alcohol **A**, separate the organic layer using a separating funnel, then distil off the solvent to obtain pure alcohol **A**.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The key challenge here is that alcohol **A** and water have the same boiling point (373 K), so simple distillation cannot separate them.
> 
> The question specifically tells you to use Table 1.1, where the key data is the melting points. The melting point of alcohol **A** is 158 K, much lower than water (273 K). Cooling to just below 0 °C freezes the water while alcohol **A** stays liquid. The solid ice can then be removed by filtration.
> 
> An alternative is the separating funnel method: dissolve alcohol **A** in an organic solvent (such as ether), which forms a separate organic layer. Use a separating funnel to drain off the aqueous layer, then distil the organic layer to remove the solvent.

parts.problemMd:
A sample of boron contains two isotopes, <sup>10</sup>B and <sup>11</sup>B, with relative abundances of 20% and 80% respectively.

Calculate the relative atomic mass of boron. Show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the relative atomic mass of boron:

- Calculate the weighted mean of the isotopic masses:

*A*<sub>r</sub>(B) = $\frac{(10\times20)+(11\times80)}{100}$ **[1 mark]**

*A*<sub>r</sub>(B) = **10.8** **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The relative atomic mass is the weighted mean of the isotopic masses. Multiply each isotopic mass by its relative abundance, sum the results, then divide by the total abundance (100 when expressed as percentages):
> 
> $\frac{(\mathrm{abundance}_{1}\times\mathrm{mass}_{1})+(\mathrm{abundance}_{2}\times\mathrm{mass}_{2})}{100}$
> 
> The relative abundance of an isotope can be given as a percentage or read directly from the mass spectrum.

parts.problemMd:

**Fig. 2.1**

Use the information in Fig. 2.1 to calculate the relative atomic mass of potassium. Show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the relative atomic mass of potassium:

- Calculate the total relative abundance:

Total abundance = 130.6 + 9.4 = 140 **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the weighted mean:

*A*<sub>r</sub>(K) = $\frac{(39\times130.6)+(41\times9.4)}{140}$ = **39.1** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Allow *A*<sub>r</sub> = 39.13 or 39.14.
> 
> Allow error carried forward from an incorrect total abundance value.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The y-axis of the mass spectrum gives relative abundance, not percentage abundance.
> 
> The total abundance is 130.6 + 9.4 = 140, not 100. Use 140 as the denominator, not 100.

parts.problemMd:
The mass spectra of octane and butane were obtained and analysed.

Construct an equation for the formation of the molecular ion of octane. State the m / e value of this molecular ion.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The equation for the formation of the molecular ion of octane and its m / e value are:
> 
> - C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub> → C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub><sup>+</sup> + e<sup>–</sup> **[1 mark]**
> - m / e = (8 x 12) + (18 x 1) = 114 **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are not required in the equation.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The molecular ion is formed when a molecule loses one electron in the mass spectrometer. Since the mass of an electron is negligible, the molecular ion has the same m / e value as the relative molecular mass of the compound.

parts.problemMd:
The mass spectrum of butane shows a molecular ion peak at *m / e* = 58.0.

Explain why there is also a smaller peak at *m / e* = 59.0 on the mass spectrum of butane.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The smaller peak at m / e = 59.0 in the mass spectrum of butane appears because:
> 
> - Some butane molecules contain a <sup>13</sup>C isotope / one carbon atom has mass 13 instead of 12, giving a molecular ion with m / e = 59 / producing an [M+1] peak **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Approximately 1.1% of all carbon atoms are <sup>13</sup>C. When a butane molecule contains one <sup>13</sup>C atom, its molecular ion has m / e = 59 rather than 58. This produces the [M+1] peak, which is always smaller than the M peak because <sup>13</sup>C is much less abundant than <sup>12</sup>C.

**Extract:**

parts.solutionMd:

> - Because it contains more carbon atoms, so there is a greater probability of one being <sup>13</sup>C **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd: State the ratio of the relative abundances of the M peak and the [M+2] peak in the mass spectra of 1-bromobutane and 1-chlorobutane.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The ratios of the relative abundances of the M and [M+2] peaks are:
> 
> - In 1-chlorobutane, M : [M+2] = 3 : 1 **[1 mark]**
> - In 1-bromobutane, M : [M+2] = 1 : 1 **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Both chlorine and bromine exist as two isotopes:
> 
> - <sup>35</sup>Cl and <sup>37</sup>Cl: <sup>35</sup>Cl is approximately three times more abundant than <sup>37</sup>Cl, giving M : [M+2] = 3 : 1 for compounds containing one chlorine atom.
> - <sup>79</sup>Br and <sup>81</sup>Br: these isotopes have approximately equal abundances, giving M : [M+2] = 1 : 1 for compounds containing one bromine atom.
> 
> The [M+2] peak arises because some molecules contain the heavier isotope of the halogen, giving a molecular ion 2 mass units heavier than the M peak.

parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the number of carbon atoms in compound **X**:

- Apply the M+1 peak formula:

n = $\frac{100\times6.5}{1.1\times100}$

n = 5.91 **[1 mark]**

Number of carbon atoms = **6** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**

> 
> n =$\frac{ ( 100 \times [ \mathrm{M} + 1 ] \text{abundance} )}{ ( 1.1 \times \mathrm{M} \text{abundance} )}$
> 
> From Fig. 1.1: the peak at *m* / *e* = 102 is the molecular ion peak (M, abundance 100%) and the peak at *m* / *e* = 103 is the M+1 peak (abundance 6.5%).

parts.solutionMd:
To suggest the molecular formula of compound **X**:

- Use the molecular ion peak:

*M*<sub>r</sub> = 102 (from M peak at *m* / *e* = 102)

- Calculate remaining mass after carbon:

102 − (6 x 12.0) = 30

- Assign oxygen and hydrogen:

30 − 16.0 (one O) = 14 → 14 hydrogen atoms

> **[exam-tip]**
> The molecular ion peak (M) at *m* / *e* = 102 gives *M*<sub>r</sub> = 102. Six carbon atoms contribute 6 × 12.0 = 72.0, leaving 30. One oxygen atom (mass 16.0) leaves 14, which corresponds to 14 hydrogen atoms. The molecular formula is therefore C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>14</sub>O.

parts.problemMd:
Boron has two naturally occurring isotopes, <sup>10</sup>B and <sup>11</sup>B. The relative atomic mass of boron is 10.8

Use this information to calculate the relative abundance of each isotope. Show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the relative abundance of each isotope of boron:

- Let the relative abundance of <sup>10</sup>B = *x*, so the relative abundance of <sup>11</sup>B = (100 − *x*)

- Substitute into the relative atomic mass equation:

*A*<sub>r</sub> = $\frac{(10\timesx)+(11\times(100-x))}{100}$

10.8 = $\frac{10x+1100-11x}{100}$

**[1 mark]**

- Rearrange and solve for *x*:

1080 = 1100 − *x*

*x* = 20

relative abundance of <sup>10</sup>B = **20**

relative abundance of <sup>11</sup>B = **80**

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct substitution into the *A*<sub>r</sub> equation and rearrangement
> 
> 1 mark for both correct values: <sup>10</sup>B = 20, <sup>11</sup>B = 80

> **[exam-tip]**
> Let the relative abundance of <sup>10</sup>B = *x*.
> 
> The two abundances must sum to 100, so <sup>11</sup>B = (100 − *x*).
> 
> Substitute into the *A*<sub>r</sub> formula: 10.8 = ((10*x*) + (11(100 − *x*))) / 100.
> 
> Solve for *x*.

parts.problemMd:
An unknown compound, **B**, is analysed and shown to have a composition of 69.7% carbon, 18.6% oxygen and the remainder is hydrogen.

The following **incomplete** mass spectrometry and infrared spectroscopy data are collected.

**Mass spectrum**

- Molecular ion peak (M) at *m* / *e* = 86
- M+1 peak at *m* / *e* = 87.0
- Fragment ion peak at *m* / *e* = 28

**Infrared spectrum**

- Sharp absorption at 1705 cm<sup>-1</sup>
- **No** broad absorption around 3200 cm<sup>-1</sup>

Calculate the molecular formula of compound **B**. Show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the molecular formula of compound **B**:

- Calculate the percentage of hydrogen:

% H = 100 − 69.7 − 18.6 = 11.7%

- Calculate the moles of each element:

moles of C = $\frac{69.7}{12.0}$ = 5.80

moles of O = $\frac{18.6}{16.0}$ = 1.16

moles of H = $\frac{11.7}{1.0}$ = 11.7

**[1 mark]**

- Find the simplest molar ratio:

C : O : H = $\frac{5.80}{1.16}$ : $\frac{1.16}{1.16}$ : $\frac{11.7}{1.16}$ = 5 : 1 : 10

Empirical formula = C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O

**[1 mark]**

- Confirm the molecular formula:

*M*<sub>r</sub> of C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O = (5 x 12.0) + (10 x 1.0) + 16.0 = 86.0

This matches the molecular ion peak at *m* / *e* = 86

Molecular formula = **C**<sub>**5**</sub>**H**<sub>**10**</sub>**O**

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for moles of C = 5.80, O = 1.16 and H = 11.7
> 
> 1 mark for correct empirical formula C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O
> 
> 1 mark for confirming molecular formula C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O with *M*<sub>r</sub> = 86 matching the molecular ion peak

> **[exam-tip]**
> When the percentage composition is incomplete, calculate the missing element's percentage by subtracting from 100: % H = 100 − 69.7 − 18.6 = 11.7%.
> 
> The molecular ion peak (M) at *m* / *e* = 86 confirms the molecular formula directly as the empirical formula C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O has a molar mass of 86.0 g mol<sup>-1</sup>, matching the M peak exactly. The M+1 peak at *m* / *e* = 87.0 arises from molecules containing one <sup>13</sup>C atom.

parts.problemMd:
Alcohol **E** is analysed using a combination of techniques. The analytical data is shown below.

**Elemental analysis by mass**

- C = 68.2%, H = 13.6%, O = 18.2%

**Mass spectrum**

- Molecular ion peak at *m* / *e* = 88.0
- Major ion peak at *m* / *e* = 45.0

Calculate the empirical formula of alcohol **E**. Deduce the molecular formula. Show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the empirical formula and deduce the molecular formula of alcohol **E**:

- Calculate the moles of each element:

moles of C = $\frac{68.2}{12.0}$ = 5.68

moles of H = $\frac{13.6}{1.0}$ = 13.6

moles of O = $\frac{18.2}{16.0}$ = 1.14

**[1 mark]**

- Find the simplest molar ratio:

C : H : O = $\frac{5.68}{1.14}$ : $\frac{13.6}{1.14}$ : $\frac{1.14}{1.14}$ = 4.98 : 11.93 : 1 ≈ 5 : 12 : 1

Empirical formula = C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O

**[1 mark]**

- Deduce the molecular formula using the molecular ion peak:

*M*<sub>r</sub> of C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O = (5 x 12.0) + (12 x 1.0) + 16.0 = 88.0

This matches the molecular ion peak at *m* / *e* = 88.0

Molecular formula = **C**<sub>**5**</sub>**H**<sub>**12**</sub>**O**

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for moles of C = 5.68, H = 13.6 and O = 1.14
> 
> 1 mark for correct empirical formula C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O
> 
> 1 mark for correct molecular formula C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O, confirmed using *M*<sub>r</sub> = 88.0 matching the molecular ion peak

> **[exam-tip]**
> Divide each percentage by the corresponding relative atomic mass to find moles, then divide by the smallest value to find the ratio. Here, O gives the smallest mole value (1.14), giving a C : H : O ratio of approximately 5 : 12 : 1.
> 
> Always verify the molecular formula against the molecular ion peak. Here, the empirical formula mass (88.0) matches *m* / *e* = 88.0, confirming the molecular and empirical formulae are the same.

parts.problemMd:
Compound **F** contains 6.98% hydrogen and 37.21% oxygen by mass. The remainder of the mass is carbon.

i) Calculate the empirical formula of compound **F**. Show your working.

[2]

ii) Explain why this empirical formula cannot be the molecular formula of compound **F**.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
i) To calculate the empirical formula of compound **F**:

- Calculate the percentage of carbon:

% C = 100 − 6.98 − 37.21 = 55.81%

- Calculate the moles of each element:

moles of C = $\frac{55.81}{12.0}$ = 4.65

moles of H = $\frac{6.98}{1.0}$ = 6.98

moles of O = $\frac{37.21}{16.0}$ = 2.33

**[1 mark]**

- Find the simplest molar ratio:

C : H : O = $\frac{4.65}{2.33}$ : $\frac{6.98}{2.33}$ : $\frac{2.33}{2.33}$ = 1.99 : 2.99 : 1 ≈ 2 : 3 : 1

Empirical formula = **C**<sub>**2**</sub>**H**<sub>**3**</sub>**O**

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for moles of C = 4.65, H = 6.98 and O = 2.33
> 
> 1 mark for correct empirical formula C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>3</sub>O

> **[exam-tip]**
> Calculate the missing percentage first: % C = 100 − 6.98 − 37.21 = 55.81%. Then divide each percentage by the relative atomic mass to find moles, and divide by the smallest value (O = 2.33) to find the simplest ratio.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) The empirical formula C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>3</sub>O cannot be the molecular formula because:
> 
> - It has an odd number of hydrogen atoms, making it impossible to form a complete, fully-bonded molecule **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For any organic molecule, the hydrogen count must be even (carbon forms 4 bonds, oxygen forms 2 bonds as any complete arrangement requires an even number of hydrogen atoms). C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>3</sub>O has only 3 hydrogen atoms (odd), so no complete bonded structure is possible.

**Extract:**

The displayed formulae and systematic names of the three possible isomers that could be compound F are:

But-3-enoic acid

cis-but-2-enoic acid / Z-but-2-enoic acid

trans-but-2-enoic acid / E-but-2-enoic acid

Compound **F** is the stereoisomer with the lowest boiling point.

Using the isomers identified in part **(d)**, state the name of compound **F**. Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The name of compound **F** is:
> 
> - cis-but-2-enoic acid / Z-but-2-enoic acid **[1 mark]**
> - The cis arrangement of substituents around the C=C reduces molecular surface area, weakening van der Waals forces, so less energy is required to overcome them **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> But-3-enoic acid is not a stereoisomer so it is excluded. Of the remaining two isomers, cis-but-2-enoic acid has both larger substituents on the same side of the C=C, giving a more compact shape, smaller surface area, weaker van der Waals forces and therefore a lower boiling point.
